edges.note: Aramaic-speaking Christianity reached Edessa early, but by what route and hands scholars genuinely disagree.
Egyptian Christianity's origins are obscure in detail, but its second-century emergence out of the same scattered network is broadly accepted.
The desert movement grew in Alexandria’s shadow; Athanasius of Alexandria wrote the Life of Antony that carried it to the world.
Jerome and Paula toured the Egyptian ascetic settlements; the circle's practice consciously imported the desert's renunciation.
Origen's textual scholarship (the Hexapla) is the direct ancestor of Jerome's Hebrew-testing project — even as Jerome turned publicly against Origen's theology.
Jerome heard Gregory of Nazianzus teach in Constantinople and calls him his teacher.
The School of Nisibis and the Persian church carry this tradition's teaching directly onward after 410.
Basil visited Egypt; the whole Greek monastic tradition claims the desert as its root.
John Cassian carried the desert's teaching to Gaul; Benedict's Rule commends his Conferences by name.
Via Gaul (Lérins, Martin of Tours); the route is secure in outline, thinner in specifics.
Post-Chalcedon Egyptian Christianity is the direct continuation of the desert tradition.
…and of Alexandria's own catechetical tradition.
The Waldensians adhered to the Reformation in 1532; how much earlier “proto-Protestant” continuity is real versus retrospective is a live scholarly argument.
The Radical Reformation defined itself against the magisterial reformers' church-state settlement as much as against Rome.
Azusa Street's leaders and vocabulary came directly out of the Holiness movement.
Aladura and Zionist movements drew on Pentecostal currents while being genuinely African-initiated — the balance is actively studied.
The Holiness movement understood itself as recovering Wesley's own doctrine of sanctification.

The Great Schism, in each side's own documents: Humbert's bull of excommunication laid on the altar of Hagia Sophia (16 July 1054); Cerularius's synodal condemnation of the legates the following week. Process honesty: 1054 was symbolic and legate-to-patriarch, not church-to-church; the 1204 sack of Constantinople sealed the estrangement (scholars dating the real rupture there - that reading Contested); the anathemas were mutually lifted in 1965.
The Black Baptist congregations (Silver Bluff c. 1773-75, First African Savannah 1788) are the Baptist parent line of the Black Church. Edge written at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
Richard Allen’s AME (1816) and AME Zion (1821) are Methodist bodies — the Methodist parent line of the Black Church. Edge written at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).

Calvin's Institutes draws explicitly and heavily on Augustine's anti-Pelagian writings (De Praedestinatione Sanctorum, Contra Julianum) for total depravity, unconditional election, and irresistible grace -- Calvin named Augustine his primary authority next to Scripture itself. A direct theological line across eleven centuries with no institutional continuity -- influence, not identity.

The census's second 'in tension with' edge — the Great Schism pattern run inside Protestantism, graded on both sides' own dated rupture texts: the five-point Doctrinal Deliverance (1910), Fosdick's 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' (21 May 1922), Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923) and the Auburn Affirmation (9 Jan 1924). The Social Gospel (IX.34) belongs inside this tension and is named here rather than given a second edge. Any present-day continuation of the argument is a matter for dated statements, not for this grade. Edge written at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14).

The a cappella wing of the Stone-Campbell movement, formed at the division the 1906 U.S. religious census recorded in its separate Churches of Christ listing. This was a formation, not a continuation: a single identity can't split into two separate successors.

The Disciples wing of the same 1906 division, on the same verified federal-census listing. No continuesAs write, for the same reason as its sibling edge. Edge written at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14).
John Cassian lived among the Egyptian monks before founding his houses at Marseilles; the Institutes and Conferences are that transmission in written form.
Benedict's Rule commends Cassian's Conferences by name and prescribes them as daily reading.
The route via Gaul (Lérins, Martin of Tours) - secure in outline, thinner in specifics.
Lérins-trained bishops staffed the Gallic sees that the Frankish church inherited.
Basil's Against Eunomius, Gregory of Nyssa's answer to Eunomius' reply, and Gregory of Nazianzus' Five Theological Orations are all directed at this party by name.
Canon 1 of Constantinople I (381) anathematizes Eunomians by name, and Theodosian legislation suppressed their assemblies.
The two wings split at Constantinople in 360, when the Homoian creed was imposed and Aetius exiled. The two are often confused with each other, but they are historically distinct movements.
Basil's On the Holy Spirit and Gregory of Nyssa's Against the Macedonians are both directed at this party.
Canon 1 of Constantinople I (381) condemns them by name, and the creed's expanded third article is the answer to them.
Gregory of Nazianzus' letters to Cledonius are the classic reply: what is not assumed is not healed.
Condemned at Rome in 377 and by name in canon 1 of Constantinople I.
Against Praxeas is the fullest Latin answer to the position, and coined much of the vocabulary the doctrine of the Trinity later used.
Hippolytus accused Callistus of sheltering the teaching; the charge is inseparable from his rivalry for the see.
Ephraim's Prose Refutations answer Bardaisan at length, and are the reason most of his position survives.
The Roman congregation of the house-church period is the same community, two generations on.
The dispute over restoring the lapsed, argued under Callistus, is what breaks open in the schism of 251.
Hilarion was Antony's disciple and brought Egyptian anchoritism to the Gaza coast.
Chariton's laura at Pharan is the form the great Judean desert monasteries of the next century inherit.
The same Christians, turned outward: Justin taught at Rome and Melito was a bishop in Asia Minor, both part of this same movement.
Justin's argument that the Word had sown seeds of truth among the philosophers is what Clement and Origen take much further.
The Protevangelium of James and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas were written during this same period and read by its churches.
Hilary ordained Martin of Tours, who founded the West's first monastery at Ligugé; the monastic world grows on ground this one kept Nicene.
De Trinitate is the major Latin answer to the Arian case, and De Synodis a primary account of the Homoian conciliar creeds.
Constantius II exiled Hilary in 356 for refusing to condemn Athanasius; the Council of Paris repudiated the creed the emperor had imposed at Ariminum.
Basil's grandmother Macrina was formed by Gregory Thaumaturgus' disciples, and Basil appeals to his practice as precedent for what is old.
Gregory studied five years under Origen at Caesarea and wrote the Panegyric on leaving; Methodius, a generation later, became Origen's first serious critic.
A substantial part of what circulates under both men's names is marked dubious or spurious by the edition itself.
Origen moved to Caesarea around 231 and taught there for twenty years; the library grew from the books he brought.
The Jerusalem entry begins in 325, where this one ends - Alexander's library and the province's episcopate are what Constantine's builders found there.
Eusebius wrote the Church History and the Life of Constantine out of this library, and lived through the persecution he recorded in Martyrs of Palestine.
Latin-speaking and roughly coeval, and nothing more than that - which is why shelving Victorinus in Africa was wrong.
Jerome reissued Victorinus' Commentary on the Apocalypse with the millenarian ending rewritten; the text survives in his revision.
The same provinces, fifty years on: Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum made Illyricum the base of the Homoian episcopate.
Jerome and Rufinus were both formed in the ascetic circle here in the 370s; the quarrel that defines I.9 is between two men who met at Aquileia.
Rufinus translated Origen into Latin, and for several works his version is the only text that survives.
Ambrose came up from Milan to preside over the Council of Aquileia in 381.
The exegetical tradition Diodore, Theodore and Chrysostom carry is usually traced to Lucian's work on the biblical text in this city.
Arius and his early backers were Lucian's pupils and used the name; the Arian party's leadership came out of this school.
Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism are opposite refusals of the same developing account of the Son, argued in the same decades.
The same enterprise carried into Latin: the charges answered are the same charges, and the strategy of claiming the philosophers is inherited.
Tertullian's Apology of 197 opens the Latin case; the priority question between it and Minucius Felix's Octavius is still unsettled.

Lactantius carried the Latin apologetic argument into Constantine's household - he tutored Crispus at Trier - and his De Mortibus Persecutorum, written from inside the settlement, stays with that entry while the rest of him stays here.
Gregory was a monk of his own foundation on the Caelian before he was bishop, and wrote the only life of Benedict there is.
Gregory sent Augustine and forty monks to Kent in 596 and directed the mission by letter for the rest of his life.
Gregory refused the patriarch of Constantinople's title of universal bishop and answered it by calling himself servant of the servants of God.

movements.name: Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich for communal life — letters, church order, worship — but its most vivid material leans on one contested corpus: Ignatius's seven letters, whose authorship and dating (c. 107–117 CE traditionally; rival readings place them decades later, even as later composition) remain a genuine, unresolved scholarly dispute. Individual, first-person voice stays thin throughout: no woman, no enslaved member, and no non-literate believer — the majority of this movement — speaks to us in words of their own.
movements.floorNote: These communities lived two centuries before the Nicene Creed was written. What they confessed is part of the raw material the creed was later drawn from, not a departure from it.
movements.relationsSummary: Parent of nearly everything on the map
movements.why: In the decades after the apostles died, these house churches held together with no fixed hierarchy and no finished New Testament - Ignatius wrote seven letters while under armed guard on his way to execution, and Rome wrote at length to settle a quarrel in Corinth.

entry.subtitle: Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity
entry.tile: In Antioch, Asia Minor, and Rome, between about 70 and 200 CE, house churches grew up on their own. No single power ruled over them — letters carried by couriers held the network together instead. Once the apostles died, how to lead a church was never settled. Some followed a single bishop with elders beside him, others a council of elders alone. In Corinth, some elders were removed from office — an account that survives only in Rome's own letter asking for them back. That letter used real command language — “submit,” “receive correction” — but Rome claimed no formal power to force it. Corinth's own side is not preserved. They marked the Lord's Supper in different ways, too. One early manual gives thanks over the cup before the bread. Neither blessing tells the story of the Last Supper. Following Jesus could mean real danger: in one province, a governor had members questioned under torture, and in another, a bishop was marched under armed guard toward Rome. But this danger came and went — never constant, never empire-wide.

movements.longDescription:
In the generations following the apostles, the earliest Christian movement had no documented church buildings and no single leadership structure. They had the Old Testament. The gospels and letters of the apostles moved between communities as copies were made and passed along, though no fixed collection had been settled yet. It was a network of faithful households, scattered across Antioch, Asia Minor, and Rome, meeting wherever they could. New believers were taught the Two Ways on the road to baptism; only then were they brought into the fellowship to share the weekly breaking of bread and prayer. Across long distances, these household communities were held together by carried letters.

Some communities were guided by a single bishop alongside elders and deacons, others by a circle of elders alone—both forms were real, and neither was settled. The questions they wrestled with had no easy answers: How do we make room for genuine doubt? How should conflict within the community be resolved? What did women's leadership look like? Following Jesus routinely meant loss of social standing, suspicion from neighbors, and periodic waves of official violence.

In his surviving letters, Ignatius of Antioch describes writing to sister churches while being marched toward Rome under armed guard — soldiers he called 'ten leopards,' who, in his own words, 'show themselves all the worse' the more kindly he treats them. Justin, who told his imperial interrogator that he taught above a public bathhouse in Rome, wrote down the earliest record of what their Sunday actually looked like—the reading of the memoirs, the common loaf and cup, and the collection gathered for orphans, widows, and travelers. Justin was executed for refusing to abandon his Lord; tradition has it that Ignatius met the same end.

The earliest outside account of these communities comes from Roman authority, not from inside the movement. Around 112 CE, the governor Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan describing an investigation: believers who had recanted told him, under threat of ordinary punishment, that these communities met before dawn to sing a hymn to Christ 'as God,' bound themselves by oath against theft and adultery, then met again later for a meal they called 'common yet harmless.' Still unsatisfied, Pliny had two enslaved women who held office among them — titled ministrae, deacons — questioned under torture. He learned, he wrote, only 'a superstition depraved and immoderate.' Their names do not survive; his letter is the earliest outside evidence that women held a formal title here at all.
voices: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote seven letters to congregations while he was marched toward Rome under armed guard, c. 107-117. Polycarp's own letter later speaks of him as already dead, though it admits not knowing the details of what happened.

Clement of Rome wrote on behalf of the Roman church to the Corinthians around the year 96, addressing a dispute over deposed leaders. The letter is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament to survive.

Polycarp of Smyrna was addressed as bishop by Ignatius, though his own letter never claims the title, opening only as 'Polycarp, and the presbyters with him.' He was put to death at Smyrna around 155; his own congregation recorded his death.
Justin Martyr was a philosopher who kept teaching Christianity as a school in Rome. He left the earliest detailed description of what their Sunday actually looked like.
Most of these communities' hosts and householders are never named in the record. The gatherings met in their homes, but no record says whose.

Two enslaved women who served among these communities, called ministrae, are named only by their Roman interrogator's own word for their office — never by their own names. A governor had them tortured around the year 112 to learn what Christians did; it is the earliest outside evidence that women here held a formal title at all.
movements.legacy:
Almost every Christian tradition descends from these early gatherings. The basic rhythm of Christian worship—assembling on the first day of the week, reading aloud from the prophets and the apostles' memoirs, and sharing the bread and the cup, whether in a full communal meal or the bread and wine alone—shows up earliest in these spaces.

With the apostles no longer there to consult, these communities had to work out how to live together: how to treat one another, how to pray, and how to forgive and restore those who fell into sin or caused division. The roles of bishop, presbyter, and deacon were already named in the apostolic writings, but trying to live out those instructions under local pressures gave the offices more concrete form.

The apostolic texts themselves gained authority in much the same way. Reading the apostles' letters aloud week after week became an enduring habit, and it was through this regular use in worship—not by an early decree—that these writings came to be heard alongside the ancient Jewish Scriptures. Carried by travelers from city to city, these letters bound scattered households together, and writings like those of Clement, Ignatius, and Polycarp were preserved and read for generations to come.

movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.name: The Second-Century Greek Apologists
movements.sourcing: Unusually good. Justin's two Apologies and the Dialogue, Athenagoras' Plea, Theophilus to Autolycus, Tatian's Address and the Epistle to Diognetus all survive whole; Quadratus and Melito survive in fragments, and Aristides was recovered only in 1889. Roughly a dozen works in hand, which is more than several other traditions here have.
movements.relationsSummary: Overlaps post-apostolic-house-church in era and largely in people - Justin taught at Rome - but is a different thing: that entry is the church's internal life, this is the same Christians turned outward, addressing emperors and an educated public that despised them.
movements.why: For eighty years, Christian writers handed Roman emperors formal defenses of their faith, answering charges of atheism and cannibalism by arguing that Greek philosophy itself had been reaching toward Christ. Justin ran a school at Rome and was executed for his teaching around 165. A generation later, Theophilus of Antioch, writing to a pagan friend, became the first Christian author on record to call God by the word 'Trinity.'
movements.longDescription: Around 124 a Christian named Quadratus handed the emperor Hadrian a written defence of his religion, and for the next eighty years others kept doing it. Aristides did it at Athens; Justin, a philosopher who kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after his conversion and ran a school at Rome, did it twice and was executed for it about 165. Athenagoras addressed Marcus Aurelius; Melito of Sardis addressed him too; Theophilus wrote three books to a pagan friend named Autolycus; an anonymous writer produced the letter to Diognetus that is still the most quoted thing any of them wrote. The charges were always roughly the same - that Christians were atheists because they had no images, cannibals because of what they said about eating a body, and disloyal because they would not sacrifice - and the answers were too. What made the enterprise interesting was the second move: rather than only denying the charges, most of them argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held, and that Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason rather than its enemies.
movements.teaser: Eighty years of Christians handing written defences to emperors who had them killed anyway - and arguing, while they did it, that Plato had been half right.
voices: Quadratus - the earliest, who gave Hadrian a defence around 124 and survives in a single paragraph
Aristides of Athens - whose apology was lost for seventeen centuries and recovered in 1889
Justin Martyr - philosopher, schoolmaster at Rome, author of two Apologies and the Dialogue with Trypho, beheaded about 165
Athenagoras of Athens - who addressed Marcus Aurelius and Commodus with the most philosophically careful of the defences
Theophilus of Antioch - who wrote three books to a pagan friend and was the first to use the word Trinity of God
Melito of Sardis - bishop, apologist to Marcus Aurelius, and author of a Paschal homily recovered in the twentieth century
The writer to Diognetus - anonymous, undated, and the most quoted of all of them
movements.legacy: Justin's argument that the Word was sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers before the incarnation gave the church a way of relating to inherited learning that it has never entirely put down, and that Clement and Origen at Alexandria took much further. The apologists also settled some of the vocabulary: Theophilus is the first surviving writer to use the word Trinity of God. And the Epistle to Diognetus' description of Christians as resident aliens - at home everywhere and strangers everywhere - has outlived every other line the movement produced.

movements.name: The Latin Apologists
movements.region: Carthage; Rome and Ostia; Sicca in Numidia; Nicomedia and Trier
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Substantial evidence survives for this tradition. Minucius Felix's Octavius (about twenty-four thousand words), Commodian's Instructiones (about fifteen thousand), and Arnobius' seven books Against the Heathen (a hundred and forty thousand) survive whole. Lactantius' writings survive at even greater length: the Divine Institutes alone runs to two hundred and forty thousand words, and with the Anger of God, the Workmanship of God, and other fragments, his surviving work totals just under half a million words. Tertullian's own corpus of thirty-two works also survives complete — the Apology, the five books Against Marcion (his longest single work, about a hundred and eighty-four thousand words), Against Praxeas, the Prescription Against Heretics, and the rest — along with the Passion of Perpetua and Felicitas, transmitted alongside his writings. In all, well over a million words survive from these five authors together. Three of the five are barely datable: Minucius Felix within a century, Commodian within three centuries; Tertullian's own dates, roughly 197 to 220, are the best anchored of the set.
movements.floorNote: Not in question for the corpus as a whole. Tertullian's own later years aligned with the New Prophecy (Montanism) out of Phrygia - a real, disclosed complication, but not a floor question: the census's own Montanism entry states plainly that the New Prophecy "held the same doctrine as the churches that condemned it," the dispute being one of authority and discipline, not of the Creed's own commitments.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Latin counterpart to the Greek apologists of the second century, a generation later and never as coherent a body. It includes Tertullian, whose Latin apologetic writing opened the tradition and gave it its vocabulary before the other authors continued it. Its clearest link to the later imperial church runs through Lactantius, who wrote his own defense during persecution and then tutored the son of the emperor who ended it.
movements.why: A Carthaginian convert named Tertullian had to invent Latin words for the Trinity and the sacraments just to defend his faith, coining terms like trinitas, persona, and substantia. The argument he opened ran a further century, through Minucius Felix's dialogue giving pagan objections their fullest voice, to Lactantius, who wrote his own defense in the middle of persecution and later tutored the emperor's son.
movements.longDescription: Carthage, 197 CE. A convert trained as a rhetorician sat down to answer the slanders against his new faith, and found that Latin had no words yet for most of what he needed to say - so he made them. Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use for the Trinity and the sacraments came substantially off Tertullian's own pen, in the Apology and in the string of treatises that followed it - Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, the Prescription Against Heretics contending that Scripture belongs to the churches that received it, five long books Against Marcion answering the one rival he judged most dangerous. In his later years he grew steadily more rigorist and aligned himself with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia, which is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint. Roughly a generation on and in a very different key, a Roman advocate named Minucius Felix wrote a dialogue set on the beach at Ostia, in which a pagan friend states the case against Christianity - it is a religion of the ignorant, its god was a criminal, Rome's greatness is proof enough that Rome's gods work - and is answered and convinced. What makes the Octavius unusual is that its author gives the other side the better speech: Caecilius' half is the fullest surviving statement of the educated pagan objection to Christianity. A century later and in a different register again, an African rhetorician at Sicca called Arnobius wrote seven furious books Against the Heathen - to persuade his own bishop that his conversion was genuine, if Jerome is to be believed - and produced along the way the most detailed account of Roman religious practice that any Christian left, because he had to describe what he was attacking. Between them, and impossible to date within three centuries, sits Commodian: eighty short poems in acrostic verse that does not scan by the old rules, aimed at ordinary people, half catechism and half warning. And at the end of the line stands Lactantius, whom Jerome makes Arnobius' pupil: a professor of Latin rhetoric summoned to Diocletian's new capital at Nicomedia, who lost the post when the persecution began and wrote the Divine Institutes in the middle of it, and who was old by the time it was over, when Constantine brought him to Trier to teach his son. What these five share is not a place or a generation. It is that each had to make the argument in Latin, in a vocabulary that had not been built to carry it - Tertullian first and most consequentially, the others after him.
movements.teaser: A Carthaginian lawyer invented the Latin words for the Trinity while defending Christians against Roman slander - and the argument he opened ran a further century, through Rome, Numidia, and the emperor's own new capitals.
voices: Tertullian of Carthage - a convert and trained rhetorician who opened the whole enterprise in 197, forged most of the Latin vocabulary of Christian argument, and grew more rigorist and Montanist-aligned in his later years
Minucius Felix - a Roman advocate whose dialogue gives the pagan side the better speech, and whose own date nobody can fix within a century
Arnobius of Sicca - a teacher of rhetoric who wrote seven books against the gods, by one account to convince his bishop that he meant it
Commodianus - who wrote catechism in acrostic verse that does not scan, and whom scholars have placed anywhere between the third century and the fifth
Lactantius - Arnobius' pupil on Jerome's account, who wrote the fullest of the Latin defences while the persecution was still running and afterwards tutored the son of the emperor who ended it
movements.legacy: The Latin vocabulary of Christian argument was made here. Tertullian coined most of the technical words Western Christians still use for the Trinity and the sacraments, and left lines that entered common Christian speech, most famously that the blood of Christians is seed; the Western habit of thinking about God, the church, and the sacraments in legal and forensic categories owes a great deal to a man trained as an advocate. Minucius Felix gave the West its model for the apologetic dialogue and preserved, inadvertently, the most complete record of what educated Romans actually said against the church. Arnobius is now read mostly by historians of Roman religion, who need him precisely because he described in detail the thing he was trying to demolish. And Lactantius' Latin was good enough that the Renaissance called him the Christian Cicero and printed him before it printed most of the Fathers - the Divine Institutes was among the first books off a press in Italy, in 1465.

movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.name: Apocryphal and Pseudepigraphal Literature in Christian Transmission
movements.informalName: The Books That Were Never Canon
movements.region: Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt, Rome, and the Latin West
movements.sourcing: Large and uneven. Around a dozen works survive - the apocryphal Acts of Andrew, John, Philip, Peter and Paul, the Protevangelium of James, the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel and Apocalypse of Peter, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, the Revelation of Moses, the Narrative of Zosimus. Dates and provenance are disputed for nearly all of them, and the received text is often centuries later than the tradition behind it.
movements.relationsSummary: Not a community and not a tradition: a body of writing that circulated across all of them. Its natural relation to every other early entry is that they read it.
movements.why: For centuries Christians copied and read stories that never entered the Bible, among them the Protevangelium of James, the source of nearly everything later believers came to know about Mary's parents and childhood. Some of these works, like the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, were originally Jewish texts that survive today only because Christian scribes kept copying them long after Judaism itself had let them go.
movements.longDescription: From about the second century onwards Christians wrote, read and copied a great deal that never went into the New Testament and was never quite meant to. Some of it fills gaps the gospels leave: the Protevangelium of James supplies Mary's parents, her childhood in the Temple and the birth in a cave, and almost everything later Christians believed about her early life comes from it rather than from scripture. Some of it carries the apostles into adventures - Andrew among cannibals, Philip at Hierapolis, Thomas in India - in narratives that read like Greek romances and often carry a strongly ascetic charge. And a third body is not Christian in origin at all: the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, the Life of Adam and Eve, the Testament of Abraham are Jewish works that survive because Christian scribes kept copying them, sometimes with Christian passages worked in, after Judaism itself had let them go. And it kept being written. The Dormition narratives that gave the church the Assumption, the tour-of-hell apocalypses that shaped medieval visions of the afterlife, Pseudo-Matthew and its Carolingian abridgement that carried Mary's childhood into the Latin West - these run to the ninth century and beyond. What holds all of it together is not a community or a doctrine. It is a fact about transmission: this is the literature the church read for centuries and never canonised.
movements.teaser: The books the church read for centuries and never put in the Bible - including the Jewish ones that survive only because Christian scribes kept copying them.
voices: The Protevangelium of James - anonymous, mid-second century, and the source of nearly everything later Christians believed about Mary's childhood
The apocryphal Acts of Andrew, John, Philip and Thomas - apostolic adventure written in the register of Greek romance, often with an ascetic edge
The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs - a Jewish work with Christian passages worked in, or a Christian work on Jewish sources; the argument is unresolved
The Gospel of Peter - condemned for its use at Rhossus by Serapion of Antioch, and recovered from an Egyptian grave in 1886
The Apocalypse of Peter - which stood near the canon's edge in the Muratorian fragment, and did not make it
movements.legacy: Marian devotion in both East and West rests substantially on the Protevangelium of James: Anna and Joachim, the presentation in the Temple, the ox and the ass, all of it entered the calendar and the iconography from a book the church never accepted as scripture. The apocryphal Acts supplied medieval art and legend with most of what it knew about the apostles' deaths. And the Jewish pseudepigrapha in this collection are the reason a large body of Second Temple literature exists at all - preserved, ironically, by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced it.

movements.name: Alexandrian Catechetical / Christian-Platonist Tradition
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Clement, Origen); school-institution question is live scholarship. One real gap: Clement's fullest surviving treatment of marriage and the body exists only in his own Greek — no public-domain English translation has ever been made of it.
movements.floorNote: This tradition's core confession does not diverge from the doctrine the Nicene Creed later stated — though one of its own greatest figures held things more loosely. Origen speculated boldly toward the soul's pre-existence and the final restoration of all things. The rupture of his own lifetime was not over these ideas: his bishop condemned his ordination, not his doctrine. The dispute over the doctrines themselves broke into open controversy only around 399–400, nearly a century and a half after his death, and a church council formally condemned them three centuries after that.
movements.relationsSummary: A contested influence on Desert Monasticism, real at one disputed point and denied as a general continuation; scholarship parent of the Bethlehem Circle
movements.why: Teachers here read Scripture in layers, the plain story and a deeper meaning beneath it, confident that Greek philosophy could serve Christ rather than threaten him - a method that shaped how much of the church has read the Bible ever since.

entry.subtitle: Alexandrian Catechetical Tradition
entry.tile: In Alexandria, from about 150 to 400 CE, teachers led seekers through a shared reading of Scripture. They read for a deeper meaning beneath the surface, one that opened onto the Logos himself. This teaching reached the literate few. Ordinary believers met the same faith another way — through baptism, the shared meal, and the yearly round of fasts and feasts. Some call this one continuous school, led by one teacher after another. Others say it was simply a series of private teachers, grouped together only in hindsight. When plague struck the city, Bishop Dionysius wrote to his own church, praising his people for nursing the sick and burying the dead. Others, he wrote, fled the city instead. Persecution could reach the school's own teachers, not only the wider community. Origen himself was imprisoned and tortured under the emperor Decius, and he died a few years later. It had already touched his boyhood, too. His father was martyred in an earlier persecution, when Origen was still just a boy.

movements.longDescription:
Alexandria was the ancient world's great city of libraries and lecture halls, and Christianity there took the same shape: a school. Teachers received enquirers, catechumens preparing for baptism, and educated pagans curious about this new philosophy, and walked them through Scripture as a text with a surface and a depth: the letter first, then the moral sense, then the spiritual meaning that opens onto the Logos himself.

Clement wrote for cultivated Greeks who wanted to know whether a Christian could keep his learning. Origen, who succeeded him, wrote commentaries across most of Scripture and produced the Hexapla, a six-column parallel edition of the Old Testament assembled to see what the Hebrew actually said — before falling out with his bishop and moving his teaching to Caesarea around 231. Historians still argue about how formal the whole thing was — whether Alexandria had one continuous institution with a succession of appointed heads, as Eusebius later described it, or a looser sequence of private Christian schools whose teachers happened to be remembered together. That tidy succession comes almost entirely from Eusebius: Clement's own writings never once describe a formal school that he headed.

The allegorical way of reading Scripture is this tradition's best-known signature, but it was never uncontested even at home. Nepos, a bishop out in the Egyptian countryside at Arsinoe, wrote a book refuting the allegorists and won real support for a plainer, literal reading — until Dionysius, by then bishop of Alexandria, spent three days in patient public conversation with Nepos's own community and brought them back around.
voices: Pantaenus was the earliest teacher named in the tradition, remembered as a philosopher who had converted from Stoicism. Clement later paid tribute to a beloved teacher as 'the true, the Sicilian bee,' though Clement himself never names him, and the identification with Pantaenus comes only from Eusebius.
Clement of Alexandria wrote for educated Greeks, arguing that philosophy had been a tutor leading them toward Christ.
Origen dominates the surviving record here: a commentator, a textual scholar, and the first Christian to attempt a systematic account of the faith.

Dionysius of Alexandria studied under Origen and later became bishop, steering the Egyptian church through persecution and plague. Of Christians who nursed the dying while an epidemic emptied the city, he wrote: they 'held fast to each other and visited the sick fearlessly... and died with them most joyfully, taking the affliction of others, and drawing the sickness from their neighbors to themselves.'

Didymus the Blind lost his sight at four, yet taught in Alexandria for decades — later tradition remembers him as heading the school in its final generation, though no surviving primary account actually says so. Jerome studied under him. Didymus's own books vanished for over fifteen centuries, until a cache of them turned up by chance in the Egyptian sand near Tura in 1941; none has yet been translated into English, so his voice here comes only through his students.

Most of the ordinary people who filled these classrooms and congregations left no words of their own. Potamiaena, a young woman the church remembered by name for her courage under execution, is typical of what survives: her story, never her own words. Everything that survives here was written by the literate few — teachers, bishops, and their own students.
movements.legacy:
The Alexandrian way of reading Scripture — that the text has depths beneath its surface, and that reading it is a lifelong formation rather than an act of information-gathering — became one of Christianity's most influential approaches, shaping how the East and West alike read Scripture for centuries.

Origen's textual scholarship set the standard for taking the original languages seriously; Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus compiled an anthology of his writings, and Ambrose and Jerome read him closely even when they were careful about saying so.

The tradition also fed directly into Egyptian monasticism, giving the desert its intellectual vocabulary.

movements.name: Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis)
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich in hymns and doctrinal teaching (Ephrem, Aphrahat's twenty-three Demonstrations); thin on ordinary believers, the daughters of the covenant's own words, and the years after Ephrem's death in 373.
movements.floorNote: This tradition holds the doctrine the Nicene Creed states. One figure inside it, the philosopher-poet Bardaisan, taught cosmological ideas his own later tradition repudiated; exactly where he stands relative to that doctrine remains an open question.
movements.relationsSummary: Parent of the Church of the East and the Syriac Orthodox Church; the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine passed into Arabic and back to Europe.
movements.why: This is the church that sang its teaching rather than argued it in treatises - Ephrem's hymns carried its doctrine, and men and women bound themselves to a covenant of celibacy and service inside the ordinary congregation, not apart from it.

entry.subtitle: Syriac Christianity of Edessa and Nisibis
entry.tile: In Edessa and Nisibis, from 200 to 410 CE, Christians taught their faith in hymn. They read Scripture as a world of types, each one answering another. They also read the four Gospels as one continuous story, not four separate books. A harmony woven a generation earlier combined the four accounts. Preachers used it for as long as this world lasted. At the heart of this community's ascetic life stood the covenant. Men and women vowed themselves to celibacy for life, serving their own congregation instead of leaving for the desert. Whether authority rested more in that vow or in a bishop's office was never settled in their own record. On the Persian side of the frontier, the king's persecution killed the bishop Simeon bar Sabbae and his clergy, and bishops after him were killed in turn. After the last of them, the bishopric of Seleucia-Ctesiphon stood empty for twenty years. Taking the post meant near-certain death.

movements.longDescription:
The first hard evidence of a Christian community at Edessa is a flood: a church building destroyed when the river overran its banks in 201, recorded in the city's own chronicle. Edessa's Christians told an older story about their beginning too—that King Abgar himself had written to Jesus and been answered—but no text earlier than the fourth century attests it, and it is best heard as the community's own cherished memory, not as history. What the record actually shows is plainer. They were a Christian people who spoke Syriac, close to the language Jesus himself spoke, and who read Scripture as a web of symbols answering each other: Eden answering the cross, the Jordan answering the font. They met the Gospel as one continuous story rather than four separate books, in a harmony a Greek-trained convert named Tatian had woven a generation earlier; Aphrahat quoted it and Ephrem preached from it for as long as this world lasted.

At the community's ascetic heart stood the covenant: men and women who vowed themselves to lifelong celibacy while remaining inside their own congregation instead of leaving for the desert, keeping the fast and the vigil and singing what the community believed. Office and vow ran side by side for this whole world's life, and who finally spoke for it was never settled. Aphrahat, remembered simply as the Persian sage, once drafted a synodal letter in the name of a council of bishops, yet whether he held that office himself, no one now can say. Persia's own bishops fought the same question in the open: Papa of Seleucia-Ctesiphon claimed to lead them all, and was contested by his own colleagues in his own lifetime. The community also knew its faith by naming what it was not, answering by name the teachings of the philosopher Bardaisan, of Marcion, and of Mani, all preached in the same cities in the same tongue.

In 338, Shapur II of Persia besieged Nisibis; Ephrem, the city's own hymnwriter, remembered its deliverance as an act of God worked through ordinary defenders, while a later account added a swarm of gnats to the story. Bishop Jacob led that defense. The Chronicle of Edessa places his death that same year; Theodoret's own church history instead has him defending the city again in 350, and the record itself never closes the question. Nisibis held until 363, when the Roman emperor Jovian ceded it to Persia and Ephrem moved west to Edessa, where he spent his last year running famine relief before he died. On the Persian side, the persecution already underway since the 340s took bishop Simeon bar Sabbae and his clergy, and left the church's chief seat empty for twenty years, since filling it meant near-certain death. Not until 410, when the Roman bishop Marutha brokered a synod with the favor of Yazdegerd I, the Persian king, did the Persian church finally receive a single settled order—the last thing this world's own record has to say.
voices: Ephrem was a deacon, first at Nisibis and then, after 363, at Edessa, and this tradition's most prolific poet: hundreds of hymns carried its doctrine in verse a congregation could sing. He spent his last year running famine relief in the city and died within the month the crisis ended.

Aphrahat, remembered simply as 'the Persian sage,' wrote twenty-three dated letters from inside the Persian empire between 336 and 345, the last of them composed deep inside Shapur's persecution. He once drafted a circular letter in a synod of bishops' own name, yet whether he held that office himself is a question his own tradition never answers.

Tatian wove the four Gospels into one continuous story a generation before this world's own window opens, and these Syriac communities read his harmony as their standard Gospel text for two centuries afterward. Greek church history also remembers him breaking with Rome and founding a rigorist sect of his own—a controversy that belongs to his life outside this Syriac world, not inside it.

Bardaisan was a philosopher and poet at the court of King Abgar the Great. His one surviving dialogue argues that free will, not the stars, decides how people live—Christians the world over follow one law, whatever horoscope they were born under. His own later tradition rejected him over a separate question, whether the body itself is raised, and exactly where he stood on it is a question the record leaves open.

Jacob, bishop of Nisibis from about 309 and a signatory at the Council of Nicaea in 325, was remembered as the city's protector through Persian siege — though even his own people could not agree on when he died: one chronicle places it in 338, the year of the first siege, another has him still at his post in 350.

The daughters of the covenant sang this tradition's hymns in every church that had them. Not one line composed by one of them survives; everything known of their voices—their vows, their singing, their service—was written by men.

Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, was ordered to collect a crushing new tax on Persia's Christians and refused. Arrested and brought before Shapur II, tradition says he was offered gifts, then threatened, and each time refused to worship the sun. He was executed with his own clergy — tradition remembers him as the first of the persecution's bishops to die for his faith. His death opened the twenty-year vacancy the Persian church endured. The year itself is disputed: 341 by the traditional count, with some historians arguing for 344 instead.
movements.legacy:
The Assyrian Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox Church, and the Eastern Catholic churches in communion with Rome all descend from this tradition, still worship in Syriac, and still sing Ephrem's hymns in their own liturgies.

Within a generation of this world's own close, the Gospel harmony these communities had read for two centuries gave way to a new translation, the Peshitta, and churches began reading the four Gospels separately again. Tradition credits Bishop Rabbula of Edessa (411–435) with the change; historians dispute whether he caused it or only presided over a shift already under way.

Missionaries carried the faith east along the trade routes into Persia and India, and by the seventh century as far as Tang-dynasty China. Centuries later, Syriac translators became the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine reached the Arabic-speaking world, and from there passed back into Europe.

A separate school of formal theological training later grew up at Nisibis—founded around 490, two generations after this world's own record closes—and became one of the ancient world's most important centres of Christian education, distinct from the teaching Jacob and Ephrem had given the same city a century earlier.

experienceToday.text: Mor Gabriel Monastery, Tur Abdin, southeastern Turkey — founded in 397 and still a working monastery and the seat of the metropolitan of Tur Abdin, one of the oldest continuously inhabited Christian monasteries on earth
