movements.name: Latin Pastoral-Congregational Christianity
movements.statusDescription: One of the traditions chosen for its era after a completed survey. Construction has not begun.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Cyprian's letters, Augustine's sermons to his own flock)
movements.floorNote: Nothing in this tradition's confession diverges from the doctrine the Nicene Creed states.
movements.relationsSummary: Confirmed distinct from the Imperial tradition; Donatism contests its interval
movements.why: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in the mid-200s, told his congregation to nurse their pagan neighbors through the plague that now bears his name, before he was beheaded outside the city in 258. A century and a half later, Augustine preached to the same Hippo congregation several times a week for thirty-five years, and stenographers took down much of what he said. There's no built conversation for this tradition here yet.
movements.teaser: Roman North Africa, c. 240s to 430 CE — the parish before the word existed: bishops burying plague victims, preaching to the same faces every week, and deciding what to do about the people who had failed.
movements.longDescription: This is the ordinary congregational life of Latin-speaking North Africa — not the councils and not the controversies, but the week in and week out work of a bishop with a flock. Cyprian became bishop of Carthage around 248, went into hiding when the emperor Decius ordered universal sacrifice, and returned to the hardest pastoral problem of the age. What to do with the thousands of his own people who had complied and now wanted back in. He organized relief through the epidemic that still bears his name, telling his congregation to nurse pagan neighbours as well as their own, and was beheaded outside Carthage in 258. A century and a half later Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius from 395 until his death in 430, preached to the same congregation several times a week for thirty-five years, with stenographers taking much of it down. Hundreds of those sermons survive, arguing, joking, scolding and consoling actual people whose situations he knew. Between the two: catechumens under instruction, baptisms at Easter, penitents doing public penance, the care of widows and the poor, and the bishop sitting as judge in his own people's disputes.
voices: Cyprian of Carthage — bishop through persecution and plague, whose letters are the fullest surviving picture of how a third-century congregation actually ran
Pontius the Deacon — Cyprian's deacon, who wrote an account of his bishop's life and death
Augustine of Hippo — bishop of Hippo Regius for thirty-five years, and the most extensively documented working pastor of the ancient world
Possidius of Calama — Augustine's friend and fellow bishop, who wrote his biography and catalogued his works
movements.legacy: The North African church itself did not survive: the Vandals took the province in the 430s, and the Arab conquest of the seventh century ended Latin Christianity there altogether. What it left behind is the working vocabulary of Western church life. Cyprian's letters became foundational for Western understandings of the bishop's office and the unity of the church. Augustine's sermons shaped Christian preaching for well over a thousand years, and the catechumenate and penitential practice worked out in these congregations became the pattern for Western sacramental discipline. Latin Christianity's basic assumptions about what a local church is were largely formed in these two African towns.

experienceToday.text: Hippo Regius and the Basilica of Saint Augustine, Annaba, Algeria — the excavated ruins of Augustine's city lie below a nineteenth-century basilica overlooking the site, both open to visitors

movements.name: Tertullian's Voice
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich corpus, one man
movements.relationsSummary: Tertullian's writing opened the entire tradition of Latin Christian argument that the Latin apologists carried on after him.
movements.why: Tertullian was the first major Christian author to write in Latin, and where the language had no words for what he wanted to say, he invented them - trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum among them. Trained as an advocate, he wrote the Apology defending Christians against Roman slander, and in his later years aligned himself with the rigorist New Prophecy movement. Cyprian, a generation on, read him every day and called him simply 'the master.'
movements.teaser: Carthage, c. 197 to 220 CE — a trained rhetorician's mind turned loose on the Christian faith, forced to invent the Latin words the West has argued in ever since.
movements.longDescription: Tertullian was the first major Christian author to write in Latin rather than Greek, which meant that a great deal of what he wanted to say had no words yet — so he made them. Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use came substantially off his pen, and his formula of one substance in three persons became the standard Latin way of stating the doctrine of God. He wrote like the advocate he was trained to be: the Apology dismantling Roman slanders against Christians, Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, and On the Prescription of Heretics contending that heretics have no standing even to cite Scripture, since the Scriptures belong to the churches that received them. In his later years he grew steadily more rigorist — against remarriage, against flight in persecution, against what he saw as a church going soft. And aligned himself with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia, which is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint.
voices: Tertullian of Carthage — the tradition is one man: a convert, probably a trained rhetorician, writing in Carthage from roughly 197 to 220
Cyprian of Carthage — not a follower, but Jerome reports that Cyprian read Tertullian every day and would ask for the volume by saying 'give me the master'
movements.legacy: No community descends from him — there is some evidence of a small group of followers in Carthage after his death, and nothing beyond that. His legacy is linguistic and rhetorical: the Latin words for the Trinity, and lines that entered the common speech of Christianity, most famously his claim that the blood of Christians is seed. Cyprian, Jerome and Augustine all read him closely, and the Western habit of thinking about God, the church and the sacraments in legal and forensic categories owes a great deal to a man who was never canonized and never quite belonged anywhere.

movements.name: Marcion / Marcionism
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Substantial, almost entirely via opponents
movements.floorNote: Marcion taught two distinct gods — the creator of the Hebrew Scriptures and a higher Father revealed by Jesus — and a Christ who only appeared to have a body. Both directly contradict the creed's confession of one God, maker of all things, and a Son truly made flesh.
movements.relationsSummary: Second-century rival the proto-orthodox defined themselves against
movements.why: Marcion, a wealthy shipowner from Sinope, concluded that the strict, law-giving God of the Hebrew Scriptures and the merciful Father revealed by Jesus could not be the same being. After the Roman church expelled him in 144 and returned his money, he built a rival network of congregations with its own edited Scripture - a version of Luke and ten letters of Paul, stripped of what he judged to be Jewish corruption.
movements.teaser: Rome and across the empire, c. 140 into the 300s CE — a shipowner who concluded the God of the Hebrew Scriptures could not possibly be the Father of Jesus, and built a rival church on that conviction.
movements.longDescription: Marcion came from Sinope on the Black Sea, made a considerable fortune in shipping, and arrived in Rome around 140 where he gave the church there a very large donation. Reading Paul on law and grace, he concluded that the just, law-giving creator of the Hebrew Scriptures and the merciful Father whom Jesus revealed were simply two different beings. And that Christ, sent by the higher God into a world he had not made, could not have taken real flesh from it. In 144 the Roman church expelled him and returned his money. He replied by organizing congregations of his own, which spread fast along the trade routes he knew and endured for centuries in the East. He gave them their own Scripture: a single gospel based on Luke and ten letters of Paul, edited to remove what he judged to be Jewish corruption, together with a book called the Antitheses setting the two Gods against one another point by point. Not one line of his own writing survives. Everything we have comes through the men who wrote to refute him, above all Tertullian, whose Against Marcion runs to five books.
voices: Marcion of Sinope — shipowner and organizer, who founded an alternative church with its own bishops and its own edited Scripture
Tertullian of Carthage — wrote five books Against Marcion, the fullest surviving account of what Marcion actually taught
Irenaeus of Lyons — one of the earliest to answer him, and the source for the story that Polycarp, meeting Marcion in the street, called him 'the firstborn of Satan'
Justin Martyr — wrote against him within Marcion's own lifetime, in a work now lost
movements.legacy: Marcionite churches faded in the West by roughly the fourth century and lingered considerably longer in Syria and the East, but nothing descends from them. What Marcion left behind is what he provoked. Congregations that had never needed to specify which books counted as Scripture discovered that they now had to, and the confession of one God, maker of heaven and earth, whose Son truly took flesh, was hammered into its sharpest early form in argument against him. How far he actually caused the New Testament canon rather than accelerated a process already under way is still debated by historians.

movements.name: Valentinian & other Gnostic Christianities
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Nag Hammadi gave real internal texts
movements.floorNote: Apparent-body Christology; pleroma vs. one Maker of all
movements.relationsSummary: Rivals the early traditions anathematized and were shaped by
movements.why: Valentinus, an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136, taught that a divine spark lies trapped within human beings and that Christ came to awaken it - a teaching offered quietly inside ordinary congregations rather than through a rival church. For eighteen centuries this movement was known only through the bishops who wrote against it, until 1945, when a buried jar near Nag Hammadi in Egypt turned out to hold their own writings, including the Gospel of Truth.
movements.teaser: Alexandria, Rome and far beyond, c. 120 to 300 CE — teachers who told the Christian story as a cosmic drama of a divine spark fallen into matter, and whose own books lay buried in an Egyptian jar until 1945.
movements.longDescription: Valentinus was an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136 and, according to Tertullian, was nearly elected bishop there. He and the students who carried his name — Ptolemy, Heracleon, Theodotus — taught that the visible world was made not by the highest God but by a lesser craftsman, that human beings carry within them a spark of the divine that has fallen into matter, and that Christ came to bring the knowledge that wakes it up. Along with related currents around teachers like Basilides, they mostly did not build rival churches: they sat in ordinary congregations and offered their teaching as the deeper meaning available to those ready for it, which is precisely what alarmed bishops like Irenaeus, whose five-volume Against Heresies of about 180 was written to drag the system into the open and refute it. For eighteen centuries they were known almost entirely through such opponents — until 1945, when farmers digging near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt turned up a sealed jar of papyrus codices in Coptic, including the Gospel of Truth, giving these currents their own voice for the first time since antiquity.
voices: Valentinus — Alexandrian teacher, later in Rome, the most influential figure of these currents and possibly the author of the Gospel of Truth
Ptolemy — a Valentinian teacher whose Letter to Flora, a patient explanation of how to read the Law of Moses, survives nearly complete
Heracleon — wrote the earliest known commentary on the Gospel of John, preserved in fragments quoted by Origen
Basilides — an Alexandrian teacher of a related but distinct system, known only through hostile summaries
Irenaeus of Lyons — their most thorough opponent, whose refutation preserved much of what they taught
movements.legacy: No community survives, and none claims descent. Their trace is double. First, the shape of what became orthodox Christianity was set partly by the labour of answering them. The insistence that the one God made matter and called it good, that the Son took real flesh and rose in a real body, and that the faith is a public rule handed down openly rather than a secret reserved for initiates, were all pressed into their enduring form in this argument. Second, since 1945 the Nag Hammadi texts have been read, translated and fought over continuously, and have reshaped how modern readers picture the diversity of the earliest Christian centuries.

experienceToday.text: The Coptic Museum, Cairo — holds the Nag Hammadi codices along with the world's largest collection of Coptic Christian art, and is open to the public

movements.name: Manichaeism
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Rich own corpus survives
movements.floorNote: Co-original dualism denies 'maker of all things'; most scholars: a distinct universal religion
movements.relationsSummary: Augustine's own former allegiance
movements.why: Mani, born in Mesopotamia in 216, broke from the Jewish-Christian sect that raised him after what he described as revelations from his heavenly twin, and went on to teach that the world is a battleground between eternal Light and Darkness in which sparks of light lie trapped in matter. He wrote his own scriptures and had them deliberately translated, and his faith spread from Persia all the way to China. Augustine of Hippo followed it as a Hearer for nine years before his conversion.
movements.teaser: From Persia to the Mediterranean and on to China, from 216 CE into the centuries beyond — a prophet who set out to found the one universal religion, and whose one intact surviving temple still stands on a hillside in Fujian.
movements.longDescription: Mani was born in Mesopotamia in 216 and raised in a Jewish-Christian baptizing sect before breaking with it after what he described as revelations from his heavenly twin. He taught that reality is the battleground of two co-eternal principles, Light and Darkness, that particles of light are trapped in the material world, and that a strict ascetic discipline sets them free. Almost uniquely among founders of his era he wrote his own scriptures and had them translated deliberately, intending a faith that could absorb and supersede Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Buddhism at once. And for a time it worked, spreading from Persia across the Roman Empire and eastward along the Silk Road into Central Asia and China. His followers divided into the Elect, who kept the full discipline, and the Hearers, who supported them and lived ordinary lives. Augustine of Hippo was a Hearer for roughly nine years before his conversion, and spent much of his later career arguing against the teachers he had once sat under. Mani himself died in custody under the Persian king Bahram I in the 270s.
voices: Mani — the founder, who wrote his own scriptures rather than leaving the task to disciples, and died in a Persian prison
Faustus of Milevis — the Manichaean bishop whose teaching Augustine sought out as a young man and later refuted at length
Augustine of Hippo — a Hearer for about nine years, then the movement's most effective Latin opponent, and an unintended preserver of its arguments
movements.legacy: In the West it was hunted by emperors and by the church and had largely vanished by the sixth century, though the word 'Manichaean' survived for centuries afterwards as an insult aimed at anyone thought too fond of dualism. In the East it lasted far longer: it was for a time the state religion of the Uyghur Khaganate from the 760s, and persisted in southern China for many centuries. Because Mani wrote his own books, and because manuscripts have been recovered over the last century from Turfan in western China, from Medinet Madi in Egypt, and in the miniature Cologne Mani Codex, this is one of the few extinct ancient religions that can now be read substantially in its own words rather than only through its enemies.

experienceToday.text: Cao'an, Jinjiang, Fujian, China — long regarded as the only intact surviving Manichaean temple, with its carved image of Mani, inscribed as part of the Quanzhou UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021

movements.name: Ebionite / Nazoraean Current
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Almost wholly hostile heresiological description
movements.floorNote: Some outside writers report that they denied Jesus's virgin birth and divinity; others report the opposite of the group they call Nazoraeans. Because nothing survives from these communities themselves, what they actually confessed cannot be established either way — an open question about the evidence, not a settled answer about their doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: These communities are the clearest evidence that Christianity began inside Judaism. Modern Messianic Jewish movements are sometimes compared to them, but no line of descent connects the two.
movements.why: Some Jewish communities of believers in Jesus kept observing Torah, circumcision, and the Sabbath long after most of the church had moved on, honoring James, the brother of Jesus, and regarding Paul as someone who had abandoned the Law. Not one word survives from these communities in their own voice - everything known of them comes through later writers who disagreed with each other and wrote from the outside, so even what they actually believed remains genuinely uncertain.
movements.teaser: Palestine and Syria, roughly the first through fourth centuries — Jewish followers of Jesus who never stopped keeping the Law, and whose own words have not survived to tell us what they actually believed.
movements.longDescription: The first Christians were Jews, and in Palestine and Syria some communities of Jewish believers in Jesus went on keeping Torah, circumcision and the Sabbath long after the wider church had moved away from them. Later heresy-hunting writers — Irenaeus, Origen, Eusebius, Epiphanius, Jerome — describe them under two names, 'Ebionites', from the Hebrew for the poor, and 'Nazoraeans', reporting that they used their own Hebrew or Aramaic gospel, honoured James the brother of Jesus, and regarded Paul as an apostate from the Law. But those writers disagree with one another, wrote from outside and often centuries later, and had every reason to sharpen the picture. The fullest account of all, Epiphanius's Panarion, is now widely judged unreliable in its details. Not one text these communities wrote about themselves survives intact — only fragments quoted by the people refuting them. And modern scholars genuinely disagree about whether 'Ebionite' and 'Nazoraean' name two distinct groups, one group under two labels, or largely a category the heresy-hunters assembled.
voices: No leader of these communities is named in any source they produced themselves. The heresy-hunters offer only 'Ebion', a supposed founder most scholars now think never existed — invented to explain a group name that in fact meant simply 'the poor'.
movements.legacy: No community descends from them. They disappear from the record by roughly the fifth century, absorbed into the wider church or back into Judaism or simply gone, and the gospel material attributed to them survives only as quotations in the writers who opposed them. What they left behind is a question rather than an institution. They are the standing reminder that Christianity began inside Judaism, and that the separation of the two was slower, later and far more contested than a tidy account allows. Modern Messianic Jewish movements are sometimes compared to them, but no line of descent connects them.

movements.name: Montanism (the New Prophecy)
movements.statusDescription: The concern is limited primary sourcing, not that prophetic leaders were involved. Surviving evidence centers on a handful of quoted oracles from three named prophets and hostile reports; whether independent community voices survive (some Phrygian inscriptions may point that way) isn't yet resolved.
movements.sourcing: Oracles, Tertullian's advocacy, Phrygian inscriptions
movements.floorNote: What the New Prophecy confessed about God, Christ and the Spirit is not what its opponents objected to — as far as the surviving evidence shows, it held the same doctrine as the churches that condemned it. The dispute was about authority and discipline: whether new prophecy could bind the church, and how strict its common life should be.
movements.relationsSummary: Named live neighbor inside Tradition I.1's milieu
movements.why: In a Phrygian village around 165, a man named Montanus began prophesying that the Holy Spirit was speaking through him. Two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, prophesied alongside him, and together they expected the New Jerusalem to descend on their own village of Pepuza. Lost for over a thousand years, that village was located by archaeologists only in 2000.
movements.teaser: Phrygia in inland Asia Minor, from around 165 CE into the centuries after — a movement convinced the Spirit was still speaking, which named the village where it expected the New Jerusalem to come down.
movements.longDescription: In a Phrygian village in the middle of the second century a man named Montanus began prophesying in ecstatic speech, and two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, prophesied alongside him. They did not call themselves Montanists — that was their opponents' label. They called it simply the New Prophecy, and their claim was that the Paraclete whom Jesus had promised was speaking now, through them. What followed was less exotic than the label suggests: stricter fasting, refusal of second marriages, a readiness to face martyrdom rather than flee it, and the expectation that the New Jerusalem would descend at Pepuza in Phrygia. It spread well beyond Asia Minor — Tertullian of Carthage became its most articulate Latin advocate — and although Asian synods condemned it and later imperial law suppressed it, communities persisted for centuries. Pepuza and its neighbour Tymion, lost for well over a thousand years, were located by archaeologists in inland Turkey only in 2000.
voices: Montanus — the prophet whose name opponents attached to the movement, though its own name for itself was the New Prophecy
Priscilla and Maximilla — the two prophetesses who spoke alongside him, and whose quoted oracles are among the very few first-person Montanist words that survive at all
Tertullian of Carthage — the movement's most articulate Latin defender, and the only sympathetic writer whose work survives in quantity
The ordinary members are the gap in the record: almost everything else comes through hostile writers such as Apollonius and the anonymous author quoted by Eusebius
movements.legacy: No church descends from the New Prophecy. Imperial suppression under Justinian in the sixth century finished it, its own writings were destroyed, and what remains is a handful of quoted oracles plus a body of Phrygian gravestone inscriptions whose Montanist identity is itself argued over. That is the honest difficulty: the surviving evidence runs overwhelmingly through the three named prophets and through their enemies, and whether an independent community voice survives anywhere is not yet settled. What outlasted the movement is the set of questions it forced: whether prophecy continued after the apostles, who may authorize it, and how a church distinguishes genuine inspiration from enthusiasm. Later renewal movements down to modern Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity have repeatedly been accused of reviving it, and have occasionally claimed the comparison themselves, though no historical line connects them.

movements.name: Novatianism
movements.statusDescription: The concern is limited primary sourcing, not that a single leader was involved. Surviving evidence centers on Novatian's own rigorist stance and rival ordination; whether an independent community voice beyond his own survives in the record isn't yet resolved.
movements.sourcing: Novatian's De Trinitate is broadly orthodox; community texture thinner
movements.floorNote: Novatian's own On the Trinity is a careful and orthodox statement of Christian doctrine, and the Novatianist bishop present at Nicaea accepted the council's creed. The break was over discipline — whether the church could readmit those who had denied the faith under persecution — not over belief.
movements.relationsSummary: Rigorist parallel communion; redundancy risk vs. Donatism noted if revisited
movements.why: When many Christians complied with the emperor Decius' order to sacrifice in 250 and then wanted back into the church, the Roman theologian Novatian argued that the church had no authority to forgive such apostasy, however much God might. His followers, who called themselves the Katharoi, 'the pure,' consecrated him as a rival bishop and spread across the empire for centuries; a Novatianist bishop even attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 and accepted its creed.
movements.teaser: Rome and across the empire, from 251 CE into the centuries after — a rival church founded the day a Roman theologian decided that Christians who had denied Christ under threat could never be readmitted.
movements.longDescription: When the emperor Decius ordered every subject of the empire to sacrifice in 250, a great many Christians complied, and once the pressure lifted they wanted to come back. Novatian — the most learned theologian in the Roman church and the first there to write substantial theology in Latin — held that the church had no authority to receive them. God might forgive apostasy, but the church could not presume to. When Cornelius, who took the lenient view, was elected bishop of Rome in 251, Novatian's supporters had him consecrated as a rival bishop, one of the earliest such rival consecrations the city had seen. His congregations called themselves the Katharoi, the pure, and they spread across the empire and lasted for centuries. At the end of the fourth century they still held several churches in Constantinople and more across Phrygia and Bithynia. What stands out is how little separated them in doctrine. Their bishop attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 and accepted its creed, and the council's eighth canon set out terms for receiving Novatianist clergy — terms they largely declined. Later tradition remembers Novatian himself as a martyr, though the record on that is not firm.
voices: Novatian — Roman presbyter and theologian, author of On the Trinity, consecrated rival bishop of Rome in 251
Cornelius — the bishop of Rome whose willingness to readmit the lapsed Novatian opposed
Cyprian of Carthage — sided with Cornelius, and much of what is known about the dispute comes through his correspondence
Acesius — the Novatianist bishop of Constantinople at Nicaea, to whom the historian Socrates reports Constantine said: set up a ladder, Acesius, and climb to heaven by yourself
The congregations themselves are thin in the record — their story is told almost entirely by outside historians rather than in their own surviving words
movements.legacy: No church descends from them; the last Novatianist communities faded in the East by around the seventh century. Two things outlasted the schism. The first is the doctrine sharpened against it — that the church is a hospital rather than a society of the already-perfect, and that no sin lies beyond the reach of the church's ministry of reconciliation — worked out by Cyprian in the moment and by Augustine at length afterwards, along with the graded system of public penance that grew out of exactly this argument. The second is Novatian's own On the Trinity, which was copied, read and valued in the mainstream church as a careful Latin statement of orthodox doctrine long after his party was gone, handed down in manuscripts among the works of Tertullian.

movements.name: The Anatolian Church in the Third Century
movements.region: Neocaesarea in Pontus, Olympus in Lycia
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Modest and mixed. Gregory's Panegyric to Origen and his Canonical Epistle survive and both are first-hand; Methodius' Banquet survives whole. But a substantial part of what circulates under both names is marked dubious or spurious by scholars, and the Life of Gregory that carries most of the stories about him was written a century later by Gregory of Nyssa.
movements.relationsSummary: The ground the Cappadocian tradition grows out of and knows it: Basil's grandmother Macrina was formed by Gregory Thaumaturgus' disciples, and Basil appeals to his practice as precedent. Origen's reach runs through it in both directions - Gregory was his devoted pupil, Methodius his first serious critic.
movements.why: Gregory of Neocaesarea, a devoted pupil of Origen, wrote a canonical letter working out, case by case, what to do with Christians who had looted alongside Gothic raiders in the 250s. A generation later, Methodius of Olympus rewrote Plato's Symposium as a Christian dialogue in which ten women take turns praising chastity, and became Origen's first serious critic before dying in the persecution around 311.
movements.longDescription: Gregory of Neocaesarea went south to study law and came back a bishop. He had fallen in with Origen at Caesarea instead, stayed five years, and left with a farewell address that is one of the warmest descriptions of a teacher anyone wrote in antiquity. What he did in Pontus after that is mostly legend - the story that he found seventeen Christians in the city and left seventeen pagans is a century later than he is - but one document survives that is not legend at all. When Gothic raiders came through in the 250s, Gregory wrote a canonical letter working out what to do about Christians who had looted alongside them, or informed, or kept what the raiders left: a bishop dealing with a wrecked province, case by case. A generation later and further south, Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia, wrote the Banquet of the Ten Virgins - a Christian rewriting of Plato's Symposium in which ten women take turns praising chastity - and became the first substantial critic of Origen, whose most devoted pupil had been Gregory. He died in the persecution around 311.
movements.teaser: Between the house churches and Nicaea, the church of Asia Minor left almost nothing behind - except a bishop's ruling on what to do with Christians who looted alongside the Goths, and ten women arguing about chastity at a banquet.
voices: Gregory Thaumaturgus - Origen's pupil, bishop of Neocaesarea, and the author of a canonical letter on a province after a raid
Methodius of Olympus - who rewrote Plato's Symposium as a Christian argument for virginity and became Origen's first serious critic
Macrina the Elder - Basil's grandmother, formed by Gregory's disciples, and the link the Cappadocians claim to this world
Origen - not of this region, but reaching into it from both ends: the teacher Gregory revered and the thinker Methodius set out to correct
movements.legacy: The Cappadocian tradition claims descent from this ground explicitly, and Basil cites Gregory's practice as precedent when he wants to argue that something is old. Gregory's Canonical Epistle entered the received canon-law collections of the East and is still there. And Methodius' Banquet is the foundation of the Christian literature of virginity - everything Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory of Nyssa later wrote on the subject is downstream of it, and its argument that chastity is a form of freedom rather than a deprivation began there.

movements.name: The Church of Antioch in the Third Century
movements.informalName: The Synod That Deposed Its Bishop
movements.region: Antioch on the Orontes, and its Syrian hinterland
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Only one document survives directly from this period: Malchion's synodal letter deposing Paul of Samosata, about three thousand words, the collective act of a council rather than an individual's book. Serapion's fragments fall just before this window. Everything else about these hundred years arrives through Eusebius, quoting archives at second hand, and through what the fourth century said about Lucian once his pupils had become notorious.
movements.floorNote: The city's church itself is not in question. But Paul of Samosata's own teaching is a live, unresolved question about where the doctrinal line falls, distinct from the other monarchian currents of the period, such as Sabellius's modalism.
movements.relationsSummary: The ground I.13 stands on, eighty years before it starts, and the seedbed of the controversy that I.23 and I.28 assess. Its relation to modalist-monarchianism is symmetry rather than descent: Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism are the two opposite ways of declining the account of the Son that the century was working out.
movements.why: In 268, a council of bishops at Antioch deposed Paul of Samosata for teaching that Christ was a man the Word had come to dwell in, rather than the Word made flesh, and for conduct they found just as troubling, including a raised throne in church and hymns sung to himself. He would not leave until the emperor Aurelian retook the city in 272 and settled the matter by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome. The council's rejection of the word 'homoousios' as something Paul had misused is a large part of why that same word was still suspect at Nicaea, sixty years later.
movements.longDescription: In 268 or thereabouts the bishops of Syria and Asia Minor met at Antioch for the third time in a few years to deal with their own metropolitan. Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East and, on the account of the council that removed him, a salaried official of the Palmyrene administration that then governed it. The charges mix doctrine with deportment: that he had a raised throne built for himself in church, that he stopped the old hymns and had new ones sung to himself, that women in his household gave scandal. The teaching at issue was that Christ was a man in whom the Word had come to dwell rather than the Word made flesh - the reading later called adoptionist. The council could not make the deposition stick, because the civil power was Palmyrene and Paul had its favour; he went only when Aurelian retook the city in 272 and settled the question of who owned the church building by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome, which is the first time a Roman emperor adjudicated a Christian dispute. The letter announcing the deposition was drafted by Malchion, who ran a rhetorical school in the city and had cross-examined Paul in front of shorthand writers. A generation later, in the same city, a presbyter named Lucian worked over the text of the Greek Bible and taught a circle of students - Arius among them - who afterwards used his name as a badge.
movements.teaser: A council removed the bishop of the greatest city in the East for what he taught and how he behaved, and could not make it stick until an emperor decided who owned the building.
voices: Paul of Samosata - bishop of Antioch and Palmyrene official, deposed for teaching that Christ was a man indwelt by the Word, surviving only in his enemies' minutes
Malchion - head of the city's rhetorical school, who cross-examined Paul before stenographers and drafted the letter that deposed him
Lucian of Antioch - biblical text-critic and martyr in 312, whose pupils, Arius among them, called themselves Lucianists
Serapion - bishop about 191 to 211, who let the Gospel of Peter be read at Rhossus, read it properly, and withdrew the permission
Aurelian - who took the city back from Palmyra in 272 and settled the dispute by asking which claimant Italy recognised
movements.legacy: Two things went out of this council into the fourth century. The word homoousios - one substance - seems to have been rejected here as something Paul had misused, which is a large part of why its adoption at Nicaea in 325 was so contentious, and why Eastern bishops who were not Arians could still be uneasy about it. And Lucian's school gave the Arian party its leadership and its self-description: Arius wrote to Eusebius of Nicomedia as one Lucianist to another. The Antiochene exegetical tradition that Diodore, Theodore and Chrysostom carry is usually traced back to Lucian's work on the text as well - which makes this century the origin of two things the next four centuries spent arguing about.

movements.name: The Church of Roman Palestine before Constantine
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Good for the end, thin for the beginning. Eusebius' Martyrs of Palestine is a first-hand record of the persecution he lived through, and fragments of Julius Africanus' letters and Chronography survive. Before that the evidence is fragments transmitted by Eusebius himself, which makes him both the principal witness and the principal filter.
movements.relationsSummary: The province Origen taught in for the last twenty years of his life, and the one Eusebius was formed in. It bridges alexandria-catechetical, whose greatest teacher moved here, and jerusalem-liturgical-pilgrimage-christianity, which begins where this ends.
movements.why: When Origen left Alexandria for Caesarea around 231, he spent his last twenty years teaching there, and a presbyter named Pamphilus built his books into the best Christian library in the ancient world. A young Eusebius trained in that library and later called himself 'Eusebius of Pamphilus' out of loyalty to his teacher. When persecution came, Pamphilus was killed in 310, and Eusebius wrote down, name by name, what he watched happen to his own province.
movements.longDescription: When Origen left Alexandria for good around 231 he went to Caesarea on the Palestinian coast, and taught there for the last twenty years of his life. What grew around him outlasted him by a long way. His books stayed, and a presbyter named Pamphilus spent his life and his money enlarging them into the best Christian library in the world - the place where the Hexapla sat, where texts were corrected and copied, and where a young man called Eusebius learned to work, and afterwards called himself Eusebius of Pamphilus out of loyalty to his teacher. Up the road at Jerusalem, Bishop Alexander had built a library of his own and was collecting letters and records; further inland at Emmaus, Julius Africanus - soldier, scholar, and correspondent of Origen - wrote the first Christian universal chronicle and a careful little treatise on why the two gospel genealogies of Jesus do not agree. Then the persecution came. Pamphilus was killed in 310 and Alexander had already died in prison; Eusebius wrote down what he had watched happen to his own province, name by name, and afterwards used the library to write the history of the church.
movements.teaser: A coastal town, a library, and the men who built it — where Origen ended up, where Eusebius learned his trade, and where the persecution of 303 was recorded by someone who watched it.
voices: Origen - who left Alexandria around 231 and taught here for the rest of his life
Alexander of Jerusalem - fellow student of Origen, founder of the Jerusalem library, dead in prison in the Decian persecution
Julius Africanus - soldier and scholar at Emmaus, author of the first Christian universal chronicle and of a letter to Origen on the book of Susanna
Pamphilus - the presbyter who spent everything on the Caesarean library, and was martyred in 310
Eusebius of Caesarea - Pamphilus' student, who called himself by his teacher's name, recorded the persecution he lived through, and wrote the church's first history out of these shelves
movements.legacy: Almost everything anyone knows about the first three Christian centuries comes through this library. Eusebius' Church History quotes documents that survive nowhere else, and it was written from shelves Pamphilus and Alexander had assembled - so the shape of early Christian memory is partly the shape of what a Palestinian library happened to hold. The Hexapla, Origen's six-column Old Testament, sat here until the Arab conquest and was consulted by Jerome. And Africanus' chronicle is the foundation Eusebius built his own chronology on, which in turn became the frame every medieval universal history used.

movements.name: The Roman Church in the Third Century
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Substantial but one-sided. Hippolytus' Refutation is the fullest account of the Roman church in these decades and is written by a man who claimed the see against its bishop; Cyprian's correspondence with Rome gives an outside view. Callistus has no surviving voice of his own.
movements.relationsSummary: Sits in the gap between post-apostolic-house-church, which ends at 200, and novatianism, which begins with the schism of 251 - the same decades those two entries bracket without covering.
movements.why: Callistus, a former slave once sent to the Sardinian mines, became bishop of Rome and led a congregation through open arguments over whether the gravely lapsed could ever be restored, and how to speak of Father and Son without naming two Gods. Hippolytus, a learned presbyter who thought him wrong on every count, set himself up as a rival bishop and wrote a Refutation that, almost by accident, preserves more about second- and third-century religious movements than any other surviving book. Callistus himself left not one word in his own voice.
movements.longDescription: Between the house-church world that ends around 200 and the Novatian schism of 251, the Roman church did most of its early growing up - and it did so in public argument with itself. Zephyrinus and then Callistus led a large and socially mixed congregation through questions that had no settled answers: whether a Christian who had committed grave sin after baptism could ever be restored, whether a noblewoman could contract a union the state would not recognise rather than lose her status, how to speak about Father and Son without saying two Gods. Hippolytus, a learned presbyter of the same city, thought Callistus wrong on all three and said so at length, eventually functioning as a rival bishop. Nearly everything known about the period comes from him, which is a problem: he is the losing party and a hostile witness. Callistus, a former slave who had been sent to the Sardinian mines, left nothing in his own voice.
movements.teaser: Rome between 200 and 260 - a former slave leading the city's church, a learned rival who called himself bishop instead, and the arguments about forgiveness and marriage that neither of them could avoid.
voices: Callistus - a former slave and convict who became bishop of Rome, and left not one word of his own
Hippolytus - the learned presbyter who opposed him, set himself up as rival bishop, and wrote nearly everything we know about it
Zephyrinus - Callistus' predecessor, whom Hippolytus judged out of his depth
Caius - the Roman presbyter whose disputation with a Montanist survives in fragments
Cornelius - bishop from 251, whose correspondence with Cyprian opens the Novatian crisis

Dionysius of Rome - bishop 259-268, whose letter against Sabellian and tritheist readings, written into the controversy with his Alexandrian namesake, is the clearest doctrinal statement the Roman see made in this century
movements.legacy: The questions argued here did not go away: whether the church can restore the gravely lapsed is what the Novatian schism of 251 and the Donatist controversy of the next century are both about, and Rome's answer - that it can - is the one the Western church kept. Hippolytus' Refutation, written to discredit Callistus, incidentally preserves more information about second and third-century religious movements than any other surviving book.

movements.name: Latin Christianity in the Danubian Provinces
movements.region: Poetovio and Sirmium in Pannonia; Noricum, Dalmatia, Moesia
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Very thin, and one voice. Victorinus of Pettau's two surviving works - On the Creation of the World and the Commentary on the Apocalypse, about nineteen thousand words together - are the only Danubian Latin Christian writing known to survive. Both reach us through Jerome, who revised the Apocalypse commentary to remove its millenarianism, so the received text is not quite what Victorinus wrote. Everything else about the region's church is known from outside it: conciliar records, Ambrose, and the paperwork of the Homoian controversy.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. The Homoian bishops who later dominate this region are assessed at I.23, not here.
movements.relationsSummary: Sits between latin-pastoral-congregational-christianity, which is Latin but Carthaginian, and homoian-arian-christianity, which is Danubian but a century later and beyond the floor. Its text reaches hieronymian-ascetic-literary by a route no other work in the corpus takes: Jerome edited it.
movements.why: Victorinus of Pettau, a bishop on the frontier river Drava, wrote the first Latin biblical commentaries around the year 300, though Jerome said he knew Greek better than his own Latin. Victorinus read the seals, trumpets, and bowls of Revelation not as a sequence but as the same events told three times over, a reading that passed into the standard Western way of reading the book even after Jerome quietly rewrote his ending to remove its literal thousand-year reign. He died in the persecution around 304.
movements.longDescription: Poetovio sat on the Drava in Pannonia Superior, a road town on the frontier, and around the year 300 its bishop was writing commentaries on scripture in Latin - the first anyone is known to have written. Jerome, who came from the same corner of the world and read him carefully, said Victorinus knew Greek better than Latin, so that his works were excellent in sense and inferior in style; what Jerome did not say, and did, was that he found the theology objectionable too. Victorinus expected a literal thousand-year reign of the saints on earth, which was ordinary enough in his own generation and had become an embarrassment by Jerome's, so when Jerome reissued the Commentary on the Apocalypse he rewrote the ending. He also kept the thing that mattered most in it. Victorinus had seen that the seals, the trumpets and the bowls are not a sequence of events but the same events told three times over, and that reading - recapitulation - is the one the Latin West went on using. He died in the persecution around 304. Within fifty years the same provinces were the base of the bishops who ran the Homoian church of the West: Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum, the Sirmium creeds of the 350s, and finally Palladius of Ratiaria, deposed at Aquileia in 381 by a council that came up from Italy to do it.
movements.teaser: The first Latin commentator on the Bible was a frontier bishop on the Drava who wrote better Greek than Latin, expected a literal thousand-year reign, and had his book quietly corrected by Jerome.
voices: Victorinus of Pettau - bishop on the Drava, the earliest Latin biblical commentator, martyred about 304
Jerome - born at Stridon on the Dalmatian-Pannonian border, who praised Victorinus' sense, disparaged his Latin, and rewrote his ending
Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum - the Danubian bishops who drove the Homoian creeds of the 350s, and whose world this region becomes
Palladius of Ratiaria - deposed at Aquileia in 381, and the last bishop of these provinces whose own argument survives in his own words
movements.legacy: Victorinus' recapitulation reading of the Apocalypse - that the seals, trumpets and bowls narrate the same events over again rather than a sequence of them - passed through Jerome's revision into Tyconius and Augustine and became the standard Western reading of the book. That is a long career for a commentary its own editor thought needed fixing. The millenarianism did not survive the same journey, which is roughly the point: what the Latin West kept of its first exegete is what its second exegete was willing to pass on.

movements.name: Desert Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich and specific — Antony's own Vita and the Apophthegmata's elder-and-disciple sayings anchor the fleet's largest shelf of verbatim quotations (59 records, well ahead of the next richest built world's 37); thinner on ordinary participants outside the sayings tradition, on the Pachomian federation's own interior life beyond its founding, and on women's own voices (a small number of amma sayings, not a fuller corpus).
movements.floorNote: The desert communities held the Nicene faith of the churches they came out of — what set them apart was a way of life, not a different doctrine. One figure inside this world, Evagrius, worked that faith into the most systematic scheme the desert ever produced; parts of it were formally condemned over a century after this world's own window closes, and the controversy that first exposed the fault line broke out within it, scattering his own circle before his ideas were ever formally judged.
movements.relationsSummary: A distinct formation world from Alexandria's own, not its continuation — though one disputed reading of its founder's letters leaves the question of contact open; parent of monastic life across the wider Christian world.
movements.why: Antony gave away his inheritance after one Gospel reading and spent decades alone at what he called the inner mountain; Pachomius built the first written rule for living the same struggle in community instead.

entry.subtitle: Desert Monasticism
entry.tile: Between about 320 and 430 CE, Christians in Egypt began leaving their villages for the desert's edge, in a movement that never really stopped. Persecution had just ended, so they invented a different kind of struggle: fighting the tempting thoughts that rise up from inside a person. This way of life took three real, different shapes. Some lived alone, testing their own choices against an elder's hard-earned wisdom. Others joined communities governed by a rule set down in writing, under an appointed leader. A third group kept mostly to their own cells, then walked in once a week to pray and share a meal together. These two kinds of authority, personal and official, existed side by side and never merged into one. None of this was as cut off from ordinary life as it might sound. Digs at one settlement found a marketplace standing among the monks' own cells. Joining this life meant giving up land, family ties, and a settled home. That cost came gradually, one step at a time, over years, not in a single break.

movements.longDescription:
By the early fourth century the last empire-wide persecution had ended, and Constantine's toleration closed off a path that had once been open to any Christian: dying for the faith. Antony, a young Egyptian landowner, gave away his family's land after hearing one Gospel reading in church — "if thou wouldest be perfect, go and sell that thou hast" — and withdrew by stages: the village's edge, an abandoned fort, then the desert's inner reaches, for the rest of his life. What his biographer Athanasius describes there is not escape but combat: the war once waged against a persecutor from outside, now fought against demons and the thoughts they whispered, from within. Teaching passed mostly in a single exchange — a younger monk asked an elder for "a word," and the elder answered in one sentence, no more. Generations later, those sentences were gathered into what other Christians would call the Sayings of the Desert Fathers and Mothers, arranged by the name of the elder who spoke them, not necessarily as anyone first heard them said.

Not everyone lived Antony's way. Around 320, a man named Pachomius founded the desert's first rule-governed community at Tabennesi in the Thebaid; by his death in 346 it had grown into a federation of nine houses for men and two for women, bound by a written rule and appointed offices rather than one elder's own example. Between the two lay a third pattern: loose settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis, where ascetics lived mostly alone but gathered weekly for worship and correction. These settlements sat closer to ordinary life than their own rhetoric of total withdrawal suggests: excavation at Kellia has uncovered at least one commercial center operating alongside the ascetic cells, real evidence of trade with the surrounding villages. Which of these actually held authority — a life earned through discipline, or an office conferred by a rule — was never settled. Even Pachomius, the rule's own founder, was remembered afterward less as an officeholder than as a father whose own example, not his rule alone, had formed his community.

What kept any of this from tipping into excess was discernment: the skill, prized above all others, of judging how much fasting, how much solitude, a particular person could actually bear. The tradition's most common story shape is an eager newcomer asking for an extreme practice and being redirected toward something more moderate. Evagrius, the most formally educated man the desert produced, tried to systematize the struggle into a scheme of his own: eight named categories of tempting thought, and a ladder rising from practice through passionlessness to contemplation. He died at Kellia in January 399, months before a controversy his own learned circle could not survive — a bishop's letter on how literally to picture God split simple monks from learned ones, and by the year's end Evagrius's circle had been driven out of Egypt. His writings survived anyway, part of them transmitted for centuries under another name.
voices: Antony gave away his family's land after hearing one Gospel reading in church and took it as addressed to himself, then withdrew by stages — the village's edge, an abandoned fort, the inner mountain — for the rest of his life. His hagiographer says he could not endure to learn letters as a boy; a handful of letters that may genuinely be his own suggest a man trained in the philosophy that same biographer denies him, and the two portraits have never been reconciled.

Pachomius founded the desert's first rule-governed community at Tabennesi around 320; by his death in 346 it had grown to nine houses of men and two of women, bound by a common rule and appointed offices. Even so, those who remembered him afterward described a father whose own example formed the community, not an officeholder alone. One of those women's houses stood a mile across the river, founded for his own sister; the rule kept the two communities from ever seeing each other's faces or hearing each other's voices in life — but required the men to carry a woman's body across the river for burial among their own when she died.

Sarah was one of a small number of women remembered by name in the desert's own teaching tradition; six of her sayings survive. When monks came to test her, she told them plainly that she was the man among them, and they were the women.

Evagrius was the most formally educated man the desert produced, ordained reader by Basil of Caesarea and deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus before he withdrew to Kellia. He organized the desert's raw, occasion-bound wisdom about tempting thoughts into the most complete scheme it ever produced, and died in January 399, months before the controversy his own circle could not survive.

John Cassian spent years among the Egyptian monks before carrying their teaching west into Latin, where the monk Benedict later read him. He also preserves the desert's own fullest answer to a hard question, worked out at length in one Conference: that the greater share of anyone's salvation belongs to grace, not to human effort — a position Western theology would later judge too generous to effort, and condemn within a generation.

Women's sayings survive by name, Sarah among them, and so do about fifteen narrated lives of named women, several with their own words reported inside the telling. What does not survive from anyone is a woman's own extended account, written in her own person and at her own length, the way this world's paradigmatic solitary figure has one.
movements.legacy:
Almost every later form of Christian monastic life descends from here. Benedict's own Rule for Western monks sends its readers directly to John Cassian's reports from Egypt, and the monasteries of Sinai and Mount Athos trace their own practice back to the same desert source.

The sayings themselves are still read as spiritual reading across Orthodox, Catholic, and Protestant traditions alike. Evagrius's eight named categories of tempting thought traveled west through Cassian and, by way of Gregory the Great two centuries later, narrowed into the seven deadly sins of Western moral teaching. One popular link doesn't actually hold: the desert's own word for the stillness they sought, hesychia, is often assumed to be the same practice as the later Byzantine Hesychast tradition and its Jesus Prayer technique — that systematized method belongs to a separate, later world and isn't part of this one's own record.

Some of the houses founded in that first Egyptian generation are still living communities. The Coptic monasteries of St Antony and St Paul near the Red Sea, and the cluster of monasteries at Wadi al-Natrun, are inhabited by monks today, on or near the same ground this world's own record describes.
