movements.name: Early Palestinian Ascetic Monasticism
movements.informalName: The Monks of Gaza and the Judean Desert
movements.region: Gaza, the Judean desert, Sinai road
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Thin and largely hagiographic. Jerome's Life of Hilarion and Life of Malchus are the main surviving witnesses and both are written to edify; Palladius and the pilgrim literature supply glimpses. Nothing here is the movement's own teaching in its own voice, which is the difference from Egypt and from Gaul.
movements.relationsSummary: Egyptian in origin - Hilarion was Antony's disciple - and the direct antecedent of chalcedonian-monasticism-judean-desert-and-gaza, which begins where this leaves off at c. 450.
movements.why: Hilarion, a disciple of Antony's, returned home to Gaza around 306 and settled in the coastal scrub, living as a solitary within reach of the villages, roads, and pilgrims of the coast rather than deep desert. In the Judean hills, Chariton founded a different pattern at Pharan, the laura, where solitaries lived apart through the week and gathered only on Sundays — the arrangement that later shaped the great monasteries of the Judean desert. Jerome told the story of the loneliest of these lives in his Life of Malchus, a monk carried off by raiders.
movements.longDescription: Hilarion came back to Gaza from Egypt in about 306, having spent time with Antony, and settled in the coastal scrub near the town he had been born in. What grew around him was recognisably Egyptian and recognisably not: monks living alone or in twos in a landscape of villages and roads rather than deep desert, close enough to the Christian and pagan populations of the coast to be constantly interrupted. In the Judean hills, Chariton founded a different arrangement at Pharan around the same decades - a laura, where solitaries lived apart through the week and came together on Sundays, which became the characteristic Palestinian form. Pilgrims passed through all of it constantly on the way to the holy places, and some of them stayed. Jerome, writing from Bethlehem, gave the movement its literature: a Life of Hilarion, and a Life of Malchus about a monk taken by Saracen raiders. Both are shaped to teach rather than to record, which leaves the period better known for its stories than for what it actually taught.
movements.teaser: Gaza and the Judean hills, c. 330 to 450 - Egyptian asceticism transplanted to a landscape full of villages, roads and pilgrims, where it invented the laura and then handed it on.
voices: Hilarion of Gaza - Antony's disciple, who brought Egyptian anchoritism to the Palestinian coast
Chariton - founder of the first laura at Pharan, the arrangement Palestinian monasticism kept
Jerome - who wrote the Life of Hilarion and the Life of Malchus from Bethlehem
Malchus - the captured monk whose story Jerome tells, and one of the few non-elite voices the period records
movements.legacy: The laura - solitaries through the week, community on Sunday - became the Palestinian form and passed into the great Judean desert monasteries of Euthymius and Sabas in the following century, and from there into the Byzantine monastic tradition. Jerome's Life of Hilarion also did something more particular: it established the saint's life as a Latin literary form, on the model of the Life of Antony, and gave the West a second template for it.

movements.name: Donatism
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Substantial but heavily via opponents (Augustine, Optatus) — a named challenge, with four texts that speak as Donatists rather than being spoken about: the Passio Donati sermon, the Passio Marculi, Macrobius’ own letter, and Tyconius’ Book of Rules.
movements.floorNote: This communion held the same Nicene doctrine as the rival church it split from. What was contested was never the Trinity, Christ's divinity, or any point of creedal belief, but a narrower and sharper question: whether a bishop's own past under persecution could void what his hand later gave.
movements.relationsSummary: Rival-sibling of the Latin pastoral congregational tradition it split from over the same persecution; its refusal of any imperial standing to judge the church is the mirror image of Imperial and Juridical Christianity's own church-state alliance, and its once-for-all rebaptism is the opposite answer Cappadocian Christianity gave to the same question of how someone from the other side comes back in.
movements.why: For a century, Roman North Africa held two rival churches side by side, each with its own bishop and basilica, over one unyielding conviction: that a bishop who had surrendered Scripture under persecution could no longer give what his office claimed to give. Nearly everything known of them survives only through the hostile writings of their opponents - Augustine chief among them.

entry.subtitle: Donatism
entry.tile: In 311/312, Caecilian was consecrated bishop of Carthage by a man accused of surrendering his copy of the scriptures when ordered to - and a rival was consecrated beside him because of it, not in his place. From that day the same see held two bishops at once, two parallel hierarchies contesting town after town across Roman North Africa, each holding its own basilicas and its own unbroken line of ordination. This is the rigorist alternative communion that grew from that refusal: not a doctrinal heresy - its confession is standard North African Latin Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy - but a communion built on one unyielding conviction, that a tainted hand cannot give what it claims to give, lived out through rebaptism, the martyrs' graves read aloud once a year, and a refusal of the Christian emperor's own standing to judge the church. It closes in 439, when a Vandal army took Carthage and removed the Roman state this whole refusal was defined against.

movements.longDescription:
In 311 or 312 — the sources support both years and this record does not choose between them — Caecilian was elected bishop of Carthage and consecrated by Felix of Aptungi, a man accused of surrendering the Scriptures to be burned under the recent persecution. A rival party would not accept a bishop ordained by a traditor's hand: they consecrated Majorinus beside him instead, not in his place, and from Majorinus's successor Donatus the movement took its name. The doctrine at stake was narrow and absolute: a sacrament's validity rises and falls on the giver's own unbroken purity, so a tainted ordination gives nothing, and everyone it touches must be washed again by a hand that can be trusted. This was never a dispute over the Trinity or Christ's divinity — both parties held the same Nicene faith — but over who could validly give what the church gives, and for a century, across much of Roman Africa, this was simply the larger of the two churches, with its own bishops, its own basilicas, and its own councils contesting the same towns as its rival.

The empire did not stay neutral. In 347, imperial commissioners sent to force the two churches into one communion met resistance in Numidia; a bishop named Marculus was seized, paraded through several towns, and thrown from a cliff called Novapetra, and this communion has kept his name, and the names of others killed with him, read aloud at their graves every year since. A rural movement called the circumcellions is attested in this same period by an imperial fine — a real, legally distinct group — though almost everything claimed about what they actually did survives only in the writing of opponents who had reason to make them look like a mob. What the record will support is existence and a name; what it will not support, cleanly, is character.

The same communion that refused any emperor's standing to say which church was the true one turned to imperial power three times when it served the case — appealing to Constantine in 313, to Julian in 361, and, in the 390s, to the same machinery it condemned everywhere else, against its own breakaway Maximianist bishops. In 411 the emperor finally ordered the whole dispute settled at law: two hundred and seventy-nine of this communion's bishops met roughly two hundred and eighty-six of the rival church's before an imperial judge at Carthage, refused the chairs he offered them, and argued for three days. The verdict went against them, and the laws that followed took their churches by name. The communion survived under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for a further century and a half, still contested and still legislated against — the last word any surviving record has on it is a set of letters Pope Gregory the Great wrote in the 590s, pressing for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism in Numidia.
movements.teaser: Roman North Africa, c. 311 to 439 CE — a whole parallel church built on one conviction, that a tainted hand gives nothing, known to history mostly through the words of the bishop who argued against it the longest.

sources.work: Augustine, On Baptism, Against the Donatists
sources.note: Seven books answering the doctrine at its most systematic — the fullest surviving reconstruction of Donatist sacramental logic, built in order to refute it.

sources.work: Optatus of Milevis, Against the Donatists
sources.note: The earliest sustained Catholic answer to the schism, written roughly five decades after the founding events it narrates; its own appended dossier of documents is the richest surviving source for the conflict.

sources.work: Augustine, Answer to the Letters of Petilian
sources.note: Three books quoting a Donatist bishop's own letters clause by clause in order to answer them — the fullest surviving Donatist voice, reaching us because it was chosen for answerability.

sources.work: Tyconius, The Book of Rules
sources.note: The one Donatist theological work that survives entire, by a writer this communion's own council condemned — and the book outlived the party that expelled him.

sources.work: The Passion of Marculus
sources.note: A hagiographic account of the death of Marculus in the Macarian persecution of 347–348; the visionary and miraculous details are carried as this tradition's own testimony, not as verified events.

sources.work: Gesta Collationis Carthaginiensis anno 411 (Acts of the Conference of Carthage)
sources.note: The transcript of the great trial at Carthage, taken down by imperial notaries — the one place in the whole surviving record where the Donatist bishops argue their own standing in their own recorded words.

sources.work: Codex Theodosianus, Book 16
sources.note: The imperial legal record, including the 412 fine naming the circumcellions by name and the 405 Edict of Unity that outlawed this communion's own rebaptism.

voices: Donatus succeeded Majorinus as bishop of Carthage around 313 and led this communion for over three decades, long enough that it took his name. Almost nothing he wrote survives; his one famous line — what has the emperor to do with the church? — reaches us only because the bishop who opposed him quoted it in order to answer it.

Petilian, bishop of Constantina from the 390s, is this communion's fullest surviving voice, and its most mediated one: his letters exist only as clauses Augustine quoted in order to refute them. At the Conference of Carthage in 411 he spoke on an open transcript instead, refusing the judge's offered chair because Christ himself had stood before a governor.

Emeritus, bishop of Caesarea, argued this communion's case at Carthage for three days, matching Augustine's own scriptural argument verse for verse and signing the record of his own words with his appeal reserved. His is the one substantial voice here that reaches us without an opponent choosing what of it to keep.

Tyconius wrote the one theological work of this communion that survives whole, was rebuked by his own bishop, and was condemned by a council around 380 for arguing the church was spread through the whole earth. He never went over to the other side — and his book outlived the party that expelled him, read for centuries by the Catholic bishop who taught from it.

Lucilla, a wealthy laywoman of Carthage, was publicly rebuked for kissing a martyr's bone before communion; money traced to her, years later in a courtroom, helped found the rival altar against Caecilian. She left no words of her own — everything known of her comes from the hostile account written to blame her for the schism.

No ordinary believer's fear or doubt survives in this communion's own words, though for long stretches it was the larger church in Africa, not a minority within it. What is known of it comes almost entirely through the men who argued against it — except for two words cut in stone at a shrine, Deo laudes, praise to God, never written down by anyone at all.
movements.legacy:
Donatism left no continuing communion of its own. Its two-party contest with the rival Catholic church did not end with the Roman empire that had tried to settle it: Vandal and then Byzantine rulers inherited the same divided towns for another century and a half, the dispute still live enough that a sixth-century pope found it worth four letters of his own.

What arguing against this communion produced outlasted it. Answering the claim that a sacrament's worth depends on the minister's own purity, Augustine reasoned his way to the claim that stuck: the church is a mixed field of wheat and weeds until harvest, not a pure remnant, and what a sacrament gives does not depend on the purity of the hand that gives it. Both became foundational Western doctrine, worked out against this communion's own most absolute conviction. Tyconius, condemned by his own church around 380, fared stranger still: his one surviving book crossed over to the side that had expelled him and shaped how Augustine himself, and centuries of readers after him, learned to read Scripture.

Excavated basilica ruins from Donatist-era Numidia, at Timgad in modern Algeria, still stand — a physical trace of a communion that otherwise left no institution behind, its own history readable mostly in the words of the church that outlasted it.

experienceToday.text: Timgad, Algeria — UNESCO World Heritage Roman ruins including a Donatist-era basilica

movements.name: Cappadocian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Basil, the Gregories, and — rare for a defeated opponent — Eunomius' own surviving Apology); several flagship attributions (Epistle 38) contested
movements.floorNote: These are among the people who wrote the creed. The language it uses for Father, Son, and Spirit is substantially theirs — though which of them wrote which formulation is not always as settled as the textbook story suggests.
movements.relationsSummary: Trinitarian and pneumatological theology paired with charitable-ascetic practice; Jerome heard Gregory of Nazianzus teach, and this world argued directly, by name, against the Eunomians and the deniers of the Spirit's divinity.
movements.why: Basil of Caesarea, his sister Macrina, and his brother Gregory of Nyssa argued the fourth century's hardest question - is the Son fully God? - while also building a famine-relief complex outside Caesarea that fed, housed, and nursed the destitute.

entry.subtitle: Cappadocian Pastoral-Monastic and Trinitarian Tradition
entry.tile: The Nicene-confessing churches of Cappadocia and Pontus lasted from about 325 to 394 CE. One family and one friendship stood at their center. They were Basil of Caesarea; his sister, Macrina; his brother, Gregory of Nyssa; and Basil's friend, Gregory of Nazianzus. Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus argued the century's hardest question. Is the Son fully God, the same way the Father is? Is the Spirit God in that same way, too? Macrina turned the family estate into an ascetic household of her own. The council that later censured them made a claim about ascetic radicals in the region. It said the radicals had already broken up households and urged enslaved people to leave their owners. Basil did not condemn that impulse. Instead, he gave it a rule to follow. It came with a vow of obedience, and a household that welcomed guests. A famine struck the region around 368. Basil, still a priest at the time, preached against the local landowners who hoarded grain, and named them. Once he became bishop, he built a complex outside Caesarea. It fed the poor, housed travelers, treated the sick, and sheltered people with leprosy. Places like it already existed elsewhere, so it was not the first. What made it unusual was its size, and how openly it stood inside the city. This world buried a martyr too. Eupsychius of Caesarea was executed under Julian in 362. Under Valens, Gregory of Nyssa was deposed and sent into exile. The charge: mishandling money. His brother Basil called it trumped up, but no record survives from the side that brought the charge. Gregory returned two years later, once political pressure on Nicene bishops eased. Then, in 381, this Nicene minority finally won the empire's favor.

movements.longDescription:
In Cappadocia and neighboring Pontus, from the years after the last empire-wide persecutions to the death of the last of a remarkable generation, one extended family and the friends around it did more than most to settle the words Christians still use about God — how settled that settlement really was is itself now a live scholarly question. Basil of Caesarea, his younger brother Gregory of Nyssa, their elder sister Macrina, and Basil's friend Gregory of Nazianzus argued the hardest question of the century — whether the Son and the Spirit are God in the same sense the Father is — while running dioceses, burying relatives, and feeding the hungry through famine.

Basil's own preaching indicted the region's grain-hoarders by name and built a hospital, hostel, and workhouse complex outside Caesarea after the famine of 368 — a genuine, near-unprecedented undertaking, though not, as later legend sometimes claims, the first of its kind anywhere. Before that, he had already spent years answering a more radical ascetic ferment loose in the region — households dissolved, slaves urged to leave their masters, fasts kept against the church's own feasts — not by condemning the impulse but by giving it a rule, an obedience, and an open door for guests instead. Macrina turned the family estate into an ascetic household of her own and, in her brother's account of her last days, taught him theology from her deathbed — the only record of her that survives; no words of her own reach us independently of his telling.

Gregory of Nazianzus carried the argument to Constantinople, where the creed most Christians still recite took its final shape in 381. The years were not peaceful throughout: this world buried its own martyr, Eupsychius of Caesarea, executed under Julian in 362, and endured a hostile imperial church under Valens that drove Gregory of Nyssa briefly into exile. Even the letter usually cited as proof the three men agreed on the technical vocabulary — Epistle 38 — is itself contested between Basil and Gregory of Nyssa in modern scholarship.
movements.teaser: Cappadocia and Pontus, c. 325 to 394 CE — a people who fought a generation over a single word in their worship, kept a door open for the poor, and buried a martyr of their own along the way.
voices: Basil, bishop of Caesarea, preached during the famine of 368 that the bread being held back belonged to the hungry and the coat in the closet belonged to the naked — then built a hospital, hostel, and workhouse complex outside the city to outlast the crisis that occasioned it. The ascetic brotherhoods he organized answered a wilder, older impulse already loose in the region, households breaking apart and the enslaved leaving their masters, by giving it walls and a rule instead of condemning it.

Macrina turned the family estate at Annisa into a community where former slaves and their one-time owners prayed and worked side by side. When her brother Gregory of Nyssa found her dying, she lay not on a bed but on planks on the ground, and owned no burial clothes of her own; what she said to him in those last hours reaches us only through the book he wrote about her afterward.

Gregory of Nazianzus wanted nothing but a quiet life of study and prayer; his friend Basil pressed him into a bishopric at a dusty road junction anyway, and he never forgave him for it, in verse and in letters both. He still carried the Trinitarian argument to Constantinople in 380, where his sermons helped give the creed its final shape.

Gregory of Nyssa, Basil's younger brother, was the most speculative of the three, writing on the soul's nature and its endless ascent into God. Exiled under Valens for years, he outlived his siblings and completed the refutation of Eunomius that Basil had left unfinished at his death.

Emmelia was mother to Basil, Macrina, and Gregory of Nyssa, and to the household this whole tradition grew from. She is credited with acquiring and enshrining relics of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste at the family's own estate chapel — the one specific act of hers to survive, and even that only in her son's telling, not her own words.

Eupsychius of Caesarea was executed under Julian in 362 — this world's own martyr, from the last years persecution was still possible. He is remembered every year at an annual feast in Caesarea; no homily on him is attested from anyone, only the feast itself.

Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste, was Basil's own ascetic mentor before their friendship broke over the Spirit's honor — Basil came to suspect him of denying the Spirit's full divinity, and said so in writing. No work of Eustathius's own survives; his side of the rupture is not tellable, only the wound as Basil recorded it.

The plateau villages beyond these cities appear in the record only as crowds fed in famine or crowds at a festival, never speaking for themselves. No woman of this world left a line in her own hand, and the losing side of every dispute here — the radical ascetics censured at Gangra, the Homoian church, Eustathius himself — survives only inside the winning side's own case against it.
movements.legacy:
Their labor on the language — one being, three persons — became the standard grammar of Christian talk about God in East and West alike and stands behind the creed recited in most churches on Sunday, though the tidy story of a fully agreed "Cappadocian settlement" is itself contested by modern scholars, who read more real variation between the three than the textbook version allows.

Basil's rules for communal ascetic life remain foundational for Eastern Orthodox monasticism, and his hospital-and-hostel complex for the sick and destitute is often named among the ancestors of the Christian hospital, though no physical trace of the complex itself has ever been securely identified.

All four are venerated as saints across the Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, and Lutheran calendars, and Gregory of Nazianzus is one of only three figures the Eastern church calls simply "the Theologian."

movements.name: Imperial and Juridical Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional (Eusebius, Ambrose, Leo); thin to silent on ordinary believers, women's own words, and the Homoian establishment's own voice
movements.floorNote: This is the tradition that convened Nicaea and eventually made its creed imperial law, so its standing on the Creed is not in doubt. It is worth saying plainly, though, that this was never obvious to the people living through it: for long stretches of the fourth century the emperor's own church was Homoian rather than Nicene. The hard questions here are about power, not about doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: Damasus's own secretary was Jerome, who carried Rome's claims into the next generation's ascetic-literary circles; the Nicene settlement received at Chalcedon in 451 is the same creed the Cappadocian churches had helped work out a generation earlier.
movements.why: Between Constantine's toleration of the church in 312 and the Council of Chalcedon in 451, bishops went from outlaws to office-holders beside a throne - and never agreed among themselves whether Rome, Constantinople, or a bishop's own moral standing held the final word.

entry.subtitle: Imperial and Juridical Christianity
entry.tile: Bishops in Rome, Constantinople, and Milan lived through a real change. It ran from Constantine's victory in 312 to the Council of Chalcedon in 451. They stopped being outlaws beneath the sword. They became office-holders beside a throne instead — settling their own disputes in council, managing imperial funds, summoned to councils at the emperor's own expense. This was not only a fight over power. At Chalcedon in 451, the council took a letter from Leo of Rome as the final word on what it means to say Christ has two natures. Whole regions, starting in Egypt, rejected that settlement at once. The split never healed. The same council also extended Constantinople's own claim to rank second among the churches, over the protest of Rome's own delegates. Three rival grounds of authority rose across this whole window. Rome claimed it from Peter. Constantinople claimed it from nearness to the throne. And Ambrose of Milan claimed that the emperor stood inside the church, not over it. The question was never settled. This world's worst hours were caused, not suffered. One was Damasus's own disputed election to the bishopric of Rome, so violent that a hundred and thirty-seven people died in a single day. Another was Theodosius's massacre at Thessalonica. His own bishop refused him the sacrament over it until he repented. Ambrose used that same refusal two years earlier for the opposite end. He shielded a bishop who had incited a mob to burn the synagogue at Callinicum. The bishop never had to pay to rebuild it, and that community got no recourse.

movements.longDescription:
For nearly three centuries the church had been an illegal association. Then, between Constantine's toleration in 313 and Theodosius's legislation at the century's end, it became first protected, then privileged, then the empire's official religion — and had to work out, very fast, what to do with that. Bishops found themselves hearing civil lawsuits, administering public building funds, and travelling to councils at imperial expense; emperors found themselves summoning those councils and expecting the results to hold.

Three answers competed for where final authority over the church now actually lay, and this world's own window closes without settling which was right. Rome traced its authority to Peter; Constantinople claimed rank because it sat beside the throne — a claim the Council of Chalcedon extended in 451 over the protest of Rome's own delegates, at the same council that received, as the last word on Christ's two natures, a letter Leo of Rome had written two years before. Ambrose of Milan staked a third claim entirely: that the emperor stood inside the church, not over it. He said those exact words from inside his own basilica in 386, besieged by the soldiers of a Homoian imperial court that wanted the building for its own worship. He would not give it up, and his congregation stayed inside with him — prepared, an eyewitness later wrote, to die with their bishop. It was there, waiting through the night, that Milan's people first sang hymns the way the Eastern churches did, a custom that, by that eyewitness's account, never stopped and spread to churches across the world. Four years later Ambrose proved the same claim again, against Theodosius himself, refusing the emperor the sacrament until he did public penance for a massacre at Thessalonica.

The hardest evidence against this world is not what was done to it, but what it did. In 366, a disputed election to the bishopric of Rome left the city so violent that a hundred and thirty-seven people were killed in a single day — the same Damasus whose reign then built the city's great martyr shrines. The same sacramental refusal that later humbled an emperor over Thessalonica had already been used once before, two years earlier, for the opposite end: protecting a bishop who had incited a mob to burn a synagogue at Callinicum from having to pay for it, and leaving the burned community no recourse at all.
movements.teaser: Rome, Constantinople, and Milan, 312 to 451 CE — a hunted church became the empire's own law, a bishop held his basilica against imperial soldiers until his people learned to sing through the night, and a disputed election in Rome left a hundred and thirty-seven dead in a single day.
voices: Constantine was the first emperor to protect and endow the church, and the first to summon a general council of its bishops. Why he did it is not settled: Lactantius, writing within a few years, has him dreaming the night before his decisive battle; Eusebius, writing after his death, has him and his whole army seeing a cross of light at midday — the two accounts do not agree, and this world's own sources never resolve which is true.

Eusebius of Caesarea wrote the first history of the church and the most admiring surviving account of Constantine's reign, once quoting the emperor calling himself a bishop of those outside the church — words no one now can be sure Constantine actually meant as a claim of office. He was his patron's panegyrist as much as his historian, and this world reads him knowing both.

Theodosius I's laws made Nicene Christianity the empire's official religion. When his soldiers massacred a crowd at Thessalonica in 390 — seven thousand dead, one historian says — his own bishop closed the altar to him and would not open it again until he had shown repentance.

Ambrose of Milan refused Theodosius the sacrament in 390 until the emperor did public penance for ordering the massacre at Thessalonica — the precedent that an emperor stands inside the church, not over it. Two years before, the same bishop had called the burning of a rival Christian sect's meeting-house at Callinicum worse than heathen, and used his standing with the emperor to spare the men who set a synagogue on fire from ever paying to rebuild it.

Leo of Rome wrote a letter on the two natures of Christ that was read aloud at Chalcedon in 451 and received as settling the question — at the same council that extended Constantinople's rank over the protest of his own delegates.

Justina, mother and dominant influence over the young emperor Valentinian II, held the Homoian faith herself and used her son's court to demand a basilica for it at Milan — backed, when Ambrose refused, by a fine of two hundred pounds of gold on the city's merchants and the imprisonment of tradespeople during Lent. Ambrose's own letter names the emperor as the one who ordered this; the record's own chronology names Justina as its real author. She survives in this world's record only through the hostile account of the bishop who refused her.

Pulcheria, empress from 414, was one of the two people whose convening power actually brought the Council of Chalcedon about in 451. Leo's own letters address her as a real principal, not a courtesy — yet nothing of her own words, on her own terms, survives.

Ordinary believers appear in this record only when they filled a basilica or a riot; not one of their own testimonies survives from this whole century and a half. Nor does the establishment they mostly lived under for decades: the Homoian church held the imperial throne itself under Constantius and Valens, yet almost nothing of its own theology survives except one battered fragment, copied by a fellow believer and partly erased as heresy before it reached us. Its likely author has a name in this record: on the dominant scholarly identification, he is Mercurinus Auxentius — the same Homoian bishop Ambrose's own sermon at the 386 basilica standoff was preached against, arguing his church's case under his predecessor's own name.
movements.legacy:
This is where most of what people mean by "the institutional church" was built: canon law, church courts, dioceses drawn along the empire's own administrative lines, and the assumption that a general council can settle a disputed doctrine for everybody.

The argument it started — where a ruler's authority over the church ends and the church's over the ruler begins — runs on through the medieval investiture disputes, the Reformation's territorial settlements, and every later fight about established churches and their disestablishment.

Its physical inheritance is still standing. The basilica, a Roman public hall rather than a temple, was the form the emperors paid for, and it remains the basic shape of church buildings across Europe. A quieter inheritance survives from the same crisis. Waiting through the siege night in 386, Ambrose's besieged congregation began singing psalms 'after the manner of the Eastern Church' — and Augustine, who was there, says the custom was 'retained from then till now' and copied by 'almost all' congregations 'throughout the rest of the world.'

movements.name: Hieronymian Ascetic-Literary Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Richest written record among the Built & Live worlds — but nearly all of it is one man's own hand. Even the one independent witness against him doesn't agree with itself: the same report of Jerome holding Paula back survives in two languages, and they diverge — a single guarded line in the Greek hardens, in a later Syriac translation, into a flat claim that she died young to escape his 'envy and evil-eyedness.'
movements.floorNote: Nothing here is in question on the Creed. Jerome was a combative defender of Nicene orthodoxy, and the circle's controversies were about asceticism, Origen's legacy, and the right basis for translating Scripture.
movements.relationsSummary: Descends scripturally from Alexandria's Origen, the same legacy this circle later fractured over with Rufinus; Jerome served as Damasus of Rome's own secretary before Bethlehem began.
movements.why: A circle of wealthy Roman women funded and led a community at Bethlehem where Jerome translated the Bible into Latin word by word from the Hebrew - work now known as the Vulgate - though nearly everything known of the women themselves survives only through his own letters.

entry.subtitle: Hieronymian Ascetic-Literary Christianity
entry.tile: Marcella, a Roman widow, had already gathered a circle of ascetic, scripturally serious women on the Aventine hill before Jerome ever arrived in 382. Jerome joined them as their teacher, a caustic, brilliant scholar with a gift for making enemies. In 384, Paula's daughter Blaesilla took up the severe fasting Jerome taught and was dead within four months. A Roman crowd's outrage at her funeral helped drive Jerome from the city in 385. Marcella did not go with him. She stayed in Rome. Clergy still brought her their hardest scripture questions until her own death in 410. Paula sailed east with her daughter Eustochium. She spent a senatorial fortune founding a men's monastery, houses for women, and a pilgrims' hostel at Bethlehem. There, Jerome went on translating the Bible into Latin, book by book from the Hebrew. He had begun the project years earlier in Rome, revising the Latin Gospels against the Greek for Pope Damasus. Scholars later called the whole project the Vulgate. Paula led the women's community until her death in 404, and Eustochium succeeded her, leading it for another decade and more. In 416, an attack tied to the Pelagian dispute set fire to the Bethlehem monasteries. Eustochium and her young niece, also named Paula, sent Rome a report of it. Innocent said fear had kept them from saying more, and what reached him was closer to rumor than complaint. He did not write back to the women. His reply went instead to John, the bishop of Jerusalem, rebuking him for letting the violence happen. Inside that rebuke, he praised the women for one thing: they had never named the man responsible. Not one word any of these women wrote in her own hand survives. Nearly everything known of them comes through Jerome's own letters. Even the claim that clergy sought out Marcella's judgment comes from a memorial Jerome wrote two years after her death. Modern historians think he was partly defending his own reputation there, not only praising hers.

movements.longDescription:
In the early 380s, Jerome arrived in Rome and joined a circle of ascetic, scripturally serious women already meeting around the widow Marcella on the Aventine. Paula, another widow, and her daughters Blaesilla and Eustochium belonged to the same circle, and all of them took Jerome as their teacher — a caustic, brilliant scholar with a gift for making enemies. In 384 Blaesilla took up the severe fasting Jerome taught and was dead within four months; at her funeral a Roman crowd shouted for the monks to be thrown in the Tiber, and Jerome's own consolation letter to the grieving Paula admits he wept writing it.

Within the year Pope Damasus, Jerome's protector, was also dead, and his position in Rome had become impossible. Paula and Eustochium sold their estates, sailed east, and founded monasteries at Bethlehem — a house for men, houses for women, a hostel for pilgrims — with Jerome installed alongside to work. What came out of it was the Vulgate: a Latin Bible rendered book by book from the Hebrew rather than the Greek everyone was used to, against fierce criticism — in one North African town, a congregation nearly rioted when its bishop read the new wording of a single word in Jonah, and Augustine wrote across the sea to warn Jerome what unsettling a people's prayed-over text could cost.

Not one word any of these women wrote in her own hand has survived; what is known of them comes only through Jerome's letters, or through others describing letters now lost. In the community's last years, an attack tied to the Pelagian dispute set fire to the Bethlehem monasteries. Eustochium sent Rome a full account of it, and the pope who answered her praised the community for one thing above all — that they had never named the man behind it.
voices: Jerome was the scholar and translator at the center of it all, and his Latin Bible became the West's standard text for a thousand years. The letters, the memorials, the record of what the women around him said and did — all of it passed through his own hand before it reached us.

Paula was a Roman widow who sold her fortune to fund the move to Bethlehem and then built and governed its monasteries and pilgrim hostel for nineteen years, until her death. The one independent witness to describe her partnership with Jerome, the historian Palladius, says the opposite of Jerome's own account: that Jerome held her back out of jealousy rather than let her surpass him.

Eustochium was consecrated to virginity as a teenage girl in Rome, the dedicatee of one of Jerome's most famous letters, and led the Bethlehem women's community for the rest of her life after her mother's death. Palladius later put the size of her community at fifty women; no other source confirms the number.

Marcella's household on the Aventine was gathering ascetic, scripturally serious women years before Jerome ever reached Rome, and he took his place inside her circle, not the other way around. By his own account, clergy still brought her their hardest scriptural questions long after he had left the city — though the only record of that standing is the letter he wrote about her after she died.

Rufinus of Aquileia had been Jerome's friend since their student days and translated Origen's own work into Latin. Their bitter public quarrel over Origen's legacy split the wider ascetic network in two, and how much of it was really about doctrine rather than about the two men themselves is a question neither side's own account can settle.

Every one of these women demonstrably wrote — Marcella's questions survive by implication in Jerome's dozens of answers, and Eustochium's report of the 416 attack reached a pope who wrote back. None of their own letters were kept. The single text that carries two of their names, a letter to Marcella signed by Paula and Eustochium, is itself judged by scholars to be Jerome's own composition in their names, not theirs.

Fabiola was a Roman noblewoman who left a husband whose vices the whole neighborhood knew, refusing to name them even to defend herself, then remarried while he still lived — a step this circle's own teaching held to be exactly as much a fault for a woman as it would have been for a man. When her second husband died she did public penance in sackcloth before all Rome and was restored to communion; afterward she founded what Jerome calls Rome's first hospital, carrying the sick in from the streets herself, and helped found a hostel for travelers at Portus. She never lived at Bethlehem, and everything known of her — the hospital and its 'first' claim included — rests on the single letter Jerome wrote after her death.
movements.legacy:
The Vulgate became the Bible of the Latin West for over a thousand years — the text medieval theology argued from, the text later translators worked from or against, and the text the Council of Trent declared authentic in 1546. Its rise was not immediate or uncontested: Augustine himself never accepted it, writing after Jerome's death that even though the Jews themselves granted his Hebrew work faithful, 'the churches of Christ judge that no one should be preferred to the authority' of the Seventy translators — and the older Greek-based Latin version he defended stayed in real use for generations afterward.

Its principle mattered as much as its content: Jerome's insistence on going back to the Hebrew rather than resting on the Greek is the ancestor of every later "back to the sources" movement, including the Renaissance and Reformation scholarship that eventually turned on the Vulgate itself.

The circle left a second, quieter pattern too — wealthy women funding, hosting, and directing serious biblical scholarship — which recurs constantly in later Christian history. The caves beneath the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, where tradition places Jerome's study, are still shown to pilgrims.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity (conversion era)
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.sourcing: Periods and transitions better attested than separable inner sub-traditions in this window
movements.relationsSummary: Formed via Cappadocia and Syriac Edessa
movements.why: By its own tradition, Armenia became the first kingdom to make Christianity its official religion, after Gregory the Illuminator — said to have spent years imprisoned in a pit — converted King Trdat and his court. Because Armenian had no script of its own, the church first taught in Greek and Syriac, until the monk Mesrop Mashtots devised an alphabet around 405 so Scripture and liturgy could be rendered into Armenian, a translation still called the Queen of Translations. The story closes at Avarayr in 451, where Armenian nobles died resisting a Persian attempt to impose Zoroastrianism.
movements.longDescription: Armenia's own tradition holds that it was the first kingdom to adopt Christianity as its official religion, when Gregory the Illuminator — imprisoned for years in a pit, by the telling — converted King Trdat and the court around the turn of the fourth century. What followed over the next century and a half is the more remarkable part. An entire national church built from nothing, catechised at first in Greek and Syriac because Armenian had no script of its own, until the monk Mesrop Mashtots devised an alphabet around 405 and the church set about putting the Bible and the liturgy into the people's own language. That translation, made under the catholicos Sahak Partev, is still called by Armenians the Queen of Translations, and it did more than any royal decree to make Christianity Armenian rather than imported. The story of these years ends at the battle of Avarayr in 451, where Armenian nobles fought a Persian attempt to impose Zoroastrianism. A defeat on the field that became the founding story of Armenian religious identity.
movements.teaser: Armenia, c. 314 to 451 — the first kingdom to make Christianity its own, which then had to invent an alphabet before it could read the Bible in its own tongue.
voices: Gregory the Illuminator — the missionary bishop credited with converting the Armenian king and court, and the church's founding patriarch
King Trdat III — the ruler whose conversion made Armenia, by its own tradition, the first Christian kingdom
Mesrop Mashtots — the monk who created the Armenian alphabet around 405 so that Scripture and liturgy could be put into Armenian
Sahak Partev — the catholicos under whom the Armenian Bible was made, still known as the Queen of Translations
Vardan Mamikonian — commander at Avarayr in 451, killed resisting a Persian attempt to impose Zoroastrianism, and remembered ever since as a martyr
movements.legacy: This one did not end. The Armenian Apostolic Church is a living communion of several million people with a worldwide diaspora, still using the alphabet Mashtots made and the liturgical language it created. That alphabet outgrew the church that commissioned it and became the vehicle of all Armenian literature, secular as well as sacred. Armenian manuscript illumination and the carved cross-stones called khachkars grew from the same root. Avarayr is still kept as a feast, and the pattern it set — religious identity as national survival — has shaped Armenian self-understanding ever since.

experienceToday.text: Cathedral and Churches of Echmiatsin, Armenia — the mother cathedral of the Armenian Apostolic Church, begun in the early fourth century, a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: Aksumite Christianity (conversion era)
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.sourcing: Same pattern as Armenia in this window; inscriptions and later narratives
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Alexandria (Frumentius consecrated by Athanasius)
movements.why: Christianity reached the Red Sea kingdom of Aksum by an almost accidental route: a shipwrecked young man from Tyre named Frumentius rose to tutor the royal household, then travelled to Alexandria and returned as the kingdom's first bishop around 330. King Ezana's own conversion is visible on his coinage, which stops carrying the disc and crescent of the old religion and starts carrying the cross — one of the earliest such declarations by any state. The faith took root in Ge'ez, the kingdom's own language, in which Scripture and liturgy were eventually rendered.
movements.longDescription: The kingdom of Aksum, straddling what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, was a Red Sea trading power with its own script and its own coinage when Christianity arrived by an almost accidental route. A young man from Tyre named Frumentius, shipwrecked and taken into the royal household, rose to be tutor and adviser, then travelled to Alexandria to ask Athanasius for a bishop. And was consecrated for the job himself, around 330. King Ezana's conversion followed, and it is legible in the most concrete way imaginable. His coins stop carrying the disc and crescent of the old religion and start carrying the cross, one of the earliest such declarations by any state anywhere. The faith took root in Ge'ez, the kingdom's own language, in which Scripture and liturgy were eventually rendered, and Frumentius's consecration bound the Ethiopian church to the Egyptian one for the next sixteen centuries. What survives from these years is mostly inscriptions, coinage, and later chronicles rather than the everyday voices of ordinary believers.
movements.teaser: Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, c. 330 to 451 — a Red Sea kingdom whose conversion you can read on its own coinage, where the crescent gives way to the cross.
voices: Frumentius — a shipwrecked traveller from Tyre who became tutor at the Aksumite court and then its first bishop, remembered in Ethiopia as Abba Salama
King Ezana — the ruler whose conversion is recorded in his own inscriptions and on his coins, which change from the disc and crescent to the cross
Athanasius of Alexandria — who consecrated Frumentius, and so began the long link between the Egyptian and Ethiopian churches
movements.legacy: This became, and remains, one of the great ancient churches of the world: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church together count tens of millions of members. It carried down a whole distinctive Christian culture — Ge'ez as a scriptural and liturgical language, a broader Old Testament canon than any other church's, drums and sistra and liturgical dance in worship, and, centuries later, the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. The link Frumentius's consecration made with Alexandria held for roughly sixteen centuries, until the Ethiopian church received a patriarch of its own in the twentieth.

experienceToday.text: Aksum, Ethiopia — the ancient capital's stelae field, royal tombs, and Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion, a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: Persian Church of the East (early)
movements.informalName: The Early Persian Church of the East
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.sourcing: Real and distinct; institutional self-identity matures after this window
movements.floorNote: The label "Nestorian" came from this church's rivals, not from itself — we judged what it actually taught from its own surviving texts, not the label its opponents pinned on it.
movements.relationsSummary: Direct heir of the Syriac tradition's Nisibis side
movements.why: This church lived east of the Roman frontier, in the Persian Empire, and Constantine's conversion of Rome made its position worse rather than better, since it let the Persian court treat Christians as a Roman foothold. Under Shapur II, the catholicos Shemon bar Sabbae was executed in the 340s after refusing to collect a punitive tax on Christians to help fund the war against Rome. When toleration eventually came, a synod at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410 gave the church a legal structure and a recognized head, and a further synod in 424 declared its bishops answerable to no authority outside Persia.
movements.longDescription: East of the Roman frontier, in the Persian Empire, were Christian communities that had never lived under a Christian emperor and never would. And Constantine's conversion made their position worse rather than better, since it let the Sassanian court read them as a Roman fifth column. The long persecution under Shapur II from about 340 killed clergy and laity in numbers this church remembered in a whole literature of martyr acts, its own head among them. The catholicos Shemon bar Sabbae was executed in the 340s after refusing to collect a punitive double tax from Christians to fund the war against Rome. When toleration eventually came, the church organized itself deliberately. A synod at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410 gave it a legal structure and a recognized head, and a further synod in 424 declared that its bishops would answer to no authority outside Persia. It worshipped in Syriac, thought in the exegetical idiom it shared with Edessa and Antioch, and was already becoming the church that would carry Christianity along the trade roads to India, Central Asia, and China.
movements.teaser: Persian Mesopotamia, c. 300 to 451 — a church that never had a Christian emperor of its own, and was persecuted at home for the conversion of the one across the border.
voices: Shemon bar Sabbae — catholicos executed in the 340s after refusing to collect a punitive tax on his own people for Persia's war with Rome
Aphrahat, called the Persian Sage — whose Demonstrations, written in the 330s and 340s, are the earliest substantial witness to this church's own thinking
Marutha of Maypherqat — bishop and envoy, whose diplomacy helped make the synod of 410 possible
Isaac — the catholicos who presided at that synod, which gave the church its legal shape under Persian rule
movements.legacy: This church did not disappear. It became the Church of the East, which for centuries had the widest geographical reach of any Christian body on earth, with bishops in India, Central Asia, and Tang-dynasty China. Its descendants are living communities today — the Assyrian Church of the East and the Ancient Church of the East, along with the Chaldean Catholic Church and the Syro-Malabar Church of Kerala. And its liturgy, including the ancient eucharistic prayer of Addai and Mari, is still in use. Its Syriac scholarship also became a bridge for learning far beyond the church. Translators from this world put Greek philosophy and medicine into Syriac and then Arabic, which is much of how that inheritance reached the medieval world.

movements.name: Antiochene Exegetical Christianity (Chrysostom-centered)
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Rich ordinary-lay ethical-formation material
movements.relationsSummary: Historical-literal exegesis vs. Alexandria's allegory; Theodore of Mopsuestia flag on record
movements.why: Where Alexandria's teachers hunted for a hidden spiritual sense beneath Scripture, Antioch's insisted on what the words actually said, and pressed hard on what that demanded of their listeners. John Chrysostom preached that way through the 380s and 390s to Antioch's tradesmen, householders, and slaves — on money, anger, and how they treated their own servants — and in 387, after crowds smashed the imperial statues, preached his sermons On the Statues to a city waiting to learn whether it would be destroyed in reprisal. Taken to Constantinople in 397 to preach the same way to the imperial court, he died in exile a decade later.
movements.longDescription: Antioch was one of the largest cities of the Roman East, and the Christianity that grew there developed a distinctive habit of reading. Where Alexandria hunted for the hidden spiritual sense beneath the text, Antioch's teachers insisted on what the words actually said in their own historical setting — and then pressed hard on what that demanded of the people in front of them. John Chrysostom, trained in rhetoric by the pagan orator Libanius and in Scripture by Diodore of Tarsus, preached in Antioch through the 380s and 390s to congregations of tradesmen, householders, and slaves: on money, on anger, on how you treat your servants, on the theatre and the racetrack, on almsgiving as a matter of justice rather than generosity. In 387, after the city's crowds smashed the imperial statues and Antioch waited to learn whether it would be destroyed in reprisal, he preached the sermons On the Statues to a terrified population. And the reason hundreds of his sermons survive at all is largely that people wanted to hear them again. At the end of 397 he was taken to Constantinople and made its archbishop, where he preached the same way to the imperial court, which is roughly why he died in exile in 407.
movements.teaser: Antioch, c. 350 to 430 — a school of preachers who refused to allegorize the hard sayings away, and told a city of shopkeepers and slaves exactly what the plain text asked of them.
voices: John Chrysostom — the preacher whose sermons on money, anger, and everyday cruelty earned him, from later generations, the name "golden-mouthed"
Diodore of Tarsus — his teacher, and the founder of the Antiochene habit of reading Scripture in its historical sense
Theodore of Mopsuestia — fellow student and the school's most systematic interpreter, whose Christology was condemned long after his death
Theodoret of Cyrrhus — bishop, historian, and commentator, the last great voice of the Antiochene reading
Libanius — the pagan rhetorician who trained Chrysostom, and a reminder that this Christianity was formed inside a still-classical education
movements.legacy: Chrysostom's sermons never stopped being read. They were quarried for medieval preaching, printed early and often in the Reformation era — Reformed and Lutheran preachers alike claimed him as an ancestor of expository preaching. And the eucharistic liturgy that carries his name is still the ordinary Sunday rite of the Eastern Orthodox churches. The Antiochene way of reading, insisting that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it, is the ancestor of the historical-grammatical method that later Western biblical scholarship made standard. The school's own fate was harsher. Theodore of Mopsuestia was condemned at Constantinople in 553, more than a century after his death, and much of his work survives only in Syriac translation preserved by the Church of the East.

experienceToday.text: The Patriarchal Church of St George, Istanbul — seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, where the relics of John Chrysostom rest after their return from Rome in 2004

movements.name: Cyrilline / Miaphysite Egyptian Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.floorNote: Rejection of Chalcedon's formula, not of the Creed's content
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of Alexandria + Desert
movements.why: When the Council of Chalcedon defined Christ as one person 'in two natures' in 451, the Egyptian church largely refused the wording, holding instead to Cyril of Alexandria's own formula against Nestorius: one incarnate nature of the Word, a single united reality rather than two things described side by side. The council deposed the Alexandrian patriarch Dioscorus, and Egypt was left with two rival hierarchies — most Egyptian Christians worshipping increasingly in Coptic rather than Greek.
movements.longDescription: When the Council of Chalcedon met in 451 and defined Christ as one person "in two natures," the Egyptian church largely refused the wording. Not because it thought Christ any less than fully God or fully human, but because it held to the formula Cyril of Alexandria had used against Nestorius twenty years earlier: one incarnate nature of the Word, a single united reality rather than two things described side by side. To Egyptian ears Chalcedon's language sounded like pulling Christ apart again; to Chalcedon's supporters, the Egyptian refusal sounded like collapsing his humanity. The council deposed the Alexandrian patriarch Dioscorus, imperial authority backed the Chalcedonian side, and Egypt was left with two rival hierarchies — one favoured by Constantinople, and one that most Egyptian Christians actually followed, worshipping increasingly in Coptic rather than Greek. Out of that separation came the Coptic Orthodox Church and the wider family of churches that made the same refusal.
movements.teaser: Egypt, from 451 — a church that would not say "in two natures," and became a separate communion rather than give up the words it had been taught to fight for.
voices: Cyril of Alexandria — whose formula for the unity of Christ, framed against Nestorius at Ephesus in 431, this tradition took as its standard
Dioscorus of Alexandria — his successor, deposed at Chalcedon in 451, and honoured by the Coptic Church as a confessor
Timothy Aelurus — elected patriarch by those who rejected Chalcedon, and among the first to argue the case at length
Severus of Antioch — the theologian, a generation later, who gave this position its most careful and lasting statement
movements.legacy: This is a living communion, not a closed chapter: the Coptic Orthodox Church of Egypt, together with the Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, Eritrean, and Indian Orthodox churches, forms the Oriental Orthodox family of tens of millions of Christians today. It preserved Coptic — the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language — as a liturgical tongue, along with a distinctive iconography, a long fasting calendar, and a monastic life descended unbroken from the desert. Modern dialogue has largely concluded that the fifth-century split was as much about vocabulary as about belief: a series of joint declarations from the 1970s onward record Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic representatives agreeing that they confess the same faith in Christ in different words.

experienceToday.text: The Hanging Church, Coptic Cairo — Saint Virgin Mary's Coptic Orthodox Church, built over a gate of the Roman fortress of Babylon and still in use

movements.name: Jerusalem Liturgical-Pilgrimage Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Strong - Egeria's eyewitness account plus unusually corroborating archaeology
movements.relationsSummary: Comparison-point for the Bethlehem Circle's distinctiveness on record
movements.why: Once Constantine's builders raised a great church complex over what they took to be the tomb of Christ in the 330s, Jerusalem's clergy built a liturgy out of commemorating the gospel on the actual day and at the actual place it happened — a Palm Sunday procession down the Mount of Olives with branches in hand, the veneration of the Cross on Good Friday, an all-night vigil at the tomb at Easter. A western pilgrim named Egeria kept a detailed diary in the early 380s recording exactly what was done and when, a manuscript lost for centuries and rediscovered in an Italian library in 1884.
movements.longDescription: Once Constantine's builders uncovered what they took to be the tomb of Christ and raised a great church complex over it in the 330s, Jerusalem became something no other city was. A place where the events of the gospel could be commemorated on the day and at the spot they were believed to have happened. Its clergy built a liturgy out of exactly that — Palm Sunday as an actual procession down the Mount of Olives with branches in hand, the veneration of the Cross on Good Friday, an all-night vigil at the tomb at Easter. And the crowds who came to see it wrote home about what they saw. One of those visitors, a woman from the Latin west named Egeria, kept a detailed travel diary in the early 380s recording precisely what was done and when. The manuscript disappeared for centuries and was rediscovered in an Italian library in 1884, and it remains the single most valuable eyewitness account of early Christian worship anywhere. What makes this community hard to pin down is the very thing that made it distinctive. It was always part settled and part passing through — resident clergy and monks, local Christians, and a constant flow of pilgrims from every corner of the Christian world.
movements.teaser: Jerusalem, c. 325 to 450 — the one city where the gospel could be commemorated on the very day and at the very spot, and where a travelling woman wrote down exactly how it was done.
voices: Cyril of Jerusalem — bishop through much of this period, whose catechetical lectures to baptismal candidates survive nearly complete
Egeria — a western pilgrim whose diary of the early 380s is the fullest surviving eyewitness account of early Christian worship
Helena — Constantine's mother, whose visit in the 320s is bound up with the tradition of the finding of the Cross and the building of the holy sites
Juvenal — the bishop who secured Jerusalem's rank as a patriarchate at Chalcedon in 451
Melania the Elder — a Roman aristocrat who founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives and helped make the city a centre of Latin ascetic life
movements.legacy: Jerusalem's calendar became everyone's calendar. Keeping Holy Week as a sequence of days, each commemorating a specific event — the Palm Sunday procession, Maundy Thursday, the Good Friday veneration of the Cross, the Easter vigil — spread west from here, and it is still how most of the Christian world keeps Easter. So did the idea of pilgrimage itself as a Christian practice, and with it the habit of building churches that copy the shape of Jerusalem's holy places. Cyril's lectures remain a primary source for how baptism and communion were explained to newcomers in the fourth century, and Egeria's diary is read wherever early liturgy is studied.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem — the complex first consecrated in 335 over the sites of the crucifixion and the tomb, still shared between several churches and open to pilgrims

movements.name: Ambrosian Milan (standalone)
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Thin alone - substantially one bishop's confrontations
movements.relationsSummary: Folded into the Imperial-Juridical tradition as one of its three phases
movements.why: In 374 the people of Milan acclaimed as their bishop a provincial governor named Ambrose who had not yet even been baptized; he was baptized and consecrated within the week. In 386 he refused to hand a basilica over to the Empress Justina's court, and his congregation occupied the building for days, singing hymns he wrote to keep their spirits up; four years later he required the emperor Theodosius to do public penance for a massacre at Thessalonica before receiving him back to the sacrament.
movements.longDescription: Milan, not Rome, was the western emperors' working capital in the late fourth century, and in 374 its people acclaimed as their bishop a provincial governor named Ambrose who had not yet even been baptized. He was baptized and consecrated within a week, and spent the next twenty-three years working out — mostly in public confrontations — what a bishop could say to power. He refused to hand a basilica over to the Empress Justina's court in 386, and his congregation occupied the building for days, singing hymns he wrote to keep their spirits up. In 390 he required the emperor Theodosius to do public penance for a massacre of civilians at Thessalonica. He was also a preacher who opened up Scripture for a restless African rhetorician sitting in his congregation — Augustine, whom Ambrose baptized at Easter in 387. And the city he shaped still carries his stamp in the rite that bears his name.
movements.teaser: Milan, 374 to 397 — an unbaptized governor acclaimed bishop by a crowd, who spent the rest of his life teaching emperors where their authority stopped.
voices: Ambrose — the governor turned bishop, hymn-writer, and the first churchman to make an emperor do public penance
Augustine of Hippo — who came to Milan as a professor of rhetoric, heard Ambrose preach, and was baptized by him at Easter 387
Monica — Augustine's mother, part of the Milanese congregation, whose deference to Ambrose's pastoral advice her son recorded
Empress Justina — regent for the young Valentinian II, and Ambrose's opponent in the struggle over the city's basilicas
Theodosius I — the emperor who submitted to Ambrose's demand for public penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390
movements.legacy: Milan still keeps the Ambrosian Rite. Its own calendar, chant, and order of worship, distinct from the Roman Rite used almost everywhere else in the Latin church, and the largest surviving non-Roman Western rite. Hymns attributed to Ambrose are still sung, and the congregational hymn-singing he made famous during the basilica occupation had a very long afterlife. His confrontation with Theodosius became a standing precedent, cited for more than a millennium, that a Christian ruler stands under the church's discipline rather than above it. And his preaching, by Augustine's own account, is a large part of the reason the West got Augustine at all. The church he founded in the 380s still stands on its site in Milan — rebuilt in Romanesque form eight centuries later — with his remains beneath its altar.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, Milan — the church Ambrose commissioned in 379-386, where his remains still lie

movements.name: The Church of Aquileia
movements.region: Aquileia and Concordia, at the head of the Adriatic
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: One work, and an unusually valuable one. Rufinus' Commentary on the Apostles' Creed - about twenty thousand words - survives, and it expounds the baptismal creed of Aquileia clause by clause while noting where that creed differs from Rome's. Nothing else from the Aquileian church survives directly: Chromatius' sermons are lost, Fortunatianus' gospel commentary was lost until 2012, and the acts of the Council of Aquileia in 381 arrive through Ambrose's own record rather than this church's own.
movements.relationsSummary: Adjacent to ambrosian-milan-standalone in region and generation, and to hieronymian-ascetic-literary in personnel - Jerome and Rufinus were formed here together and quarrelled elsewhere. Its transmission relation to alexandria-catechetical is the consequential one: Rufinus is why Origen survives in Latin at all.
movements.why: Around 404, Rufinus of Concordia sat down in his home church at Aquileia and wrote out the creed used there at baptism, explaining it line by line for people about to say it — and noted, a little pointedly, that this creed already contained the clause about Christ's descent into hell, which Rome's did not. It is the earliest evidence that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font. Rufinus had belonged to a circle of young ascetics gathered at Aquileia in the 370s that also included Jerome, before their friendship broke apart in the bitterest literary quarrel the Latin church produced.
movements.longDescription: Aquileia stood where the roads from Italy, the Danube and the Balkans met at the head of the Adriatic, and in the fourth century it was among the largest cities of the empire and among the more consequential churches of the West; its basilica floor mosaics from the 310s are still there. In the 370s a group of young ascetics gathered in the city whom Jerome afterwards remembered as a chorus of the blessed. He was one of them. So was Rufinus of Concordia, and the friendship between those two ended thirty years later in the bitterest literary quarrel the Latin church produced. In 381 Ambrose came up from Milan and presided over a council at Aquileia that deposed the last two Homoian bishops of the Danube provinces. And around 404 Rufinus, home in Italy after decades in Egypt and Palestine, sat down and wrote out the creed his own church used at baptism, explaining it line by line for people about to say it. That is why anyone knows that the Aquileian creed called the Father invisible and impassible where Rome's did not, and that it already contained the clause about the descent into hell, which Rufinus points out - a little pointedly - that the Roman creed does not have. It is the earliest evidence that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
movements.teaser: A commentary written to explain the local baptismal creed is the only reason anyone knows the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
voices: Rufinus of Concordia - monk at Aquileia, translator of Origen into Latin, and the man who wrote his home church's creed down
Chromatius - bishop from 388, patron of both Rufinus' and Jerome's translation work, whose own sermons are not in this corpus
Fortunatianus - bishop in the 340s and 350s, author of the earliest Latin gospel commentary, lost until a manuscript was identified in 2012
Jerome - who spent his twenties here among what he called a chorus of the blessed, and later wrote against the man he had shared it with
Ambrose of Milan - who came up the road in 381 to preside over the council that finished the Homoian bishops of Illyricum
movements.legacy: The Apostles' Creed as the Latin West came to recite it is not the Roman text alone. The descent into hell, which every later version carries, is first attested here - Rufinus notes that the Roman creed lacks it - and it entered the received Western text from the provincial creeds rather than from Rome. Rufinus' commentary is also the earliest systematic exposition of a creed in Latin and the model for the genre. And his translations - Origen, Eusebius, the Clementine Recognitions, Basil, the Sentences of Sextus - are the channel through which a great deal of Greek Christianity reached the Latin Middle Ages, often as the only text that survives.

movements.name: The Gallic Nicene Episcopate
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Strong and concentrated. Hilary's De Trinitate (190,000 words), De Synodis and Homilies on Psalms all survive, and Sulpitius Severus' Sacred History gives the Gallic narrative from inside. What is thin is anyone but Hilary: the bishops he wrote to are known mostly through him and through the conciliar record.
movements.relationsSummary: The other half of fourth-century Gaul, and deliberately separate from gallic-monastic-ascetic-christianity: an episcopate resisting an imperial creed, not a monastery. The two touch at one point that matters - Martin of Tours was Hilary's disciple, and the monastic world grows out of the ground this one defended.
movements.why: In 356 the emperor Constantius II exiled Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, to Phrygia for refusing to condemn Athanasius — a miscalculation, since Hilary spent his exile learning the eastern debates from the inside and wrote home a patient account of what the eastern creeds actually said. He returned with De Trinitate, a massive Latin answer to Arianism, and when he came home around 360 the Gallic church repudiated the Homoian creed that had been imposed at Ariminum. He had already ordained a young ex-soldier, Martin, who was living as a monk at Ligugé.
movements.longDescription: In 356 the emperor Constantius II, who wanted a single creed his bishops would all sign, exiled the bishop of Poitiers to Phrygia for refusing to condemn Athanasius. It was a miscalculation. Hilary spent four years in the Greek-speaking East learning the eastern debates from the inside, and wrote back to the Gallic bishops to explain them - De Synodis, a patient account of what the eastern creeds actually said and where they could and could not be met. He also wrote De Trinitate, a massive Latin answer to Arianism running to some 190,000 words. When he was allowed home around 360, the Gallic church repudiated the Homoian creed that had been imposed at Ariminum, at a council in Paris. Hilary went on to attack Auxentius, the Homoian bishop of Milan, with less success. He died in 367. The province he left behind was securely Nicene, Latin, and in possession of a theological vocabulary it had not had before - and a young ex-soldier named Martin, whom Hilary had ordained, was already living as a monk at Ligugé.
movements.teaser: An emperor exiled the bishop of Poitiers to shut him up, and got back the longest anti-Arian book in Latin and a province that would not sign his creed.
voices: Hilary of Poitiers - exiled for refusing to condemn Athanasius, and the West's principal theologian of the Trinity before Augustine
Constantius II - the emperor who wanted one creed signed by everyone, and whose exile of Hilary produced the opposite of what he intended
Auxentius of Milan - the Homoian bishop Hilary attacked and failed to dislodge
Sulpitius Severus - whose Sacred History narrates the Gallic side of the Arian crisis
Martin of Tours - Hilary's disciple, whom he ordained, and the bridge to the monastic Gaul that follows
movements.legacy: Hilary's De Trinitate gave Latin theology its first full-scale treatment of the doctrine, and Augustine, who did the second, worked with it in view. The Gallic repudiation of Ariminum at Paris also mattered practically: it kept the western provinces out of the Homoian settlement that the Gothic kingdoms would later inherit, so that the Frankish conversion two centuries on was to a Nicene church rather than an Arian one. And Hilary ordained Martin, which makes this episcopate the immediate ancestor of the monastic Gaul that grew up beside it.

movements.name: Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich in volume — Cassian's Institutes and Conferences, Vincent's Commonitory, and a body of writing about Martin all survive — but uneven in kind: the Marseilles and Lérins material is the school's own teaching, while almost everything about Martin comes through one admirer's hagiography. It is thinner than that volume suggests on the daily life of the community itself: no woman's own words survive from either house, and the surviving edition of Cassian has had its sexual-discipline material removed by a later editor.
movements.relationsSummary: Descended from Egyptian desert monasticism through Cassian, who had lived among the Egyptian monks before founding his houses at Marseilles; the seedbed of the Merovingian Gallic church that follows it, and - through Lérins and Tours - of Irish monasticism.
movements.why: Martin of Tours, a soldier who asked to leave the army to serve Christ unarmed, became a bishop who never stopped living like a monk; two generations later, monks at Lerins and Marseilles carried the wisdom of the Egyptian desert into a colder climate and a different church.

entry.subtitle: Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity
entry.tile: This tradition grew up around bishops who never stopped living as monks, and around wisdom first learned in the deserts of Egypt. Its first figure, Martin, was a Roman soldier. Almost everything we know of him comes from one admirer's writing — Sulpitius Severus was not present for the events he describes. Martin told Caesar that he was now a soldier of Christ, and asked to leave the army; he even offered to walk unarmed toward the enemy line. By about 360, he had gathered a few companions near Poitiers. Some years later, the people of Tours seized him and made him their bishop. He kept living as a monk outside the city walls. Two generations later, Honoratus founded a monastery on the island of Lérins, off the Mediterranean coast. He became bishop of Arles himself, and other monks from the island followed him into the office, at Arles and at Riez. Around the same years, John Cassian founded two houses at Marseilles. He had spent years among the fathers of Egypt. He wrote down what he had learned there, adapting their customs to a colder climate and a different church. At Lérins, the monk Vincent wrote a rule for telling real growth in the faith from a corruption dressed up as one. Augustine had written to a monastery in North Africa about grace and human effort. Word of his treatise reached Gaul. It was the monks of Marseilles, not Martin's own Tours, who pushed back hardest. Augustine then wrote two more treatises answering them directly. Through the southern houses ran one argument, never fully settled: how much of a monk's progress comes from God's own gift, and how much from his own effort. The story ends around the year 450, with that question still open.
