sources.note: Founder-generation interior voice: aphoristic self-scrutiny, no system.

sources.work: Guigo I, Consuetudines Cartusiae (Customs, c. 1127)
sources.note: The order's foundational legislation: cell, silence, and capped community size. Available only in Latin and French (Sources Chretiennes 313); no complete English translation exists.

sources.work: Adam of Eynsham, Magna Vita Sancti Hugonis (Life of Hugh of Lincoln) (trans. Douie & Farmer, Oxford Medieval Texts, 2 vols)
sources.note: Lived Carthusian texture through the order's one very public member, written by his own chaplain.

sources.work: Gordon Mursell, The Theology of the Carthusian Life in the Writings of St. Bruno and Guigo I (Analecta Cartusiana 127, 1988)
sources.note: The thinness of English scholarship mirrors the order's deliberate silence.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 'Monastic and religious orders, c.1100-c.1350' (B. P. McGuire)

movements.longDescription: In 1084 Bruno of Cologne, who had been a leading master of the schools at Reims, gave up his career, took six companions into a high, hard valley in the Alps above Grenoble, and built a life with almost nothing in it: each man in his own cell with a small garden, meeting the others only for the night office, part of the Mass, and a weekly walk. Guigo I, the fifth prior, wrote the customs down around 1127 — cell, silence, and a strict cap on how many could live in any one house — and Guigo II's Ladder of Monks, a short account of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God, became one of the most widely used descriptions of prayer in the Western church. Deliberately, the order produced almost no public figures. The one great exception was Hugh, prior of the English charterhouse at Witham and then bishop of Lincoln, whose chaplain wrote him up in unusual detail. The Grande Chartreuse is still a working monastery, and the order has kept substantially the same shape ever since. A traditional saying has it that the Carthusians were never reformed because they were never deformed.
movements.teaser: The Alps above Grenoble, from 1084 onward — hermits who built a monastery out of separate cells and near-total silence, then kept it almost unchanged for nine hundred years.
voices: Bruno of Cologne — master of the schools at Reims, who gave up his career to found the first charterhouse in 1084
Guigo I — fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, who wrote down the order's customs and left a book of unsparing private meditations
Guigo II — author of The Ladder of Monks, the short treatise on reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation that became the West's standard map of prayer
Hugh of Lincoln — the order's one very public member, a Carthusian prior who became an English bishop and was written up at length by his own chaplain
movements.legacy: The order is still living and still small, which is exactly what it intended. Its longest reach is Guigo II's Ladder of Monks: the four-step pattern of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God passed into the general devotional vocabulary of the West and is still taught today, often by people who have never heard of the Carthusians. The charterhouse plan — a great cloister ringed by individual cells and gardens — became a recognisable building type across Europe, and several former charterhouses now serve as museums and galleries. The liqueur the monks of the Grande Chartreuse still make has kept the name in ordinary circulation long after most people forgot what it belonged to.

experienceToday.text: Saint-Pierre-de-Chartreuse, France — the Museum of the Grande Chartreuse at La Correrie, two kilometres below the monastery itself, which remains closed to visitors

movements.name: Canons Regular / Victorine School
movements.informalName: The Canons Regular and the Victorines
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — rich textually, moderate in community texture, with its distinctiveness from the Cistercian and university traditions named as the real test it would have to pass. Both dates were corrected at the Freeze from numbers that matched nothing to 1108 and 1246, and the Premonstratensians were routed inside this canons-regular family rather than given their own entry.
movements.sourcing: Rich textually; community texture moderate
movements.relationsSummary: Bridge between cloister and the schools; the Premonstratensians (Norbert’s reformed canons, 1120/21) ride inside this canons-regular family’s story
movements.why: Canons regular lived under a rule like monks but kept working in the world — serving churches, running hospitals, teaching — and the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris became the movement's greatest school after William of Champeaux withdrew there in 1108. Hugh of St Victor argued that every art and science, rightly ordered, leads toward wisdom, while Richard of St Victor mapped the stages of contemplation more carefully than anyone before him in the Latin West. Adam of St Victor supplied the abbey's own sung liturgy, the sequences that outlasted the school itself.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1108 (William of Champeaux settles at Saint-Victor — the school's actual beginning; the old 1100 matched nothing); end 1246 (death of Thomas Gallus, last major Victorine thinker; alt 1173 on record) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Hugh of St Victor, Didascalicon (trans. Jerome Taylor, Columbia, 1961; newer trans. Harkins in Victorine Texts in Translation)
sources.note: The school's program: all the arts ordered to wisdom.

sources.work: Richard of St Victor, The Twelve Patriarchs, The Mystical Ark, Book Three of the Trinity (trans. Grover Zinn, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1979)
sources.note: Contemplative theology built on communal reading.

sources.work: Liber ordinis Sancti Victoris (the abbey's customary)
sources.note: The abbey's customary: offices, discipline, and hospitality set out in daily detail. Available only in Latin (CCCM 61), with no English translation.

sources.work: Victorine Texts in Translation (ed. Feiss et al., New City Press/Brepols, multi-volume)
sources.note: Modern annotated corpus incl. Hugh on love and formation and Adam of St Victor's liturgical sequences - the school's sung, ordinary face.

sources.work: Paul Rorem, Hugh of Saint Victor (OUP, 2009)
sources.note: Standard one-volume entry to the school.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 (McGuire); cf. ch. 5 'The theological framework' (L. Smith)

movements.longDescription: Canons regular were clergy who lived in community under a rule — usually the Rule of St Augustine. But who, unlike monks, kept working in the world: serving churches, running hospitals, teaching. The most influential of their houses was the abbey of Saint-Victor on the left bank of Paris, where the master William of Champeaux withdrew from the schools in 1108 and where his successors built a way of learning that refused to choose between the classroom and the cloister. Hugh of St Victor argued in the Didascalicon that every art and science, rightly ordered, leads toward wisdom; Richard of St Victor mapped the stages of contemplation more carefully than anyone in the Latin West had yet done. Adam of St Victor wrote the sequences the abbey sang. The school's line ran down to Thomas Gallus, who died in 1246, and the abbey itself no longer stands.
movements.teaser: Paris and the abbey of Saint-Victor, 1108 to 1246 — clergy under a rule who would not choose between the cloister and the classroom, and worked out a theology of contemplation in the middle of a university town.
voices: William of Champeaux — the Paris master who withdrew to Saint-Victor in 1108 and began the school there
Hugh of St Victor — the school's greatest teacher, whose Didascalicon ordered all learning toward wisdom
Richard of St Victor — his successor, author of the West's most careful account of the stages of contemplation
Adam of St Victor — poet of the liturgical sequences the abbey sang, the school's ordinary, singing face
Norbert of Xanten — founder in 1120 of Prémontré, the reformed canons who carried this way of life across northern Europe
Thomas Gallus — the last major Victorine thinker, who died in 1246
movements.legacy: The abbey is gone, but the way of life is not: canons regular still exist, and Norbert's Premonstratensians remain an order today. The Victorines' real bequest was intellectual. Hugh's insistence that the arts and sciences belong inside the search for God, and Richard's stage-by-stage analysis of contemplation, were read and quarried by nearly everyone who wrote on prayer in the later Middle Ages — Bonaventure most of all. And the abbey's sequences stayed in the liturgy long after the school that composed them had gone quiet.

movements.name: The Franciscan Movement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), immense in scale, with its famous layered-hagiography problem carried rather than resolved — the tier system exists for exactly that. Its lay third order was routed inside its own story at the Freeze, and the shape of its Era 6 receiver, which carries only the Fraticelli splinter and the Observant reform, was flagged forward as an open gap.
movements.sourcing: Rich, with a famous layered-hagiography problem — sources built up over time in overlapping layers of legend and memory.
movements.relationsSummary: Sibling-rival of the Dominicans; parent of Observants and Spirituals; its lay third order (Order of Penance, 1221) rides inside its own story
movements.why: Francis of Assisi gave away a merchant's inheritance to preach and care for lepers in the streets of Italy's fast-growing towns, and by 1209 the friars who joined him owned nothing, begged, and worked rather than withdrawing behind monastery walls. Clare of Assisi built the movement's women's branch and wrote the first monastic rule known to have been composed by a woman. Within a generation of Francis's death in 1226 the order was fighting bitterly over how literally his poverty had been meant, a quarrel serious enough that his own brothers rewrote his life story more than once.

sources.work: Francis's own writings (Testament, both Rules, Canticle of the Creatures, letters), in Francis of Assisi: Early Documents, vol. 1 (ed. Armstrong, Hellmann & Short, 1999; free online)
sources.note: The founder's undisputed first-person layer, kept distinct from all hagiography.

sources.work: The layered hagiography: Francis of Assisi: Early Documents, vols. 1-3 (1999-2001) - Celano's Lives, Legend of the Three Companions, Assisi Compilation, Bonaventure
sources.note: Printed in datable layers, with a scholarly apparatus that lets readers trace how the sources built up over time.

sources.work: Clare of Assisi: Early Documents (ed. Regis Armstrong, rev. 2006)
sources.note: Clare's letters to Agnes of Prague and her Form of Life (the first monastic rule written by a woman) - the movement's female branch in its own voice.

sources.work: Scripta Leonis, Rufini et Angeli (writings of Brother Leo and companions; ed./trans. Rosalind Brooke, Oxford Medieval Texts, 1970)
sources.note: The companions' counter-memory against the official portrait; central evidence in the poverty dispute.

sources.work: Augustine Thompson, Francis of Assisi: A New Biography (Cornell, 2012)
sources.note: Deliberately source-critical, layer by layer.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 3 'Religious poverty and the search for perfection' (Kienzle); cf. ch. 4 (McGuire)

movements.longDescription: Francis of Assisi was a cloth merchant's son who gave away his inheritance, took the gospel's instructions to the apostles as a literal rule of life, and began preaching and caring for lepers in the towns of central Italy. By 1209 others had joined him and Pope Innocent III gave the group verbal approval. What made the movement new was that it did not withdraw behind walls — the friars owned nothing, begged, worked, and preached in the streets of the fast-growing commercial towns. Clare of Assisi built the movement's women's branch and wrote her own Form of Life, the first monastic rule known to have been composed by a woman, and a third order let married lay people live a version of the same discipline without leaving ordinary life. Within a generation of Francis's death in 1226 the order was quarrelling bitterly over how literally his poverty had been meant. A fight that eventually split it into Spirituals and Conventuals, and that also produced repeated rewritings of his own life story, by his own brothers, within living memory of him.
movements.teaser: Assisi and then most of the known world, from 1209 — a merchant's son who took the gospel's poverty literally, and an order that began arguing about what he meant almost before he was buried.
voices: Francis of Assisi — the founder, whose Testament, Rules and Canticle of the Creatures survive in his own words
Clare of Assisi — founder of the movement's women's branch and author of the first monastic rule known to be written by a woman
Brother Leo — Francis's companion and secretary, whose recollections preserve a counter-memory to the order's official portrait
Thomas of Celano — the first biographer, commissioned to write Francis's life and then commissioned to write it again
Bonaventure — minister general and theologian, whose authorized life of Francis was meant to settle the quarrel over him
movements.legacy: The Franciscans are still one of the largest religious families in the world, in several branches, with a lay third order alongside them. Beyond the order, the movement changed the ordinary furniture of Western devotion: the Christmas crib, which Francis is credited with staging at Greccio in 1223. The Stations of the Cross, spread through Europe largely by Franciscans; an affectionate attention to Christ's humanity and to the poor; and a strand of Christian language about creation — the Canticle of the Creatures, with its brother sun and sister moon. That is quoted constantly to this day. The basilica raised over Francis's tomb at Assisi carries some of the most famous fresco cycles in European art.

experienceToday.text: Assisi, Italy — the Basilica of Saint Francis, built over his tomb from 1228 and frescoed by Cimabue, Giotto and Simone Martini

movements.name: The Dominican Order
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base — constitutions, formation treatises, and sworn canonization-inquest testimonies, which give it an unusually direct evidentiary footing for the era.
movements.sourcing: Rich: constitutions, canonization-inquest sworn testimonies, formation treatises
movements.relationsSummary: Sibling-rival of the Franciscans; parent of the German convent-mysticism tradition
movements.why: Dominic de Guzmán, a Spanish cathedral canon, concluded that the church was losing arguments with dissenters because its preachers travelled with baggage while their opponents walked and fasted — so he built an order backwards from that single purpose: friars trained in theology, poor and mobile, planted immediately in the new universities at Paris and Bologna. Its 1216 constitution even ruled that the order's own rule did not bind under sin, so it could never get in the way of study. The order's convents of women, especially in the German lands, became one of the few places in medieval Europe where women wrote theology and were read.

sources.work: Simon Tugwell (ed.), Early Dominicans: Selected Writings (Classics of Western Spirituality, 1982)
sources.note: Jordan of Saxony's Libellus, the Nine Ways of Prayer, Humbert of Romans' Treatise on the Formation of Preachers, and the early constitutions in an appendix.

sources.work: The canonization process of St Dominic (Bologna and Toulouse, 1233), in F. C. Lehner, Saint Dominic: Biographical Documents (1964)
sources.note: Friars and lay witnesses under oath on what Dominic actually did.

sources.work: Jordan of Saxony, letters to Diana d'Andalo (trans. Gerald Vann, To Heaven with Diana!, 1960)
sources.note: The master general's correspondence with the Bologna nuns - the order's women's side and its interior register.

sources.work: Gerard de Frachet, Vitae Fratrum (Lives of the Brethren, c. 1260)
sources.note: Communal self-portrait in anecdote: dormitory, road, deathbed - ordinary texture. English translation: Conway, 1924.

sources.work: M. Michele Mulchahey, 'First the Bow is Bent in Study': Dominican Education before 1350 (PIMS, 1998)
sources.note: The formation system as system.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 (McGuire); cf. ch. 9 'The Word and its diffusion' (Jansen)
sources.note: Preaching is the order's reason for existing.

movements.longDescription: Dominic de Guzmán was a Spanish cathedral canon who, travelling through Languedoc, concluded that the church was losing the argument with dissenters because its own preachers arrived on horseback with baggage while their opponents walked and fasted. His answer was an order built backwards from a purpose: friars trained in theology, living poor and mobile, whose stated reason for existing was preaching. Approved in 1216, the Order of Preachers wrote itself a constitution of unusual sophistication — elected superiors, representative chapters, and a clause stating that the rule did not bind under sin, so that it could never get in the way of study — and planted itself immediately in the new universities at Paris and Bologna. Its convents of women, in the German lands especially, became one of the very few settings in medieval Europe where women wrote theology and were read.
movements.teaser: Toulouse, Paris and Bologna, from 1216 — an order built backwards from a single purpose, and the rare medieval institution that put its whole reason for existing into its own name.
voices: Dominic de Guzmán — the Castilian canon who founded the order and was canonized within thirteen years of his death
Jordan of Saxony — his successor as master general, who wrote the order's account of its own beginnings and whose letters to the Bologna nun Diana d'Andalo survive
Diana d'Andalo — the Bolognese woman who founded the convent of St Agnes and to whom Jordan wrote
Humbert of Romans — master general and author of a detailed treatise on how to form a preacher
Gerard de Frachet — compiler of the Lives of the Brethren, the order's portrait of itself in dormitory and roadside anecdotes
movements.legacy: The Dominicans are still here, and much of what they built outlasted the century. The constitutional machinery of elected superiors and representative chapters, a permanent commitment to study as itself a form of religious life, and the university theology that Albert the Great and Thomas Aquinas produced inside the order and that still anchors Catholic thought. Their German convents fed the mystical writing associated with Meister Eckhart, Johannes Tauler and Henry Suso. The order also supplied the church with much of its inquisitorial personnel, which belongs to the same inheritance and is not separable from it. The rosary's spread through Europe was carried largely by Dominicans, though the traditional story that Dominic himself received it is legend rather than history.

experienceToday.text: Bologna, Italy — the Basilica of San Domenico, where Dominic is buried in a shrine carved by Nicola Pisano, Niccolò dell'Arca and the young Michelangelo

movements.name: Athonite & Comnenian Byzantine Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) as the era's Orthodox monastic anchor and the parent of hesychasm. One sourcing nuance was carried rather than smoothed over: Symeon the New Theologian's corpus is Constantinopolitan — the entry's Comnenian half — not Athos proper. Its c. 963 start, which precedes the era, stands under the adopted start-before-era rule.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: founders' typika, Symeon the New Theologian's corpus
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of the iconophile tradition; parent of hesychasm
movements.why: In 963 the monk Athanasios founded the Great Lavra on Mount Athos with imperial backing, and the peninsula grew into a federation of monasteries each governed by its own written charter, a typikon setting down everything from diet to liturgy. In Constantinople in the same period, Symeon the New Theologian preached that God could be known directly and consciously, in experienced light, and was pushed out of his monastery for insisting on it. Between them, these houses shaped the disciplines of interior prayer that the next century would gather up and name hesychasm.

sources.work: Byzantine Monastic Foundation Documents (ed. Thomas & Constantinides Hero, Dumbarton Oaks, 5 vols, 2000; free online)
sources.note: The founders' typika are complete in English: Athanasios's Great Lavra documents, the Evergetis typikon, Pantokrator, and more - legislation, liturgy, diet, and charity in lived detail.

sources.work: Symeon the New Theologian, The Discourses (trans. deCatanzaro, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1980)
sources.note: Catecheses actually preached to his monks — formation as it was delivered, and the era's boldest claim of direct experience of God. One nuance worth naming: Symeon's own writing comes from Constantinople, representing the 'Comnenian' half of this tradition rather than Mount Athos itself.

sources.work: Symeon the New Theologian, Hymns / Divine Eros (trans. Daniel Griggs, SVS Press, 2010)
sources.note: The same claim in first-person poetry.

sources.work: Holy Men of Mount Athos (ed./trans. Greenfield & Talbot, Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library, 2016)
sources.note: Lives of the mountain's founders incl. Athanasios of Athos - Athonite hagiography in facing-page translation.

sources.work: Rosemary Morris, Monks and Laymen in Byzantium, 843-1118 (CUP, 1995)
sources.note: Standard study of the monastic world's social ecosystem: patrons, property, holy men.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 4 'The rise of hesychasm' (Krausmuller); cf. ch. 3 'The culture of lay piety in medieval Byzantium' (Gerstel & Talbot)

movements.longDescription: In 963 the monk Athanasios, with the backing of a Byzantine emperor, founded the Great Lavra on the mountainous peninsula of Athos in northern Greece, and the loose scatter of hermits already living there began to take the shape it has kept ever since. A self-governing federation of monasteries, each running on a written charter, a typikon, in which its founder set down exactly what the house was for, down to the diet, the liturgy and the charity. In Constantinople in the same period Symeon the New Theologian preached to his monks that God can be known directly and consciously, in experienced light, and was pushed out of his monastery for pressing the claim so hard. Between them the Athonite houses and the capital's monasteries carried the disciplines of interior prayer that the following century would gather up and name hesychasm.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos and Constantinople, 963 to 1300 — a mountain of monasteries governed by their founders' written charters, and the monks who insisted God could be known directly and not merely believed in.
voices: Athanasios the Athonite — founder of the Great Lavra in 963 and effectively the organizer of Athonite monasticism
Symeon the New Theologian — abbot in Constantinople whose sermons and hymns claimed direct experience of God, and who was exiled for insisting on it
The founders of the Evergetis monastery in Constantinople — whose typikon was copied and adapted more widely than any other, from Athos to the Slavic lands
movements.legacy: Mount Athos never stopped. Its monasteries have been continuously occupied since this period, still governed by their own charters, and it is one of the very few places on the whole map of Christian history where a visitor can find something doing today what it was doing a thousand years ago. The prayer practices formed here fed directly into hesychasm and the Palamite theology of the next century, and from there into the whole later devotional life of Orthodoxy — the Jesus Prayer, and eventually the Philokalia. Athonite typika were adapted by Georgian, Serbian, Bulgarian and Russian founders, exporting a model of monastic government across Eastern Europe.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the Great Lavra, founded in 963 and still the senior monastery of the mountain; entry requires a permit and is open to men only

movements.name: The Beguines
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), and named the flagship for the marginalized-voices duty the census sets itself: Hadewijch, Mechthild of Magdeburg and Marguerite Porete are first-person women's voices, the rarest commodity in the atlas, all in verified modern translation. Its 1310 end, Porete's burning, crosses the era boundary once as a principled straddle rather than an artifact.
movements.sourcing: RICH in first-person women's voice - the rarest commodity in the whole atlas (Hadewijch, Mechthild, Porete)
movements.relationsSummary: Lay women's movement outside every standard structure; suppression pressure is part of its own story
movements.why: Beginning in the late twelfth century, women across the Low Countries and the Rhineland lived religious lives with no vows, no rule and no enclosure, keeping their own property or working in cloth and nursing the sick in walled courtyard communities called beguinages. Some of them wrote, which is what makes them extraordinary: Hadewijch's visions and letters, Mechthild of Magdeburg's Flowing Light of the Godhead, and Marguerite Porete's Mirror of Simple Souls are among the very few medieval accounts of religious life told from the inside by the women living it. Porete was burned in Paris in 1310, and two years later the Council of Vienne moved against the beguine life itself.

sources.work: Hadewijch, The Complete Works (trans. Mother Columba Hart, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1980)
sources.note: Visions, letters, and poems in Middle Dutch - a beguine directing other women's formation, in her own voice.

sources.work: Mechthild of Magdeburg, The Flowing Light of the Godhead (trans. Frank Tobin, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1998)
sources.note: Begun as a beguine, finished at Helfta; includes her defense of writing as an unlettered woman.

sources.work: Marguerite Porete, The Mirror of Simple Souls (trans. Ellen Babinsky, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1993)
sources.note: The movement's boldest theology, and its martyrdom — Porete was burned in 1310 — carried in the fate of one book. Her theology of the soul's freedom also overlaps with the Free Spirit heresy of the same period.

sources.work: Jacques de Vitry, Life of Marie d'Oignies, in Mary of Oignies: Mother of Salvation (ed. Mulder-Bakker, Brepols, 2006)
sources.note: A sympathetic outside view from a churchman, and the account that won the movement its first toleration — written, though, in the idealizing frame of a saint's life.

sources.work: Walter Simons, Cities of Ladies: Beguine Communities in the Medieval Low Countries, 1200-1565 (Penn, 2001)
sources.note: The standard social history - courtyards, labor, and rents behind the mystics.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 20 'On the margins of religious life... beguines and beghards' (Simons); cf. ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)
sources.note: The volume's co-editor writes on this exact movement.

movements.longDescription: From the late twelfth century, women in the towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland began living religious lives without joining any order: no lifelong vows, no rule, no enclosure. They kept their own property or worked — often in cloth — lived alone or in walled courtyard communities called beguinages, prayed, and nursed the sick and the dying. Some of them wrote, and that is what makes them extraordinary on any map of medieval Christianity: Hadewijch's visions and letters, Mechthild of Magdeburg's Flowing Light of the Godhead, Marguerite Porete's Mirror of Simple Souls are among the very few medieval accounts of a religious life told from the inside by the women actually living it. Because they fitted no category, they attracted suspicion: Porete was burned in Paris in 1310, and in 1312 the Council of Vienne moved against the beguine life itself.
movements.teaser: The towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland, c. 1190 to 1310 — women who lived a religious life under no rule and no vows, wrote about it in their own words, and were finally condemned for fitting nowhere.
voices: Marie d'Oignies — the movement's first widely known figure, whose life was written by a sympathetic churchman and helped win the beguines early toleration
Jacques de Vitry — the cleric who wrote that life and defended the movement at Rome
Hadewijch — a beguine of the Low Countries whose visions, letters and poems in Middle Dutch guided other women's formation
Mechthild of Magdeburg — who began The Flowing Light of the Godhead as a beguine and finished it at the convent of Helfta, defending along the way her right to write as an unschooled woman
Marguerite Porete — author of The Mirror of Simple Souls, burned at Paris in 1310 for refusing to withdraw it
movements.legacy: The beguinages themselves outlasted the suppression by centuries. Whole courtyard quarters in Bruges, Leuven and other Flemish towns still stand, lived in and intact, and are now protected as world heritage. The writing survived too, though not always under its author's name. Porete's Mirror circulated anonymously for six hundred years and was read as an orthodox devotional classic until scholars identified it as hers in the twentieth century. Hadewijch and Mechthild are read today as major theologians in their own right, and the movement as a whole has become one of the standard reference points in the history of women's religious life.

experienceToday.text: Bruges, Belgium — the Princely Beguinage Ten Wijngaerde, founded in 1244, still standing around its garden

movements.name: The Waldensians
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), and named the map's clearest dissent-that-survived thread. Its evidence splits by period — inquisition registers early, genuine internal literature later, with the Liber Antiheresis flagged Latin-only and its representativeness contested. The 1300–1517 gap its continuing thread jumps was flagged to the succession walk rather than closed here.
movements.sourcing: Hostile-source problem early (inquisition registers), genuine internal literature later
movements.floorNote: No plain-reading doctrinal question - discipline, not doctrine, was the charge
movements.relationsSummary: The map's clearest 'dissent that survived' thread - joins the Reformed tradition in 1532
movements.why: Around 1173 a rich merchant of Lyon named Valdes gave away his property, had Scripture translated into the language people actually spoke, and began preaching in the streets — his confession of faith was entirely orthodox, and he was condemned in 1184 only for preaching without a licence. Driven from the cities, the movement survived three and a half centuries of persecution in the Alpine valleys between France and Italy, with its own travelling ministers and its own books. In 1532 its representatives met the Reformers at Chanforan and joined the Reformed tradition, carrying a line of protest from twelfth-century Lyon straight into the Reformation.

sources.work: Valdes's Profession of Faith (1180) and the early Waldensian dossier, trans. in Wakefield & Evans, Heresies of the High Middle Ages (Columbia, 1969; repr. 1991)
sources.note: The founder's own orthodox confession - evidence the charge was discipline, unauthorized preaching, not doctrine.

sources.work: Durand of Osca, Liber Antiheresis (c. 1190s; ed. Selge, 1967)
sources.note: The earliest inside theological text, from the first generation; its author later reconciled with Rome, so how representative it is remains debated. Available only in Latin; no English translation exists.

sources.work: Bernard Gui, Inquisitor's Guide, Waldensian section (trans. Janet Shirley, 2006), plus 13th-c. inquisition registers
sources.note: Written by the persecutors: how they described Waldensian practice. The depositions preserve ordinary believers' voices that no inside text records.

sources.work: Euan Cameron, Waldenses: Rejections of Holy Church in Medieval Europe (Blackwell, 2000)
sources.note: Source-critical standard; warns against reading later Waldensian identity back into the 1170s.

sources.work: Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent: Persecution and Survival, c.1170-c.1570 (CUP, 1999)
sources.note: Covers the survival arc down to the 1532 union with the Reformed tradition.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller); cf. ch. 3 (Kienzle)
sources.note: Biller is the leading Waldensian specialist.

movements.longDescription: Around 1173 a rich merchant of Lyon named Valdes gave away his property, had parts of Scripture translated into the language people actually spoke, and began preaching in the streets. His confession of faith was entirely orthodox. What he would not do was stop preaching without a licence, and in 1184 the bull Ad abolendam condemned him and his followers for exactly that. Driven out of the cities, the movement survived in the Alpine valleys between France and Italy for three and a half centuries of intermittent persecution, with its own travelling ministers and its own books. In 1532 its representatives met the Reformers at Chanforan and threw in with the Reformed tradition. Which is why a single line of protest can be followed from twelfth-century Lyon into the Reformation without a break.
movements.teaser: Lyon and the Alpine valleys, from about 1173 — a merchant who gave away everything to preach, condemned not for what he believed but for preaching without permission, and a movement that outlived everyone who condemned it.
voices: Valdes of Lyon — the merchant who gave away his wealth, commissioned Scripture in the vernacular, and would not stop preaching
Durand of Osca — a first-generation Waldensian whose theological defence of the movement survives, and who later reconciled with Rome
Bernard Gui — the Dominican inquisitor whose handbook describes Waldensian practice from the outside, and whose registers preserve the words of ordinary believers recorded nowhere else
movements.legacy: The Waldensian church is still here. Having joined the Reformed tradition at Chanforan in 1532, it survives as the Waldensian Evangelical Church, based in the same Piedmontese valleys and now united with Italy's Methodists. One of the very few medieval movements condemned by Rome that never disappeared and never had to be reconstructed out of its enemies' files. Its long habit of vernacular Scripture and lay preaching anticipated, and then joined, the Reformation.

experienceToday.text: Torre Pellice, Italy — the Waldensian Cultural Centre Foundation and its historical museum, in the Alpine valleys where the community survived

movements.name: Zagwe Ethiopian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — moderate in sourcing here and richer in the next era, so its work in this window is holding the spine. At the Freeze a stated fork was decided in favour of ending it at 1270, the Solomonic restoration, with a rename from 'Zagwe & Early Solomonic' to match; that removed a 30-year double-coverage with its successor entry, and the alternative of moving the successor's start was shown and declined.
movements.sourcing: Moderate here, rich next era - a window-setting call
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of Aksum; formal dependence on the Coptic patriarchate
movements.why: Under the Zagwe dynasty, the Ethiopian church kept its head bishop, the abun, permanently on loan as a monk sent from the Coptic patriarchate in Egypt, even though the kingdom itself was fully independent. Its most famous achievement is the group of eleven churches carved downward out of solid rock at Lalibela, laid out to recall Jerusalem at a time when the real Jerusalem had become unreachable. In 1270 the dynasty was displaced by Yekuno Amlak, whose Solomonic line justified its rule through the Kebra Nagast for the next seven centuries.
movements.dateRationale: End 1270 (Solomonic restoration — Yekuno Amlak): fixes a 30-year double-coverage with its continuesAs target V.7 (starts 1270); renamed from 'Zagwe & Early Solomonic' to match the corrected window (the Early Solomonic story belongs to V.7). The move-V.7 alternative was shown and declined — 1270 is V.7's genuine gravity start (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Kebra Nagast (The Glory of Kings) (trans. E. A. Wallis Budge, 1922; free online)
sources.note: The Solomonic dynasty's charter myth, compiled and redacted in the early 14th century - royal ideology from just after this period, not the Zagwe's own self-description. Budge's translation is dated but remains the standard available edition.

sources.work: Gadla Lalibela (Life of King Lalibela) (ed./French trans. Perruchon, 1892)
sources.note: Zagwe royal hagiography. No English translation exists, and the Life was written after the king it praises died.

sources.work: Lalibela's rock-hewn churches (material culture) + land grants and marginalia in gospel books (e.g. the Golden Gospel of Dabra Libanos)
sources.note: The era's most eloquent contemporary witnesses are carved and written into stone and manuscript margins, not narrated. Covered mainly in specialist publications.

sources.work: Taddesse Tamrat, Church and State in Ethiopia, 1270-1527 (Oxford, 1972)
sources.note: Available on archive.org. Still the field's standard frame, by an Ethiopian historian.

sources.work: Marie-Laure Derat, L'enigme d'une dynastie sainte et usurpatrice: les rois zagwe (2018)
sources.note: Current Zagwe scholarship revising the Solomonic-propaganda picture. French only; no English translation.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, 'Church and nation: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tawahedo church (from the thirteenth to the twentieth century)' (Crummey)

movements.longDescription: After the old Aksumite kingdom faded, a dynasty called the Zagwe ruled the Ethiopian highlands from the twelfth century, and under them the Ethiopian church went on doing what it had done for eight hundred years — with one striking peculiarity of constitution: its head bishop, the abun, was not Ethiopian but a monk sent from the Coptic patriarchate in Egypt, so a wholly independent kingdom kept its senior churchman permanently on loan from another country. The dynasty's most famous achievement is the group of eleven churches cut downward out of solid rock at the town now called Lalibela, after the king who commissioned them, laid out to recall Jerusalem at a time when Jerusalem itself had become unreachable. In 1270 the Zagwe were displaced by Yekuno Amlak, whose line claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba — a claim set out in the Kebra Nagast, compiled in the generations after the takeover and used to justify Ethiopian kingship for the next seven centuries.
movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 1137 to 1270 — a kingdom that carved its churches downward into living rock, ruled by a church whose senior bishop was always a foreigner sent from Egypt.
voices: Gebre Meskel Lalibela — the Zagwe king who commissioned the rock-hewn churches that carry his name and who became a saint of the Ethiopian church
Yekuno Amlak — the ruler who ended the Zagwe in 1270 and founded the Solomonic line
The abuns of this period — Coptic monks sent from Alexandria to head a church whose language and kingdom were not their own, and who left little personal record behind them
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the largest ancient churches in the world today, and it runs in an unbroken line through this period. Lalibela's churches are not ruins: they are working parish churches, with priests and pilgrims, and remain one of the great pilgrimage destinations of African Christianity. The Solomonic claim launched in these years shaped Ethiopian politics until 1974, when the last emperor to bear the title Lion of Judah was deposed.

experienceToday.text: Lalibela, Ethiopia — eleven churches cut downward out of the living rock in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and still in use for worship

movements.name: Maronite Christianity
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 5 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3): thin-to-moderate early, with much of its early history being later reconstruction under polemical pressure — the census's own line, confirmed rather than softened. Its start was decided at a stated fork in favour of keeping 1100 with an Era 4 origin note, rather than backward-extending to c. 685 on tradition-internal evidence.
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate early; much early history is later reconstruction under polemical pressure
movements.floorNote: Contested historiography (monothelete question) is about the past record, not present confession
movements.relationsSummary: West Syriac liturgical family; unique early union with Rome
movements.why: The Maronites take their name from the Syriac monk Maron, and by the medieval period were a distinct West Syriac church whose monasteries and hermitages were cut straight into the cliffs of Mount Lebanon. Their early history is unusually hard to recover, because much of what is told about it was written later, under argument over whether the community had once held that Christ had only one will. When the crusaders arrived, the Maronites entered communion with Rome — William of Tyre describes the union around 1182, and in 1215 the patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti travelled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council to settle its terms.

sources.work: Kitab al-Huda (Book of Guidance; Syriac-to-Arabic trans. by Bishop David, 1059; ed. Fahed, 1935)
sources.note: The community's own law-liturgy-theology compendium - the lived internal rulebook. Available only in Arabic and French; no English translation exists.

sources.work: Thomas of Kaphartab, Ten Chapters (11th c.)
sources.note: Pre-union Maronite apologetics defending the one-will christology - inside evidence bearing on the contested monothelete question, which concerns the historical record rather than the church's present confession. No English translation exists.

sources.work: William of Tyre on the Maronite union with Rome (1180s), in A History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea (trans. Babcock & Krey, 1943)
sources.note: An outside view: the union described through Latin crusader eyes. William frames it with hostility, calling the Maronites' prior teaching heresy.

sources.work: Kamal Salibi, Maronite Historians of Mediaeval Lebanon (Beirut, 1959)
sources.note: Available on archive.org. A classic dissection of how later Maronite historians rebuilt the early record under polemical pressure.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse, 1986; repr. Gorgias 2005)
sources.note: Critical counter-history; itself contested by Maronite traditionalists - the historiography is a live confessional argument on both sides.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, Part III 'East Christianities (eleventh to fourteenth century): Copts, Melkites, Nestorians and Jacobites'
sources.note: Maronites are not named in the chapter title, though they fall within its scope of medieval Eastern Christianity.

movements.longDescription: The Maronites take their name from a Syriac monk, Maron, and from the monastery built around his memory. By the medieval period they were a distinct church of the West Syriac liturgical family, concentrated in the mountains and gorges of Lebanon, where their monasteries and hermitages were cut straight into the cliffs. Their early history is unusually hard to recover, because much of what is told about it was written down later and under argument. Specifically over whether the community had once held that Christ had only one will, a position the wider church had rejected. What is clear is that when the crusaders arrived, the Maronites entered into communion with Rome: William of Tyre describes the union around 1182, and in 1215 the Maronite patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti travelled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council, after which a papal bull set out the terms of the union.
movements.teaser: Mount Lebanon, consolidating through this era — a Syriac church of cliffside monasteries whose own early history is fought over, and the one Eastern church to enter a lasting communion with Rome in the Middle Ages.
voices: Maron — the Syriac hermit of late antiquity the church is named for
Thomas of Kaphartab — an eleventh-century Maronite writer whose Ten Chapters defends the one-will Christology that later Maronite historians would deny the community had ever held
Jeremiah al-Amshitti — the patriarch who travelled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215
William of Tyre — the crusader archbishop whose history is the main outside account of the union, written from a frankly Latin point of view
movements.legacy: The Maronite Church is very much alive: one of the largest Eastern Catholic churches, the largest Christian community in Lebanon, and with a worldwide diaspora. The union begun here has held for eight centuries and made the Maronites the working model for later Eastern Catholic churches — communion with the papacy alongside a Syriac liturgy and a patriarch of their own. The Qadisha valley, where the monasteries and hermitages are carved into the cliff faces, remains a place of pilgrimage and is protected as world heritage.

experienceToday.text: Northern Lebanon — the Qadisha (Kadisha) Valley, whose cliffside monasteries and hermitages are the historic heart of Maronite monastic life, with the cedar forest above it

movements.name: Military-Religious Orders (Templars, Hospitallers)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — institutionally rich with a thin interior voice, and the Templar trial testimony flagged as coerced rather than read as inside evidence. The entry's own open question, whether this is a tradition or an institution, was left standing for any build to face, alongside the question of holy violence its floorNote names.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally; interior voice thin
movements.floorNote: No creedal question — these orders held the ordinary faith of the Latin church. The hard question they raise is holy violence, and it is a real one.
movements.relationsSummary: These orders fused monastic vows with arms, something the church had never authorized before, and Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their defense, In Praise of the New Knighthood. The Hospitallers continued after the fall of Acre in 1291, moving their base to Rhodes in 1310 and remaining there into the sixteenth century.
movements.why: The Hospitallers began as a hospital in Jerusalem caring for pilgrims, calling the sick 'our lords the sick,' and only later took on a military role, while the Templars began as knights guarding the pilgrim roads and were given a monastic rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Bernard of Clairvaux defended the fusion of vows and arms in his In Praise of the New Knighthood, arguing that a knight who killed in this cause was not a homicide but a 'malicide' — a killer of evil. Both orders grew rich running castles, estates and banking networks, and when Acre fell in 1291 the Templars were arrested, tortured into confession, and suppressed by 1312.

sources.work: The Rule of the Templars (trans. J. M. Upton-Ward, Boydell, 1992)
sources.note: Primitive Rule, hierarchical statutes, penances - the fused monastic-military life in regulated detail, down to horses and mess discipline.

sources.work: Bernard of Clairvaux, In Praise of the New Knighthood (De laude novae militiae) (trans. Greenia, Cistercian Fathers 19)
sources.note: The apologia for the fused monastic-military life; the era's theology of holy violence stated plainly.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber & Keith Bate, The Templars: Selected Sources (Manchester Medieval Sources, 2002)
sources.note: Foundation documents, papal bulls, charters, letters from the East, and trial documents. The trial testimony was extracted under torture (1307-12) and should be read as coerced, not free confession.

sources.work: The Hospitallers' Rule and statutes (trans. E. J. King, The Rule, Statutes and Customs of the Hospitallers, 1934)
sources.note: The order's own legislation, with its 'lords the sick' care obligation - the charitable half of the fusion. This is an older translation.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber, The New Knighthood: A History of the Order of the Temple (CUP, 1994)
sources.note: Standard history, foundation to suppression.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 (McGuire) + ch. 11 'Christendom and Islam' (Nirenberg)
sources.note: No single chapter is dedicated to the military orders specifically; coverage is split across these two chapters.

movements.longDescription: In the decades after the First Crusade, two kinds of institution fused into something the church had never authorized before. The Hospitallers began as a hospital in Jerusalem caring for pilgrims — they called the sick 'our lords the sick' — and only later took on a military role. The Templars began as a small band of knights guarding the pilgrim roads, took monastic vows, and were given a rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their defence, In Praise of the New Knighthood, arguing that a man who killed in this cause was not a homicide but, in his coinage, a malicide — a killer of evil. Both orders grew enormously rich, ran castles, estates and banking networks from the Latin East across Europe, and lost their reason for existing when Acre fell in 1291. The Templars were arrested in France in 1307, made to confess under torture, and suppressed in 1312.
movements.teaser: The Latin East and Iberia, 1120 to 1291 — men who took monastic vows of poverty, chastity and obedience and then went to war, defended in their own time by the most admired churchman in Europe.
voices: Hugh de Payens — the knight who founded the Templars and became their first master
Bernard of Clairvaux — who wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood, the era's most influential defence of holy violence
Gerard — the founder-figure of the Hospital in Jerusalem, remembered as the beginning of the order's care of the sick
Jacques de Molay — the last Templar master, burned in Paris in 1314 after years of imprisonment and forced confession
movements.legacy: One of the two orders is still going. The Hospitallers moved to Rhodes, then Malta, and continue today as the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a hospitaller body with a legal personality of its own, alongside Protestant orders of St John in Britain and Germany out of which St John Ambulance grew — the medical vocation outlived the military one by many centuries. The Templars did not survive, and their destruction left a very long afterlife in legend and conspiracy writing that has almost nothing to do with the historical order. What both left physically is architecture. Castles across the eastern Mediterranean and Iberia, and round churches in Europe built in imitation of the Holy Sepulchre, of which London's Temple Church is the best known.

experienceToday.text: London, England — the Temple Church, consecrated in 1185 as the Templars' English headquarters, with its round nave and its floor of knightly effigies

movements.name: Cathars / Albigensians
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence recorded — dualist theology per the claimed Liber de duobus principiis; the Lyon Ritual as claimed inside practice; docetic Christology at census-claim strength; texts’ status and the movement’s coherence contested in scholarship — disclosed
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Inquisition records plus the movement's own surviving ritual
movements.floorNote: By every account we have, they taught that the visible material world was not the good God's making, and that Christ only appeared to have a body — both outside the common Christian creed. Their own voice has not survived to test it against.
movements.relationsSummary: Target of crusade and inquisition - which the map names without softening
movements.why: From the 1140s, communities in Languedoc with their own ministers and their own initiation rite taught that the visible material world was not the good God's making, a dualism that placed them outside the councils' Christianity. In 1209 the papacy launched a crusade against them, and at the siege of Montségur in 1244 roughly two hundred of their ministers walked into a fire rather than recant; the last known Languedoc perfect, Guillaume Bélibaste, was burned in 1321. Almost everything known about them comes from the people who destroyed them, and historians still argue over how much of 'Catharism' was ever a coherent movement at all.
movements.dateRationale: Start c. 1143 (Eberwin of Steinfeld's Cologne letter — first solid western description); end 1321 (Bélibaste burned — documented Languedoc Catharism ends; one boundary crossing, allowed) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Book of the Two Principles (Liber de duobus principiis, c. 1240s-60s), trans. in Wakefield & Evans, Heresies of the High Middle Ages (1969), p. 511
sources.note: Radical-dualist theology from the circle of John of Lugio (Italy). Non-Catholic authorship is broadly accepted, but whether it speaks for 'the Cathars' (esp. Languedoc) is exactly what Pegg and Moore deny.

sources.work: The Cathar Rituals (Occitan Lyon ritual; Latin Florence ritual), trans. in Wakefield & Evans (1969), p. 465
sources.note: The consolamentum liturgy. Scholars still debate whether this really reflects a coherent Catharism, or a small literate circle later projected back onto Languedoc.

sources.work: Biller, Bruschi & Sneddon (ed./trans.), Inquisitors and Heretics in Thirteenth-Century Languedoc (Brill, 2011) - Toulouse depositions 1273-82
sources.note: A hostile source, but the only place ordinary believers' voices survive — filtered through the interrogators' own categories; the words 'Cathar' and 'perfect' are largely the inquisitors', not the deponents'.

sources.work: Rainerius Sacconi, Summa de Catharis (1250), in Wakefield & Evans
sources.note: A hostile source from a former insider: a 'heretic' of seventeen years who turned Dominican inquisitor — uniquely informed, and uniquely motivated to condemn what he'd left.

sources.work: Antonio Sennis (ed.), Cathars in Question (York Medieval Press, 2016)
sources.note: The coherence debate itself: Pegg ('The Paradigm of Catharism; or, the Historians' Illusion'), Moore, Biller, Hamilton, Taylor, Stoyanov face to face - the honest state of the question.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller)
sources.note: Biller is a leading voice on one side of the live debate, not a neutral summary of it; read alongside Sennis.

movements.longDescription: From the 1140s, church writers in the Rhineland and then in southern France describe communities with their own ministers, their own initiation rite, and a teaching that the visible material world was not the work of the good God. A dualism that placed them outside Christianity as the councils had defined it. In Languedoc they had noble protection and something close to a parallel church, and in 1209 the papacy launched a crusade against them: two decades of war, then inquisition, then the siege of Montségur in 1244, where roughly two hundred of their ministers walked into a fire rather than recant. The last known Languedoc perfect, Guillaume Bélibaste, was burned in 1321. Almost everything known about them comes from the people who destroyed them, and historians now argue seriously about how much of 'Catharism' was a coherent movement at all and how much was a category assembled by inquisitors out of scattered local dissent.
movements.teaser: Languedoc, c. 1143 to 1321 — a dissenting church with its own ministers and its own initiation, destroyed by crusade and inquisition, and known almost entirely through the records of the men who destroyed it.
voices: Guilhabert de Castres — the most prominent Cathar bishop of Languedoc in the movement's strongest years
Bertrand Marty — the bishop who led some two hundred of his people into the fire at Montségur in 1244
Rainerius Sacconi — a former member of seventeen years who became a Dominican inquisitor and wrote the fullest surviving description of their beliefs: uniquely informed and thoroughly hostile at once
Guillaume Bélibaste — the last known Languedoc perfect, burned in 1321
movements.legacy: Nothing of the movement itself survived; it was extinguished, and no continuing community descends from it. What it left behind belongs mostly to the people who suppressed it. The Albigensian Crusade attached Languedoc to the French crown, and the papal inquisition was built in the 1230s largely to deal with this problem and then became a permanent institution that long outlived its original target. In the modern Languedoc the Cathars have been rediscovered as regional heritage, and ruined hilltop castles are marketed as 'Cathar country', though the ruins standing today are mostly later rebuildings and the popular picture of the movement owes as much to romantic reconstruction as to the sources.

experienceToday.text: Ariège, southern France — the ruined Château de Montségur, above the field where roughly two hundred Cathars were burned in March 1244 (the standing walls are a later rebuilding)

movements.name: Joachimite Current
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: A reading-program more than a community
movements.floorNote: Joachim submitted his writings to Rome, and Rome took him up on it: the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 condemned his book on the Trinity while leaving his person and his monastery in good standing. The later expectation of a coming age of the Spirit was condemned in its most extreme forms, not in his.
movements.relationsSummary: Where it became communal, it lives inside the Franciscan Spirituals' story
movements.why: Joachim of Fiore, a Calabrian abbot, read history as moving through three ages — of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, with the third not far off — and died in 1202 before any of it arrived. The current his reading started spread especially among Franciscans, who saw their own movement described in it, until a 1254 book making the claim explicit was condemned and the current fixed on 1260 as the year the new age would open. When the year passed without incident, the expectation did not simply vanish — it fed into the bitter Franciscan quarrel over poverty that followed.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1202 (Joachim's death — the posthumous current is the entry's stated subject; the old 1200 matched nothing) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Joachim of Fiore, selections in Bernard McGinn, Apocalyptic Spirituality (Classics of Western Spirituality, 1979)
sources.note: Joachim's letters and key texts plus Spiritual-Franciscan material - both ends of the current in one translated volume, with Reeves's preface.

sources.work: Joachim of Fiore, major works: Liber de Concordia, Expositio in Apocalypsim, Psalterium decem chordarum
sources.note: The authentic baseline against which the pseudo-corpus is measured. Latin text; critical editions exist (MGH), and E. R. Daniel produced a partial translation of the Concordia, but no complete English translation exists.

sources.work: The pseudo-Joachimite corpus (Super Hieremiam, Super Esaiam, the Vaticinia)
sources.note: The texts that actually carried the current after c. 1240, written by others under Joachim's name. Latin only; no English translation.

sources.work: Salimbene de Adam, Chronicle (trans. Baird, Baglivi & Kane, MRTS, 1986)
sources.note: An ex-Joachimite friar's first-person memoir: expectation caught, shared in friaries, pinned to Frederick II, dropped when 1260 passed - communally carried expectation observed from inside; includes the 1254 Eternal Evangel scandal (Gerard of Borgo San Donnino) and the hostile commission record known as the Protocol of Anagni. The current rested on communal expectation more than on Joachim's own person, within Franciscan circles.

sources.work: Marjorie Reeves, The Influence of Prophecy in the Later Middle Ages: A Study in Joachimism (Clarendon, 1969)
sources.note: The standard study, built on the distinction between Joachim himself and the broader Joachimist movement his ideas inspired. Reeves and Salimbene both document real episodes of communal expectation inside Franciscan circles, not just an individual reading program.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4
sources.note: See also ch. 3 (Kienzle) for the Franciscan context this current grew within.

movements.longDescription: Joachim of Fiore was a Calabrian abbot who read history as a pattern with a shape: three ages, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the third still to come and not far off. He died in 1202, and the current that carried his reading afterwards was never an order or a church. It was a way of reading the Bible and the calendar together, and it spread especially among Franciscans, who found in it a description of their own movement. In 1254 a young friar published an Introduction to the Eternal Gospel that made the claim explicit and scandalous, and it was condemned. The current then fixed on 1260 as the year the new age would open. The year came and went. Some let it go, and some carried the expectation on into the bitter Franciscan quarrel over poverty, where it did most of its later work.
movements.teaser: Calabria and then the Franciscan houses of Europe, 1202 to 1300 — not an order but a way of reading history, which named the year the world would change and kept going after the year had passed.
voices: Joachim of Fiore — the Calabrian abbot whose reading of history the current is named for, and who died in 1202 before any of it happened
Gerard of Borgo San Donnino — the Franciscan whose Introduction to the Eternal Gospel of 1254 made the claim public and was condemned for it
Salimbene de Adam — a friar who caught the expectation, watched 1260 pass, and wrote a candid first-person account of letting it go
Much of the current is anonymous — the texts that actually carried it after about 1240 were written by other hands under Joachim's name
movements.legacy: No community descends from it, and the Florensian order Joachim founded was absorbed long ago. What the current left behind is a habit of mind: the idea that history moves in ages toward a coming age of the Spirit kept resurfacing in Western thought long after anyone was reading Joachim directly. In Franciscan reform movements, in radical politics, and in the recurring modern language of a 'third age' or a new spiritual era. Joachim himself stayed readable enough that Dante placed him in paradise. His abbey at San Giovanni in Fiore still stands and still holds his remains.

experienceToday.text: San Giovanni in Fiore, Calabria, Italy — the Florense Abbey, founded by Joachim and holding his remains

movements.name: 'Free Spirit' Heresy
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Substantially a construct of its persecutors (scholarly consensus since Lerner)
movements.floorNote: Cannot be assessed - the 'movement' may never have existed as described
movements.relationsSummary: Beguine suppression used it as a charge
movements.why: In 1312 the Council of Vienne's decree Ad nostrum listed eight errors said to belong to a 'sect of the Free Spirit,' chiefly that a soul perfected in this life needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer — and interrogators then went looking for people who held them, finding them because the questions supplied the answers. Robert Lerner's 1972 study concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed; what existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards, and a charge that could be laid against any part of it. Marguerite Porete's own book, once separated from the label, has since been read as a serious work of theology.

sources.work: Marguerite Porete, The Mirror of Simple Souls (trans. Ellen Babinsky, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1993)
sources.note: The one substantial text by a person condemned under what became the Free Spirit charge; she never claims the label, and whether the Mirror teaches what Ad nostrum condemned is precisely the question. The overlap with Beguine history is real: the suppression of beguines used this same charge.

sources.work: The trial of Marguerite Porete and Guiard of Cressonessart (Paris, 1310), trans. in Sean L. Field, The Beguine, the Angel, and the Inquisitor (Notre Dame, 2012)
sources.note: The inquisitorial process records that made her the emblematic case for the charge - documents from the persecuting side, not a neutral account.

sources.work: Ad nostrum, Council of Vienne (1312), trans. in Tanner, Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils (1990)
sources.note: The eight-error decree that legally defined 'the sect of the Free Spirit'; its errors were partly extracted, and distorted, from Porete's Mirror.

sources.work: Interrogation records of accused beghards and beguines (e.g. John of Brunn; the Schweidnitz interrogations, 1332)
sources.note: The 'movement' as it survives in the record: answers shaped by the questioners' own template. Partial translations exist, including in Lerner's own apparatus.

sources.work: Robert E. Lerner, The Heresy of the Free Spirit in the Later Middle Ages (California, 1972)
sources.note: The consensus-setting study: no organized sect ever existed - a persecutors' construct laid over a wide spectrum of mystical piety.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller); cf. ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)

movements.longDescription: In the early fourteenth century the church declared that a sect existed. The decree Ad nostrum, issued at the Council of Vienne in 1312, listed eight errors said to be held by a 'sect of the Free Spirit'. Chiefly that a soul perfected in this life becomes incapable of sin and needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. Interrogators then went looking for people who held them, and found them, because the questions supplied the answers. Modern research, above all Robert Lerner's study of 1972, concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed. What existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards, and a charge that could be laid against any part of it. The movement named here probably was not real; the charge and its victims certainly were.
movements.teaser: The Rhineland and the Low Countries, thirteenth and fourteenth centuries — a heresy that was defined before anyone had been found holding it, and that most historians now think never existed as an organized movement at all.
voices: Marguerite Porete — burned at Paris in 1310, and the one person condemned under this charge who left a substantial book in her own voice; she never used the label, and whether her Mirror of Simple Souls teaches what Ad nostrum condemned is precisely the disputed question

The rest are known only as defendants — men and women like John of Brunn, whose recorded words come out of interrogation and follow the questioners' template closely enough that they cannot safely be read as their own
movements.legacy: Nothing continued, because there was most likely nothing there to continue. What the episode left behind is the charge itself, which stayed available for two centuries afterwards against mystical writing and against religious women living outside enclosure. It also left one of the clearest lessons in the historian's craft: that a heresy can be manufactured out of a decree, a questionnaire and enough pressure. Marguerite Porete's book, once separated from the label, has been read since the twentieth century as a serious work of theology.

movements.name: The Georgian Golden Age
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — chronicles, typika, hymnography and the Gelati material give it a moderate base, with access flags carried on the Georgian-language editions. Its end was set to 1245, Queen Rusudan's death and the Mongol tributary submission, replacing a round-number 1250.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: chronicles, typika, hymnography, hagiography (Gelati academy)
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of II.10 - restores the Georgian lane, silent since 622; partner of Byzantine monasticism
movements.why: David IV, called the Builder, broke the Seljuk hold on Georgia at the battle of Didgori in 1121 and founded the monastery of Gelati in 1106 as an academy where philosophy, astronomy and rhetoric were taught alongside the liturgy, with the Neoplatonist Ioane Petritsi among its scholars. Under his great-granddaughter Tamar the kingdom reached its widest extent, with frescoed churches and a literature of its own. The age ended not through decline but through conquest, closing with the Mongol submission and Queen Rusudan's death in 1245.
movements.dateRationale: End 1245 (Queen Rusudan's death / Mongol tributary submission — the golden age's actual close; the old 1250 was a round number) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Kartlis Tskhovreba (the Georgian Chronicles): Robert W. Thomson, Rewriting Caucasian History (Clarendon, 1996)
sources.note: Annotated English translation of the medieval corpus via the 13th-century Armenian adaptation, which reaches only to c. 1125 - it does not cover the later Golden Age. A complete English translation of the Georgian corpus (ed. S. Jones, Tbilisi, 2014) also exists.

sources.work: Tamara Grdzelidze (trans.), Georgian Monks on Mount Athos: Two Eleventh-Century Lives of the Hegoumenoi of Iviron (Bennett & Bloom, 2009)
sources.note: The hagiography in the movement's own voice: George the Hagiorite's Life of John and Euthymios, and the Life of George.

sources.work: Typikon of Gregory Pakourianos for Petritsoni/Bachkovo (1083), in Byzantine Monastic Foundation Documents (Dumbarton Oaks, 2000; free online)
sources.note: A Georgian grandee's monastic foundation, with its Georgians-only clause, available in English.

sources.work: Hymnography and the Gelati world: 'Shen khar venakhi' ('Thou art a Vineyard', attrib. King Demetre I); Gelati academy translations (Ioane Petritsi); Gelati mosaics
sources.note: Available mainly in specialist and Georgian-language editions; some attributions are traditional rather than firmly documented.

sources.work: Antony Eastmond, Royal Imagery in Medieval Georgia (Penn State, 1998)
sources.note: Standard English analysis of royal-sanctity ideology (Davit the Builder to Tamar) through monuments - material culture doing work the chronicles cannot.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 1 'The Byzantine commonwealth 1000-1500' (Shepard)
sources.note: No chapter is dedicated specifically to Georgia; this chapter is the nearest anchor, though its coverage of Georgia specifically has not been confirmed page by page.

movements.longDescription: For two and a half centuries Georgia was a real power in the Caucasus, and its church rose with it. David IV, called the Builder, broke the Seljuk hold at the battle of Didgori in 1121, and in 1106 had begun the monastery of Gelati, which was also an academy: philosophy, astronomy, rhetoric and Greek taught alongside the liturgy, with the Neoplatonist Ioane Petritsi among its scholars. Under his great-granddaughter Tamar the kingdom reached its widest extent, its churches were covered in frescoes, and its language was given a literature to match. The age ended not in decline but in conquest — after the Mongol invasions Georgia became a tributary state, and the death of Queen Rusudan in 1245 closes the age.
movements.teaser: Georgia, c. 1000 to 1245 — a mountain kingdom at its height, with an academy at Gelati teaching philosophy beside the liturgy, ended not by decay but by the Mongols.
voices: David IV the Builder — the king who broke the Seljuk hold at Didgori in 1121 and founded Gelati in 1106
Ioane Petritsi — the Neoplatonist philosopher and translator of Proclus who taught at the Gelati academy
Queen Tamar — under whom the kingdom reached its greatest extent, and who was canonized by the Georgian church
George the Hagiorite — the Georgian abbot at Iviron on Mount Athos, who revised the Georgian scriptures and wrote the lives of his predecessors there
Queen Rusudan — Tamar's daughter, whose reign saw the Mongol submission and whose death in 1245 closes the age
movements.legacy: The Georgian Orthodox Church is still the national church of Georgia, in a line running straight through this period. Gelati survives, with its twelfth-century mosaic of the Virgin and centuries of wall painting, and David the Builder is buried at its gate. What the age produced in Georgian — the chronicles, the hymnody, the translations made at Gelati, and beside them Rustaveli's great secular poem — remains the foundation of the national literature. The hymn traditionally attributed to King Demetre I, 'Thou Art a Vineyard', is still sung in Georgian churches and concert halls today.

experienceToday.text: Kutaisi, Georgia — the Gelati Monastery and its academy, founded by David the Builder in 1106, with its mosaics and medieval frescoes

movements.name: Serbian & Bulgarian Medieval Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a moderate-to-rich base with a native genre of its own — the zhitija, or royal saints' lives — alongside typika and chrysobulls, with access flags carried on the non-English editions. Its 1396 end is the era's heaviest overhang at 96 years; the Freeze kept it under the straddle rule's letter rather than capping it, with whether the rule's intent should cap such overhangs left as a standing question.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: typika, royal saints' lives (zhitija - a native genre), chrysobulls
movements.relationsSummary: Children of Byzantium/Athos; carried hesychasm into the Slavic lands; fixes the Slavic lane's Kyiv-to-Moscow jump
movements.why: When the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanja abdicated in 1196 to become a monk, his son Rastko — already a monk on Mount Athos as Sava — joined him there, and together they founded the Serbian house of Hilandar. Sava secured an autocephalous Serbian church in 1219 and became its first archbishop, while in Bulgaria a restored patriarchate at Tarnovo gathered its own literary school around the cult of hermits like John of Rila. Both churches carried hesychast prayer out of Greek and into the Slavic world, eventually reaching Russia.

sources.work: St Sava of Serbia: Life of St Symeon (Stefan Nemanja) + the Karyes and Hilandar/Studenica typika
sources.note: Founder-family sanctity and legislation in one hand: the zhitija genre's fountainhead and the typika corpus (adapted from Evergetis).

sources.work: Domentijan and Teodosije, Lives of St Sava (13th c.)
sources.note: The native royal-saint genre, built around the dynasty's own monk-king.

sources.work: Kiril Petkov, The Voices of Medieval Bulgaria, Seventh-Fifteenth Century (Brill, 2008)
sources.note: The Bulgarian side's primary corpus in English: inscriptions, charters, seals, graffiti, church records, including the Synodicon of Boril (1211), a hostile anti-Bogomil source, and John of Rila materials.

sources.work: Royal chrysobulls and charters: Nemanja's Hilandar founding charter; Ivan Asen II's Tarnovo column inscription; monastic land charters
Dimitri Obolensky, Six Byzantine Portraits (Oxford, 1988)
sources.note: Includes a standard scholarly portrait of Sava; frames both churches inside his Byzantine Commonwealth model (a frame, not a verdict).

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 1 'The Byzantine commonwealth 1000-1500' (Shepard)
sources.note: The Balkans are this chapter's core ground.

movements.longDescription: When the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanja abdicated in 1196 and became a monk, and his youngest son Rastko — already a monk on Mount Athos under the name Sava — joined him there, the two founded Hilandar, a Serbian house on the Holy Mountain. From it the shape of Serbian church life was set: Athonite charters adapted for Serbian monasteries, and a ruling family that produced its own saints and then wrote their lives. Sava secured an autocephalous Serbian church in 1219 and became its first archbishop. In Bulgaria the restored patriarchate at Tarnovo did something comparable, gathering a literary school around it and the cult of hermits like John of Rila. Both churches were the road by which hesychast prayer travelled out of Greek and into Slavonic, and from there eventually to Russia. And Bulgaria was overrun by the Ottoman advance at the end of the fourteenth century, with Serbia following within two generations.
movements.teaser: The Balkans, c. 1170 to 1396 — Serbian and Bulgarian monasteries that took their rule from Mount Athos, wrote their own kings into the calendar of saints, and carried hesychast prayer into the Slavic world.
voices: Stefan Nemanja — the Serbian ruler who abdicated, became the monk Symeon, and died at Hilandar
Sava of Serbia — his son, co-founder of Hilandar, first archbishop of an autocephalous Serbian church from 1219, author of its monastic charters and of his father's life
Domentijan and Teodosije — the monks who wrote the lives of Sava and gave the Serbian royal-saint genre its classic form
John of Rila — the tenth-century Bulgarian hermit whose monastery became the centre of Bulgarian monastic life
Euthymius of Tarnovo — the last medieval Bulgarian patriarch and head of the Tarnovo literary school, who revised the Slavonic liturgical books
movements.legacy: Both churches survive, as the Serbian and Bulgarian Orthodox Churches. So do their buildings, which are among the most visited in the region — Studenica, where Nemanja is buried, and Rila, still Bulgaria's largest monastery. While Hilandar remains one of the twenty ruling monasteries of Mount Athos. The literary legacy outran the politics. The Tarnovo school's revised Slavonic texts, and the hesychast spirituality carried inside them, travelled north and shaped Russian church life for centuries, and the zhitija, the lives of the royal saints, are foundational texts of Serbian literature to this day.

experienceToday.text: Kraljevo district, Serbia — Studenica Monastery, founded by Stefan Nemanja in the late twelfth century, with its white marble churches and Byzantine frescoes
