Rila Mountains, Bulgaria — Rila Monastery, the country's largest, built around the memory of the hermit John of Rila

movements.name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run as one of the two Great Schism principals - the pre-banked gap. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Cerularius's synodal edict, Anna Komnene's Alexiad, Komnenian synodal records, the Nicaea exile church's documents, Lyons 1274 acta
movements.relationsSummary: The eastern side of the Great Schism, under Patriarch Michael Cerularius: the Komnenian dynasty's restoration, the Latin sack of Constantinople in 1204 and the exile to Nicaea, the return to the capital in 1261, and the union with Rome offered at the Council of Lyon in 1274 and then rejected. This church remained in lasting tension with the Latin papal church in Rome.
movements.why: In July 1054 a papal legate laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and walked out, and the patriarch Michael Cerularius condemned him in return — though neither man believed at the time that he had divided Christendom permanently. The estrangement hardened in 1204, when a crusading army sacked Constantinople, installed a Latin patriarch, and drove the imperial church into exile at Nicaea for nearly sixty years before its return in 1261. In 1274, needing Western help, Emperor Michael VIII accepted union with Rome at the Second Council of Lyon, but his own clergy and monks refused it and the union collapsed.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 (the Schism) to 1300 (era end; the church continues — era-6 receiver at the A1.E6 run) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In July 1054 a papal legate laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia during the liturgy and walked out. The patriarch, Michael Cerularius, condemned him in return. Neither man believed he had divided Christendom, and for a long time nobody treated the breach as final. But the estrangement between the Greek and Latin churches did not heal, and it hardened catastrophically in 1204, when a crusading army sacked Constantinople, installed a Latin patriarch, and drove the imperial church into exile at Nicaea for nearly sixty years. The Byzantines returned in 1261. In 1274, needing Western help against his enemies, Emperor Michael VIII accepted union with Rome at the Second Council of Lyon. His own clergy and monks refused it, and the union collapsed.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, and Nicaea in exile, 1054 to 1300 — the eastern half of a quarrel nobody at the time thought was permanent, made permanent by a crusader army.
voices: Michael Cerularius — the patriarch at the centre of the events of 1054
Anna Komnene — imperial princess and historian, whose Alexiad is one of the great first-hand accounts of the age and of her father's dealings with Latins and heretics alike
Michael VIII Palaiologos — the emperor who retook Constantinople in 1261 and then accepted a union with Rome that his own church rejected
The monks and lower clergy — collectively the decisive voice against union in 1274, remembered as a body rather than as named individuals
movements.legacy: This is the eastern half of a division that has still not been repaired: the Eastern Orthodox churches today trace their institutional continuity through this church, and the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople remains the first see among them. The sack of 1204 left a memory that shaped Orthodox attitudes to the West for centuries; Pope John Paul II offered an apology for it in 2001, nearly eight hundred years later. And the pattern set in 1274 — union agreed by an emperor and refused by his own clergy and people — would repeat at Florence in 1439 with the same result. The same church continued into the next era through the Palaiologan period.

movements.name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
movements.informalName: The Roman Church of the Reform Popes
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run as the other Great Schism principal - the church every Latin era-5 entry lived inside, absent in every era. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Humbert's bull, Dictatus Papae, Investiture Contest dossiers, Lateran I-IV constitutions, Innocent III's registers
movements.relationsSummary: The western side of the Great Schism: Leo IX's reform circle, the Investiture Contest, the Lateran councils, and the rise of the papal monarchy, in lasting tension with the Byzantine church. This era's story also carries the national churches of the age — Anselm and Becket's England, Capetian France, and the Reconquista — along with the rise of the universities, scholastic theology, and the crusading ransom orders.
movements.why: A circle of reformers around Pope Leo IX set out in the mid-eleventh century to free the church from lay lords who appointed its bishops and sold its offices, and ended by claiming for the papacy an authority no bishop of Rome had held before — Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 asserted that the pope alone could depose an emperor, producing the Investiture Contest and the scene of Emperor Henry IV waiting in the snow at Canossa. What followed was a working papal monarchy, with canon law codified in Gratian's Decretum and legates and councils across Latin Christendom. Under Innocent III, the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 legislated for the whole Latin church, from the definition of the eucharist to a requirement that every Christian confess once a year.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1049 (Leo IX opens the reform era; start-before-era extension granted at this Freeze) to 1300 (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In the middle of the eleventh century a circle of reformers around Pope Leo IX set out to free the church from the lay lords who appointed its bishops and sold its offices. And ended by claiming for the papacy an authority no bishop of Rome had exercised before. Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 asserted, among much else, that the pope alone could depose an emperor. The resulting Investiture Contest ran for half a century and produced the extraordinary scene of Emperor Henry IV waiting in the snow outside Canossa. What followed was a working papal monarchy. Canon law codified, legates everywhere, a run of great councils at the Lateran, and under Innocent III, who reigned from 1198 to 1216, a papacy that arbitrated between kings, authorized the new friars, called crusades, and in 1215 legislated at the Fourth Lateran Council for the whole Latin church — from the definition of the eucharist to the requirement that every Christian confess once a year.
movements.teaser: Rome and all of Latin Christendom, c. 1049 to 1300 — the church every Western order and movement of the age lived inside, remade from a local bishopric into a monarchy that could summon kings.
voices: Leo IX — the reforming pope whose circle set the whole movement going
Humbert of Silva Candida — the cardinal who drafted the reform's sharpest arguments and delivered the excommunication at Constantinople in 1054
Gregory VII — pope of the Dictatus Papae and of the confrontation with Henry IV
Gratian — the canonist whose Decretum, compiled around 1140, gave the Western church a usable body of law
Innocent III — under whom the papal monarchy reached its widest reach, and who summoned the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215
movements.legacy: It never stopped: this is the Roman Catholic Church, and the institutional shape worked out here — a legally defined papal primacy, a professional canon law, a college of cardinals electing the pope, general councils legislating for the whole church — is substantially the shape it still has. Fourth Lateran's requirements of annual confession and Easter communion formed lay Catholic practice for the next seven centuries. So did darker parts of the same programme: the same council imposed distinguishing dress on Jews and Muslims living in Christian territory, and the machinery of inquisition took its permanent form in these decades. The claims made here are also the ones the Reformation would eventually be a protest against. The same institution continued into the next era through Avignon and the Fifth Lateran Council.

experienceToday.text: Rome, Italy — the Archbasilica of St John Lateran, the pope's own cathedral and the setting of the great Lateran councils of 1123, 1139, 1179 and 1215

movements.name: Kievan Rus' Christianity, 1054-1240
movements.informalName: The Church of Kyiv and the Caves
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich with tier care: the Kyiv Caves Paterik and Primary Chronicle are later compilations reaching back into this window; Theodosius's tradition
movements.relationsSummary: A continuation of Rus' Christianity's first generations, centered on the Kyiv Caves Monastery, with native-born metropolitans appearing alongside the usual Greek ones sent from Constantinople. It ended with the Mongol sack of Kyiv in 1240.
movements.why: In the two centuries after Yaroslav the Wise died in 1054, the Kyiv Caves Monastery grew from a hermit's hillside cave — dug by Anthony — into a community under its abbot Theodosius, who gave it a Byzantine rule built on humility, manual work and care for the poor. Out of that monastery came bishops, chronicles and a native literature, even though the church was formally headed by Greek metropolitans sent from Constantinople. It ended abruptly when the Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 (Yaroslav's death — III.8's gated end) to 1240 (Mongol sack of Kyiv); the 1240-1340 yoke gap to V.8 stays disclosed, routed to A1.E6 (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In the two centuries after Yaroslav the Wise died in 1054, the Christianity that had arrived in Rus' only two generations earlier put down roots of its own. Its centre was the Caves Monastery at Kyiv, begun by a hermit named Anthony in a hillside cave above the Dnieper and turned into a community by Theodosius, its third abbot, who gave it a Byzantine rule and a distinctive emphasis on humility, manual work and care for the poor. Out of that monastery came bishops, chronicles, and a book of stories about its own monks. The church was formally a metropolitanate of Constantinople, usually headed by a Greek, but native metropolitans appeared and a native literature and a native calendar of saints grew up around the princely dynasty. It ended abruptly: the Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240.
movements.teaser: Kyiv, Novgorod and Vladimir-Suzdal, 1054 to 1240 — a young church growing its own saints, chronicles and monasteries out of a hillside cave, until the Mongols ended it in a single season.
voices: Anthony of the Caves — the hermit who dug the first cave in the hillside above the Dnieper
Theodosius of the Caves — the abbot who made it a community, and whose insistence on humility and manual work set the tone of Rus' monasticism
Hilarion of Kyiv — the first native-born metropolitan and author of the Sermon on Law and Grace, the earliest surviving work of Rus' theology
Nestor — the monk traditionally credited with much of the Primary Chronicle and with early lives of the Rus' saints
Boris and Gleb — the murdered princes who became the first saints canonized in Rus', venerated for refusing to fight back
movements.legacy: The Caves Monastery survived the sack and is still there — the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, with its underground galleries of relics — one of the most important monastic sites in the Orthodox world and, in the twenty-first century, contested ground between rival Ukrainian church jurisdictions. The literature this church produced, the Primary Chronicle above all, is the foundation document of East Slavic history, and the cult of Boris and Gleb, princes venerated precisely for not fighting back, became a distinctive strand in Slavic sanctity. Who inherits Kyiv's legacy — Kyiv, Moscow, or both — is a question with live political weight to this day, and the century of Mongol rule that followed 1240 leaves a real gap in the record between this church and the Muscovy that later claimed it.

experienceToday.text: Kyiv, Ukraine — the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, the Monastery of the Caves, begun in the eleventh century above the Dnieper

movements.name: Armenian Christianity in Cilicia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate with a first-rank interior voice: Nerses Shnorhali's corpus (ecumenical letters to Manuel I, prayers, laments); Nerses of Lambron; catholicosate records at Hromkla
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Coptic churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The Armenian church in exile became a kingdom's church: the catholicosate moved to the fortress of Hromkla in 1151, Nerses Shnorhali carried on ecumenical correspondence with the Byzantine emperor seeking reunion between the Armenian and Greek churches, and Levon I was crowned king in 1198. The kingdom itself fell in 1375.
movements.why: After the Seljuk conquest of the Armenian homeland, Armenians resettled in Cilicia on the Mediterranean coast, where the catholicos moved his seat to the fortress of Hromkla in 1151. There Nerses Shnorhali, 'the Gracious,' wrote the finest Armenian religious poetry of the age and carried on a long, generous correspondence with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I about reuniting the Armenian and Greek churches — a reunion that never happened. The Cilician church spent the following century negotiating instead with the neighboring Latin crusader states, a closeness some Armenians welcomed and others resented deeply.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1080 (Rubenid consolidation; catholicosate at Hromkla 1151) to 1300 (era end; the kingdom falls 1375 — era-6 receiver flagged) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: After the Seljuk conquest of the Armenian homeland, Armenians resettled in Cilicia on the Mediterranean coast, where a principality grew into a kingdom — Levon I was crowned in 1198. And the Armenian church went with them. In 1151 the catholicos moved his seat to Hromkla, a fortress above the Euphrates, and there Nerses Shnorhali, 'the Gracious', wrote the finest Armenian religious poetry of the age and conducted a long and remarkably generous correspondence with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I about reuniting the Armenian and Greek churches. The reunion never happened. The Cilician church spent the following century negotiating instead with the Latin crusader states next door. A closeness that some Armenians welcomed and others resented deeply, and that shaped the church's arguments with itself for generations.
movements.teaser: Cilicia, on the Mediterranean coast, c. 1080 to 1300 — an Armenian church in exile that became a kingdom's church, whose greatest poet spent his life writing letters trying to end a seven-hundred-year division.
voices: Nerses Shnorhali — catholicos, poet and hymn-writer, whose letters to Emperor Manuel I are the era's most serious attempt at reunion between the Armenian and Byzantine churches
Nerses of Lambron — archbishop of Tarsus, who pushed the same conciliatory line further and was attacked at home for it
Levon I — crowned king of Armenian Cilicia in 1198, who bound the kingdom closely to the Latin West
Toros Roslin — the illuminator working at Hromkla whose manuscripts are regarded as the summit of Armenian book art
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church continues, and this period is a load-bearing part of it: the catholicosate established here still exists as the Catholicosate of Cilicia, now seated at Antelias in Lebanon, one of the two catholicosates of the Armenian church. Shnorhali's hymns and prayers are still sung and prayed, and his long penitential prayer cycle remains one of the most used devotional texts in Armenian. The manuscript illumination produced in Cilicia in these years, Roslin's above all, is among the treasures of medieval art.

experienceToday.text: Gaziantep province, Turkey — Rumkale, the Euphrates fortress the Armenians knew as Hromkla and used as their catholicosate, now reached by boat from Halfeti

movements.name: The Syriac Renaissance
movements.informalName: The Age of Michael and Bar Hebraeus
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich - the strongest eastern attestation of the era: Michael the Syrian's chronicle (the greatest in Syriac), Dionysius bar Salibi's commentaries, Bar Hebraeus's polymath corpus
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Coptic churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The West Syriac church's intellectual summit, reached under Muslim rule and during the crusader period. A later medieval decline followed.
movements.why: Living under Muslim rule, and for a while alongside the crusader states, the Syriac Orthodox Church produced its best writing in four hundred years in this period. Michael the Syrian, patriarch from 1166, compiled a world chronicle that quotes at length from earlier writers whose own books are otherwise lost, while Dionysius bar Salibi commented on the whole Bible and the liturgy. Gregory Bar Hebraeus, who died in 1286, wrote across history, theology, canon law, grammar, astronomy and medicine in both Syriac and Arabic, while serving as his church's chief bishop for the eastern provinces under Mongol rule.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 to 1300 (era window; Michael the Syrian 1166-1199 and Bar Hebraeus d. 1286 inside) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Syriac Orthodox Church lived under Muslim rule, and for a while alongside the crusader states, in the country between the Euphrates and the Tigris. And in exactly this period it produced its best writing in four hundred years. Dionysius bar Salibi commented on the whole Bible and on the liturgy. Michael the Syrian, patriarch from 1166, compiled a world chronicle that remains one of the most valuable historical sources for the medieval Middle East, not least because he quotes at length from earlier writers whose books are otherwise lost. And Gregory Bar Hebraeus, who died in 1286, wrote across nearly everything — history, theology, canon law, grammar, astronomy, medicine, and a collection of jokes. In both Syriac and Arabic, and did it while serving as his church's chief bishop for the eastern provinces under Mongol rule.
movements.teaser: The Jazira and Melitene, 1054 to 1300 — a church living inside other people's empires that answered by writing everything down: a world chronicle, commentaries on the whole Bible, and one polymath who covered nearly every subject there was.
voices: Dionysius bar Salibi — bishop of Amid, who commented on the entire Bible and on the liturgy
Michael the Syrian — patriarch from 1166, whose chronicle preserves whole earlier histories that would otherwise have vanished
Bar Hebraeus — maphrian of the East, historian, theologian, grammarian, astronomer and physician, who wrote in Syriac and Arabic and whose learning was admired well beyond his own church
movements.legacy: The Syriac Orthodox Church continues today, with its patriarchate now in Damascus and a large diaspora. The books written here never went out of use. Michael's chronicle and Bar Hebraeus's histories are still primary sources for anyone working on the medieval Middle East, and Bar Hebraeus's canonical and grammatical works stayed standard in the Syriac churches for centuries. This period is generally reckoned the last great flowering of Syriac letters before the long contraction that followed, which is why later Syriac writers kept looking back to it.

experienceToday.text: Mount Alfaf, near Mosul, Iraq — the Syriac Orthodox monastery of Mor Mattai, long associated with Bar Hebraeus and still maintained by the church

movements.name: The Church of the East under the Mongols
movements.informalName: The Church of Bar Sauma and Yahballaha
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate with a genuine inside travel text: the History of Rabban Bar Sauma and Yahballaha III; Kerait conversion tradition; Prester John material rides inside as labeled legend
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the same faith as the wider Church of the East.
movements.relationsSummary: The Church of the East gained new access at the Mongol court: Rabban Bar Sauma's embassy to Europe in 1287, and the election of his former pupil as Patriarch Yahballaha III, who held the office from 1281 until his death in 1317.
movements.why: When the Mongols swept west, many of the peoples they absorbed — the Kerait and the Öngüd among them — were already Christian in the Church of the East tradition, as were several of the great khans' wives and mothers, giving the church real access at the Mongol court. In 1281 a monk who had travelled the whole width of Asia from China was elected catholicos as Yahballaha III, while his teacher Rabban Bar Sauma ended up as the Ilkhan's ambassador to the West, reaching Rome and the courts of France and England and writing the journey down. Yahballaha died in 1317, and the church's favour at court did not survive him.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1220 (the Mongol rise carries the church back into documented view) to 1317 (Yahballaha III's death; one boundary crossing — the 1300+note branch was shown and declined) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Church of the East had spread far into Central Asia centuries earlier, and when the Mongols swept west a good many of the peoples they absorbed — the Kerait and the Öngüd among them — were already Christian in this tradition, as were several of the great khans' wives and mothers. For a few decades the church that Latin Europe called Nestorian had extraordinary access: tolerated and sometimes favoured at the Mongol court, and in 1281 a monk who had travelled the whole width of Asia from China was elected its catholicos as Yahballaha III. His teacher, Rabban Bar Sauma, had set out with him on pilgrimage toward Jerusalem and ended up instead as the Ilkhan's ambassador to the West, reaching Rome and the courts of France and England and writing the journey down — one of the very few medieval descriptions of Europe by a traveller from Asia. Yahballaha died in 1317, and the favour did not survive him.
movements.teaser: Central Asia, Persia and China, c. 1220 to 1317 — the church Europe called Nestorian, briefly favoured at the Mongol court, whose head had walked there from China and whose ambassador reached Rome and Paris.
voices: Yahballaha III — catholicos from 1281 to 1317, a monk from the far east of the Mongol world elected to head a church whose politics were not his own
Rabban Bar Sauma — his teacher and travelling companion, sent west as the Ilkhan's envoy in 1287, whose account of Rome and the Frankish courts survives
Sorghaghtani Beki and Doquz Khatun — Christian women of the Mongol ruling house whose position gave the church much of its access at court
movements.legacy: The Church of the East still exists, but this was its last period of long reach. The Mongol elite in Persia turned to Islam within a generation of Yahballaha's death, and the fourteenth century brought the catastrophe — Timur's campaigns above all — that reduced a church once stretching from Cyprus to China to a mountain remnant in Hakkari. Its traces are now mostly archaeological: Syriac gravestones scattered across Central Asia, Christian tomb carvings in the Chinese port cities. The account of Bar Sauma's embassy remains the single most remarkable thing this period produced.

movements.name: The Carmelites
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Rule of Albert, written between 1206 and 1214, survives, but interior voice beyond the Rule itself is thin in this period. The order's great voices, Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross, belong to a later century.
movements.relationsSummary: One of the mendicant orders alongside the Franciscans and Dominicans: hermits on Mount Carmel who received a rule of life from Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, later approved as a formal Rule in 1247, after migrating west in the 1230s and 1240s as the crusader states contracted.
movements.why: Between 1206 and 1214, hermits living in a wadi on Mount Carmel asked Albert, the patriarch of Jerusalem, for a written way of life, and what he gave them was short and severe: separate cells, silence, work, daily Mass and constant meditation on the law of the Lord. As the crusader states contracted, the hermits moved into England, France and Italy, where their rule was adapted into a mendicant order and approved by Innocent IV in 1247. They kept the mountain in their name and, in later retellings, traced their origins all the way back to the prophet Elijah.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1206 (Albert's formula vitae, 1206-1214 — survey's c. 1200 sharpened on the Rule's own dating) to 1300 (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Some time between 1206 and 1214 a group of Latin hermits living in a wadi on Mount Carmel above the bay from crusader Acre asked Albert, the patriarch of Jerusalem — who kept his seat at Acre — for a written way of life. What he gave them was short and severe: separate cells, silence, work, daily Mass, and constant meditation on the law of the Lord. As the crusader states contracted the hermits moved west, into England, France and Italy, where a hermit's rule made little sense in a town — so the life was adapted into a mendicant order alongside the Franciscans and Dominicans, and Innocent IV approved the revised Rule in 1247. The order kept the mountain in its name and in its self-understanding, and traced its origins, in its own later retellings, all the way back to the prophet Elijah.
movements.teaser: Mount Carmel and then the towns of Europe, c. 1206 to 1300 — hermits on a Holy Land mountain who lost the mountain, moved to Europe, and had to work out what a hermit is for in a city.
voices: Albert of Jerusalem — the patriarch who wrote the hermits their short rule between 1206 and 1214
Innocent IV — the pope who approved the adapted Rule in 1247, turning the hermits into a mendicant order
The first Carmelites are anonymous — the community that asked Albert for a rule left no names, and the order's own accounts of its earliest years were written much later
movements.legacy: The Carmelites are still here, and their greatest period was still ahead of them. The sixteenth-century Spanish reform that produced Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross grew directly out of this rule, and their writings became the standard vocabulary of Western contemplative prayer. The brown scapular, one of the most widespread Catholic devotional objects, comes from the order. Though the story of its being handed to Simon Stock in a vision is a later legend rather than documented history. Albert's Rule itself remains the order's foundation text, one of the shortest and most durable religious rules in the Western church.

experienceToday.text: Haifa, Israel — the Stella Maris monastery on Mount Carmel, the Carmelites' house on the mountain the order is named for

movements.name: Balkan Bogomilism, 1054-1300
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence carried forward from III.13 (register; one verified witness, two [S]; own voice unrecovered)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run as the receiver of III.13's register - the movement demonstrably continues. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Hostile-only: Anna Komnene on Basil the physician's burning (c. 1100-1118), Zigabenos's commissioned Panoplia chapter, the Synod of Tarnovo's anathemas (1211, Book of Boril).
movements.floorNote: Everything known about them comes from people writing against them, and by those accounts they held that the visible, material world was not the good God's making — a position outside the common Christian creed. Their own voice has not survived. The Bosnian Church, which older accounts often folded into this movement, is treated separately here; most current scholarship no longer regards the two as the same thing.
movements.relationsSummary: A continuation of an earlier Bogomil current: Basil burned in the Hippodrome under Alexios I, Zigabenos wrote against them, Tarnovo anathematized them in 1211; claimed parent of the Cathars - a claim, not an established line of descent.
movements.why: By this period the Bogomils, who began in tenth-century Bulgaria, held no church buildings, no clergy in the ordinary sense and no sacraments as the wider church understood them, teaching that the material world and the visible church alike belonged to an evil power. Around 1100 the emperor Alexios I had a Bogomil teacher named Basil brought to Constantinople, drew out his beliefs by pretending to be a convert, and had him burned in the Hippodrome — a story his daughter Anna Komnene tells, and which the theologian Euthymios Zigabenos was commissioned to write up for refutation. A synod at Tarnovo anathematized them again in 1211, and not one line survives that a Bogomil wrote about themselves.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 to 1300 (continues-cap convention; the survey's c. 1230 branch was shown and declined — no event; last anchor Tarnovo 1211) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Bogomils began in tenth-century Bulgaria and were still there, and in Byzantine territory, throughout this period. What their opponents describe is a movement with no church buildings, no clergy in the ordinary sense, no sacraments as the church understood them, and a teaching that the material world and the institutions of the visible church alike belonged to an evil power. Around the turn of the twelfth century the emperor Alexios I had a Bogomil teacher called Basil brought to Constantinople, drew out his beliefs by pretending to be a convert, and had him burned in the Hippodrome. The emperor's daughter Anna Komnene tells the story, and Alexios commissioned the theologian Euthymios Zigabenos to write the movement up for refutation. In 1211 a synod at Tarnovo anathematized them again. Not one line survives that a Bogomil wrote about themselves.
movements.teaser: Bulgaria, Thrace and Macedonia, 1054 to 1300 — a movement that rejected the visible church entirely, known to us only in the words of the emperors, bishops and synods that hunted it.
voices: Basil the physician — a Bogomil teacher tricked into explaining his beliefs by the emperor Alexios I and burned in the Hippodrome at Constantinople
Euthymios Zigabenos — the theologian commissioned to write against them, whose chapter is the fullest surviving description of their teaching
Anna Komnene — the imperial historian who recorded Basil's interrogation and death
No Bogomil voice survives — every name we have was recorded by an enemy, and nothing written by the movement itself has ever been recovered
movements.legacy: Nothing continued, and almost nothing remains — no buildings, no books, no descendants. Their long afterlife is instead an argument. Medieval writers, and many modern ones, have treated the Bogomils as the source of the Western dualist movements, the Cathars especially, and the English word 'bugger' descends by way of 'Bulgar' from that association. Whether any actual line of transmission ran from the Balkans to Languedoc is disputed and probably unprovable. The Bosnian Church, often bundled in with them in older accounts, is now generally handled by scholars as a separate question.

movements.name: The Latin Church of Outremer
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 5 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally (patriarchate records, canons of the Holy Sepulchre, pilgrim liturgy); interior devotional voice thinner than the military orders' - disclosed
movements.relationsSummary: A transplanted Latin church with its own hierarchy: patriarchates of Jerusalem (1099, Greek patriarch expelled - the Schism lived on the ground) and Antioch; moves to Acre 1187, falls with it 1291
movements.why: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, the conquerors built a whole Latin church on top of an existing Christian landscape, installing a Latin patriarchate and expelling the Greek patriarch, with the canons of the Holy Sepulchre at its center and a liturgy shaped by processions to the holy places themselves. It governed a population that was mostly not Latin — Greek, Syriac, Armenian, Muslim — with dealings that ranged from workable accommodation to outright dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre, and when Acre fell in 1291 the church of Outremer ended with it.
movements.dateRationale: 1099 (Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem erected) to 1291 (fall of Acre) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099 the conquerors did not simply add a diocese. They built a whole Latin church on top of an existing Christian landscape, erecting a Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem and expelling the Greek patriarch, and then another at Antioch. For nearly two centuries this transplanted hierarchy ran parishes, cathedrals and an enormous pilgrim traffic to the holy places, with the canons of the Holy Sepulchre at its centre and a distinctive liturgy shaped by processions to the sites themselves. It governed a population that was mostly not Latin — Greek, Syriac, Armenian, Muslim — and its dealings with those communities ranged from workable accommodation to plain dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre, and when Acre fell in 1291 the church of Outremer ended with it.
movements.teaser: Jerusalem, Antioch, Acre and Cyprus, 1099 to 1291 — a whole Latin church transplanted onto ground that already had four of its own, which lasted exactly as long as the states that carried it.
voices: Daimbert of Pisa — an early Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, whose quarrels with the kingdom's rulers set the pattern of friction between church and crown
William of Tyre — archbishop, chancellor of the kingdom, and the great historian of Outremer, whose chronicle is the indispensable source for it
Jacques de Vitry — bishop of Acre, preacher and letter-writer, who described the mixed society he found there in unusual detail
The Greek patriarchs of Jerusalem in exile — displaced in 1099 and continuing their line from Constantinople, a standing reminder that this church was built by removing another
movements.legacy: It left no continuing institution in the East. When Acre fell, the Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem became a title without a diocese and stayed that way for more than five centuries, until it was restored as a working see in 1847. What survived instead is stone and story. The church of the Holy Sepulchre, largely rebuilt in this period, is substantially the building pilgrims enter today, and crusader castles and churches from Acre to Cyprus are among the best-preserved medieval buildings in the region. William of Tyre's history became the standard Western account of the crusades for centuries. The long memory of Outremer among Eastern Christians, who experienced it as occupation rather than liberation, is part of the legacy too.

experienceToday.text: Akko (Acre), Israel — the old city, where the Hospitallers' vaulted halls and much of the crusader street plan survive beneath and beside the later Ottoman town

movements.name: Coptic Christianity, Fatimid to Mamluk
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred pending source verification (Era 5 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run with its attestation carried [S] - a named source-base verification is required before any build. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: The clearest evidence comes from its 13th-century Copto-Arabic golden age: the al-Assal brothers' canon-law and theological writings, and Patriarch Cyril III ibn Laqlaq's own record.
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Ethiopian churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.why: Egypt's Christians lived under a poll tax and alternating tolerance and persecution through the Fatimid period, and slowly shifted from Coptic into Arabic as their everyday language. In the thirteenth century, one Cairo family — the four sons of al-Assal — turned that shift into a renaissance, writing canon law, theology, biblical scholarship and Coptic grammars and dictionaries in Arabic to keep the old language from being lost. Their patriarch for part of that stretch, Cyril III ibn Laqlaq, was a learned and combative man who gathered the church's authority into his own hands.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1054 to 1300 — attestation [S]; window and anchors require the named source-base verification before any build (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: By this period Egypt's Christians had lived under Muslim rule for four centuries, and the shape of their life was set by that: a poll tax, stretches of tolerance under the Fatimids alternating with sharp episodes of persecution, and a slow shift out of Coptic and into Arabic as the everyday language. What they did with Arabic is the surprise. In the thirteenth century a single Cairo family, the sons of al-Assal, produced a body of work — canon law, theology, biblical scholarship, philosophy, and Coptic grammars and dictionaries written in Arabic to keep the old language from being lost entirely — that amounted to a renaissance of Coptic learning in a new tongue. Their patriarch for part of that stretch, Cyril III ibn Laqlaq, was a learned and combative man who spent his reign gathering the church's authority into his own hands.
movements.teaser: Egypt, c. 1054 to 1300 — a church losing its own language and answering by writing its whole inheritance down again in Arabic, in what turned out to be its greatest literary century.
voices: The awlad al-Assal — four brothers of one Cairo family, al-Safi, al-Mu'taman, al-As'ad and al-Amjad, whose canon law, theology, biblical scholarship and Coptic grammars are the heart of this period's achievement
Cyril III ibn Laqlaq — patriarch from 1235 to 1243, a cultivated and contentious man who reorganized the church's government around himself
movements.legacy: The Coptic Orthodox Church is very much alive — the largest Christian community in the Middle East — and runs unbroken through this period. The work done here lasted: the al-Assal brothers' canonical collections stayed authoritative in the Coptic church for centuries and were carried south into Ethiopia, where the Fetha Nagast, the law book of the Ethiopian state into the twentieth century, derives from al-Safi's canons. Their grammars and dictionaries are much of the reason the Coptic language is recoverable at all today. The Hanging Church in Old Cairo, which served as the patriarch's seat for most of this period, is still standing and still in use.

experienceToday.text: Old Cairo, Egypt — the Hanging Church of St Mary, built over a Roman gatehouse and the residence of the Coptic patriarchs through most of this period

movements.name: The Humiliati
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 5 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate, verified: condemned in Ad abolendam (1184), reconciled by Innocent III (1201) as three orders; rule and order documents survive
movements.relationsSummary: Lay penitential wool-workers condemned alongside the Waldensians and then re-absorbed - the mirror-image of IV.8: same 1184 condemnation, opposite outcome
movements.why: In twelfth-century Lombardy, lay wool-workers and weavers took up plain dress, manual labor and a rejection of the oath-taking and violence expected of feudal society, calling themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' Condemned alongside the Waldensians in 1184 for preaching without permission, they took the opposite path: Pope Innocent III reconciled them in 1201, organizing them into three orders, two religious and one for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life. They remained a real presence in northern Italian towns for roughly two centuries, until the movement was suppressed by papal bull in 1571.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1170 to 1300 (Ad abolendam 1184 and the 1201 reconciliation inside the window) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In twelfth-century Lombardy, groups of lay wool-workers and weavers began living out a simple, demanding vision of penitence — plain dress, manual labor, and a rejection of the oath-taking and violence expected of feudal society. And called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' In 1184 they were condemned alongside the Waldensians for preaching without official permission, but where the Waldensians' story became one of lasting separation, theirs took the opposite turn. Pope Innocent III reconciled them in 1201, organizing them into three recognized orders. Two religious, one for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life under a shared rule. For roughly two centuries afterward they remained a real presence in northern Italian towns, their rule and community records still surviving, until the movement was formally suppressed by papal bull in 1571.
movements.teaser: Lombardy, c. 1170 to 1300 — lay wool-workers who traded feudal violence and oath-taking for penitence and plain labor, condemned alongside the Waldensians and then, unlike them, welcomed back.

sources.work: Catholic Encyclopedia: Humiliati
sources.note: Overview of origins, rule, papal reconciliation, and 1571 suppression.

voices: No individual founder is named in the record — the Humiliati were fundamentally a lay collective, organized by trade and locality rather than around a founding figure
movements.legacy: No clear record survives of lasting influence beyond their own two centuries — when the order was suppressed by papal bull in 1571, its distinct identity ended with it.

movements.name: The English Mystics and Devout
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich, first-person and vernacular, carrying two women's voices, with the census's own judgment that Margery Kempe's Book may be the atlas's best ordinary-believer document left standing. Its end was moved to c. 1440, when the corpus's last major document was completed, replacing a 1450 that matched nothing.
movements.sourcing: Rich, first-person, and vernacular, with two women's voices at its center: Julian of Norwich's Showings and Margery Kempe's Book, which may be the richest surviving account of an ordinary medieval believer's own life.
movements.relationsSummary: Carthusians copied and preserved these texts (documented transmission)
movements.why: Julian of Norwich, enclosed for decades in a cell beside a Norwich church, kept revising her account of sixteen revelations until it reached the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe, a mother of fourteen who could not write, dictated a book about her pilgrimages, her uncontrollable public weeping, and the heresy examinations she survived. Both voices reach us mainly because Carthusian monks copied and preserved the texts.
movements.dateRationale: End c. 1440 (Margery Kempe's Book completed c. 1436-38 [S] - the corpus's last major document; the old 1450 matched nothing; keep-1450-as-reception alt was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Julian of Norwich, Showings (trans. Colledge & Walsh, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1978; Short and Long Texts)
sources.note: A named woman's first-person theological writing, revised over a lifetime, in the vernacular. A modern critical alternative exists: Watson & Jenkins, The Writings of Julian of Norwich (2006).

sources.work: The Book of Margery Kempe (trans. Barry Windeatt, Penguin Classics, 1985)
sources.note: An illiterate townswoman's dictated life: pilgrimage, weeping, heresy examinations survived - among the richest surviving accounts of an ordinary medieval believer's life. It was dictated to two scribes, and the priest-scribe's shaping hand is part of the text.

sources.work: The teaching corpus: Richard Rolle, The Fire of Love; Walter Hilton, The Scale of Perfection; The Cloud of Unknowing
sources.note: The movement's formation texts, written for anchoresses, recluses, and devout laity. Editions: Penguin (trans. Wolters); Hilton in Classics of Western Spirituality (trans. Clark & Dorward, 1991).

sources.work: The Carthusian transmission layer: the unique Kempe MS (BL Add. 61823, Mount Grace annotations), the Amherst MS of Julian's Short Text, The Chastising of God's Children; plus Arundel's Constitutions (1409) as counter-pressure
sources.note: Physical evidence that Carthusians copied and preserved these texts, set against the era's censorship of vernacular theology.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Varieties of Vernacular Mysticism 1350-1550 (Presence of God vol. 5, 2012)
sources.note: Current standard frame; Nicholas Watson's censorship scholarship is the key work on the Arundel context.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)
sources.note: Coverage of the English vernacular mystics specifically within this chapter is inferred rather than confirmed page by page.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1330 to 1440 — hermits, anchoresses and a weeping townswoman who wrote about God in English, in the first person, when almost nobody else did.
movements.longDescription: Across a single century a scattering of English men and women began writing about the inner life of prayer in their own language rather than in Latin — Richard Rolle the Yorkshire hermit with his Fire of Love, Walter Hilton with the Scale of Perfection, and the anonymous author of The Cloud of Unknowing, all writing for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars. Two of the voices are women's. Julian of Norwich, an anchoress enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church, spent decades revising an account of sixteen revelations she had received during a near-fatal illness, arriving at the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe, a brewer's wife and mother of fourteen from Bishop's Lynn who could not write, dictated to scribes a book about her pilgrimages, her uncontrollable public weeping and the heresy examinations she survived. The closest thing the period leaves us to an ordinary believer's own life story. That any of it reaches us at all is largely owed to Carthusian monks, who copied the texts and kept them safe.
voices: Richard Rolle — Yorkshire hermit whose Fire of Love helped make devotional writing in English popular
Walter Hilton — Augustinian canon whose Scale of Perfection became the era's standard guide to the interior life
The anonymous author of The Cloud of Unknowing — never identified, writing for a single young disciple about praying beyond thought
Julian of Norwich — anchoress of Norwich, the first woman known to have written a book in English
Margery Kempe — a Lynn townswoman who could not write and dictated her life instead, producing what is often called the first autobiography in English
movements.legacy: The writings outlived their authors by way of a long silence. Margery Kempe's Book was known only from a few short printed extracts until the single surviving manuscript was identified in a private family library in 1934, and Julian's Revelations circulated quietly among Carthusians and English exiles for centuries before reaching a wide readership in the twentieth. Both are now among the most read of all medieval English religious books. Julian is commemorated each May in the Church of England's calendar, and her cell — destroyed centuries ago, its foundations uncovered after wartime bombing and rebuilt — is again a place people travel to pray in.

experienceToday.text: St Julian's Church, Norwich — the rebuilt cell on the site of Julian's anchorhold, open daily

movements.name: Rhineland Mysticism & the Friends of God
movements.informalName: The Rhineland Mystics and the Friends of God
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base of sermons and sister-books, with one tier-care nuance carried: the sermons survive 'as delivered' only through listeners' transcripts, and the sister-books are collective women's memory rather than individual witness. Eckhart's condemnation stayed where its floorNote puts it — an intra-Catholic language contest, carried rather than resolved.
movements.sourcing: Rich: sermons as delivered to convents; sister-books as collective women's memory
movements.floorNote: Eckhart was condemned over how he said things, not over what the Creed says — and the argument about him has never really been settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Dominican line; feeds Devotio Moderna and (via Theologia Deutsch) Luther
movements.why: Dominican preachers here had to invent a German vocabulary for the inner life the language did not yet have, and Meister Eckhart pushed it furthest, speaking of a 'birth of God' within the soul in terms that got him tried for heresy and, after his death, condemned by papal bull. Much of what survives does so because nuns wrote sermons down as they were preached and compiled their own convents' sister-books. Out of the same circle came the Theologia Deutsch, a book Martin Luther printed twice and said had taught him more about God than almost anything but the Bible and Augustine.

sources.work: Meister Eckhart, The Essential Sermons, Commentaries, Treatises and Defense (trans. Colledge & McGinn, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1981)
sources.note: Latin and German works, with his trial Defense. The papal bull In agro dominico (1329) condemned 28 of his propositions, taken out of context, after his death - an institutional condemnation that has shaped how his legacy has been read ever since.

sources.work: Johannes Tauler, Sermons (trans. Shrady, CWS, 1985) and Henry Suso, The Exemplar (trans. Tobin, CWS, 1989)
sources.note: Tauler preaching to Dominican nuns; Suso's Life of the Servant, co-produced with Elsbeth Stagel - a man's interior life reaching us through a woman's editorial hand. These sermons survive as listeners' transcripts and convent copies, not the preacher's own manuscript.

sources.work: The Dominican convent Sister-Books (Schwesternbuecher: Toess, Unterlinden, Engelthal, St Katharinental and kin); study-with-translations: Gertrude Jaron Lewis, By Women, for Women, about Women (PIMS, 1996)
sources.note: Nuns writing their own communities' graces, austerities, and deaths - collective women's memory in its own genre. English translations exist only piecemeal.

sources.work: Theologia Deutsch (trans. Bengt Hoffman, The Theologia Germanica of Martin Luther, CWS, 1980)
sources.note: The anonymous Frankfurt priest's treatise from the Friends of God milieu. The standard English translation is made from Luther's own 1518 edition, so the Luther connection is built into how the text reaches English readers at all. Rulman Merswin's Friends-of-God literature stands behind it.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Harvest of Mysticism in Medieval Germany (Presence of God vol. 4, 2005)
sources.note: Current standard on exactly this ecosystem, Eckhart through the Sister-Books.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)

movements.teaser: The Rhineland and Switzerland, c. 1300 to 1400 — Dominican preachers who tried to say in German what theology had only ever said in Latin, and the nuns who wrote it down.
movements.longDescription: Along the Rhine a generation of Dominican preachers — Meister Eckhart, Johannes Tauler, Henry Suso — began preaching in German to convents of nuns and to devout lay people, and in doing so had to invent a vocabulary for the inner life that the language did not yet have. Eckhart pushed furthest, speaking of the ground of the soul and of a birth of God within it in terms that got him put on trial for heresy. He died before the case closed, and in 1329 a papal bull condemned twenty-eight propositions drawn from his work, which is how his memory reached everyone who came after. Around Strasbourg and Basel a mixed circle of clergy and laypeople who called themselves Gottesfreunde, the Friends of God, carried the same piety outside the cloister, and out of that milieu came the anonymous Theologia Deutsch. Much of what survives survives because women preserved it. Nuns took sermons down as they were delivered, convents compiled sister-books recording their own communities' lives, and Elsbeth Stagel worked with Suso on the book of his own life.
voices: Meister Eckhart — Dominican preacher and master of theology at Paris, tried for heresy at the end of his life and condemned after his death
Johannes Tauler — Eckhart's most widely read successor, preaching to nuns and townspeople at Strasbourg
Henry Suso — wrote the Life of the Servant, an unusually personal spiritual autobiography, together with his correspondent Elsbeth Stagel
Elsbeth Stagel — Dominican nun of Töss, Suso's collaborator, and the writer credited with her convent's sister-book
Rulman Merswin — a Strasbourg banker who gave up his business for the Friends of God and endowed their house on the Green Isle
movements.legacy: Its influence ran far past its own century. The Devotio Moderna in the Low Countries grew in its wake, and the Theologia Deutsch reached Martin Luther, who printed it twice — a partial text in 1516 and a fuller one in 1518. And wrote that apart from the Bible and Augustine no book had taught him more about God and about himself. Tauler's sermons went on being read by Catholics and Protestants alike for centuries. Eckhart, condemned in his own lifetime, was rediscovered in the nineteenth century and has been read ever since by philosophers, theologians and religious writers well outside the church that condemned him.

movements.name: Devotio Moderna / Brethren of the Common Life
movements.informalName: The Brethren of the Common Life
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base — customaries, the brothers' and sisters' lives, rapiaria and the Imitation — and named a rare both-directions ancestor, feeding Luther's schooling and Jesuit pedagogy alike. Its end was moved to 1517 under the continues-cap convention, replacing a round-number 1500, since its houses ran into the sixteenth century and dissolved under the Reformation.
movements.sourcing: RICH: customaries, brothers' and sisters' lives, rapiaria, the Imitation of Christ
movements.relationsSummary: Parent-influence on both Luther's schooling and Jesuit pedagogy - a rare both-directions ancestor
movements.why: Geert Grote gave up a wealthy career to gather devout men and women into households that lived in common without ever taking vows, supporting themselves by copying manuscripts. Their habit of keeping a personal notebook of gathered readings, a rapiarium, produced Thomas a Kempis's Imitation of Christ, the most copied Christian book after the Bible. Their schools shaped Erasmus and touched Luther's own education, and the same disciplined, interior devotion later fed into Jesuit formation.
movements.dateRationale: End 1517 (continues-cap: the houses run into the 16th c. and dissolve under the Reformation; the old 1500 was a round non-event; keep-1500+note alt was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Devotio Moderna: Basic Writings (ed./trans. John Van Engen, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1988)
sources.note: Geert Grote's own writings (incl. Resolutions and Intentions - a layman's self-rule), lives of the Brothers and Sisters, customary material, from Latin and Middle Dutch - founder's voice and communal texture in one volume.

sources.work: Thomas a Kempis, The Imitation of Christ (c. 1418-27)
sources.note: The movement's mass-formation engine - the era's most copied book after the Bible, grown out of the rapiarium practice. Countless editions exist, with no single standard translation.

sources.work: The sisters' houses literature: vitae of the Sisters of the Common Life at Deventer (Master Geert's House) and Diepenveen
sources.note: Collective women's memory in the movement's own genre; partly available in Van Engen's volume, though the fuller corpus survives only in Middle Dutch.

sources.work: Gerard Zerbolt of Zutphen, The Spiritual Ascents, plus the rapiarium practice
sources.note: The movement's method text - interiorized, graded devotion for people in ordinary life - and its distinctive excerpt-book genre.

sources.work: John Van Engen, Sisters and Brothers of the Common Life (Penn, 2008)
sources.note: Current standard, by the corpus's own translator.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 26 'Empowerment through reading, writing and example: the Devotio Moderna' (Goudriaan)
sources.note: A dedicated chapter, one of the strongest reference fits for this movement. Its influence on Luther and the Jesuits reaches beyond 1500, but the movement's own historical window closes around that year.

movements.teaser: The Low Countries, c. 1380 to 1517 — devout townspeople who lived in common without taking vows, kept notebooks of what they read, and produced the most copied book of the Middle Ages after the Bible.
movements.longDescription: It began with Geert Grote, a wealthy and worldly Deventer scholar who gave up his career, opened his own house to a group of devout women, and started preaching repentance in the towns of the IJssel valley. After his death in 1384 his followers organized: Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life, living together and supporting themselves by copying manuscripts and other ordinary work, without vows and without leaving ordinary society, alongside a stricter branch of canons at Windesheim. What held them together was less a doctrine than a method — a plain, interior, methodical devotion, and the habit of keeping a rapiarium, a personal notebook of gathered passages to return to. One such gathering, worked up by Thomas à Kempis at a house near Zwolle, became the Imitation of Christ. The houses also took in schoolboys and shaped the Latin schools of towns like Deventer and Zwolle, which is how the movement's formation reached far more people than ever joined it.
voices: Geert Grote — Deventer deacon and preacher whose turn from a wealthy career started the movement
Florens Radewijns — Grote's successor, who gathered the scattered devout into the Brothers of the Common Life
Gerard Zerbolt of Zutphen — set out the movement's graded method of interior devotion for people living ordinary lives
Thomas à Kempis — canon at Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, credited with the Imitation of Christ

No single founding figure holds the women's side of the movement: the Sisters' houses at Deventer and Diepenveen recorded their lives collectively, in books written by and about the community rather than any one member
movements.legacy: The Imitation of Christ never stopped circulating. After the Bible it is the most widely copied and printed Christian book of the era, and it is still in print in dozens of languages. The movement's schooling shaped people who then went in opposite directions. Erasmus was educated at Deventer, Luther spent a school year at Magdeburg in a household connected with the Brethren, and the ordered, interior, personal devotion the movement taught fed into Jesuit formation a century later. The houses themselves did not survive the century they helped bring about; most dissolved during the Reformation.

movements.name: Hesychasm & the Palamite Synthesis
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — theologically rich in Palamas's Triads, the synodal tomoi and Cabasilas as a lay-facing formation voice, but narrower in communal texture than the era's Tier 1 set. The institutional side of its story was placed in the Palaiologan patriarchal entry added at the same gate, and its succession from the Athonite entry, until then carried only in prose, was regularized as an identity link.
movements.sourcing: Rich theologically; Cabasilas is a genuinely lay-facing formation voice
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of Athonite line; parent of the Philokalia line (Eras 7-8)
movements.why: Monks on Mount Athos practiced hesychia, sitting in stillness and repeating the Jesus Prayer until some reported seeing an uncreated light. When the scholar Barlaam mocked the practice, Gregory Palamas defended it by arguing that God is unknowable in his essence yet truly given in his energies, a case that church councils upheld between 1341 and 1351. Alongside the monks, the layman Nicholas Cabasilas wrote The Life in Christ to show that the same life in God reached people who would never enter a monastery.

sources.work: Gregory Palamas, The Triads (ed. Meyendorff, trans. Gendle, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1983)
sources.note: In Defense of the Holy Hesychasts (1338-41) - the synthesis's cornerstone in the movement's leading voice.

sources.work: The synodal tomoi of 1341, 1347, 1351 (and 1368), in Norman Russell, Gregory Palamas: The Hesychast Controversy and the Debate with Islam (Translated Texts for Byzantinists, Liverpool, 2020)
sources.note: The conciliar documents that made hesychasm the Orthodox norm, most translated into English for the first time here. These are the winning side's records - the anti-Palamite side (Barlaam, Akindynos, Gregoras) is largely untranslated and reaches us mainly through its condemnations.

sources.work: The hesychast method texts: Nikephoros the Monk On Watchfulness, ps.-Symeon's method, Gregory of Sinai - as carried in the Philokalia (vol. 4, trans. Palmer, Sherrard & Ware)
sources.note: The Philokalia is a 1782 compilation - a later, retrospective anthology of these 14th-century texts, not a contemporary one.

sources.work: Nicholas Cabasilas, The Life in Christ (trans. deCatanzaro, SVS Press, 1974)
sources.note: Sacramental life for people outside the monastery, by a lay theologian of hesychast Thessalonica. His Commentary on the Divine Liturgy is a companion work.

sources.work: John Meyendorff, A Study of Gregory Palamas (1959; Eng. 1964), with Norman Russell, Gregory Palamas and the Making of Palamism in the Modern Age (OUP, 2019)
sources.note: Classic frame plus current corrective on how 'Palamism' was retrospectively systematized.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 4 'The rise of hesychasm' (Krausmuller)
sources.note: This era is the chapter's home ground - a direct fit.

movements.teaser: Mount Athos and Thessalonica, c. 1300 to 1400 — monks who repeated a single sentence of prayer until it prayed itself, and the archbishop who argued that what they saw was really God.
movements.longDescription: On Mount Athos monks had long practised hesychia, stillness. Sitting alone, controlling the breath, and repeating the Jesus Prayer until it continued of itself — and some of them reported seeing an uncreated light. When the Calabrian scholar Barlaam ridiculed the practice, Gregory Palamas, an Athonite monk who later became archbishop of Thessalonica, answered him in the Triads. God is unknowable in his essence and yet genuinely given in his energies, so what the praying monk meets is God himself and not some created substitute. The argument ran for two decades and was settled by councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351, which vindicated Palamas and made the hesychast position the standard of Orthodox theology. Beside it stands a very different voice. Nicholas Cabasilas, a layman of Thessalonica, who wrote The Life in Christ to show that the same life in God was given through the sacraments to people who would never enter a monastery.
voices: Gregory Palamas — Athonite monk and archbishop of Thessalonica, who gave the practice its theological defence
Gregory of Sinai — carried the hesychast method from Athos into the Balkans
Nicholas Cabasilas — a layman of Thessalonica who wrote about the same life in God for people outside the monastery
Barlaam of Calabria — the scholar whose attack on the hesychasts forced the whole argument into the open
Philotheos Kokkinos — the bishop who wrote up the council's decree, and who later, as patriarch, had Palamas declared a saint in 1368
movements.legacy: It became, and remains, the mainstream of Orthodox theology and prayer. Palamas was declared a saint in 1368, and the second Sunday of Great Lent is still kept in his memory across the Orthodox world. The texts of the hesychast masters were gathered in 1782 into the Philokalia, which carried the practice into Russia and Romania, into the nineteenth-century monastic revival, and — through the anonymous Russian book The Way of a Pilgrim. Into the hands of ordinary readers who had never seen a monastery. The Jesus Prayer is prayed today by a great many people who have never heard of the fourteenth-century controversy that defended it.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the monastic peninsula where the practice took shape, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (visits are by permit and restricted to men)

movements.name: Lollardy
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on the honest mix its sourcing names — hostile trial records that nonetheless preserve ordinary artisans' and women's own stated beliefs, alongside real internal texts. The person-defined check its floorNote ordered was run at this gate and cleared: the movement outgrew Wycliffe, and the beliefs the records preserve are scripture-centred rather than Wycliffe-centred.
movements.sourcing: Hostile trial records preserving ordinary artisans' and women's stated beliefs, plus real internal texts
movements.floorNote: No creedal question: Lollards disputed the church's wealth, its authority and its sacramental teaching, not the Creed. Nor is this simply one man's following — the movement outlasted Wycliffe by well over a century, and what the trial records preserve are ordinary believers' own scripture-centred convictions rather than an Oxford theologian's system.
movements.relationsSummary: Contested influence line to the English Reformation
movements.why: Lollardy grew out of Oxford theologian John Wycliffe's attacks on church wealth and papal authority into a movement carried mainly by ordinary people: weavers, smiths, tailors, wives, and widows who met in each other's houses to read scripture aloud in English. England made burning for heresy the law in 1401 and drove the movement underground after a failed rising in 1414, yet the trial records built to convict Lollards ended up preserving some of the fullest surviving statements of what ordinary medieval believers actually thought. Around two hundred and fifty manuscripts of the Wycliffite Bible still survive, more than of any other Middle English text.

sources.work: John Wyclif's own corpus: Trialogus (trans. Stephen E. Lahey, CUP, 2013), with the Latin works in the Wyclif Society editions
sources.note: The academic source the movement outgrew — kept distinct here from the movement's own later texts, since Lollardy demonstrably became more than Wyclif's own teaching.

sources.work: Anne Hudson (ed.), Selections from English Wycliffite Writings (CUP, 1978; repr. Toronto MART, 1997)
sources.note: Twenty-seven texts of 1385-1425 by the movement itself - Twelve Conclusions, Bible tracts, polemic, doctrine.

sources.work: English Wycliffite Sermons (ed. Hudson & Gradon, 5 vols, Oxford, 1983-96)
sources.note: The movement's formation machinery: a complete vernacular preaching corpus for the liturgical year.

sources.work: Norman Tanner (ed.), Heresy Trials in the Diocese of Norwich, 1428-31 (Camden 4th ser. 20, 1977)
sources.note: These are the persecutors' own records, including abjurations extracted under coercion — hostile evidence, but evidence that still preserves ordinary artisans' and women's stated beliefs (Hawisia Moone's recorded confession is a digest of lay Lollard belief). Foxe's later martyrology is a partisan, later account.

sources.work: Anne Hudson, The Premature Reformation (Oxford, 1988), with Shannon McSheffrey, Gender and Heresy (1995)
sources.note: The field's standard, plus the contested question of women's actual place in Lollard communities.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 28 'Wycliffism and Lollardy' (Ghosh)
sources.note: A dedicated chapter, a direct fit for the 1380-1520 period covered here. The contested question of Lollardy's influence on the English Reformation belongs to the Reformation period itself.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1380 to 1520 — artisans and household readers who wanted the Bible in English, and got a century and a half of heresy trials for it.
movements.longDescription: Lollardy grew out of the teaching of the Oxford theologian John Wycliffe — who attacked church wealth and papal authority, denied transubstantiation, and argued that scripture should be available in English. But it quickly became something much wider than him. Its adherents were mostly ordinary people: weavers, smiths, tailors, wives and widows who owned or shared vernacular scripture, met in one another's houses to read it aloud, and doubted images, pilgrimage and the priest's power over the sacrament. The response was severe. Burning for heresy was made law in England in 1401, Archbishop Arundel's constitutions of 1409 forbade unlicensed translation of scripture into English, and Sir John Oldcastle's failed rising in 1414 made Lollardy treason as well as heresy. After that the movement went underground and survived as scattered household networks into the 1520s. Almost everything we know about those households comes from the records their prosecutors kept — because to convict someone you first had to write down what they said.
voices: John Wycliffe — the Oxford theologian whose writings gave the movement its arguments, though it outlived and outgrew him by well over a century
Sir John Oldcastle — the knight whose rising in 1414 failed and turned Lollardy into a political crime; he was executed in 1417
William Sawtrey — a parish priest, the first person burned for heresy in England, in 1401
Hawisia Moone — a Norfolk woman whose confession at the heresy trials of 1428-31, extracted under pressure, is one of the fullest surviving statements of what ordinary Lollards believed
movements.legacy: Whether Lollardy fed directly into the English Reformation is still argued over by historians. What is not in doubt is that Lollard communities in the Chilterns, Essex, Coventry and Kent were still being prosecuted in the 1520s, exactly where and when the first English evangelicals appear, and that some of the same families turn up in both sets of records. Its most concrete survival is physical: around two hundred and fifty manuscripts of the Wycliffite Bible still exist, more than of any other Middle English text. A strange sort of monument for a movement its opponents believed they had stamped out.

movements.name: The Hussite & Bohemian Brethren Movement
movements.informalName: The Hussites and the Bohemian Brethren
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), and named unique as a functioning non-Roman national church a century before Luther. Two record corrections landed at the Freeze: an origin note recording that its Prague formation (1402–14) precedes Hus's burning, and a fix to its renewal line, which had placed the Moravians at Herrnhut in the wrong era. The absence of an Era 7 entry for its Unitas segment was flagged forward rather than filled.
movements.sourcing: Rich: confessions, hymnody, discipline records
movements.relationsSummary: A functioning non-Roman national church a century before Luther. It took shape in Prague between 1402 and 1414, before Hus was burned, and its stricter branch was later renewed as the Moravian Church at Herrnhut in Saxony.
movements.why: Jan Hus preached reform in Czech for over a decade before being burned as a heretic in 1415, and the shock turned a university movement into a national one built around a single demand: that ordinary lay people, not only priests, should receive the wine at communion. Hussite armies beat back crusade after crusade, and in 1436 Bohemia won something no other medieval dissent ever had, legal recognition for its own church. A stricter, pacifist branch, the Unity of the Brethren, printed what is often called the first hymnbook in a European vernacular by 1501.

sources.work: The Letters of John Hus (trans. Matthew Spinka, Manchester, 1972)
sources.note: All 105 surviving letters and documents, from Latin and Czech - his own voice, including the Constance prison letters.

sources.work: Peter of Mladonovice, John Hus at the Council of Constance (trans. Spinka, Columbia, 1965)
sources.note: The eyewitness Relatio by Hus's companion - a sympathetic account that also embeds the council's own hostile record of the charges and condemnation.

sources.work: The Four Articles of Prague (1420), Hussite and Taborite manifestos, war songs, and chronicle excerpts, in Thomas Fudge, The Crusade against Heretics in Bohemia, 1418-1437 (Crusade Texts in Translation 9, Ashgate, 2002)
sources.note: 208 documents from Czech, German, and Latin, most translated into English for the first time - the movement's own program and its enemies' bulls printed side by side.

sources.work: The Unity of Brethren (from 1457): Gregory the Patriarch's letters, the Brethren's confessions, discipline ordinances, and hymnody culminating in the first printed vernacular hymnal (1501); Peter Chelcicky's Net of Faith as its intellectual spring
sources.note: Confessions, hymnody, and discipline records from the movement's second, pacifist generation. English translations exist only piecemeal, mostly through Moravian-tradition scholarship.

sources.work: Howard Kaminsky, A History of the Hussite Revolution (California, 1967), with Thomas Fudge, Jan Hus: Religious Reform and Social Revolution in Bohemia (2010)
sources.note: The standard history, alongside a current entry.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 28 'Wyclif's Bohemian reception' (Ghosh) and ch. 15 'Sacramental life' (Rubin)
sources.note: No chapter is dedicated specifically to the Hussites; these are the nearest anchors - one on Wyclif's Bohemian reception, the other on utraquism as a sacramental claim.

movements.teaser: Bohemia, 1415 to 1517 — a whole country that took communion in both kinds, was crusaded against five times for it, and kept its own church anyway.
movements.longDescription: Jan Hus preached reform in Czech at Prague's Bethlehem Chapel for more than a decade before the Council of Constance burned him as a heretic in 1415. The shock turned a university movement into a national one. Its emblem was the chalice — the insistence that ordinary lay people, and not only priests, should receive the wine at communion. And its programme was set out in the Four Articles of Prague in 1420. When crusades were called against Bohemia, the Hussite armies under Jan Žižka and then Prokop the Bald beat them one after another, and in 1436 the Compacts of Basel conceded what no other medieval dissent ever won: legal recognition. Out of that settlement two bodies grew. The Utraquist church held the parishes and, under George of Poděbrady, for a time the crown itself. And from 1457 the Unity of the Brethren, a smaller, stricter, pacifist body formed at Kunvald under the influence of the layman Petr Chelčický, which by 1501 had printed what is often called the first hymnbook in a European vernacular.
voices: Jan Hus — preacher at Bethlehem Chapel and rector of Prague university, burned at Constance in 1415
Jakoubek of Stříbro — the theologian who restored the chalice to the laity in 1414, giving the movement its emblem
Jan Žižka — the one-eyed and later wholly blind commander who made the Hussite field armies unbeatable
Petr Chelčický — a layman whose Net of Faith rejected war, oaths and social rank, and shaped the Unity of the Brethren
Gregory the Patriarch — founder of the Unity of the Brethren at Kunvald in 1457
movements.legacy: It did not end in 1517. The Utraquist church and the Unity of the Brethren went on as Bohemia's non-Roman churches for another full century, producing the Kralice Bible and, in Jan Amos Comenius, a last bishop who became one of Europe's great educational reformers, before the Habsburg suppression of the 1620s drove them into exile. Remnants of the Unity survived underground and resurfaced in 1722 at Herrnhut in Saxony as the Moravian Church, which still exists worldwide. In Bohemia the memory never went away. 6 July, the day Hus was burned, is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, and Luther, reading Hus a century later, concluded that 'we are all Hussites without knowing it.'

experienceToday.text: Bethlehem Chapel, Prague — rebuilt on its medieval foundations and surviving walls, where Hus preached in Czech

movements.name: The Ethiopian Monastic Flowering
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) and named the atlas's strongest non-European medieval candidate on its own record — royal chronicles and saints' lives in quantity, with the royal-sponsorship gravity treated as a source condition rather than passed over. One nuance was carried: Zara Yaqob's own writings are simultaneously an inside voice and a persecutor's voice toward the Estifanosites. Its end was capped at 1517, the real break of the Gragn war belonging to the next era.
movements.sourcing: RICH: royal chronicles, saints' lives in quantity (royal-sponsorship gravity needs care)
movements.relationsSummary: A continuation of the earlier Aksumite and Zagwe Christian tradition, carried forward under the new Solomonic dynasty.
movements.why: When the Solomonic dynasty took the Ethiopian throne in 1270, a monastic expansion led by Tekle Haymanot and the followers of Ewostatewos carried churches deep into newly conquered regions. The Ewostathians were persecuted for generations over their insistence on keeping Saturday as well as Sunday as a Sabbath, until the emperor Zara Yaqob finally conceded the point in 1450, the same emperor who, as a theological author himself, persecuted the monks of Estifanos for refusing his own required observances. It was all written down in Ge'ez: royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast, the book that gave the dynasty its claimed descent from Solomon and Sheba.
