movements.dateRationale: End 1517 (continues-cap for a living tradition; the real break - the Gragn war 1529-43 [S] - is era 7's and would be a forbidden double-straddle from the 1270 start; keep-1500+note alt was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The royal chronicles: The Glorious Victories of Amda Seyon (trans. Huntingford, Oxford, 1965) and the chronicle of Zara Yaqob (ed./French trans. Perruchon, 1893)
Kebra Nagast (The Glory of Kings) (trans. Budge, 1922; free online)
sources.note: The Solomonic dynasty's own charter myth. Its dating is a live scholarly argument: the text as it survives is an early-14th-century compilation claiming much older authority.

sources.work: The gadl literature of the era's own movements: Gadla Ewostatewos and Gadla Estifanos (Getatchew Haile, The Ge'ez Acts of Abba Estifanos of Gwendagwende, CSCO, 2006)
sources.note: The Estifanosite acts are the persecuted dissenters' own memory of refusing royal-cult conformity under Zara Yaqob — a real counterweight to the royally-sponsored sources that dominate elsewhere.

sources.work: Zara Yaqob's own writings: Mashafa Berhan (Book of Light) and Mashafa Milad
sources.note: A reforming king writing theology and enforcing it — an inside voice for the royal reform, but a hostile source for the movements it condemned, including the Estifanosites.

sources.work: Taddesse Tamrat, Church and State in Ethiopia, 1270-1527 (Oxford, 1972)
sources.note: Still the standard account for exactly this window, written by an Ethiopian historian; current French scholarship (Derat) supplements it.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, 'Church and nation: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tawahedo church (from the thirteenth to the twentieth century)' (Crummey)
sources.note: A direct fit — this period is the chapter's opening ground.

movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 1270 to 1517 — an independent Christian kingdom whose monks argued with its emperors, and often won.
movements.longDescription: When the Solomonic dynasty took the Ethiopian throne in 1270, claiming descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, it did so alongside a monastic expansion that carried churches and monasteries deep into newly conquered regions. The network Tekle Haymanot built in Shewa, and the northern houses founded by the followers of Ewostatewos. The relationship between crown and cloister was contested throughout. The Ewostathians insisted on keeping Saturday as well as Sunday as a Sabbath and were harried for generations before the emperor Zara Yaqob finally conceded the point at a council in 1450. And Zara Yaqob, himself a theological author who reorganized the church and pressed Marian devotion on it, persecuted the monks of Estifanos when they refused the prostrations and observances he demanded. All of it was written down in Ge'ez — royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast, the book that gave the dynasty its Solomonic charter.
voices: Tekle Haymanot — the monastic founder whose Shewan network of houses carried the church across the expanding kingdom
Ewostatewos — whose insistence on keeping both Saturday and Sunday as Sabbaths made his followers a persecuted movement for a century, until the church conceded
Zara Yaqob — emperor, theological author and church reformer, and the persecutor of the monks who would not conform
Estifanos — leader of the monks who refused the emperor's required observances, and who died in confinement for it
movements.legacy: This is a living church. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church still keeps the outcome of the Sabbath argument, still sings the Marian hymnody Zara Yaqob's reign promoted, still worships in Ge'ez, and still traces its great monastic houses to the founders of these centuries. The manuscripts of the period — illuminated gospels, gadl lives of the saints, hymn collections — form one of the largest bodies of medieval Christian literature produced outside Europe. The tradition carried on through the wars and upheavals of the century that followed into the church of tens of millions of members it is today.

movements.name: Muscovite Monastic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — lives, skete rules and the possessors/non-possessors polemics give it a moderate-to-rich base, with the peasant voice acknowledged as thin. Its monastic frame was kept deliberately and said so at the gate: the 1448 autocephaly rides inside this entry rather than prompting a separate institutional one.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: lives, skete rules, the possessors/non-possessors polemics; peasant voice thin
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Kievan + hesychast lines; parent of the Old Believers' tradition and later renewal
movements.why: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the forests north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone, and within a generation his monastery's disciples had founded dozens more, pushing deep into what Russians called the northern Thebaid. The era's sharpest argument was over monastic wealth: Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors wanted monks poor and silent, Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors wanted monasteries endowed and socially useful, and the possessors won at a council in 1503. Andrei Rublev painted his Trinity icon, now the most famous icon ever made, for Sergius's own monastery.

sources.work: Epiphanius the Wise, Life of Sergius of Radonezh (c. 1417-18)
sources.note: The movement's founding hagiography, by Sergius's own disciple. It survives only as reworked through Pachomius the Serb's redactions. English translation is available only in abridged form, in Zenkovsky's Medieval Russia's Epics, Chronicles, and Tales.

sources.work: Nil Sorsky, The Authentic Writings (trans. David Goldfrank, Cistercian Studies 221, 2008; alt. Maloney, CWS)
sources.note: The non-possessor leader's own writings: the Predanie, the Ustav, and four authentic letters - the hesychast tradition transplanted north.

sources.work: Joseph of Volokolamsk, The Monastic Rule of Iosif Volotsky (trans. Goldfrank, Cistercian, 1983)
sources.note: The possessor side's own legislation, so both sides of the possessors/non-possessors dispute are represented in their own words, not through summary.

sources.work: The monastic colonization record: northern founders' lives (Kirill of Beloozero; Zosima and Savvatii of Solovki), foundation charters and land acts; Stoglav (1551) retrospectives
sources.note: Expansion into the Russian north as the movement's lived, economic form. The Stoglav-era (1551) material reflects back on this period from about a century later. The voice of ordinary peasants appears only indirectly, filtered through monastic land documents.

sources.work: David B. Miller, Saint Sergius of Radonezh, His Trinity Monastery, and the Formation of the Russian Identity (2010)
sources.note: Current standard study of cult and colonization together.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, 'Russian piety and Orthodox culture 1380-1589' (Stella Rock)
sources.note: This chapter's time span covers this period directly.

movements.teaser: The Russian north, c. 1340 to 1517 — monks who walked into the forest to be alone, and ended up settling a country.
movements.longDescription: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the woods north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone. Within a generation the monastery that grew up around him had sent out disciples who founded dozens more, pushing ever deeper into the northern forests in what later Russians called the northern Thebaid. The texts followed — Epiphanius the Wise's life of Sergius, the skete rules of Nil Sorsky. And so did the art, since Andrei Rublev's Trinity was painted in Sergius's memory for his own monastery. The period also produced the sharpest argument in Russian church history. Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors held that monasteries should own no land and no peasants and should live by their own labour, while Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors held that endowed monasteries could feed the poor, train clergy and carry the church's work. The possessors won it at the council of 1503. In the middle of all this, in 1448, Russian bishops elected their own metropolitan without waiting on Constantinople — the beginning of an independent Russian church.
voices: Sergius of Radonezh — the hermit whose Trinity monastery became the centre of Russian monastic life and, later, of Russian national memory
Epiphanius the Wise — Sergius's disciple and biographer, who wrote the movement's founding life
Stephen of Perm — missionary to the Komi, for whom he devised an alphabet and translated the services
Nil Sorsky — leader of the non-possessors, who wanted monks poor, few and silent
Joseph of Volotsk — leader of the possessors, who wanted monasteries endowed, disciplined and socially useful
Andrei Rublev — monk and icon painter, whose Trinity was made for Sergius's own monastery
movements.legacy: Almost everything that follows in Russian Christianity runs back through here. Sergius's foundation is still a working lavra and a spiritual centre of the Russian Orthodox Church; the hesychast prayer this generation received from the Greeks resurfaced in the elder movement of the nineteenth century. And the argument between possessors and non-possessors about monastic wealth has been re-fought in Russian religious writing ever since. Rublev's Trinity became the most famous icon ever painted.

experienceToday.text: Trinity Sergius Lavra, Sergiev Posad — Sergius's own foundation, still a working monastery and a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Observant Reform & Popular Preaching
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on Bernardino's sermon-cycles taken down as spoken, with an access limit noted — the 1427 cycle has no complete English translation. The person-defined question its record carried was cleared at this gate: the movement is multi-founder and multi-order, its legitimacy resting on the Rule strictly observed, with the boundary that Savonarola alone would fail that test kept verbatim. Its dates were anchored to c. 1368 (Brugliano) and 1517 (Ite vos).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Bernardino's sermon-cycles taken down as spoken - near-transcripts of mass lay formation
movements.floorNote: No creedal question. Nor does the movement stand or fall with a single figure: it had many founders across several orders, and its claim rested on keeping the Rule strictly rather than on any leader's person. Savonarola, the one Observant whose following really did gather around himself, is the exception rather than the pattern.
movements.relationsSummary: A merge/split test vs. the mendicant traditions, in the Phase One record's own style; the Spanish observance’s context includes the converso crisis (1391-1492) - carried as context with process honesty, never endorsement
movements.why: The Observance began small, with Paoluccio Trinci's handful of friars keeping the Rule strictly at Brugliano in 1368, before spreading across the Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians, and Benedictines alike. Its public face was mass preaching: the forty-five sermons Bernardino of Siena gave in 1427 were taken down live by a listener in the crowd, asides and all, about as close as anyone gets to hearing rather than reading a medieval sermon. Its legacy is mixed: it left behind the low-interest pawn-banks called monti di pietà, still trading today, but John of Capistrano's preaching also drove the persecution of Jewish communities, most notoriously at Breslau in 1453.
movements.dateRationale: Start c. 1368 (Brugliano - Paoluccio Trinci's documented origin; keep-1400 alt was shown); end 1517 (Ite vos, the Franciscan Observance's institutional terminus, doubling as the era boundary; alt 1498 was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Bernardino of Siena, the 1427 Siena sermon cycle (reportatio of Benedetto di maestro Bartolomeo; standard ed. Delcorno, 1989, Italian)
sources.note: Forty-five vernacular sermons taken down as they were spoken, audience reactions included - close to a live recording of a medieval sermon. English translation exists only in selections.

sources.work: John of Capistrano: letters, treatises, and eyewitness accounts of the 1451-56 central-European preaching tours
sources.note: Mass preaching at Vienna, Nuremberg, and Breslau. This includes the movement's darkest episode: at Breslau in 1453, Capistrano led the trial and burning of Jews on host-desecration charges. Those trial records are testimony extracted under coercion by the persecuting side, not neutral evidence. Largely untranslated (Acta Sanctorum; Hofer).

sources.work: The Observance as structure: Observant constitutions and statutes (e.g. the Martinian constitutions, 1430), vicariate records, Bernardino's Latin model-sermon collections
sources.note: The movement's institutional self-organization across Franciscan, Dominican, Augustinian, and Benedictine families. Latin editions only.

sources.work: The reform's women in their own words: Colette of Corbie's Constitutions for the Poor Clares; Caterina Vigri of Bologna, The Seven Spiritual Weapons
sources.note: The Observance's female branch as authors, not subjects - a woman legislating a reform, and an Observant Poor Clare's own formation book.

sources.work: James Mixson & Bert Roest (eds.), A Companion to Observant Reform in the Late Middle Ages and Beyond (Brill, 2015)
sources.note: Current standard, cross-order by design. Treats Savonarola within the Observant frame - on his own he would not fit a movement defined by a single person, since the Observance was always broader than any one figure.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 29 'Observant reform in religious orders' (Roest); cf. ch. 30 'Public purity and discipline' (Rusconi)
sources.note: A dedicated chapter by the Companion's co-editor - a direct fit.

movements.teaser: Italy and Spain, c. 1368 to 1517 — friars who went back to the strict rule, and then preached it to whole cities standing in the square.
movements.longDescription: The Observance began as an argument inside the religious orders: that the Rule should be kept as it was written, not as generations of dispensation had relaxed it. It started small, with Paoluccio Trinci's handful of friars at Brugliano in 1368, and spread across the Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Benedictines alike, until reformed houses formed rival provinces alongside the unreformed ones. Its public face was preaching. Bernardino of Siena drew whole towns into the piazza for sermon cycles that ran for weeks. The forty-five sermons he preached at Siena in 1427 were taken down as he spoke by a listener in the crowd, asides and audience reactions included, which is about as close as anyone gets to hearing a medieval sermon rather than reading one. John of Capistrano did the same across central Europe. The movement's darker side belongs in the same account: Capistrano's preaching also drove the persecution of Jewish communities, most notoriously at Breslau in 1453.
voices: Paoluccio Trinci — began the Franciscan Observance with a few friars at Brugliano in 1368
Bernardino of Siena — the movement's great preacher, whose Siena sermons of 1427 survive as a listener's near-transcript
John of Capistrano — preached to enormous crowds across central Europe, and led the persecution of Jews at Breslau in 1453
Colette of Corbie — reformed the Poor Clares and wrote constitutions for her own branch of the order
Caterina Vigri of Bologna — Observant Poor Clare, painter and writer, whose Seven Spiritual Weapons is a formation book written by a woman for women
movements.legacy: The Observance won. When Leo X divided the Franciscans in 1517 the Observants took the larger share and the order's leadership, and the reforming impulse ran on into the Capuchins a decade later. The same reformed-against-unreformed pattern shaped the Dominicans and Augustinians too, and Observant houses became a seedbed of the Catholic reform of the following century. Two smaller things passed into ordinary use and outlived the movement: the monti di pietà, low-interest municipal pawn-banks promoted by Observant friars from the 1460s as an alternative to ruinous lending — the one established at Siena in 1472 still trades as a bank today. And the radiant IHS monogram Bernardino held up at the end of his sermons, which became a fixture of Catholic devotional art.

experienceToday.text: Basilica of San Bernardino, L'Aquila — built for Bernardino of Siena in the decades after his death, reopened in 2015 after earthquake repairs

movements.name: Late-Medieval Lay Parish Piety
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) for reaching the constituency every other tradition reaches only at its edges, on evidence that is rich but oblique — churchwardens' accounts, wills and primers show practice more than interior voice. Its link to Borromean Milan was reclassified at the gate as exemplar-succession rather than identity: the continuesAs field was removed and the relation carried in prose, given the 43-year gap and the region jump.
movements.sourcing: Rich but oblique: churchwardens' accounts, wills, primers - practice more than interior voice
movements.relationsSummary: This is the religion of the ordinary laity — the everyday practice every other tradition on this map reaches only at its edges. Something like it was built again a generation later in the intensely parish-centred Catholicism of Carlo Borromeo's Milan.
movements.why: For most people in late-medieval England, Christianity was the parish: the mass seen from the nave, the guild joined, the light paid for before an image, the church ale that funded the roof. Ordinary laymen elected as churchwardens managed the money and, on their own initiative, rebuilt naves, raised towers, and hired carvers, while cheap printed books of hours put the same daily prayers into any household that could afford them. Almost none of these people wrote about what they believed; what survives instead is the record of what they did with their money and their time.

sources.work: Churchwardens' accounts: Morebath (ed. Binney, 1904), All Saints' Bristol (ed. Burgess), Bassingbourn and kin
Books of hours and primers: The Prymer or lay folks' prayer book (ed. Littlehales, EETS, 1895-97) and the mass-market horae
sources.note: The ordinary household's actual prayer equipment, surviving in thousands of worn copies.

sources.work: Wills and gild records: bequests for obits, lights, and fabric; the 1389 gild returns; The Lay Folks Mass Book (EETS)
sources.note: Practice documented at the moment of death and in fraternity - the two points where ordinary people wrote themselves down.

sources.work: John Mirk, Festial (ed. Powell, EETS, 2009-11)
sources.note: The era's most-copied English sermon collection, written for parish priests preaching to lay congregations - the closest surviving proxy for what the pew actually heard.

sources.work: Eamon Duffy, The Stripping of the Altars: Traditional Religion in England, c.1400-c.1580 (Yale, 1992; 2nd ed. 2005), with The Voices of Morebath (2001)
sources.note: Duffy's revisionism is a position in a live historiographical argument, not a settled conclusion.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 15 'Sacramental life' (Rubin); cf. ch. 21 'Saints and pilgrimages' (Vauchez)
sources.note: The parish's sacramental round is this chapter's ground. Its coverage ends in 1517, before this practice's continuation into Tridentine parish renewal, which a later volume would cover.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1400 to 1517 — the religion of people who left no writings, reconstructed from what they paid for, prayed from, and left behind in their wills.
movements.longDescription: For most people in late-medieval England, Christianity was the parish. The mass seen from the nave, the yearly round of feasts and processions, the guild you joined, the light you paid to keep burning before an image, the church ale that funded the roof. It was not passive. Churchwardens — ordinary laymen, elected and accountable to their neighbours. Collected and spent the money, and their accounts show parishes rebuilding naves, raising towers, buying vestments and hiring carvers on their own initiative. Books of hours, soon printed by the thousand, put the same daily prayers into the hands of any household that could afford them, and sermon collections like John Mirk's Festial tell us roughly what the pew was hearing. Almost none of these people wrote about what they believed. What survives instead is the record of what they did with their money and their time — a different kind of evidence, and in some ways a more candid one.
voices: No founder, leader or spokesman — this is the religion of the ordinary parish, and it reaches us through churchwardens, guild members and will-makers who are named in the records but who wrote nothing about themselves
movements.legacy: Much of it is still standing. The great parish churches of East Anglia, the Cotswolds and the West Country were built or rebuilt in these decades out of ordinary parishioners' giving, and their towers, painted screens and carved roofs are the largest surviving artefact of late-medieval lay religion anywhere. Most of the rest was deliberately taken apart. The English Reformation abolished the guilds and chantries, whitewashed the paintings and broke up the images, so that what we know of the practice comes largely from accounts that record first its purchase and then its destruction. Something like it was built again elsewhere: the intensely parish-centred Catholicism of Carlo Borromeo's Milan, a generation later, ran on the same instincts under very different rules.

movements.name: Taborite Radicalism
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Chronicled largely by opponents and moderate Hussites
movements.floorNote: No creedal question — Tabor stripped worship back to what it could find in scripture, but the argument was about practice and property, not the Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: Radical wing of V.6
movements.why: In 1420 the most radical wing of the Hussite movement built a fortified town in southern Bohemia, named it Tabor after the mountain of the Transfiguration, and expected Christ's imminent return. When the world did not end, the community stayed, stripping worship down to what it could find in scripture, no vestments, no purgatory, no cult of saints, and for a time holding property in common under its own elected bishop. Its wagon-fort armies broke crusade after crusade before moderate Hussites themselves destroyed the Taborite forces at Lipany in 1434.
movements.dateRationale: String aligned to its own principled numbers (Tabor's founding 1420 to its capitulation 1452); no numeric change (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Taborite manifestos and chiliast articles (1419-20), with the priests' adventist letters, in Fudge, The Crusade against Heretics in Bohemia (Ashgate, 2002)
sources.note: The radicals' own program, in English - mountain assemblies, community of goods, the avenging Christ. Genuine inside texts survive, despite Tabor being chronicled mostly by its opponents.

sources.work: Nicholas of Pelhrimov (Biskupec), Taborite confession and chronicle (Chronicon Taboritarum)
sources.note: The movement's own bishop defending Taborite doctrine and recording its history - the strongest inside text. Available only in Latin editions (Hoefler).

sources.work: Lawrence of Brezova, Hussite Chronicle; John Pribram, The Lives of the Taborite Priests; Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini's account of Tabor (1451)
sources.note: Prague moderates writing against Tabor (Pribram's tract is an intra-Hussite heresiology), plus a later outside papal observer. Partial English translation available via Fudge.

sources.work: Howard Kaminsky, A History of the Hussite Revolution (California, 1967)
sources.note: Still the standard for Tabor's theology-into-politics arc, built directly on these sources.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 28 'Wyclif's Bohemian reception' (Ghosh) and ch. 15 'Sacramental life' (Rubin)
sources.note: No chapter is dedicated specifically to the Hussites or Taborites; these are the nearest anchors, shared with the wider Hussite movement this radical wing belongs to.

movements.teaser: Southern Bohemia, 1420 to 1452 — Hussite radicals who built a town on a hill expecting the world to end, and became the most feared army in Europe instead.
movements.longDescription: In 1420 the most radical wing of the Hussite movement founded a fortified town in southern Bohemia and named it Tábor, after the mountain of the Transfiguration, in the expectation that Christ was about to return and only a few chosen places would be spared. The year passed, the world continued, and the community stayed. Tabor stripped worship down to what it could find in scripture — vernacular liturgy, no vestments, no purgatory, no cult of the saints — elected its own bishop in Nicholas of Pelhřimov, and in its early years held property in common. It also fielded the Hussite wars' most effective army, whose wagon-fort tactics under Jan Žižka and then Prokop the Bald broke crusade after crusade. In the end it was the moderate Hussites of Prague who destroyed it, shattering the Taborite field armies at Lipany in 1434. The town itself surrendered to George of Poděbrady in 1452, and its bishop died in confinement.
voices: Nicholas of Pelhřimov, called Biskupec — the elected Taborite bishop, who defended and chronicled the community's teaching and died a prisoner
Jan Žižka — the Hussite commander who made Tabor's wagon-forts unbeatable, and who also turned on radicals he judged had gone too far
Prokop the Bald — the priest who led the Taborite field armies after Žižka's death
movements.legacy: As a church, nothing continued: Tabor's worship and its community of goods ended with its surrender. Its influence ran two other ways. The wagon-fort tactics its armies perfected were studied and copied across central Europe for a century afterward. And the revulsion of Petr Chelčický and others at what armed radicalism had produced helped push the Unity of the Brethren, founded a few years after Tabor's fall, toward a deliberate and permanent pacifism. The town itself is still there.

experienceToday.text: The Hussite Museum, Tábor — in the old town hall of the town the Taborites founded, with the medieval tunnels beneath it

movements.name: Fraticelli (Spiritual Franciscan rigorists)
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Inquisition-era records
movements.floorNote: Declared heretical over poverty doctrine and obedience, not the creed
movements.relationsSummary: Rupture inside the Franciscan family
movements.why: When Pope John XXII ordered the strictest Franciscans to give up their insistence on absolute poverty, four who refused were burned at Marseille in 1318, and in 1323 he declared it heretical to believe Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. Those who still would not submit, called fraticelli, survived for another century and a half in scattered communities across Italy and Provence, supported by lay sympathizers such as the beguins of Languedoc, who venerated the burned friars as martyrs and were hunted for it in turn. A trial at Rome in the 1460s finally ended them.
movements.dateRationale: End c. 1466 (the great Fraticelli trial at Rome - documented Fraticelli's effective end; the old 1420 matched nothing; the minimum string-only fix was shown); string corrected to 14th-15th c. (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Angelo Clareno, A Chronicle or History of the Seven Tribulations of the Order of Brothers Minor (trans. Burr & Daniel, Franciscan Institute, 2005)
sources.note: The Spirituals' own martyr-history of their persecution inside the order — the movement's own voice, openly partisan and hagiographic in frame. Genuine internal literature survives here, not only inquisition-era records.

sources.work: Peter of John Olivi: the usus pauper treatises and the Apocalypse commentary (condemned 1326)
sources.note: The theological wellspring the rigorists carried - the intellectual layer beneath the movement.

sources.work: John XXII's bulls: Sancta Romana and Gloriosam ecclesiam (1317-18), Cum inter nonnullos (1323)
sources.note: A hostile, institutional source: the papacy's own bulls constituting 'fraticelli' as a legal category and declaring the doctrine of absolute poverty heretical — the obedience-and-property rupture in the church's own words.

sources.work: Inquisition records: the Marseilles friars burned 1318; Bernard Gui's Fraticelli/beguin sections; the Languedoc beguin depositions - English access via Louisa Burnham, So Great a Light, So Great a Smoke (Cornell, 2008)
sources.note: Both hostile and coerced: lay men and women who venerated the burned friars as martyrs are known almost only through their interrogations.

sources.work: David Burr, The Spiritual Franciscans: From Protest to Persecution in the Century after Saint Francis (Penn State, 2001)
sources.note: The standard account, built on both the inside literature and the trial record.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 3 'Religious poverty and the search for perfection' (Kienzle); cf. ch. 23 'Repression and power' (Arnold)
sources.note: This movement sits exactly between these two chapters' subject matter.

movements.teaser: Italy and Provence, the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries — friars who would not give up absolute poverty after the pope made it a heresy to believe in.
movements.longDescription: The Franciscans had argued for a century about how literally to take Francis's poverty, and in the 1310s and 20s the argument was closed by force. John XXII ordered the strictest friars to conform, had four of them burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing, and in 1323 declared it heretical to hold that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. Turning a devotional ideal into a condemned proposition. Those who would not submit became the fraticelli, 'little brothers', a name their prosecutors used as a legal category as much as a description. They survived for another century and a half in the Marches of Ancona, in Provence and in scattered Italian and Greek communities, supported by lay sympathizers. Among them the beguins of Languedoc, who venerated the burned friars as martyrs and were hunted for it. A major trial at Rome in the 1460s effectively ended them.
voices: Angelo Clareno — leader of the surviving rigorists and author of their own history of the order's persecutions
Peter of John Olivi — the theologian of restricted use whose writings the rigorists carried; his Apocalypse commentary was condemned in 1326, decades after his death
Pope John XXII — the pope who made absolute poverty a heresy and gave the fraticelli their name as a category in law
movements.legacy: No community survived and no church descends from them. What survived was the argument. The poverty controversy forced both sides into working out theories of ownership, use and right that fed directly into later Western thinking about property, and the friars who fled the papal court over it — William of Ockham among them — turned the quarrel into political philosophy. It also left the beguins of Languedoc, remembered now almost entirely through the interrogations that destroyed them, and it left the poverty question itself, which kept returning inside the Franciscan family every time it reformed.

movements.name: Inquisition-Record 'Sects' (Adamites and kin)
movements.informalName: The Sects of the Inquisition Records
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Heresiological artifacts in the Free Spirit pattern
movements.why: The Bohemian Adamites of 1421, described in hostile chronicles as a naked, communal, apocalyptic band on an island, and wiped out by the Taborites, left no voice of their own behind. The wider 'heresy of the Free Spirit' survives mainly through a list of errors condemned at the Council of Vienne that circulated among inquisitors as a template, and historians since Robert Lerner's 1972 study have concluded that much of what later depositions 'found' was produced by that template rather than discovered by it. Some of these people were certainly real; what they are recorded as believing may say more about their interrogators than about them.

sources.work: The Bohemian 'Adamites' of 1421: accounts in Lawrence of Brezova's chronicle and later in Aeneas Sylvius; partial English via Fudge's Hussite-crusade volume
sources.note: Hostile, and doubly filtered: a community exterminated by Zizka's own Taborites — radicals describing the radicals they killed. No inside voice survives.

sources.work: Free Spirit-pattern interrogations: John of Bruenn's deposition; the Schweidnitz beguine interrogations (1332)
sources.note: A hostile, coerced source: answers shaped by the questioners' own template for what heresy should look like — the same pattern seen in other Free Spirit cases.

sources.work: The heresiological template itself: Ad nostrum (Vienne, 1312; trans. in Tanner, Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, 1990) and circulating inquisitors' error-lists
sources.note: A hostile construction: the template document that could generate a 'sect' on paper, whether or not one existed in practice.

sources.work: Robert E. Lerner, The Heresy of the Free Spirit in the Later Middle Ages (California, 1972)
sources.note: The scholarly consensus: such "sects" are substantially constructs of the persecutors' own template. For the Adamite case, modern Hussite scholarship (Kaminsky; Fudge) weighs how much reality lay under the atrocity stories.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 23 'Repression and power' (Arnold); cf. ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller)
sources.note: A close fit with the repression chapter: the absence of any inside voice is the central fact these sources show, since no self-standing account from within these groups survives.

movements.teaser: Central Europe, the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries — groups that may have been movements, or may have been what the interrogators already expected to find.
movements.longDescription: Some of the 'sects' in the medieval record are known only from the documents that condemned them. The Bohemian Adamites of 1421 — described as a naked, communal, apocalyptic band on an island in southern Bohemia — appear in the chronicles of people who despised them and in the account of a later outside observer, and the Taborites destroyed them, so no voice from inside survives at all. The wider 'heresy of the Free Spirit' works much the same way. A list of errors condemned at the Council of Vienne circulated among inquisitors as a template, and much of what later depositions 'found' matches that template closely enough that historians since Robert Lerner's work in 1972 have concluded a good deal of it was produced by the questioning rather than discovered by it. Some of these people were certainly real, and some of what they were accused of may well have been true. But the evidence is one-sided, extracted under coercion, and shaped in advance by the questions.
voices: No voice from inside any of these groups survives. Every name we have — John of Brünn, the beguines interrogated at Schweidnitz in 1332, the Adamites of 1421 — reaches us only as a defendant in someone else's record, answering questions written before they were asked
movements.legacy: Nothing institutional survives, and in some cases there may have been nothing to survive: several of these 'sects' may never have existed in the form the records describe. What they left instead is a caution that historians now take seriously. That a confident, detailed list of what a group believed can be an artefact of the procedure that produced it rather than a description of anybody's faith.

movements.name: The Latin Papal Church (Avignon to Fifth Lateran)
movements.informalName: The Church of Avignon, Schism, and Councils
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.18's receiver - the era's headline gap. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Avignon registers, Schism dossiers from all obediences, Constance and Basel acta, Fifth Lateran constitutions; the era of the papacy's own record-keeping explosion
movements.relationsSummary: Seven popes at Avignon (1309-1377); the Great Western Schism (1378-1417) healed at Constance (Martin V, 1417); Basel and the conciliar contest (Haec sancta, Frequens [S on decree specifics]); the Renaissance papacy; Fifth Lateran closes 16 March 1517. Carries inside its story: conciliarism, the Templar trial, Catherine of Siena and Bridget of Sweden (the Avignon-era prophetic women), the Pragmatic Sanction, and the converso context (1391 pogroms, 1478 Inquisition, 1492 expulsion - carried as context with process honesty, never endorsement)
movements.why: In 1309 the popes moved their court to Avignon for nearly seventy years, and when they finally returned to Rome a disputed election left the Latin church with two rival popes, then three. The schism was ended not by a pope but by the Council of Constance, which deposed the rivals, elected Martin V in 1417, and declared that a general council holds its authority directly from Christ, a claim the papacy spent the next generation working to defeat. The Renaissance popes who followed rebuilt Rome around the Vatican Library, the Sistine Chapel, and the new St Peter's, and the Fifth Lateran Council closed its own reform program, having changed very little, just seven months before Luther posted his theses.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.18's gated end) to 1517 (Fifth Lateran's last session, 16 March 1517) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Avignon, Rome and all of Latin Christendom, 1300 to 1517 — two centuries in which the papacy left Rome, split three ways, was put on trial by its own councils, and came back as a Renaissance court.
movements.longDescription: In 1309 Clement V settled the papal court at Avignon, and for nearly seventy years the popes governed the Latin church from the Rhône rather than the Tiber, building the largest Gothic palace in Europe and an administration to match. The return to Rome in 1377 produced something worse. A disputed election the following year left two popes, an attempt to fix it in 1409 left three, and the schism divided every kingdom, university and religious order in the West for a generation. It was ended not by a pope but by a council. Constance, which removed the rival claimants, elected Martin V in 1417, and declared that a general council holds its authority immediately from Christ. The decades after that were a contest over whether that was true, settled in the papacy's favour by the 1440s. The popes who followed rebuilt Rome, founded the Vatican Library, commissioned the Sistine Chapel and began the new St Peter's. The Fifth Lateran Council, which decreed a programme of reform that changed very little, closed on 16 March 1517 — seven months before Luther's theses.
voices: Boniface VIII — whose claim of papal supremacy over kings in 1302 collapsed the following year at the hands of the French crown
Catherine of Siena — a lay Dominican whose letters pressed Gregory XI to bring the papacy back to Rome
Bridget of Sweden — a widowed noblewoman whose revelations, addressed to popes and kings, made the same demand
Martin V — elected at Constance in 1417, the pope who ended the schism
Julius II — who began the rebuilding of St Peter's in 1506
movements.legacy: This is a continuous institution: the same church, reorganized by the Council of Trent a generation later, is the Roman Catholic Church of today. Its material legacy from these centuries is unmissable — the papal palace at Avignon, the Vatican Library, the Sistine Chapel, the basilica of St Peter's begun in 1506. Its constitutional legacy is quieter and longer-running. The conciliar claim that a general council can judge a pope was defeated but never quite died, resurfacing in Gallicanism, in later Catholic reform movements, and in the arguments around the First Vatican Council four and a half centuries afterward. And the reforms that the fifteenth century's councils repeatedly voted and failed to enforce were still outstanding when Luther wrote.

experienceToday.text: The Palais des Papes, Avignon — the popes' fortress-palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site open to visitors year-round

movements.name: The Byzantine Church, Palaiologan Era
movements.informalName: The Church of the Empire's Last Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.17's receiver. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally: the hesychast councils' tomoi (1341/1347/1351), Ferrara-Florence acta (Laetentur Caeli, 1439), Mark of Ephesus's corpus, Gennadius Scholarius's pre-1453 corpus (his patriarchate belongs to VI.17's window); the patriarchal register survives for stretches
movements.relationsSummary: The patriarchal institution of the empire's last century and a half: receives the hesychast councils synodally (V.4 carries the movement and theology - scope split deliberate), signs Florence (1439) and repudiates it at home, falls with the City (29 May 1453); hands to VI.17 (Orthodoxy under the Ottomans, starts 1453) - the clean two-way handoff
movements.why: With the Ottomans closing in, the Byzantine emperor and patriarch signed a union with Rome at the Council of Florence in 1439 in exchange for military help that never adequately came; Mark of Ephesus alone among the Greek bishops present refused to sign, and the union was rejected at home by monks, clergy, and the city itself. Constantinople fell five months after the union was finally proclaimed in Hagia Sophia, on 29 May 1453. The same dying empire produced some of Byzantium's finest art, the mosaics of the Chora church and the painted churches of Mystras among them.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.17's gated end) to 1453 (the fall of Constantinople - meeting VI.17's 1453 start, the clean handoff) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 1300 to 1453 — the church of a dying empire, which in the end chose its theology over its survival.
movements.longDescription: In its last century and a half the Byzantine church governed the shrinking remnant of an empire and still did some of its most consequential work. Synods at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 ruled in favour of the hesychast monks and made Gregory Palamas's theology the standard of Orthodoxy. Then came the harder question. With the Ottomans closing in, the emperor and the patriarch went to Italy and in 1439 signed a union with Rome at the Council of Florence, in exchange for military help that never adequately came. Mark of Ephesus refused to sign. At home the union was rejected by monks, by much of the clergy and by the city, and when it was finally proclaimed in Hagia Sophia in December 1452 it was met with open hostility. Five months later, on 29 May 1453, Constantinople fell. The same era produced the Palaiologan revival in art — the mosaics of the Chora church, the painted churches of Mystras. Some of the finest work Byzantium ever did, made while the state around it was collapsing.
voices: Gregory Palamas — whose theology the synods of these decades established as the Orthodox standard
Mark of Ephesus — the one Greek bishop at Florence who refused to sign the union, and became Orthodoxy's symbol of that refusal
Bessarion — a Greek archbishop who accepted the union, remained in Italy as a cardinal, and whose library helped carry Greek learning west
Gennadios Scholarios — opponent of the union, and the first patriarch of Constantinople under Ottoman rule
movements.legacy: The patriarchate outlived the empire. Within months of the conquest the sultan installed Gennadios Scholarios as patriarch, and the church became the governing institution of the Orthodox population under Ottoman rule for the next four centuries — a continuous line reaching the Ecumenical Patriarchate of today. The union of Florence was formally repudiated and is still a live memory in Orthodox-Catholic relations. And the scholars who left for Italy, Bessarion among them, carried Greek manuscripts and Greek teaching with them into the Renaissance.

experienceToday.text: Mystras, Greece — the ruined Byzantine city of the Palaiologan era, with its painted churches, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: The Waldensians in the Alps
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.8's receiver - the inherited flag the survey reads as cannot-land-by-silence (the survey's gloss of the Freeze record's general discipline, re-attributed at Review Round 1). Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: The barbes' own manuscript books and the inquisition records of the communities they served [S on specific items]; the 1487 crusade bull and its aftermath documented from both sides
movements.floorNote: No question — the charge against them was always discipline and obedience, not doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: The scattered communities the barbes circuit on foot; Innocent VIII's 1487 crusade bull and the Cattaneo crusade (1487-88) - survived; the thread the 1532 Chanforan synod (VI.10) receives at the era-7 gate
movements.why: A century after being condemned, the Waldensians had become something no medieval dissenting movement was supposed to be: a durable, organized underground church, its members living openly as Catholic parishioners and privately as something else. It was held together by the barbes, itinerant preachers who travelled in pairs, memorized scripture in the vernacular, and carried small hand-copied books on a circuit of scattered households across the Alps. They survived a crusade Pope Innocent VIII called against them in 1487, and in 1532 joined the Protestant Reformation outright.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 to 1517 (era window; the 1487-88 Cattaneo crusade survived inside; VI.10's Chanforan 1532 receives at the era-7 gate) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: The Cottian Alps and beyond, 1300 to 1517 — an outlawed church of scattered households, held together by preachers who walked to them.
movements.longDescription: A century and more after being condemned, the Waldensians had become something no medieval dissent was supposed to be: a durable, organized, underground church. Its members lived openly as ordinary Catholic parishioners and privately as something else, in the high valleys of the Cottian Alps between Piedmont and Dauphiné, and in scattered communities in Provence, in Calabria and Apulia, in Germany and Bohemia. What held it together were the barbes — 'uncles'. Itinerant preachers who travelled in pairs, memorized large amounts of scripture in the vernacular, carried small hand-copied books, and worked a circuit of the households. Their existence was known and repeatedly attacked; in 1487 Innocent VIII proclaimed a crusade against them, and the campaign that followed tore through valleys on both sides of the Alps. They survived it.
voices: The barbes are named individually only rarely, and mostly in the records of the people prosecuting them — the church was built so that no single figure held it together, and its continuity rested on the circuit of preachers and the households that sheltered them
movements.legacy: They are the one medieval dissenting movement still here. In 1532, at a synod at Chanforan in the Angrogna valley, the Waldensians of the Alps joined the Protestant Reformation, and the church that resulted still exists as the Waldensian Evangelical Church, based in the same valleys, now in union with Italy's Methodists, with a sister church in Argentina and Uruguay and congregations founded by emigrants in the United States. The valleys themselves keep the memory in place names, in caves and hidden meeting-places, and in a museum network the church runs.

experienceToday.text: Torre Pellice, Italy — the Waldensian Cultural Centre Foundation and its historical museum, in the Alpine valleys the barbes' circuit ran

movements.name: The Church of the East — Timur's Catastrophe and the Hakkari Remnant
movements.informalName: The Mountain Remnant of Asia's Great Church
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.22's terminal receiver. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin and partly late: patriarchal succession lists, colophons, and Timothy II's 1318 synod records survive, but the catastrophe itself is documented mostly from outside the church.
movements.floorNote: No question — the same communion this church has always been in.
movements.relationsSummary: Patriarch Yahballaha III died in 1317 as anti-Christian persecution closed in, and Timur's campaigns between the 1380s and 1405 destroyed the church's lowland dioceses. Survivors held out in the Hakkari mountains — along with the community in India, the one province Timur's armies never reached. In 1552 the church split when part of it entered communion with Rome.
movements.why: For centuries the Church of the East had been the most geographically extensive church on earth, reaching from Baghdad to Central Asia, India, and China, but Timur's campaigns between the 1380s and 1405 destroyed its lowland dioceses along with much of the population that sustained them. What survived did so purely by geography: communities in the Hakkari mountains and around Lake Van and Urmia, where the patriarchate relocated and, over the following century, became hereditary within a single family. The one province Timur never reached was the community on India's Malabar coast, which kept receiving bishops from a patriarch who now governed from a mountain village.
movements.dateRationale: 1317 (Yahballaha III's death - IV.22's gated end) to 1517 (era end; the 1552 Sulaqa split is era 7's) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: From Mesopotamia to the Kurdish mountains, 1317 to 1517 — the collapse of the most widely spread church in the medieval world into a handful of highland valleys.
movements.longDescription: For centuries the Church of the East had been the most geographically extensive church on earth, with metropolitan provinces running from Baghdad across Central Asia to India and China. It ended within a lifetime. When the patriarch Yahballaha III — a monk born far to the east among the Öngüd — died in 1317, the Mongol rulers of Persia had already turned to Islam and made Christians a persecuted minority in Mesopotamia. Then Timur's campaigns between the 1380s and 1405 destroyed the lowland dioceses outright, along with much of the population that had sustained them. What survived did so by geography: communities in the Hakkari mountains and around Lake Van and Urmia, where the patriarchate relocated and where, over the fifteenth century, the office became hereditary within a single family, passing from uncle to nephew. The one province Timur never reached was the community on the Malabar coast of India, which went on receiving bishops from a patriarch who now governed from a mountain village.
voices: Yahballaha III — the last patriarch of the church's Mongol-era expansion, who died in 1317 as the persecutions closed in
Timothy II — patriarch in the years just before the collapse, whose synod of 1318 is among the last acts of the old order
Beyond the patriarchs, the people of this era reach us mainly as names in manuscript colophons — scribes recording who they were, where they were copying, and what was happening around them
movements.legacy: The remnant endured. The hereditary patriarchate that formed in the mountains split in 1552, when part of the church entered communion with Rome, and the two lines run to the present as the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church. Their Syriac liturgy and their manuscript tradition are carried now by communities largely dispersed by the persecutions and displacements of the twentieth century. And the Indian province that outlasted the catastrophe became the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, whose descendants number several million.

movements.name: Terminal Christian Nubia (Late Makuria and Dotawo)
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as III.18's terminal receiver. Era-slot fork (era-6 with standing-rule extension [lead lean] vs adding to Frozen Era 5) is Mark's - AND the III.18 continuesAs write is validator-legal only under the era-5 branch (4->6 is forbidden); under the era-6 lean the relation is carried in a named-gap register line. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Archaeology-grade at both ends (Barshambu's 1317 stela in the converted throne hall; the Gebel Adda letter naming King Joel, 1484; Faras and Tamit inscriptions); inside literary voice thin - the III.18 disclosure pattern
movements.relationsSummary: The Nubian story's actual end: Dongola's throne hall becomes a mosque (1317), Makuria fragments, the successor kingdom of Dotawo persists to King Joel (documented 1484), then the record falls silent (a possible Queen Gaua c. 1520s carried as live-scholarship nuance)
movements.why: Christian Nubia had held the Nile above Egypt since the sixth century, with cathedrals, bishops, and a literature written in Old Nubian, Greek, and Coptic. Its ending took four centuries: the throne hall of the royal palace at Dongola was converted into a mosque in 1317, the kingdom of Makuria fragmented, and a smaller successor kingdom, Dotawo, held on downstream, still issuing documents in Old Nubian under its own king and bishop. The last ruler anyone can name, King Joel, is documented in 1484, and after that the record simply falls silent, no conquest, no massacre, just a population that gradually became Muslim.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 (III.18's gated end) to c. 1484 (King Joel of Dotawo, the last documented; Gaua c. 1520s carried as nuance). Era-6 slot ruled at the Freeze under a standing-rule extension; the III.18 succession FIELD is withheld (4->6 forbidden) - the relation is this entry's named register line (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: The Middle Nile, 1054 to about 1484 — the slow ending of a Christian kingdom that had held the Nile above Egypt for eight hundred years.
movements.longDescription: Christian Nubia had been a going concern since the sixth century: kingdoms with cathedrals and bishops, a literature in Old Nubian, Greek and Coptic, and treaties that kept Muslim Egypt at a distance. Its ending took four centuries and left an unusually physical record. In 1317 the throne hall of the royal palace at Dongola was converted into a mosque, and the stone that records it is still legible. Makuria fragmented after that, and a smaller successor kingdom, Dotawo, persisted downstream around Gebel Adda and Qasr Ibrim, still issuing documents in Old Nubian, still with a king and a bishop. The last of them anyone can name is King Joel, documented in 1484. After that the record simply stops — no conquest, no massacre, no final synod; just documents that cease, and a population that over the following generations became Muslim.
voices: Almost no one from these centuries speaks to us directly. The names we have — King Joel of Dotawo, the bishops in their epitaphs, the officials in the Old Nubian documents from Qasr Ibrim — are names on deeds and tombstones rather than voices, and no Nubian account of the church's own ending survives
movements.legacy: No church continued and no community carried the tradition forward. What survived is material, and was very nearly lost as well. When the Aswan High Dam was built in the 1960s an international rescue campaign lifted the wall paintings out of the cathedral at Faras before the reservoir covered it, and exceptionally dry conditions at Qasr Ibrim preserved a large archive of Old Nubian, Greek, Coptic and Arabic documents. Because of that salvage, a Christian civilization that left no descendants is better documented now than it was a century ago, and its painting can be seen in museums in Warsaw and Khartoum.

experienceToday.text: The Faras Gallery, National Museum in Warsaw — the rescued wall paintings from Faras cathedral, the only permanent display of medieval Nubian painting in Europe

movements.name: The Franciscan Order — Spirituals Crisis to the Great Division
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run - the inherited Franciscan-shape flag resolved as the order's own era-6 entry (the A5-inside-V.14 alternative stays stated). Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: the poverty-controversy dossiers (Quorundam exigit 1317, Cum inter nonnullos 1323), Observant and Conventual records, Ite vos (1517); Clareno and Olivi's internal literature beyond the inquisition record
movements.floorNote: No question — the poverty condemnations were about obedience and property, not the Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: The order between IV.4 (ends 1300) and the 1517 division: the Spirituals crisis (Marseille burnings 1318), Conventual/Observant polarization, Leo X's Ite vos (29 May 1517) splitting the family in two; V.12 Fraticelli and V.9's Franciscan wing are its two named wings
movements.why: By 1300 the Franciscans were an enormous international order with universities and libraries, built by a founder who had told them to own nothing, a strain that broke in the 1310s and 20s when Pope John XXII ordered the strictest friars to conform and had four burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing. The order's minister general, Michael of Cesena, fled the papal court with the philosopher William of Ockham rather than accept John XXII's ruling that owning nothing at all was itself heretical. The argument reshaped into a long split between Conventuals, who kept the order's endowments, and Observants, who rebuilt strict Rule-keeping from 1368, until Pope Leo X divided the family formally in two in 1517.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.4's end) to 1517 (Ite vos, 29 May 1517 - the Great Division) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Across Latin Christendom, 1300 to 1517 — two centuries in which Francis's order argued with itself about poverty until the pope cut it in two.
movements.longDescription: By 1300 the Franciscans were an enormous international order with universities, libraries and buildings, and a founder who had told them to own nothing. The strain broke in the 1310s and 20s. The Spirituals, who wanted the Rule kept to the letter, were ordered to conform; four were burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing. And in 1323 John XXII declared it heretical to teach that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all, which put the order's own official self-understanding on the wrong side of the law. The minister general Michael of Cesena fled the papal court with William of Ockham rather than accept it. The argument did not end so much as change shape, into a long polarization between Conventuals, who accepted the order's endowments and urban convents, and Observants, who from 1368 built up reformed houses keeping the Rule strictly. Leo X ended the pretence of a single order on 29 May 1517, dividing the family formally in two.
voices: Ubertino da Casale — the Spirituals' most forceful advocate at the papal court
Angelo Clareno — led the surviving rigorists and wrote their own history of the order's persecutions
Michael of Cesena — minister general, who defied John XXII over poverty and fled Avignon in 1328
William of Ockham — the philosopher who left with him, and who turned the poverty quarrel into a theory of rights and of the limits of papal power
Pope John XXII — who closed the poverty question by declaring one side of it heretical
movements.legacy: The order is still here, and still divided along the line drawn in 1517. The Order of Friars Minor and the Conventual Franciscans both date their separate legal existence from that bull, and the Capuchins broke away from the Observants a decade later, making three. Beyond the family, the poverty controversy left a real intellectual inheritance. The arguments about use, ownership and right worked out in it, above all by Ockham, fed into later Western thinking about property and about the limits of authority. And the Observant reform that grew out of the crisis became one of the main engines of Catholic renewal in the century that followed.

movements.name: The Bosnian Church (Krstjani)
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run - the question Era 5 routed here, carried with the identification debate honest. Status fork (plain candidate [lead lean] vs Contested-Evidentiary) is Mark's; the c. 1230s start fork has BOTH branches open (standing-rule extension, or start 1300 + origin note if declined). Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Largely external (papal condemnations, Ragusan records); Gost Radin's 1466 testament is the one great inside document - and it reads orthodox, a cross drawn down its margin
movements.floorNote: The old identification of the krstjani as Bogomil dualists has been rejected by most scholarship since the 1970s, so this is not a case of a church known to have departed from Nicene belief. What they actually held is still debated; that the church existed, with its hierarchy of djed, gost and starac and its own monastic houses, is not in doubt. It is treated here as a Slavonic-rite church standing between Rome and Orthodoxy, with the ambiguity acknowledged rather than resolved.
movements.relationsSummary: The autonomous church of medieval Bosnia, condemned by Rome as heretical but defended by its own kings. It ended with the Ottoman conquest: Bosnia fell in 1463, and Gost Radin's testament of 1466 is its last substantial surviving document. The old identification of the church with Bogomil dualism is rejected by most current scholarship.
movements.why: Medieval Bosnia had a church of its own, standing between Catholic Hungary and Orthodox Serbia. Its members called themselves simply krstjani, 'Christians,' worshipped in Slavonic, and were organized under a djed, a 'grandfather,' with gosts and starci beneath him. Rome repeatedly condemned them as heretics while Bosnia's own kings protected them, but what they actually believed remains genuinely disputed: the old identification with Bogomil dualism has been rejected by most historians since the 1970s, and the one substantial document written from inside, Gost Radin's 1466 will, reads like conventional Christianity, a cross drawn down its margin.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1230s (standing-rule extension granted at the Freeze, as drafted) to 1463 (the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia; Radin's testament 1466 just past) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Medieval Bosnia, c. 1230s to 1463 — an independent church whose members called themselves simply Christians, and whose beliefs are still argued over.
movements.longDescription: Between Catholic Hungary and Orthodox Serbia, medieval Bosnia had a church of its own. Its members called themselves krstjani, Christians. It used a Slavonic liturgy, and it had its own hierarchy headed by a djed, a 'grandfather', with gosts and starci under him and communities called hiže, houses, scattered through the countryside. Rome repeatedly condemned it as heretical and periodically sent friars against it, while Bosnia's own rulers protected and made use of it. What its members actually believed remains genuinely disputed. The long-standing identification of them with Bogomil dualism has been rejected by most historians since the 1970s, and the one substantial document written from inside — the will of Gost Radin, made in 1466 — reads like conventional Christianity, with a cross drawn down its margin. Bosnia fell to the Ottomans in 1463, and the church did not outlast the kingdom.
voices: Gost Radin — a senior figure of the church and a courtier, whose testament of 1466 is the only substantial document written from inside it
Ban Kulin — the ruler at whose court, in 1203, an abjuration was made that stands at the disputed beginning of the whole story
Beyond a handful of djeds and gosts who witnessed royal charters, the church's members are anonymous
movements.legacy: Nothing continued. After the Ottoman conquest the krstjani disappear from the record within a generation or two, absorbed into Islam, Catholicism and Orthodoxy, and no later church claims descent from them. What remains is inscriptional and archaeological: charters and grave inscriptions naming djeds and gosts, and the stećci, the great carved limestone tombstones of medieval Bosnia and its neighbours. Though those were raised by Catholics and Orthodox as well, and the once-popular idea that they are specifically a Bosnian Church monument is no longer accepted. The church's other legacy is the argument about it, which became part of Bosnian national self-understanding in the twentieth century and is still running.

experienceToday.text: Stećci medieval tombstone graveyards — 28 necropolises in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Armenian Christianity after the Kingdom (Sis to Etchmiadzin)
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.20's receiver segment. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin after Shnorhali's generation, but colophons are rich: the era's Armenian voice survives mostly in scribes' margins, the notes copyists left at the ends of the manuscripts they made.
movements.floorNote: No question — the ancient miaphysite confession, unchanged.
movements.relationsSummary: The kingdom falls (Sis 1375; Levon V dies in exile 1393); the catholicosate remains at Sis until a national council elects a catholicos at Etchmiadzin (1441) - the seat moves home, with Sis continuing as a second catholicosate. No other Armenian source in the record covers 1441 to 1915, the longest gap in its own documentary history.
movements.why: The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia spent the fourteenth century squeezed between Mamluk Egypt and a Latin Europe pressing for union with Rome, a union its own clergy and people repeatedly resisted. After the kingdom fell to the Mamluks in 1375 and its last king died in exile in Paris in 1393, the catholicosate stayed at Sis for two more generations before a national council in 1441 elected a catholicos at Etchmiadzin, the church's original see, left behind nearly a thousand years earlier. Sis kept its own line of succession too, so the church has had two catholicosates ever since.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.20's gated end) to 1441 (the catholicosate returns to Etchmiadzin - the national spine relocates home) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: From Cilicia to Ararat, 1300 to 1441 — a church that lost its kingdom and moved its see back to where it had started.
movements.longDescription: The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia on the Mediterranean spent the fourteenth century under pressure from Mamluk Egypt and from Latin Europe at the same time: repeated attempts to seal a union with Rome, pressed by kings who needed western help, were resisted by clergy and people who saw the church's independence at stake. The kingdom fell in 1375 when the Mamluks took Sis, and its last king died in exile in Paris in 1393. The catholicosate stayed at Sis for two more generations, increasingly cut off from the great majority of Armenians living far to the east under other rulers, until in 1441 a national council meeting at Vagharshapat elected a catholicos at Etchmiadzin — the church's original see, left behind nearly a thousand years earlier — and the centre of Armenian church life moved home. Sis did not surrender its own succession, so the church has had two catholicosates ever since. Much of what we hear from Armenians of this period comes from colophons. The notes scribes wrote at the ends of the manuscripts they copied, recording who they were and what was happening around them.
voices: Levon V — the last king of Armenian Cilicia, who died in exile in Paris in 1393
Grigor Tatevatsi — theologian of the monastic university at Tatev, whose teaching stiffened Armenian resistance to union with Rome
Kirakos of Virap — elected catholicos at Etchmiadzin in 1441, first of the restored line
The scribes of the colophons — mostly anonymous copyists whose notes at the ends of manuscripts are this era's fullest Armenian account of itself
movements.legacy: Etchmiadzin has been the Mother See of the Armenian Apostolic Church ever since 1441, and remains so today. The see at Sis, whose holder did not move, kept its own succession and continues as the Catholicosate of Cilicia, based since the 1930s at Antelias in Lebanon. The two sees still in communion with one another. The manuscripts of these centuries, colophons and all, form the core of the Matenadaran collection in Yerevan, and the colophon habit has left historians one of the most detailed running records of ordinary catastrophe and survival anywhere in the medieval world.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the Mother See the church returned to in 1441, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Maronite Christianity — the Union Formalized
movements.informalName: The Maronites of Lebanon and Cyprus
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.10's receiver - closing the dead-end with the thread's own defining event inside the window. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin to moderate, and much of it from the Roman side: the Florence union act of 1445 and the Fifth Lateran reception of 1516. Little survives from the patriarchal archive itself for this period.
movements.floorNote: No question — the monothelete dispute is an argument about the church's early history, not about what Maronites confess now.
movements.relationsSummary: Mamluk raids on the Kesrwan around 1305 displaced Christian populations. The Maronites' long-claimed union with Rome — their own self-understanding as a church that was never out of communion with Rome — was formalized when the Maronites of Cyprus were received into union at the Council of Florence on 7 August 1445, and affirmed again during the Fifth Lateran Council in 1516.
movements.why: The Maronites, a Syriac-speaking church of the Lebanese mountains with a patriarch based in the Qadisha valley, survived Mamluk campaigns against the Kesrwan around 1305 largely by remoteness, tucked into monasteries and rock-cut hermitages that armies found too costly to reach. Their long-claimed friendship with Rome was made formal in this era: at the Council of Florence in 1445 the Maronites of Cyprus were received into union with the Roman church, a relationship affirmed again during the Fifth Lateran Council in 1516. Unlike almost every other Eastern church, the Maronites hold that they were never out of communion with Rome at all.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.10's gated end) to 1517 (era end; the union formalized inside - Florence 1445, Fifth Lateran reception 1516) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Mount Lebanon and Cyprus, 1300 to 1517 — a mountain church that turned a long-claimed friendship with Rome into a formal, permanent union.
movements.longDescription: The Maronites were a Syriac-speaking church of the Lebanese mountains, with a patriarch based in the Qadisha valley and communities on Cyprus as well. The fourteenth century opened badly, with Mamluk campaigns against the Kesrwan around 1305 that displaced Christian populations, and for most of the period the church survived largely by remoteness. Monasteries and rock-cut hermitages tucked into a gorge that armies found expensive to enter. Its relationship with Rome, claimed since the crusader period, was made explicit in this window: at the Council of Florence, in an act of 7 August 1445, the Maronites of Cyprus were formally received into union with the Roman church, and the relationship was affirmed again during the Fifth Lateran Council in 1516. Unlike almost every other Eastern church, the Maronites hold that they were never out of communion with Rome at all — a self-understanding that this era's documents put on paper.
voices: Named individuals are scarce in this window: the patriarchs of the period are known mainly from succession lists and from the Roman documents addressed to them, and the era's Maronite voice survives chiefly in liturgical manuscripts and scribes' notes rather than in personal writing
movements.legacy: It is a living church. The Maronite Church remains in full communion with Rome, is the largest Christian body in Lebanon, and has a worldwide diaspora. Its patriarch still carries the title of Antioch, and the Syriac liturgy of these centuries is still in use in developed form. The Qadisha valley stayed the patriarchate's refuge for centuries afterward, and its monasteries and hermitages are still there.

experienceToday.text: Ouadi Qadisha (the Holy Valley) and the Forest of the Cedars of God, Lebanon — the gorge that sheltered the Maronite patriarchate and its monasteries, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: St Thomas Christians, 1300-1517
movements.informalName: The Malabar Church before the Portuguese
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run with St-Thomas-pattern honesty. No continuesAs from III.11 - the eras are non-adjacent; the 1054-1300 gap stays a named register. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin, though richer than in the previous period: a manuscript (Vatican Syriac 22) copied at Cranganore in 1301 — the oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India, naming Patriarch Yahballaha III — plus fourteenth-century travelers' notices, the record of a delegation to the patriarch around 1490 and the bishops' letter of 1504, and accounts from Vasco da Gama's 1498 voyage.
movements.floorNote: No question — the same communion this church has always been in.
movements.relationsSummary: A manuscript colophon from 1301 shows the community's link to its patriarch in Mesopotamia still held, and later correspondence with the catholicos confirms the link continued. Like the remnant that survived in the Hakkari mountains, this was one of the few provinces of the Church of the East that Timur's campaigns never reached.
movements.why: Christians on India's Malabar coast, tracing their founding to the apostle Thomas and worshipping in Syriac, belonged to the Church of the East and received their bishops from a patriarch far away in Mesopotamia. A manuscript copied at Cranganore in 1301, the oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India, names the patriarch Yahballaha III in its colophon, showing the link still held, and the community itself was an established, high-status trading group with privileges from local Hindu rulers. Around 1490 a delegation travelled to the patriarch asking for bishops, and the bishops who returned wrote home in 1504 describing both the community and the first arrival of Portuguese ships.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 to 1517 (era window; the 1301 Cranganore colophon opens it, the 1490/1504 correspondence [S] closes it; both adjacent gaps stay named) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: The Malabar coast, 1300 to 1517 — an Indian church worshipping in Syriac and governed from Mesopotamia, in the last two centuries before Europe arrived.
movements.longDescription: On the pepper coast of south-west India there had been Christians for longer than anyone could document, who traced their founding to the apostle Thomas, worshipped in Syriac, and belonged to the Church of the East, receiving their bishops from its patriarch far away in Mesopotamia. In this window they come into focus. A Syriac manuscript copied at Cranganore in 1301 — the oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India — names the patriarch Yahballaha III in its colophon, showing the link intact. Socially the community was no marginal minority but an established, high-status trading group with privileges from Hindu rulers and a headman of its own. By the late fifteenth century, with the church's Mesopotamian heartland shattered, the connection had to be actively maintained. A delegation travelled to the patriarch around 1490 asking for bishops, and the bishops who came back wrote home in 1504 describing the community — and the arrival of Portuguese ships.
voices: Yahballaha III — the distant patriarch named in the 1301 Cranganore colophon, the era's clearest evidence that the link to Mesopotamia held
Mar Jacob — one of the bishops sent from Mesopotamia after the delegation of about 1490, who served in Malabar into the Portuguese period
The community is otherwise largely anonymous in this window: its record survives in manuscript colophons and in letters written about it rather than by it
movements.legacy: The community is still here. The centuries after 1517 brought Portuguese pressure, the Synod of Diamper in 1599 and the Coonan Cross revolt of 1653, which between them divided the St Thomas Christians into the several churches they remain — Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholics, the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian churches, the Mar Thoma Church and others — together numbering several million people in Kerala and around the world. Syriac is still used liturgically among them, and the claim of apostolic origin from Thomas that this era's documents already take for granted is still the community's defining self-description.

movements.name: Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich in both directions, with Luther's corpus on one side and the congregations' own lived record on the other, including women's voices in verified modern editions (Argula von Grumbach, Katharina Zell). The visitation records carry a care note: what they show about ordinary knowledge is itself a live scholarly debate. The Augustinian Hermits were routed into this entry's record as Luther's seedbed rather than given an entry of their own.
movements.sourcing: RICH at every level - including visitation records showing what villagers actually knew (disillusioning and honest)
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of late-medieval piety and its protest against Rome, becoming a rival to Rome and a sibling rival to the Reformed churches.
