The Augustinian Hermits, Luther's own religious order, were its seedbed: the order's houses in Lutheran lands were absorbed into the new movement, while its Catholic houses continued within the Catholic Church.
movements.why: Luther's own writings are enormous, but the Saxon visitation records of 1527-28 tell a different story: sent out to examine parish after parish, the visitors found many villagers knew far less of the new faith than the pamphlets implied. The same decades also produced women publishing under their own names, like Argula von Grumbach and Katharina Schütz Zell, defending the evangelical cause in print.

sources.work: Luther's Works (American Edition, 55 vols + new series, Concordia/Fortress), incl. the Small and Large Catechisms (1529) and the hymns as used texts
The Saxon visitation records (from 1527-28, with Melanchthon's Instructions for the Visitors) and church ordinances in Sehling, Die evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts
sources.note: Shows what villagers actually knew. Mostly untranslated German archival material. Historians disagree on how to read it: Strauss's 'failure' reading (Luther's House of Learning, 1978) versus critics like Scribner and Kittelson; the debate is part of what the record means.

sources.work: Argula von Grumbach, A Woman's Voice in the Reformation (ed./trans. Matheson, T&T Clark, 1995); Katharina Schuetz Zell, Church Mother (ed./trans. McKee, Chicago, 2006)
sources.note: Women's voices in their own published words; Zell writes from Strasbourg, within the wider evangelical world.

sources.work: The confessional documents: Augsburg Confession (1530), Book of Concord (1580; ed. Kolb & Wengert, Fortress, 2000), read against parish registers the ordinances mandated
Susan Karant-Nunn, The Reformation of Ritual (Routledge, 1997), with Strauss (1978) as classic provocation
sources.note: A lived-practice view of parish religion.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 1 'Martin Luther, reformer' (Hendrix), with ch. 2 (Brady) and ch. 4 (Lehmann)

movements.longDescription: Wittenberg was a small Saxon university town when one of its theology professors, an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther, wrote 95 theses against the sale of indulgences and sent them to the archbishop of Mainz on 31 October 1517. Tradition also holds that he nailed a copy to the door of the Castle Church, the university's usual notice board for an academic debate — but that detail comes only from an account written decades later, after Luther's death, and historians still disagree over whether it happened. Within a few years a movement had grown around him that reorganised worship, emptied monasteries, and put the Bible, a catechism and a hymnbook into ordinary German households. What that looked like from the pew is documented unusually well. From 1527-28 the Saxon churches sent visitors out to examine parish after parish, and their reports are frank about how little many villagers actually knew. The movement settled its own arguments in writing — the Augsburg Confession of 1530, then the Book of Concord of 1580. And the churches shaped by it spread north and east across Germany and Scandinavia, where they remain.
movements.teaser: Saxony and then northern Europe, 1517 to 1580 — a university town's quarrel over indulgences that ended with catechisms, hymnbooks and a new confession of faith in ordinary households.
voices: Martin Luther — Wittenberg theology professor whose 1517 protest began the movement, and whose catechisms and hymns shaped its ordinary worship
Philipp Melanchthon — Luther's colleague, author of the Augsburg Confession (1530) and of the instructions that sent visitors out to inspect Saxon parishes
Katharina von Bora — former nun who married Luther and ran the household that became the movement's most-watched model of a pastor's family
Argula von Grumbach — Bavarian noblewoman who published pamphlets under her own name in the 1520s defending the evangelical cause
Katharina Schütz Zell — Strasbourg pastor's wife who published devotional writing, hymn collections and open letters in her own name
movements.legacy: It became the Lutheran churches — an ongoing communion of tens of millions across Germany, Scandinavia, the Baltic and North America, and, through later missions, Africa and Asia. Its most durable everyday bequest is less doctrinal than liturgical and musical: congregational hymn-singing in the local language, the small catechism learned by heart at home, and a tradition of church music that runs from Luther's own tunes through to Bach.

experienceToday.text: The Luther museums in Lutherstadt Wittenberg, Germany — Luther's own house and Melanchthon's, a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: The Reformed Cities - Zurich & Geneva
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: RICH - Geneva's consistory registers are among the best ordinary-life archives in Christian history
movements.relationsSummary: Parent of the Scottish, Huguenot, Dutch, and Puritan traditions
movements.why: Zwingli tested every inherited church practice at Zurich through public disputation before the whole city; five years later and without ever meeting him, Calvin built the same conviction at Geneva through catechesis and a Consistory that held ordinary conduct to account.

entry.subtitle: The Reformed Cities - Zurich & Geneva
entry.tile: On 1 January 1519, Huldrych Zwingli, newly appointed Leutpriester at Zurich's Grossmunster, began preaching straight through the Gospel of Matthew rather than following the fixed lectionary - the first act of a reform that tested every inherited practice against Scripture and kept only what the text would warrant. The First and Second Zurich Disputations (1523) carried that testing into public, civic argument before the whole city; Zwingli died in battle at the Second War of Kappel in 1531, and his successor Heinrich Bullinger held Zurich's own pastorate for four decades after him. Geneva's own reform opened separately - its 1526 alliance with Bern, its 1536 break from Savoy - and was joined that same year by John Calvin, whose ministry, once consolidated under the 1541 Ecclesiastical Ordinances, built a Consistory of pastors and lay elders to hold the whole city's ordinary conduct to account. Zwingli and Calvin never met; their ministries did not overlap. What formally bridges the two cities is the Consensus Tigurinus (1549), a jointly negotiated statement on the Lord's Supper - evidence of two reforms arriving independently at language neither could disown, not of any earlier contact between their founders. The window's close at 1650 is the census's own administrative continues-cap for a still-living tradition, not a historical rupture: this pattern continues unbroken into the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed, and English Puritanism.

movements.dateRationale: End 1650 (continues-cap; living — the old 1600 matched nothing; alts 1566/keep-1600 were shown) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Zurich leg: Zwingli's writings (Sixty-Seven Articles 1523; On True and False Religion 1525; LCC Zwingli and Bullinger), disputation records, the Prophezei and Zurich Bible (1531)
Calvin's corpus: Institutes (1559; trans. Battles, ed. McNeill, LCC 1960), Ecclesiastical Ordinances (1541), Geneva Catechism, sermons and letters
sources.note: Teaching-and-order layer, kept distinct from the discipline texture.

sources.work: Registers of the Consistory of Geneva in the Time of Calvin, vol. 1: 1542-1544 (ed. Kingdon, Lambert & Watt, trans. McDonald, Eerdmans, 2000)
sources.note: Minutes kept by the very body doing the disciplining — an institutional record, not a neutral one.

sources.work: The Genevan Psalter as lived piety: Marot and Beze metrical psalms (complete 1562), La Forme des prieres (1542), psalm-singing practice
sources.note: The movement's ordinary devotional voice.

sources.work: Scott Manetsch, Calvin's Company of Pastors (OUP, 2013), with Bruce Gordon, Calvin (Yale, 2009)
sources.note: Current standards, the first built on the registers.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 6 (Kingdon, Calvin/Geneva), with ch. 5 (Blickle) and ch. 7 (Greengrass)
sources.note: Reference author is also the registers' editor.

movements.longDescription: Two Swiss city-states, a generation apart, worked out what a whole town would look like if its church were rebuilt from Scripture: Zurich under Huldrych Zwingli from 1519, which stripped images and the Mass out of its churches. And Geneva after 1536 under John Calvin, whose Ecclesiastical Ordinances of 1541 gave the city pastors, teachers, elders and deacons, and a consistory that met every week. Geneva's consistory registers survive, and they are startlingly ordinary — quarrels between neighbours, absent husbands, people who had not been to church. Which makes this one of the best pictures anywhere of what a church actually did about the daily conduct of ordinary people. From these two cities the Reformed pattern travelled: Scotland, France, the Netherlands and English Puritanism all trace back here.
movements.teaser: Zurich and Geneva, 1519 to 1650 — two small cities that rebuilt church and civic life out of Scripture, and kept the minutes.
voices: Huldrych Zwingli — Zurich's people's priest from 1519, whose preaching and public disputations carried the city into reform
Heinrich Bullinger — Zwingli's successor, who steadied Zurich for four decades and corresponded with Protestants across Europe
John Calvin — the French exile who gave Geneva its church order, its catechism, and the Institutes
Theodore Beza — Calvin's successor at Geneva and co-author of the metrical psalter the Reformed world sang
Marie Dentière — former abbess turned Genevan reformer, who published in her own name arguing that women could speak about Scripture
movements.legacy: Reformed and Presbyterian churches worldwide descend from these two cities, and so do four traditions this map carries separately. The Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed and English Puritanism. Beyond doctrine the everyday inheritance is a style: plain whitewashed interiors with the pulpit at the centre, congregational psalm-singing in the language people spoke, and church government by elected elders rather than by bishops.

experienceToday.text: The International Museum of the Reformation, Geneva — beside St Peter's Cathedral, in the old cloister where the city voted for reform
The Grossmünster, Zurich — Zwingli's own church, still open to visitors

movements.name: The Anabaptist Movements
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base read with genre care — the Martyrs Mirror and the Hutterite Chronicle alongside the movement's own hymnody, with the court testimonies flagged as coerced rather than taken as plain inside voice. Its end was moved to 1650, bringing the Dordrecht Confession (1632) back inside its own window; the previous 1600 had stranded it.
movements.sourcing: RICH in ordinary inside voice: court testimonies, prison hymns, the Martyrs Mirror, Hutterite Chronicle
movements.floorNote: The mainstream of the movement held the historic creeds' teaching about God and Christ, though Menno Simons and the Dutch wing taught a distinctive doctrine of Christ's heavenly flesh that their neighbours disputed. The era's anti-Trinitarian groups are a separate story, told elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: Persecuted by Lutheran, Reformed, and Catholic traditions alike - a loud tension in the sources; parent of the free-church line
movements.why: In January 1525, a small group in Zurich baptized one another as adults, and Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic authorities alike hunted them down for it. What survives from inside the movement is unusually direct: court testimony, prison hymns and a martyr book, the Martyrs Mirror, still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes today.
movements.dateRationale: End 1650 (continues-cap; living; the Dordrecht Confession 1632 [S] rescued in-window — the old 1600 stranded it; alt c. 1632 was shown) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The confessions and leaders' corpus: Schleitheim Articles (1527) with Sattler's trial record (The Legacy of Michael Sattler, ed./trans. Yoder, 1973); Menno Simons, The Complete Writings (trans. Verduin, ed. Wenger, 1956); Dirk Philips, Enchiridion
sources.note: Swiss and Dutch wings speak in their own words.

sources.work: The court testimonies: Taeuferakten series (Quellen zur Geschichte der Taeufer); Sources of South German/Austrian Anabaptism; Harder, Sources of Swiss Anabaptism
sources.note: Hostile, coerced evidence: interrogations conducted under threat and torture, recorded by the persecuting authorities. Ordinary believers speak only through the persecutor's pen.

sources.work: Martyrs Mirror (van Braght, 1660; Eng. trans. Sohm) with the Ausbund prison hymns (from 1564)
sources.note: A 1660 Dutch Mennonite compilation, not a contemporaneous archive, but it embeds authentic prison letters, including Anneken Jans's 1539 testament — a rare quantity of women's voices.

sources.work: The Chronicle of the Hutterian Brethren, vol. 1 (trans./ed. the Hutterian Brethren, Plough, Rifton, 1987), with the Hutterite community ordinances
sources.note: Inside institutional memory covering 1528-1665, including the only account of the first believers' baptism. It's a self-vindicating genre, written to defend the community's own memory.

sources.work: Roth & Stayer (eds.), A Companion to Anabaptism and Spiritualism, 1521-1700 (Brill, 2007)
sources.note: The current standard reference on the movement's diverse, multiple origins ('polygenesis').

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 3 (McLaughlin, the radical Reformation)

movements.longDescription: In January 1525 a handful of men in Zurich, impatient with how slowly their own city's reform was moving, baptised one another as adults — and were hunted for it. Anabaptists held that baptism belonged to those who could confess faith for themselves, that the church was a voluntary body rather than a whole society, and, for most of them, that a Christian could neither swear oaths nor take up the sword. Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed authorities alike treated this as sedition and executed them by the hundreds. The survivors regrouped: Hutterite communities holding goods in common in Moravia, and in the Low Countries the congregations gathered by a former priest, Menno Simons, whose name their descendants still carry.
movements.teaser: Swiss lands, Moravia and the Low Countries, 1525 to 1650 — believers who baptised one another as adults and were hunted for it by every other church of their century.
voices: Conrad Grebel — Zurich radical, among the first to be re-baptised in January 1525
Felix Manz — drowned in the Limmat at Zurich in 1527, the movement's first martyr at Protestant hands
Michael Sattler — former Benedictine prior, principal author of the Schleitheim Articles of 1527 and executed that same year
Menno Simons — Dutch priest who left his parish in 1536 and gathered the scattered congregations that took his name
Anneken Jans — executed at Rotterdam in 1539, whose testament written for her infant son survives in the movement's own martyr book
movements.legacy: The movement survives directly: Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites and Brethren all descend from it, and the wider free-church principle — that membership is a voluntary adult commitment and that the church should not be an arm of the state — became one of the most widely adopted Protestant ideas in the world. Its martyr book, the Martyrs Mirror of 1660, is still printed and still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes.

experienceToday.text: The Täuferhöhle near Bäretswil, Switzerland — the cave in the hills outside Zurich where hunted Anabaptists met to worship, reachable on a short marked walk
The Menno Simons monument at Witmarsum, Friesland — freely accessible, on the site where he is said to have preached to his congregation

movements.name: The English Reformation & Elizabethan Settlement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the Prayer Book as lived formation, with churchwardens' evidence continuing from the late-medieval parish entry's base. Its end was extended at the Freeze to 1650 so that it carries the Stuart century itself rather than leaving a 47-year micro-entry, the Elizabethan-close alternative having been shown and declined; the absence of any Church of England entry between 1650 and 1815 was flagged forward.
movements.sourcing: Rich: liturgy (BCP), martyrology, visitation, wills tracking belief-change across decades
movements.relationsSummary: Shaped by Lutheran and Reformed influences taking root in England, and the parent of both the Anglican tradition and the dissenting Protestant churches that broke from it. Its story extends through the Stuart century, from the 1604 Hampton Court Conference to the Westminster Assembly.
movements.why: What changed English religion was less a confession of faith than a book: the Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549 and revised through 1662, fixed the words the whole country had to say together every week. Ordinary wills from the same parishes show belief shifting under people's feet, as the phrases they used about the soul and the dead changed decade by decade.
movements.dateRationale: End 1650 (continues-cap, absorbing the Stuart church — Hampton Court, the KJV, Laud, the Westminster Assembly [S]; the 1603 Elizabethan-close + separate-segment branch was shown); the era-8 Anglican hole stays flagged (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662 (ed. Cummings, Oxford World's Classics, 2011), with the primers and Books of Homilies
sources.note: These are the texts ordinary England actually prayed, and the homilies show what parishioners actually heard from the pulpit.

sources.work: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1563+; online variorum TAMO edition)
sources.note: Worth reading with care: this is martyrology — real documentary content (examinations of ordinary believers, many women) inside an openly polemical frame that shifted across editions; it also digests the Marian regime's own hostile records.

sources.work: Visitation articles and injunctions (Frere & Kennedy, Alcuin Club, 1910) with churchwardens' accounts spanning the changes (Morebath and neighboring parishes)
sources.note: This parish paperwork carries the story of Morebath and its neighbors across the religious changes of the period, showing continuity on the ground.

sources.work: Wills tracking belief-change across decades (soul-bequest preamble series), with Jewel's Apology (1562) and Hooker, Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (1593-)
Duffy, The Stripping of the Altars (Yale, 1992/2005), part II, with Peter Marshall, Heretics and Believers (Yale, 2017)
sources.note: Duffy's revisionist frame is carried here as one interpretive lens, not a final verdict.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6

movements.longDescription: England's Reformation began as a king's quarrel — Henry VIII's break with Rome in the 1530s. And only afterwards became a change in what people believed, swinging hard toward Protestantism under Edward VI, back to Rome under Mary I, and settling under Elizabeth I into a church that kept bishops and cathedrals while preaching a Protestant gospel. What actually altered English religion was less a confession of faith than a book. The Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549 and revised in 1552, 1559 and 1662, which fixed the words the whole country was required to say together, week after week. The change can be watched from below in churchwardens' accounts and in the wills of ordinary people, whose formulas about the soul and the dead shift decade by decade. And the settlement held, uneasily, until the civil wars of the 1640s broke it open again.
movements.teaser: England, the 1530s to 1650 — a reformation carried less by a confession of faith than by a book of prayer the whole country had to say aloud together.
voices: Thomas Cranmer — Archbishop of Canterbury and chief architect of the Book of Common Prayer, burned at Oxford in 1556
Elizabeth I — whose settlement of 1559 fixed the shape of the English church for centuries
John Jewel — Bishop of Salisbury, whose Apology of 1562 defended that settlement to the rest of Europe
Richard Hooker — its theologian, author of Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity from 1593
John Foxe — martyrologist whose Acts and Monuments gave English Protestantism its memory of the Marian burnings
movements.legacy: It became the Church of England, and through it the worldwide Anglican Communion. Its most far-reaching bequest is verbal: the cadences of the Book of Common Prayer and of the King James Bible of 1611 shaped English-language worship, and phrases from both — 'till death us do part', 'ashes to ashes, dust to dust' — passed into ordinary speech far beyond any church. The dissenting traditions that later broke away from it, Puritan, Congregational and Baptist, are equally its children.

movements.name: The Scottish Reformation & Kirk
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), on kirk-session discipline records the census rates denser still than Geneva's. Its distinctness from its Genevan parent — a national-covenantal formation logic of its own — stands as the real uniqueness test any build would have to pass.
movements.sourcing: RICH - kirk-session discipline records even denser than Geneva's
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Geneva; distinct national-covenantal formation logic (a real uniqueness test)
movements.why: Scotland's kirk sessions kept records even denser than Geneva's, mostly over small quarrels between neighbours who then had to keep living side by side. Its ambition was bigger than any single city's: a whole nation bound together by public covenant, most visibly in the National Covenant of 1638.

sources.work: John Knox, History of the Reformation in Scotland (ed. Dickinson, 1949) and Works (ed. Laing)
sources.note: A partisan, first-person history written by one of the movement's own protagonists. The Kirk went on to outgrow Knox himself.

sources.work: Scots Confession (1560), First Book of Discipline (1560), Second Book of Discipline (1578), Book of Common Order
sources.note: A national church's own self-design.

sources.work: Kirk-session registers: Register of the St Andrews Kirk Session 1559-1600 (ed. Hay Fleming, SHS, 1889-90), with Perth, Aberdeen, and rural session books
sources.note: Shows day-to-day church discipline at a national scale, filtered through the institutional concerns of the session itself. The claim that these records are 'denser than Geneva's' rests on Margo Todd's authority and hasn't been independently checked.

sources.work: The National Covenant (1638) with subscription records; Archibald Johnston of Wariston's Diary; the Scottish Psalter
sources.note: Covenanted piety seen from inside one intense, first-person conscience, with psalm-singing as an ordinary devotional voice.

sources.work: Margo Todd, The Culture of Protestantism in Early Modern Scotland (Yale, 2002), with Jane Dawson, John Knox (Yale, 2015)
sources.note: The current standard work on lived Kirk discipline, built on the session registers, along with the current standard biography of Knox.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6
sources.note: This volume has no chapter dedicated to Scotland; the closest is chapter 8, by Benedict.

movements.longDescription: In 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished papal authority and adopted a Reformed confession of faith, and the church that followed set out to remake a whole nation rather than a single city: a minister and a school in every parish, and in each parish a kirk session of elders meeting to deal with quarrels, drunkenness, broken promises and sexual misconduct. Those session registers survive in extraordinary quantity, which makes Scotland the best-documented case anywhere of church discipline as it was actually administered. Usually over small matters, among neighbours who then had to go on living beside each other. The Kirk's covenanting instinct, the idea of a whole people bound to God by public oath, came to a head in the National Covenant of 1638 and in the conflicts that followed it.
movements.teaser: Scotland, 1560 to 1650 — a church that set out to reform an entire nation parish by parish, and wrote down what it found there.
voices: John Knox — preacher and polemicist, the Reformation's loudest Scottish voice and the author of its partisan first history
Andrew Melville — who pressed the Kirk toward a fully presbyterian government in the decades after Knox's death
Archibald Johnston of Wariston — lawyer, co-drafter of the National Covenant of 1638, and a relentless diarist of his own conscience
movements.legacy: It became the Church of Scotland, and through emigration and mission the worldwide Presbyterian family. Its ambition of a school in every parish left Scotland unusually literate for its time, and its habit of government by elected elders sitting in courts of the church — session, presbytery, assembly — was carried onto every continent. Metrical psalm-singing in the Scottish manner is still heard in Gaelic congregations today.

experienceToday.text: John Knox House on Edinburgh's Royal Mile — a 1470s townhouse and museum, now part of the Scottish Storytelling Centre

movements.name: The Huguenots
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on synod acts, memoirs, martyrologies and refugee narratives. Its start was moved to 1559, the first national synod at Paris and the church's own organizational birth, replacing a soft 1550s.
movements.sourcing: Rich: synod acts, memoirs, martyrologies, refugee narratives
movements.relationsSummary: Grew directly out of Calvin's Geneva, and became one of history's clearest examples of a persecuted community scattering into exile across an entire continent.
movements.why: French Protestants organised themselves before any king told them to, adopting a confession of faith and a book of discipline in secret in 1559. After a century of civil war and the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, several hundred thousand chose exile over conversion — and gave the English language the word 'refugee.'
movements.dateRationale: Start 1559 (first national synod, Paris [S] — the church's own organizational birth; c. 1550s alt was shown) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Gallican Confession (1559) and Discipline ecclesiastique, with the national synod acts (Quick, Synodicon in Gallia Reformata, 1692, English)
sources.note: A persecuted national church's complete self-governing record.

sources.work: Jean Crespin, Histoire des martyrs (1554 and expansions)
sources.note: An early example of the Reformed martyrology genre taking shape — documentary letters presented within a shaping, partisan frame. Available in full only in French.

sources.work: Memoirs and refugee narratives: Charlotte Arbaleste de Mornay's memoirs (Eng. trans. Crump, 1926); Jean Migault's Journal (dragonnades and flight)
sources.note: A woman's massacre-survival account and a schoolmaster's family refugee narrative from the 1680s.

sources.work: The Marot-Beze Psalter in Huguenot practice - sung at the stake, in battle, in secret assemblies
sources.note: Psalm-singing was the tradition's most ordinary act — and, sung at the stake or in secret, its most defiant.

sources.work: Barbara Diefendorf, Beneath the Cross (OUP, 1991), with Philip Benedict, Christ's Churches Purely Reformed (2002), chapters
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 8 'The second wave of Protestant expansion' (Benedict), with ch. 15 (Gregory)
sources.note: The chapter's author, Philip Benedict, is the tradition's leading historian.

movements.longDescription: France's Protestants organised themselves before any ruler told them to. In 1559 delegates met secretly in Paris to adopt a confession of faith and a book of discipline, creating a national church inside a Catholic kingdom. What followed was nearly a century of civil war and precarious tolerance — the St Bartholomew's Day massacres of August 1572, the Edict of Nantes in 1598 that gave them legal existence and fortified towns, then the slow erosion of that edict until Louis XIV revoked it in 1685. Rather than convert, several hundred thousand left, carrying their trades, their psalters and their memory of what it was to flee into England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, Switzerland, South Africa and the American colonies.
movements.teaser: France, 1559 to 1685 — a church that organised itself in secret, survived a century of civil war, and then scattered across the world rather than convert.
voices: Gaspard de Coligny — Admiral of France and the Huguenots' leading noble protector, killed at the outset of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572
Philippe Duplessis-Mornay — statesman and theologian, the movement's chief negotiator and apologist
Charlotte Arbaleste de Mornay — his wife, whose memoirs record her own escape from the 1572 massacre
Jean Crespin — Genevan printer whose martyrology gathered the letters and last words of executed French Protestants
movements.legacy: The tradition still exists in France, in the united Protestant church that grew out of it, and the dispersion left permanent traces abroad. Huguenot surnames, silk-weaving and watchmaking trades, and congregations founded in London, Berlin, Amsterdam, Cape Town and Charleston. The English word 'refugee' comes from the French réfugié, a word that came into use for them.

experienceToday.text: The Musée du Désert in the Cévennes, France — the memorial museum of Huguenot persecution and clandestine worship, in the farmhouse country where it happened

movements.name: Recusant English Catholicism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — moderate-to-rich, with women unusually visible in its record because the household was the church. The run left standing the entry's own observation that this repeats the Era 1 house-church dynamic sixteen centuries on.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; women unusually visible because households were the church
movements.relationsSummary: A household-based church forced underground by persecution, echoing how the earliest Christians met and organized in private homes centuries before institutional churches existed.
movements.why: After 1559, English Catholics who refused to attend their parish church were fined as recusants, and from 1585 it was treason for a priest even to set foot in the country. What survived was a church of private houses, with priests hidden in walls and the women of the household — legally less exposed than their husbands — effectively running the congregation.

sources.work: John Gerard, The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest (trans. Caraman, 1951); William Weston's autobiography
sources.note: Inside accounts of the household church, written for edification within the mission — a partisan, inside-voice genre.

sources.work: The women who ran the church: Mush's True Report of the Life and Martyrdom of Mrs Margaret Clitherow; Smith's life of Lady Magdalen Montague; recusancy prosecutions of women who shielded priests
sources.note: The life of Margaret Clitherow was written by her own confessor to advance her sainthood cause, so it's a hagiographic work, not a neutral biography.

sources.work: The state's record: recusant rolls, quarter-session presentments, interrogation and trial records (incl. examinations under torture)
sources.note: Hostile, administrative records, some obtained under coercion — the community's shape has to be reconstructed from its persecutors' own bookkeeping.

sources.work: The devotional equipment: Rheims New Testament (1582), Douai OT, A Manual of Prayers (1583), secret-press books, Southwell's poetry and epistles
sources.note: What the households actually read and prayed.

sources.work: John Bossy, The English Catholic Community 1570-1850 (1975), with Alexandra Walsham, Church Papists (1993/1999)
sources.note: Walsham's work corrects an earlier picture of a hard line between recusants and conformists, showing a wide grey zone in between.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 15 'Persecutions and martyrdom' (Gregory)
sources.note: Directly relevant to a community shaped by persecution.

movements.longDescription: After Elizabeth I's settlement of 1559, English Catholics who would not attend their parish church were fined as recusants — refusers. And from 1585 it was treason for a priest ordained abroad even to set foot in the country. What survived was a church that had retreated into private houses. Mass said in an upstairs room, priests hidden in cavities built into chimneys and stairwells, and households in which the woman of the house, legally less exposed than her husband, effectively ran the congregation. Well over a hundred priests and lay people were executed under these laws, and the community that remained was small, anchored in gentry households, and stubborn.
movements.teaser: England, 1559 to 1650 — a church driven back into private houses, with priests hidden in the walls and the women of the household keeping it alive.
voices: Margaret Clitherow — York butcher's wife, pressed to death in 1586 for harbouring priests
Edmund Campion — Jesuit missioner, executed at Tyburn in 1581
Robert Southwell — Jesuit priest and poet, executed in 1595, whose verse was read well beyond Catholic circles
Nicholas Owen — lay Jesuit carpenter who built the priest-holes in houses across England and died under torture in 1606
John Gerard — Jesuit who escaped from the Tower of London and wrote an account of his years on the run
movements.legacy: The community survived. English Catholicism continued unbroken through the penal years and re-emerged legally in the nineteenth century, and forty of its martyrs were canonised together in 1970 as the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales. Its most tangible remains are the houses themselves — priest-holes still shown to visitors in country manors. And a devotional literature, above all Southwell's poetry, that outlived the persecution which produced it.

experienceToday.text: Harvington Hall, Worcestershire — a moated Elizabethan manor with seven surviving priest-holes, several attributed to Nicholas Owen

movements.name: Puritanism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) for exactly the interior-voice premium this project prizes: diaries and conversion narratives are its native genre, at ordinary levels. Its 1660 end crosses the era boundary once as a principled straddle, and the Baptist entry beginning in 1609 inside this window was noted as born within its separatist story.
movements.sourcing: RICH in first-person interior voice at ordinary levels - diaries and conversion narratives are its native genre
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Geneva + the English settlement's tensions; parent of the evangelical line
movements.why: Puritans thought the English Reformation had stopped halfway, and their sharpest distinctiveness was interior: they kept diaries examining their own hearts and told conversion narratives — an account of how God had brought them to faith — aloud before the whole congregation. Pressed at home, thousands carried that habit across the Atlantic to New England from 1630.

sources.work: The diaries: Lady Margaret Hoby (1599-1605, earliest known Englishwoman's diary); Nehemiah Wallington's notebooks (London artisan); Samuel Ward's student diary
The conversion narratives: Thomas Shepard's Cambridge, MA congregation relations (God's Plot, ed. McGiffert; The Confessions, ed. Selement & Woolley)
sources.note: Lay men's and women's conversion accounts as delivered for church admission. Worth remembering the setting: these narratives were performed for a gate-keeping audience, which shaped how they were told.

sources.work: Practical divinity as used: Perkins (A Golden Chain; casuistry), Rogers's Seven Treatises, Bayly's Practice of Piety, Dod & Cleaver on household government
sources.note: The how-to shelf of godly living - catechesis and conduct rather than system.

sources.work: The church-order record: An Admonition to Parliament (1572), Marprelate tracts (1588-89), subscription/deprivation records, the Dedham classis minutes (1582-89)
sources.note: The movement's own semi-clandestine presbytery keeping minutes inside the establishment.

sources.work: Collinson, The Elizabethan Puritan Movement (1967), with Coffey & Lim (eds.), The Cambridge Companion to Puritanism (2008)
sources.note: Field-defining classic and current survey.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6

movements.longDescription: Puritans were the English Protestants who thought the Elizabethan settlement had stopped halfway. That a church with bishops, surplices and a set liturgy still carried too much of what the Reformation was meant to clear away. Their real distinctiveness lay less in church furniture than in the inner life. They kept diaries, examined their own hearts in writing, and made the conversion narrative — an account of how God had brought you to faith, told aloud before a congregation. A normal thing for ordinary men and women to produce. Pressed at home, thousands sailed for New England from 1630. Those who stayed came to dominate the Long Parliament and the Westminster Assembly, and after the Restoration of 1660 were ejected from the Church of England altogether.
movements.teaser: England and New England, c. 1560 to 1660 — Protestants who thought the reform had stopped halfway, and who wrote down the state of their own souls in extraordinary detail.
voices: William Perkins — Cambridge preacher whose practical divinity shaped the movement's teaching on conscience and assurance
Lady Margaret Hoby — Yorkshire gentlewoman whose diary of 1599-1605 is the earliest known diary kept by an Englishwoman
Nehemiah Wallington — London woodturner who filled some fifty notebooks with the record of his spiritual life
Thomas Shepard — minister at Cambridge, Massachusetts, who wrote down his congregation's spoken conversion narratives
Richard Baxter — Kidderminster pastor whose writing on pastoral work and the Christian life outlasted the movement's political defeat
movements.legacy: Puritanism did not survive as a church of its own, but it left more behind than most movements that did. English Congregationalism, Presbyterianism and much of the Baptist tradition come straight out of it, and so does the culture of early New England, including Harvard, founded in 1636 to train its ministers. Its books stayed in print — Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, written by a man formed in that world, became one of the most widely read books in English. And its insistence on personal conversion runs directly into the evangelical revivals of the following century.

experienceToday.text: The Old Ship Meeting House, Hingham, Massachusetts — built in 1681, the only surviving seventeenth-century Puritan meetinghouse in the United States and still in use

movements.name: Dutch Further Reformation & Refuge Culture
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), conditionally — the entry's own question, whether it is supporting context or a tradition in its own right, was left open at the Freeze as a standing scope line rather than answered. Dort (1618–19) is now named both here and in the Remonstrant entry added at the same gate.
movements.sourcing: Rich
movements.relationsSummary: Historians still debate whether this is a distinct tradition or simply the devotional intensity of Dutch Reformed church life at the time. Its practical piety later fed into German Pietism and, through the Dutch Reformed diaspora, reached South Africa and North America.
movements.why: The Dutch Republic became the printing house and shelter of much of Europe's religious dissent, home to English separatists, French and Flemish refugees, and Jews expelled from Iberia. Inside its own Reformed church, preachers pressed for a precise, examined daily godliness that contemporaries called the Nadere Reformatie, the 'further Reformation.'

sources.work: The Nadere Reformatie corpus: Teellinck (The Path of True Godliness, Eng. trans. 2003), Voetius's practical works, Udemans
sources.note: Precision piety, in its own authors' words — most of it remains untranslated.

sources.work: Anna Maria van Schurman, Whether a Christian Woman Should Be Educated (trans. Irwin, Chicago, 1998) and correspondence
sources.note: A woman's learned voice within this piety. Her later Labadist work, the Eukleria, belongs to a later period.

sources.work: Consistory and refuge records: Dutch Reformed kerkeraad minutes (Amsterdam and provincial towns); stranger-church records of Emden, London Austin Friars, Norwich
sources.note: Congregational discipline and refugee administration recorded in the communities' own books.

sources.work: Judith Pollmann, Religious Choice in the Dutch Republic (1999), with Fred van Lieburg's Dutch-piety scholarship
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 8 'The second wave of Protestant expansion' (Benedict)
sources.note: The Netherlands falls within this chapter's broader scope.

movements.longDescription: The Dutch Republic won independence from Spain as a Reformed country, but a strange one. The Reformed church was the public church while a large minority never joined it, and the Republic became the printing house and the shelter of much of Europe's religious dissent. English separatists, French and Flemish refugees, Jews expelled from Iberia, and books that could be published nowhere else. Inside the Reformed church itself a movement of preachers pressed for something beyond correct doctrine, urging precise, examined, daily godliness on their congregations; contemporaries called it the Nadere Reformatie, the further or closer Reformation. It was a movement of pastors and their books rather than of institutions, and historians still argue whether it is a tradition in its own right or the devotional temperature of a whole society.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, c. 1570 to 1650 — a republic that sheltered Europe's dissenters while its own preachers pressed for a reformation of daily life.
voices: Willem Teellinck — Middelburg minister usually named as the movement's founder, author of manuals of practical godliness
Gisbertus Voetius — Utrecht theologian who joined rigorous scholastic theology to insistent practical piety
Anna Maria van Schurman — the Republic's most celebrated learned woman, who argued in print that women should be educated
movements.legacy: Its books travelled. Translated into German, this Dutch practical divinity fed directly into German Pietism, and through the Dutch Reformed diaspora it reached South Africa and North America. The refuge culture left the wider mark. The Republic's habit of tolerating in private what it would not endorse in public, and its printing trade, put ideas into circulation across Europe that had nowhere else to go.

movements.name: The Waldensian-Reformed Union
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a moderate-to-rich base. Its succession from the Alpine Waldensian entry was written at this gate, completing a chain the earlier record could carry only as an influence edge; whether that older edge should now retire was left open rather than decided.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich
movements.relationsSummary: Medieval dissent grafted into Reformed Protestantism without losing its own memory. The community was granted full civil emancipation in Italy in 1848.
movements.why: The Waldensians had already survived three centuries as an underground movement of lay preachers when, in 1532, they joined the young Reformed churches at a meeting in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont and paid for a new French Bible. Their communities were massacred at Easter 1655, an atrocity that drew protests across Protestant Europe and a sonnet from John Milton.

sources.work: The Synod of Chanforan decisions (1532) and the Olivetan Bible (1535) - the union's concrete deliverable, financed by the Waldensian communities
sources.note: The Chanforan decisions survive only through later copies and transcriptions, not an original protocol.

sources.work: The valleys' own historians: Lentolo's manuscript history (1560s), Gilles, Histoire ecclesiastique des eglises vaudoises (1644), Leger, Histoire generale (1669)
sources.note: Insider history carrying the medieval memory forward into Reformed identity. Léger wrote as an advocate after 1655 and included contested, possibly backdated 'ancient' documents — the act of memory-keeping is itself part of the evidence. Available only in French and Italian.

sources.work: Samuel Morland, The History of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piemont (1658) - the 1655 Piedmont Easter massacre dossier with survivor depositions
sources.note: Written by a sympathetic outsider — Cromwell's envoy — from a Protestant-international advocacy standpoint. Covers the massacre and its aftermath from 1655 onward.

sources.work: Euan Cameron, The Reformation of the Heretics: The Waldenses of the Alps 1480-1580 (Oxford, 1984), with Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent (CUP, 1999)
sources.note: Cameron's book covers exactly this transition into union with the Reformed churches.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6
sources.note: This volume has no chapter dedicated to the Waldensians; the closest are chapter 8 (Benedict) and chapter 15 (Gregory).

movements.longDescription: The Waldensians had already survived three centuries of suppression as an underground movement of lay preachers when, in 1532, their representatives met at Chanforan in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont and agreed to join the young Reformed churches. And to pay for a new French translation of the Bible, which appeared in 1535 as the Olivétan Bible. It was an unusual graft: an old dissenting tradition became a Reformed church with ministers, confessions and printed books, without letting go of its own memory of the centuries before. That memory was tested repeatedly, most brutally in the Piedmont massacre of Easter 1655, which drew protests from across Protestant Europe and a famous sonnet from John Milton.
movements.teaser: The Alpine valleys of Piedmont, 1532 to 1655 — a medieval underground three centuries old that walked out into the open and became a Reformed church.
voices: Pierre Olivétan — the translator whose French Bible of 1535 the Waldensian communities paid for
Guillaume Farel — Reformed preacher who pressed the union at the 1532 assembly at Chanforan
Jean Léger — Waldensian pastor and historian who gathered survivors' accounts of the 1655 massacre
movements.legacy: The Waldensian Church still exists — since the nineteenth century out of the valleys and across Italy, with a sister church in Argentina and Uruguay, and since 1979 in union with Italian Methodists. Its valleys remain a place of pilgrimage for Protestants, and its sheer longevity made it a standing reference point for later Protestants looking for a church older than the Reformation.

experienceToday.text: The Museo Storico Valdese at Torre Pellice, in the Waldensian valleys of Piedmont — the tradition's own historical museum, beside the hall where its synod still meets

movements.name: The Society of Jesus
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on an oceanic archive — Ignatius's autobiography and Exercises alongside the Relations — with founder-corpus gravity named as a discipline any build would have to apply, rather than counted as a straightforward strength.
movements.sourcing: RICH to a fault (oceanic archive); founder-corpus gravity needs standard discipline
movements.relationsSummary: Spearhead of Catholic reform; parent of the mission-born traditions
movements.why: Ignatius of Loyola was a soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball, and the long convalescence that followed produced the Spiritual Exercises, a structured month of prayer that shaped everyone the order later trained. Rather than retreat into a cloister, the Jesuits became a mobile body of teachers and missionaries, running some 250 colleges by 1600 and sending men as far as India, Japan, China, Brazil and Canada.

sources.work: Ignatius of Loyola: Personal Writings (trans. Munitiz & Endean, Penguin, 1996/2004 - Reminiscences, Spiritual Diary, select letters), with the Spiritual Exercises and the Constitutions
sources.note: The founder's own voice, and the Society's own self-design.

sources.work: The Letters and Instructions of Francis Xavier (trans. Costelloe, Institute of Jesuit Sources, 1992)
sources.note: The mission's outward reach, in its first protagonist's own letters — though reporting home to superiors carries its own genre pressures.

sources.work: The Jesuit Relations (Thwaites 73 vols; Greer's selection, Bedford, 2000) and the litterae annuae system
sources.note: The Society's serialized self-reporting, written for an edifying purpose and shaped by its intended audience.

sources.work: The non-founder texture: Ratio Studiorum (1599, Eng. trans.), college records, Nadal's exhortations, Marian congregation/sodality registers
sources.note: Shows the Society's ordinary, everyday footprint through schooling and lay religious associations.

sources.work: John W. O'Malley, The First Jesuits (Harvard, 1993)
sources.note: The standard scholarly account, written to counter mythologized readings of the order's founding.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 10 'New religious orders' (Donnelly), with ch. 9 (Bireley)

movements.longDescription: Ignatius of Loyola was a Basque soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball in 1521. During a long convalescence he read the lives of the saints, and the notes he made about his own inner experience became the Spiritual Exercises, a structured month of prayer that afterwards shaped everyone the order trained. The Society of Jesus was approved by Rome in 1540 and grew astonishingly fast. Not as a monastic order in a cloister but as a mobile body of preachers, confessors, schoolmasters and missionaries, running dozens of colleges across Europe within a generation, and some two hundred and fifty by 1600, and sending men to India, Japan, China, Brazil and Canada. By 1650 its members were at once the Catholic Church's most effective teachers and its most controversial operators, admired and resented in roughly equal measure.
movements.teaser: Rome and then the world, 1540 to 1650 — a mobile order of teachers and missionaries founded by a wounded soldier, and the most argued-about body in the Catholic Church.
voices: Ignatius of Loyola — founder, author of the Spiritual Exercises and of the Society's Constitutions
Francis Xavier — one of the first companions, who carried the mission to India and Japan and died in 1552 within sight of China
Matteo Ricci — mathematician and missionary in China, who learned classical Chinese and wrote for Confucian scholars
Peter Canisius — whose catechisms shaped Catholic teaching across German-speaking Europe
Roberto de Nobili — missionary in south India who took up the life of a Hindu ascetic in order to be heard
movements.legacy: The Society still exists and is the largest religious order of men in the Catholic Church; in 2013 one of its members became the first Jesuit pope. Its lasting institutional bequest is education — a worldwide network of schools and universities. And its lasting spiritual one is the Spiritual Exercises, still made as eight-day and thirty-day retreats by Catholics and, increasingly, by Protestants. Its missionaries' letters home also gave Europe some of its first sustained descriptions of Japan, China and the Americas.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Gesù, Rome — the Society's mother church, holding Ignatius's tomb and the rooms where he lived and wrote

movements.name: Tridentine Parish Renewal - Borromean Milan
movements.region: Lombardy, model for the Catholic world
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on rich institutional records plus visitation material giving ordinary texture. Its 1610 end was kept and its reason put on the record for the first time — Borromeo's canonization that year; at the same gate this entry became the named exemplar for the late-medieval parish world's Catholic-reform continuation.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional + visitation ordinary-texture
movements.relationsSummary: The Catholic mirror of Wittenberg's parish question
movements.why: Archbishop Charles Borromeo took the Council of Trent's decrees and worked out what they meant for one ordinary parish: founding seminaries, walking visitations through remote alpine valleys, and issuing instructions detailed enough to help standardise the enclosed confessional box still found in Catholic churches. When plague struck Milan in 1576, he stayed in the city rather than flee it.
movements.dateRationale: End 1610 kept — principled but previously unstated: Borromeo's canonization (1610 [S]) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Acta Ecclesiae Mediolanensis (1582) - Borromeo's provincial councils, diocesan synods, and instructions (incl. Instructiones fabricae, 1577)
sources.note: The model diocese's own legislation, later adopted across the Catholic world. Available only in Latin and Italian.

sources.work: The Milan visitation records - Borromeo's and successors' parish visitations across the archdiocese
sources.note: A Catholic counterpart to the Lutheran Saxon visitation records, showing ordinary parish life. Largely archival material in Italian.

sources.work: Lay formation records: Schools of Christian Doctrine rules and catechist rosters (laymen and laywomen teaching), confraternity statutes and registers
sources.note: Shows the renewal as ordinary people's weekly practice.

sources.work: Giussano's Life of St Charles Borromeo (1610; Eng. trans. 1884) and the canonization-process testimony (1604-10)
sources.note: Written for a hagiographic purpose; the canonization testimony is structured, guided evidence rather than a free-standing account.

sources.work: Wietse de Boer, The Conquest of the Soul (Brill, 2001), with Headley & Tomaro (eds.), San Carlo Borromeo (1988)
sources.note: The current standard work on how Borromeo's discipline was actually lived.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 9 'Redefining Catholicism: Trent and beyond' (Bireley), with ch. 12 (Ditchfield)

movements.longDescription: The Council of Trent decided what Catholic reform ought to mean; Milan under Archbishop Charles Borromeo showed what it looked like in a parish. From 1565 Borromeo set about redesigning a whole archdiocese around the question of what a parish priest was actually for — founding seminaries to train them, holding provincial councils and diocesan synods, walking his own visitations through remote alpine valleys, and issuing minutely detailed instructions on everything from the fabric of a church building to the enclosed confessional box, which his diocese did much to standardise. He also mobilised the laity, through Schools of Christian Doctrine in which ordinary men and women taught catechism to children and through confraternities that organised charity. When plague struck Milan in 1576 he stayed in the city, and his reputation as a pastor was made.
movements.teaser: Milan and Lombardy, 1560 to 1610 — an archbishop who took the Council of Trent's decrees and worked out, parish by parish, what they would actually change.
voices: Charles Borromeo — Archbishop of Milan, whose visitations, seminaries and instructions became the model for Catholic reform elsewhere; canonised in 1610
Federico Borromeo — his younger cousin and successor, who carried the programme on and founded the Ambrosian Library
Castellino da Castello — the priest who began Milan's Schools of Christian Doctrine, the lay catechism classes Borromeo went on to expand
movements.legacy: Borromeo's Milan became the template. His Acta Ecclesiae Mediolanensis, published in 1582, circulated as a working handbook for bishops across the Catholic world, and the parish shape it describes — a trained resident priest, regular catechism, the confessional, the visitation — lasted into the twentieth century. Charles Borromeo remains one of Catholicism's most widely invoked patrons of bishops and seminarians, and his diocese still keeps the Ambrosian rite that long predates him.

movements.name: Mission-Born Christianities (Kirishitan Japan; Kongo; China; New Spain/Andes)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — uneven by region but genuinely moderate-to-rich in each named case, with the missionary-pen gravity its floorNote names carried at full strength as a source-asymmetry problem. Its start was moved back to 1491, João I of Kongo's baptism, the previous 1549 having been the Japan wing's date doing four regions' duty. The question of splitting the family into distinct traditions was put to the gate and held rather than answered.
movements.sourcing: Uneven by region but genuinely moderate-to-rich in each named case; heavy missionary-pen gravity; real native voices (Japan, Kongo especially)
movements.floorNote: No question about their creedal faith. The hard question here is a different one: with nearly all the surviving records written by missionaries, how much of what we can read is the mission's story rather than the converts' own.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of the Jesuit missions and the wider Catholic Reformation, and became the root of Christianity's spread as a truly global religion in the centuries that followed.
movements.why: In Kongo, King Afonso I adopted the faith and left letters in his own voice; in Japan, a savage prohibition drove Christian communities underground, where hidden believers kept a transmitted faith alive for roughly two hundred and fifty years without a single priest. Almost everything else written about these communities came from missionaries' own pens, which makes whose story survives — the mission's or the converts' — a real and open question.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1491 (Joao I of Kongo baptized — the Era 6 gate's resolved back-extension landing here; strengthened by New Spain 1524/Guadalupe 1531 [S]; 1549 was the Japan wing's date doing four regions' duty). The family split question was HELD at this gate (A5-now stands; Japan's arc confirmed inside) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Kirishitan Japan: Dochirina Kirishitan (1591/1600 catechism as used); Fabian Fucan's Myotei mondo (1605) and Ha Daiusu (1620) in Elison, Deus Destroyed (Harvard, 1973); Tenchi Hajimari no Koto (trans. Whelan, 1996); martyr acts and fumi-e apostasy registers
sources.note: Fucan wrote first as a convert apologist, then later as an apostate attacking the faith he'd left. The fumi-e apostasy registers are hostile, coerced evidence — produced under a torture regime designed to force apostasy.

sources.work: Kongo: the letters of King Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga, c. 1509-1540s) in Brasio, Monumenta Missionaria Africana (Eng. excerpts in documentary readers); the Kikongo Doutrina christaa (1624)
sources.note: A genuine African Christian ruler's own voice: he requested teachers and protested the slave trade. (Dona Beatriz, a later prophetic figure from 1704, belongs to a subsequent period.)

sources.work: China: Ricci, The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (trans. Lancashire & Hu, 1985); the converts' own texts - Xu Guangqi, Yang Tingyun; Kouduo richao (Li Jiubiao's Diary of Oral Admonitions, trans. Zuercher, 2007)
sources.note: Lists converts' own texts first. The Kouduo richao (Diary of Oral Admonitions) shows ordinary convert experience directly.

sources.work: New Spain/Andes: Nahuatl testaments (The Testaments of Culhuacan); Guaman Poma, Nueva coronica y buen gobierno (1615); the Huarochiri Manuscript (trans. Salomon & Urioste, Texas, 1991); extirpation-trial records
sources.note: The Huarochiri Manuscript exists only because a Spanish extirpator of idolatry commissioned it, and the extirpation trial records are hostile evidence. Guaman Poma gives a native Andean Christian voice writing under colonial pressure.

sources.work: Regional standards: Higashibaba, Christianity in Early Modern Japan (2001); Thornton's Kongo-Christianity scholarship; Standaert (ed.), Handbook of Christianity in China vol. 1 (2001); Mills, Idolatry and Its Enemies (1997)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 27 'The naturalisation of Andean Christianities' (Mills) and ch. 29 'Christianity shaped by the Chinese' (Standaert)
sources.note: These two chapters directly cover two of the four regions here (the Andes and China). There's no dedicated chapter on Japan or Kongo; the nearest is chapter 30, by Zupanov and Hsia.

movements.longDescription: Between the 1490s and the middle of the seventeenth century, Christian communities took root far outside Europe under very different conditions. The kingdom of Kongo, whose ruler Afonso I adopted the faith and whose letters survive in his own voice. Japan, where a Jesuit mission from 1549 gathered a large Christian population before a savage prohibition drove the survivors underground. China, where Jesuits and Chinese converts argued out how the Christian God could be spoken of in a Confucian idiom. And Spanish America, where conquest and mission arrived together and Andean and Nahua Christians made something of their own out of what they were given. Almost everything written about these communities was written by missionaries, which makes the deepest question about them a hard one — how much of what survives is the mission's story and how much the converts'. And Japan and Kongo are where converts' own voices most clearly break through.
movements.teaser: Japan, Kongo, China and the Americas, 1491 to 1650 — Christian communities born far outside Europe, most of whose surviving records were written by the missionaries rather than by them.
voices: Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga) — king of Kongo from about 1509, whose own letters argue with Portugal about the slave trade and about his church
Fabian Fucan — Japanese convert, later apostate, who wrote first for Christianity and then against it
Xu Guangqi — Chinese scholar-official and convert, Matteo Ricci's collaborator and co-translator of Euclid into Chinese
Guaman Poma de Ayala — Andean nobleman whose vast illustrated letter to the king of Spain protests what colonial Christianity had become
movements.legacy: These are the beginnings of Christianity as a genuinely global religion, and several of them were never broken. The hidden Christians of Japan kept a transmitted faith for roughly two hundred and fifty years without priests, and their villages are now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Latin American and Philippine Catholicism, with their processions, confraternities and local devotions, grew directly out of this period, and Kongolese Christianity shaped religion on both sides of the Atlantic, including among enslaved Africans in the Americas.

experienceToday.text: The Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region, Japan — ten villages, a castle site and a cathedral, inscribed by UNESCO in 2018
Visitor guide to the Nagasaki hidden Christian sites, Japan National Tourism Organization

movements.name: Anti-Trinitarian Currents (Servetus; Polish Brethren/Socinians; Transylvanian Unitarians)
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — by the movement’s own confessions (Racovian Catechism; the standard English translation rests on the 1680 recension); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Real internal literature (the Racovian Catechism is candid)
movements.floorNote: They rejected the Trinity and said so plainly in their own confessions of faith — a clear divergence from the Nicene Creed, declared in their own words rather than alleged by opponents. Noting that divergence is not a judgement on what was done to them: Servetus was burned at Geneva in 1553, and the Polish Brethren were expelled from Poland in 1658.
movements.relationsSummary: The radical left edge of the Reformation. Michael Servetus was burned by Geneva's own council in 1553, and the Polish Brethren were expelled from Poland in 1658.
movements.why: Following the Reformation's own appeal to 'Scripture alone,' Michael Servetus published against the doctrine of the Trinity in 1531 and was burned at Geneva in 1553. The idea survived further east: the Polish Brethren built a printing academy at Raków, and Transylvania's 1568 Edict of Torda gave a Unitarian church legal standing under the preacher Ferenc Dávid. Their case for religious toleration, made by people with the most to lose from its absence, outlasted their own persecuted communities.
movements.dateRationale: String aligned to numerics; start 1517 is boundary-structural — the first real anchor is De Trinitatis Erroribus (1531 [S]) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Michael Servetus, On the Errors of the Trinity (1531; trans. Wilbur, Harvard, 1932) and Christianismi Restitutio (1553)
sources.note: The movement's first voice, in his own words.

sources.work: The Geneva process, 1553: trial records of Servetus and Calvin's Defensio orthodoxae fidei (1554)
sources.note: A hostile, institutional record — Servetus's answers were given while on trial for his life, a plainly coercive setting.

sources.work: The Racovian Catechism (1605; trans. Rees, 1818 - archive.org)
sources.note: The movement's own confession of faith — a candid, published self-statement of non-trinitarian doctrine in their own words. Note on the text: Rees's translation is of the 1680 Latin recension, not the original 1605 edition.

sources.work: G. H. Williams (ed.), The Polish Brethren (Harvard Theological Studies, 1980) - documents 1601-1685; Socinus's works (Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum); Transylvanian materials (Francis David; the 1568 Torda edict context)
sources.note: The communities' own records, including Raków's pacifist, communal social life — this movement was more than just its Christology. Much remains untranslated.

sources.work: E. M. Wilbur, A History of Unitarianism: Socinianism and Its Antecedents (1945), with current scholarship (Mortimer, Reason and Religion in the English Revolution, 2010; the Polish school on Rakow)
sources.note: Wilbur writes as a Unitarian himself, so this is sympathetic, inside-perspective historiography rather than a neutral outside account.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 3 (McLaughlin, the radical Reformation)

movements.longDescription: The Reformation's appeal to Scripture alone led a minority to a conclusion the rest found intolerable: that the doctrine of the Trinity was not taught in the Bible. Michael Servetus published against it in 1531 and was burned at Geneva in 1553 with the city council's approval and Calvin's agreement. The idea survived further east, where the Polish Brethren built a printing town and academy at Raków and issued the Racovian Catechism in 1605, and where the Transylvanian diet's Edict of Torda in 1568 gave a Unitarian church legal standing under the preaching of Ferenc Dávid. Poland expelled the Brethren in 1658; the Transylvanian church is still there.
movements.teaser: Poland and Transylvania, 1517 to 1650 — Reformation radicals who followed 'Scripture alone' to a denial of the Trinity, and were driven out by every other church for it.
voices: Michael Servetus — Spanish physician and theologian, burned at Geneva in 1553
Fausto Sozzini (Socinus) — Italian exile whose thought gave the Polish Brethren their systematic shape and his name to 'Socinianism'
Ferenc Dávid — Transylvanian preacher and first bishop of the Unitarian church, who died in prison in 1579
movements.legacy: The Transylvanian church still exists, now the Hungarian Unitarian Church in Romania and Hungary, and is very likely the oldest continuously existing Unitarian body in the world. The Polish Brethren, expelled in 1658, scattered into the Netherlands and beyond, where their writings fed into Dutch and English rational theology and, at some distance, into later Unitarianism. Their argument for religious toleration — made by people with the most to lose from its absence — outlasted their communities.

movements.name: Schwenckfelders
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Modest but real internal corpus
movements.floorNote: They diverge on one point: Schwenckfeld taught that Christ's humanity was heavenly rather than ordinary flesh, and his followers suspended the sacraments. Neither position denies Christ's full divinity, which is why their standing relative to the historic creeds is genuinely arguable rather than settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Spiritualist wing of the Reformation
movements.why: Caspar Schwenckfeld broke with Luther over a conviction that outward things — preaching, sacraments, church order — could never do what only Christ's inward work could accomplish. In 1526 he urged that the Lord's Supper be suspended until Christians could agree what it actually was, a 'standing still' his followers kept for generations, meeting in houses and copying his writings out by hand.
movements.dateRationale: String aligned to the capped numerics (the extend-past-cap branch was shown); origin note: Schwenckfeld's break runs from the 1520s (Stillstand 1526 [S]) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Corpus Schwenckfeldianorum (19 vols, 1907-61), incl. the Great Confession on Christ's glory (1540)
sources.note: The 'celestial flesh' Christology and the Stillstand ('standing still') documented in his own words, across a 19-volume collected corpus. Mostly in Latin and German; English translations exist only as piecemeal selections.

sources.work: The community's own texture: Silesian conventicle letters and devotional manuscripts, the Schwenkfelder hymn and prayer-book tradition, the 1734 Pennsylvania migration records and Gedaechtnistag
sources.note: Evidence of the small fellowship's continuity across two centuries, held at the Schwenkfelder Library in Pennsburg.

sources.work: The condemnations: Lutheran polemic and the Formula of Concord article against the 'Schwenkfeldians' (1577); Silesian suppression records; Jesuit mission pressure (1719-25)
sources.note: Hostile sources — the majority churches' own filter on the community's memory. The 1719-25 material comes from a later period than the rest.

sources.work: R. Emmet McLaughlin, Caspar Schwenckfeld, Reluctant Radical (Yale, 1986)
sources.note: The standard modern study.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 3 (McLaughlin, the radical Reformation)
sources.note: The chapter's author is also the movement's standard biographer.

movements.longDescription: Caspar Schwenckfeld was a Silesian nobleman who welcomed Luther's reform and then broke with it, concluding that outward means — preaching, sacraments, church order — could not do what only the inward work of Christ could do. In 1526 he urged that the Lord's Supper be suspended until Christians could agree what it was, a 'standing still' his followers kept for generations, and he taught a distinctive doctrine of the glorified, heavenly flesh of Christ that Lutherans and Reformed alike condemned. His followers never built a church in the ordinary sense. They met in houses, copied his writings out by hand, and were harried in Silesia for two centuries until a remnant emigrated to Pennsylvania in the 1730s.
movements.teaser: Silesia and later Pennsylvania, from the 1540s — followers of a nobleman who suspended the Lord's Supper rather than fight over it, and kept a church of houses and handwritten books.
voices: Caspar Schwenckfeld von Ossig — Silesian nobleman and reformer, who broke with Luther over the sacraments and the inward work of Christ
Adam Reissner — humanist scholar and follower, whose hymn 'In dich hab ich gehoffet, Herr' is still sung
Beyond its founder the movement produced few prominent leaders — it survived as scattered households copying, hiding and passing on his writings
movements.legacy: A small Schwenkfelder Church still exists in south-eastern Pennsylvania, descended from the families who emigrated in the 1730s, and it keeps a heritage library and an annual thanksgiving marking their arrival. The movement's larger mark is as a witness: an early, articulate case that inward faith matters more than outward form, argued from inside the Reformation rather than against it.

movements.name: Family of Love & Spiritualists (Franck, Niclaes)
movements.informalName: The Family of Love and the Spiritualists
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Real texts; communities deliberately invisible
movements.floorNote: These writers read the creeds' content symbolically and inwardly rather than as statements about outward, historical realities, which raises a real question about how far they held the historic faith in the sense the creeds intended. A second question hangs over the Family of Love in particular: how far it was a tradition and how far it was one man, Hendrik Niclaes. The evidence cuts both ways — English Familist households continued for decades after his death, but the movement was built around him as an inspired prophet — and neither question has a settled answer here.
movements.relationsSummary: Quiet influence on later dissent
movements.why: Sebastian Franck concluded that the true church had been invisible since the apostles, with God's word spoken inwardly to people of every nation rather than housed in any institution. Hendrik Niclaes went further and built a secret fellowship, the Family of Love, whose members conformed outwardly to whatever church their country demanded while keeping their real convictions hidden — so well hidden that England hunted them by royal proclamation in 1580.
movements.dateRationale: Start c. 1540 (Niclaes's founding [S]; Franck's activity 1520s-42 as origin note) — the old 1517 predated the movement it names (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Sebastian Franck: Chronica (1531), Letter to Campanus (in Williams & Mergal, Spiritual and Anabaptist Writers, LCC, 1957), 280 Paradoxes (trans. Furcha)
Hendrik Niclaes's own writings: Evangelium Regni, Terra Pacis, epistles and ordinances (English prints of the 1570s)
sources.note: Hendrik Niclaes's own prophetic self-presentation — elected 'godded man,' his writings styled as scripture. This is the founder-shaped side of the movement's own evidence.

sources.work: The schism record: Hendrik Jansen van Barrefelt ('Hiel') and his separate following after breaking with Niclaes (c. 1573); the Plantin circle's quiet adherence
sources.note: Authority here was contested and the movement survived the contest — evidence that cuts both ways: a founder-shaped rupture, but also a fellowship that outlived it.

sources.work: The English Familists: the 1580 proclamation, member examinations and recantations, Rogers's The Displaying of an horrible secte (1578); against these, wills, parish offices, and outward conformity of known Familist families persisting decades after Niclaes's death (Marsh's evidence base)
sources.note: Both hostile (the polemic and the proclamation) and coerced (the examinations and recantations). The wills and parish-conformity records are the counter-evidence, shaped by the community's own structure: it was a community without its prophet, invisible by design, the same pattern seen in other communities that survived by staying unseen.

sources.work: Alastair Hamilton, The Family of Love (1981), with Christopher Marsh, The Family of Love in English Society, 1550-1630 (CUP, 1994)
sources.note: Standard continental and English studies. Marsh is the community-evidence base.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 3 (McLaughlin, the radical Reformation)

movements.longDescription: Some of the Reformation's most radical figures concluded that no visible church was worth joining at all. Sebastian Franck, a former priest turned printer and chronicler, held that the true church had been invisible since the apostles and that God's word was spoken inwardly to individuals of every nation. Hendrik Niclaes, a merchant in the Low Countries, went further and founded one. The Family of Love, a secretive fellowship whose members were expected to conform outwardly to whatever church their country required while holding their real convictions inside. Familists were hunted by royal proclamation in England in 1580. And precisely because they conformed so well, historians still argue about how many there were and how long they lasted.
movements.teaser: The Rhineland, the Low Countries and England, c. 1540 to 1600 — spiritualists who held that the true church was invisible, and a secret fellowship whose members outwardly conformed to everything.
voices: Sebastian Franck — printer, chronicler and spiritualist, who held that the true church had been invisible since the apostles
Hendrik Niclaes — merchant who founded the Family of Love and published its books under the initials H.N.
Hendrik Jansen van Barrefelt ('Hiël') — who broke with Niclaes around 1573 and led a following of his own
movements.legacy: Neither group survived as an institution. Franck's writings, though, were read and reprinted for centuries by people looking for a Christianity without an institution, and reached the later mystical and spiritualist strands of Protestantism. The Familists' habit of outward conformity makes their influence almost impossible to trace — which is exactly what they intended — but their books circulated among Dutch printers and English readers, and the arguments for toleration made in the following century drew on that world.

movements.name: Orthodoxy under the Ottomans - Parish, Millet & Neomartyrs
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — neomartyrologies and parish and monastic registers give it a moderate base, with the ordinary interior voice acknowledged as thinner mid-period. Its window was segmented at 1650 to end a straddle that crossed two era boundaries, the whole-arc exception having been shown and declined for consistency. The Lucaris affair was routed inside its story on the stated principle that the church, not the man, is the tradition.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: neomartyrologies (incl. documented pastoral preparation of martyrs), parish/monastic registers; ordinary interior voice thinner mid-period
movements.relationsSummary: A continuation of Byzantine Orthodoxy after Constantinople fell in 1453, following on from the earlier fall of Tarnovo, when the patriarch Euthymius went into exile and the Balkan despotate's church carried on. The Patriarchate of Peć was restored in 1557.
