The controversy around Patriarch Cyril Lucaris — his Greek College ties, his Calvinist-sounding Confession of 1629, his death in 1638, and the church councils that later repudiated his teaching — belongs to the church's own story, not just to the man.
movements.why: After Constantinople fell in 1453, the sultan recognised the Ecumenical Patriarch as both civil and religious head of the empire's Orthodox Christians, who lived for centuries afterward as a tolerated but subordinate community. The period produced a distinctive kind of saint, the neomartyr, executed for refusing to convert — sometimes prepared for that death beforehand by a confessor.
movements.dateRationale: SEGMENTED at 1650 (the old 1821 crossed two era boundaries — the forbidden shape; the whole-arc-exception branch was shown and declined for consistency); the era-8 segment (1650-1821, incl. Jerusalem 1672 [S]) is created at the A1.E8 gate (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The neomartyrologies: Nikodemos the Hagiorite, Neon Martyrologion (1799); English access via Vaporis, Witnesses for Christ: Orthodox Christian Neomartyrs of the Ottoman Period 1437-1860 (SVS, 2000); Ottoman execution records as the hostile-administrative layer
sources.note: Worth reading with genre in mind: the collection is itself a late-18th-century spiritual project. It documents a real pastoral texture — spiritual fathers preparing, and sometimes dissuading, would-be martyrs.

sources.work: The Jeremias II-Tuebingen correspondence: Augsburg and Constantinople (trans. Mastrantonis, Holy Cross, 1982)
sources.note: The patriarch's three Answers (1576-81) - captive Orthodoxy defining itself against the Reformation in its own measured voice.

sources.work: The Lucaris controversy, both sides: Cyril Lucaris's Confession (1629) and the condemnations - Synod of Constantinople (1638), Synod of Jerusalem with Dositheus's Confession (1672; trans. Robertson, 1899)
sources.note: An internal boundary contest under double outside pressure (Protestant embassies, Roman missions), with documents surviving from both sides of the dispute.

sources.work: Parish/millet texture: patriarchal berats (Ottoman appointment warrants), kadi-court records used by Christians, parish and monastic registers, Athonite archives
sources.note: Church life seen through the sultan's own bureaucracy — an outside, administrative pen, not the church's own voice.

sources.work: Steven Runciman, The Great Church in Captivity (1968), with Papademetriou, Render unto the Sultan (2015)
sources.note: The classic account, dated in parts, paired with a current corrective.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 7 'The Great Church in captivity 1453-1586' (Zachariadou), with ch. 6 'Mount Athos and the Ottomans' (Zachariadou)
sources.note: This period runs past where this particular volume ends; a related chapter (Kitromilides, "Orthodoxy and the West") may also be relevant but hasn't been directly confirmed.

movements.longDescription: When Constantinople fell in 1453 the Orthodox Church did not disappear; it was reorganised. The sultan recognised the Ecumenical Patriarch as head of the empire's Orthodox Christians — a civil as well as a religious office, taxing, judging and appointing. And for the next four centuries most Orthodox Christians lived as a tolerated but subordinate community under Muslim rule. Parish and monastic life continued, Mount Athos kept its monasteries, and a distinctive kind of saint appeared. The neomartyr, executed for refusing to convert or for returning to the faith after having converted, sometimes prepared for that death by a confessor beforehand. The period also produced the strangest episode in Orthodox history, the patriarch Cyril Lucaris, whose Calvinist-sounding Confession of 1629 was repudiated by a succession of church councils after his death in 1638.
movements.teaser: Anatolia, the Balkans and the Greek islands, 1453 to 1650 — the Orthodox Church living as a tolerated community inside a Muslim empire, and producing a new kind of martyr.
voices: Gennadios Scholarios — the first patriarch appointed after the conquest, who negotiated the church's place under its new rulers
Jeremias II — patriarch who corresponded with Lutheran theologians at Tübingen in the 1570s and consecrated Moscow's first patriarch in 1589
Cyril Lucaris — patriarch whose 1629 Confession read as Calvinist, and who was put to death by the Ottoman authorities in 1638
Nikodemos the Hagiorite — the later Athonite monk who gathered the scattered accounts of these martyrs into a single collection
movements.legacy: This is the church that came through. The Ecumenical Patriarchate is still at the Phanar in Istanbul, and the Orthodox churches of Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia and Romania all passed through these centuries. The neomartyrs are commemorated in the Orthodox calendar to this day. The millet arrangement, under which a religious community handled much of its own law and taxation, also shaped the way Balkan national identities later formed around their churches.

movements.name: St. Thomas Christians under Portuguese Pressure - Diamper & the Coonan Cross
movements.informalName: The St. Thomas Christians at the Coonan Cross
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — moderate-to-rich for this window in synod acts and missionary records, with those acta flagged as hostile to the tradition they absorbed. Its succession from the preceding St Thomas segment was written direct at this gate on a stated fork, with the 82-year gap disclosed rather than filled by a thin intermediate entry.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich FOR THIS WINDOW: synod acts, missionary records (hostile-pen gravity), community tradition - resolves III.11's thin-early-sources problem
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of III.11; the 1653 oath's lines become today's Kerala churches; VIII.27 descends from it
movements.why: The Christians of the Malabar coast traced their church to the apostle Thomas and had worshipped in Syriac under bishops from the Church of the East for centuries, until a 1599 synod placed them under Latin jurisdiction and ordered their Syriac books corrected or burned. Resentment broke open in 1653, when a crowd gathered at a stone cross, tied ropes to it, and swore they would no longer obey the Jesuits — the Coonan Cross Oath, named for a cross said to have bent under the strain.

sources.work: The Synod of Diamper acta (1599): Eng. trans. Michael Geddes (1694); critical ed. Scaria Zacharia, The Acts and Decrees of the Synod of Diamper 1599 (Kottayam, 1994)
sources.note: Hostile to the tradition it absorbed: the decrees Latinize the community and condemn its East Syriac books, many of which were burned or corrected under the synod's own orders — which is why the earlier record is so thin. The community's practices survive mainly as a list of things condemned.

sources.work: Gouvea, Jornada of Archbishop Menezes (1606; Eng. trans. Malekandathil, 2003)
sources.note: The fullest contemporary description of the community, but written by its conqueror's own chronicler.

sources.work: The community's own layer: surviving Kerala Syriac manuscripts (HMML digitization), the East Syriac liturgical and canonical tradition, palm-leaf (ola) records, transmitted memory of the copper-plate privileges
sources.note: The inside voice, fragmentary because the synod burned so many of its books — that destruction is itself part of the evidence. Largely uncatalogued and untranslated.

sources.work: The Coonan Cross oath (1653): community tradition of the oath's wording, contemporary Carmelite and Jesuit reports of the revolt, correspondence around Mar Thoma I's consecration
sources.note: The oath's text is preserved only through tradition, in variant forms, and the surviving reports come from pens sympathetic to the mission side. This event marks the origin of today's division among Kerala's churches.

sources.work: Frykenberg, Christianity in India (OUP, 2008), relevant chapters, with Istvan Perczel's Kerala Syriac manuscript studies
sources.note: Perczel's manuscript discoveries have directly revised the earlier picture of how thin the sources are.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5; vol. 6, ch. 30 (Zupanov & Hsia)
sources.note: Volume 5 has no chapter dedicated to the St Thomas Christians; the closest is chapter 22 (O'Mahony, on Syriac Christianity, though it focuses on the modern period). Zupanov is a specialist on the Malabar missions.

movements.longDescription: The Christians of the Malabar coast traced their church to the apostle Thomas and had for centuries received their bishops from the Church of the East, worshipping in Syriac. The Portuguese found this puzzling and then intolerable, and in 1599 Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes convened a synod at Diamper that placed the community under Latin jurisdiction, revised its liturgy, and ordered its Syriac books corrected or burned. Half a century of resentment came to a head on 3 January 1653, when a crowd gathered at a stone cross in Mattancherry, tied ropes to it and swore they would no longer obey the Jesuits. The Coonan Cross Oath, so called because the cross was said to have bent under the strain.
movements.teaser: The Malabar coast, 1599 to 1665 — an ancient Indian church forced under Roman jurisdiction, and the oath sworn at a bent cross that split it in two.
voices: Aleixo de Menezes — Archbishop of Goa, who convened the Synod of Diamper in 1599
Archdeacon Thomas (Mar Thoma I) — the community's own leader, made bishop by his own people after the 1653 oath
Ahatallah — the Syrian bishop whose disappearance in Portuguese custody helped trigger the revolt of 1653
movements.legacy: The division made in 1653 is still the shape of Christianity in Kerala. Those who returned to Rome became the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church, now one of the largest Eastern Catholic churches in the world. Those who did not are the ancestors of the Malankara Orthodox, Jacobite, Mar Thoma and related churches. All of them still worship in liturgies descended from the Syriac tradition Diamper set out to correct, and the bent cross at Mattancherry is still there.

experienceToday.text: Holy Cross Church, Mattancherry, Kochi — the parish church where the Coonan Cross Oath was sworn in 1653, with the granite cross still standing
Kerala Tourism's account of the Coonan Cross Oath and its site

movements.name: Philippine Catholicism
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 7 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) for this window — the pasyon is inside voice by definition, though its text-survival carries a dating nuance. Its window was segmented at 1650 under the same ruling applied to Ottoman Orthodoxy: the former end crossed three era boundaries, and its 2026 figure was a generated-date artifact rather than a claim.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: the pasyon (vernacular passion epic chanted in homes - inside voice by definition), confraternity records, rich devotional documentation
movements.relationsSummary: Grew directly out of Spanish colonial Catholicism, brought by friars following the start of Spanish rule in 1565.
movements.why: The first book printed in the islands, the Doctrina Christiana of 1593, appeared in Spanish and in Tagalog written in both Latin letters and the local baybayin script. Out of that vernacular habit grew the pasyon, the Passion of Christ told as a long verse epic and chanted in ordinary homes through Holy Week, a practice still kept today.
movements.dateRationale: SEGMENTED at 1650 (the old end 'present'/2026 crossed three era boundaries; same ruling as VI.17 for consistency; the 2026 numeric was a generated-date artifact); later segments at later gates (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Doctrina Christiana (1593) - the first Philippine imprint, Tagalog and Spanish, in Latin script and baybayin
sources.note: Catechesis in the converts' own script from the very first year. A facsimile of the Library of Congress copy has been digitized.

sources.work: The mission record: Chirino's Relacion de las Islas Filipinas (1604), the orders' chronicles (Plasencia's customs accounts); translations in Blair & Robertson, The Philippine Islands
sources.note: The fullest early descriptions of Filipino Christian life — but written by the missionaries themselves, not the converts.

sources.work: The pasyon and confraternity layer: cofradia records and parish devotional documentation; the pasyon/pabasa tradition of home chanting
sources.note: The earliest surviving pasyon text is Aquino de Belen's, from 1704 — later than this period. The account here rests on the broader devotional practice of the Spanish era, not on that specific text.

sources.work: Phelan, The Hispanization of the Philippines (1959), with Rafael, Contracting Colonialism (1988)
sources.note: A classic framing work, plus the current standard on translation and conversion.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6
sources.note: This volume has no chapter dedicated to the Philippines; the closest is the mission cluster in Part V, chapters 27-30.

movements.longDescription: Spanish rule in the Philippines began in 1565, and with it came friars — Augustinians first, then Franciscans, Jesuits, Dominicans and Recollects. Who baptised, gathered scattered settlements into parishes and built stone churches at their centres. What grew there was not simply transplanted Spanish religion. The first book printed in the islands, the Doctrina Christiana of 1593, appeared in Spanish and in Tagalog written both in Latin letters and in the local baybayin script, and lay confraternities took on much of the work of devotion. Out of that vernacular habit came the tradition the islands are still known for — the pasyon, the Passion of Christ told as a long verse epic and chanted in ordinary houses through Holy Week — though the surviving pasyon texts date from the century after this one.
movements.teaser: The Philippines, 1565 to 1650 — the first century of a Catholicism that learned to speak Tagalog, printed in baybayin, and ended up being sung at home.
voices: Miguel López de Legazpi — commander of the 1565 expedition that began Spanish rule, and the mission with it
Andrés de Urdaneta — Augustinian friar and navigator on that expedition, who found the return route across the Pacific
Juan de Plasencia — Franciscan who wrote down Tagalog customs and law and worked on the first catechisms in the language
Pedro Chirino — Jesuit whose account of 1604 is a principal source for the mission's first decades
movements.legacy: It became one of the largest Catholic populations on earth — the Philippines is today the largest Christian country in Asia — and its devotional culture of patronal fiestas, confraternities, the Black Nazarene procession in Manila and the chanted pasyon at Holy Week descends directly from this period. Four of the churches begun in these centuries are now a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Filipino Catholics have since become one of the world's largest migrant Christian populations, carrying those devotions everywhere they go.

experienceToday.text: The Baroque Churches of the Philippines — four churches of the Spanish period, including San Agustín in Manila, inscribed by UNESCO in 1993
San Agustín Church, Intramuros, Manila — completed in 1607 and the oldest stone church in the country

movements.name: The Union of Brest & Ruthenian Greek Catholic Christianity
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 7 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) on a moderate base — synodal acts, brotherhood records and polemical literature, polemic being a native genre here. Its date string was disambiguated to c. 1700 to match its own numbers, with the eighteenth-century reading left as material for the next era's sweep rather than quietly resolved.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: synodal acts, brotherhood records, polemical literature (polemic as native genre)
movements.relationsSummary: A communion born inside an argument - East-and-West identity tension as daily formation; sibling-rival of VI.21; parent of IX.21. Restores a whole absent communion family
movements.why: In 1596, most Orthodox bishops of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth accepted communion with Rome while keeping their Byzantine liturgy, Church Slavonic and married clergy — while their opponents met in the same town and rejected it outright, producing two rival hierarchies that argued in print for a century. Its most famous bishop, Josaphat Kuntsevych, was killed by a hostile crowd at Vitebsk in 1623.
movements.dateRationale: String disambiguated to c. 1700 (matches the numeric; the 18th-century reading is era-8 sweep material) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The union documents: the 33 articles (1595), the acta of the two simultaneous Brest synods of 1596 (union and anti-union - both records carried), papal and royal instruments, in Documenta Unionis Berestensis (ed. Welykyj)
sources.note: Available only in Latin and Church Slavonic.

sources.work: The polemical literature, both sides: Ipatii Potii's union apologetics; Meletij Smotryc'kyj's Threnos (1610, as Orthodox) and his later pro-union works after converting; English access via Frick's scholarship and the Harvard Library of Early Ukrainian Literature
sources.note: Polemic was this tradition's native genre, and both sides' literature is treated as formative. Smotryc'kyj's own switch from the Orthodox to the pro-union side is itself evidence of the identity tension at stake.

sources.work: Brotherhood records: the Lviv Stauropegial brotherhood statutes, registers, and school records, with Vilnius and kin
sources.note: Lay confraternities formed the backbone of Orthodox resistance — a rare glimpse of lay agency in this era's Eastern sources.

sources.work: The Uniate church's early life: Metropolitan Rutsky's Basilian reform and pastoral correspondence; Josaphat Kuntsevych - pastoral record, murder (1623), canonization-process testimony
sources.note: The Kuntsevych material is hagiographic and drawn from canonization-process testimony, so it's structured, guided evidence. The violence during this period ran in both directions.

sources.work: Borys Gudziak, Crisis and Reform: The Kyivan Metropolitanate, the Patriarchate of Constantinople, and the Genesis of the Union of Brest (Harvard, 1998)
sources.note: The current standard work on the subject.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 18 'Latin Christianity and eastern Orthodoxy' (Dmitriev)
sources.note: Directly covers this borderland region.

movements.longDescription: In 1596 most of the Orthodox bishops of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth met at Brest and accepted communion with Rome while keeping their Byzantine liturgy, their Church Slavonic, their calendar and their married clergy. Their opponents met in the same town at the same time and rejected it outright, so what the union produced was not one church but two rival hierarchies claiming the same people and arguing in print for a century. The new church had to explain itself constantly — to Rome, to the Orthodox it had left, and to Latin bishops who never quite treated it as an equal. And that argument became the ordinary condition of its life rather than an occasional crisis. Its most famous figure, Archbishop Josaphat Kuntsevych, was killed by a hostile crowd at Vitebsk in 1623.
movements.teaser: Ruthenia — today's Ukraine and Belarus — from 1596: a church born inside an argument, Byzantine in worship and Roman in obedience, and never allowed to forget either half.
voices: Ipatii Potii — bishop, chief architect of the union and its most persistent apologist
Josaphat Kuntsevych — Uniate archbishop of Polotsk, killed by a crowd at Vitebsk in 1623
Meletij Smotryc'kyj — polemicist who wrote the most eloquent Orthodox lament against the union, and years later joined it
Josyf Rutsky — metropolitan who reformed the Basilian monks and gave the church its institutional shape
movements.legacy: It survives as the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church and the Belarusian Greek Catholic Church, and it became the model for the Byzantine-rite unions that followed, one branch of the wider family of Eastern Catholic churches — Eastern in worship, in communion with Rome — that now exists around the world. Suppressed by the Russian Empire in the nineteenth century and again by the Soviet Union in 1946, the Ukrainian church survived underground and re-emerged in 1989 as the largest Eastern Catholic church anywhere.

movements.name: The Kyiv-Mohyla Orthodox Revival
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on academy records, catechisms and brotherhood statutes, with textual care noted on its printed Confession, which was revised before publication. Its 1700 end crosses the era boundary once — a single principled crossing under the straddle rule.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: academy records, catechisms, brotherhood statutes
movements.relationsSummary: Orthodoxy answering Reformation/Counter-Reformation pressure with its own confessional formation; the response to VI.20's union
movements.why: Orthodox Kyiv answered the Union of Brest not with a lament but with a school: a lay brotherhood founded a college in 1615, and Metropolitan Petro Mohyla built it on the Jesuit model — Latin, rhetoric, philosophy, theology — on the reasoning that a church cannot defend itself against arguments it cannot read. He also gave the church its own confession of faith and a service book, the Trebnyk of 1646, that fixed how priests actually celebrated the sacraments.

sources.work: Mohyla's confessional corpus: the Orthodox Confession (Kyiv synod 1640; Syrigos's revision approved Iasi 1642; Eng. trans. from Overbeck 1898 onward) and the Short Catechism (1645)
sources.note: The printed Confession is Syrigos's Greek revision, not exactly the original Kyiv text; the 1645 Short Catechism stays closer to Mohyla's own hand. Together they show Orthodoxy answering Reformation and Tridentine pressure with its own confessional formation.

sources.work: The Trebnyk of 1646 (Mohyla's Euchologion) with its pastoral rubrics
sources.note: The revival's most parish-facing text — formation carried out through worship itself.

sources.work: Academy and brotherhood records: the Kyiv Epiphany brotherhood statutes and school records, the Mohyla Collegium's curriculum, disputation, and panegyric materials
sources.note: Latin-style schooling put in service of Orthodoxy — the underlying identity tension is visible in the syllabus itself.

sources.work: The apologetic-patristic layer: Kopystens'kyj's Palinodija (1620s) and the Kyiv Caves Lavra press's patristic and hagiographic printing program
sources.note: The revival's scholarly self-defense and publishing arm.

sources.work: Ihor Sevcenko, 'The Many Worlds of Peter Mohyla' (HUS, 1984), with current Kyivan-academy scholarship (Sharipova/Charipova)
sources.note: A classic orientation essay, plus current archive-based studies.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 18 'Latin Christianity and eastern Orthodoxy' (Dmitriev)
sources.note: No dedicated chapter on this Ruthenian revival was found in volume 5.

movements.longDescription: Orthodox Kyiv answered the Union of Brest not with a lament but with a school. A lay brotherhood founded one in 1615, and Petro Mohyla, metropolitan from 1633, turned it into a college on the Jesuit model — Latin, rhetoric, philosophy, theology. On the reasoning that a church cannot defend itself against arguments it cannot read. He also gave the Kyivan church its own instruments. An Orthodox Confession of faith, approved in revised form by a council at Iaşi in 1642, a short catechism, and a great service book, the Trebnyk of 1646, which regularised how priests were actually to celebrate the sacraments. It is the clearest case anywhere of a tradition taking up its rivals' tools in order to remain itself.
movements.teaser: Kyiv, 1615 to 1700 — Orthodoxy answering Counter-Reformation pressure by building an academy, a catechism and a confession of its own.
voices: Petro Mohyla — metropolitan of Kyiv, founder of the college that bears his name and author of its confessional books
Yelysei Pletenetsky — archimandrite of the Kyiv Caves monastery, who built up its printing press
Zakhariia Kopystensky — his successor and a polemicist, whose Palinodia defended Orthodoxy against the union
movements.legacy: The Kyiv Mohyla Academy became the leading school of the Orthodox Slavic world and supplied Russia with its educated clergy for a century. One reason Peter the Great's church reforms have a distinctly Kyivan accent. Mohyla's Confession was accepted well beyond Ukraine and remained a standard Orthodox reference text into modern times. The academy itself, closed under Soviet rule, was refounded in 1991 and is now a leading Ukrainian university.

movements.name: The Tridentine Church
movements.informalName: The Church of Trent and the Counter-Reformation
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run as V.14's receiver - the era's headline gap, the big-church hole's third appearance. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Trent's acta and catechism, the reformed liturgical books, Propaganda Fide's archive, the new orders' records; the era of Catholic record-keeping remade
movements.relationsSummary: The Catholic Church's answer to the Reformation: the Council of Trent's three periods between 1545 and 1563, the resulting Roman Catechism and Tridentine Missal, Pope Sixtus V's reorganized curia, and the missionary office Propaganda Fide founded in 1622. Its story also includes the Index of Forbidden Books and the Roman Inquisition, new active orders such as the Capuchins, a wider generation of lay devotion, the Greek College in Rome, and the Catholic remainder of the Augustinian Hermits after the Reformation split the order.
movements.why: The Council of Trent met across three widely separated periods between 1545 and 1563, restating Catholic teaching on Scripture, justification and the sacraments, and ordering bishops to actually live in their dioceses and found seminaries to train priests. What followed was thorough standardisation — a single Roman Catechism, Missal and Breviary for the whole Latin church — alongside new active orders, the Capuchins, Ursulines and Oratorians, doing pastoral work the older monastic rules had never been designed for.
movements.dateRationale: 1517 (era boundary; V.14's gated end) to 1650 (era end; the era-8 Roman hole stays flagged) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Catholic Church's answer to the Reformation took decades to assemble and then held for four centuries. The Council of Trent met in three widely separated periods between 1545 and 1563, restating Catholic teaching on Scripture and tradition, justification and the sacraments, and — as important in practice — ordering bishops to reside in their dioceses and to found seminaries. What followed was wholesale standardisation: a Roman Catechism, a revised Missal and Breviary issued for the whole Latin church, and in 1622 a Roman office for the missions, Propaganda Fide. The same period produced the Roman Inquisition and the Index of Forbidden Books, and a wave of new active orders — Capuchins, Ursulines, Oratorians — doing work the older monastic rules had never been designed for.
movements.teaser: Rome and Latin Christendom, 1517 to 1650 — a church that answered the Reformation with a council, a catechism and a single missal, and built a system that lasted until the 1960s.
voices: Pope Paul III — who finally convened the Council of Trent in 1545, after decades of delay
Pope Pius V — who issued the Roman Catechism, Breviary and Missal that carried Trent's decisions into every parish
Charles Borromeo — Archbishop of Milan, whose diocese became the working model of what Trent's decrees meant on the ground
Angela Merici — founder of the Ursulines in 1535, the first order of women organised for the teaching of girls
Robert Bellarmine — Jesuit cardinal whose controversial writings were the era's standard Catholic reply to Protestant theology
movements.legacy: This is the Catholic Church most people picture before the twentieth century. The Latin Mass in the form fixed in 1570, the seminary-trained parish priest, the catechism learned by rote, the confessional, the teaching and nursing orders. That framework governed Catholic life until the Second Vatican Council of 1962-65 revised it — and the older Mass is still celebrated today by communities that have kept it. The missionary and educational institutions built in this period carried Catholicism to every continent.

experienceToday.text: The Museo Diocesano Tridentino, Trento — in the palace on the cathedral square, with a gallery devoted to the Council of Trent itself

movements.name: The Russian Church, Stoglav to the Eve of Nikon
movements.informalName: The Church of the First Patriarchs
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run as V.8's receiver. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich institutionally: the Stoglav's hundred chapters, patriarchal records, chronicles, and saints' lives. Ordinary lay voices are thinner here than in other Reformation-era traditions.
movements.relationsSummary: The Stoglav council met under Ivan IV in 1551. Moscow became a patriarchate in 1589, when the visiting Ecumenical Patriarch Jeremiah II consecrated Job as the first Patriarch of Moscow. The church became the country's rallying point through the Time of Troubles, with Patriarch Hermogenes at its center, and Patriarch Filaret later governed alongside his son, the tsar. What followed — Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms of the 1650s and the resulting schism — belongs to the next chapter of this story.
movements.why: A council held in Moscow in 1551, its rulings arranged in a hundred chapters and known as the Stoglav, tried to regulate everything from icon painting to the conduct of priests. In 1589 the visiting Ecumenical Patriarch consecrated Metropolitan Job as the first Patriarch of Moscow, and when the Russian state collapsed during the Time of Troubles, the church became the country's rallying point — Patriarch Hermogenes died in confinement rather than bless a foreign claimant to the throne.
movements.dateRationale: 1517 (era boundary; V.8's gated end) to 1650 (boundary-cap: Nikon 1652 and the raskol are era 8's) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In the century and a half after 1517 the Russian Church became something new: a national church with a patriarch of its own. A great council held in Moscow in 1551, its decisions arranged in a hundred chapters and so known as the Stoglav, tried to regulate everything from icon painting to the conduct of priests. In 1589 the visiting Ecumenical Patriarch Jeremias II consecrated Metropolitan Job as the first Patriarch of Moscow, making formal what Muscovy already believed about itself. Then came the Time of Troubles, when the state effectively collapsed and the church became the country's rallying point — Patriarch Hermogenes died in confinement rather than endorse a foreign claimant to the throne — and afterwards Patriarch Filaret, the young tsar's own father, governed alongside him. All of this stands immediately before the liturgical corrections of the 1650s that would tear the church apart.
movements.teaser: Muscovy, 1517 to 1650 — the century in which the Russian church gained its own patriarch, held the country together when the state failed, and set itself up for the schism to come.
voices: Metropolitan Macarius — who presided over the Stoglav council of 1551 and gathered Russia's saints and writings into vast compilations
Job — Metropolitan of Moscow, consecrated in 1589 as the first Patriarch of Moscow
Hermogenes — patriarch who refused to bless a foreign claimant during the Time of Troubles and died in confinement in 1612
Filaret — patriarch and father of the first Romanov tsar, who governed church and state together until 1633
movements.legacy: The patriarchate created in 1589 was abolished by Peter the Great in 1721 and restored only in 1917. And the Moscow Patriarchate is now the largest Orthodox church in the world. What this century built — a national church closely bound to the state, and a body of liturgical practice widely believed to be untouchably ancient — also set up the catastrophe that followed. When Patriarch Nikon corrected the service books against Greek originals in the 1650s, many refused, and the Old Believers who broke away over it remain a distinct communion today.

movements.name: The Czech Churches' Last Century (Utraquists and Unitas)
movements.informalName: The Church of Kralice and White Mountain
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run as V.6's homeless receiver. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: the Bohemian Confession of 1575, the Kralice Bible (1579-93, the first complete Czech Bible translated from the original languages), Unity of the Brethren discipline records, and Comenius's writings from exile.
movements.relationsSummary: A non-Roman national church in its last century of survival: the 1609 Letter of Majesty guaranteed its religious freedom, the Bohemian revolt followed, and the 1620 Battle of White Mountain led to the 1627-28 suppression, when Comenius led the Unity of the Brethren into exile. A remnant survived underground and later became the seed of the Moravian Church at Herrnhut.
movements.why: The Utraquists insisted that ordinary laypeople receive both bread and wine at communion, a demand that outlived the Hussite wars that produced it and won real legal standing in the 1609 Letter of Majesty. The 1620 Battle of White Mountain crushed that settlement, and by 1627-28 the Habsburgs had outlawed the church outright, sending its last bishop, Jan Amos Comenius, into exile with much of his flock — leaving behind the Kralice Bible, the first complete Czech translation made directly from the original languages.
movements.dateRationale: 1517 to c. 1627 (the suppression decrees — the story IS the ending; the 1620 White Mountain alternative was shown) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: A century before Martin Luther, Bohemia already had its own reform-minded national church — the Utraquists, who insisted that the laity receive both bread and wine at communion, and the Unity of the Brethren who grew alongside them. Surviving as a tolerated, functioning body long after the Hussite wars that gave it birth. Its final century opens with real legal standing, the 1609 Letter of Majesty guaranteeing religious freedom, and closes in catastrophe: the 1620 Battle of White Mountain crushed Bohemian Protestant resistance, and by 1627-28 the Habsburgs had outlawed the church outright, forcing its bishop, the scholar and educator Jan Amos Comenius, into permanent exile along with much of his flock. In between, the church produced lasting work — the Bohemian Confession of 1575 and the Kralice Bible, the first complete Czech translation from the original languages — leaving behind a body of literature that outlasted the institution itself.
movements.teaser: Bohemia and Moravia, 1517 to c. 1627 — a reform church older than Luther's, living on borrowed legal time until its bishop Comenius led its people into permanent exile.

sources.work: Bible of Kralice (1579-93)
sources.note: The first complete Czech Bible translated from the original languages, the Unity of the Brethren's lasting literary work.

voices: Jan Blahoslav — Unity bishop who began the Kralice Bible translation and built its educational and printing base
Jan Amos Comenius — the church's last bishop, who led its people into exile and became one of the era's most influential educational reformers
movements.legacy: Its story didn't end with the 1627-28 suppression. A remnant of the Unity of the Brethren survived underground for nearly a century in Bohemia and Moravia, and in 1722 their descendants found refuge on a German nobleman's estate at Herrnhut — becoming the seed of the modern Moravian Church, one of Protestantism's most influential missionary movements.

experienceToday.text: Herrnhut, Germany — the Moravian Church's founding town, still a living community and a UNESCO World Heritage Site
The Comenius Mausoleum, Naarden, Netherlands — his tomb and museum, open to the public

movements.name: Ethiopian Christianity — Gragn to Fasilides
movements.informalName: The Church that Survived Two Empires
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run as V.7's receiver - its predecessor's own dateRationale names this story as era 7's. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: A genuine inside voice survives: royal chronicles, Emperor Galawdewos's Confession of 1555, and anti-Catholic polemics from the Jesuit century. The wars of this period destroyed many manuscripts, which itself limits what can be known.
movements.relationsSummary: Ahmad Gragn's jihad devastates the church (1529-43); Wayna Daga (1543) saves it; the Jesuit interlude ends in Susenyos's Catholicism (1622), popular revolt, and Fasilides's restoration and expulsion of the Jesuits (1632) - the era's inversion: the Counter-Reformation as outside pressure on an ancient church
movements.why: From 1529 the armies of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, remembered as Gragn, burned Ethiopian churches, monasteries and manuscripts on a scale that still limits what can be known of earlier Ethiopian history, until the invasion broke at the Battle of Wayna Daga in 1543. The Portuguese help that won that battle brought Jesuits who later converted Emperor Susenyos to Catholicism — provoking a revolt so fierce that his son Fasilides expelled the Jesuits, restored the ancient church, and built a new capital at Gondar.
movements.dateRationale: 1517 (era boundary; V.7's gated end) to 1650 (era end; Fasilides's restoration 1632 inside) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02) living corrected to true at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark) — the lane is alive via IX.20 (the VII.23 same-shape case, survey discrepancy 4).
movements.longDescription: Ethiopian Christianity nearly ended in this period and then reasserted itself twice over. From 1529 the armies of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi — remembered as Gragn, the left-handed — swept through the highlands, burning churches and monasteries and destroying manuscripts on a scale that still limits what can be known about earlier Ethiopian history. The invasion was broken only at the battle of Wayna Daga in 1543, with Portuguese help. That help brought Jesuits, and after decades of argument Emperor Susenyos converted to Catholicism and tried to impose it, provoking a revolt so fierce that he abdicated in 1632. His son Fasilides expelled the Jesuits, restored the ancient church, and built a new capital at Gondar.
movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, 1517 to 1650 — a church that survived an invasion which burned its libraries, then expelled the missionaries who had come with its rescuers.
voices: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi ('Gragn') — the Adal commander whose campaigns from 1529 devastated the Ethiopian church
Emperor Galawdewos — who fought the invasion to its end and wrote a Confession defending Ethiopian practice against Catholic criticism
Emperor Susenyos — who converted to Catholicism and abdicated in 1632 when his attempt to impose it provoked revolt
Emperor Fasilides — who restored the traditional church, expelled the Jesuits, and founded the new capital at Gondar
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church survives as one of the largest of the Oriental Orthodox churches, with tens of millions of members, still keeping its own calendar, its Ge'ez liturgy, its long fasts and the tabot at the centre of every church. Gondar's castles and painted churches, built in the century after the expulsion, are a UNESCO World Heritage site. And the memory of this period — an invasion survived, a foreign form of the faith refused — remains part of how the church understands itself.

experienceToday.text: Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar, Ethiopia — Fasilides's walled royal city, with its castles and churches, inscribed by UNESCO in 1979

movements.name: The Remonstrants and Dort
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 7 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Remonstrance of 1610, the acts and canons of the Synod of Dort, Simon Episcopius's writings, and the exile Brotherhood's own records.
movements.floorNote: The movement as it stood in this period held the historic creeds without dispute; its quarrel with its opponents was about predestination, not about the doctrine of God. The later drift of some Remonstrant thinkers toward anti-Trinitarian positions belongs to a different story on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The sharpest internal contest inside Reformed Protestantism in this era: the Five Articles of 1610, judged and condemned by the Synod of Dort in 1618-19, about two hundred ministers deposed, and the Remonstrant Brotherhood driven into exile until toleration returned in the 1630s. The Brotherhood continued afterward with its own seminary in Amsterdam, later associated with the theologian Philipp van Limborch.
movements.why: After Jacobus Arminius raised doubts about how strictly predestination should be taught, his followers set out five articles in the Remonstrance of 1610 — a quarrel that swallowed Dutch politics and sent the statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt to the scaffold in 1619. The Synod of Dort answered with five canons of its own, deposing some two hundred ministers, until toleration returned in the 1630s and the exiles came home to build a church of their own.
movements.dateRationale: 1610 (the Remonstrance) to 1650 (era end; the Brotherhood continues — era-8 sweep material) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Dutch Reformed minister Jacobus Arminius had doubts about how strictly predestination should be taught, and after his death in 1609 his supporters set them out in five articles — the Remonstrance of 1610. Asking the government to allow their view. The quarrel that followed swallowed the young Dutch Republic, mixing theology with politics until it ended on a scaffold. The statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, the Remonstrants' protector, was executed in 1619. The Synod of Dort, meeting through the winter of 1618-19 with delegates from Reformed churches across Europe, condemned the Remonstrance and answered it with five canons of its own. Some two hundred ministers were deposed and their leaders driven into exile — until toleration returned in the 1630s and they came home to build a church of their own.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, 1610 to 1650 — five articles about predestination that split a republic, sent a statesman to the scaffold, and produced canons still argued over today.
voices: Jacobus Arminius — Leiden professor whose questions about predestination began the controversy
Simon Episcopius — the Remonstrants' spokesman at Dort and chief theologian of the church they built in exile
Hugo Grotius — jurist and Remonstrant sympathiser, imprisoned for his part in the affair and famously smuggled out in a book chest
Johan van Oldenbarnevelt — the Republic's leading statesman and the Remonstrants' protector, executed in 1619
movements.legacy: Both sides outlived the quarrel. The Remonstrant Brotherhood still exists as a small Dutch church, with its own seminary in Amsterdam. The Canons of Dort became one of the three confessional standards of the Dutch Reformed tradition worldwide, and the five points they answer are still taught in Reformed churches as the shorthand summary of Calvinism. 'Arminian', meanwhile, became a permanent label in English-language theology, taken up a century later by John Wesley and through him by the whole Methodist family.

experienceToday.text: The Grote Kerk in Dordrecht — where the Synod of Dort opened and closed, with a permanent exhibition about it in the south aisle chapels

movements.name: The Scandinavian Reformation Kingdoms
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run - the receiver the post-1104 Scandinavian gap has waited four eras for. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally [S on items]: church ordinances (Denmark-Norway 1536/37), the Uppsala Synod's acta (1593, verified), hymnals and visitation records; ordinary voice via the hymnal tradition
movements.relationsSummary: Two established national churches emerged: Denmark-Norway's decisive break in 1536/37, and Sweden's slower path from the 1527 Diet of Västerås to the 1593 Uppsala Synod, which committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. Iceland's Reformation was complete by 1550.
movements.why: Sweden's break began at the Diet of Västerås in 1527, when Gustav Vasa seized the church's property, and wasn't completed until the Uppsala Synod of 1593 committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. Denmark-Norway moved faster and harder: Christian III arrested the bishops outright in 1536, and Icelandic resistance ended only in 1550, with the execution of the island's last Catholic bishop.
movements.dateRationale: 1520s (Vasteras 1527 [S]) to 1650 (era end; both kingdoms continue as established churches) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In Scandinavia the Reformation arrived from the top down and stayed. Sweden's break began at the Diet of Västerås in 1527, when Gustav Vasa took the church's property and its independence, and was only completed at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, which committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. In Denmark-Norway it came faster and harder. Christian III won a civil war, arrested the bishops outright in 1536, and the church ordinance drawn up with Luther's colleague Johannes Bugenhagen reorganised the churches of Denmark, Norway and Iceland at a stroke. Icelandic resistance ended in 1550 with the execution of the island's last Catholic bishop. What followed everywhere was the long, slow business of translating Bibles and hymnbooks and teaching a rural population its catechism.
movements.teaser: Denmark-Norway and Sweden-Finland, the 1520s to 1650 — Reformations settled by kings and diets, then taught to whole rural nations out of hymnbooks and catechisms.
voices: Gustav Vasa — king of Sweden, who took the church's wealth and set the kingdom's course at Västerås in 1527
Olaus Petri — preacher and writer, the leading voice of the Swedish Reformation and closely associated with its first Swedish New Testament
Christian III — king of Denmark-Norway, who arrested the bishops in 1536 and imposed a Lutheran church order
Johannes Bugenhagen — the Wittenberg pastor who drafted that ordinance and crowned Christian III
Mikael Agricola — Finnish bishop whose translations effectively created written Finnish
movements.legacy: These became the Lutheran churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland — still the largest churches in their countries, and in several cases still formally established or closely tied to the state. Their most durable everyday inheritance is linguistic: the vernacular Bibles and hymnbooks of this period helped standardise written Swedish, Danish and Finnish. The parish register, kept from this era for baptisms, marriages and burials, also made Scandinavia one of the most thoroughly documented populations on earth.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity — Etchmiadzin and New Julfa
movements.informalName: The Church of the Great Migration
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 7 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run as V.21's receiver - halving the Armenian spine's longest gap. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: colophons, the New Julfa church-building record, merchant-network documents, Arakel of Tabriz (Davrizhetsi)'s history from the 1660s, and material on Etchmiadzin under Safavid rule.
movements.floorNote: No question — this is one of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches, whose difference from the Chalcedonian churches is about how Christ's divinity and humanity are described, not about whether he is God.
movements.relationsSummary: Shah Abbas deports about 300,000 Armenians (1604-05, the Great Migration); New Julfa rises at Isfahan from 1605 - churches within years, and the merchant network that funds the church; Etchmiadzin's catholicoi continue under Safavid rule.
movements.why: In 1604-05, Shah Abbas I deported the population of Julfa and much of eastern Armenia into Persia as part of a scorched-earth campaign, and many died on the road. Survivors resettled across the river from Isfahan in New Julfa, where Armenian merchants built a trading network stretching from Amsterdam to Manila and used it to fund a new cathedral, the Vank, while the mother see at Etchmiadzin worked to rebuild itself under Safavid rule.
movements.dateRationale: 1517 to 1650 (era window; the Great Migration 1604-05 and New Julfa's rise inside; the 1441-1517 spine remainder stays disclosed) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Caught between the Ottoman and Safavid empires, Armenians lived through one of the great forced migrations of their history: in 1604-05 Shah Abbas I, pursuing a scorched-earth strategy against the Ottomans, deported the population of Julfa and much of eastern Armenia into Persia, and many died on the road. Those who survived were settled in a new quarter across the river from Isfahan, New Julfa, where the cathedral known as the Vank was established in 1606 and where Armenian merchants built one of the most far-reaching trading networks in the world, from Amsterdam to Manila, funding their church as they went. Meanwhile the mother see at Etchmiadzin, now under Safavid rule, worked to rebuild itself as the centre of Armenian church life.
movements.teaser: Armenia and Isfahan, 1517 to 1650 — a church deported en masse into Persia that rebuilt itself in a new city and paid for itself by trade.
voices: Shah Abbas I — the Safavid ruler whose scorched-earth deportation of 1604-05 created New Julfa
Movses III of Tatev — catholicos who led the rebuilding of Etchmiadzin around 1630
Khachatur Kesaratsi — bishop of New Julfa, who set up the first printing press in Persia in the 1630s
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church continues, with Etchmiadzin still its mother see and the residence of its catholicos. New Julfa is still an Armenian quarter of Isfahan, with working churches and the Vank cathedral's museum. The merchant network built in this period seeded Armenian communities and churches from India to the Mediterranean, and the memory of forced displacement became part of how the Armenian church tells its own story.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church and a UNESCO World Heritage site
The Vank Cathedral in New Julfa, Isfahan — the Armenian quarter's cathedral, founded in 1606, with its museum

movements.name: The Carmelite Reform and the Spanish Mystics
movements.informalName: The World of Teresa and John
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (Era 7 Step 0; corpus verification follow-up named)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run - the completeness gap the inherited flags missed. Corpus dates [S] this session; verification follow-up named before any build. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Teresa's Life, Way of Perfection, and Interior Castle, along with her foundations narrative, and John of the Cross's poems and commentaries — among the era's deepest first-person accounts of inner spiritual experience, including a woman's voice writing in her own words.
movements.floorNote: No question (intra-Catholic reform, Inquisition-shadowed - the shadow is part of its story)
movements.relationsSummary: Teresa founds San Jose (1562); John joins (1568); the Discalced province is recognized (1580-93); Teresa dies 1582, canonized 1622; connects to the medieval Carmelite order and lives inside the wider Tridentine Catholic reform while speaking in its own unmistakable voice.
movements.why: After more than twenty years in a large, comfortable convent, Teresa of Ávila concluded she wasn't living the life she had promised, and in 1562 founded a small house under a stricter rule of poverty, enclosure and long silent prayer. She wrote books about prayer she never intended to publish, and the friar who joined her reform, John of the Cross, wrote some of his finest poetry during nine months imprisoned by his own brethren.
movements.dateRationale: 1562 (San Jose [S]) to 1622 (Teresa's canonization [S]); corpus dates verification-conditioned, follow-up named (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Teresa of Ávila had spent more than twenty years as a Carmelite nun in a large, comfortable, sociable convent when she concluded that the life she had promised was not the life she was living. In 1562 she founded a small house, St Joseph's in Ávila, under a stricter rule — poverty, enclosure, few sisters, long hours of silent prayer. And spent the rest of her life travelling Spain founding others, arguing with officials, and writing books about prayer she had never intended to publish. In 1568 a young friar, John of the Cross, joined the reform on the men's side and became its greatest poet. Both were watched by the Inquisition and opposed from inside their own order, and John spent nine months imprisoned by his own brethren. Which is when he wrote some of his finest verse.
movements.teaser: Castile, 1562 to 1622 — a nun who rebuilt her order from a single small house, and the friar-poet who joined her, between them writing the era's deepest accounts of prayer.
voices: Teresa of Ávila — founder of the reform and author of the Life, the Way of Perfection and the Interior Castle
John of the Cross — friar and poet, author of the Dark Night and the Spiritual Canticle, imprisoned by his own order in 1577
Jerónimo Gracián — the reform's first provincial and Teresa's confidant, who defended it through its worst internal conflicts
Ana de Jesús — Teresa's companion, who carried the reform into France and the Low Countries after her death
movements.legacy: The Discalced Carmelites are still a worldwide order of friars and nuns. Teresa's and John's writings became permanent classics of Christian spiritual literature far beyond Catholicism, read by Protestants, by poets and by psychologists, and both were later declared Doctors of the Church — Teresa in 1970, the first woman ever so named. Their vocabulary passed into ordinary English: the 'dark night of the soul', the 'interior castle'.

experienceToday.text: The Convento de San José in Ávila, Spain — Teresa's first foundation of 1562, now also housing the Museo Teresiano

movements.name: The Church of the East — the Schism of 1552
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 7 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 7 Step 0 run as V.17's receiver. The named-gap alternative stays stated. Added at the Era 7 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin: mostly succession lists and colophons. Sulaqa's profession of faith and consecration at Rome are documented from the Roman side.
movements.floorNote: No question — both patriarchal lines belong to the same ancient communion and share the same faith.
movements.relationsSummary: Opponents of hereditary succession elect Yohannan Sulaqa; he professes at Rome (1553), is consecrated in St Peter's, and is martyred (1555) - the Chaldean line begins and the communion carries two rival patriarchates ever after; kin story: VI.18 (Malabar) is the same communion's other era-7 ordeal
movements.why: By the sixteenth century, the Church of the East's highest office had become hereditary, passing from uncle to nephew within a single family. In 1552 a dissenting party elected a monastery superior, Yohannan Sulaqa, who travelled to Rome, was consecrated patriarch there in 1553, and was arrested and killed on his return home in 1555 — beginning a division into two rival patriarchates that has never fully healed.
movements.dateRationale: 1517 (era boundary; V.17's gated end) to 1650 (era end; the 1552-55 Sulaqa arc inside; both patriarchal lines continue) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: By the sixteenth century the patriarchate of the Church of the East — once a communion that had reached as far as China — had contracted to the mountains and plains of Mesopotamia, and its highest office had become hereditary, passing from uncle to nephew inside a single family. In 1552 a party opposed to that arrangement elected a monastery superior, Yohannan Sulaqa, and sent him to Rome. He made a profession of faith there, was consecrated patriarch in 1553, returned home, and was arrested and killed in 1555. The line he had begun continued anyway, and from that point the ancient communion has carried two rival patriarchates — a division that has never fully healed.
movements.teaser: Mesopotamia and Rome, 1552 to 1555 — a disputed election that sent a monk to the pope and left an ancient church with two patriarchs ever after.
voices: Yohannan Sulaqa — monastery superior elected by the dissenting party, consecrated at Rome in 1553 and killed in 1555
Shemon VII Ishoyahb — the hereditary patriarch whose succession the dissenters rejected
Abdisho IV Maron — Sulaqa's successor, who continued the new line and its relationship with Rome
movements.legacy: The division is still the shape of the communion, though not in the way the 1552 parties would have guessed. The line Sulaqa began eventually drifted back out of communion with Rome and continued as the Assyrian Church of the East, now largely a diaspora church with its patriarchate at Erbil, while the older line he had challenged entered communion with Rome in the nineteenth century and became the Chaldean Catholic Church, today the largest Christian body in Iraq. Both still use the East Syriac liturgy, including the ancient Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the two churches have been in formal dialogue since the 1990s.

movements.name: The Quakers (Religious Society of Friends)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — journals are the movement's own native genre, with Woolman and women's ministry records among them. Its floor question was addressed rather than deferred: early Friends were kept off the register on purpose, since rejecting creedal subscription is a question about the form of confession rather than a divergence in content, and this run seats only the seventeenth-and-eighteenth-century window. Its end moved to 1815 once a six-entry cluster of round-1800 ends was identified as a generated default rather than six judgments.
movements.sourcing: RICH - journals are the movement's own native genre; meeting records dense; Woolman's Journal a moral-formation classic
movements.floorNote: A carefully-stated case rather than a simple one. The earliest Friends affirm Christ's divinity in plain terms, but they reject the practice of signing up to a creed at all — which is an argument about the form of confession rather than a disagreement about its content. Later Quakerism spread out considerably, so the answer depends on which century and which body of Friends is being asked about.
movements.relationsSummary: Radical child of the Puritan ferment; parent-influence on abolition
movements.why: Quakers built their worship around silence, waiting until someone felt moved by the Spirit to speak, and refused any oath or hat-honor to social superiors — convictions that filled English jails with them in the seventeenth century. Women preached on the same footing as men from the movement's earliest days, and it was a Quaker tailor, John Woolman, who spent decades traveling from meeting to meeting until Friends in America made owning slaves grounds for exclusion.
movements.dateRationale: End 1815 (continues-cap; living) — the old 1800 was part of a six-entry generated-default cluster, replaced (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.36 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The Journal of George Fox (ed. John L. Nickalls, CUP, 1952; reissued 2010), with the epistles to the meetings
sources.note: The journal genre was the movement's own native form, not just Fox's.

sources.work: Margaret Fell, Women's Speaking Justified (1666) and Works (1710); the separate women's meetings' minute books (from the 1670s)
sources.note: Women's ministry defended in print from inside the leadership; women's business meetings as standing church government.

sources.work: John Woolman, The Journal and Major Essays (1774; ed. Moulton, OUP, 1971); Elizabeth Ashbridge, Some Account; the published Friends' journals corpus as a genre
sources.note: A moral-formation classic; the journal genre beyond the founder.

sources.work: The sufferings archive: the Great Book of Sufferings (from 1675) and Besse, A Collection of the Sufferings of the People Called Quakers (1753); Katharine Evans & Sarah Cheevers's Malta captivity narrative (1662)
sources.note: Persecution documented by the movement's own record-keeping, compiled for advocacy purposes; women's prison voice in their own words.

sources.work: Rosemary Moore, The Light in Their Consciences: Early Quakers in Britain 1646-1666 (Penn State, 2000), with Angell & Dandelion (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Quaker Studies (2013)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in the 'Great Britain and Ireland' chapter (Clark) and the toleration chapter

movements.longDescription: In the turmoil of the English Civil War years, a shoemaker's apprentice named George Fox began telling anyone who would listen that Christ could teach his people himself. That every person carried an inward light, that no paid clergy or consecrated building was needed, and that a meeting could sit in silence until someone was moved to speak. Friends refused oaths, hat-honour and titles, refused to fight, and let women preach on the same footing as men. Thousands of them were fined, jailed and transported for it, and they kept a running written record of their own sufferings as they went. By the eighteenth century the movement had settled into a quieter, disciplined life of meetings and plain dress, and turned outward. The New Jersey tailor John Woolman spent decades travelling among Friends, pressing them to free the people they held as slaves, until the American yearly meetings made slaveholding a bar to membership.
movements.teaser: England and the Atlantic world, 1650s to 1815 — a movement that sat in silence waiting for God to speak, refused to swear an oath or take off its hat to any man, and went to prison for both.
voices: George Fox — the movement's founding preacher, whose Journal became the pattern for a whole tradition of Quaker spiritual autobiography
Margaret Fell — of Swarthmoor Hall, organizer and financier of the early movement and author of Women's Speaking Justified (1666)
John Woolman — New Jersey tailor whose journal and decades of patient travelling turned Friends against slaveholding
Katharine Evans and Sarah Cheevers — Friends held for years by the Inquisition on Malta, who wrote their own captivity narrative (1662)
movements.legacy: The Religious Society of Friends is a living body on both sides of the Atlantic, though it divided in the nineteenth century into unprogrammed, evangelical and pastoral branches that persist to this day. Its wider mark is out of all proportion to its size. Quaker campaigning was central to abolition in Britain and America, Quaker refusal to swear or to fight helped push conscience into English law, and Pennsylvania began as a Quaker experiment in governing without an established church. The plain meeting house, the silent meeting and the practice of testing a decision until the whole gathering can consent are all still recognizably theirs.

experienceToday.text: Swarthmoor Hall, Ulverston, Cumbria — Margaret Fell's house, the early movement's headquarters, open to visitors with its gardens and café

movements.name: German Pietism - Spener, Francke, Halle
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on correspondence networks, conversion narratives and institutional records. Its c. 1750 end was kept but relabelled honestly as a soft round-off rather than an event, with c. 1727 shown as the alternative; Württemberg Pietism was named inside its scope at the same gate so that it is no longer stranded.
movements.sourcing: Rich: correspondence networks, conversion narratives, institutional records
movements.relationsSummary: Pietism grew out of Lutheran devotion together with the influence of Dutch Reformed precisianism, and gave rise in turn to the Moravian Church and the wider Protestant missionary movement. Württemberg Pietism, associated with Johann Albrecht Bengel, belongs within this same movement.
movements.why: In 1675 the Lutheran pastor Philipp Jakob Spener argued that correct doctrine preached from the pulpit wasn't enough — Christians needed to meet in small groups, read Scripture together, and expect real change in their lives. That conviction built an orphanage at Halle that grew into schools, a press, and a network reaching across Europe, and sent Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg to Tranquebar in South India in 1706, one of the first organized Protestant missions out of Europe.
movements.dateRationale: End c. 1750 KEPT, stated as a soft round-off (alt c. 1727, Francke's death, was shown) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Spener, Pia Desideria (1675; trans. Tappert, Fortress, 1964), with the collegia pietatis practice it launched

Francke's conversion narrative (1690/91 Lebenslauf) and works; the Halle institutional record - orphanage reports (Segensvolle Fusstapfen, 1701ff.), the global correspondence network, Canstein Bible Institute records
sources.note: The Halle archives (Franckesche Stiftungen) are largely untranslated from German.

sources.work: Johanna Eleonora Petersen, The Life of Lady Johanna Eleonora Petersen, Written by Herself (1718; trans. Becker-Cantarino, Chicago, 2005); lay conversion-narrative compilations (Reitz, Historie der Wiedergebohrnen, 1698-)
sources.note: Women's and lay voices; part of the movement's own conversion-narrative genre.

sources.work: Freylinghausen, Geistreiches Gesangbuch (Halle, 1704; expanded 1714)
sources.note: Hymnody in actual use - household and conventicle piety in its own medium. Available only in German.

sources.work: Douglas Shantz, An Introduction to German Pietism (Johns Hopkins, 2013), with W. R. Ward, The Protestant Evangelical Awakening (CUP, 1992)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann), with 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' (Ward)
sources.note: Strong fit: Lehmann is a Pietism specialist.

movements.longDescription: In 1675 a Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt, Philipp Jakob Spener, published a short book called Pia Desideria arguing that correct doctrine correctly preached was not enough. Christians needed to meet in small groups, read Scripture together, and expect their lives to change. What followed was less a new church than a renewal movement inside the Lutheran state churches, and its centre became Halle, where August Hermann Francke built an orphanage that grew into a complex of schools, a printing house and a Bible institute, funded by donations and tied to correspondents across Europe, Russia, India and North America. Pietism gave German Protestantism the conversion narrative as a genre and a great body of new hymnody, and through Halle's graduates it launched one of the first organized Protestant missions sent out from Europe, when Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau sailed for the Danish trading post at Tranquebar in South India in 1706.
movements.teaser: Germany, 1675 to about 1750 — a renewal inside the Lutheran state church that answered cold orthodoxy with small groups and conversion stories, and built an orphanage in Halle that grew into a world-spanning enterprise.
voices: Philipp Jakob Spener — Frankfurt pastor whose Pia Desideria (1675) set the movement's programme and launched its small-group meetings
August Hermann Francke — built the Halle orphanage, schools and press that became Pietism's institutional engine
Johanna Eleonora Petersen — published her own life story in 1718, one of the first autobiographies written and printed by a German woman
Johann Anastasius Freylinghausen — compiled the Halle hymnbook (1704) that carried the movement's piety in its sung form
Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg — Halle-trained, sailed in 1706 for Tranquebar in South India, translating the New Testament into Tamil
movements.legacy: Pietism never became a denomination of its own — it stayed inside the Lutheran churches and eventually dissolved as a distinct party — but almost everything it touched outlived it. The Moravians at Herrnhut came out of its orbit and through them John Wesley; the Protestant missionary movement's first sustained institutional base was at Halle. And the Halle foundations themselves are still standing and still working in Saxony-Anhalt, orphanage buildings, library, cabinet of curiosities and all. Its habits — small groups meeting midweek to read Scripture, and the expectation that a Christian can tell the story of their own conversion — are now so ordinary across evangelical Protestantism that their origin is easy to miss.

experienceToday.text: The Francke Foundations, Halle, Germany — Francke's orphanage complex, library and historic school buildings, still in use and open to visitors

movements.name: Radical Pietism & the Brethren (Dunkers, Ephrata)
movements.informalName: The Radical Pietists and the Brethren
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a moderate-to-rich base. Its position between Pietism and Anabaptism was left standing as a real uniqueness test rather than settled, and its end moved to 1815 as part of the correction of the round-1800 default cluster.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich
movements.relationsSummary: Between Pietism and Anabaptism - a real uniqueness test
movements.why: In 1708, eight separatists waded into the river Eder at Schwarzenau in Germany and baptized one another, joining Pietist inward renewal to Anabaptist convictions — baptism only for believing adults, plain living, and refusal to bear arms. Driven to Pennsylvania, one of them, Conrad Beissel, founded the celibate community at Ephrata, where a sisterhood called the Roses of Saron composed austere music and hand-lettered manuscripts unlike anything else made in colonial America.
movements.dateRationale: End 1815 (continues-cap; living; the round-1800 cluster replaced) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Alexander Mack, Rights and Ordinances (1713) and Basic Questions, with the Schwarzenau (1708) accounts, in Durnbaugh (ed.), European Origins of the Brethren (1958) and The Brethren in Colonial America (1967)
sources.note: The movement's own documents, in the standard English documentary editions.

sources.work: Gottfried Arnold, Unparteiische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie (1699-1700), with Hochmann von Hochenau's confession (1702)
sources.note: Radical Pietism's historiographical manifesto and separatist matrix. Untranslated in full.

sources.work: Chronicon Ephratense (1786; trans. Hark, 1889), with Ephrata's registers and Beissel's writings
sources.note: The community's own history, written in an insider, hagiographic style.

sources.work: The Ephrata sisterhood (Roses of Saron) writings, the convent's Fraktur and music manuscripts, the Turtel-Taube hymnbook (1747)
sources.note: A women's spiritual community documenting itself in text, script, and song. Held in archives at the Ephrata Cloister and Winterthur.

sources.work: Jeff Bach, Voices of the Turtledoves: The Sacred World of Ephrata (Penn State, 2003), with Durnbaugh's historical scholarship
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann) and Ward's awakenings chapter

movements.longDescription: Where mainstream Pietism stayed inside the Lutheran church, a radical wing walked out of it — separatists who held that the true church had fallen away centuries earlier and that no state establishment could be mended. In 1708, at Schwarzenau in the little county of Wittgenstein — one of the few German territories that would leave separatists alone — eight of them baptized one another in the river Eder and became the Brethren, joining Pietist inwardness to Anabaptist convictions: baptism only for believers, plain living, and refusal of the sword. Persecution pushed them to Pennsylvania from 1719, where they became one of the first German-speaking religious cultures in colonial America; and where one of them, Conrad Beissel, founded the celibate community at Ephrata, which produced its own austere music, its own hand-lettered Fraktur manuscripts, and a sisterhood, the Roses of Saron, who wrote and sang their own hymns.
movements.teaser: Germany and then Pennsylvania, 1690s to 1815 — separatists who rebaptized one another in a German river in 1708, crossed the Atlantic, and built a singing, manuscript-making cloister in the Pennsylvania woods.
voices: Alexander Mack — led the first Brethren baptisms at Schwarzenau in 1708 and wrote the movement's founding tracts
Gottfried Arnold — radical Pietist historian whose Impartial History of Churches and Heretics (1699-1700) retold church history from the dissenters' side
Ernst Christoph Hochmann von Hochenau — itinerant separatist preacher whose 1702 confession shaped the circle Mack came out of
Conrad Beissel — founder of the Ephrata community, composer of its hymnody and author of its rule
The Roses of Saron — Ephrata's sisterhood, who produced much of the community's music, illuminated manuscripts and written work
movements.legacy: It became an ongoing family of churches: the Brethren bodies of North America — the Church of the Brethren and its relatives. Descend directly from the Schwarzenau baptisms, and they carried the plain-dress, peace-church strand of American Christianity alongside the Mennonites and the Quakers. Ephrata itself died out, but its buildings survive as a Pennsylvania state historic site, along with its Fraktur, its hymnbooks and a body of choral music unlike anything else written in colonial America. The radical Pietist habit of printing — Christopher Sauer's press in Germantown produced the first Bible printed in a European language in North America — left its own long mark on American publishing.

experienceToday.text: Ephrata Cloister, Ephrata, Pennsylvania — the original eighteenth-century community buildings, preserved as a state historic site and open to visitors

movements.name: The Moravian Church at Herrnhut
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on what the run called the era's strongest sourcing line — daily congregational diaries, choir records, and thousands of member memoirs, including women's and formerly-enslaved members'. At the Freeze its succession from the Czech churches was ruled an identity link across the 1627–1722 hidden-seed century, resting on the census's own literal-renewal claim and refugee-carried continuity, with the 95-year gap disclosed and the episcopal-consecration argument carried as supporting rather than load-bearing.
movements.sourcing: RICH to an almost unique degree: daily congregational diaries, choir records, thousands of member memoirs (Lebenslaeufe), the Losungen since 1731
movements.floorNote: No creedal question; the Sifting Time's excesses are a tension the sources themselves name and correct
movements.relationsSummary: This community is a direct renewal of the old Bohemian Unity of the Brethren, carried across the hidden century between its suppression in 1627 and the refugees' arrival at Herrnhut in 1722. Its episcopal succession was renewed through the Jablonski-Nitschmann consecration of 1735, tying it formally back to the old Unity. It had a decisive influence on John Wesley, and began sending missionaries decades before any other Protestant body did.
movements.why: In 1722 a handful of refugee families slipped out of Bohemia, remnants of a reformed church that had survived underground for nearly a century, and built the village of Herrnhut on a Saxon nobleman's land. The community kept prayer running in shifts around the clock, wrote up its life in a diary every single day, and from 1732 sent out missionaries — to the enslaved of St Thomas, to Greenland, to Suriname — on a scale no other Protestant body approached for another two centuries.
movements.dateRationale: End 1815 (continues-cap; living; alt 1760 Zinzendorf shown; the round-1800 cluster replaced) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The Herrnhut congregational record: Gemein-Diarium (daily diary), Brotherly Agreement (12 May 1727), the 13 August 1727 communion account, choir records, the Losungen (printed annually since 1731)
sources.note: A community writing itself down daily. The Unity Archives are largely untranslated.

sources.work: The Lebenslaeufe: thousands of member memoirs, incl. women's (selection in Faull, Moravian Women's Memoirs, Syracuse, 1997) and formerly-enslaved members' (Rebecca Protten's letters and memoir materials)
sources.note: An unusually deep record of ordinary voices.

sources.work: Zinzendorf's corpus: discourses, litanies, hymns
sources.note: Zinzendorf's own writings, kept distinct from the congregation's communal record. The excesses of the Sifting Time (1743-50) are named and corrected in the community's own records.

sources.work: Mission diaries: St Thomas (from 1732; Friedrich Martin's diaries; the 1739 enslaved converts' petition-letters), Greenland, Shekomeko/Bethlehem Native congregations; Oldendorp's Historie (1777)
sources.note: The converts' words survive only as recorded by missionaries, within contexts of slavery and dispossession.

sources.work: Craig Atwood, Community of the Cross (Penn State, 2004), with Jon Sensbach, Rebecca's Revival (Harvard, 2005)
sources.note: Sensbach's book recovers Rebecca Protten's story.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' (Ward), with 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann)
sources.note: Both are a direct fit for this movement.

movements.longDescription: In 1722 a handful of families slipped over the Bohemian border into Saxony. The remnant of the Unity of the Brethren, which had survived underground for nearly a century after the Habsburgs outlawed the Czech reform church.
