Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf let them settle on his estate, the village they built was called Herrnhut, and after years of quarrelling among the refugees and the other seekers who joined them, a communion service on 13 August 1727 became the moment the community always afterwards dated its renewal from. What followed was extraordinary for a settlement of a few hundred people. A prayer watch kept in shifts around the clock, a congregation organized into 'choirs' by age and situation, a diary written up every single day, and thousands of ordinary members setting down their own life stories. From 1732 they began sending missionaries — to the enslaved people of St Thomas, to Greenland, to Suriname, to the Native congregations of Pennsylvania and New York. On a scale nothing else in Protestantism came near: a village of a few hundred people sending out more missionaries in twenty years than the whole of Protestant Europe had sent in two centuries.
movements.teaser: Saxony and then the world, 1722 to 1815 — a refugee village of a few hundred that wrote down every day of its life, prayed in shifts around the clock, and sent out missionaries on a scale no other Protestant church came near.
voices: Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf — the Saxon nobleman who gave the refugees land and became the community's leader, preacher and hymn-writer
Christian David — the carpenter who guided the first Moravian families out of Moravia to Herrnhut in 1722 and cut the first tree
Leonhard Dober and David Nitschmann — the first two missionaries, sent in 1732 to the enslaved people of St Thomas in the Caribbean
Rebecca Protten — born enslaved in the Caribbean, a Moravian evangelist among the enslaved of St Thomas, whose own letters survive
Anna Nitschmann — leader of the single sisters' choir and one of the community's central figures in her own right
movements.legacy: The Moravian Church is a living worldwide body, and far larger outside Europe than in it. The great majority of its members are in Tanzania and the Caribbean, the long fruit of the mission work begun in 1732. Its most consequential single contact was with a young Anglican priest: John Wesley met Moravians in a storm at sea and again in London, and the Methodist revival carries their fingerprints. The Losungen, a book of daily Scripture texts drawn by lot at Herrnhut and printed every year since 1731, is still published and read in dozens of languages. One of the longest unbroken publishing runs in the world. And the hidden-seed story ended well: a church suppressed in Bohemia in 1627 has descendants in every continent.

experienceToday.text: Herrnhut, Germany — the Moravian Church's founding town, still a living community and a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: The Methodist Revival
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich at every level, from journals and class-meeting records to thousands of member narratives and the hymn corpus. Its end moved to 1815 under the continues-cap convention, with Wesley's death (1791) and the Plan of Pacification (1795) named as the tradition's own hinges — the discarded round-1800 sat astride both without being either.
movements.sourcing: RICH at every level: journals, class-meeting records, thousands of member narratives, the hymn corpus
movements.relationsSummary: Methodism grew from Puritan piety and Moravian influence inside the Church of England, and became the parent of the Holiness movement and, through Holiness, of Pentecostalism. It is also a parent tradition of the Black Church in America, through Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal Church, founded in 1816, and the AME Zion Church, founded in 1821.
movements.why: In May 1738, John Wesley felt his heart 'strangely warmed' at a meeting in London and began preaching holiness and assurance to crowds shut out of ordinary church pulpits, so he and George Whitefield preached in open fields instead. What made the revival last was Wesley's habit of organizing converts into weekly classes of a dozen, each expected to give an honest account of their lives, while his brother Charles set the movement's whole theology to thousands of singable hymns.
movements.dateRationale: End 1815 (continues-cap; living) — Wesley's death (1791) and the Plan of Pacification (1795 [S]) named as the tradition's own hinges; the round-1800 artifact replaced (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.34 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Wesley's Journal and the Works of John Wesley (Bicentennial Edition, Abingdon, 1975-), sermons, A Plain Account of Christian Perfection
sources.note: Wesley's own writings, kept distinct from the connexion's communal record.

sources.work: The class meeting and connexional machinery: General Rules (1743), band and class records and class papers, society and circuit records, annual Conference Minutes (from 1744)
sources.note: The movement's lived organizational core, in records scattered across archives, chiefly the Methodist Archives in Manchester.

sources.work: Charles Wesley's hymns: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780), with Charles's journal
sources.note: Hymnody as actually used: the movement's theology in its sung, memorized, everyday form.

sources.work: Women's and ordinary voices: Wesley-Crosby correspondence (1761), Mary Bosanquet Fletcher's 1771 letter, Hester Ann Rogers's Account, the Arminian Magazine (1778-) lay narratives; Richard Allen's conversion c. 1777 at the era's edge
sources.note: The women's-preaching debate in its own protagonists' words; a vehicle for ordinary members' narratives. Allen's narrative wasn't published until 1833, and the Primitive Methodist accounts (from 1807) come from a later period than this movement's core years.

sources.work: Henry Rack, Reasonable Enthusiasm (1989; 3rd ed. 2002), with David Hempton, Methodism: Empire of the Spirit (Yale, 2005)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' (W. R. Ward)
sources.note: A direct fit for this movement.

movements.longDescription: John Wesley was an Oxford-trained Church of England priest whose methodical little religious society had earned him a mocking nickname and whose mission to Georgia had ended in failure. Until, at a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, in May 1738, he felt his heart 'strangely warmed' and began preaching assurance and holiness to anyone who would stand still for it. Shut out of many pulpits, he and George Whitefield preached in fields and at pit-heads to crowds of thousands. But Wesley did something rarer than preaching, which was to organize, dividing converts into 'classes' of a dozen who met weekly to give an account of their lives, licensing lay preachers to ride circuits, and holding an annual conference. His brother Charles wrote the movement's theology into thousands of hymns, so that people who could not have read a treatise sang one instead. Wesley meant all of this to renew the Church of England from inside and insisted to the end that he had not left it. After his death in 1791 the connexion became a separate church anyway.
movements.teaser: Britain and then America, 1738 to 1815 — a priest who could not get a pulpit preached in fields instead, then organized everyone who listened into weekly classes that had to give an honest account of themselves.
voices: John Wesley — the movement's preacher and organizer, who rode an estimated quarter of a million miles and never formally left the Church of England
Charles Wesley — wrote thousands of hymns that carried the revival's theology in singable form
George Whitefield — the revival's most powerful open-air preacher on both sides of the Atlantic, and Wesley's Calvinist counterpart and friendly rival
Mary Bosanquet Fletcher — argued in a 1771 letter to Wesley for a woman's right to preach, and won his qualified agreement
Francis Asbury — carried the connexion across the American frontier and became the shaping figure of American Methodism
Richard Allen — converted as a young enslaved man in the 1770s, later founder of the African Methodist Episcopal Church
movements.legacy: It became one of the largest church families in the world. The British connexion separated from the Church of England after Wesley's death, American Methodism organized itself as a church in 1784, and out of that stem came the nineteenth-century Holiness movement and, from Holiness, Pentecostalism. Now the fastest-growing form of Christianity on earth. Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal Church, founded in 1816, made Methodism one of the foundations of the Black Church in America. And the hymns stayed: 'O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing', 'Love Divine, All Loves Excelling' and 'Hark! the Herald Angels Sing' are all Charles Wesley's.

experienceToday.text: Wesley's Chapel and the Museum of Methodism, City Road, London — the chapel Wesley opened in 1778, his house next door, and his grave behind it

movements.name: The Evangelical Awakening in New England
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1): the revival narratives were the era's own documentation project, with Edwards's case histories of ordinary people at their centre. Its middle- and southern-colonies duty was named at the gate, while the entry's own question — whether Britain and New England are one tradition or two — was left standing as its record's open call. Its date string was aligned to c. 1760, with 1770 shown as an outer alternative.
movements.sourcing: Rich - revival narratives were the era's own documentation project (Edwards's case histories of ordinary people)
movements.relationsSummary: The awakening grew out of New England Puritanism and became a parent of later American revival culture and the missionary movement. It also reached into the middle and southern colonies, through preachers like the Tennents and the revival at Hanover, Virginia — though historians are divided on whether that counts as part of the same movement or a separate one. Through the Black and Native Christian writing it produced, it stands among the parent traditions of the Black Church in America.
movements.why: When an ordinary Massachusetts congregation began converting in waves during the winter of 1734–35, its pastor Jonathan Edwards did something unusual: he wrote down what happened case by case, including a four-year-old girl and a young woman the town had thought beyond hope. The awakening split New England's churches between defenders and critics of the revival, and produced the first substantial body of Christian writing by Black and Native people in the colonies.
movements.dateRationale: String aligned; c. 1760 the awakening's close (outer alt 1770, Whitefield's death [S], shown) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Edwards's corpus: A Faithful Narrative (1737, with the Hutchinson and Bartlet case histories), The Distinguishing Marks (1741), Religious Affections (1746), Life of Brainerd (1749) - Works of Jonathan Edwards (Yale; WJE Online)
sources.note: Life of Brainerd belongs to the missionary-biography genre, which shaped how Edwards told the story.

sources.work: The conversion-narrative genre: Nathan Cole's Spiritual Travels; Sarah Osborn's diaries and memoir (ed. Brekus, Sarah Osborn's Collected Writings, Yale, 2017); Sarah Edwards's 1742 narrative; The Christian History (1743-45, ed. Prince)
sources.note: The revival's serialized self-documentation.

sources.work: Black and indigenous voices: Phillis Wheatley (Whitefield elegy 1770; Poems 1773), Jupiter Hammon, Lemuel Haynes (sermons; Liberty Further Extended ms. c. 1776), Samson Occom (Short Narrative of My Life, 1768; hymns); Richard Allen's ministry begins a generation later
sources.note: These voices mostly date from the 1760s-70s, a generation after the main revival years, but are carried here as the awakening's direct fruit. Occom's own account describes discrimination within the mission system in the first person.

sources.work: The contested revival: Chauncy, Seasonable Thoughts (1743); Davenport's Confession and Retractions (1744); Separate congregations' records and Isaac Backus's early diary
sources.note: Chauncy writes from inside the opposition — a hostile source, though his dossier is itself full of revival data. Backus's diary marks the point where the Separate movement became Baptist — the same transition covered under the Baptist history.

sources.work: Thomas Kidd, The Great Awakening (Yale, 2007), with George Marsden, Jonathan Edwards: A Life (Yale, 2003)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' (Ward), with 'British and French North America to 1765' (Noll)
sources.note: Noll's chapter frames the real question of whether this is one tradition or two.

movements.longDescription: It began in the winter of 1734-35 in Northampton, Massachusetts, where the town's minister, Jonathan Edwards, watched an ordinary Connecticut Valley congregation come apart and remake itself in a wave of conversions. And then did something unusual: he wrote down what had happened, case by case, including a young woman the town had thought beyond hope and a four-year-old girl. When the English preacher George Whitefield toured the colonies from 1739, scattered local revivals became a general one, with itinerants crossing parish lines and crowds gathering in the open air. It split New England's churches: the New Lights defended the awakening, the Old Lights — Charles Chauncy of Boston foremost among them — attacked it as enthusiasm and disorder, and hundreds of Separate congregations broke away, a great many of them becoming Baptist. It also produced the first substantial body of Christian writing by Black and Native people in the colonies.
movements.teaser: New England, 1734 to about 1760 — a revival that its own pastor wrote down as it happened, conversion by conversion, and that split the region's churches in two.
voices: Jonathan Edwards — Northampton pastor and theologian who documented the revival in A Faithful Narrative (1737) and defended it in Religious Affections (1746)
George Whitefield — the itinerant English preacher whose 1739-40 tour turned local revivals into a general awakening
Sarah Osborn — Newport schoolmistress who led religious meetings in her own house, including for enslaved and free Black people, and left extensive diaries
Charles Chauncy — Boston minister and the revival's most formidable critic, whose Seasonable Thoughts (1743) is itself full of revival evidence
Samson Occom — Mohegan preacher and ordained Presbyterian, who wrote a first-person account of his life and of the discrimination he met
Phillis Wheatley — enslaved in Boston, whose published poems included an elegy for Whitefield
movements.legacy: It left no church of its own — the awakening ran through existing Congregational parishes and broke some of them — but it reshaped American religion permanently. It made the revival meeting and the itinerant preacher normal instruments, filled the Baptist churches with Separate converts, and produced in Edwards the most substantial theologian America has yet made, still argued over three centuries later. It seeded the first generation of Black and Native Christian writing in North America. And the missionary societies of the following century traced their impulse back to it, often explicitly, through Edwards's Life of David Brainerd.

movements.name: The Old Believers
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich inside voice: Avvakum's autobiography, verified in the source pass, is a first-person masterpiece. Its floorNote was cited approvingly at the gate as a clean example that the floor is the Creed and not liturgical correctness. Its end moved to 1815, with Edinoverie (1800) named so that a previously near-principled accident became a stated reason.
movements.sourcing: RICH inside voice: Avvakum's autobiography is a first-person masterpiece; community rules; later merchant records
movements.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here at all. Old Believers held exactly the same creed as the church they left — the split was about ritual: how to make the sign of the cross, how to spell the name of Jesus, which way a procession should walk around a church.
movements.relationsSummary: The Old Believers grew out of Muscovite Christianity, standing as the enduring counterpart to the official church's Nikonian reforms. Edinoverie, established in 1800, sits on the boundary shared between the two churches. In 1846 the priestly Old Believers restored their own episcopate through the Belokrinitsa hierarchy.
movements.why: When Patriarch Nikon corrected the Russian service books in the 1650s — changing how the faithful crossed themselves and how Jesus's name was spelled — a large part of the church refused to accept it as a mere detail and was anathematized for it in 1666. Their great voice, Archpriest Avvakum, wrote the first sustained autobiography in Russian from an underground prison before he was burned at the stake in 1682, and the movement survived in the forests and Siberia, in some communities by mass self-immolation rather than submission.
movements.dateRationale: End 1815 (continues-cap; living) — Edinoverie (1800 [S]) named so the old near-principled accident becomes a stated fact (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Archpriest Avvakum: The Life Written by Himself (ed./trans. Brostrom, Michigan Slavic, 1979; new trans. Gluck & Brostrom, Columbia Russian Library, 2021), with his Pustozersk letters and petitions
sources.note: A first-rank inside voice, written in an underground earthen prison, 1669-75.

sources.work: Boyarynia Feodosia Morozova: Avvakum's letters to her and the Tale of Boiarynia Morozova (trans. in Ziolkowski's edition, 2000)
sources.note: A noblewoman starved to death for the old rite (1675); women were numerically central in the priestless communities.

sources.work: The communities' own layer: the Solovki petitions (1667) and siege record (1668-76); the Vyg community - Pomorskie otvety (1723, bespopovtsy self-defense), Semyon Denisov's Vinograd Rossiiskii and Solovki-fathers history; popovtsy settlement records (Vetka, Kerzhenets); community rules
sources.note: Denisov's work follows the martyrology genre, so read it with that framing in mind. The division between priestly and priestless communities appears directly in the sources. Largely available only in untranslated Russian editions.

sources.work: The establishment record: the 1666-67 Moscow council's acts and anathemas, state persecution decrees (1685 articles), interrogation records
sources.note: The schism documented by its persecutors; testimony given under threat of death, so treat it as coerced evidence.

sources.work: Robert Crummey, The Old Believers and the World of Antichrist (Wisconsin, 1970) and Old Believers in a Changing World (2011), with Georg Michels, At War with the Church (Stanford, 1999)
sources.note: Michels complicates the movement's early coherence. The later merchant records referenced elsewhere are 19th-century, later than this movement's founding period.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 13 'Eastern Orthodoxy in Russia and Ukraine in the age of the Counter-Reformation', with 'The Russian Orthodox Church in imperial Russia 1721-1917' (Dixon)
sources.note: The Dixon chapter's number is inconsistent across listings - cited as ch. 14 in some, ch. 15 in others.

movements.longDescription: In the 1650s Patriarch Nikon set out to correct the Russian service books and rituals against contemporary Greek practice — two fingers in the sign of the cross became three, the spelling of Jesus's name changed, processions reversed direction. And a great part of the Russian church refused. To them the old rite was not a detail but the faith itself, handed down and now being altered by a church they concluded had fallen; the council of 1666-67 anathematized them, and the state hunted them for generations. Their great voice was Archpriest Avvakum, who wrote his own life story from an underground prison at Pustozersk before he was burned in 1682 — the first sustained autobiography in Russian, plain-spoken, furious and unexpectedly funny. Cut off from bishops, the movement divided between those who found priests and those who concluded the priesthood had ended altogether, and survived in the far north, the forests and Siberia, in some cases by mass self-immolation rather than submission.
movements.teaser: The Russian north and Siberia, 1666 to 1815 — Christians who would not change how they crossed themselves, and who took to the forests, the prisons and sometimes the fire rather than accept a corrected service book.
voices: Archpriest Avvakum — the movement's leading writer and martyr, who composed his autobiography in an earth-prison and was burned at the stake in 1682
Boyarynia Feodosia Morozova — a noblewoman who gave up her rank for the old rite and was starved to death in an underground cell in 1675
Patriarch Nikon — the reformer whose corrections caused the split, and who was himself deposed by the same council that condemned his opponents
Semyon Denisov — of the Vyg community on the White Sea, who wrote the movement's own histories and helped compose the Pomorian Answers (1723)
movements.legacy: Old Belief is still practised. Several Old Believer churches exist today — in Russia, Romania, the Baltic states, Alaska, Oregon and South America — some with their own bishops, some with no clergy at all, keeping pre-Nikonian chant, icons and books. Their stubbornness preserved a whole layer of medieval Russian religious culture that the official church had modernized away. Old icon-painting styles, znamenny chant and manuscript practices survived in these communities and were later recovered from them by collectors and scholars. Russian literature never let the schism go either; the raskol runs through the nineteenth-century novel as the standing question of what faithfulness actually costs.

experienceToday.text: The Rogozhskoye settlement, Moscow — since 1771 the spiritual centre of the largest Old Believer church, with its cathedrals and old-rite services

movements.name: The Hesychast Revival - Paisius & the Philokalia
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — lives, letters, and the anthology-making itself read as formation evidence. Two boundary matters were settled around it at the Freeze: under the Kollyvades seam ruling this entry keeps the Philokalia while the movement itself sits with an Era 9 entry, and its pre-existing succession write to the Optina tradition, made outside any gate, was ratified here.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: lives, letters, the anthology-making itself as formation evidence
movements.relationsSummary: Revival of the Palamite line; direct source of the Optina tradition
movements.why: In 1746 a young monk named Paisius Velichkovsky went looking through the monastery libraries of Mount Athos for old Greek teaching on inward prayer that almost nobody read anymore, and set his community to translating it into Slavonic at Neamț in Moldavia. Printed as the Philokalia at Venice in 1782 and in Paisius's own Slavonic version at Moscow in 1793, that anthology carried a monk's teaching on the Jesus Prayer out to ordinary readers, and fed directly into the elders of Optina and the anonymous classic The Way of a Pilgrim.

sources.work: Philokalia (Venice, 1782; comp. Macarius of Corinth and Nicodemus the Hagiorite; Eng. trans. Palmer, Sherrard & Ware, Faber, 1979-)
sources.note: The anthology itself is formation evidence in its own right — an editorial act aimed at monastics and laity alike.

sources.work: Paisius Velichkovsky: his unfinished autobiography and Mitrofan's Life (Featherstone trans., Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute, 1990), the Slavonic Dobrotolubiye (1793), letters and rule for Neamt
Nicodemus the Hagiorite: A Handbook of Spiritual Counsel (CWS, 1989), Concerning Frequent Communion (with Macarius), Unseen Warfare (reworking of Scupoli); the Kollyvades controversy documents
sources.note: The revival as a contested movement — both sides of the Kollyvades dispute are represented here; that it borrows from the Catholic writer Scupoli is itself worth noting.

sources.work: The living chain of teachers and students: Neamt's translation school and multinational community records; the starets-disciple correspondence into Russia
sources.note: The Optina elders' tradition flowered a generation later.

sources.work: Bingaman & Nassif (eds.), The Philokalia: A Classic Text of Orthodox Spirituality (OUP, 2012), with Kallistos Ware's essays and Chetverikov's Starets Paisii Velichkovskii (Eng. trans. 1980)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 8 'Orthodoxy and the West: Reformation to Enlightenment' (Kitromilides), with ch. 6 'Mount Athos and the Ottomans' (Zachariadou)
sources.note: A direct fit for this period.

movements.longDescription: In 1746 a young Ukrainian monk named Paisius Velichkovsky arrived on Mount Athos and began working through its monastery libraries for the old Greek texts on inner prayer that almost nobody was reading any more. He gathered a community, moved with it to Moldavia, and at Neamț built a translation workshop where monks turned those fathers into Slavonic; meanwhile on Athos, Macarius of Corinth and Nicodemus the Hagiorite assembled the same material into an anthology printed at Venice in 1782 under the title Philokalia, 'the love of the beautiful'. Paisius's Slavonic version, the Dobrotolubiye, was printed in Moscow in 1793, and the effect was enormous and largely unplanned: a body of monastic teaching on the Jesus Prayer and the watching of one's own heart, gathered for specialists, went into general circulation and reached ordinary lay readers.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos, Moldavia and Russia, 1746 to 1815 — monks who went looking in old libraries for forgotten teaching on inward prayer, printed what they found, and handed it to everybody.
voices: Paisius Velichkovsky — gathered and translated the hesychast fathers into Slavonic at Neamț, and rebuilt the elder-and-disciple relationship as a living practice
Nicodemus the Hagiorite — co-compiler of the Greek Philokalia (Venice, 1782) and a prolific writer of spiritual guidance
Macarius of Corinth — bishop and co-compiler of the Philokalia, and a leading voice for frequent communion
Mitrofan — Paisius's disciple, whose Life of his teacher preserves most of what is known about him
movements.legacy: This is one of the clearest cases anywhere of a book changing a church. The Philokalia is still in print and still read — the standard English translation has been appearing volume by volume since 1979. And the Russian tradition it fed produced the elders of Optina, the anonymous nineteenth-century classic The Way of a Pilgrim, and, through both, the spiritual world of Dostoevsky's novels. Twentieth-century Orthodox theology in the West drew on it heavily, and the Jesus Prayer is now practised far outside the monasteries the texts were written in. Neamț Monastery still stands and still functions, with Paisius's relics in it; he was canonized in 1988.

experienceToday.text: Neamț Monastery, Romania — Paisius's community and translation centre, a working monastery where his relics are kept

movements.name: Port-Royal Jansenism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on the record of a self-documenting community — memoirs, letters, and Pascal from its orbit. Its floorNote's distinction was left standing rather than reopened: an intra-Catholic grace controversy, in which papal condemnation is not floor failure.
movements.sourcing: Rich: a self-documenting community (memoirs, letters, Pascal from its orbit)
movements.floorNote: No question of creed arises. This was an argument among Catholics about grace and free will; Port-Royal was condemned by Rome, but being condemned in that dispute is not the same thing as departing from the church's confession of faith.
movements.relationsSummary: Augustine's long shadow inside the Tridentine church
movements.why: The convent of Port-Royal, reformed into severity by the young abbess Angélique Arnauld, read Augustine on grace harder than the Jesuits or the French crown could tolerate, and men of rank gave up their careers to live plainly nearby and write in its defense — among them Blaise Pascal, whose Provincial Letters mocked Jesuit moral reasoning so well that the mockery outlived the quarrel. When a core of the nuns refused to sign a formulary swearing to a matter of fact they said they had no way of knowing, Louis XIV had them dispersed in 1709 and the buildings pulled down to the cemetery.

sources.work: The nuns' own records: Mere Angelique Arnauld's letters and Relations; Angelique de Saint-Jean's Relation de captivite (1664-65); the Constitutions and the nuns' collective Relations on the signature crises
sources.note: The community's own voice: women's conscience under institutional siege, in their own words.

sources.work: Pascal from its orbit: The Provincial Letters (1656-57) and Pensees (1670)
sources.note: The Provinciales are themselves a polemic, worth reading as one.

sources.work: The theological controversy and the destruction record: Jansen's Augustinus (1640), Arnauld's De la frequente communion (1643), Quesnel's Reflexions morales; Cum occasione (1653), the Formulary, Unigenitus (1713); the destruction of 1709-11
sources.note: A hostile, institutional source: the church's own condemnation and destruction paperwork, which also documents this community's actual end.

sources.work: The memoir tradition: Racine's Abrege de l'histoire de Port-Royal, Fontaine's and du Fosse's memoirs, the Memoires pour servir a l'histoire de Port-Royal
sources.note: This community's own habit of documenting itself — an insider-advocate genre, worth reading as such.

sources.work: Daniella Kostroun, Feminism, Absolutism, and Jansenism: Louis XIV and the Port-Royal Nuns (CUP, 2011), with Alexander Sedgwick, Jansenism in Seventeenth-Century France (1977)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Jansenism and the international suppression of the Jesuits' (Van Kley)
sources.note: Aston's 'Continental Catholic Europe' sits beside it.

movements.longDescription: Port-Royal was a Cistercian convent outside Paris, reformed into severity by a young abbess, Angélique Arnauld, and it became the centre of a movement that read Augustine on grace harder than the Jesuits or the French crown could tolerate. Around it gathered the solitaires — men of rank who gave up their careers to live plainly near the abbey, teach in its small schools and write. And in its orbit stood Blaise Pascal, whose Provincial Letters mocked Jesuit moral reasoning so effectively that the mockery outlived the quarrel. Rome condemned five propositions said to be contained in Jansen's Augustinus, and the nuns were required to sign a formulary declaring both that the propositions were heretical and that they were in the book. A core of them refused, on the ground that no one could compel them to swear to a matter of fact they had no way of knowing. Louis XIV lost patience: the nuns were dispersed in 1709 and the buildings pulled down, down to digging up the cemetery.
movements.teaser: France, 1640 to 1710 — a convent that would not swear to something it could not know, and a king who answered by scattering the nuns and levelling the buildings.
voices: Angélique Arnauld — abbess from childhood, who reformed Port-Royal into the strict community the movement grew around
Angélique de Saint-Jean Arnauld d'Andilly — wrote the Relation de captivité, her own account of interrogation and confinement during the signature crisis

Antoine Arnauld — the family's theologian, whose On Frequent Communion (1643) set the movement's tone, and who was stripped of his Sorbonne doctorate in 1656 for defending the nuns' distinction between fact and doctrine
Blaise Pascal — mathematician and writer in Port-Royal's orbit, whose Provincial Letters defended it and whose Pensées were unfinished at his death
Cornelius Jansen — the Flemish bishop whose posthumous Augustinus (1640) gave the movement its name and the controversy its text
movements.legacy: The house was destroyed and the movement formally beaten, yet almost nothing about it actually disappeared. Pascal's Provincial Letters and Pensées became permanent French classics, and the Port-Royal schools' methods, along with the Port-Royal Logic and Grammar, shaped European education for generations. The quarrel outlived the abbey too: Jansenism became a political force in eighteenth-century France and fed the campaign that suppressed the Jesuits, and it produced one lasting institution. The small Church of Utrecht in the Netherlands, which consecrated its own archbishop without Rome in the 1720s and became the root of the Old Catholic churches. The abbey ruins and the farm beside them are now a French national museum.

experienceToday.text: Musée national de Port-Royal des Champs, Magny-les-Hameaux, France — the abbey ruins, the granges and a national museum on a thirty-hectare estate

movements.name: The Welsh Revival Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — rich for its size, with ordinary and women's voices prominent, though the corpus is in Welsh and carries a translation-layer flag. A tier-care note was added on Ann Griffiths, whose work reaches the record through oral transmission.
movements.sourcing: Rich for its size, in Welsh (translation-layer flag); ordinary and women's voices prominent (Ann Griffiths)
movements.relationsSummary: Sibling of Methodism with its own language-tradition; parent of the 1904 revival
movements.why: The Welsh revival ran in its own language from 1735, when Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland began preaching and organizing converts into the seiat, a small meeting where members told each other honestly how things stood with their souls. Its hymn writer William Williams Pantycelyn gave Welsh Christianity a national songbook, and so, more quietly, did Ann Griffiths, a farmer's daughter whose hymns survive only because her maid Ruth Evans memorized them and Ruth's husband wrote them down after Ann died at twenty-nine.

sources.work: Howell Harris's Trevecka diaries (c. 300 ms. volumes, National Library of Wales) and autobiographical accounts
sources.note: One of the century's densest self-records of an itinerant preacher; largely unpublished.

sources.work: Williams Pantycelyn: the hymn corpus (from Aleluia, 1744), Theomemphus (1764), The Experience Meeting (Drws y Society Profiad; Eng. trans. Bethan Lloyd-Jones, 1973)
sources.note: Hymnody as actually used, plus the movement's own manual for its small-group structure. Available in English translation.

sources.work: Ann Griffiths: hymns and letters (d. 1805) - composed orally, held in Ruth Evans's memory, transcribed posthumously by John Hughes
sources.note: A rare woman's voice from the revival. It reached us only through memory and a later transcription by someone else, so two layers of transmission stand between her and the page.

sources.work: The seiadau (experience meetings) records and rules, Daniel Rowland's Llangeitho communion seasons, the Trevecka letters (converts' correspondence)
sources.note: The revival's lived organizational core, comparable to Methodism's class meetings. Records are archival, in Welsh.

sources.work: Derec Llwyd Morgan, The Great Awakening in Wales (Epworth, 1988), with Geraint Tudur, Howell Harris (2000) and Eryn White's seiadau scholarship
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in 'Great Britain and Ireland' (Clark) and Ward's awakenings chapter

movements.longDescription: The Welsh revival began independently of England and in its own language: in 1735 Howell Harris, a schoolmaster from Trefeca, and Daniel Rowland, a curate at Llangeitho, were converted within months of each other and began preaching to whoever would gather. What grew was not only a wave of feeling but a structure. The seiat, or experience meeting, a small society where members told one another honestly how things stood with their souls, described in a handbook written by the movement's poet, William Williams Pantycelyn. Williams gave Welsh Christianity a hymn corpus that became a national possession, and so, more quietly, did Ann Griffiths, a farmer's daughter who composed her hymns aloud and never wrote them down. They survive because her maid Ruth Evans held them in memory and Ruth's husband set them on paper after Ann died at twenty-nine.
movements.teaser: Wales, 1735 to 1815 — a revival that happened in Welsh, met in small groups to tell the truth about itself, and left the country a body of hymns it still sings.
voices: Howell Harris — the Trefeca layman whose relentless itinerant preaching and enormous diaries drove the revival's first decades
Daniel Rowland — curate of Llangeitho, whose communion seasons drew people on foot from across Wales
William Williams Pantycelyn — the movement's hymn-writer and the theorist of its experience meetings; his 'Guide me, O thou great Jehovah' is sung far beyond Wales
Ann Griffiths — composed her hymns orally; they reached the page only because her maid Ruth Evans remembered them and Ruth's husband John Hughes wrote them down
Thomas Charles — organized the revival's Sunday schools and was among the founders of the British and Foreign Bible Society in 1804
movements.legacy: It became a church: the Calvinistic Methodists ordained their own ministers in 1811 and are now the Presbyterian Church of Wales, and the revival's wider effect made Nonconformity rather than the established church the ordinary religion of Wales for a century and a half. Its Sunday schools taught a great part of the nation to read Welsh, which is one reason the language came through industrialization alive. And the singing tradition it created runs straight on to the revival of 1904-05 and, less obviously but just as really, into Welsh choral culture generally.

experienceToday.text: The Howell Harris Museum at Trefeca, Powys — Harris's own community buildings in the Brecon Beacons, with a museum of the Welsh revival

movements.name: The Antonian Movement in Kongo
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 8 Step 0; c2 contested-on-record)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) — its evidence is moderate but missionary-pen and hostile, needing gravity discipline. Its person-defined question was run at this gate as the criterion's fifth live application and recorded as genuinely contested across two limbs, with the transmission condition named and the question left open rather than closed; the syncretism question was kept separate and un-run. Its end was corrected to 1706, matching the entry's own string, the previous 1708 having matched no event.
movements.sourcing: Moderate but real - missionary eyewitnesses (hostile pen; gravity discipline needed)
movements.floorNote: Two questions sit on this movement, and neither has been settled. The first is whether it can be described apart from the person of the prophetess herself, since her revelation is what defined it — the argument runs both ways, because the restoration programme she called for outlasted her and her ideas persisted after her death. The second is how far its teaching departed from the Christianity it grew out of. Both are complicated by the fact that nearly everything known about it comes through the missionaries who destroyed it.
movements.relationsSummary: Christianity already two centuries African producing its own prophetess - crushed at the stake
movements.why: By 1700 the Kingdom of Kongo had been Christian for two centuries but its capital lay abandoned, broken by war and the slave trade. In 1704 a young noblewoman, Kimpa Vita, announced that Saint Anthony spoke through her and led thousands of followers back to reoccupy the ruined capital, insisting Christ and the saints should be understood as Kongolese rather than European — a claim that ended with her burned at the stake in 1706.
movements.dateRationale: End 1706 (Beatriz burned 2 Jul 1706, verified — matches the entry's own string; the old numeric 1708 matched nothing; alt 1709, Sao Salvador retaken, shown) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Bernardo da Gallo's and Lorenzo da Lucca's Capuchin relations - the only contemporary documentation of Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita's movement, incl. her interrogation, trial, and burning (1706)
sources.note: Her voice survives only through the pen of the men who condemned her. Italian originals; available in English chiefly through Thornton's translations.

sources.work: The Salve Antoniana - the movement's own reworked prayer, recoverable through da Gallo's transcription/summary
sources.note: An inside text that survives only through hostile transmission, reconstructed by Thornton.

sources.work: The Kongo-Christian documentary matrix: the court's correspondence (Pedro IV's era), the Kikongo catechism tradition (1624 Doutrina), Sao Salvador church records
sources.note: Documents the two-century-old African Christianity without which this movement can't be understood. Editions include Brasio's Monumenta Missionaria Africana.

sources.work: John Thornton, The Kongolese Saint Anthony: Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita and the Antonian Movement, 1684-1706 (CUP, 1998), with Cecile Fromont, The Art of Conversion (UNC, 2014)
sources.note: Thornton is the standard work, built on the Capuchin records read critically, against their hostile grain.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Christianity in Africa' (Sanneh)

movements.longDescription: By 1700 the Kingdom of Kongo had been Christian for two centuries — its kings baptized, its capital São Salvador full of churches, its catechism printed in Kikongo. And it was also in ruins, broken by civil war and the slave trade, its capital abandoned. In 1704 a young noblewoman named Kimpa Vita, baptized Beatriz, announced that she had died and been possessed by Saint Anthony of Padua, and that he now spoke through her. The kingdom must be reunited, the capital reoccupied, and Christ and the saints understood as Kongolese rather than European. Thousands followed her back into São Salvador. Two Capuchin missionaries persuaded the restored king to arrest her, and in July 1706 she was burned as a heretic.
movements.teaser: The Kingdom of Kongo, 1704 to 1706 — a young woman who said Saint Anthony spoke through her, led thousands back into a ruined Christian capital, and was burned for it two years later.
voices: Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita — the young noblewoman who said she was possessed by Saint Anthony and led the movement; burned at the stake in July 1706
Bernardo da Gallo — the Capuchin missionary who interrogated her, and whose hostile report is very nearly the only record of what she taught
Pedro IV — the Kongolese king who first tolerated and then executed her, and who reoccupied São Salvador after her death

The movement's own voice reaches us almost entirely through the pens of the men who destroyed it — including its reworked prayer, the Salve Antoniana, which is known only because a missionary wrote it out in order to refute it
movements.legacy: The movement was crushed within two years and left no church behind it. What it left is harder to see but real. São Salvador was reoccupied and the kingdom partially reunited, which is what she had called for, and the idea of a Christianity understood in Kongolese terms did not die with her. Historians now read her as one of the earliest documented African Christian prophets, and she has become a figure of memory in Angola and across the Atlantic diaspora. Mbanza Kongo, the old capital, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its sixteenth-century cathedral ruins still standing.

experienceToday.text: Mbanza Kongo, Angola — the old Kongolese capital and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with the ruins of its sixteenth-century cathedral

movements.name: Shakers
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — Christ’s second appearing identified with the founder, by the community’s own published confession (the 1808 Testimony and church covenants); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Luminous community records
movements.floorNote: The Shakers' own published confession — The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing (1808), together with their church covenants — identifies Christ's second coming with the founder, Ann Lee. That is a plain departure from the historic creeds, on their own account. The earliest accounts of the founding generation come either from hostile former members or from testimony collected thirty years later, so some caution is warranted there.
movements.relationsSummary: Radical edge of the era's prophetic currents
movements.why: The Shakers grew from a small circle of Manchester dissenters who worshipped with shaking, dancing and ecstatic speech, transformed by one of them, Ann Lee, who had buried four children and came to believe celibacy was the way out of the world's fallenness. Their communities held property in common, let men and women govern jointly, and treated work itself as worship; their own published confession identified Christ's second coming with Ann Lee, and the villages they built were so plain and exact that Shaker furniture and architecture remain reference points in American design today.
movements.dateRationale: End 1815 (the era-8 register cap, settling the pair with VII.13 — the four-convention family shape banked for era 9); origin note: the 1747 Wardley society precedes the 1774 numeric start [S] (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Our Ever Blessed Mother Ann Lee (Hancock, 1816)
sources.note: The society's compiled oral testimony about the founding generation, gathered more than 30 years after Ann Lee's death; women's voices are structurally central to it.

sources.work: The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing (1808; Youngs), the church covenants (from 1795), the Millennial Laws
sources.note: The society's own confession, stating the second-coming claim in their own words.

sources.work: The lived community record: village journals and daybooks, membership rolls, hymnody (Millennial Praises, 1813; the gift-song tradition)
sources.note: The richest record starts from the 1790s gathering onward; the founding generation itself is documented only retrospectively or by hostile sources.

sources.work: Valentine Rathbun, An Account of the Matter, Form, and Manner of a New and Strange Religion (1781); Amos Taylor's narrative (1782); the 1780 Albany imprisonment records
sources.note: Ex-member polemic that forms the earliest documentation of Ann Lee's generation - an asymmetry worth noting, since hostile and later accounts dominate the early record.

sources.work: Stephen Stein, The Shaker Experience in America (Yale, 1992)
sources.note: Covers both readings of the Shakers: the identification of Mother Ann with Christ's second appearing in their own confession, and the institutional growth under Meacham and Wright after her death.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in Ward's 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' chapter, at the radical-prophetic periphery

movements.longDescription: The Shakers began among a small group of dissenters in Manchester who worshipped with shaking, dancing and ecstatic speech, and were transformed by one of them. Ann Lee, a factory-hand who had buried four infant children and came to believe that celibacy was the way out of the world's fallenness. In 1774 she led eight followers to New York, and the communities that grew after her death in 1784 became one of the most successful communal experiments in American history. Property held in common, men and women living apart but governing jointly, work treated as a form of worship. Their published confession identified Christ's second appearing with Ann Lee herself, which set them apart from the churches around them, and their dancing worship gave them the name their neighbours used. What they built was startlingly beautiful: villages of plain, exact buildings, furniture pared down to its function, and thousands of songs.
movements.teaser: England and then America, 1774 to 1815 — a celibate communal society founded by a Manchester factory-hand, which built the plainest and most beautiful villages in America and sang thousands of songs.
voices: Ann Lee — the Manchester woman the society called Mother Ann, who led the first eight believers to America in 1774
Joseph Meacham and Lucy Wright — reorganized the scattered believers after her death into ordered villages under joint male and female leadership
Benjamin Seth Youngs — principal author of The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing (1808), the society's own published statement of what it believed
movements.legacy: The society still exists, barely — a single small community at Sabbathday Lake, Maine, has carried it into the twenty-first century. Its material legacy is far larger than its membership ever was. Shaker furniture and architecture are permanent reference points in American design, several of the villages are museums visited by hundreds of thousands of people a year, and the Shaker song 'Simple Gifts' entered the wider culture when Aaron Copland used it in Appalachian Spring. They were also inventive in practical things, from the flat broom to packaged garden seeds sold by mail, and ran them as businesses that paid for the villages.

experienceToday.text: Hancock Shaker Village, Pittsfield, Massachusetts — twenty original Shaker buildings including the Round Stone Barn, with the farm and gardens still worked

movements.name: Swedenborgian New Church
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — new-revelation authority and non-trinitarian theology by its own account (the record-mandated Era 8 disposition); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich founder corpus
movements.floorNote: By its own account this church rests on a body of new revelation given to Emanuel Swedenborg, and its confession — set out in his True Christian Religion and in the church's own liturgies — is not trinitarian in the creedal sense: God is one person, Jesus Christ. Both points are taken from the church's own statements rather than from outside criticism. It is an unusual case in one respect: the authority claim is bound to one man, but the body itself was formed by readers after his death.
movements.why: Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swedish scientist who, in his mid-fifties, began having visions and spent the rest of his life writing an enormous body of theology in Latin — describing heaven and hell, the inner meaning of Scripture, and a God who is one person, Jesus Christ, rather than three. He never founded a church and died in 1772, so the New Church that formed afterward, first in Manchester and London in the 1780s and then in Baltimore and Philadelphia, was built entirely by people who had only ever known him through his books.
movements.dateRationale: String aligned to the cap; origin note: reading societies 1783, New Church organized 1787 [S]; Swedenborg d. 1772 (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Swedenborg's corpus: Arcana Coelestia (1749-56), Heaven and Hell (1758), True Christian Religion (1771) - New Century Edition (Swedenborg Foundation)
sources.note: The claimed revelatory corpus and its non-trinitarian reading of Christianity, in its own words.

sources.work: The church's own organizational record: the London reading circle, the 1787 separation, first General Conference minutes (1789), the New Church liturgy (1790); Hindmarsh's Rise and Progress (pub. 1861)
sources.note: Shows the readers' movement becoming an organized church only after the founder's death - the founder's own writings are not the same as the church's own record. Hindmarsh's account is a participant memoir written fifty years after the events it describes.

sources.work: The reception network: New-Jerusalem Magazine, reading societies (Manchester printing society, 1782; James Glen's American lectures, 1784; Baltimore society, 1792)
sources.note: Shows how a book-borne church actually spread; ordinary readers' voices survive here and there.

sources.work: Jane Williams-Hogan's New Church scholarship, with Rose et al. (eds.), Scribe of Heaven: Swedenborg's Life, Work, and Impact (Swedenborg Foundation, 2005)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in the 'Christian Enlightenment' (Rosenblatt) and 'Enlightenment critique of Christianity' (Jacob) chapters
sources.note: Swedenborg's work sits on the seam between Christian orthodoxy and Enlightenment religious critique.

movements.longDescription: Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swedish mining engineer, anatomist and member of the House of Nobles who, in his mid-fifties, began having visions and spent the rest of his life writing an enormous body of theological work in Latin — accounts of heaven and hell, of the inner meaning of Scripture, and of a Christianity in which God is one person, Jesus Christ, rather than three. He never founded a church and died in London in 1772; the church came afterwards, and it was made by readers. Reading societies formed in Manchester and London in the 1780s, a separate New Church congregation organized in London in 1787, the first General Conference met in 1789, and the books crossed the Atlantic, where societies formed in Baltimore and Philadelphia in the 1790s.
movements.teaser: England and America, 1780s to 1815 — a church that assembled itself out of readers, years after the visionary whose books they were reading had died.
voices: Emanuel Swedenborg — Swedish scientist and civil servant turned visionary writer, who died in London in 1772 without founding anything
Robert Hindmarsh — the London printer who gathered the first readers into a congregation and later wrote the movement's own account of its origins
James Glen — gave the first Swedenborgian lectures in America, at Philadelphia in 1784
movements.legacy: It became a small but continuous denomination, with New Church bodies still active in Britain, the United States and elsewhere. Its reach through literature and art went far beyond its membership. Blake, Emerson, Balzac, Baudelaire and Yeats all read Swedenborg, and Helen Keller and John Chapman — 'Johnny Appleseed', who distributed Swedenborgian tracts along with his seedlings — were adherents. Bryn Athyn, Pennsylvania, built as a New Church centre, has a cathedral and a college still in use, and the Swedenborg Society in London has been publishing his works since 1810.

experienceToday.text: Swedenborg House, Bloomsbury, London — the Swedenborg Society's home since 1925, with a library, archive, bookshop and hall open to the public

movements.name: Quietist Controversy (Molinos, Guyon)
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Real texts and trial records
movements.floorNote: A spirituality contest inside the Catholic tradition, not a community
movements.relationsSummary: Adjacent to Port-Royal's tradition
movements.why: Miguel de Molinos taught a prayer of total interior passivity — stop even asking, and let God act — until he was arrested in 1685 and dozens of his propositions condemned. The argument moved to France around the widow Jeanne Guyon, whose similar teaching found a defender in the archbishop Fénelon and an implacable opponent in Bossuet; Guyon spent years imprisoned, including in the Bastille, and Fénelon read out his own submission from his own pulpit when Rome condemned him in 1699.
movements.dateRationale: End 1699 (Cum alias — Fenelon's condemnation [S]; the old 1700 was round) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Molinos, The Spiritual Guide (1675); the Inquisition process (1685-87) and Coelestis Pastor's 68 condemned propositions (1687)
sources.note: The condemned-proposition lists reflect the prosecutor's framing, and confessions were extracted under trial pressure.

sources.work: Madame Guyon: A Short and Easy Method of Prayer (1685), her autobiography, the prison narratives (Mourad & Guenin-Lelle, The Prison Narratives of Jeanne Guyon, OUP, 2012)
sources.note: A woman's voice at the center of the controversy, documented under real institutional pressure - the autobiography was written under her spiritual directors' orders and revised while she was imprisoned.

sources.work: The Fenelon-Bossuet contest: Maximes des saints (1697), Bossuet's Relation sur le quietisme, the 1699 condemnation (Cum alias)
sources.note: The controversy's public record, in both principals' own words.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Crisis of Mysticism: Quietism in Seventeenth-Century Spain, Italy, and France (2021), with Patricia Ward, Experimental Theology in America (2009)
sources.note: Ward covers the Protestant afterlife of Guyon's texts.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Continental Catholic Europe' (Aston)
sources.note: The nearest chapter covering this intra-Catholic spirituality dispute.

movements.longDescription: In 1675 a Spanish priest living in Rome, Miguel de Molinos, published The Spiritual Guide, teaching a prayer of total interior passivity: stop striving, stop even asking, and let God act. It was hugely popular until it was not; Molinos was arrested in 1685 and sixty-eight propositions drawn from his work were condemned in 1687. The quarrel then moved to France, around Jeanne Guyon, a widow whose Short and Easy Method of Prayer taught something similar, and who found a defender in Fénelon, archbishop of Cambrai, and an implacable opponent in Bossuet, bishop of Meaux. Guyon spent years in confinement, including in the Bastille; Fénelon's defence of her was condemned by Rome in 1699, and he read out his own submission from his own pulpit.
movements.teaser: Spain and France, 1675 to 1699 — an argument about whether the highest prayer is to stop trying, which cost one priest his freedom, one widow years in the Bastille, and an archbishop his standing at court.
voices: Miguel de Molinos — Spanish priest whose Spiritual Guide (1675) set off the controversy; condemned in 1687 and imprisoned for the rest of his life
Jeanne Guyon — widow and spiritual writer whose Short and Easy Method of Prayer made the dispute a French one; imprisoned for years, and author of her own prison narratives
François Fénelon — archbishop of Cambrai, who defended the substance of Guyon's teaching in Maximes des saints (1697) and submitted publicly when Rome condemned it
Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet — bishop of Meaux and the prosecution's voice, who broke Fénelon's position at Louis XIV's court
movements.legacy: The condemnation ended quietism as a movement inside Catholicism, but not the texts. Guyon's writings had a long second life among Protestants — translated, reprinted and read warmly by Pietists, Quakers and Methodists. So that a condemned French Catholic widow became devotional reading in English-speaking evangelicalism, and still is. Fénelon's Telemachus and his letters of spiritual direction stayed in print and are read to this day. The word 'quietism' itself survived as a term of criticism for any spirituality thought too passive.

movements.name: Camisard Prophetism
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Persecution-born ecstatic prophecy, documented in trials and memoirs
movements.relationsSummary: Aftermath of the Huguenot tradition's suppression
movements.why: After Protestantism was outlawed in France in 1685, ordinary people in the Cévennes — many of them children and young women with no pastors left to guide them — began falling into trance and speaking as they believed the Spirit directed. A shepherd girl named Isabeau Vincent was the first widely reported case, and by 1702 the movement had become an armed revolt, led in the field by a twenty-year-old baker's apprentice, Jean Cavalier, with prophets traveling alongside the fighters to direct them.
movements.dateRationale: End 1710 (the revolt's end [S]; the old 1780 aftermath reading belongs to the Church of the Desert's story); prophetism from 1688 [S] as origin note (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Le Theatre sacre des Cevennes (London, 1707; ed. Misson; Eng. as A Cry from the Desart) - sworn depositions of exiled Camisard prophets (Marion, Fage, Cavalier)
sources.note: The movement's own voices, in exile; the collection was assembled to defend the French Prophets in London, so it's an advocacy compilation.

sources.work: Memoirs: Jean Cavalier, Memoirs of the Wars of the Cevennes (1726); Abraham Mazel's and Elie Marion's memoires; the child- and women-prophets record (Isabeau Vincent, 1688, via pastoral and hostile observers)
sources.note: Participant memoirs, written some years after the events; the material on Vincent comes through outside observers, not her own words.

sources.work: The persecution record: intendants' interrogation and trial records, abjuration registers, galley rolls (Tournier's Les galeres de France series), execution records
sources.note: The movement's shape here is reconstructed from its persecutors' own records; testimony was given under torture and threat.

sources.work: W. Gregory Monahan, Let God Arise: The War and Rebellion of the Camisards (OUP, 2014), with Lionel Laborie, Enlightening Enthusiasm (Manchester, 2015)
sources.note: Laborie covers the movement's afterlife among exiles in London.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann), with the toleration chapter
sources.note: The nearest chapter covering the Huguenot aftermath.

movements.longDescription: After Louis XIV outlawed Protestantism in 1685, the Protestants of the Cévennes were left with no pastors, no churches and no legal existence. And out of that vacuum came prophecy. From 1688 ordinary people, many of them children and young women, began falling into trance and speaking in what they took to be the voice of the Spirit. The first widely reported was a shepherd girl, Isabeau Vincent, who preached in her sleep. In 1702 the movement turned to armed revolt. Bands of peasants known as Camisards fought royal troops through the mountains for two years, led by men like Jean Cavalier, a baker's apprentice of twenty, with prophets travelling alongside the fighters and directing them. The rising was broken by 1704 and the last resistance ended by 1710; some of the prophets escaped to London, where they caused a fresh sensation as the 'French Prophets'.
movements.teaser: The Cévennes, 1700 to 1710 — a peasant war fought by people who had no pastors left, and who took their orders from prophets, some of them children.
voices: Isabeau Vincent — the shepherd girl whose prophesying from 1688 was the first case to be widely reported
Jean Cavalier — a baker's apprentice who became the revolt's most capable commander before negotiating terms in 1704
Abraham Mazel and Élie Marion — Camisard leaders who wrote their own memoirs; Marion carried the prophecy to London
Pierre Laporte, called Rolland — Camisard captain, killed in 1704; the museum of the whole period stands in the house where he was born
movements.legacy: The Camisards left no church of their own — French Protestantism rebuilt itself without them, in a completely different key, sober and clandestine. What the prophets left was a wave that carried. The exiles in London published sworn accounts of their experiences, drew crowds and ridicule, and shaped English and continental arguments about religious enthusiasm for a generation, with echoes reaching later revival movements. In the Cévennes the memory was never allowed to fade, and it is still marked by an assembly held every September at the Musée du Désert.

experienceToday.text: Musée du Désert, Mialet, Cévennes — the museum of the Huguenot underground and the Camisards, in the birthplace of the Camisard leader Rolland

movements.name: The Baptists
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on church minute books, covenants, Bunyan's Grace Abounding and association records. Its end moved to 1815, bringing the founding of the BMS (1792) — the record's own named hinge — inside the window; the handoff of its Black Baptist thread was flagged forward to the next era, where an explicit parent pointer was later written.
movements.sourcing: RICH: church minute books, covenants, Bunyan's Grace Abounding, association records
movements.relationsSummary: The Baptists grew out of Puritan-Separatist ferment in England. They arrived at Anabaptist-like convictions about believer's baptism largely on their own — historians are divided on how much direct contact there was between the two movements. From the Baptists came William Carey's missionary movement and the Black Baptist churches, which in turn became one of the founding traditions of the Black Church in America.
movements.why: In 1609 an exiled English congregation in Amsterdam concluded that baptism belonged only to believers who could profess faith for themselves, and its pastor John Smyth baptized himself and then the rest. The churches that grew from that governed themselves in writing, week by week, in minute books and covenants — John Bunyan wrote Grace Abounding during twelve years in Bedford gaol for preaching without a license — and in 1792 a shoemaker named William Carey persuaded a small association of ministers to found a missionary society before sailing for India himself.
movements.dateRationale: End 1815 (continues-cap; living) — the BMS founding (1792 [S], the record's own named hinge) inside; the round-1800 cluster replaced (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.35 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The confessional record: First London Confession (1644/46), Second London Confession (1677/1689), Standard Confession (1660), Orthodox Creed (1678), with local church covenants
sources.note: The two wings' self-statements; the documents any independent-origins argument runs on. Whether Baptists descend in part from the continental Anabaptists is itself a genuinely contested question among historians.

sources.work: Bunyan: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666) and The Pilgrim's Progress (1678)

Church minute books and association records: Broadmead (Bristol) records, Fenstanton/Warboys/Hexham church books (Underhill's editions), association circular letters, Philadelphia Baptist Association minutes (1707-)
sources.note: Women members' testimony and cases are visible throughout, though filtered through the church's own institutional minutes.

sources.work: Women's and Black voices: Agnes Beaumont, The Narrative of the Persecutions of Agnes Beaumont (1674); George Liele's letters and account (1791; congregations from c. 1773-75) and David George's autobiographical narrative (1793)
sources.note: A Bedford congregation woman's own persecution story; enslaved and formerly-enslaved preachers' own words.

sources.work: Michael Watts, The Dissenters, vol. 1 (OUP, 1978), with David Bebbington, Baptists Through the Centuries (Baylor, 2010)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: the 'Great Britain and Ireland' chapter (Clark), Ward's awakenings chapter, and Noll for America

movements.longDescription: In 1609 an exiled English congregation in Amsterdam concluded that baptism belonged to believers who could profess faith for themselves, and its pastor John Smyth baptized himself and then the rest — the beginning of the English Baptists. Two streams developed, General Baptists holding that Christ died for all and Particular Baptists holding to a Calvinist election, and both organized as gathered churches. Bodies of ordinary people who covenanted together, chose their own ministers, disciplined their own members and wrote it all down in minute books, week after week. They were persecuted hard under the Restoration — John Bunyan spent twelve years in Bedford gaol for preaching without a licence and wrote Grace Abounding there. And they became one of the strongest voices in English for liberty of conscience. In America they grew explosively out of the awakening, and the movement's outward turn came in 1792, when a Northamptonshire shoemaker named William Carey persuaded a small association of ministers to found a missionary society and then sailed for India himself.
movements.teaser: England and then America, 1609 to 1815 — congregations of ordinary people who baptized believers only, governed themselves in writing week by week, and went to prison for preaching without a licence.
voices: John Smyth — pastor of the exiled English congregation in Amsterdam that took the first step in 1609
Thomas Helwys — brought the first Baptist church back to England in 1612 and wrote one of the earliest English pleas for complete liberty of conscience, extending it to Jews and Muslims
John Bunyan — Bedford tinker and preacher, imprisoned twelve years, author of Grace Abounding and The Pilgrim's Progress
Agnes Beaumont — a young woman of Bunyan's congregation who wrote her own account of the scandal and persecution she faced
George Liele and David George — formerly enslaved preachers who founded some of the first Black Baptist congregations in America and then carried the movement to Jamaica and Sierra Leone
William Carey — Northamptonshire shoemaker whose 1792 appeal founded the Baptist Missionary Society; he spent the rest of his life in India
movements.legacy: Baptists are now one of the largest Protestant families in the world. The tradition's argument that no magistrate has authority over belief passed into Rhode Island's founding under Roger Williams and, through a long line of Baptist petitioning, into the American constitutional settlement on religion. Carey's society opened the era of Protestant foreign missions and was quickly imitated across the denominations. And the Black Baptist churches founded by Liele, George and their successors became one of the central institutions of African American life, and the ground from which the civil rights movement later grew.

experienceToday.text: Bunyan Meeting and the John Bunyan Museum, Bedford — the church on the site of Bunyan's own congregation, with a museum of his life and imprisonment

movements.name: Colonial Latin American Devotional Catholicism
movements.informalName: The Devotional World of New Spain and Peru
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 8 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on cofradía books, canonization processes and convent writings, women's among them — Úrsula de Jesús, an Afro-Peruvian woman's own voice, verified in the source pass. Its c. 1600 start was kept with the overlap against the mission-born family disclosed on purpose rather than tidied away, and its 1810 end kept with its reason, Hidalgo's Grito, put on the record for the first time.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: cofradia books, canonization processes, convent writings (women's among them)
movements.relationsSummary: This continues the earlier missionary Catholicism of Spanish America into its settled, everyday form. It is the popular piety that the twentieth-century base communities later re-read "from below." The California missions, founded from 1769 under Junípero Serra, belong within this same New Spain-wide devotional world.
movements.why: Ordinary religious life across colonial Spanish America ran through the cofradías — lay confraternities, often organized by trade, parish, or race, that maintained a saint's image, buried their own members, and paid for their funerals. The era produced homegrown saints like Rose of Lima and Martín de Porres, convent writers including Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz and the formerly enslaved Úrsula de Jesús, whose dictated spiritual diary survives in her own words, and the shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe at Tepeyac, which became the devotional heart of Mexico.
movements.dateRationale: Start c. 1600 KEPT with the VI.13 overlap DISCLOSED on purpose (Rose of Lima d. 1617 [S] is genuinely this register's content; the align-to-1650 branch was shown); end 1810 KEPT, rationale stated: Hidalgo's Grito (Sep 1810 [S]) — the independence rupture (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The cofradia books: confraternity records across New Spain and Peru, incl. indigenous confraternities' books and Black brotherhoods' records (Afro-Peruvian and Afro-Brazilian rosary confraternities)
sources.note: A lay-run devotional economy that was the ordinary institutional life of the piety; the records themselves were kept under clerical oversight.

sources.work: Convent writings, women's: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea (1691; trans. Arenal & Powell); Madre Maria de San Jose's autobiography (ed. Myers & Powell); Ursula de Jesus, The Souls of Purgatory (ed./trans. van Deusen, UNM, 2004)
sources.note: An enslaved-then-freed convent servant's dictated spiritual diary, begun in 1650 - an enslaved woman's own religious voice, though filtered through the confessor who took her dictation. The convent's racial hierarchy is visible within it.

sources.work: The canonization processes: Rose of Lima (canonized 1671), Martin de Porres (process testimony from the 1660s, ordinary witnesses incl. Afro-Peruvians), Mariana de Quito
sources.note: Canonization-process testimony is structured and led by the questioners, but it remains the era's densest record of ordinary devotees speaking for themselves.

sources.work: The devotional-practice layer: the Guadalupan corpus (Nican Mopohua, published 1649 in Huei tlamahuicoltica; its dating and authorship are still debated), shrine and pilgrimage records, novena imprints; Inquisition and extirpation records that policed popular devotion
sources.note: The records that policed popular devotion come from a hostile administrative source.

sources.work: William B. Taylor, Magistrates of the Sacred (Stanford, 1996), with Asuncion Lavrin, Brides of Christ (Stanford, 2008)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, ch. 19 'Christianity in Iberian America' (Riley)
sources.note: A direct fit for this movement, with the chapter number confirmed.

movements.longDescription: Once the first missionary generation had passed, Catholicism in Spanish America settled into being the ordinary religion of whole societies, and its real institutions were local: the cofradías, lay confraternities that maintained an altar or an image, buried their members and paid for their funerals, organized by trade, by parish and often by race — with indigenous confraternities and Black brotherhoods running their own devotional life. Its saints were homegrown: Rose of Lima, canonized in 1671 as the first saint of the Americas, and Martín de Porres, the mixed-race Dominican lay brother of the same city. Its convents produced writers of the first rank, among them Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz in Mexico, who defended a woman's right to study, and Úrsula de Jesús in Lima, an enslaved woman later freed, whose spiritual diary survives in her own dictated words. Above all it produced Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose shrine at Tepeyac became the devotional centre of Mexico and eventually a symbol of Mexican identity itself.
movements.teaser: New Spain and Peru, about 1600 to 1810 — the centuries when Catholicism stopped being a mission and became the ordinary religion of a continent, held together by lay confraternities and their own saints.
voices: Rose of Lima — canonized in 1671, the first saint of the Americas
Martín de Porres — Dominican lay brother of Lima, son of a Spanish nobleman and a free Black woman, remembered for his care of the poor and the sick
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz — Mexican nun, poet and scholar, whose Respuesta a Sor Filotea (1691) defended a woman's right to learn
Úrsula de Jesús — an enslaved and later freed woman in a Lima convent, whose dictated spiritual diary survives
Juan Diego — the indigenous man to whom Our Lady of Guadalupe is said to have appeared at Tepeyac in 1531; canonized in 2002
movements.legacy: This is a living tradition rather than a closed one. Latin America holds the largest Catholic population on earth, and the devotional shape the faith took in these centuries — the shrine, the patronal feast, the confraternity, the image carried in procession — is still how it is practised by most of its people. Guadalupe's basilica in Mexico City is the most visited Marian shrine in the world. And this popular piety was the ground the base communities of the twentieth century stood on when they began reading Scripture from below.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mexico City — the shrine at Tepeyac, the most visited Marian pilgrimage site in the world

movements.name: Orthodoxy under the Ottomans — the Second Act
movements.informalName: The Millet Church from Jerusalem 1672 to 1821
movements.statusDescription: The Era 7 Freeze segmented VI.17 at 1650 and mandated this receiver's creation at the A1.E8 gate. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: the Jerusalem 1672 acta and Dositheus's Confession (verified), patriarchal records, neomartyr acts [S on collections]; ordinary parish voice thinner
movements.relationsSummary: This covers Ottoman Orthodoxy's second act: the Synod of Jerusalem under Dositheus in 1672, the East's own answer to the Council of Trent; the century that produced the largest number of neomartyrs; the rise of Phanariot influence; and the abolition of the Serbian patriarchate of Peć in 1766 and the archbishopric of Ohrid in 1767. The Serbian Great Migration of 1690 placed the Karlovci church outside the Ottoman millet system from that date. The story ends with Patriarch Gregory V hanged at the Patriarchate's gate at Easter 1821.
movements.why: For a century and a half, the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople was both a church leader and an arm of Ottoman government, collecting taxes and judging marriages for Orthodox subjects while patriarchs themselves were deposed and restored constantly. In 1672 the Synod of Jerusalem answered Calvinist ideas that had been spreading under an Orthodox name, and the arrangement ended violently in 1821, when Patriarch Gregory V was hanged in his vestments from the gate of his own patriarchate — a gate that has stayed welded shut ever since.
movements.dateRationale: 1650 (the segment boundary ruled at the Era 7 Freeze) to 1821 (Gregory V hanged, Easter 1821, verified; one legal 1815 crossing) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.28 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
