movements.longDescription: For a century and a half after 1650 the Orthodox church of the Ottoman Empire was both a church and an arm of the state: the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople answered to the Sultan for the obedience of all Orthodox subjects, collected their taxes and judged their marriages and inheritances. It was a position of real power and total insecurity — patriarchs were deposed and restored constantly. And it came increasingly to be held under the influence of the Phanariots, the wealthy Greek families of Constantinople's Phanar quarter who supplied the empire's interpreters and the princes of its Danubian provinces. In 1672 the Synod of Jerusalem, under Patriarch Dositheus, issued a confession answering the Calvinist ideas that had been circulating under an Orthodox name — the East's own equivalent of the West's confessional settlements. That power also worked against its neighbours: the Serbian patriarchate of Peć was abolished in 1766 and the archbishopric of Ohrid in 1767, both absorbed into Constantinople. It ended violently — when the Greek revolt broke out in 1821, Patriarch Gregory V was hanged in his vestments from the gate of his own patriarchate.
movements.teaser: Anatolia, the Balkans and the Greek islands, 1650 to 1821 — a church that was also a department of the Ottoman state, and whose patriarch was hanged from his own front gate when that arrangement finally broke.
voices: Dositheus II of Jerusalem — presided over the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672, whose confession became the standard Orthodox answer to Protestant theology
Gregory V of Constantinople — patriarch hanged at the gate of the patriarchate at Easter 1821, in reprisal for the Greek revolt
The Phanariots — the Greek families of Constantinople's Phanar quarter who supplied the empire's interpreters and Danubian princes, and who shaped the patriarchate's politics
The neomartyrs — Orthodox Christians executed for refusing Islam or for returning to Christianity after converting, whose accounts their own church collected and circulated
movements.legacy: The arrangement kept Orthodox Christianity intact through centuries of Muslim rule, at the price of tying the church to a foreign state and of Greek ecclesiastical dominance over Slavs and Arabs. A resentment that shaped every Balkan church that came after. When the empire's Christian provinces became nations in the nineteenth century, each took its own church with it, and the pattern of national Orthodox churches that exists today is the direct result. Gregory V's gate at the Phanar has never been opened since 1821: it is welded shut and painted black, and the patriarchate is still there behind it.

experienceToday.text: St George's Cathedral at the Phanar, Istanbul — the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, with the gate sealed since Gregory V was hanged from it in 1821

movements.name: The Catholic Church of the Ancien Régime
movements.informalName: The Church from Unigenitus to the Concordat
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run as VI.22's receiver - the Roman hole's third recurrence closed. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally: the bull Unigenitus (1713) and the records of the Jansenist controversy it caused, the documents of the Jesuits' suppression in 1773, the revolutionary-era records including the 1790 Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the record of Pius VI's captivity, and the 1801 Concordat.
movements.relationsSummary: This was the era's largest institutional story inside the Catholic Church: the Gallican Articles, the bull Unigenitus, and the Jansenist crisis it set off in France; the expulsion and suppression of the Jesuits between 1759 and 1773; the catastrophe of the French Revolution, which split the clergy between those who swore the required oath and those who refused, and left Pope Pius VI to die a prisoner in 1799; and the Concordat and the standoff between Pius VII and Napoleon that followed, ending with the Jesuits restored in 1814. The same period held the Quietist controversy, a Jansenist current that ran through the eighteenth century, Alphonsus Liguori's founding of the Redemptorists, and the broader current of Catholic Enlightenment thought.
movements.why: Rome's condemnation of Jansenism in the bull Unigenitus (1713) set off a fifty-year political crisis in France, and within decades the Catholic monarchies themselves turned on the church's most effective order, forcing the pope to suppress the Jesuits altogether in 1773. Then came the Revolution — church property seized, clergy split by a forced oath, and Pope Pius VI dying a French prisoner in 1799 — until his successor Pius VII signed a concordat with Napoleon, was imprisoned by him in turn, and lived to restore the Jesuits in 1814.
movements.dateRationale: 1650 to 1815 (era cap; the in-era alternative 1801, Concordat, was shown) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.29 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: This was the Catholic Church at the height of its establishment and on the edge of its worst crisis: enormously wealthy, woven into the monarchies of Europe, and increasingly unable to control them. Rome's condemnation of Jansenism in the bull Unigenitus (1713) turned into a fifty-year political crisis in France, with parlements and bishops fighting over it. Then the Catholic monarchies turned on the church's most effective order, expelling the Jesuits from Portugal, France, Spain and Naples and forcing the pope to suppress the Society altogether in 1773. Then came the Revolution: church property nationalized, clergy required to swear to a Civil Constitution that split them into jurors and refractories, thousands killed or driven abroad, and Pope Pius VI carried off to die a French prisoner in 1799. His successor signed a concordat with Napoleon in 1801, was imprisoned by him in turn, outlived him, and restored the Jesuits in 1814.
movements.teaser: Rome and Catholic Europe, 1650 to 1815 — the church at its most established and its most helpless, which lost its greatest order to its own kings and then nearly lost everything to a revolution.
voices: Clement XI — issued Unigenitus in 1713, the condemnation of Jansenism that convulsed the French church for fifty years
Clement XIV — suppressed the Society of Jesus in 1773 under pressure from the Catholic crowns
Pius VI — died in 1799 a prisoner of the French Republic at Valence
Pius VII — signed the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon, was imprisoned by him for years, outlived him, and restored the Jesuits in 1814
Alphonsus Liguori — founder of the Redemptorists and the era's most influential moral theologian and mission preacher
movements.legacy: It survived, which was not obvious in 1799. The Revolution stripped away the wealth and political entanglement that had defined the church for centuries, and what emerged after 1815 was poorer, more clerical and far more oriented toward Rome. The ultramontane Catholicism of the nineteenth century is the direct product of this catastrophe. The suppression and restoration of the Jesuits, the loss of the church lands, and the concordat as a way of settling with a secular state all set terms the church has operated under ever since. Its parish churches, seminaries and religious orders across Europe are still, physically, largely those of this period.

movements.name: The Restoration and Georgian Church of England
movements.informalName: The Established Church of the Long Eighteenth Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run as VI.4's receiver - the flagged Anglican hole closed. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich: the 1662 Prayer Book as lived formation, visitation records, SPCK and SPG archives, and parish registers, continuing a long documentary tradition for the English church.
movements.relationsSummary: The restoration of the bishops in 1660, the Act of Uniformity of 1662, and the Great Ejection of roughly two thousand ministers defined church and dissent in a single stroke. The Toleration Act of 1689 produced the nonjurors, and the church founded its first missionary societies, the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701. This is the church that Methodism grew up inside, and eventually out of.
movements.why: When the monarchy returned in 1660, so did the bishops and the Prayer Book, and the Act of Uniformity of 1662 forced out about two thousand ministers who wouldn't accept both, creating English Dissent as a permanent fact in a single day. The same church founded the first Anglican missionary societies, the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701, watched several hundred clergy including its own Archbishop of Canterbury walk out rather than break an oath to the old king in 1689, and was the church John and Charles Wesley were born in, ordained in, and never meant to leave.
movements.dateRationale: 1660 (Restoration episcopacy) to 1815 (era cap) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.30 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: When the monarchy came back in 1660 so did the bishops and the Prayer Book, and the Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every minister to accept both. About two thousand refused and were ejected from their livings on a single day, creating English Dissent as a permanent fact. The church that remained was the established church of the long eighteenth century, and it has had a poor press — pluralism, absentee clergy, comfortable sermons. But it was also the church of the Prayer Book as ordinary people actually knew it, of parish registers and charity schools, and of the first Anglican missionary societies, the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701. It had its own principled casualties. The nonjurors, several hundred clergy including the Archbishop of Canterbury, who would not swear allegiance to William and Mary in 1689 while James II lived, and walked out rather than break an oath. And it was the church John and Charles Wesley were born in, ordained in, and never meant to leave.
movements.teaser: England, Wales, Ireland and the colonies, 1660 to 1815 — the established church of the long eighteenth century, which created Dissent in a single day in 1662 and then grew Methodism inside itself.
voices: Gilbert Sheldon — Bishop of London in 1662 and Archbishop of Canterbury from the following year, the architect of the terms that produced the Great Ejection
William Sancroft — Archbishop of Canterbury who refused the oath to William and Mary in 1689 and led the nonjurors out
Thomas Bray — founded the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701, the church's first educational and missionary societies
Joseph Butler — bishop and philosopher, whose Analogy of Religion (1736) was the era's most serious Anglican answer to deism
Hannah More — writer and educator of the church's evangelical wing, whose cheap tracts and village schools reached an enormous readership
movements.legacy: It continues as the Church of England, and a great deal of what people recognize as Anglican comes from this stretch: the 1662 Prayer Book, still the church's legal standard. The parish interiors with their box pews and galleries; and the settled expectation that an established church will contain parties that disagree with each other. Its missionary societies planted congregations across the Atlantic world and became the institutional seed of the worldwide Anglican Communion. And the ejection it caused in 1662 gave England a permanent Nonconformist tradition that shaped its politics for two centuries.

movements.name: The Russian Church — Nikon to the Holy Synod
movements.informalName: The Church of the Reforms and the Synod
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run as VI.23's receiver - the establishment line whose absence left the census carrying the raskol's protest but not the church it protested against. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: the acts of the 1666-67 council, the Spiritual Regulation of 1721, synodal and seminary records, and saints' lives including those of Mitrofan and Tikhon of Zadonsk. The ordinary believer's voice comes through more thinly here than in accounts of the revival movements.
movements.relationsSummary: Patriarch Nikon's reforms of 1652 and the council of 1666-67 are the establishment side of the story whose other side is the Old Believers, a related but separate tradition born of the same split rather than a successor to this one. Peter the Great left the patriarchal office empty from 1700 and replaced it with the Holy Synod in 1721. The state secularized monastic lands in 1764, and in 1686 the Kyiv metropolia was transferred into this church's jurisdiction. In 1794 it sent the Valaam mission to Alaska, including Herman of Kodiak, and in 1800 it established Edinoverie, a formal arrangement on the shared boundary with the Old Believers.
movements.why: Patriarch Nikon tried to correct Russia's service books and assert the church's authority over the tsar in the 1650s, and lost both fights — deposed by the same council that condemned the split his reforms caused. Peter the Great settled the larger argument by leaving the patriarchal office empty after 1700 and abolishing it in 1721, replacing it with a Holy Synod watched over by a state official, yet the same church still produced Tikhon of Zadonsk's widely read devotional writing and sent monks from Valaam across the Pacific to Alaska in 1794.
movements.dateRationale: 1652 (Nikon patriarch [S]) to 1815 (era cap; the Synod 1721 verified inside) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.31 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Patriarch Nikon, elected in 1652, set out to correct Russian service books against Greek models and to assert the priesthood's authority over the tsar's. And lost both fights: the corrections split the church permanently, and Nikon himself was deposed by the council of 1666-67 that condemned his opponents. Half a century later Peter the Great settled the second argument the other way. When the patriarch died in 1700 Peter simply left the office empty, and in 1721 he abolished it, replacing it with a Holy Synod of clergy, watched over by a lay official the tsar appointed. The church became, in effect, a department of the imperial government and stayed one for two hundred years. Catherine II completed the process in 1764 by confiscating the monastic estates. Yet the same church produced Tikhon of Zadonsk's gentle devotional writing, a serious seminary system, and in 1794 sent monks from Valaam across the Pacific to Alaska.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1652 to 1815 — a church that lost its patriarch to a tsar's pen, was run for two centuries as a government department, and still sent monks to Alaska.
voices: Patriarch Nikon — whose liturgical corrections split the church and whose claim to authority over the tsar ended in his own deposition
Peter the Great — left the patriarchal throne empty from 1700 and abolished it in 1721, replacing it with the Holy Synod
Feofan Prokopovich — the archbishop who drafted the Spiritual Regulation of 1721 that reorganized the church under the crown
Tikhon of Zadonsk — bishop who resigned his see for a monastery and wrote some of the most widely read Russian devotional literature of the century
Herman of Alaska — one of the Valaam monks sent to Kodiak in 1794, who stayed and took the side of the Alaska Natives against the fur company
movements.legacy: The synodal arrangement lasted until 1917, and the church restored the patriarchate almost as soon as the empire fell. The whole shape of modern Russian church-and-state relations was set in this period and is still argued about. Its Alaskan mission planted an Orthodox Christianity that survives among Native communities there to this day, the only Orthodox church established in North America before the nineteenth century. And the tension it created, an official church tied to the state with intense spiritual life running alongside and underneath it, produced both the Optina elders of the following century and the sharp religious searching of Russian literature.

movements.name: The Church of the Desert
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run as VI.6's receiver - the completeness gap the inherited flags missed. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: the Desert synod records from 1715 onward, galley and prison records including those of Marie Durand's imprisonment in the Tour de Constance, the papers of Antoine Court and Paul Rabaut, and correspondence from the Protestant refuge abroad.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the story of what survived after Louis XIV's 1685 Revocation of the Edict of Nantes outlawed French Protestantism. Antoine Court's first Desert synod in 1715 began rebuilding a proscribed church in hiding, at the cost of galley slavery and, for Marie Durand, thirty-eight years imprisoned in the Tour de Constance. The Edict of Toleration in 1787 finally ended that illegality. The Camisard prophetic uprising belongs to this same story's opening decades.
movements.why: When Louis XIV outlawed French Protestantism in 1685, its people met at night in ravines and quarries, calling what they did 'the Desert' after Israel's wilderness. In 1715 a twenty-year-old lay preacher, Antoine Court, began rebuilding an actual church there — holding a synod, restoring ordained ministry, and founding a seminary at Lausanne to train pastors who returned knowing they could hang for it — while Marie Durand spent thirty-eight years imprisoned in a tower rather than recant, until the Edict of Versailles finally granted Protestants a civil existence again in 1787.
movements.dateRationale: 1685 (the Revocation - VI.6's gated end) to 1787 (the Edict of Toleration, verified - the story's own resolution; the 1815-cap alternative was shown) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: When Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, French Protestantism was simply abolished. Its churches were pulled down, its pastors expelled, its people forbidden to emigrate and required to attend Mass. Those who stayed called what they did next 'the Desert', after Israel's wilderness — they met at night in ravines, quarries and woods, several hundred at a time, with lookouts posted. In 1715 a twenty-year-old lay preacher named Antoine Court gathered a handful of others and set about rebuilding an actual church. He held a synod, restored ordained ministry and discipline, discouraged the prophesying that had led to the Camisard rising, and founded a seminary at Lausanne to train pastors who went back over the border knowing they could hang for it. The penalties were exactly that — pastors executed, men sent to the galleys for life, women shut up in towers, Marie Durand among them for thirty-eight years. Until the Edict of Versailles in 1787 finally gave Protestants a civil existence again.
movements.teaser: Languedoc and the Cévennes, 1685 to 1787 — a church that was legally abolished and rebuilt itself in quarries and forests, holding synods for the seventy-two years from its first one to the day it was made legal again.
voices: Antoine Court — the young lay preacher who rebuilt an organized Protestant church in hiding from 1715 and founded the Lausanne seminary that supplied it with pastors
Paul Rabaut — the Desert's leading pastor for decades, living hidden in the hills of Languedoc
Marie Durand — held in the Tour de Constance at Aigues-Mortes for thirty-eight years without recanting; the word 'RESISTER' carved into the tower's stone is traditionally credited to its prisoners
Rabaut Saint-Étienne — Paul Rabaut's son, who carried the case for toleration into French national politics and helped secure the 1787 edict
movements.legacy: It survived, and it is the direct ancestor of the Reformed Church in France. The church that came into the open after 1787 was Antoine Court's church, organized in synods and served by trained pastors. The Revolution finished what the edict began, and Rabaut Saint-Étienne sat in the National Assembly that declared freedom of religion in 1789 — he was guillotined four years later. In the Cévennes the memory is deliberately kept: the Musée du Désert stands in a Camisard leader's birthplace, and an assembly gathers there every September.

experienceToday.text: Musée du Désert, Mialet, Cévennes — the museum of the French Protestant underground, in a Cévenol farmhouse, with an assembly held there each September
The Tour de Constance, Aigues-Mortes — the tower where Protestant women, Marie Durand among them, were held for decades; open as a national monument

movements.name: The Melkite Greek Catholic Split
movements.informalName: The Church of the 1724 Antioch Split
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 8 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: succession records of Cyril VI's 1724 election and his 1729 recognition by Rome, correspondence with Rome's missionary administration, and material from Aleppo's Arabic Christian printing presses.
movements.relationsSummary: At Athanasius III's death the Damascus party elects the pro-Roman Cyril VI Tanas (1724, verified); Constantinople consecrates Sylvester instead; the Antiochian patriarchate splits permanently and the Melkite Greek Catholic communion - alive today - begins; kin-shape to the Brest (VI.20) and Maronite (V.22) unions, both seated; the Orthodox side of the split lives inside VII.18's scope
movements.why: When the Patriarch of Antioch died in 1724, Damascus elected Cyril VI Tanas, who favored union with Rome, but Constantinople refused to accept him and consecrated a rival instead — permanently splitting one Arabic-speaking, Byzantine-rite community into two churches that share the same liturgy, language, and often the same families to this day. Rome recognized Cyril's line in 1729, and the resulting Melkite Greek Catholic church was pressed hard by Ottoman authorities for generations before gaining any recognized civil standing of its own.
movements.dateRationale: 1724 (Cyril VI's election, verified) to 1815 (era cap) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) living corrected to true at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark) — its own E8 record calls it a still-living communion.
movements.longDescription: When the Patriarch of Antioch died in 1724, the Christians of Damascus elected Cyril VI Tanas, who favoured union with Rome. Constantinople refused to accept him and consecrated a rival, Sylvester, a Greek monk from Cyprus. The Antiochian patriarchate never reunited. What followed was the permanent division of one Arabic-speaking, Byzantine-rite community into two churches — one in communion with Rome, recognized by the pope in 1729, and one with Constantinople — sharing the same liturgy, the same language and frequently the same families. The Catholic side, based at Damascus, Aleppo and the monasteries of Mount Lebanon, was pressed hard by Ottoman authorities acting on Orthodox complaints, and was not granted a recognized civil standing of its own until well into the nineteenth century.
movements.teaser: Damascus, Aleppo and Mount Lebanon, from 1724 — one Arabic-speaking Byzantine-rite church that elected two patriarchs and never became one church again.
voices: Cyril VI Tanas — elected patriarch at Damascus in 1724 and recognized by Rome in 1729, the first patriarch of the Melkite Greek Catholic Church
Sylvester of Antioch — the Cypriot monk consecrated by Constantinople as the rival patriarch, who governed the Orthodox side of the split for nearly fifty years
Euthymios Saifi — bishop of Tyre and Sidon in the decades before the split, whose pro-Roman work and religious order prepared the ground for it
movements.legacy: Both churches are alive. The Melkite Greek Catholic Church has a patriarch of Antioch today, is present across the Middle East and in a large diaspora in the Americas, Europe and Australia, and worships in Arabic in the Byzantine rite while in communion with Rome. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch continues alongside it. The split also fixed a pattern that recurs across the Christian East — an Eastern-rite church in union with Rome standing beside its Orthodox mother church, with all the ordinary difficulty that creates. Through Aleppo's presses and schools, the Melkites became significant carriers of Arabic Christian literature.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity — the Mekhitarists and the Catholic Patriarchate
movements.informalName: The Church of San Lazzaro and Bzommar
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 8 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run as VI.28's receiver segment (the VI.28 precedent continued). Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Mekhitarist scholarship is itself part of the source base, built on San Lazzaro's press and manuscript collection; the 1742 patriarchate's own records; and documentation of millet politics in the Ottoman capital.
movements.floorNote: Two Armenian churches appear together here: the ancient Armenian Apostolic Church, which stands outside the Chalcedonian definition of Christ's two natures, and the Armenian Catholic line established in 1742.
movements.relationsSummary: Mekhitar of Sebaste founded his congregation in 1701 and settled it on San Lazzaro in Venice in 1717, where it became the diaspora's scholarly engine. Inside the Ottoman millet system, tension grew between the Armenian Apostolic Church and Armenians in communion with Rome. In 1742 Benedict XIV confirmed Abraham Petros I as Catholic patriarch of Cilicia, with a seat established at Bzommar in 1750.
movements.why: In 1701 Mekhitar of Sebaste founded a congregation devoted to gathering, editing, and printing the Armenian inheritance for a people scattered across empires, and settled it on the island of San Lazzaro in Venice in 1717, where its press and library of thousands of manuscripts effectively created modern Armenian lexicography. Meanwhile, inside the Ottoman capital, Armenians in communion with Rome grew numerous enough that Benedict XIV confirmed a separate Armenian Catholic patriarch in 1742, seated at Bzommar in Mount Lebanon from 1750.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1700 (Mekhitar's congregation 1701 [S]) to 1815 (era cap) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.32 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Mekhitar of Sebaste founded a religious congregation in 1701 with a purpose as much scholarly as devotional. To gather, edit and print the Armenian inheritance for a people scattered across empires. Driven out of Ottoman territory, he and his monks were given the small island of San Lazzaro in the Venetian lagoon in 1717, and turned it into one of the great centres of Armenian learning — a press, a library of thousands of manuscripts, and the dictionaries and translations that effectively created modern Armenian lexicography. Meanwhile, inside the Ottoman capital, the growing number of Armenians in communion with Rome created a problem the millet system had no room for. In 1742 Benedict XIV confirmed Abraham Petros I as Catholic patriarch of Cilicia, with a seat established at Bzommar in Mount Lebanon in 1750. The Armenian Apostolic Church remained overwhelmingly the larger body, but from that point there were two Armenian churches, and the argument between them was fought out in the politics of Constantinople.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, Venice and Mount Lebanon, about 1700 to 1815 — a scattered people's church that built its scholarly engine on a Venetian island and acquired a second hierarchy it had not asked for.
voices: Mekhitar of Sebaste — founded his congregation in 1701 and settled it on the island of San Lazzaro in Venice in 1717
Abraham Petros I Ardzivian — confirmed by Benedict XIV in 1742 as the first Armenian Catholic patriarch of Cilicia
The Mekhitarist scholars of San Lazzaro — collectively the editors, printers and lexicographers whose work preserved and standardized written Armenian
movements.legacy: Both institutions are still there. The Mekhitarist monastery on San Lazzaro degli Armeni continues, with a library of some four and a half thousand Armenian manuscripts, and receives visitors by arrangement — Lord Byron rowed out to it in 1816 to learn Armenian and helped the monks with a grammar. The Armenian Catholic Church endures as a small Eastern Catholic church with its patriarchal seat historically at Bzommar in Lebanon. And the Mekhitarists' printing and philology laid much of the groundwork for the nineteenth-century Armenian cultural revival, the Zartonk.

experienceToday.text: San Lazzaro degli Armeni, Venice — the Mekhitarist monastery, library and press, on its own island in the lagoon; visits by arrangement

movements.name: The Church of Utrecht
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred pending source verification (Era 8 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run, verification-conditioned: its anchors are [S] this session; the named follow-up runs before any build. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The 1723 chapter election and the 1724 Varlet consecration are recorded in standard historical references; the Utrecht chapter's own archives and the later records of the Union of Utrecht provide fuller documentation of the church's early history.
movements.floorNote: No question of creed arises. This church held, and holds, the Catholic faith it always had; the break with Rome was over jurisdiction — who may appoint a bishop — and over the grace controversy of the previous century, neither of which touches the creed.
movements.relationsSummary: This church grew out of the Jansenist quarrel: the Utrecht cathedral chapter elected Cornelius Steenoven without Rome's approval in 1723, and Dominique Varlet consecrated him in 1724. The small communion that resulted survived and became the root of the later Old Catholic Union of Utrecht.
movements.why: When Rome refused for years to confirm an archbishop for the tolerated but legally unrecognized Catholic church of the Dutch Republic, its cathedral chapter fell back on what it held to be its own ancient right and elected Cornelius Steenoven itself in 1723. A French missionary bishop, Dominique Varlet — already in trouble with Rome himself — consecrated him the following year, giving the small church a valid succession and a permanent breach with the papacy in the same act, though it kept the Catholic faith in everything else.
movements.dateRationale: 1723 (the chapter election [S]) to 1815 (era cap); verification-conditioned (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.33 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Catholic Church in the Dutch Republic was a church without legal standing, tolerated in hidden chapels, and its clergy had absorbed a good deal of the Jansenist temper of the age. When Rome refused for years to confirm any archbishop for Utrecht, the cathedral chapter fell back on what it held to be its own ancient right and, in 1723, elected Cornelius Steenoven itself. A French missionary bishop, Dominique Marie Varlet — himself already in trouble with Rome — consecrated him in 1724, which gave the small church a valid succession and a permanent breach with the papacy in the same act. It stayed Catholic in everything else, went on electing its own bishops, and survived on a few thousand members for a century and a half.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, from 1723 — a Catholic chapter that got tired of waiting for Rome, elected its own archbishop, and has been electing them ever since.
voices: Cornelius Steenoven — elected by the Utrecht chapter in 1723 and consecrated in 1724, the first archbishop of the separated Utrecht church
Dominique Marie Varlet — the French missionary bishop who performed the consecration, and who spent the rest of his life in the Netherlands under Roman censure
movements.legacy: It is still there, and it grew a family. When the First Vatican Council defined papal infallibility in 1870, Catholics in Germany, Switzerland and Austria who rejected the definition needed bishops, and Utrecht — the one Western church with an unquestioned Catholic succession outside Rome — supplied them. The resulting Old Catholic churches bound themselves together in the Declaration of Utrecht in 1889, and that Union of Utrecht continues today, in full communion with the Anglican churches since 1931. St Gertrude's Cathedral in Utrecht is its mother church.

experienceToday.text: St Gertrude's Cathedral, Utrecht — the mother church of the Old Catholic Church of the Netherlands and of the wider Union of Utrecht

movements.name: English Old Dissent — Presbyterians and Congregationalists
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run - the Great Ejection's other half. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich for the academies and for hymnody, including Isaac Watts's own work; congregational records; and documentation of the Salters' Hall controversy.
movements.floorNote: No question arises about the tradition itself, which held the historic creeds. But one strand of it moved: at Salters' Hall in 1719 a majority of London's Dissenting ministers declined to require ministers to subscribe to a trinitarian formula, and over the following century many English Presbyterian congregations drifted toward Arian and then Unitarian belief. That drift is named here rather than hidden — it is where the later British Unitarian churches came from.
movements.relationsSummary: The roughly two thousand ministers ejected from the Church of England in 1662 built a lasting tradition: the dissenting academies, Isaac Watts and the hymn revolution he began, and the 1719 Salters' Hall meeting, after which many Presbyterian congregations drifted toward Arian and then Unitarian belief while the Congregationalists stayed orthodox and were reinvigorated by the eighteenth-century revival. Together with the Quakers and the Baptists, this tradition makes up the wider family of English Dissent.
movements.why: About two thousand ministers were put out of the Church of England on a single day in 1662, and the Presbyterian and Congregationalist traditions that grew from the ejection built their own dissenting academies, teaching mathematics and modern languages when Oxford and Cambridge largely didn't. Isaac Watts, one of their ministers, broke the old rule that only the Psalms could be sung in worship and wrote hymns instead, while a 1719 meeting at Salters' Hall split the tradition quietly: many English Presbyterian congregations drifted over the following century toward Arian and then Unitarian belief, while the Congregationalists stayed orthodox.
movements.dateRationale: 1662 (the Great Ejection, verified) to 1815 (era cap) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: On St Bartholomew's Day 1662 about two thousand ministers who could not accept the restored Prayer Book and episcopal ordination were put out of the Church of England, and English Presbyterianism and Congregationalism became permanently separate traditions rather than parties inside one church. Barred from the universities, they built their own: the dissenting academies, which taught mathematics, science and modern languages when Oxford and Cambridge largely did not, and educated a striking share of the country's scientists, manufacturers and reformers. Their other great contribution was sung. Isaac Watts, a Congregational minister, broke the convention that only the Psalms could be sung in worship and wrote hymns instead, which is why English-speaking Christians sing 'When I Survey the Wondrous Cross' and 'Joy to the World'. The tradition also had a fault line: at Salters' Hall in London in 1719 a majority of Dissenting ministers declined to require subscription to a trinitarian formula, and over the following century many English Presbyterian congregations moved toward Arian and then Unitarian belief, while the Congregationalists stayed orthodox and were reinvigorated by the revival.
movements.teaser: England and Wales, 1662 to 1815 — two thousand ministers ejected in a single day, who built their own schools, invented the English hymn, and quietly divided over the Trinity.
voices: Richard Baxter — the most influential of the ejected ministers, whose devotional writing was read far beyond Dissent
Isaac Watts — Congregational minister who effectively created the English hymn
Philip Doddridge — Northampton minister and academy tutor, hymn-writer, and author of The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul (1745)
Joseph Priestley — chemist, Dissenting minister and academy tutor, whose Unitarian convictions and radical politics eventually drove him out of England
movements.legacy: Both halves continue. English Congregationalism ran on into the United Reformed Church and the Congregational Federation, carrying the gathered-church principle into the modern world. The Presbyterian congregations that had moved toward Unitarianism became the core of British Unitarianism. The academies' effect on English intellectual and industrial life was out of all proportion to Dissent's numbers, and the long campaign to remove the legal disabilities Dissenters lived under shaped a century of British politics. Watts's and Doddridge's hymns are sung every week in churches that have never heard of Old Dissent.

experienceToday.text: Bunhill Fields, London — the Nonconformists' burial ground, where Bunyan, Isaac Watts, Daniel Defoe and William Blake are buried; open as a public garden

movements.name: Early American Unitarians & Universalists
movements.informalName: The Liberal Dissent of the New Republic
movements.region: New England, the mid-Atlantic, and London
movements.statusWord: Floor findings recorded separately — Unitarian thread by its own confessions; Universalist thread arguably floor-clean (Era 8 gate); register
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run as a register entry with the two threads analyzed SEPARATELY in the era doc's Section A: the Unitarian thread is plain-reading beyondFloor by its own confessions (VI.14's register-kin resuming after 1650); the Universalist thread is a soteriology dispute, arguably floor-clean - both argued there, neither decided. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: records of Murray's Gloucester congregation from 1779, the Winchester Profession of 1803, Hosea Ballou's Treatise on Atonement, King's Chapel's revised 1785 prayer book, and the record of the Essex Street Chapel founded in 1774.
movements.floorNote: Two different questions need to be kept separate here. The Unitarian thread states plainly, in its own confessions, that it does not hold the Trinity — a clear divergence from the historic creeds, on its own account. The Universalist thread is a different matter: its claim is that God will finally save everyone, which is an argument about salvation rather than about the creed, and may not touch the creed at all. Neither is treated as a fully settled question.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1785 King's Chapel in Boston revised its prayer book to remove the Trinity. English Unitarian precedent came earlier still, with the opening of the Essex Street Chapel in London in 1774. Separately, John Murray organized the Universalists at Gloucester in 1779, and they adopted the Winchester Profession in 1803. Both threads only became formal denominations later, with the American Unitarian Association founded in 1825.
movements.why: Two distinct movements converged in the new American republic. John Murray, an English preacher who believed God would finally save everyone, gathered a Universalist congregation at Gloucester, Massachusetts in 1779, while in 1785 King's Chapel in Boston — an Anglican congregation left leaderless by the Revolution — revised its own prayer book to remove the Trinity, years before either movement had an actual denomination.
movements.dateRationale: 1770 (Murray's arrival in America [S]; earliest named event Essex Street 1774) to 1815 (era cap; the AUA 1825 consolidation is era 9's) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.37 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Two separate movements, often confused with one another, converged in the new American republic. The Universalists came first in organized form. John Murray, an English preacher who had absorbed the doctrine that God will finally save everyone, arrived in America in 1770 and gathered a congregation at Gloucester, Massachusetts in 1779, and a general convention adopted the brief Winchester Profession in 1803. The Unitarian thread came from inside New England Congregationalism and from English precedent — Theophilus Lindsey opened the Essex Street Chapel in London in 1774, and in 1785 King's Chapel in Boston, an Anglican congregation left leaderless by the Revolution, revised its Book of Common Prayer to remove the Trinity. Neither had a denomination yet; those came in the 1820s, after this period closes.
movements.teaser: New England and the mid-Atlantic, 1770 to 1815 — two liberal movements, one holding that God saves everyone and one that God is one person, both organizing churches before either had a denomination.
voices: John Murray — English preacher who brought organized Universalism to America and gathered the Gloucester congregation in 1779
Judith Sargent Murray — essayist and playwright, a leading Universalist voice and an early American advocate of women's education
Hosea Ballou — whose Treatise on Atonement (1805) gave American Universalism its distinctive theology
James Freeman — the King's Chapel minister who revised its prayer book along Unitarian lines in 1785
Theophilus Lindsey — resigned his Church of England living and opened the Essex Street Chapel in London in 1774
movements.legacy: Both became denominations in the following decade — the American Unitarian Association in 1825, the Universalists consolidating their conventions. And in 1961 the two merged into the Unitarian Universalist Association, which continues. Their cultural influence in nineteenth-century New England was far larger than their numbers. Harvard, the Transcendentalists, and a great deal of American reform work in education, prisons and abolition came out of this milieu. King's Chapel in Boston still uses a descendant of its 1785 prayer book.

experienceToday.text: King's Chapel, Boston — the 1754 stone church that became America's first Unitarian congregation in 1785, on the Freedom Trail and open for tours

movements.name: The Ruthenian Uniate Church — Zamość to the Partitions
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 8 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run as VI.20's receiver segment. Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the acta of the Synod of Zamość (1720), partition-era records, and Galician diocesan archives.
movements.relationsSummary: The Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated the church, importing Latin devotional practices into its Byzantine rite, at what became its numerical peak. The partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795 placed most of its people under Catherine II's Russia, whose forced-reversion campaigns of 1794-96 stripped away most of its parishes within two years. Austrian Galicia became the church's real zone of survival.
movements.why: A century after the Union of Brest, the Greek Catholic church of the Ruthenian lands held the loyalty of most of the region's peasantry, and the Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated it while importing Roman devotional practices into its Byzantine rite. When the partitions of Poland handed most of its people to Catherine II's Russia, which treated the union as an amputation to be reversed, forced-reversion campaigns from 1794 stripped away the great majority of its parishes within two years — leaving Austrian Galicia, where the Habsburgs funded the clergy's education, as the church's real survival zone.
movements.dateRationale: 1700 to 1815 (era window; Zamosc 1720 [S] and the partitions inside) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.38 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: A century after the Union of Brest, the Greek Catholic church of the Ruthenian lands — today's Ukraine and Belarus — was at its numerical height, holding the loyalty of most of the peasantry of the eastern Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated it and also latinized it, importing Roman devotional practices into a Byzantine rite and settling its identity as something distinctly its own rather than a temporary arrangement. Then the political ground vanished: the partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795 handed most of the church's people to Catherine II's Russia, which regarded the union as an amputation to be reversed, and campaigns of forced reversion from 1794 stripped it of the great majority of its parishes within two years. What survived did so in Austrian Galicia, where the Habsburgs raised the Greek Catholic clergy's status and paid for their education. And where the church became, over the following century, the carrier of Ukrainian national identity.
movements.teaser: Ruthenia and Austrian Galicia, 1700 to 1815 — a church at its height that lost most of its people in two years, when the state that had protected it ceased to exist.
voices: Lev Kishka — metropolitan who presided over the Synod of Zamość in 1720, the assembly that shaped the church for two centuries
Catherine II of Russia — under whose rule the forced reversions of 1794-96 transferred most of the church's parishes to Orthodoxy
Maria Theresa and Joseph II — the Habsburg rulers who put the Greek Catholic clergy of Galicia on a legal footing with the Latin clergy and funded their seminaries
movements.legacy: The Galician remnant became one of the most consequential churches in Eastern Europe. The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church carried Ukrainian language, schooling and national feeling through the nineteenth century, was suppressed outright by Stalin in 1946, survived underground for four decades as the largest banned church in the world, and came back into the open in 1989. It is a substantial living church today. Its cathedral of St George in Lviv, built in the decades after Zamość, remains its historic centre. The Belarusian and central Ukrainian branches, dissolved in this period and again in 1839, did not recover.

experienceToday.text: St George's Cathedral, Lviv — built 1744-1760, the historic mother church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church

movements.name: Philippine Catholicism — Era-8 Segment
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred pending source verification (Era 8 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 8 Step 0 run per VI.19's own segment mandate, verification-conditioned ([S] anchors; the explicit-deferral alternative was shown). Added at the Era 8 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The records of the mature friar-parish system, documentation of the British occupation of Manila (1762-64), the visitation-controversy dossiers, and records of the 1768 Jesuit expulsion's effects are all well documented. The pasyon's earliest surviving text, from 1704, is the period's one real inside voice from ordinary Filipino Christians.
movements.relationsSummary: This continues the story of Philippine Catholicism into the period when the friar-parish system matured. It covers the British occupation of Manila in 1762-64, the ongoing dispute over whether bishops could inspect the friars' parishes, and the 1768 expulsion of the Jesuits. The unresolved question of native Filipino clergy sharpened over this period, building toward the crisis of 1872.
movements.why: By the mid-seventeenth century the Philippines were the one substantially Christian society in East or Southeast Asia, built parish by parish around Spanish friars who were often the only European in town and the only one who could preach in the local language. Filipino Christianity found its own voice inside that arrangement in the pasyon, a long verse account of Christ's passion chanted by ordinary people through Holy Week in their own houses — the earliest surviving text dates to 1704 — even as the century's real strain built around whether Filipino priests, and not only Spanish friars, could ever hold parishes of their own.
movements.dateRationale: 1650 to 1815 (era window; verification-conditioned; the explicit-deferral branch was shown) (Era 8 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03) continuesAs (identity) written at the Era 9 Freeze — receiver VIII.39 (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: By the middle of the seventeenth century the Philippines were the one substantially Christian society in East or Southeast Asia, and its basic unit was the friar parish: a Spanish religious — Augustinian, Dominican, Franciscan, Recollect or Jesuit — often the only Spaniard in a town, holding both spiritual and civil authority over a population whose language he had learned and which he alone among the officials could preach in. Filipino Christianity took its own shape inside that arrangement, above all in the pasyon, a long verse narrative of Christ's passion in the vernacular, chanted by ordinary people through Holy Week in their own houses. The earliest surviving text dates from 1704, and the practice continues. The century's strains were institutional: a long fight over whether bishops could inspect the friars' parishes, the British occupation of Manila in 1762-64, the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1768, and above all the question of whether Filipino secular priests could hold parishes at all. Which became the great grievance of the century that followed.
movements.teaser: The Philippines, 1650 to 1815 — the one substantially Christian society in East or Southeast Asia, run parish by parish by friars, where ordinary people chanted the passion of Christ in their own language and their own houses.
voices: Gaspar Aquino de Belén — wrote the earliest surviving Tagalog pasyon (1704), the poem that gave Filipino Christianity its most enduring popular form
Basilio Sancho de Santa Justa — archbishop of Manila from 1767, who pressed for the friars to submit to episcopal visitation and for parishes to be given to Filipino secular clergy
The friar orders — Augustinians, Franciscans, Dominicans, Recollects and Jesuits — who between them held the parishes and, with them, most of the effective government of the countryside
movements.legacy: This is a living church and a very large one. The Philippines has one of the largest Catholic populations in the world, and the devotional culture of these centuries is still recognizably what is practised — the pasyon chanted through Holy Week, the town fiesta for the patron saint, the processions. The unresolved question of the period, whether Filipino priests could run Filipino parishes, produced the executions of the three priests remembered as Gomburza in 1872 and fed directly into the national revolution and into the independent Philippine church that broke from Rome in 1902. The friar churches themselves survive: four of them, San Agustín in Manila among them, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

experienceToday.text: The Baroque Churches of the Philippines — four surviving Spanish-era churches inscribed by UNESCO, including San Agustín in Intramuros, Manila

movements.name: The Black Church in America
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on rich inside-voice evidence — slave narratives, with their editorial-frame gravity named, spirituals as communal theology, and Allen's and Jarena Lee's autobiographies. At the Freeze its parentage was named in full for the first time: the Baptist line, the New England revival world, and the Methodist parent an earlier flag had missed, two of those links also landing as 'formed' edges. Its 1906 end is principled twice over — the era cap, and this lane's own next act at Azusa.
movements.sourcing: RICH and inside-voice: slave narratives (editorial-frame gravity named), spirituals as communal theology, conversion accounts, Allen's and Jarena Lee's autobiographies
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of revival Christianity, transformed in the praise house into something distinctly its own. Independent Black Baptist congregations trace back to Silver Bluff (around 1773–75) and First African Baptist in Savannah (1788); Richard Allen organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816, and the AME Zion Church followed in 1821. Its worship fed directly into the 1906 Azusa Street revival and, generations later, into the leadership of the civil rights movement.
movements.why: Independent Black congregations were already meeting by the 1770s, and in 1816 Richard Allen organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church after being pulled up from his knees in a segregated gallery. Because much of the South forbade enslaved people to read, this tradition's theology survives mainly in what it sang and told — the spirituals, conversion accounts, and Jarena Lee's own published life story. Its worship fed directly into the 1906 Azusa Street revival and, a half-century later, into the leadership of the civil-rights movement.
movements.dateRationale: Start c. 1770s (incoming-class, banked at E8: Silver Bluff c. 1773-75 [S]); end 1906 principled twice over — the era cap AND this lane’s own next act (Azusa 1906, IX.1) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Richard Allen, The Life Experience and Gospel Labors (pub. 1833); the 1794 yellow-fever vindication pamphlet (with Absalom Jones); AME Doctrines and Discipline (1817) and General Conference minutes; Daniel Coker, A Dialogue between a Virginian and an African Minister (1810)
sources.note: The founding bishop's own narrative and the church's own records from the start.

sources.work: Jarena Lee, The Life and Religious Experience of Jarena Lee (1836; expanded 1849); Zilpha Elaw, Memoirs (1846); Julia Foote, A Brand Plucked from the Fire (1879)
sources.note: Black women preachers' own narratives (Lee self-published, with Allen's authorization recorded in her own words), collected in Andrews's Sisters of the Spirit.

sources.work: Slave narratives as primary religious texts: Douglass, Narrative (1845, with the appendix on slaveholding religion); Sojourner Truth, Narrative (1850 - dictated); God Struck Me Dead (Fisk interviews, 1920s); WPA ex-slave narratives (1930s)
sources.note: These narratives carry real editorial filters: abolitionist framing, dictation rather than self-authorship in some cases, and interviewer bias. The Fisk and WPA interviews were recorded in the 1920s and 1930s, decades after the events they describe.

sources.work: Spirituals as communal theology: Slave Songs of the United States (1867) and the Fisk Jubilee Singers' repertoire; with David Walker, Appeal (1829) and The Confessions of Nat Turner (1831, recorded by Thomas R. Gray)
sources.note: The spirituals survive here through white transcription and concert-stage arrangement, both real filters on the original oral form. Walker's Appeal is a direct work of Black prophetic writing. Turner's Confessions were recorded by Thomas R. Gray, a white lawyer, from a captive man facing execution - a hostile and coercive context for the text.

sources.work: Albert J. Raboteau, Slave Religion (OUP, 1978; updated 2004), with Milton Sernett (ed.), African American Religious History: A Documentary Witness (Duke, 2nd ed. 1999)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated chapter on the Black church; chapter 35 (Kalu) touches on the Atlantic diaspora as related context.

movements.longDescription: Before the Civil War most Black Christians in America worshipped under white supervision. And made something else of it anyway, in praise houses, brush arbours and night meetings where the preaching, the singing and the theology were their own. Independent congregations appear from the 1770s (Silver Bluff in South Carolina, First African Baptist in Savannah in 1788), and in 1816 Richard Allen, who had walked out of a Philadelphia Methodist church with the rest of its Black members after a trustee pulled Absalom Jones up off his knees in the segregated gallery, organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church — the first Black denomination of national reach; AME Zion followed in 1821. Because the law in much of the South forbade the enslaved to read, the tradition's theology comes down to us largely in what it sang and told: the spirituals, conversion accounts, and self-published narratives like Jarena Lee's. By 1906 it was a whole world of its own. Denominations, colleges, newspapers and a worship life that was about to reshape global Christianity from a mission on Azusa Street.
movements.teaser: The United States, c. 1770s to 1906 — a church born in praise houses and hush harbours, whose theology was sung long before it was allowed to be written down.
voices: Richard Allen — founder and first bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, whose own narrative tells the story of its beginning

Absalom Jones — Allen's co-worker in Philadelphia, the first Black priest ordained in the Episcopal Church, and co-author of their 1794 defence of the Black nurses who stayed through the yellow-fever epidemic
Jarena Lee — the first woman authorized to preach in the AME Church, who self-published her own spiritual autobiography in 1836
Daniel Coker — Baltimore preacher and early AME leader whose 1810 Dialogue put the case against slavery into print
Zilpha Elaw and Julia Foote — Black women preachers whose published memoirs record a ministry the churches only partly made room for
movements.legacy: It is still here, and it is enormous. The AME, AME Zion and CME churches and the Black Baptist conventions are among the largest Christian bodies in the United States, alongside colleges and publishing houses founded in this very window. Its worship went straight into the Azusa Street revival of 1906 and from there into worldwide Pentecostalism, and its music — the spirituals, and then gospel — became one of the most widely borrowed sounds in the world. In the twentieth century its congregations supplied the meeting halls, the money, the songs and most of the leadership of the American civil-rights movement.

experienceToday.text: Mother Bethel A.M.E. Church, Philadelphia — Richard Allen's congregation, founded 1794, on the oldest parcel of land continuously owned by African Americans in the United States

movements.name: The Second Great Awakening & Camp-Meeting Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). The entry's own test — whether revivalism is a tradition or an era-atmosphere — was left standing rather than settled, and the question of a later revivalist successor was answered at the Freeze by scope lines naming Finney and Moody inside existing entries rather than by extending this window or adding a row. An origin note was added recording McGready's Logan County work, Red River and Cane Ridge.
movements.sourcing: Rich
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Methodist/Edwardsean lines; parent of Restorationist and Holiness traditions
movements.why: At Cane Ridge in August 1801, crowds estimated as high as twenty thousand camped in the woods for a week of preaching, weeping, and shouting. Methodist circuit riders and Baptist preachers carried that pattern across the frontier, and by the 1830s Charles Finney was teaching revival as a method that could be worked deliberately rather than simply awaited. Two later movements, the Stone-Campbell Restoration and the Holiness movement, grew directly out of this ferment.
movements.dateRationale: Kept c. 1795-1840 stated; origin note: McGready’s Logan County work 1797, Red River 1800, Cane Ridge 1801 [S]; the revivalism successor question resolved by scope-line (Finney-Moody named lines), not extension (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Itinerants' own accounts: Barton Stone's autobiography (1847, incl. Cane Ridge eyewitness); Peter Cartwright, Autobiography (1856); James B. Finley, Autobiography (1853); Francis Asbury's Journal
sources.note: These are firsthand accounts from circuit-riding preachers. The autobiographies were written well after the events they describe, so treat them as retrospective accounts rather than contemporary records.

sources.work: Charles G. Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835) and Memoirs (1876; critical ed. Rosell & Dupuis, 1989)
sources.note: Finney theorized revival from inside the movement, but his writing postdates the camp-meeting practices it discusses and should be read as later reflection, not a contemporary account of Cane Ridge-era revivalism.

sources.work: The camp meeting's own practice record: songsters and choruses; Methodist quarterly-meeting, conference, and class records; Cane Ridge (1801) participant testimonies
sources.note: This is the revival's own lived practice and sung theology. Sources are scattered across archives and editions, and not all are easy to access.

sources.work: Women's and Black participants: conversion narratives in the Methodist Magazine; Zilpha Elaw's camp-meeting preaching (Memoirs, 1846); John F. Watson, Methodist Error (1819)
sources.note: Watson's Methodist Error is a hostile insider's complaint, but it happens to be the earliest description of Black chorus and ring-shout practice, which gives it real evidential value despite the author's hostility.

sources.work: Nathan Hatch, The Democratization of American Christianity (Yale, 1989), with Paul Conkin, Cane Ridge: America's Pentecost (Wisconsin, 1990)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)

movements.longDescription: At the turn of the nineteenth century, settlers on the Kentucky and Tennessee frontier began travelling for days by wagon to sacramental gatherings that ran for a week at a time — and something broke loose. At Cane Ridge in August 1801 the crowd was estimated at anywhere from ten to twenty thousand people, camped in the woods around a log meeting house, with several preachers going at once and people weeping, shouting and falling to the ground. Methodist circuit riders and Baptist farmer-preachers carried the pattern across the continent, and by the 1830s Charles Finney was writing up the revival as a method that could be worked deliberately rather than waited for. Whether or not it counts as a tradition of its own, it changed what an entire continent expected conversion to feel like.
movements.teaser: The American frontier, 1795 to 1840 — week-long camp meetings in the woods that reset what a whole continent expected conversion to feel like.
voices: James McGready — the Presbyterian minister whose Logan County, Kentucky, sacramental meetings from 1797 set the pattern
Barton W. Stone — hosted the Cane Ridge meeting of 1801 and left an eyewitness account of it
Francis Asbury — the Methodist bishop who rode the circuits and organized the itinerant preaching system that spread the revival
Peter Cartwright — frontier circuit rider whose blunt, funny autobiography is the genre's best-known example
Charles G. Finney — the lawyer-turned-evangelist who theorized the revival into a repeatable method in his Lectures on Revivals (1835)
movements.legacy: It made revivalism a permanent feature of American religion rather than an occasional event, and handed on a whole toolkit still in use — the protracted meeting, the altar call, the anxious bench, the campground and its choruses. Two traditions came directly out of its ferment: the Stone-Campbell Restoration movement and, by way of Methodism's perfectionist wing, the Holiness movement and eventually Pentecostalism. Its campgrounds outlived the frontier, turning into summer resorts, Chautauqua assemblies and conference centres that are still in use.

experienceToday.text: Cane Ridge Meeting House, near Paris, Kentucky — the 1791 log meeting house where the great revival of 1801 was held, preserved inside a protective stone shell and open seasonally

movements.name: The Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on journals, congregational records and debate transcripts — debating was the movement's native genre. It was kept off the register on purpose and said so: its subscription-versus-content concerns and Stone's reservations were read as movement-level historical description, not confessional deviation by its own text. Its 1906 end was kept with its rationale written for the first time — the federal religious census's separate Churches of Christ listing, the rare case where the era cap and the story's own event coincide.
movements.sourcing: Rich: journals, congregational records, debate transcripts (debating was the native genre)
movements.floorNote: The movement refused to make subscription to any creed a test of fellowship — "no creed but the Bible" — while its mainstream nonetheless taught the content the historic creeds state. Barton Stone himself held reservations about how the doctrine of the Trinity had been worded, and those are part of the record; they were a strand inside the movement rather than its confession. This is a description of what the movement actually did, not a charge against it.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of the Awakening + Presbyterian line
movements.why: In 1804 Barton Stone dissolved his own Presbyterian presbytery rather than keep a denominational name, and five years later Thomas Campbell published a plea for "no creed but the Bible and no name but Christian." The two movements merged in 1832, and Alexander Campbell argued their case in public debates that ran for days and that he then published himself. By 1906, a movement founded to end division had recorded one of its own, when the federal census counted the Churches of Christ separately for the first time.
movements.dateRationale: End 1906 kept and its rationale WRITTEN: the 1906 federal religious census’s separate Churches-of-Christ listing (verified) — the division’s own recorded moment; the rare case where era cap and the story’s own event coincide; start 1801 (Cane Ridge, incoming-class) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Founding documents: Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery (1804); Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
sources.note: These founding documents state the movement's 'no creed but the Bible' position in its own words.

sources.work: The journals (native genre per census): Christian Baptist (1823-30), Millennial Harbinger (1830-70), Stone's Christian Messenger (1826-45)
sources.note: These journals were the movement's own periodicals. Stone's reservations about how the doctrine of the Trinity was worded appear in the Messenger's exchanges.

sources.work: Debate transcripts: Campbell-Walker (1820), Campbell-McCalla (1823), Campbell-Owen (1829), Campbell-Purcell (1837), Campbell-Rice (1843)
sources.note: Public debate was one of this movement's characteristic genres, and these transcripts were published verbatim by the movement itself.

sources.work: Congregational minute books; Stone's 1847 autobiography; pioneer-preacher memoir literature ('Raccoon' John Smith biography)
sources.note: Treat the memoir material as retrospective and hagiographic - written well after the fact and admiring in tone. Black congregations from this era are documented mainly through white church minutes, a real filter on the record.

sources.work: Foster, Blowers et al. (eds.), The Encyclopedia of the Stone-Campbell Movement (Eerdmans, 2004), with Richard Hughes, Reviving the Ancient Faith (Eerdmans, 1996)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 (Noll), with 'The growth of voluntary religion' (Bebbington)
sources.note: The Bebbington chapter's exact number in this volume could not be confirmed.

movements.longDescription: On opposite sides of the Appalachians, two sets of Presbyterians came independently to the same conclusion. That the creeds and denominational names Christians used to define themselves were the very things keeping them apart. Barton W. Stone and his colleagues dissolved their own presbytery in 1804 with a document called the Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery. Five years later Thomas Campbell published the Declaration and Address, and with his son Alexander built a movement around the plea for no creed but the Bible and no name but Christian. In 1832 the two groups shook hands and merged. Debating was their native genre — Alexander Campbell argued in public for days at a stretch against sceptics, Presbyterians and a Roman Catholic bishop, and published the transcripts himself — and by 1906, when the federal religious census listed the Churches of Christ separately for the first time, a movement founded to end division had recorded a division of its own.
movements.teaser: The American frontier, 1801 to 1906 — preachers who wanted no creed but the Bible and no name but Christian, and who argued the case in public debates that ran for days.
voices: Barton W. Stone — Kentucky preacher who dissolved his own presbytery in 1804 rather than keep a denominational name
Thomas Campbell — author of the Declaration and Address (1809), the movement's founding plea for Christian unity
Alexander Campbell — his son, the movement's editor, debater and college founder, known as the sage of Bethany
Walter Scott — the evangelist who reduced the movement's gospel to a plan simple enough to count on five fingers
"Raccoon" John Smith — frontier preacher who helped broker the 1832 union of the Stone and Campbell movements
movements.legacy: Three living streams descend from it — the Churches of Christ, the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), and the Christian Churches and Churches of Christ — together numbering several million people worldwide, along with the colleges, journals and mission agencies they built. Its habits travelled further than its name: weekly communion in an otherwise low-church setting, baptism by immersion of believers, congregational independence, and a deep suspicion of anything that looks like a required creed.

experienceToday.text: The Alexander Campbell Mansion, Bethany, West Virginia — Campbell's home, study and family cemetery, a National Historic Landmark open by guided tour

movements.name: The Holiness Movement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on evidence that is rich, testimony-native and unusually women-prominent, Phoebe Palmer's parlour serving as the movement's engine. Keswick was named as a line in this entry's orbit at the Freeze rather than given a row of its own.
movements.sourcing: RICH, testimony-native, women-prominent (Phoebe Palmer's parlor as a movement's engine)
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of Methodism's teaching on Christian perfection and became the immediate parent of Pentecostalism. The Keswick Convention, begun in 1875, carried the same current in a quieter, more Anglican form in Britain.
movements.why: In the 1830s, a New York doctor's wife named Phoebe Palmer simplified Methodist teaching on holiness into a step any believer could take at once, and her Tuesday afternoon parlour meeting ran for decades. Because believers were expected to testify to their own sanctification out loud, the movement's native literature is ordinary people's own accounts of what happened to them — none more striking than Amanda Berry Smith, born enslaved, who preached across England, India, and West Africa.

sources.work: Phoebe Palmer: The Way of Holiness (1843), Entire Devotion to God (1845), Promise of the Father (1859); the Tuesday Meeting records (from 1835); her Guide to Holiness editorship
sources.note: Palmer's own writings, including a book-length defense of women's ministry.

sources.work: The testimony literature: Guide to Holiness (1839-); love-feast and camp-meeting testimonies; National Camp Meeting Association records (Vineland 1867, Manheim 1868)
sources.note: Testimony was this movement's characteristic genre: ordinary believers testifying to their own experience of sanctification. Some of these editions and archives are not easy to access.

sources.work: Amanda Berry Smith, An Autobiography: The Story of the Lord's Dealings with Mrs. Amanda Smith, the Colored Evangelist (1893)
sources.note: A formerly enslaved woman's own account of sanctification, transatlantic evangelism, and the racism she met inside the movement - one of the strongest firsthand voices from inside it.

sources.work: The transatlantic/Keswick wing: William Arthur, The Tongue of Fire (1856); Hannah Whitall Smith, The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life (1875) and letters; Keswick Convention records (1875-)
sources.note: This covers the movement's British, Keswick wing. Robert Pearsall Smith's public scandal and withdrawal from ministry is part of that record and worth noting when weighing these sources.

sources.work: Melvin Dieter, The Holiness Revival of the Nineteenth Century (1980; 2nd ed. 1996), with Vinson Synan, The Holiness-Pentecostal Tradition (Eerdmans, 2nd ed. 1997)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, 'The growth of voluntary religion' (Bebbington) with 'Women preachers and the new orders' (Holmes & O'Brien); ch. 22 (Noll) beside them
sources.note: Exact chapter numbers for the Bebbington and Holmes & O'Brien chapters could not be confirmed; the Noll chapter is chapter 22.

movements.longDescription: Methodism had always taught that God could make a believer actually holy in this life, and in the 1830s a New York doctor's wife named Phoebe Palmer took that teaching, simplified it into a step anyone could take at once, and began hosting a Tuesday afternoon meeting in her parlour that ran for decades and drew bishops as well as neighbours. From that parlour the Holiness movement spread through camp meetings organized from 1867, through the Guide to Holiness and a flood of cheap devotional print, and across the Atlantic, where it took a quieter and more Anglican form at the Keswick Convention from 1875. Because sanctification had to be testified to out loud, the movement's native literature is ordinary people's accounts of their own experience rather than the writings of its leaders. Women were prominent throughout, and its single most remarkable voice belongs to Amanda Berry Smith, born enslaved, who preached in England, India and West Africa and wrote her own life.
movements.teaser: North America and Britain, 1835 to 1906 — a movement launched from a New York parlour, teaching that God could make an ordinary believer holy now, and asking them to say so out loud.
voices: Phoebe Palmer — whose Tuesday Meeting and books made entire sanctification a step an ordinary believer could take, and who defended women's preaching at book length
Amanda Berry Smith — born enslaved, an evangelist across three continents, and the author of one of the era's most striking spiritual autobiographies
Hannah Whitall Smith — Quaker author of The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life (1875), the movement's best-selling book
William Arthur — British Methodist whose The Tongue of Fire (1856) gave the movement much of its transatlantic vocabulary
John Inskip — Methodist minister who led the national camp-meeting association that carried Holiness preaching across America from 1867
movements.legacy: It became a family of ongoing denominations — the Church of the Nazarene, the Wesleyan Church, the Free Methodist Church, the Church of God (Anderson) and others. And it is the immediate parent of Pentecostalism. The leaders, the vocabulary and the expectation of a second, transforming work of the Spirit all came out of Holiness circles into the Azusa Street revival of 1906. Through Keswick it also shaped a whole strand of evangelical devotional language, the deeper life and the surrendered will, that is still in use by people who have never heard the movement's name.

experienceToday.text: The Keswick Convention, Cumbria — the Lake District gathering founded in 1875, still held every summer

movements.name: The Oxford Movement & Anglo-Catholic Revival
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on tracts, memoirs, parish records and the sisterhoods' archives — the first Anglican women's orders since the Reformation. At the Freeze it gained the host it had lacked: a renewal-inside relation was named in both directions with the Victorian Church of England entry added at the same gate, and a lane note was recorded acknowledging that an Anglo-Catholic revival sits in the Protestant lane by inheritance.
movements.sourcing: Rich: tracts, memoirs, parish records, the sisterhoods' archives (first Anglican women's orders since the Reformation)
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of the high-church strand of the Church of England's post-Reformation settlement, as a renewal movement within the Victorian Church of England.
movements.why: In 1833 John Keble preached against Parliament's interference in the church, and a circle of Oxford dons began arguing in their Tracts for the Times that the Church of England was a branch of the ancient catholic church rather than a creature of the state. The next generation carried that argument into ordinary parishes — vestments, incense, weekly communion, and slum missions — at the cost of ritual prosecutions that sent a few priests to prison. It also revived something England had not had since the Reformation: women's religious orders, beginning with the Park Village sisterhood in 1845.

sources.work: Tracts for the Times (1833-41, ending with Newman's Tract 90), with Keble's Assize Sermon 'National Apostasy' (1833)
sources.note: These tracts are the movement's manifesto literature, published serially.

sources.work: Newman, Apologia Pro Vita Sua (1864); Keble, The Christian Year (1827); Froude's Remains (1838-39); Pusey's sermons and letters
sources.note: Newman's Apologia is a retrospective, defensive account written years after the events. Froude's Remains was published after his death and shaped by its editors. Keble's Christian Year is the movement's own devotional poetry.

sources.work: The sisterhoods' archives: Park Village (1845), Sellon's Devonport Society, CSMV Wantage, CSJB Clewer - rules, annals, letters
sources.note: These are the first Anglican women's religious orders since the Reformation, documenting themselves in their own rules, annals and letters. Hostile anti-sisterhood pamphlets from the period survive alongside them as the opposing view. Some of these community archives are not easy to access.

sources.work: Ritualist parish records (St Alban's Holborn, St Peter's London Docks); the ritual-prosecution record (Public Worship Regulation Act 1874; Bishop King's trial 1888-90)
