sources.note: Some of this practice is documented through the courts that prosecuted it, a hostile legal filter worth keeping in mind.

sources.work: Peter Nockles, The Oxford Movement in Context (CUP, 1994), with Brown & Nockles (eds.), The Oxford Movement: Europe and the Wider World 1830-1930 (CUP, 2012)

Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, 'Anglicanism, Presbyterianism and the religious identities of the United Kingdom' (Wolffe); 'Women preachers and the new orders' (Holmes & O'Brien) for the sisterhoods
sources.note: Exact chapter numbers for these two chapters could not be confirmed.

movements.longDescription: In July 1833 John Keble preached an Oxford sermon on national apostasy, protesting Parliament's reorganization of the Irish bishoprics, and a group of Oxford dons began issuing Tracts for the Times arguing that the Church of England was not a creature of the state but a branch of the ancient catholic church, with bishops in unbroken succession and a sacramental life to match. The argument split them: John Henry Newman's Tract 90 in 1841 tried to read the Thirty-Nine Articles in a catholic sense, and four years later he left for Rome, while Keble and Edward Pusey stayed and worked. The next generation carried it out of the university and into the parishes — vestments, incense, candles, weekly communion, and slum missions in the worst districts of London and the industrial cities. At the cost of ritual prosecutions in which a few priests went to prison. It also gave England something it had not had since the Reformation: women's religious orders, beginning with the Park Village sisterhood in 1845.
movements.teaser: England, 1833 to 1906 — Oxford dons who reached back over their own Reformation, and a generation of parish priests who were taken to court for what they did with the result.
voices: John Keble — poet and priest whose 1833 Assize Sermon is conventionally taken as the movement's starting gun
John Henry Newman — its most brilliant writer, whose Tract 90 broke the movement open and who left for Rome in 1845
Edward Bouverie Pusey — the Hebrew professor who stayed, and whose name became a byword for the whole party
Richard Hurrell Froude — the young firebrand of the original circle, whose posthumously published papers scandalized Victorian England
Priscilla Lydia Sellon — founder of the Devonport sisterhood, among the first women to lead a religious community in the Church of England since the Reformation
movements.legacy: Anglo-Catholicism became a permanent party inside Anglicanism and is still there, worldwide — its ceremonial, its parish schools and its slum priests changed what an ordinary English church service looks and sounds like, and the religious orders it revived are still in existence. Its hymn-writers and translators put a great deal of ancient and medieval material into English hymnals used far outside its own circles, and its recovery of early liturgy fed into the twentieth-century liturgical reforms of churches that had no sympathy with its politics at all. Newman went the other way and became a cardinal; he was canonized by the Roman Catholic Church in 2019.

experienceToday.text: Pusey House, Oxford — built as Pusey's memorial in 1884, with its chapel open daily and a library that is one of the great collections on the Oxford Movement

movements.name: The Salvation Army
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a record that is rich and ordinary-facing by design, keeping statistics on every soul and soup bowl. Its floorNote's distinction was left standing: non-observance of the sacraments is a matter of practice, not creed, and raises no floor question.
movements.sourcing: RICH and ordinary-facing by design (statistics on every soul and soup bowl)
movements.floorNote: The Salvation Army does not baptize or celebrate communion. That is a matter of practice rather than of belief — what it confesses is entirely conventional Christian doctrine — and it is worth saying plainly rather than leaving a visitor to guess.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Holiness + Methodist lines
movements.why: William Booth gave up his Methodist pulpit in 1861 to preach in the streets of London's East End, and by 1878 his Christian Mission had renamed itself an Army, with ranks, uniforms, and brass bands to drown out hecklers. Catherine Booth had already argued, in 1859, that women should be commissioned as officers on equal terms with men, and the Army counted everything it did, soul by soul and meal by meal, in the scheme for shelters and labour it published as In Darkest England in 1890.

sources.work: William Booth, In Darkest England and the Way Out (1890); Orders and Regulations; The War Cry (1879-)
sources.note: The movement's own program, internal discipline, and weekly self-record.

sources.work: Catherine Booth, Female Ministry (1859) and Papers on Aggressive Christianity (1880); the Hallelujah Lasses' testimonies and women officers' records
sources.note: Catherine Booth's own defense of women's preaching. The Army commissioned women as officers from the start, making this an unusually large-scale institutional record of women's ministry.

sources.work: The ordinary-facing record: corps statistics, converts' testimonies in The War Cry, rescue-home and slum-sisters casebooks
sources.note: This is the Army's own statistical record, down to individual converts and meals served. Keep in mind it's the Army's own bookkeeping of the poor it served, not an independent account.

sources.work: The opposition record: Skeleton Army riots in press and court records; anti-Army pamphlets; the 1885 Eliza Armstrong case record
sources.note: This is hostile and legal material - opposition press, court records, and the Eliza Armstrong case file - not the Army's own account.

sources.work: Pamela J. Walker, Pulling the Devil's Kingdom Down (California, 2001), with Norman Murdoch, Origins of the Salvation Army (Tennessee, 1994)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, 'The growth of voluntary religion' (Bebbington) with 'Women preachers and the new orders' (Holmes & O'Brien)
sources.note: Exact chapter numbers for these two chapters could not be confirmed.

movements.longDescription: William Booth, a Methodist preacher who could not settle inside a denomination, gave up his pulpit in 1861, and by 1865 was preaching in the streets of London's East End to people the churches were not reaching and did not particularly want. In 1878 his Christian Mission renamed itself an Army — with a General, ranks, uniforms, flags and brass bands to drown out the hecklers. And its officers were commissioned regardless of sex from the beginning, on Catherine Booth's insistence and the published argument she had made for it in 1859. It fed and housed as much as it preached: In Darkest England (1890) laid out a whole scheme of shelters, labour yards, rescue homes and emigration, and the Army counted everything it did, soul by soul and meal by meal. Mobs attacked it, magistrates fined it, and by 1906 it was working on every inhabited continent.
movements.teaser: East London and then the world, 1865 to 1906 — a mission that turned itself into an army, put women in command from the start, and kept the books on every soul and every soup bowl.
voices: William Booth — founder and first General, who moved from Methodist pulpit to East End street corner and never went back
Catherine Booth — co-founder, preacher, and the author of the 1859 argument that settled women's ministry in the Army before it began
Bramwell Booth — their son and the Army's chief of staff, central to the 1885 campaign against child prostitution and to the prosecution that followed it
George Scott Railton — the Army's first commissioner, who took it to the United States in 1880
The Hallelujah Lasses — the young women officers who opened much of the Army's early work, and took most of the street violence for it
movements.legacy: It is still here and still working, one of the largest charitable and religious organizations in the world, active in well over a hundred countries and running shelters, disaster relief, rehabilitation programmes and thrift shops that many people use without ever thinking of it as a church. Its brass bands and its Christmas kettles became part of the ordinary furniture of public life in a dozen countries, and its model of organized, uniformed, professionally administered Christian social work was copied widely.

experienceToday.text: The Salvation Army International Heritage Centre, William Booth College, London — the movement's own archive and museum, open by appointment

movements.name: The Missionary Movement's Native Churches (Serampore India; Sierra Leone & the Niger; Pacific Islands; China Coast & CIM)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), with its source asymmetry carried at full strength — the record is missionary-pen-weighted, and the run held that real native inside voices, Crowther's journals, Pastor Xi and the island teachers' narratives among them, must anchor any build. At the Freeze the boundaries of its four named wings were fixed: East Africa, Madagascar and Alaska were ruled outside them and given rows of their own, while Liberia was named inside this orbit.
movements.sourcing: Rich but missionary-pen-weighted; real native inside voices exist and must anchor any build (Crowther's journals, Pastor Xi, island teachers' narratives)
movements.relationsSummary: These churches descend from Pietist, Moravian, Methodist and Catholic mission lines, and they became the parents of the Christian traditions now flourishing across the global South. Converts also became missionaries in their own right — Lott Carey's mission to Liberia in 1821, sent by Black American churches, is one example.
movements.why: Samuel Ajayi Crowther, freed as a boy from a slave ship, translated the Bible into Yoruba and in 1864 became the first African bishop in the Anglican Communion, only to be forced aside by his own missionary society in 1890. In the Pacific it was Polynesian teachers, not Europeans, who carried the faith from island to island, often at the cost of their lives, while in China the former opium addict known as Pastor Xi built a network of congregations he led himself. Across India, West Africa, the Pacific, and the China coast, churches planted by foreign missions were run and spread almost immediately by converts the missions had not planned for.

sources.work: Samuel Ajayi Crowther: journals (incl. the 1841 Niger Expedition journal), his 1837 enslavement-and-rescue narrative, letters, Yoruba translation work; WITH the 1890-91 Niger crisis record in the CMS archives
sources.note: Crowther's own writing is likely the fullest surviving self-record by an African bishop of this century. It also documents his own society's later treatment of him - sidelined under colonial and racial pressure from within the CMS in his last years.

sources.work: Pacific island teachers' narratives: The Works of Ta'unga (ed. Crocombe, 1968); Joeli Bulu, The Autobiography of a Native Minister in the South Seas (1871); the islander-teacher corpus as a class
sources.note: Joeli Bulu's autobiography passed through missionary translation and editorial mediation before publication. Hundreds of Polynesian teachers carried the Pacific mission forward; their record survives partly in their own words and partly through missionary writers who recorded it for them.

sources.work: India and China inside voices: Krishna Pal's hymns and letters (Serampore, 1800-); Liang Fa, Good Words to Admonish the Age (1832); Pastor Hsi (Xi Shengmo) - hymns and accounts via Mrs Howard Taylor's CIM biography
sources.note: Pastor Xi's hymns and accounts survive mainly through Mrs Howard Taylor's missionary-authored biography - a real editorial filter to keep in mind. Liang Fa's tract had an afterlife of its own: it later helped inspire the leader of the Taiping Rebellion.

sources.work: The societies' archives WITH flags: Carey's Enquiry (1792) and Serampore Form of Agreement (1805); Sierra Leone Native Pastorate records; CMS/LMS/WMMS station diaries; CIM records and China's Spiritual Need and Claims (1865); women's missionary society records (zenana missions, women's boards)
sources.note: This material is weighted toward missionary authorship and entangled with the colonial administrations of the day. It includes records from women's missionary societies, such as the zenana missions to secluded women in India.

sources.work: Lamin Sanneh, Translating the Message (Orbis, 1989; 2nd ed. 2009), with Brian Stanley, The Bible and the Flag (1990) and Andrew Porter, Religion versus Empire? (Manchester, 2004)
sources.note: Sanneh argues that Bible translation into local languages gave converts agency to make the faith their own. Stanley and Porter are standard studies of the relationship between mission and empire.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, chs. 27 & 34 (Stanley), with regional chs. 29 (Frykenberg), 30 (Bays & Grayson), 33 (Piggin & Davidson), 35 (Kalu)
sources.note: These chapters give strong, direct coverage across the regions this record spans.

movements.longDescription: Between 1793 and 1906 European and American missionary societies planted churches across India, West Africa, the Pacific and the China coast. And almost immediately those churches began to be run, staffed and spread by local Christians the societies had not planned for. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, enslaved as a boy in Yorubaland and freed by an anti-slavery patrol, translated the Bible into Yoruba and in 1864 became the first African Anglican bishop, only for the next generation of the same society to force him aside in 1890. In the Pacific it was hundreds of Polynesian teachers, not Europeans, who carried Christianity from island to island, often at the cost of their lives. In China the preacher Liang Fa wrote a tract in 1832 whose stray reading by Hong Xiuquan helped set the Taiping upheaval in motion, and the former opium addict known as Pastor Xi built a network of his own converts inland. What holds these four wings together is a single problem. Nearly everything written about them was written from the mission's side, and the native voices that do survive are what any honest telling has to be built on.
movements.teaser: India, West Africa, the Pacific and the China coast, 1793 to 1906 — churches founded by foreign missions and carried onward, almost at once, by converts the missions had not planned for.
voices: Samuel Ajayi Crowther — freed from a slave ship as a boy, translator of the Bible into Yoruba, and in 1864 the first African bishop in the Anglican Communion
Krishna Pal — the first Indian baptized at Serampore, in 1800, and a Bengali hymn-writer
Ta'unga — Cook Islands teacher and missionary to New Caledonia, one of the few Pacific evangelists whose own writings survive
Joeli Bulu — Tongan missionary to Fiji, whose autobiography is a rare first-person account from an islander evangelist
Liang Fa — the first ordained Chinese Protestant preacher, whose 1832 tract passed into hands he never intended
Xi Shengmo (Pastor Hsi) — Confucian scholar and former opium addict who founded refuges and led a Chinese-run network of congregations in Shanxi
William Carey and Hudson Taylor — the English missionaries whose Serampore mission and China Inland Mission set the pattern for the wider movement
movements.legacy: Much of the Christianity of Africa, Asia and the Pacific descends from these churches, and the global South is now the numerical centre of the faith: the Anglican Church of Nigeria, the churches of South India, the Pacific island churches and the Chinese church all run back through this window. The translation work left a second legacy nobody planned. Hundreds of languages given a written form, a grammar and a printed literature for the first time, which preserved them as much as it preserved anything doctrinal. And the treatment of Crowther in his last years became a lesson African Christians drew directly. It is one of the roots of the independent African church movements of the following century.

experienceToday.text: Serampore College, West Bengal — founded in 1818 by William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward, and still teaching

movements.name: The Haugean Awakening
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, smaller frame (Era 9 Step 0; c2 cleared on the community limb)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered deferred on a smaller frame, on Hauge's own 33 books and letters plus the friends'-societies records. Its person-defined check was run at this gate as the criterion's eighth live application and cleared on the community limb — the movement demonstrably outgrew its founder into a broad lay culture. Its end was moved to 1842, the repeal of the Conventicle Act and the movement's own legal resolution.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: Hauge's own 33 books and letters; friends' societies' records
movements.floorNote: A fair question about any movement named for its founder is whether it was really a tradition or just one man's following. The Haugeans clearly outgrew Hauge: the friends' societies kept their own records, ran their own businesses, and went on meeting for generations after his death in 1824, and the lay culture he set going long outlived him.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Pietism inside the Lutheran establishment
movements.why: In 1796 a Norwegian farmer's son named Hans Nielsen Hauge had a religious experience in his father's field and set out on foot to preach, defying a law that reserved religious meetings to the parish clergy. He wrote thirty-three books and founded mills and trading businesses to support the network of "friends" that grew around him, while the state answered by imprisoning him for most of the following decade. Those friends' societies kept meeting and trading long after his death in 1824, until the law he had defied was finally repealed in 1842.
movements.dateRationale: End 1842 (the Conventicle Act repealed — the movement’s own legal resolution [S]); start 1796 (Hauge’s call [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Hauge's own corpus: his 33 books and tracts (from Betragtning over Verdens Daarlighed, 1796), his letters to the friends' network, and his Testament to his Friends (1821)
sources.note: Hauge was a lay peasant preacher who ran his own itinerant press. Most editions are in Norwegian, with only limited material translated into English.

sources.work: The prosecution record: the 1804-14 case under the Conventicle Act - interrogation records, commission files, Hauge's prison writings
sources.note: This is hostile legal material: the founder documented at length by the state church that prosecuted and jailed him.

sources.work: The friends' societies' records: haugianere society minutes, correspondence and business networks, lay preachers' memoirs; Hauge's authorization of women itinerant speakers in his letters
sources.note: These records show the movement's own societies continuing to meet, correspond, and run businesses well beyond Hauge's own lifetime - evidence the movement outgrew its founder. Hauge's letters also document his authorization of women as itinerant speakers.

sources.work: Andreas Aarflot, Hans Nielsen Hauge: His Life and Message (Augsburg, 1979), with Joseph Shaw, Pulpit Under the Sky (1955)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8 (chapter assignment hedged): nearest Bebbington's voluntary-religion and Thompson's popular-religion chapters
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated Scandinavian or Nordic chapter; these are the nearest topical fits.

movements.longDescription: In 1796 a Norwegian farmer's son named Hans Nielsen Hauge had a religious experience while working in his father's field, and set out on foot to tell people about it. Which was against the law, because Norway's Conventicle Act reserved religious meetings to the parish clergy. He wrote thirty-three books and tracts, walked thousands of miles, and founded mills, paper works and trading businesses to support the network of "friends" that grew around him; the state answered by arresting him in 1804 and keeping him in prison and under prosecution for most of the following decade. The movement long outlasted the man: after his death in 1824 the friends' societies went on meeting and trading, and in 1842 the Conventicle Act itself was repealed.
movements.teaser: Norway, 1796 to 1842 — a farmer's son who walked the country preaching without a licence, wrote thirty-three books, built factories to pay for it, and spent most of a decade in prison.
voices: Hans Nielsen Hauge — lay preacher, author of thirty-three books, industrial entrepreneur, and prisoner of the state church for most of a decade

Beyond Hauge himself the movement was deliberately lay and collective — the "friends" ran their own societies, businesses and meetings, and it is those local networks rather than any named successor that carried it on after his death
movements.legacy: Haugean piety became one of the permanent layers of Norwegian Lutheranism: a lay preaching culture, a network of mission societies and prayer houses, and a suspicion of clerical monopoly that outlived the law it was reacting against. Norwegian emigrants carried it into the American Midwest, where Haugean congregations became one of the founding strands of Norwegian-American Lutheranism. In Norway today Hauge is honoured about equally as a revivalist and as an entrepreneur, which would have puzzled almost nobody who knew him.

experienceToday.text: Hans Nielsen Hauge's Memorial Museum, Rolvsøy, Fredrikstad — his birthplace, a protected building from around 1730, with a visitor centre and guided tours

movements.name: The Reveil & Inner-Mission Awakening
movements.informalName: The Réveil and the Inner Mission
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a rich institutional and personal record, with the deaconess motherhouses named as a genuine women's tradition inside it. Its own split test — one tradition or national siblings — was left open, and French Protestantism was routed as named lines in its orbit rather than given a segment of its own. Its c. 1880 end was kept and stated as such, Wichern's death in 1881 having been shown as a near-principled alternative and not adopted.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional + personal; the deaconess motherhouses are a genuine women's tradition inside it
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Pietist/Moravian lines
movements.why: After the Napoleonic wars, awakened piety across Switzerland, France, the Netherlands, and Germany turned quickly into institutions: Johann Hinrich Wichern's Rauhes Haus for street children in Hamburg, opened in 1833, grew into a whole programme of organized Christian social work. At Kaiserswerth in 1836, Theodor and Friederike Fliedner founded a deaconess motherhouse that trained women as nurses, and one of its visitors in 1851 was Florence Nightingale. Wichern also left something almost everyone has met without knowing it — he made the first Advent wreath, for the children in his care, in 1839.
movements.dateRationale: End kept c. 1880 stated (Wichern d. 1881 [S] the near-principled alternative, shown not adopted); start 1815 boundary, crossing nothing (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Geneva/French Reveil voices: Malan's Chants de Sion (1841); Adolphe Monod, Les Adieux (1856); Felix Neff's Alpine letters; Merle d'Aubigne's histories; Bourg-de-Four/Oratoire society records
sources.note: Les Adieux was dictated on a deathbed, worth reading with that in mind; d'Aubigne writes advocacy history, not a disinterested account.

sources.work: The Dutch leg: da Costa, Bezwaren tegen den geest der eeuw (1823); Groen van Prinsterer's writings; the Afscheiding (1834) secession acts and persecution record
sources.note: Real state pressure — fines and forced billeting on the separatist congregations — appears throughout, alongside the seceded churches' own minutes.

sources.work: German Inner Mission and the deaconess motherhouses: Wichern's Denkschrift (1849) and Rauhes Haus records; Fliedner's Kaiserswerth records (from 1836) - deaconess annals, training registers, sisters' correspondence
sources.note: The motherhouse's own pen frames the sisters' record here, not the sisters' own unmediated voice.

sources.work: Timothy C. F. Stunt, From Awakening to Secession (T&T Clark, 2000), with Nicholas Hope, German and Scandinavian Protestantism 1700-1918 (OUP, 1995)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8: 'Christianity and the Creation of Germany' (Steinhoff), and David Bebbington's writings on the evangelical awakening
sources.note: Its several national strands are kept distinct here by design, rather than merged into one composite story.

movements.longDescription: After the Napoleonic wars a wave of personal religious awakening ran through the Protestant churches of Switzerland, France, the Netherlands and Germany — in Geneva against a comfortable rationalist establishment, in the Netherlands to the point of secession from the state church in 1834, everywhere with an insistence that faith had to be felt and not merely inherited. What distinguished it was what it built. Johann Hinrich Wichern's Rauhes Haus for street children in Hamburg (1833) grew into the Inner Mission, a whole programme of organized Christian social work. At Kaiserswerth in 1836 Theodor and Friederike Fliedner founded a deaconess motherhouse that trained women as nurses and teachers, and one of its visitors in 1851 was Florence Nightingale. By the time the generation was over, awakened piety in these countries had turned into a permanent network of hospitals, orphanages, schools and training houses.
movements.teaser: Switzerland, France, the Netherlands and Germany, 1815 to 1880 — an awakening that turned personal conversion into hospitals, orphanages and the first Protestant order of nursing sisters.
voices: Johann Hinrich Wichern — founder of the Rauhes Haus in Hamburg and of the Inner Mission, who argued that social work was the church's own business
Theodor and Friederike Fliedner — founders of the Kaiserswerth deaconess motherhouse in 1836, which trained women for nursing, teaching and prison visiting
César Malan — Geneva preacher and hymn-writer, dismissed by the city's church for the fervour of his preaching
Adolphe Monod — the Réveil's greatest French preacher, whose deathbed addresses were taken down and published
Félix Neff — evangelist and practical reformer among the isolated Protestant villages of the French Alps
Isaac da Costa and Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer — the Dutch Réveil's poet-polemicist and its political thinker
movements.legacy: The German Diakonie — the Protestant social-service network the Inner Mission became — is still one of the largest welfare providers in Europe, and the deaconess model spread across the Protestant world and into the professionalization of nursing. The Dutch secession of 1834 grew into a major strand of Reformed Christianity in the Netherlands and, through emigration, in North America. And Wichern left one thing almost everyone has met without knowing it. He made the first Advent wreath at the Rauhes Haus in 1839, so the children in his care could count the days to Christmas.

experienceToday.text: Das Rauhe Haus, Hamburg — Wichern's institution of 1833, still a working diaconal organization on the same site

movements.name: Restorationist-Apocalyptic Ferment & Adventism
movements.statusWord: Creedal question — two window-specific findings recorded (Era 9 Step 0); resolution belongs to era 10’s window
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich - the movement documented itself compulsively (including the Great Disappointment's morning-after accounts)
movements.floorNote: Early Adventist leaders, including some of the movement's founders, explicitly rejected the doctrine of the Trinity in this era's documents — most notably the 1872 Declaration of Fundamental Principles. The Seventh-day Adventist Church's official confession became trinitarian in 1931. A separate, related question — how much authority Ellen G. White's own prophetic claims carry relative to Scripture — isn't fully settled by this window of its history. CLOSURE NOTE (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14): the era-10 case this row's disposition charged is completed on IX.44 — the 1931 yearbook statement and the 1980 Dallas Fundamental Beliefs (both verified) are the dated own-voice resolution of the window question, and Ellen White's death in 1915 followed by the movement's continued institutional life completes the community limb of the person-defined run.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of the Awakening's ferment
movements.why: In the 1830s and 40s, thousands of Americans followed Baptist farmer William Miller's calculation that Christ would return around 1844, and when the date passed without incident, most walked away in what believers still call the Great Disappointment. A remnant did not: Hiram Edson, reinterpreting the date's meaning in a vision on his own farm the morning after, helped build what became the Seventh-day Adventist Church. The movement is unusual for writing down its own failed prediction, and its own reckoning with it, rather than pretending it never happened.

sources.work: The Millerite layer: Miller, Evidence from Scripture and History (1836); Signs of the Times and Midnight Cry; the Great Disappointment morning-after accounts (Hiram Edson's manuscript; Washington Morse and others)
sources.note: Edson's account of his vision was written retrospectively, decades after the event it describes.

sources.work: Ellen White: Early Writings, Spiritual Gifts (1858-64), Testimonies for the Church (1855-), Steps to Christ (1892), with the church's own account of her visions and prophetic office
sources.note: These are the movement's own foundational texts, including the church's own account of Ellen White's visions and her claimed prophetic office.

sources.work: The church's own institutional print: Review and Herald (1850-), the 1863 General Conference organization records, the 1872 Declaration of Fundamental Principles
sources.note: The 1872 Declaration reflects the movement's early anti-trinitarian position. The church's official confession later became trinitarian, a change documented in its own institutional print.

sources.work: The wider ferment and the hostile/apostate record: Advent Christian records; Rachel Oakes Preston and the sabbath link; Uriah Smith and J. N. Andrews; D. M. Canright, Seventh-day Adventism Renounced (1889)
sources.note: Canright left the church, and his book is a hostile, ex-member's account rather than neutral description.

sources.work: George Knight, A Search for Identity (2000), with David L. Rowe, God's Strange Work: William Miller and the End of the World (Eerdmans, 2008) and Ronald Numbers, Prophetess of Health (1976; 3rd ed. 2008)
sources.note: Numbers's book is a critical scholarly study of Ellen White that remains contested within the church itself.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated chapter on Millerism or Adventism.

movements.longDescription: In the 1830s and 40s, thousands of Americans across denominations followed Baptist farmer William Miller's calculation that Christ would return around 1844 — and when the date passed without incident, in what believers still call the Great Disappointment, most walked away disillusioned. A determined remnant didn't: they reread their calculations, concluded the date had marked something other than Christ's visible return, and built lasting communities around that reinterpretation, most enduringly the Seventh-day Adventist Church and a cluster of related Adventist bodies. What makes the story unusual is how openly it was told — the movement wrote down its own failed prediction and its own morning-after reckoning with it. And that same instinct for self-documentation carried into its later history, including its own internal debate over the Trinity in its earliest decades, formally settled in its 1931 statement of belief.
movements.teaser: New England and beyond, 1831 to 1906 — a movement that dated Christ's return, watched the date pass in silence, and chose to write down its own disappointment rather than pretend it never happened.
voices: William Miller — the Baptist farmer-turned-preacher whose calculations sparked the movement
Hiram Edson — reinterpreted the 1844 date's meaning the morning after the Great Disappointment, in a vision on his own farm
Joseph Bates — convinced the movement's other founders to keep the seventh-day Sabbath
Ellen G. White — the movement's central prophetic voice, whose visions and writings shaped its lasting institutions
movements.legacy: This ferment became an ongoing denomination — the Seventh-day Adventist Church, now a global body of tens of millions, along with smaller related Adventist bodies that trace back to the same movement.

experienceToday.text: The William Miller Farm, Low Hampton, New York — his restored home, the chapel he built, and Ascension Rock, open for tours

movements.name: The Optina Elders & Russian Ascetic Renewal
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a profoundly inside-voice record — thousands of letters of spiritual direction to laypeople, alongside the Way of a Pilgrim. At the Freeze a renewal-inside relation was named in both directions with the Synodal Century entry added at the same gate, and a scope note recorded that John of Kronstadt is a parish figure rather than an Optina elder, so his line is shared with that entry, where it fits better.
movements.sourcing: RICH and profoundly inside-voice: thousands of letters of spiritual direction to laypeople; Way of a Pilgrim; John of Kronstadt's diary
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of the Philokalia tradition of ascetic prayer and became the world Dostoevsky drew on for The Brothers Karamazov. Its spirituality carried forward into twentieth-century émigré Orthodox theology, as a renewal movement within the wider Russian Orthodox Church of the same era.
movements.why: At a forest hermitage founded in 1821 near Kozelsk, elders known as startsy kept their door open to anyone who came, and those they could not see in person they answered in thousands of pages of letters written to ordinary people rather than to monks. From the 1840s the monastery also ran a press, putting the Greek ascetic fathers into Russian for laypeople for the first time. Dostoevsky came in 1878 after the death of his small son, and turned what he found there into the elder Zosima.

sources.work: The elders' letters: Macarius of Optina (Eng. sel. Russian Letters of Spiritual Direction, trans. de Beausobre, 1944); Ambrose of Optina's letters; Leonid; the skete's records
sources.note: Thousands of letters of monastic direction addressed to ordinary lay people. Most of this correspondence remains untranslated from Russian.

sources.work: The Philokalia-in-Russian line: Paisius's Slavonic Dobrotolubiye (1793); Optina's own publishing enterprise (from 1846, with Kireevsky); Theophan the Recluse's Russian Dobrotolubiye (1877-89) and letters; Brianchaninov, The Arena
sources.note: This shows the renewal as a translation and publishing effort, with the elders themselves working as editors and translators.

sources.work: The lay side: The Way of a Pilgrim (Kazan, 1880s); John of Kronstadt, My Life in Christ; pilgrims' memoirs of Optina (Leontiev)
sources.note: The Way of a Pilgrim's author is unknown, and its textual history is debated among scholars.

sources.work: The Dostoevsky-adjacent layer: The Brothers Karamazov's Zosima (1880, after the 1878 visit to Ambrose); Kireevsky/Slavophile essays; the Tolstoy visits
sources.note: This is the renewal's literary and cultural afterlife - Dostoevsky's fiction and the Slavophile essays it inspired - rather than firsthand documentation of the movement itself.

sources.work: Irina Paert, Spiritual Elders: Charisma and Tradition in Russian Orthodoxy (Northern Illinois, 2010), with Leonard Stanton, The Optina Pustyn Monastery in the Russian Literary Imagination (1995)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 15 'The Russian Orthodox church in imperial Russia 1721-1917' (Dixon)

movements.longDescription: At a small monastery in the forest near Kozelsk, south of Moscow, a hermitage founded in 1821 became the centre of something Russian Orthodoxy had never had at this scale. Elders — startsy — who kept the door open to anyone who walked up to it. Peasants, students, landowners and novelists queued outside the cell of Father Ambrose, and the elders who could not see everyone answered by letter, leaving thousands of pages of spiritual direction addressed not to monks but to ordinary people trying to live ordinary lives. They were also publishers: from the 1840s, with the Slavophile thinker Ivan Kireevsky, Optina ran a press that put the Greek ascetic fathers into Russian and made a monastic literature available to laypeople for the first time. Dostoevsky came in 1878 after the death of his small son, and turned what he found there into the elder Zosima.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1821 to 1906 — a forest monastery where monks kept a door open to anyone who knocked, and answered by letter the thousands who could not come.
voices: Leonid of Optina — the first of the elders, who brought the practice of eldership to the hermitage in the 1820s
Macarius of Optina — his successor, and the driving force behind the monastery's publishing work
Ambrose of Optina — the most sought-after of them all, who received visitors daily for decades and whom Dostoevsky met
Ivan Kireevsky — Slavophile philosopher and lay collaborator who helped the monastery become a publishing house
Theophan the Recluse — not an Optina monk, but the bishop whose Russian Philokalia and vast correspondence belong to the same renewal
movements.legacy: The Soviet state closed Optina in 1918 and killed or scattered its monks, but the monastery was returned to the church in 1987 and is active again, receiving thousands of pilgrims a year, with the elders now canonized. The books it printed did more travelling than the monks. The Philokalic spirituality it made available in Russian carried into the émigré theology of twentieth-century Paris and from there into English, and The Way of a Pilgrim, with its Jesus Prayer, became one of the very few Orthodox devotional books widely read in the West — J. D. Salinger built a novel around it in 1961.

experienceToday.text: Optina Pustyn, near Kozelsk, Kaluga region — the monastery of the elders, returned to the church in 1987 and receiving pilgrims again

movements.name: The Kollyvades & Greek Renewal
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered deferred on a smaller frame — moderate-to-rich, with new-martyr preparation documented as pastoral practice. Its own merge-or-split test against the Paisian revival was left standing, and the Era 8 seam ruling was carried forward unchanged: a sibling and renewal relation, not an identity link, was named with the national-churches entry added at this gate.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; new-martyr preparation as documented pastoral practice
movements.relationsSummary: A sibling movement to the Paisian revival among Slavic Orthodox monks, part of the same broader eighteenth-century wave of ascetic renewal but a separate development within Greek Orthodoxy.
movements.why: The dispute began over which day to hold memorial services for the dead, and the monks who insisted on the older practice were mocked with a nickname for the boiled wheat served at them. What they produced was serious: a 1782 anthology of Greek ascetic writing on prayer, the Philokalia, and an argument for frequent communion against a general practice of receiving only once or twice a year. Under Ottoman rule they also prepared, deliberately and pastorally, people who expected to be executed for refusing to convert, and wrote up their deaths in a New Martyrologion in 1799.

sources.work: The Kollyvades fathers' own texts: the Philokalia (1782); Concerning Frequent Communion; Nicodemus's Handbook of Spiritual Counsel; Athanasios Parios; the controversy record (memorial-services dispute, Athonite expulsions)
sources.note: This includes voices from both sides of the controversy over memorial services.

sources.work: New-martyr preparation: Nicodemus's New Martyrologion (1799) with the documented pastoral practice of preparing candidates for martyrdom under Ottoman rule
sources.note: This material is hagiographic in genre, and the executions are recorded only from the Christian side.

sources.work: The renewal's spoken and diffused layer: Kosmas Aitolos's teachings and prophecies as recorded by hearers, his school-founding mission and martyrdom (1779); island circles (Paros, Hydra, Chios) in disciples' lives and correspondence
sources.note: Kosmas himself wrote almost nothing; what survives comes through his hearers' memory. Treat the disciples' lives of him as hagiographic in genre.

sources.work: Constantine Cavarnos, St. Nicodemos the Hagiorite (1974), with Kitromilides's essays on the Orthodox world of the era
sources.note: Cavarnos writes from an insider, devotional stance; Kitromilides writes as an academic historian.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 8 'Orthodoxy and the West: Reformation to Enlightenment' (Kitromilides), with ch. 6 'Mount Athos and the Ottomans' (Zachariadou)

movements.longDescription: It began as an argument about when to hold memorial services for the dead — Saturday, as tradition had it, or Sunday, as convenience on Mount Athos had made usual. And the monks who insisted on the older practice were nicknamed for the boiled wheat, kollyva, served at those services. The quarrel was small; what came out of it was not. Its leaders argued for frequent communion against a general practice of receiving perhaps once or twice a year, and in 1782 published in Venice the Philokalia, an anthology of Greek ascetic writers on prayer that became one of the most influential books ever printed in Orthodoxy. Under Ottoman rule they also did something with few parallels anywhere in Christian history. They prepared, pastorally and deliberately, people who expected to be executed for refusing to convert, and then wrote up their deaths in a New Martyrologion in 1799. For their trouble the Kollyvades were driven off Athos and scattered through the islands.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos and the Greek islands, 1750s to 1860s — monks mocked over a quarrel about boiled wheat, who published the book that reshaped Orthodox prayer.
voices: Nicodemus the Hagiorite — the movement's great editor and compiler, co-editor of the Philokalia and author of a handbook of spiritual counsel
Macarius of Corinth — bishop and co-editor of the Philokalia, and the movement's advocate of frequent communion
Athanasios Parios — its most combative theologian and defender in the controversy
Kosmas Aitolos — itinerant preacher who founded hundreds of village schools across Greek lands and was executed in 1779; he wrote almost nothing, and survives in what his hearers wrote down
movements.legacy: The Philokalia went straight out of Greek. Paisius Velichkovsky translated it into Slavonic in 1793, Theophan the Recluse into Russian later in the century, and English translations in the twentieth century put it into the hands of readers with no Orthodox background at all. Frequent communion, the practice the Kollyvades were mocked for, is now ordinary across most of the Orthodox world. The movement is generally read as the seed of the modern Greek Orthodox revival, and its leading figures have since been canonized by the church that once expelled them.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the monastic republic where the dispute began; visits require a permit and, by the peninsula's own ancient rule, are open to men only

movements.name: The Coptic Revival — Cyril IV and After
movements.informalName: The Coptic Revival under Cyril IV
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a moderate institutional and biographical base, with its own note that the richer window may be the twentieth century left standing. It was renamed at this Freeze so the title matches its window — Cyril IV died in 1861 while the entry runs to 1906, and its subject is the revival he launched — and its succession into the next era, written before any gate, was ratified here with the 34-year internal gap disclosed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate (institutional and biographical; the richer window may be the 20th century)
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of the long Egyptian lane; parent of the Sunday School revival

movements.longDescription: The Coptic Orthodox Church entered the nineteenth century poor, largely untaught, and reduced in the eyes of most outsiders to a survival. And then in 1854 a young patriarch took office and spent seven years changing that. Cyril IV founded schools, including one for girls at a time when that was nearly unheard of in Egypt, brought in a printing press, built a library, and set about educating clergy who had mostly learned the liturgy by ear. He died suddenly in 1861, not yet fifty, in circumstances still argued about. What he started did not stop. An elected lay communal council from 1874, a Coptic press and newspapers from the 1870s, and the schools that would eventually produce the twentieth-century Sunday School movement out of which the modern Coptic renaissance came.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 1854 to 1906 — seven years of a reforming patriarch, and a church long counted out beginning to teach itself again.
voices: Cyril IV — patriarch from 1854 to 1861, remembered by Copts as the Father of Reform, who founded the schools and imported the press

Much of what followed him ran through institutions rather than individuals — the elected lay council of 1874 and the Coptic newspapers of the 1870s onward — and the reformers behind them are far less well documented in accessible sources than the patriarch himself
movements.legacy: Everything the modern Coptic Church is known for was made possible here. The Sunday School movement that grew out of Cyril's schools, formally organized from 1918, produced the generation of teachers, monks and bishops who repopulated the desert monasteries and led the church through the twentieth century, and the Coptic diaspora carried that renewal to Europe, North America and Australia. The Coptic Orthodox Church remains the largest Christian community in the Middle East.

experienceToday.text: The Coptic Museum, Old Cairo — the world's largest collection of Coptic Christian art and manuscripts, in the middle of Coptic Cairo's ancient churches

movements.longDescription: In 1830 a young man in western New York named Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon — which he said he had translated from golden plates shown to him by an angel — and on 6 April that year organized a church around it. Its members were driven out of Ohio, then Missouri, then Illinois, where a mob killed Smith in the Carthage jail in 1844. Under Brigham Young most of them crossed the plains from 1847 and settled the Salt Lake valley, laying out towns, irrigation systems and eventually a territory largely of their own making. The nineteenth-century church practised plural marriage openly from 1852, which brought decades of federal prosecution before its president formally renounced the practice in 1890 and Utah entered the Union six years later. Its members documented themselves relentlessly: the Relief Society's minute book, Eliza R. Snow's poems and trail diaries, and Emmeline B. Wells's newspaper make up one of the fullest records any nineteenth-century American religious community left behind.
movements.teaser: New York to the Great Basin, 1830 to 1906 — a new scripture, a church driven west across a continent, and a desert territory built very largely from scratch.
voices: Joseph Smith — founder, translator and publisher of the Book of Mormon, killed by a mob in Illinois in 1844
Emma Hale Smith — his wife, first president of the Relief Society, and compiler of the church's first hymnbook
Brigham Young — who led the migration west in 1847 and organized the Utah settlements
Eliza R. Snow — poet, hymn-writer and Relief Society leader, one of the movement's most influential women
Emmeline B. Wells — editor of the Woman's Exponent from 1877 to 1914 and a leading Utah suffragist
movements.legacy: It is a large and growing worldwide church, headquartered in Salt Lake City, with millions of members on every continent and one of the most extensive volunteer missionary programmes of any religious body. Its genealogical archives, built for its own theological reasons, have become a resource used by family historians of every background in the world. And its settlement pattern is still legible on the ground: grid-plan towns, irrigation canals and ward meetinghouses across the American Intermountain West.

experienceToday.text: The Church History Museum, Salt Lake City — the church's own museum of its nineteenth-century origins and migration, opposite Temple Square, free to enter

movements.longDescription: In the early 1870s a young Pittsburgh clothing merchant named Charles Taze Russell gathered a small circle to study the Bible without reference to inherited denominational teaching, and in 1879 began a magazine, Zion's Watch Tower and Herald of Christ's Presence. Around the magazine grew an international network of readers who called themselves Bible Students, distributed Russell's six-volume Studies in the Scriptures by the million, worked door to door as colporteurs, and gathered for annual conventions from 1893. The movement was built on printing and personal distribution from the very start, which is why its record of itself is unusually complete for a body of its size. The name Jehovah's Witnesses, and the tightly centralized organization the movement is known for today, came later — after Russell's death in 1916, under his successor Joseph Franklin Rutherford.
movements.teaser: Pittsburgh and outward, 1870s to 1906 — a Bible study circle that became a printing house, and a magazine that built a worldwide readership on foot, door by door.
voices: Charles Taze Russell — founder, editor of Zion's Watch Tower from 1879, and author of the six-volume Studies in the Scriptures
Maria Frances Russell — his wife and an early Watch Tower writer and speaker, later estranged from him in a separation that became public
The colporteurs — the ordinary readers who sold and gave away the movement's literature full time, and whose reports in the magazine are its own account of how it actually grew
movements.legacy: It became one of the most recognizable religious movements in the world. Several million active members in nearly every country, still organized around door-to-door work and one of the largest religious publishing operations anywhere, in hundreds of languages. Its members' refusals — of military service, of flag salutes, of blood transfusions — produced a long series of court cases, and some of the resulting judgments, particularly in the United States, became landmark free-speech and religious-liberty precedents that now protect everyone.

experienceToday.text: Jehovah's Witnesses' world headquarters and educational centre, Warwick and Patterson, New York — public guided tours and exhibits, run by the organization itself

A second and separate question is how far the movement is defined by one person — Mary Baker Eddy governed it personally, by her own written rules, until her death in 1910. Both points are recorded here as factual description of what the movement's own texts say, not as a judgment of it or of its members.

Her congregations have no ordained clergy and no sermons in the usual sense — two lay readers read the same lesson from the Bible and her book in every branch church in the world on a given Sunday. The practitioners who did most of the movement's actual work, then as later, were overwhelmingly women, and their printed healing testimonies are its characteristic literature.

movements.longDescription: Mary Baker Eddy was a New England woman in poor health for most of her early life who, after a recovery in 1866 that she attributed to reading the Gospels, spent nine years working out what she had understood and published it in 1875 as Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures. Around the book she organized a church in 1879, a college to train practitioners, and a set of periodicals that carried the healing testimonies of ordinary members. Its congregations have no ordained clergy, no sacraments and no sermons in the usual sense. Two lay readers read aloud from the Bible and from Eddy's book, the same lesson in every branch church in the world on any given Sunday. Eddy governed the movement closely through the Manual of The Mother Church, written in 1895, until her death in 1910. And the practitioners who did most of its actual work were, then as later, overwhelmingly women.
movements.teaser: New England and outward, 1875 to 1906 — a church with no clergy and no sermons, built around one book and the healings its readers reported.
voices: Mary Baker Eddy — founder, author of Science and Health, and the movement's governing authority to the end of her life

The practitioners — the mostly female healers whose printed testimonies in the church's own periodicals are the movement's characteristic literature and the main record of how ordinary members experienced it
movements.legacy: It is an ongoing denomination, much smaller now than at its height, with branch churches and reading rooms in many cities and its landmark complex in Boston. Its most widely felt legacy is a newspaper. The Christian Science Monitor, founded by Eddy in 1908 in her late eighties, became a respected international daily that has won multiple Pulitzer Prizes and is read by people with no connection to the church at all. Its position on medical treatment has also been the subject of repeated legal and public debate over the years, particularly where children are concerned.

experienceToday.text: The Mary Baker Eddy Library and the Mapparium, Boston — the church's library and its 1935 stained-glass globe, open to the public

His followers organized into small congregations called ecclesias, with no clergy and members teaching and presiding in turn, and in 1864 took the name Christadelphians largely so they could claim conscientious-objector status in the American Civil War. Robert Roberts gave them a magazine that has run continuously since that year and a statement of faith they still use.

movements.longDescription: John Thomas was an English doctor who emigrated to America in 1832, nearly drowned in a shipwreck on the way, and resolved that if he survived he would work out the Bible's teaching for himself rather than take it on anyone's authority. He concluded that most of what the churches taught had been added long after the apostles, and set out the alternative in Elpis Israel in 1848. His followers organized as "ecclesias" — small congregations with no clergy, where members taught and presided in turn. And in 1864 adopted the name Christadelphians, brothers of Christ, largely so they could claim conscientious-objector status in the American Civil War. Robert Roberts, a Scottish printer's apprentice who became the movement's second great figure, gave them a magazine that has run continuously since 1864 and a written confession, the Birmingham Statement of Faith, that they still use.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1848 to 1906 — a doctor who set out to start the Bible again from scratch, and small lay congregations who took a new name so they could refuse to fight.
voices: John Thomas — English physician and emigrant whose Elpis Israel (1848) set out the movement's whole reading of Scripture
Robert Roberts — his younger colleague, who founded The Christadelphian magazine in 1864 and drafted the statement of faith the community still uses
movements.legacy: It continues as a small worldwide body — tens of thousands of people in autonomous ecclesias across Britain, North America, Australia, Africa and elsewhere — with no clergy, no central headquarters, the same statement of faith, and a magazine published without a break since 1864. Its tradition of conscientious objection outlasted the war it was named for. Christadelphians were among the recognized objectors in both world wars, and their case files are part of the legal record of conscience in Britain and the United States.

movements.name: Catholic Apostolic Church (Irvingites)
movements.statusWord: No floor question — the office-defined c2 run recorded (Era 9 Step 0); the question stays genuinely open
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Real liturgical and institutional record
movements.floorNote: The Catholic Apostolic Church was trinitarian and creedally conventional; there is no question at all about its doctrine. What is genuinely open is a different question — whether a body whose entire existence rested on twelve restored apostles counts as a tradition in its own right or as a movement defined by an office. It answered that question about itself more plainly than most: when the last apostle died in 1901 it ordained no successors and let its ministry lapse, yet its congregations went on worshipping for another half-century.
movements.relationsSummary: A German branch broke away in 1863, specifically to keep calling new apostles, and became the New Apostolic Church, which today has millions of members, mostly in Africa and Europe.
movements.why: Between 1830 and 1831, members of Edward Irving's fashionable London congregation began speaking in tongues and prophesying, convinced that Christ's return was near, and the church that grew out of it restored twelve apostles to prepare for it. Because the apostles were held to be irreplaceable, no successors were ever ordained, and as they died one by one the church's ministry simply ran out. When the last apostle died in February 1901, its congregations entered what they called the time of silence, continuing to worship with no one left who could ordain anyone.
movements.dateRationale: End 1901 kept, principled: the last of the twelve restored apostles (Francis Woodhouse) died 3 Feb 1901 [S] and the church, by its own theology, ordained no successors — the story closes itself; start 1832 (Newman Street church [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.note: The women's voices at the movement's origin survive only as transmitted through others' accounts, a real filter. Baxter's Narrative of Facts is a former prophet's recantation, written after he left the movement and turned critic.

sources.note: This liturgy is among the century's richest liturgical creations, and shows the church in its own most characteristic register.

sources.note: This documents a church continuing to record its own life even after the apostolic office that had defined it lapsed.

sources.note: Flegg's is the standard study; he has his own connection to the tradition, which is worth noting.

sources.note: No chapter in this reference volume is dedicated to this movement; these are the nearest topical fits.

movements.longDescription: In 1830 and 1831, people in the fashionable London congregation of the Scottish preacher Edward Irving began speaking in tongues and prophesying — something almost nobody in Britain had expected to see again. And Irving was deposed by his presbytery for his teaching and died in 1834, before the movement that bears his name had really taken shape. What emerged was a church built on the conviction that Christ was about to return and had restored the apostolate to prepare for it. Twelve men were called as apostles, and around them grew a fourfold ministry, church buildings on a near-cathedral scale, and one of the richest liturgies composed in the nineteenth century. Because the apostles were held to be irreplaceable, no successors were ordained. As they died, the church's ministry simply ran out, and when the last of them died in February 1901 its congregations entered what they called the time of silence. Continuing to worship, with nobody left who could ordain anyone.
movements.teaser: Britain, 1832 to 1901 — a church that expected the world to end, restored twelve apostles to meet it, and then quietly ran out of clergy when the last of them died.
voices: Edward Irving — the Scottish preacher whose London congregation was where it began, deposed in 1833 and dead in 1834; the movement is named for him although he was never one of its apostles
Mary Campbell and Margaret Macdonald — the young women in western Scotland whose 1830 prophecies and tongues touched the whole thing off, and whose words survive only in other people's accounts
John Bate Cardale — the London lawyer called as the first of the twelve apostles, and the principal author of the church's liturgy
Henry Drummond — banker, politician and patron, on whose Albury estate the prophetic conferences met
Francis Valentine Woodhouse — the last surviving apostle, who died on 3 February 1901, after which no more ordinations were possible
movements.legacy: The liturgy outlived the church that wrote it. Scholars of worship studied it long after the congregations fell silent, and it drew on Eastern, Roman and Anglican sources in a combination nobody else had attempted. Its buildings survive and are still in use by other congregations — the great church in Gordon Square, London, is Grade I listed. And a German branch that broke away in 1863 precisely because it wanted to keep calling new apostles became the New Apostolic Church, which today has millions of members, mostly in Africa and Europe. The original body itself has no ministry left and, by its own theology, cannot acquire one.

experienceToday.text: The Church of Christ the King, Gordon Square, London — built 1850-54 as the Catholic Apostolic Church's central church, Grade I listed and still in use for worship

movements.name: Oneida Community
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — perfectionism and complex marriage under one founder’s total authority, both grounds (proposed and recorded, Era 9); register retained

movements.floorNote: Oneida diverged from historic Christian teaching on two counts, both stated in its founder's own published writings: John Humphrey Noyes taught that his followers were already free of sin, and he reorganized marriage and sexual life around that claim under his own personal authority. The community also settled the question of its own continuity — in 1881 it dissolved itself and became a joint-stock company.
movements.why: In 1848, John Humphrey Noyes gathered a community at Oneida in upstate New York to live as though sin were already conquered, replacing marriage with what they called complex marriage and submitting to a formal system of group criticism. They also worked hard at manufacturing, making animal traps, silk thread, and eventually tableware, to pay their way. Under outside pressure Noyes left for Canada in 1879, and in 1881 the community voted itself out of existence and became a joint-stock company instead.

sources.work: The community's own record: The Circular/Oneida Circular, the First Annual Report (1849), daily journals, mutual-criticism records, the stirpiculture records (1869-79)
sources.note: Diary-depth self-documentation, including the real question of consent and coercion inside the community's practice of complex marriage — not smoothed over.

sources.work: Members' voices: Tirzah Miller's diaries (ed. Fogarty, Desire and Duty at Oneida, 2000); ex-members' accounts and the 1879-81 breakup correspondence; Prof. John Mears's public campaign
sources.note: A woman member's own inside record, though the founder's authority visibly presses on it. Mears writes as a hostile outside critic.

sources.work: Lawrence Foster, Religion and Sexuality (Illinois, 1984), with Spencer Klaw, Without Sin (Penguin, 1993)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)

movements.longDescription: John Humphrey Noyes taught that a Christian could be wholly free of sin in this life, and in 1848 he gathered a community at Oneida in upstate New York to live as though the kingdom had already arrived. They held property in common, replaced marriage with what they called complex marriage — in which every member was in principle married to every other. Submitted to a formal system of group criticism, and from 1869 ran a selective breeding programme they named stirpiculture. They also worked hard and paid their way, manufacturing animal traps, silk thread and eventually tableware. Outside campaigning and internal strain finished it. Noyes left for Canada in 1879, and in 1880 the community voted itself out of existence, reorganizing on New Year's Day 1881 as a joint-stock company.
movements.teaser: Upstate New York, 1848 to 1881 — a community that believed sin was already over, abolished marriage among themselves, and finally voted itself into a cutlery company.
voices: John Humphrey Noyes — founder and, to the end, the community's sole governing authority
Tirzah Miller — his niece, whose diaries are the fullest surviving inside account by a member, and show the pressure of that authority as well as the life
John Mears — the Hamilton College professor whose public campaign against the community in the late 1870s helped bring the outside pressure that ended it
movements.legacy: As a religious body it left nothing — no successor community, no continuing church, no doctrinal descendants. As a business it left a great deal. Oneida Limited became one of the best-known tableware manufacturers in the world, and its flatware sat on ordinary tables for generations without the faintest hint of where it came from. The Mansion House the community built still stands and is a National Historic Landmark, run as a museum and inn.

experienceToday.text: Oneida Community Mansion House, Oneida, New York — the community's own building, now a museum with period rooms, guided tours and lodging

movements.name: Spiritualism / New Thought
movements.statusDescription: Outside the Constitution's own sense of a Christian movement — named and explained, never silently dropped.
movements.floorNote: Neither Spiritualism nor New Thought is a confessionally Christian movement in the historic sense. They grew up alongside nineteenth-century Christianity, borrowed a good deal of its vocabulary, and overlapped with it socially — but they are not traditions within it. They are named here only because visitors often ask where they belong.
movements.why: In March 1848, two young sisters in a farmhouse at Hydesville, New York, said they were communicating with the dead through rapping sounds, and within a few years séances and spirit circles had spread through the United States and Britain. Running alongside it was New Thought, a family of teachers descended from the Maine healer Phineas Quimby who held that right thinking heals. Both movements borrowed heavily from Christian vocabulary but grew up alongside the churches rather than inside them, and neither teaches specifically Christian doctrine.
movements.dateRationale: Start corrected to 1848 (the Fox sisters at Hydesville [S]) — the previous numerics were an era-window fill artifact; end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Spiritualism's own texts: Andrew Jackson Davis, The Principles of Nature (1847); the Fox sisters' record (1848; Margaret Fox's 1888 confession and recantation); Emma Hardinge Britten, Modern American Spiritualism (1870); women's platform mediumship (Cora L. V. Scott)
sources.note: Named here for context, since participants will rightly ask about it, though Spiritualism is not a Christian tradition. These are advocacy chronicles from inside the movement; women's leadership was structurally central to it, including the famous Fox sisters' confession and later recantation of fraud.

sources.work: New Thought's own texts: Quimby's manuscripts (pub. 1921); Warren Felt Evans; Emma Curtis Hopkins; the Fillmores' Unity (1889-)
sources.note: Included for context only. Quimby's manuscripts were edited after his death, worth weighing with that in mind; the contested question of how much Mary Baker Eddy depended on Quimby is noted here, not settled (see also Christian Science).

sources.work: The investigative record: the Seybert Commission report (1887); SPR investigations; the fraud-exposure literature
sources.note: Investigative and hostile: adversarial pens that were themselves part of how the movement came to be publicly known.

sources.work: Ann Braude, Radical Spirits (1989; 2nd ed. 2001), with Catherine Albanese, A Republic of Mind and Spirit (Yale, 2007)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)

movements.longDescription: In March 1848 two young sisters in a farmhouse at Hydesville, New York, said they were communicating with the dead through rapping sounds, and within a few years séances, mediums and spirit circles had spread through the United States and Britain, drawing in reformers, grieving families and scientists who wanted to test the claims. Running alongside it, and partly overlapping, was New Thought. A family of teachers descended from the Maine healer Phineas Quimby who held that mind governs matter and that right thinking heals. Both borrowed Christian vocabulary heavily and grew in the same nineteenth-century soil as the revivals, but neither is a Christian tradition; they are named here only because visitors reasonably ask where they fit. Spiritualism's public credibility took a heavy blow in 1888, when Margaret Fox declared before an audience in New York that she and her sister had produced the original raps by cracking their toe joints — a confession she withdrew a year later.
movements.teaser: North America and Britain, 1848 to 1906 — table-rapping in a New York farmhouse and a mind-over-matter gospel, both grown up beside the churches without belonging to them.
voices: Margaret and Kate Fox — the sisters at Hydesville in 1848, whose rappings started it, and whose later confession and retraction have been argued over ever since
Andrew Jackson Davis — the self-taught seer whose writings supplied Spiritualism with much of its theology before the Fox sisters made it a movement
Emma Hardinge Britten — medium, lecturer and the movement's first serious chronicler
Phineas Quimby — the Maine clockmaker and mental healer at the head of the New Thought line
Emma Curtis Hopkins — the teacher who trained most of New Thought's founding generation
Charles and Myrtle Fillmore — founders of Unity in 1889, the largest of the New Thought bodies
movements.legacy: Spiritualist churches still exist in Britain and the United States, and the effort to test their claims scientifically produced the Society for Psychical Research in 1882 and, indirectly, a whole field of investigation. New Thought became ongoing denominations — Unity, Religious Science and their relatives — but its far larger legacy escaped religion altogether. Its language of mind over circumstance runs straight into twentieth-century positive-thinking, self-help and prosperity literature read by millions who have never heard of Quimby.

movements.name: Korean Catholic Origins
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on martyrs' letters and trial records — a pre-missionary church documented by the missionaries who finally reached it. Its 1886 end was kept with its rationale written for the first time, the France–Korea treaty ending the persecution era, and the 1886–1904 seam was disclosed forward to the next gate rather than absorbed here.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: martyrs' letters and trial records; the pre-missionary church documented by the missionaries who finally reached it
movements.relationsSummary: The Korean Catholic Church was self-founded by lay Confucian scholars before any priest arrived, a singular case of lay initiative in Catholic history. Roughly ten thousand martyrs died in the persecutions that followed. It stands as a precursor to the Protestant missions that later took root in Korea.
movements.why: Korea is the only country where the Catholic Church began without a missionary: in the late eighteenth century a circle of Confucian scholars near Seoul studied Chinese-language Catholic books, convinced themselves, and sent Yi Sung-hun to Beijing to be baptized in 1784. He came home and baptized the rest, and the church he founded was written in Korean from the start, reaching women, servants, and the poor as fast as the educated elite. The Choson state read it as treason against the Confucian order, and roughly ten thousand Korean Catholics were killed in successive purges between 1801 and 1866.
movements.dateRationale: End 1886 kept, principled: the France-Korea treaty ending the persecution era [S]; the 1886-1904 seam disclosed to era 10 (IX.2’s origin lines); start 1784 (Yi Sung-hun’s Beijing baptism [S], incoming-class) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The self-evangelized church's own documents: Chong Yak-chong, Chugyo yoji (c. 1798-1801, vernacular han'gul catechism); the community's letters to Beijing and Rome (1784-, incl. the 1811 letter to the Pope); Yi Byeok's Essence of Sacred Doctrine
sources.note: This is the lay church teaching itself, in its own hand. The attribution of the Essence of Sacred Doctrine to Yi Byeok is debated among scholars. English-language access is chiefly through Baker and Rausch's translations.

sources.work: The Hwang Sa-yong silk letter (1801)
sources.note: A believer's appeal written on silk during the Sinyu persecution, intercepted by authorities. It survives only in the persecutors' own archive, and it combines genuine faith testimony with a politically sensitive appeal for foreign intervention - both parts of the record, without softening either.

sources.work: The persecution records: Sinyu (1801), Kihae (1839), Pyongo (1846), Pyongin (1866) interrogation and execution records in the Choson annals and police archives
sources.note: These are the persecutors' own records: the martyrs' testimony as it survives through interrogation and torture, not their own words freely given.

sources.work: Women's voices: Columba Kang Wan-suk (catechist, executed 1801) in trial records and martyrology; the women catechists' cell-structure centrality; Daveluy's martyr-account compilations
sources.note: This material passes through two filters: hostile court records and later hagiographic compilation. Daveluy's martyr-account compilations were made by missionaries who reached Korea only after these events, adding another layer of outside mediation.

sources.work: Don Baker with Franklin Rausch, Catholics and Anti-Catholicism in Choson Korea (Hawai'i, 2017), with James Grayson, Korea: A Religious History (rev. ed. 2002)
sources.note: The current standard study, including English translations of the Chugyo yoji and the silk letter.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 30 'Christianity in East Asia: China, Korea and Japan' (Bays & Grayson)
sources.note: Grayson is a specialist in Korean church history, making this a direct fit.

movements.longDescription: Korea is the only country in the world where the Catholic Church began without a missionary. In the late eighteenth century a circle of Confucian scholars near Seoul studied Chinese-language Catholic books, convinced themselves, and sent one of their number, Yi Sung-hun, to Beijing to be baptized in 1784. He came home and baptized the others, and a church of several thousand people existed before a priest had ever set foot in the country. It was written in Korean from the start — Chong Yak-chong's catechism was in the vernacular script rather than in the scholarly Chinese of the elite. Which is part of why it reached women, servants and the poor as fast as it reached the literati. The Choson state read it as treason against the Confucian order, and the church spent a century under persecution, with something on the order of ten thousand Korean Catholics killed in successive purges between 1801 and 1866, until a treaty with France in 1886 finally brought the killing to an end.
movements.teaser: Korea, 1784 to 1886 — the one church in the world that converted itself out of books, and then paid for it with some ten thousand lives.
voices: Yi Sung-hun — sent to Beijing by his study circle and baptized there in 1784, he came home and baptized the rest
Yi Byeok — one of the founding scholars of the circle, credited with the earliest Korean writing on the faith
Chong Yak-chong — author of the first Korean-language catechism, written for people who could not read Chinese; executed in 1801
Kang Wan-suk — a noblewoman and catechist who ran much of the underground church in Seoul, executed in 1801
Andrew Kim Taegon — the first Korean-born Catholic priest, executed in 1846 at the age of twenty-five

Hwang Sa-yong — author of the 1801 letter on silk, intercepted before it reached Beijing, which lay in the state tribunal's archive for nearly a century before the church recovered it, and is now in the Vatican
movements.legacy: It became one of the largest and most active Catholic communities in Asia — several million people in South Korea today, in a church that still traces its beginning to laypeople rather than clergy and takes considerable pride in the fact. In 1984 Pope John Paul II canonized 103 of its martyrs in Seoul itself rather than in Rome, and further beatifications followed in 2014. The execution grounds are now national shrines, and the martyrs' letters and trial testimony remain among the most vivid first-person religious documents anywhere in nineteenth-century Asia.

experienceToday.text: Jeoldusan Martyrs' Shrine, Seoul — the riverside cliff where Catholics were executed in 1866, now a church and museum holding the martyrs' relics and records

movements.name: Laestadianism & the Nordic Revivals
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on sermons, movement periodicals and later oral histories, with the Sami dimension named as carrying real marginalized-voice value. Its end was aligned to the 1906 era cap, replacing a round-1900 artifact, and a scope note recorded that the Swedish low-church revivals sit inside its Nordic plural deliberately rather than by accident.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: sermons, movement periodicals, later oral histories; the Sami dimension adds real marginalized-voice value
movements.relationsSummary: Laestadianism is part of Pietism's long line in the Lutheran north, marked by its practice of spoken absolution between believers, and its communities are still alive today. The Swedish low-church revivals led by Carl Olof Rosenius, whose mission society formed in 1856, and P. P. Waldenström, whose Mission Covenant Church formed in 1878, are counted alongside it as part of the same broader Nordic revival movement.
