movements.why: Lars Levi Laestadius, a Swedish Lutheran pastor and botanist of partly Sami descent, had his preaching changed entirely by an 1844 conversation with a young Sami woman he called Mary, and the revival that followed carried fierce, local-language preaching and an end to drinking through Sami and Finnish parishes. Its most distinctive practice is confession and absolution spoken face to face between ordinary believers, rather than pronounced from a pulpit. The same century's low-church revivals in Sweden, led by Carl Olof Rosenius and P. P. Waldenström, are counted as part of the same Nordic movement.
movements.dateRationale: End aligned to the 1906 era cap (living; round-1900 artifact replaced); start 1844 (Laestadius and Milla Clementsdotter [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: Laestadius's own corpus: sermons/postillas; Darhushjonet; Ens Ropandes Rost i Oknen (1852-54); Fragments of Lappish Mythology (1840s)
sources.note: The sermons survive through transcription and copying, so treat the text as mediated rather than a direct transcript. Fragments of Lappish Mythology is Laestadius's own account of Sami religion - his own partly-Sami background complicates that positioning, worth keeping in mind. Only partial English translation exists.

sources.work: The Sami dimension: Milla Clementsdotter ('Lapp Mary' of Asele, 1844) - known through Laestadius's own account; Juhani Raattamaa's letters and the lay-reader network; the Kautokeino uprising trials (1852)
sources.note: Milla Clementsdotter's own voice survives only through Laestadius's account of her, a real filter on the record. The Kautokeino trial records are hostile legal material, from a state court condemning the Sami revivalists it tried.

sources.work: The lived practice record: spoken absolution and liikutuksia in sermons, movement periodicals, and later collected oral histories; firstborn-network village-meeting records
sources.note: The oral histories in this collection were recorded well after the events they describe, so treat them as retrospective. Most sources are in Finnish or Swedish and not easy to access in translation.

sources.work: The wider Nordic revivals: Paavo Ruotsalainen's letters and the herannaisyys meeting culture; C. O. Rosenius's Pietisten (1842-) and the Swedish lasare networks
sources.note: Ruotsalainen's letters are a lay peasant leader's own record - thin, but genuine. Each national strand of this wider revival should be kept distinct from the others.

sources.work: Juha Pentikainen's Laestadius scholarship (incl. the Fragments critical edition), with Warren Hepokoski's Laestadian-movement surveys
sources.note: The English-language scholarship on this movement is notably thin.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8 (chapter assignment hedged): nearest Thompson's popular-religion and Bebbington's voluntary-religion chapters
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated Nordic or Scandinavian chapter; these are the nearest topical fits.

movements.longDescription: Lars Levi Laestadius was a Swedish Lutheran pastor and a serious botanist, of partly Sami descent, serving parishes in Lapland that were being destroyed by alcohol — and in 1844 a conversation with a young Sami woman he called Mary changed his preaching entirely. What followed spread through the Sami and Finnish north: fierce sermons in the local languages, an end to drinking, and intense emotional expression in meetings that startled outsiders. Its most distinctive practice is confession and spoken absolution between ordinary believers — forgiveness declared face to face by a neighbour rather than pronounced from a pulpit. It was never only his: the same century brought Paavo Ruotsalainen's awakening in Finland and, in Sweden, the low-church revivals of Carl Olof Rosenius and P. P. Waldenström — a wider family of Nordic revivals, not just one man's movement.
movements.teaser: Lapland and the Nordic north, 1844 to 1906 — a revival among Sami and Finnish parishes where ordinary believers forgave each other's sins out loud.
voices: Lars Levi Laestadius — pastor, botanist and preacher, of partly Sami descent, whose sermons set the revival going
Milla Clementsdotter — the young Sami woman whose 1844 conversation with Laestadius he credited with changing everything; her own words survive only in his account of them
Juhani Raattamaa — the lay schoolmaster who became the movement's real organizer and the architect of its practice of spoken absolution
Paavo Ruotsalainen — the unlettered Finnish farmer at the centre of Finland's own awakening
Carl Olof Rosenius — Swedish lay preacher and editor whose journal Pietisten carried the low-church revival across Sweden
Paul Petter Waldenström — theologian and preacher behind the Swedish Mission Covenant of 1878
movements.legacy: Laestadian communities are alive across northern Finland, Sweden and Norway and among emigrant descendants in the American upper Midwest, now divided into several distinct and generally conservative branches. It is one of very few European revival movements with a substantial indigenous constituency, and Sami has remained a language of its preaching. The Swedish revivals in the same entry left their own institutions. The mission society Rosenius helped inspire and the Mission Covenant Church, whose American cousin became the Evangelical Covenant Church.

experienceToday.text: The Laestadius Museum and cottage, Pajala, Sweden — the rectory and cabin where Laestadius lived from 1851 until his death in 1861, with his herb garden

movements.name: Plymouth Brethren & Dispensational Formation
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (Era 9 Step 0; c2 cleared on the community limb)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on movement periodicals, Darby's vast corpus, assembly records and Müller's narratives. Its person-defined check was run at this gate as the criterion's ninth live application and cleared on the community limb — the 1848 Open/Exclusive division shows the body was never reducible to Darby — with the Exclusive wing's later Darby-centrism named as the honest counter-note. Its end was aligned to the 1906 era cap, replacing a round-1900 artifact.
movements.sourcing: Rich: movement periodicals, Darby's vast corpus, assembly records, Mueller's narratives
movements.floorNote: There is a fair question about a movement so shaped by one man's mind: was it a tradition, or Darby's following? The 1848 division answers it — the movement split into Open and Exclusive Brethren and both halves went on, which a body reducible to its founder could not have done. The honest counter-note is that the Exclusive wing afterwards centred itself heavily on Darby's own authority.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of evangelical dissent; via Scofield reshaped how millions read Scripture; influence on the Bible-institute tradition
movements.why: In the late 1820s a handful of Dublin Christians, among them a dentist, a lawyer, and a young curate named John Nelson Darby, began meeting to break bread together with no ordained clergy and no denominational name. Darby also worked out a scheme dividing history into dispensations and expecting Christ to remove the church before a final tribulation, a way of reading the Bible almost unknown before him. George Müller ran orphanages in Bristol for thousands of children on the principle of never asking anyone for money, publishing the accounts to prove it.
movements.dateRationale: End aligned to the 1906 era cap (living; round-1900 artifact replaced); start 1827 (Dublin gatherings [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: J. N. Darby, Collected Writings (34 vols.) and letters; the 1848 Bethesda division documents (both sides' circulars)
sources.note: Darby's corpus is vast and centers heavily on him personally, worth keeping distinct from the movement's own broader record. The 1848 division documents show the Open and Exclusive streams diverging and continuing on their own, beyond Darby himself.

sources.work: George Muller, A Narrative of Some of the Lord's Dealings with George Muller (1837-) and the Bristol orphanage annual reports; Scriptural Knowledge Institution records
sources.note: Muller's own bookkeeping of answered prayer, published as an ordinary-facing genre for a general readership.

sources.work: Periodicals and assemblies: The Christian Witness (1834-); assembly minute books; A. N. Groves's memoir and 1836 letter to Darby; women's presence chiefly in hymnody (Frances Bevan) and missionary letters (Harriet Groves)
sources.note: Groves's 1836 letter to Darby is the movement's own earliest internal critique. Women's presence in the surviving record is thin - itself a reflection of the restrictions the assemblies placed on women's public roles, not an absence of women in the movement.

sources.work: Tim Grass, Gathering to His Name (Paternoster, 2006), with F. Roy Coad, A History of the Brethren Movement (1968) and Ernest Sandeen, The Roots of Fundamentalism (Chicago, 1970)
sources.note: Sandeen is the key study of dispensationalism's formation. Scofield's later reshaping of Darby's scheme belongs to the following era, not this one.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, 'The growth of voluntary religion' (Bebbington)
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated chapter on the Brethren movement; this is the nearest topical fit.

movements.longDescription: In the late 1820s a handful of dissatisfied Christians in Dublin — among them a dentist, a lawyer and a young Anglican curate named John Nelson Darby — began meeting to break bread together with no ordained clergy, no denominational name and no set liturgy, and assemblies on the same pattern spread through Britain and then the world. Darby also worked out a way of reading the Bible that divided history into distinct dispensations, kept Israel and the church permanently separate, and expected Christ to remove the church before a final tribulation — a scheme almost unknown before him and enormously consequential after. Alongside the theology ran an equally characteristic practice. George Müller ran orphanages in Bristol for thousands of children on the principle of never asking anyone for money and publishing the accounts. In 1848 the movement split over how far assemblies were answerable to one another, into the Open and Exclusive Brethren, and both halves carried on.
movements.teaser: Dublin, England and then the world, 1827 to 1906 — a few people breaking bread without clergy, whose way of reading prophecy went on to shape how millions read the Bible.
voices: John Nelson Darby — former Anglican curate, the movement's dominant mind and the architect of dispensationalism
Anthony Norris Groves — dentist, missionary to Baghdad and India, and the author of the movement's earliest internal criticism of Darby
George Müller — who housed and educated thousands of orphans in Bristol without ever soliciting a donation, and published the books to prove it
Benjamin Wills Newton — the Plymouth leader whose clash with Darby precipitated the 1848 division
J. G. Bellett — one of the original Dublin circle, and its most sympathetic memoirist
movements.legacy: Open and Exclusive assemblies exist worldwide to this day, and Müller's Bristol work continues as a charitable trust with a museum in one of the original orphan houses. But the movement's real reach is elsewhere: Darby's dispensational scheme, packaged in the notes of the Scofield Reference Bible from 1909 and taught in the Bible institutes, became the default end-times framework of American evangelicalism and lies behind most popular prophecy writing and preaching of the last hundred years — read by millions who have never heard of the Brethren.

experienceToday.text: The George Müller Museum, Ashley Down, Bristol — in one of the original orphan houses, telling the story of the 17,000 children who lived there; free entry

movements.name: The Sunday School & Bible-Institute Movement
movements.informalName: The Sunday School and Bible-Institute Movement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a rich institutional record with teachers' and students' memoirs. Its own ecology question — whether this is a tradition, or a set of formation technologies operating inside other traditions — was left standing as a genuine test. Its c. 1900 end was kept and stated as a judgment rather than a default, the entry making no living-continuation claim that would call for an era cap.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally, with teachers' and students' memoirs
movements.relationsSummary: A pair of lay-formation methods that worked at industrial scale, from Robert Raikes's Sunday schools (from 1780) to D. L. Moody's Bible institute model (from 1886).
movements.why: In 1780, a Gloucester newspaper owner named Robert Raikes hired four women to teach the town's factory children to read on their one free day, and publicized the results in his own paper until the idea spread across Britain and America. By the mid-nineteenth century, Sunday schools staffed almost entirely by unpaid women volunteers were teaching literacy alongside religion to millions of working-class children. A century later the same instinct produced the Bible institute — schools like D. L. Moody's in Chicago, opened in 1886, that trained ordinary lay people as evangelists and missionaries in a year or two.
movements.dateRationale: End kept c. 1900 STATED (living:false — no cap claim; round-1900 trio member, judged not defaulted); start 1780 (Raikes) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The founding and institutional layer: Raikes's Gloucester Journal notices (1783-) and correspondence; Sunday School Union (1803-) and American Sunday School Union records (incl. the Mississippi Valley Enterprise, 1830); the Uniform Lesson records (1872)
sources.note: This is lay religious formation carried out at industrial scale, documented in its own institutional paperwork.

sources.work: Teachers' and students' memoirs: teachers' periodicals and memoirs; working-class scholars' recollections in laboring autobiographies; women teachers' predominance as structural fact
sources.note: The students' own voice survives mostly through memoirs written later in life, so treat it as retrospective rather than contemporary.

sources.work: The Bible-institute layer: Moody Bible Institute founding records (1886) with Emma Dryer's founding work and letters; Moody's sermons and correspondence; YMCA and convention records
sources.note: Emma Dryer's role in founding the institute is a woman's institutional founding voice that is only thinly documented.

sources.work: Anne Boylan, Sunday School: The Formation of an American Institution 1790-1880 (Yale, 1988), with Thomas Laqueur, Religion and Respectability (Yale, 1976)
sources.note: Boylan is the American standard and Laqueur the British standard; Laqueur centers the working-class students themselves rather than the institutions.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, 'The growth of voluntary religion' (Bebbington) with ch. 22 (Noll - number verified)
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated chapter on religious education; the Bebbington chapter's exact number could not be confirmed.

movements.longDescription: In 1780 a Gloucester newspaper proprietor named Robert Raikes hired four women to teach the town's factory children to read on Sunday — their one free day — and then publicized the results in his own paper. The idea travelled with extraordinary speed, and by the middle of the nineteenth century Sunday schools were teaching literacy along with religion to millions of working-class children in Britain and America, staffed overwhelmingly by unpaid women volunteers and organized by unions that supplied lessons, prizes and books at industrial scale. A century after Raikes the same instinct produced the Bible institute: schools like D. L. Moody's in Chicago, opened in 1886, that took ordinary lay people rather than university graduates and trained them in a year or two as evangelists, teachers and missionaries. Together they are the machinery by which most ordinary Christians of the industrial age actually learned the faith.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1780 to about 1900 — the machinery by which most ordinary Christians of the industrial age learned to read, and learned the faith.
voices: Robert Raikes — the Gloucester newspaperman who hired the first teachers in 1780 and then advertised the results into a movement
Thomas Stock — the curate who worked with Raikes on the first school and is easily the more forgotten of the two
D. L. Moody — the evangelist whose Chicago institute of 1886 became the model Bible school
Emma Dryer — the educator who did much of the founding work behind Moody's institute, and whose part in it is thinly documented compared with his
movements.legacy: Sunday school became a near-universal feature of Protestant congregational life worldwide and stayed there. The graded, standardized lesson series invented in the 1870s is still the shape of most children's curricula. Historians credit the movement with a substantial share of working-class literacy in nineteenth-century Britain, for many children the only schooling they got. The Bible institutes turned into colleges, and their graduates staffed the twentieth-century missionary agencies, radio ministries and publishing houses that carried evangelical Christianity around the world.

experienceToday.text: Gloucester, England — the city where Raikes started, with St Mary de Crypt church and the surviving schoolroom, and Raikes's own house still standing in the old centre

movements.name: The Student Volunteer Movement & Edinburgh 1910
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on SVM records, volunteers' diaries and letters, and conference reports. A title-and-window line was added at the Freeze so the record reads honestly: the entry is named for Edinburgh 1910, an event sitting outside its own era, inside its one legal boundary crossing.
movements.sourcing: Rich: SVM records, volunteers' diaries and letters, conference reports
movements.relationsSummary: Known by its watchword, "the evangelization of the world in this generation." The 1910 World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh was its summit, and it became the parent of both the modern ecumenical movement and the independent evangelical missionary agencies that followed. It continued seamlessly into the International Missionary Council, founded in October 1921.
movements.why: In the summer of 1886, a hundred students at a Massachusetts conference signed a declaration that they were willing to become foreign missionaries, and over the next thirty years the movement they founded sent roughly twenty thousand young Americans and Britons overseas under the watchword "the evangelization of the world in this generation." Its summit was the 1910 World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh, where two of the few non-Western delegates said the necessary thing to the twelve hundred gathered: V. S. Azariah of India asked for friends rather than masters, and Cheng Jingyi of China asked for one Chinese church free of European denominational divisions.
movements.dateRationale: String aligned; one legal boundary crossing — the entry is NAMED for an event (Edinburgh 1910) inside its legal tail, outside its own era, stated deliberately; start 1886 (Mount Hermon Hundred [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The SVM's own records: the Mount Hermon record (1886), declaration cards, watchword literature, quadrennial convention reports (1891-); Mott, The Evangelization of the World in This Generation (1900)
Volunteers' diaries and letters: candidates' and missionaries' correspondence; women volunteers' letters and diaries; Grace Wilder's origin role
sources.note: Women were the majority of the volunteer force, and the women's missionary movement's own records are central to this history. Grace Wilder's own role, though, is recorded mostly through others' accounts of her, not her own words.

sources.work: Edinburgh 1910's own record: the nine published volumes (Commission reports and proceedings); the non-Western delegates' interventions - Azariah's 'give us friends' address, Cheng Jingyi's unity speech
sources.note: Colonized voices inside the summit, verbatim in the conference's own record — though worth noting how few there were: a handful among 1,200 delegates.

sources.work: Brian Stanley, The World Missionary Conference, Edinburgh 1910 (Eerdmans, 2009), with Michael Parker, The Kingdom of Character (1998)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 34 'Missions and empire, c.1873-1914' (Stanley)
sources.note: Its author, one of the volume's co-editors, works directly on this subject.

movements.longDescription: In the summer of 1886 a hundred students at a conference in Massachusetts signed a declaration that they were willing and desirous to become foreign missionaries, and over the next thirty years the Student Volunteer Movement they founded put something on the order of twenty thousand young Americans and Britons on ships, under the watchword "the evangelization of the world in this generation." Its summit was the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910, where twelve hundred delegates met to plan the work as one enterprise instead of a hundred competing ones. Two of the very few non-Western delegates used their few minutes to say the necessary thing: V. S. Azariah of India asked the room, to its face, for friends rather than masters, and Cheng Jingyi of China told it that the Chinese church wanted to be one church and had no use for European denominational divisions. Both were right, and it took the rest of the century to act on it.
movements.teaser: North America, Britain and the world, 1886 to 1920 — a generation of students who volunteered by the thousand, and the conference where they were told, politely, to let go.
voices: John R. Mott — the movement's organizer and the chairman of Edinburgh 1910, later a Nobel Peace Prize laureate
Robert Wilder — one of the original hundred, who toured the campuses and turned a conference pledge into a movement
Grace Wilder — his sister, whose part in the movement's origins is real and recorded almost entirely through other people
J. H. Oldham — Edinburgh's secretary, whose continuation work turned a conference into an institution
V. S. Azariah — Indian delegate, later the first Indian Anglican bishop, whose Edinburgh address asked Western missionaries for friendship rather than supervision
Cheng Jingyi — Chinese delegate whose short speech for a united, non-denominational Chinese church is the most quoted thing said at the conference
movements.legacy: Edinburgh's continuation committee became the International Missionary Council in 1921 and fed into the World Council of Churches in 1948: the modern ecumenical movement dates its own beginning to that room. The same generation's evangelistic energy went the other way, into the independent missionary agencies that multiplied through the twentieth century, so that one gathering is claimed as an ancestor by two movements that spent the following century largely apart. The Student Volunteer Movement itself never recovered from the First World War and had effectively ended by mid-century.

movements.name: Indonesian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on mission records read with gravity, the Batak church's own records and revival testimonies. Its open-ended present tail was segmented at 1906 under the census's segment discipline, leaving the era-10 segment — the 1965–71 Timor revival and the HKBP's growth — for that era's own gate to create rather than inherited by silence.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: mission records (with gravity), the Batak church's own records, revival testimonies
movements.relationsSummary: Ludwig Nommensen's mission gave rise to the HKBP, among the largest Lutheran bodies on earth. The Timor revival of 1965-71 belongs to the same story. Indonesia is now one of the largest Christian communities in the Muslim-majority world.
movements.why: German missionaries reached the Batak highlands of North Sumatra in 1861, where Ludwig Nommensen worked for more than fifty years, and the church that grew there gave itself a written order in 1881 and is now among the largest Lutheran bodies anywhere in the world. Further west in Java, a teacher known as Kiai Sadrach gathered thousands of followers into congregations that kept Javanese forms and Javanese leadership, which the Dutch missions regarded with deep suspicion at the time. It is now read as the archipelago's clearest early case of Christianity built on local terms.
movements.dateRationale: Present-tail segmented: the era-9 segment caps at 1906 per the census’s segment discipline; the era-10 segment (the 1965-71 Timor revival, HKBP growth) is the A1.E10 gate’s to create; start 1861 (Nommensen [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The Batak church's own records: the HKBP 1881 church order, synod minutes, congregation registers; Batak teachers' and pastors' writings and church press; first evangelists' accounts
sources.note: This is an indigenous church's own institutional record, growing first inside and then beyond the mission that planted it.

sources.work: Mission records WITH gravity: Nommensen's letters and reports (Rheinische Missionsgesellschaft archives, Wuppertal); the Joseph Kam-era Moluccan records; Minahasa mission records
sources.note: This material carries a double filter: it is mission-authored, and it operates inside the Dutch colonial administration even though the mission itself was German.

sources.work: The indigenous-initiative leg: Kiai Sadrach's Javanese communities (c. 1870s-90s) - the mission's hostile-suspicious file AND the community's own practice and continuity
sources.note: This combines the mission's own suspicious file on Sadrach with the community's own practice and continuity - both sides of the record. It is the clearest case in this period of Christianity built on indigenous terms.

sources.work: Revival testimonies: Toba conversion-era and mass-movement testimonies (1880s-1900s, largely through mission transcription); the 1965-71 Timor revival flagged as past this era's window
sources.note: The Toba conversion testimonies survive largely through mission transcription, a filter worth noting. The Timor revival of 1965-71 falls outside this era's time window and belongs to a later period of the same story.

sources.work: Jan Aritonang & Karel Steenbrink (eds.), A History of Christianity in Indonesia (Brill, 2008), with Sutarman S. Partonadi, Sadrach's Community and Its Contextual Roots (Rodopi, 1990)
sources.note: The standard history, written largely by Indonesian scholars, together with the dedicated study recovering Sadrach's community.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8 (chapter assignment hedged): nearest ch. 32 (Francisco, Filipino Christianity) and ch. 34 (Stanley) - both numbers verified
sources.note: This reference volume has no dedicated chapter on Indonesia or the Netherlands Indies; these are the nearest topical fits.

movements.longDescription: Christianity had been present in the eastern Indonesian islands since the Portuguese and the Dutch East India Company, but the churches that matter most today were built in the nineteenth century and, very quickly, by Indonesians. German missionaries reached the Batak highlands of North Sumatra in 1861, where Ludwig Nommensen spent more than fifty years. The church that grew there gave itself a written order in 1881 and is now among the largest Lutheran bodies anywhere in the world. Further west, in Java, a Javanese teacher known as Kiai Sadrach gathered thousands of followers into congregations that kept Javanese forms, Javanese leadership and Javanese ways of teaching. Which the Dutch missions regarded with deep suspicion at the time, and which is now read as the archipelago's clearest early case of Christianity on local terms. Almost everything written about all of this in the period was written by the missions; the churches' own records are what let it be read the other way round.
movements.teaser: Sumatra, Java and the eastern islands, 1861 to 1906 — churches planted by foreign missions and rebuilt, almost at once, on Indonesian terms.
voices: Ludwig Ingwer Nommensen — German missionary among the Toba Batak from 1862 until his death in 1918, buried at Sigumpar in North Sumatra
Kiai Sadrach — Javanese teacher who built a large network of congregations on Javanese terms, and was distrusted by the Dutch missionaries for it
Joseph Kam — the Dutch pastor whose work in the Moluccas from 1815 revived the older island churches left over from the Company era

The Batak evangelists and teachers — the local preachers who did most of the actual spread of the church into the highlands, recorded in the church's own registers rather than in the mission's published accounts
movements.legacy: Indonesia now has one of the largest Christian populations of any Muslim-majority country in the world, numbering in the tens of millions, and the Batak church founded in this window counts several million members on its own. A fact that would surprise most people's mental map of where Lutherans live. The universities, schools and hospitals that grew out of the mission remain, one of them carrying Nommensen's name. The great Timor revival of 1965 to 1971, one of the largest recorded in the twentieth century, belongs to the next chapter of the same story.

experienceToday.text: The Batak Christian Protestant Church (HKBP), North Sumatra — the church founded in this window, still one of the largest in Indonesia and a member of the World Council of Churches

movements.name: Northeast India Revivals & the Mar Thoma Reform
movements.informalName: The Northeast India Revivals and the Mar Thoma Reform
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on church records, revival accounts and hymnody in local languages. Its present tail was segmented at 1906 on the same discipline applied to the Indonesian entry, and a scope note was recorded naming what it does not carry: this entry holds the reform wing of 1889, while the Malankara Orthodox majority after the court verdict has no row — a named absence left for a later gate, with the backward 1665–1836 gap likewise disclosed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: church records, revival accounts, hymnody in local languages
movements.relationsSummary: The Mar Thoma Church is an ancient-rite church that added evangelical reform, continuing the St. Thomas Christian tradition of Kerala. After the 1889 court verdict split the community, the larger Malankara Orthodox (Jacobite) body carried on as a separate tradition. Independent revivals in the Khasi, Mizo and Naga hills, meanwhile, made those regions among the most thoroughly Christian on earth.
movements.why: In 1836 a seminary teacher named Abraham Malpan revised Kerala's ancient Syriac liturgy into Malayalam, keeping the old rite but reforming it from within. A thousand miles away, revival swept the Khasi, Mizo and Naga hills and gave those languages their first written hymns, composed rather than translated.
movements.dateRationale: Present-tail segmented: the era-9 segment caps at 1906 (the Khasi revival 1905-06 at the boundary [S]; the Mizo revivals are era 10’s); the era-10 segment is the A1.E10 gate’s to create; start 1836 (Abraham Malpan’s reform liturgy [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The Mar Thoma reform's own documents: Abraham Malpan's revised liturgy (1836ff.); the reformers' 1836 memorial; Mathews Mar Athanasius's records; synod records and service books; the Travancore Royal Court litigation record (to 1889)
sources.note: This is an ancient-rite church's own liturgical act of reform, documented in its own texts. The court record is adversarial legal material, not the church's own voice.

sources.work: The hill revivals' own record: Khasi revival (1905-06, Mairang) and Mizo revival (1906ff.) accounts; hymnody in local languages (Khasi and Mizo revival hymns; lengkhawm zai); indigenous evangelists' and converts' accounts
sources.note: This hymnody was composed directly in Khasi and Mizo, not translated - the revivals' own theological voice in their own languages. The accounts survive partly self-recorded and partly through mission transcription.

sources.work: Church records WITH mission filters: Welsh Calvinistic Methodist records (Khasi/Mizo hills); American Baptist records (Naga hills, Assam); presbytery/assembly and association minutes
sources.note: The earliest records here are missionary-authored, though indigenous leaders had taken over most church governance by the end of this period. The wider colonial administrative context - the Inner Line regulations and military expeditions into the hills - shapes this record.

sources.work: Robert Eric Frykenberg, Christianity in India: From Beginnings to the Present (OUP, 2008), with Frederick S. Downs, History of Christianity in India vol. V pt. 5: North East India (CHAI, 1992)
sources.note: Frykenberg is the standard covering both wings of this story; Downs is the standard regional study.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 29 'Christians and religious traditions in the Indian empire' (Frykenberg)
sources.note: This chapter gives direct coverage of both wings of this story.

movements.longDescription: In 1836 a teacher at the seminary in Kottayam, Abraham Malpan, revised the Syriac liturgy that Kerala's St Thomas Christians had used for centuries — cutting what he judged unscriptural and putting the service into Malayalam so ordinary people could follow it. The reform divided the ancient community, and after decades of argument and litigation a royal court verdict in 1889 separated the two parties for good. The reforming wing carried on as the Mar Thoma Syrian Church, an Eastern church that kept its ancient rite and its evangelical conscience together, while the larger body continued as the Malankara church. A thousand miles to the northeast, in the Khasi, Mizo and Naga hills, small congregations planted by Welsh and American missions caught fire on their own. Village preachers and singers carried revival through the hills, most famously the Khasi awakening of 1905-06, and hill languages received their first written hymnody out of the same process, composed rather than translated.
movements.teaser: Kerala and the hill country of northeast India, 1836 to 1906 — an ancient Syriac church reforming its own liturgy at one end of India, and hill villages singing their first hymns in their own languages at the other.
voices: Abraham Malpan — the Kottayam seminary teacher whose 1836 revision of the Syriac liturgy began the Mar Thoma reform
Mathews Mar Athanasius — the reform party's metropolitan, consecrated in 1842, who carried it through its first decades of conflict
Thomas Jones — the Welsh missionary who gave the Khasi language its written form in the 1840s
Edwin W. Clark — the American Baptist who, with Naga converts, began the mission in the Naga hills in 1872
movements.legacy: The Mar Thoma Syrian Church is still here, with dioceses in India and among Indian communities abroad, and its annual Maramon Convention on the sandy bed of the Pamba river remains one of Asia's largest Christian gatherings. The hill churches did more than survive. Mizoram and Nagaland are today among the most thoroughly Christian regions on earth, Presbyterian and Baptist respectively, and the revival hymnody composed in those years is still what their congregations sing.

movements.name: Orthodoxy after 1821 — the National Churches
movements.informalName: The Millet Church Breaks into Nations
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: the Greek autocephaly acts (1833; Tomos of 1850, verified), the Exarchate firman (1870, verified), the 1872 council acta (verified); parish texture thinner
movements.relationsSummary: The hanging of Patriarch Gregory V in 1821 opened the break-up of a single Ottoman-era Orthodox community into national churches: Greek autocephaly (declared 1833, recognized by the Tomos of 1850), the Bulgarian Exarchate (1870), and recognition for Serbia (1879) and Romania (1885). A council in 1872 condemned phyletism, organizing churches by nationality rather than place, even as the practice went on spreading.
movements.why: The Greek revolt of 1821 began with the hanging of the Patriarch of Constantinople at his own gate, and by the century's end Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia and Romania had each won their own self-governing church. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned the practice of organizing churches by nationality rather than by place, even as it kept happening anyway.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1821 (Gregory V hanged — seamless to VII.18’s legal tail); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Under Ottoman rule the Orthodox of the Balkans had been governed as a single religious community answering to the Patriarch of Constantinople. The Greek revolt of 1821 — which opened with the hanging of Patriarch Gregory V at the gate of his own residence — broke that arrangement apart, and as each new nation won independence its church claimed self-government. Greece declared its church self-governing in 1833 and was formally recognized by Constantinople in 1850, Bulgaria won an imperial decree creating a national exarchate in 1870, Serbia was recognized in 1879 and Romania in 1885. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned phyletism — organizing the church by ethnic nation rather than by place — even as national churches went on multiplying anyway. What the century produced was not one church breaking up so much as a family of them, each with its own synod, its own language of worship, and its own claim on a people.
movements.teaser: Greece, the Balkans and Constantinople, 1821 to 1906 — Orthodoxy under one Ottoman roof breaking into national churches, each new nation claiming a church of its own.
voices: Gregory V of Constantinople — the patriarch hanged at the gate of his own residence in 1821, whose death opened the century
Theoklitos Pharmakidis — the churchman who argued for and drafted the 1833 declaration of Greek self-government
Konstantinos Oikonomos — his opponent, who defended the Patriarchate's authority and the older canonical order
Antim I — first exarch of the Bulgarian Exarchate created in 1870
movements.legacy: These are the churches that make up Orthodoxy today: the Church of Greece and the Bulgarian, Serbian and Romanian patriarchates all date their modern independence to this century, and the pattern they set — a self-governing church per nation — became the normal shape of the Orthodox world. So did the argument the 1872 council started. Wherever Orthodox jurisdictions overlap on the same ground, as they do throughout the diaspora, the question of whether a church is defined by place or by people comes straight back.

movements.name: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century
movements.informalName: The Church of Pius IX and Leo XIII
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: the acts of Vatican I, whose definitions were promulgated on 18 July 1870, the encyclical corpus (Mirari Vos, the Syllabus, Rerum Novarum), and the literature of the era's devotional revolution.
movements.relationsSummary: From Gregory XVI to Leo XIII, this era saw Pius IX define the Immaculate Conception in 1854, issue the Syllabus of Errors, and see the First Vatican Council define papal infallibility, followed by the end of the Papal States. Leo XIII faced the Kulturkampf in Germany and issued Rerum Novarum. The century also saw the Marian apparitions at Lourdes and a broader wave of devotion to Rome, alongside the growth of missionary Catholicism, the Catholic immigrant church in the United States, and the restoration of the Catholic hierarchy in England in 1850.
movements.why: Pius IX spent decades cataloguing what he saw as the errors of the modern age, then in July 1870 saw the First Vatican Council declare the pope infallible, just weeks before Italian troops ended a thousand years of papal rule over Rome. His successor Leo XIII turned the church toward the modern world instead, declaring in 1891 that workers had a right to a living wage and to organize.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.19); end 1906 era cap; Vatican I 18 Jul 1870 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Between the fall of Napoleon and the eve of the First World War, the Catholic Church lost a state and gained a papacy. Gregory XVI and then Pius IX met the liberal century head-on: Pius defined the Immaculate Conception in 1854, catalogued the errors of the age in the Syllabus of 1864, and in July 1870 saw the First Vatican Council define papal infallibility. Weeks before Italian troops entered Rome and ended the Papal States. Stripped of territory, the papacy grew in reach instead: bishops and ordinary Catholics looked to Rome as never before, new congregations of sisters and brothers staffed schools and hospitals across the world, and mass devotion gathered around Marian apparitions like Lourdes in 1858. Under Leo XIII the church that had spent decades condemning the modern world began to negotiate with it, most consequentially in Rerum Novarum (1891), which put the church on the side of a worker's right to a living wage and to organize.
movements.teaser: Rome and the Catholic world, 1815 to 1906 — a papacy that lost its last territory in the same weeks it was declared infallible, and grew in reach as it shrank on the map.
voices: Pius IX — the longest-reigning pope, who defined the Immaculate Conception, issued the Syllabus of Errors, and lost the Papal States
Leo XIII — his successor, who opened the church's engagement with industrial society in Rerum Novarum (1891)
Bernadette Soubirous — the Pyrenean girl whose 1858 visions made Lourdes the century's great pilgrimage site
John Henry Newman — the English convert whose theology of conscience and of doctrinal development ran alongside, and sometimes against, the century's Roman current
Nicholas Wiseman — first archbishop of Westminster after the Catholic hierarchy was restored in England in 1850
movements.legacy: This is the Catholic Church still recognizably in place — a worldwide body governed from Rome, with the papacy at its centre in a way earlier centuries would not have recognized. Vatican I's definition remains binding doctrine; Rerum Novarum founded the tradition of Catholic social teaching that every pope since has extended; Lourdes still receives millions of pilgrims a year. The century also left a fracture line, in the Catholics who could not accept 1870 and became the Old Catholics, and a set of questions the church would only take up again at the Second Vatican Council.

movements.name: The Victorian Church of England
movements.informalName: The Established Church of the Long Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich: the parties' own publications, Essays and Reviews (1860), records of the Gorham case, documentation of the 1867 Lambeth Conference, and parish-revival records.
movements.relationsSummary: The Oxford Movement was a renewal movement within this church. The era was defined by party divisions between evangelicals, high churchmen and broad churchmen, a wider crisis of faith, and the first Lambeth Conference in 1867, when the church's overseas missions became a worldwide Communion.
movements.why: Evangelical, high church and broad church parties fought so hard over what the Church of England should believe that their quarrels went to court: a case over infant baptism in 1850, and prosecutions that put clergymen in prison over candles and vestments. By 1867 the church's overseas missions had produced so many bishops that the first Lambeth Conference had to be called just to hold them together.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.20); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Church of England entered the nineteenth century as a comfortable establishment and left it a contested one. Three parties argued for its soul. Evangelicals who had inherited the awakening's fervour and its campaigns against slavery and squalor, high churchmen who rediscovered the church's catholic inheritance, and broad churchmen who wanted room for the new biblical criticism and the new geology. The quarrels went to law: the Gorham case of 1850 over what baptism does, the storm over the essayists of 1860 who applied critical methods to Scripture, ritual prosecutions that put clergymen in prison over vestments and candles. Underneath the controversies the church rebuilt itself, in thousands of new buildings and slum parishes at home and in a mission network abroad that by 1867 had produced enough overseas bishops that a first Lambeth Conference had to be called to hold them together.
movements.teaser: England and its empire, 1815 to 1906 — an established church arguing with itself over Rome, over Darwin and over the Bible, while quietly turning into a worldwide communion.
voices: Charles Simeon — the Cambridge evangelical whose long ministry shaped a generation of parish clergy
Lord Shaftesbury — the evangelical layman behind the century's factory, mining and child-labour reforms
Samuel Wilberforce — bishop of Oxford, the era's great diocesan organizer and Darwin's most famous public sparring partner
Frederick Denison Maurice — theologian of the broad church and of Christian socialism, dismissed from his professorship over his view of eternal punishment
John William Colenso — bishop of Natal, whose critical work on the Pentateuch and defence of his Zulu converts split the colonial church
Charles Longley — archbishop of Canterbury, who convened the first Lambeth Conference in 1867
movements.legacy: The Church of England is still established in England, and the conference it improvised in 1867 became the standing instrument of an Anglican Communion of tens of millions across the world. The parties formed in this century are still recognizable as evangelical, Anglo-Catholic and liberal, and so are their arguments — only now conducted across the whole Communion rather than inside one country's church. The century also left the physical church most English people picture: Victorian gothic parish buildings, surpliced choirs and hymnbooks, all of them inventions of this period rather than inheritances from before it.

movements.name: The Russian Church — the Synodal Century
movements.informalName: The Church of Filaret and Pobedonostsev
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich institutionally: Filaret's catechism, the Synodal Bible (finished 1876), synodal records, missionary-society archives, and the parish writings of John of Kronstadt.
movements.relationsSummary: Governed under Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow and, later, the state-appointed ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev. Sent missions to the Altai peoples and to Japan (from 1861, under Nikolai), and reached the 1905 toleration edict that opened the way to the council that restored the patriarchate. The Optina elders' renewal movement grew within this church, and Alaska was one of its missions. It stood in tension with the separate Old Believer Belokrinitsa hierarchy, founded in 1846, and with the evangelical Stundist movement that broke from it.
movements.why: For a century Russia's church had no patriarch of its own, governed instead by a lay official answering to the tsar. Metropolitan Filaret spent decades pushing through a Russian-language Bible against long resistance, finished in 1876, while later the ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev used the same church to enforce religious uniformity on Old Believers, Eastern Catholics and evangelicals alike.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.21); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: For this whole century the Russian Orthodox Church had no patriarch. It was governed by a Holy Synod whose chief lay officer, the ober-procurator, answered to the tsar — an arrangement that produced both an immense institution and a cramped one. Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow gave Russia its standard catechism and pressed for decades for a Bible in modern Russian, finished in 1876 over long resistance. Missions went out to the Altai peoples, to Alaska and to Japan. Monasteries and their elders drew crowds, and a parish priest, John of Kronstadt, became the most sought-after confessor in the empire. But under Konstantin Pobedonostsev, ober-procurator for a quarter-century, the church was also the instrument of a policy of religious uniformity that pressed hard on Old Believers, Eastern Catholics and evangelicals alike. When toleration was finally decreed in 1905, the church immediately began preparing the council that would give it back its own head.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1815 to 1906 — a church with no patriarch, run by a lay official of the tsar, that produced a Bible, a missionary empire and a famous parish priest while waiting a century to govern itself again.
voices: Filaret (Drozdov) of Moscow — metropolitan for nearly half a century, author of the church's catechism and champion of the Russian Bible
Makary (Glukharev) — founder of the Altai mission, who translated Scripture into the languages of Siberian peoples
Nikolai (Kasatkin) of Japan — sent to Hakodate in 1861, he built a Japanese Orthodox church staffed by Japanese clergy
John of Kronstadt — the parish priest whose eucharistic preaching and charity drew the whole empire to a naval town
Konstantin Pobedonostsev — the lay ober-procurator whose long tenure defined the era's policy of religious uniformity
movements.legacy: The Bible Filaret fought for is still the Russian Orthodox Church's standard translation, and the missionary churches begun in this period — in Japan, in Alaska — are still there. Its deepest legacy is the council it spent the century waiting for. The preparatory work of 1905-06 became the Moscow Council of 1917-18, which restored the patriarchate just as the revolution arrived that would try to destroy it.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity — the Zartonk Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: the text of the 1863 Constitution itself, National Assembly records, and documents from the Evangelical split.
movements.relationsSummary: The Zartonk century produced the Armenian National Constitution of 1863, which gave lay delegates power to limit the Patriarch's authority. Converts of American missionaries were expelled from the Apostolic Church and organized as the Armenian Evangelical Church in 1846, recognized by the Ottoman state as a separate Protestant community in 1850. The century ended in the Hamidian massacres of 1894-96.
movements.why: Because the Ottoman state treated the Armenian church as the legal body of the whole nation, a century of awakening in language, schools and printing ran largely through it. Its 1863 National Constitution gave lay delegates a formal check on the Patriarch's own authority, an unusual arrangement that outlived the massacres of 1894-96 that closed the century in blood.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.24); end 1906 era cap RULED over the 1915 branch — 1906-1915 left to era 10 (IX.27 receives) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Zartonk — awakening — is what Armenians call their nineteenth century. A revival of language, schools, printing and civic life carried largely inside the church, because under Ottoman rule the church was the nation's legal body. Its central document is the Armenian National Constitution of 1863, which seated lay delegates in a national assembly and limited what the Patriarch of Constantinople could do alone, an unusual experiment in giving a laity formal power over its own hierarchy. The century also divided the community: converts of American missionaries were expelled from the Apostolic Church and organized as the Armenian Evangelical Church in 1846, recognized by the Ottoman state as a separate Protestant community in 1850, while an Armenian Catholic patriarchate continued alongside. And it ended in blood — the Hamidian massacres of 1894-96 killed tens of thousands and emptied whole districts.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, Anatolia and the Caucasus, 1815 to 1906 — a national awakening carried by a church, which wrote its people a constitution and then watched the massacres begin.
voices: Mkrtich Khrimian, called Hayrik — editor, bishop, patriarch of Constantinople and later catholicos, the era's great popular voice for the Armenian peasantry
Nerses Varzhapetian — patriarch of Constantinople, who took the Armenian case to the Congress of Berlin in 1878
Grigor Odian — among the young Constantinople intellectuals who drafted the Armenian National Constitution of 1863
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church remains the national church of Armenia and of a diaspora this century's emigrations began. The Armenian Evangelical Church founded in 1846 and the Armenian Catholic Church are both still here, small and continuous. The habit of lay representation written into the 1863 constitution survived into the Apostolic Church's later governance. And the awakening's institutions — its schools, presses and newspapers — carried a national literature and a national self-understanding that the catastrophe of the following decade would scatter across the world but not extinguish.

movements.name: The Old Catholic Churches — Utrecht to the Union
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Declaration of Utrecht (1889), Döllinger's writings, and the churches' own synodal records.
movements.relationsSummary: Formed when German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics rejected the First Vatican Council's definition of papal infallibility. Ignaz von Döllinger was excommunicated in 1871, and Utrecht consecrated Joseph Hubert Reinkens as the first bishop of the German Old Catholics in 1873. In 1889 five bishops signed the Declaration of Utrecht, founding the Union of Utrecht.
movements.why: When German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics refused the pope's new claim to infallibility in 1870, an old Dutch church at Utrecht, out of communion with Rome since an eighteenth-century dispute but still holding valid bishops, consecrated one of their own. The five bishops who signed the 1889 Declaration of Utrecht professed the faith of the undivided church of the first thousand years, then dropped required celibacy for priests and put the liturgy into the language of the people.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 RULED over the 1870 formation-event branch (segment continuity with VII.25; the pre-1870 Utrecht line carried, not a head-gap); Declaration of Utrecht 24 Sep 1889 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: There had been a small church at Utrecht out of communion with Rome since an eighteenth-century quarrel over Jansenism left it electing its own archbishops. It stayed a Dutch curiosity until 1870, when the First Vatican Council defined papal infallibility and a body of German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics — professors, priests and laypeople, with the church historian Ignaz von Dollinger at their head — refused to accept it. Excommunicated, they needed bishops, and Utrecht had them: Joseph Hubert Reinkens was consecrated for the German Old Catholics in 1873 by a bishop of that line. In 1889 five bishops signed the Declaration of Utrecht, binding these churches into a union that professed the faith of the undivided church of the first thousand years and rejected the papal claims of 1870. And then went on to drop compulsory celibacy for clergy and to put the liturgy into the language of the people.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland, 1815 to 1906 — Catholics who could not accept the pope's 1870 infallibility, and an old Dutch church that had bishops to spare.
voices: Ignaz von Dollinger — the Munich church historian whose refusal of the 1870 definition made him the movement's intellectual founder; excommunicated in 1871
Joseph Hubert Reinkens — first bishop of the German Old Catholics, consecrated by the see of Utrecht in 1873
Hermanus Heykamp — bishop of Deventer, the Utrecht-line bishop who consecrated him
Eduard Herzog — first bishop of the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland
movements.legacy: The Union of Utrecht is still there: a small communion of national churches in the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Poland and the Czech lands. Its most consequential work turned out to be ecumenical. The Bonn conferences Dollinger convened in the 1870s were among the first modern meetings of Old Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox theologians at one table, and in 1931 the Old Catholics and the Church of England entered full communion by the Bonn Agreement — one of the earliest such agreements between separated Western churches, and a model for many since.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Methodism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: connexional minutes, the Primitive Methodist magazine, documents from the 1844 split, and records from the 1881 ecumenical conference.
movements.relationsSummary: British Wesleyan Methodism consolidated into a settled denomination. The Primitive Methodists formed after the 1807 Mow Cop camp meeting, becoming a settled connexion by 1811-12, known for their women itinerant preachers and working-class base. In America, the Methodist family split into northern and southern churches in 1844 over slavery, after Black Methodists had already formed their own churches, the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816 and the AME Zion Church in 1821.
movements.why: Methodism split repeatedly as it grew. In Britain, working-class converts who found the Wesleyan church too respectable formed the Primitive Methodists after an 1807 camp meeting, sending women itinerant preachers into the pit villages, while in America, Black Methodists refused equal standing built their own churches, the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816 and the AME Zion Church in 1821, years before slavery split the wider American church in two.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.5); end 1906 era cap; Primitive Methodists (Mow Cop 1807, connexion 1811-12 [S]) A5 inside (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: A movement that began as a society inside the Church of England spent the nineteenth century becoming a worldwide family of churches, and dividing as it grew. In Britain the Wesleyan connexion consolidated into a respectable denomination, and those who found it too respectable went their own way: the Primitive Methodists, born at an open-air camp meeting on Mow Cop in 1807 and a settled connexion by 1811-12, took the gospel into the pit villages behind working-class preachers, a striking number of them women. In America, Methodism became the largest Protestant body in the country and then split down the middle over slavery in 1844 into northern and southern churches that would not reunite for nearly a century. Black Methodists, refused equal standing, had already built churches of their own — the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816, the AME Zion Church in 1821. By 1881 the family was scattered enough that it needed a world conference simply to speak to itself.
movements.teaser: Britain, North America and the mission fields, 1815 to 1906 — a revival grown into a worldwide church, divided by class at one end of the Atlantic and by slavery at the other.
voices: Hugh Bourne and William Clowes — the Staffordshire preachers whose 1807 camp meeting on Mow Cop began the Primitive Methodists
Jabez Bunting — the administrator who shaped, and centralized, British Wesleyan Methodism for a generation
Richard Allen — founding bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816
James Varick — first superintendent of the AME Zion Church
William Taylor — the itinerant preacher, later missionary bishop, whose work ran from the California goldfields to India and Africa
movements.legacy: Methodism became one of the largest Protestant families in the world: the United Methodist Church and British Methodism, the AME, AME Zion and CME churches, and Methodist churches across Africa and Asia all descend from this century's expansion. Its machinery outlasted it too — the class meeting, the itinerant preacher, the connexional conference. So did its conviction that holiness is meant to be practical and available now, which passed through the Holiness movement into Pentecostalism and from there into a very large share of world Christianity.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Baptists
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate to rich: association minutes, Spurgeon's own writings, and the Southern Baptist Convention's 1845 founding documents.
movements.relationsSummary: Spurgeon preached to thousands weekly at the Metropolitan Tabernacle. The Southern Baptist Convention formed in 1845 out of the split over slavery. Landmarkism traced an unbroken Baptist succession back to the apostles, and the Down-Grade Controversy divided British Baptists late in the century.
movements.why: Baptists never agreed to be governed from anywhere, yet by the century's end Charles Haddon Spurgeon alone was preaching to thousands weekly and selling printed sermons in the millions. Late in life he broke with fellow Baptists over what he called the Down-Grade, certain they were quietly abandoning doctrines they had been ordained to preach, in the same decades that saw American Baptists split in 1845 after Southern churches were refused a slaveholding missionary appointment.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.16); end 1906 era cap; distinctiveness caveat on the record (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Baptists began the century as a scattering of self-governing congregations and ended it as one of the largest Protestant families in the English-speaking world, without ever agreeing to be governed from anywhere. In London, Charles Haddon Spurgeon preached weekly to thousands at the Metropolitan Tabernacle and published sermons that sold in the millions. Late in life he broke with the Baptist Union over what he called the Down-Grade, convinced his fellow ministers were quietly giving up the doctrines they had been ordained to preach. In America the family split in 1845, when Baptists in the South, refused a slaveholding missionary appointment, formed the Southern Baptist Convention. Running alongside was Landmarkism, which held that only true Baptist congregations were churches at all and traced an unbroken Baptist succession back to the apostles.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1815 to 1906 — congregations that answered to no bishop, arguing their way into becoming one of Protestantism's largest families.
voices: Charles Haddon Spurgeon — London's Metropolitan Tabernacle preacher, whose printed sermons reached a worldwide readership
James Robinson Graves — the editor and controversialist who gave Landmarkism its shape
William Bullein Johnson — first president of the Southern Baptist Convention, formed at Augusta, Georgia, in 1845
John Clifford — the Baptist Union leader who stood on the other side of Spurgeon in the Down-Grade dispute
movements.legacy: The bodies formed in this century are still the shape of Baptist life. The Southern Baptist Convention became the largest Protestant denomination in the United States, and the Baptist Union of Great Britain and its counterparts continue. Spurgeon's sermons have never gone out of print, and the Down-Grade Controversy became a template for the fundamentalist-modernist battles of the century after. The era also produced two of Baptist history's most consequential lines: the Black Baptist churches of America, and the overseas mission movement that Baptists largely began.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Quakerism — the Separations
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich for the separations: both sides kept their own minutes and epistles. The overlap with abolition and the women's rights movement is documented in Friends' own records.
movements.relationsSummary: The Hicksite separation of 1827–28 was the defining split of the century for the Society of Friends. It was followed by a further division between the evangelical Gurneyite and conservative Wilburite wings, and by a pastoral-system revival that introduced planned worship and paid ministers to part of the movement.
movements.why: Friends split first in 1827-28 over Elias Hicks' teaching that the Inward Light, not the Bible or a doctrine of atonement, stood at the heart of the faith, then split again between evangelical and conservative wings. Out of the evangelical stream came something Quakers had never had before: revival meetings, planned worship, and paid pastors, so that by the century's end some meetings sat in silence while others sang hymns and listened to sermons.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.1); end 1906 era cap; the Hicksite separation 1827-28 [S] is the century event (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Society of Friends came into the nineteenth century intact and left it in pieces. In 1827-28 the American yearly meetings tore apart over Elias Hicks, a Long Island farmer and travelling minister who held that the Inward Light, not the Bible or a doctrine of atonement, was the heart of the faith. Those who followed him and those who opposed him became separate bodies meeting in separate houses. Within twenty years the evangelical side divided again, between followers of the English banker-minister Joseph John Gurney and the conservative John Wilbur. Out of the Gurneyite stream came something Friends had never had — revival meetings, planned worship and paid pastors. So that by the century's end some Quaker meetings still sat in silence while others sang hymns and listened to a sermon. Through all of it Friends kept up the work they were best known for: abolition, prison reform, and the women's rights movement several of them helped to launch.
movements.teaser: North America and Britain, 1815 to 1906 — a people known for silence dividing three ways over what the silence was for, while leading the fights against slavery and for women's rights.
voices: Elias Hicks — the travelling minister whose preaching on the Inward Light precipitated the separation of 1827-28
Joseph John Gurney — the English evangelical Friend whose teaching shaped the largest branch of American Quakerism
John Wilbur — his conservative opponent, whose followers kept to the older quietist discipline
Lucretia Mott — Hicksite minister and abolitionist, a principal organizer of the 1848 Seneca Falls women's rights convention
Levi Coffin — the Indiana Friend whose house was one of the busiest stations on the Underground Railroad
movements.legacy: All three streams are still here: the pastoral, evangelical Friends who are now the majority of Quakers worldwide — most of them in Kenya and Latin America. The unprogrammed liberal meetings, and the small conservative bodies that kept the older ways. Friends' public work outlasted their divisions. The peace testimony survived the separations intact, the relief agencies that grew from it were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947, and the Quaker practice of seeking the sense of a meeting rather than counting votes has been borrowed far outside the Society.

movements.name: American Unitarianism & Universalism — the Consolidations
movements.statusWord: Floor Question carried — VII.27’s two-thread separation re-carried (Unitarian beyondFloor at own-confession strength; Universalist arguably floor-clean), the Transcendentalist third thread named Outside-A4-adjacent (Era 9 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: Channing's 1819 sermon, the AUA's founding in 1825, Emerson's 1838 Divinity School Address, and convention records from both movements.
movements.floorNote: Two different questions here, and they get different answers. The Unitarian side placed itself outside the Nicene creed's confession of the Trinity by its own explicit teaching — that is the movement's own account of itself, not an outsider's charge. The Universalist side is a separate case: its defining claim was about the scope of salvation rather than about the doctrine of God, and much of it would sit comfortably inside Nicene bounds. A third strain, the Transcendentalists, moved past the question of Christian doctrine altogether.
movements.relationsSummary: William Ellery Channing's 1819 Baltimore sermon named and defined the movement, and the American Unitarian Association organized on 25 May 1825. The Universalists built their own conventions on a separate track. A third strain, the Transcendentalists, pushed past Christian doctrine altogether.
movements.why: The Universalists built their movement on a single conviction, that God would in the end save everyone, while the Unitarians organized around William Ellery Channing's 1819 sermon and an explicit rejection of the Trinity. A generation later, Ralph Waldo Emerson pushed further still, leaving the pulpit to tell Harvard's divinity students in 1838 to seek religion in intuition and nature rather than historical revelation.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1819 (Channing’s Baltimore sermon [S]; AUA organized 25 May 1825, verified); end 1906 register-cap convention (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Two movements that had grown up separately in New England spent this century turning themselves into organized denominations. In 1819 William Ellery Channing preached an ordination sermon in Baltimore that gave liberal Congregationalists both a name and a platform, and in 1825 they founded the American Unitarian Association. The Universalists, who taught that God would in the end save everyone, built their own conventions on a separate track. Within a generation the Unitarian side produced a third thing it had not expected. Ralph Waldo Emerson left the ministry and told Harvard's divinity students in 1838 to look for religion in intuition and nature rather than historical revelation, and the Transcendentalists carried that further than most of their elders wanted to go. What held the movements together was less a shared creed than a shared refusal of creeds, along with a strong practical bent — toward schools, prisons, asylums and abolition.
movements.teaser: New England and the mid-Atlantic, 1819 to 1906 — liberal churches that made a principle of having no creed, and organized themselves anyway.
voices: William Ellery Channing — whose 1819 Baltimore sermon named and defined American Unitarianism
Hosea Ballou — the Universalist preacher whose Treatise on Atonement (1805) shaped the movement's theology
Ralph Waldo Emerson — Unitarian minister turned essayist, whose 1838 Divinity School Address broke with historical Christianity
Theodore Parker — the radical Unitarian preacher and abolitionist who pushed the movement's boundaries hardest
Dorothea Dix — the Unitarian reformer whose campaigns transformed the treatment of the mentally ill
movements.legacy: Both bodies survived, and in 1961 merged into the Unitarian Universalist Association, still a functioning denomination in North America. Their wider mark is out of proportion to their numbers. The Transcendentalists' essays became a permanent part of American literature, and the causes the movement threw itself into — abolition, public education, humane treatment of prisoners and the mentally ill. Long outlived the theological arguments that produced them.

movements.name: The Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church — Polotsk to Galicia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the acts of the Synod of Polotsk (1839), Galician diocesan records, and Sheptytsky's early writings.
movements.relationsSummary: The Synod of Polotsk in 1839 dissolved the union with Rome across the Russian Empire, transferring roughly a million and a half people to Russian Orthodoxy; the Chełm eparchy followed in 1875. The church survived only under Austrian rule in Galicia, where it became the institutional engine of Ukrainian national life, especially under Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky from 1900. It stood in natural tension with the Russian Orthodox Church, which absorbed the dissolved dioceses.
movements.why: At the Synod of Polotsk in 1839, bishops declared their church reunited with Russian Orthodoxy and roughly a million and a half Eastern-rite Catholics were transferred by decree; a further eparchy followed in 1875, some of it by force. Under Austrian rule in Galicia the church survived instead, its priests doubling as the schoolteachers, editors and cooperative organizers of a Ukrainian people who had almost no other leadership of their own.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.28); end 1906 era cap; Synod of Polotsk 12 Feb 1839 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Millions of Belarusians and Ukrainians worshipped in the Byzantine rite while in communion with Rome, an arrangement dating from a union of 1596. In the Russian Empire it was abolished by decree. At the Synod of Polotsk in February 1839, bishops led by Joseph Semashko declared their church reunited with Russian Orthodoxy, and roughly a million and a half people were transferred with a stroke of the pen. The remaining eparchy of Chelm followed in 1875, with resistance in some villages broken by force. What survived did so under Austrian rule in Galicia, where the Greek Catholic Church became not only a church but the institutional backbone of Ukrainian national life. Its clergy the schoolteachers, editors and co-operative organizers of a people who had almost no other leadership. At the turn of the century Andrey Sheptytsky took the metropolitan see of Lviv and began the long tenure that would carry the church through everything the next fifty years brought.
movements.teaser: Belarus, Ukraine and Austrian Galicia, 1815 to 1906 — an Eastern church in communion with Rome dissolved by decree in one empire and turned into a nation's backbone in the other.
voices: Joseph Semashko — the bishop who engineered the Synod of Polotsk in 1839 and led his church into the Russian Orthodox Church
Andrey Sheptytsky — metropolitan of Lviv from the turn of the century, who made the Galician church a national institution
Markiyan Shashkevych — the Greek Catholic priest and poet whose writing helped begin the Ukrainian literary revival in Galicia
The villagers of Pratulin — thirteen Greek Catholics killed in 1874 for refusing to surrender their church, later beatified as martyrs
movements.legacy: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church is the largest Eastern Catholic church in the world today, and everything it survived afterwards — Soviet liquidation in 1946, four decades underground, its re-emergence in 1989. Rested on the Galician base built in this century. In the lands where the union was dissolved by decree, it never came back. The church's habit of carrying a national culture as well as a liturgy, formed here, is still one of the most distinctive things about it.

movements.name: Philippine Catholicism — Gomburza to the Aglipayan Schism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: secularization-era records, documentation of the 1872 Gomburza executions, records from the church question during the Revolution, and the Iglesia Filipina Independiente's own founding texts.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of the secularization controversy and the 1872 Gomburza executions, which fed directly into the Philippine independence movement. The Iglesia Filipina Independiente was proclaimed in 1902 as the Spanish colonial-era church question came to a head, and it later adopted a trinitarian Declaration of Faith in 1947.
movements.why: The 1872 garrotting of three priests, Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, remembered together as Gomburza, did more to fuel the independence movement than their campaign for Filipino-run parishes ever had; Jose Rizal dedicated his second novel to their memory. Three decades later a labor organizer, Isabelo de los Reyes, proclaimed an independent Philippine church and put the former revolutionary chaplain Gregorio Aglipay at its head.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.29); end 1906 era cap; the Aglipayan proclamation 1902 [S] in-window (its doctrinal drift is era 10’s, window-noted) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Spanish friars had run the Philippine church for three centuries, and the century's great church fight was over whether Filipinos could run their own parishes. The secularization campaign — transferring parishes from Spanish religious orders to diocesan clergy, most of them native-born — turned into a national grievance, and in 1872, after a mutiny at the Cavite arsenal, three priests who had championed it were garrotted: Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, remembered ever since by the single name Gomburza. Their execution did more for the independence movement than their campaign ever had; Jose Rizal dedicated his second novel to their memory. When Spanish rule ended, part of the church went with it. In 1902 the labour organizer Isabelo de los Reyes proclaimed an Iglesia Filipina Independiente and named the former revolutionary chaplain Gregorio Aglipay its head, and for a few years a substantial minority of Filipino Catholics followed it.
movements.teaser: The Philippines, 1815 to 1906 — three priests garrotted over who should run the parishes, and a national church proclaimed thirty years later in the ruins of Spanish rule.
voices: Pedro Pelaez — the Manila cathedral canon who first pressed the case for Filipino priests in Filipino parishes
Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora — the three priests executed in 1872, remembered together as Gomburza
