Gregorio Aglipay — the priest and revolutionary chaplain who became the first head of the Iglesia Filipina Independiente
Isabelo de los Reyes — the writer and labour organizer who proclaimed the independent church in 1902
movements.legacy: The Iglesia Filipina Independiente is still a functioning church, and since 1961 has been in full communion with the Episcopal Church and the wider Anglican Communion. The Catholic Church it broke from remained the country's majority faith and, over the following decades, got what the secularization campaign had asked for: a Filipino hierarchy drawn from Filipino clergy. Gomburza became a national memory more than a churchly one — three priests' names on monuments and in schoolbooks, taught as the beginning of a country.

movements.name: The Church of the East & the Chaldean Consolidation
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is thin to moderate: succession records, and mission archives, including the American mission at Urmia from 1834 and the Archbishop of Canterbury's mission from 1886.
movements.relationsSummary: John Hormizd was confirmed as Chaldean patriarch in 1830, consolidating the modern Chaldean Catholic Church as a single body in communion with Rome. The line that stayed independent kept its seat at Qudshanis and became known as the Assyrian Church of the East.
movements.why: This was once a missionary church whose bishops reached from Baghdad as far as China; by the nineteenth century it had shrunk to a mountain village in Hakkari and a rival line recognized by Rome in 1830 as the Chaldean Catholic Church. When the Archbishop of Canterbury sent a mission to the remaining Assyrian line in 1886, he instructed it to strengthen the ancient church rather than convert its people.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815; end 1906 era cap; John Hormizd confirmed 1830 [S]; NO continuesAs back to VI.30 (165-year gap — the E8 named-gap disclosure is the bridge) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Church of the East — the church that once sent bishops from Baghdad as far as China — entered this century reduced to the mountains and plains of the Ottoman-Persian borderland and divided between rival patriarchal lines, one in communion with Rome and one not. In 1830 Rome confirmed John Hormizd as patriarch of Babylon, consolidating the Chaldean Catholic Church as a single body. The line that stayed independent kept its seat in the mountain village of Qudshanis in Hakkari, its patriarchate passing from uncle to nephew, and its people came to be known as the Assyrian Church of the East. Both then found themselves courted by outsiders. American Congregationalist missionaries settled at Urmia in the 1830s and gave the region a printing press and schools in the spoken Syriac of the day. From 1886 the Archbishop of Canterbury sent a mission expressly instructed to strengthen the ancient church rather than convert its members.
movements.teaser: Mesopotamia, the Hakkari mountains and Urmia, 1815 to 1906 — the oldest missionary church in Asia, reduced to two patriarchates and a mountain village, and rediscovered by Western missions.
voices: John Hormizd — confirmed patriarch in 1830, the figure in whom the modern Chaldean Catholic Church consolidated
Joseph Audo — Chaldean patriarch who resisted Roman centralization over his church's jurisdiction, including at the First Vatican Council
Justin Perkins — the American missionary who established the Urmia press and printed Scripture in the spoken Syriac of the region
movements.legacy: Both churches are still here, and both are now largely churches of exile. The Chaldean Catholic Church remains the largest Christian body native to Iraq. The Assyrian Church of the East, driven out of the Hakkari mountains during the First World War, spent most of the twentieth century with its patriarch abroad and only returned the seat to Erbil in 2015. The Urmia press left a quieter legacy: printing Scripture and schoolbooks in the language people actually spoke helped make modern Aramaic a written literary language, which it has remained.

movements.name: The Confessional Lutheran Revival & the Emigrations
movements.region: Prussia, Saxony, Bavaria; N. America; Australia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: the Prussian Union documents of 1817, records of the 1838 emigrant sailing, the Missouri Synod's founding documents from 1847 and its newspaper Der Lutheraner, and the Erlangen theological corpus.
movements.relationsSummary: The Prussian Union of 1817 forced a merger of Lutheran and Reformed congregations. The Old Lutherans who refused were persecuted, leading to the Saxon emigration of 1838 and the founding of the Missouri Synod in 1847. In Germany the same instinct produced Neo-Lutheranism at Erlangen and Wilhelm Löhe's Neuendettelsau institutions, while Lutherans who emigrated to Australia shared the same root.
movements.why: When Prussia's king ordered Lutheran and Reformed congregations merged in 1817, some Lutherans chose exile over compliance, sailing for Missouri and South Australia rather than sign. The Saxon company that reached Missouri had to depose its own leader for misconduct within months of landing, and it was out of that chastened remnant that C. F. W. Walther built the Missouri Synod of 1847, a church that made subscribing to the old confessions the actual condition of belonging.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1817 (the Prussian Union, verified — the confession-defining provocation); end 1906 era cap; Saxon emigration Nov 1838 and Missouri Synod 26 Apr 1847 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: In 1817 the king of Prussia ordered his Lutheran and Reformed subjects into a single united church. Many Lutherans complied; some would not, holding that a confession of faith is not something a state can merge. These Old Lutherans were fined, had their services broken up and their pastors imprisoned — and rather than conform, whole congregations emigrated. Some went to South Australia in 1838 under Pastor August Kavel. A Saxon company sailed for Missouri the same year and had to depose its own leader for immorality within months of landing. Out of that chastened remnant, under the young pastor C. F. W. Walther, came the Missouri Synod of 1847. A church that made subscription to the Lutheran confessions the condition of fellowship, and built its own schools, seminaries and German-language press to keep them. In Germany the same instinct produced a scholarly renewal at Erlangen, and at Neuendettelsau, Wilhelm Lohe's training of pastors and deaconesses for emigrant congregations overseas.
movements.teaser: Prussia, Saxony and Bavaria, then Missouri and South Australia, 1817 to 1906 — Lutherans who would not let a king merge their confession, and sailed rather than sign.
voices: Johann Gottfried Scheibel — the Breslau theologian whose refusal of the Prussian Union made him the Old Lutherans' first leader
C. F. W. Walther — the Saxon emigrants' pastor, first president of the Missouri Synod and editor of Der Lutheraner
Martin Stephan — the Dresden pastor who led the Saxon emigration of 1838 and was deposed by his own colonists soon after arrival
August Kavel — who led Prussian Old Lutherans to South Australia in 1838
Wilhelm Lohe — the Bavarian pastor whose Neuendettelsau institutions sent pastors and deaconesses to emigrant churches on three continents
movements.legacy: The churches this produced are on three continents still: the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Synod in North America, the Lutheran Church of Australia, and the independent Lutheran churches of Germany. Their parochial schools became one of the largest Protestant school systems in the United States. The wider legacy is a pattern rather than an institution. A church defined by a written confession rather than by a state, a nation or a revival, which became one of the standing options in Protestant life and remains an argument Protestants have with each other.

movements.name: Malagasy Christianity — the Self-Carried Church
movements.informalName: The Church that Grew under Persecution
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The record carries a real inside voice: martyr accounts, including Rasalama's from 1837, Malagasy hymnody, and the memorial churches built by survivors, alongside London Missionary Society archives as the outside frame.
movements.relationsSummary: The London Missionary Society arrived in 1818/1820, and the first baptisms took place in 1831. Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity in 1835, and Rasalama was martyred in 1837. The church then grew for twenty-five years with no missionaries at all. Ranavalona II converted in 1869, and the French conquest of 1895-96 ended the kingdom that housed the church.
movements.why: Missionaries gave Madagascar's language its first written form and, by 1835, a complete Bible, the same year Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity outright and drove them out. For the next quarter-century believers had no foreign clergy at all, only the Bible and hymns they had been left, and when missionaries were finally allowed back they found far more Christians than they had left behind.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1818 (LMS arrival window [S]; first baptisms 1831 verified); end 1895 principled (the French conquest [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The London Missionary Society reached Madagascar in 1818, and its most consequential work turned out to be alphabetical. Within a decade Malagasy had a written form, a printing press and, by 1835, a complete Bible. Then the door slammed. Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity in 1835 and expelled the missionaries. Rasalama, the first Malagasy martyr, was speared in 1837, and for the next quarter-century believers were hunted, enslaved, and thrown from the cliff at Ampamarinana above the capital. The church did not merely survive the persecution. It grew through it, without foreign clergy, on the Bible it had been left and hymns its own people wrote, and when the missionaries were allowed back they found far more Christians than they had left behind. Ranavalona II was baptized in 1869 and burned the royal talismans, and the church became the establishment it had once been martyred by, until the French conquest of 1895 ended the kingdom that housed it.
movements.teaser: Madagascar, 1818 to 1895 — a church whose missionaries were expelled and whose members were speared and thrown off cliffs, and which was larger at the end of the persecution than at the start.
voices: David Jones and David Griffiths — the Welsh missionaries who gave Malagasy its written form and its first complete Bible
Rasalama — the first Malagasy Christian martyr, speared in 1837
Rafaravavy — the noblewoman who survived the first wave of persecution, escaped the island, and carried the church's story abroad
Ranavalona I — the queen whose 1835 edict outlawed Christianity and began the persecution
Ranavalona II — the queen baptized in 1869, who burned the royal talismans and made the kingdom Christian
movements.legacy: Christianity is still the majority faith of Madagascar, and the churches grown from this period remain among the island's largest institutions. In Antananarivo four memorial churches stand on the sites where believers were killed, built by the people who had survived them. The story travelled further than the island did. The Malagasy persecution became one of the most retold missionary narratives of the nineteenth century, a standard illustration in sermons and mission magazines wherever the question was whether a church could hold together with no clergy and no protection at all.

movements.name: East African Christianity & the Uganda Martyrs
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: the record of the martyrs across both Anglican and Catholic communions, from 1885-87 and canonized in 1964, accounts of the wave of Baganda evangelists, and Church Missionary Society and White Fathers archives.
movements.relationsSummary: Johann Ludwig Krapf began mission work on the coast in 1844, and the Universities' Mission to Central Africa followed in 1857. The Church Missionary Society and the Catholic White Fathers reached Buganda in 1877 and 1879. Anglican and Catholic pages together became the Uganda Martyrs, executed between 1885 and 1887, with Charles Lwanga burned at Namugongo in 1886. By the 1900 Agreement that settled Buganda's relations with Britain, it was a Christian kingdom. The revival movement that swept the same churches decades later grew out of this same soil.
movements.why: When the kabaka Mwanga II turned on Buganda's Anglican and Catholic converts in 1885-87, he killed both kinds together, the largest group burned alive at Namugongo under Charles Lwanga, who is said to have arranged his own pyre. The persecution did not stop the faith's spread; Baganda converts carried it outward as evangelists to neighboring kingdoms faster than any mission society could have managed on its own.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1844 (Krapf at Mombasa [S]); end 1906 era cap; Lwanga and companions 3 Jun 1886 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Christianity came back to East Africa along the coast first — Johann Ludwig Krapf landed at Mombasa in 1844 and began the language and mapping work later missions relied on — and then inland to the kingdom of Buganda, where Anglican missionaries arrived in 1877 and French Catholic White Fathers in 1879. Their converts were largely young men of the royal court, and when the kabaka Mwanga II turned on them between 1885 and 1887 he killed both kinds together: Anglican and Catholic pages executed side by side, the largest group burned alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886 under the leadership of Charles Lwanga, who is said to have arranged his own pyre. Persecution did what it often does. The church grew, and Baganda converts carried it outward as evangelists into the surrounding kingdoms faster than any mission society could have, so that by the agreement of 1900 that settled Buganda's relations with Britain, it was a Christian kingdom.
movements.teaser: The East African coast and the kingdom of Buganda, 1844 to 1906 — Anglican and Catholic converts burned together at Namugongo, and a church that spread out of their ashes across the region.
voices: Johann Ludwig Krapf — the German Lutheran in Anglican service whose 1844 landing at Mombasa opened inland East Africa to mission
Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe — first of the martyrs, killed in 1885 for rebuking the kabaka
Charles Lwanga — leader of the Catholic pages, burned at Namugongo on 3 June 1886 and canonized in 1964
James Hannington — first Anglican bishop of Eastern Equatorial Africa, killed on the road into the kingdom in 1885
Mwanga II — the kabaka whose persecution of 1885-87 created the martyrs
Apolo Kivebulaya — a Muganda convert who spent his life as an evangelist among the peoples west of the kingdom
movements.legacy: Uganda became one of the most heavily Christian countries in Africa, and the martyrs are honoured on both sides of the division that produced them — canonized by the Catholic Church in 1964, commemorated in the Anglican calendar, with shrines of both communions at Namugongo that draw enormous crowds every 3 June. The pattern set here mattered as much as the memory. African Christians carrying the faith to neighbouring peoples on their own initiative is how Christianity actually spread across this region, and the revival that swept these same churches from the 1930s grew out of the same soil.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs at Namugongo, Uganda — built over the place where Charles Lwanga and his companions were burned, with the Anglican martyrs' shrine nearby

movements.name: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
movements.informalName: The Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace
movements.statusWord: Floor Question (register) — new-revelation and sonship claims at own-text strength [S]; person-defined ground plain; shelf ruled REGISTER over Outside-A4 at the Era 9 Freeze; ended 1864
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Strong for the movement's own voice: it printed its own scriptures and edicts. Hostile Qing and missionary accounts survive alongside them, and modern scholarship, notably Jonathan Spence's, draws on both.
movements.floorNote: Hong Xiuquan claimed to be God's second son and the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and the kingdom's own printed scriptures rest on that claim. Both the claim and the authority built on it sit outside anything the historic creeds confess — recorded here as a description of what the movement's own texts say, not as a verdict on the people caught up in it.
movements.relationsSummary: Hong Xiuquan founds the God Worshippers; the Heavenly Kingdom declared 1851, Nanjing taken 1853, falls 1864; ~20 million dead (verified) — the century’s largest Christianity-adjacent movement and its largest catastrophe; VIII.7’s China wing needs this row to point at
movements.why: Hong Xiuquan, a village schoolteacher who had failed China's imperial examinations four times, came to believe after rereading a Christian tract that he was God's second son and the younger brother of Jesus Christ. The kingdom he and his followers built on that conviction banned opium and footbinding, held land in common, and lasted eleven years before the war fought to destroy it killed an estimated twenty million people.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1850 (the God Worshippers’ rising); end 1864 (the Kingdom falls) — both the movement’s own dates; register shelf RULED over the Outside-A4 branch (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Hong Xiuquan was a village schoolteacher in Guangdong who failed the imperial examinations four times. After one failure he collapsed into a delirium and saw visions he could not interpret until, years later, he reread a Christian tract handed to him in the street. From it he concluded that the old man in his vision had been God the Father, the elder brother beside him Jesus Christ, and that he himself was God's second son, sent to sweep China clean of demons. The God Worshippers he and his cousin Feng Yunshan gathered in Guangxi became an army. They proclaimed the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace in 1851, took Nanjing in 1853 and held it for eleven years — banning opium, alcohol and footbinding, destroying idols and ancestral tablets, holding land in common, and printing their own scriptures alongside the Bible. The war fought to destroy them was among the deadliest in human history, with estimates of the dead running to twenty million, and when Nanjing fell in 1864 Hong was already dead and the kingdom went with him.
movements.teaser: Southern China, 1850 to 1864 — a failed examination candidate who concluded he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and the kingdom founded on that conviction, which cost perhaps twenty million lives.
voices: Hong Xiuquan — the examination candidate turned Heavenly King, who identified himself as the younger brother of Jesus Christ
Feng Yunshan — his cousin and closest colleague, who built the God Worshippers into a mass movement in Guangxi
Yang Xiuqing — the East King, who claimed to speak with the voice of God the Father and dominated the kingdom until he was killed in 1856
Hong Rengan — the Heavenly King's cousin, who had lived among Protestant missionaries in Hong Kong and returned in 1859 with a programme for modernizing the kingdom
Issachar Jacox Roberts — the American Baptist missionary with whom Hong studied for a few months in 1847, and who declined to baptize him
movements.legacy: The Heavenly Kingdom left no church. Its institutions were destroyed with it in 1864 and no continuing body traces its descent from Hong Xiuquan. What it left instead was consequence. The Qing dynasty was permanently weakened by the war and by the regional armies raised to win it; the lower Yangtze countryside took generations to recover. And Chinese officials and villagers alike had been handed a reason to associate Christianity with rebellion and mass death, a suspicion that later missionaries met everywhere they went. Later Chinese revolutionaries, Sun Yat-sen among them, looked back on the Taiping as forerunners, and the movement remains a fixture of Chinese historical memory and museum display.

movements.name: Japanese Christianity — the Hidden Christians’ Emergence & the Meiji Church
movements.informalName: The Church that Survived Two Centuries in Hiding
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The record carries a real inside voice: the 1865 Ōura declaration, dated to the day, Kakure oral tradition, the records of the Protestant bands, and Uchimura's own writings.
movements.relationsSummary: On 17 March 1865, Urakami villagers revealed themselves at Ōura, and roughly 30,000 hidden believers came forward in the months that followed. The Urakami community faced a final persecution until 1873. Some, the Kakure, chose to stay separate from the visible church. Protestant bands grew alongside, including Uchimura Kanzo's Mukyōkai movement founded in 1901, and Nikolai's Russian Orthodox mission dated from 1861.
movements.why: On 17 March 1865 a group of villagers walked into a newly opened church in Nagasaki and quietly told the priest their hearts were the same as his, descendants of Christians driven underground more than two centuries earlier who had kept baptism, prayer and a liturgical calendar with no priest at all. Not everyone who surfaced rejoined the visible church; some, the Kakure, chose to keep the faith exactly as they had received it, and remain separate to this day.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1865 RULED over the 1861 Nikolai branch (the Ōura revelation of 17 Mar 1865, verified — the reveal the hidden-church story waits on); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: On 17 March 1865, weeks after a French church opened in Nagasaki's foreign settlement, a group of villagers from nearby Urakami came in, and one woman quietly told the priest that the hearts of all present were the same as his, and asked where the statue of Mary was. They were descendants of Christians driven underground in the 1600s, who had kept baptism, prayers and a liturgical calendar for over two hundred years without a single priest. In the months that followed tens of thousands more made themselves known. The government's ban was still in force, and the Urakami villagers were deported and held until 1873. When it was lifted, a Christianity of three kinds grew quickly in Meiji Japan. Catholic parishes rebuilt around the emerging hidden communities, Protestant bands of samurai-class students at Yokohama, Kumamoto and Sapporo, and a Russian Orthodox mission that Nikolai of Japan had begun in 1861 and staffed largely with Japanese clergy. Not all the hidden Christians rejoined: some, the Kakure, kept the tradition exactly as they had received it, and remain separate to this day.
movements.teaser: Nagasaki and Meiji Japan, 1865 to 1906 — villagers who walked into a new church and revealed that their families had kept the faith for two and a half centuries without a priest.
voices: Bernard Petitjean — the French priest at Oura to whom the Urakami villagers revealed themselves in 1865
Nikolai (Kasatkin) of Japan — the Russian monk who arrived at Hakodate in 1861 and built a Japanese Orthodox church
Niijima Jo — who left Japan illegally to study in America and returned to found Doshisha in Kyoto
Uchimura Kanzo — Sapporo Band convert who founded the Non-Church movement, a Christianity without clergy or sacraments
movements.legacy: Christianity in Japan stayed small — roughly one per cent of the population then and now — but its institutions outlasted the century. Doshisha and other mission-founded universities, the Orthodox cathedral in Tokyo that Nikolai built, and a Catholic community around Nagasaki that is still the largest in the country. The hidden Christians' story became the basis of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Nagasaki-region sites in 2018, and it has had a long literary afterlife, most famously in Endo Shusaku's novel Silence.

experienceToday.text: Oura Church, Nagasaki — the church where the hidden Christians revealed themselves in 1865, a National Treasure of Japan and open to visitors
Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region — the villages, islands and churches inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage property in 2018

movements.name: The Haitian Church — Rupture to Concordat
movements.informalName: The Church of the First Black Republic
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is thin and weighted toward outside observers: concordat documents from 1860, state records, and later church histories.
movements.relationsSummary: Schism from Rome across the whole post-independence period (verified — no Rome-trained clergy; the state runs the church; the Catholic-Vodou creole field forms in the vacuum); the Concordat signed 28 Mar 1860 (verified) — the story’s own resolution; start 1804 precedes the era once, disclosed (the story is indivisible)
movements.why: For fifty-six years after independence, Haiti's parishes were served by men of irregular standing, some genuine priests under suspension, some who had simply taken the title, since Rome refused to recognize the new republic at all. In that long vacancy, Catholic sacraments and feast days wove together with Vodou practice inherited from West Africa into a religious life most Haitians have held as one thing rather than two.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1804 RULED over the 1815 branch (one disclosed pre-era reach — the story is indivisible); end 1860 RULED over the era-cap branch (the Concordat of 28 Mar 1860, verified — the story’s own resolution, the VII.22-1787 pattern) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: When Haiti declared independence in 1804 as the first Black republic, its church was cut adrift. Rome would not recognize the new state, the French clergy had fled or been killed, and for more than half a century no properly appointed bishop and almost no seminary-trained priest arrived. The state filled the gap, appointing its own clergy, and the parishes were served by men of irregular standing. Some genuine priests under suspension, some who had simply assumed the title. In that long vacancy Haitian religious life took the shape it has largely kept: Catholic sacraments, feast days and saints woven together with Vodou practice inherited from West Africa, held by most Haitians as one thing rather than two. The rupture formally ended on 28 March 1860, when Haiti and the Holy See signed a concordat restoring a regular hierarchy. And began a much longer argument about what to do with everything that had grown up in the meantime.
movements.teaser: Haiti, 1804 to 1860 — the first Black republic's church, left for fifty-six years without Rome, a bishop or a seminary, and what grew in the gap.
voices: Fabre Geffrard — the president whose government concluded the 1860 concordat that restored Haiti's ties with Rome

The clergy of the schism years are poorly recorded — most of the men who served Haitian parishes between 1804 and 1860 arrived without appointment and left little written trace, and what record survives was largely written by outsiders
movements.legacy: The hierarchy the 1860 concordat established is still the framework of the Haitian Catholic Church, the country's largest institution. The creole religious world formed during the schism is also still there, and the church's relationship to it — stretches of quiet accommodation alternating with campaigns to stamp it out, most violently the anti-superstition drives of the 1940s — has been one of the defining questions of Haitian religion ever since.

movements.name: The Alaskan Mission — Herman’s Decades & Veniaminov
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: Veniaminov's own journals and Aleut translations, Herman's Spruce Island record, and records of the native clergy who kept the church going after 1867.
movements.relationsSummary: Veniaminov reached Unalaska in 1824 and created Aleut and Tlingit alphabets and translations. Herman lived out his last decades as a hermit, dying in 1836. Veniaminov was made bishop, taking the name Innocent, in 1840. After Russia sold Alaska in 1867, the church stayed on as a native church under its own Alaska Native clergy.
movements.why: Herman, a hermit monk on Spruce Island, spent his last decades fighting the Russian trading company over its treatment of the Alutiiq children in the school and orphanage he ran for them. Ioann Veniaminov, arriving at nearby Unalaska in 1824, gave Aleut its first alphabet and translated Scripture into it, and when Russia sold Alaska in 1867 and went home, the church he helped build stayed on, kept alive by Alaska Native clergy in their own languages.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1824 (Veniaminov at Unalaska 29 Jul 1824, verified); end 1906 era cap; the church stays after the 1867 sale [S] (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Russian Orthodoxy reached Alaska with the fur trade, and two very different men made it stay. Herman, a lay monk who had come with the first mission in 1794, spent his last decades alone on Spruce Island near Kodiak, running a school and an orphanage for Alutiiq children and quarrelling with the trading company over its treatment of them. In 1824 a young married priest, Ioann Veniaminov, arrived at Unalaska and did the work of a linguist. He devised an alphabet for Aleut, translated the Gospel of Matthew and a catechism into it, and wrote an account of the islands and their people that scholars still use. Widowed, he became a monk, was made bishop in 1840 as Innocent, and rose eventually to be Metropolitan of Moscow. What the two of them built proved unexpectedly durable. When Russia sold Alaska in 1867 and the Russians went home, the church stayed, in the hands of Alaska Native clergy and lay readers who kept the services going in their own languages.
movements.teaser: Kodiak, the Aleutians and the Alaskan mainland, 1824 to 1906 — a hermit monk, a priest who wrote the Aleut alphabet, and a church that stayed on after the empire that brought it sold the territory and left.
voices: Herman of Alaska — the lay monk of Spruce Island, defender of the Alutiiq against the fur company; canonized in 1970 as the first saint of Orthodox America
Ioann Veniaminov, later Saint Innocent — priest at Unalaska from 1824, creator of the Aleut alphabet, then bishop of Alaska and finally Metropolitan of Moscow
Iakov Netsvetov — the first Alaska Native priest, who served the Yukon mission for twenty years
Tikhon (Bellavin) — bishop of the American diocese at the turn of the century, later patriarch of Moscow
movements.legacy: Orthodoxy is still a living Alaska Native tradition, with dozens of parishes serving villages across the Aleutians, the Kodiak archipelago and the Yukon-Kuskokwim delta, many of them keeping services in Yup'ik, Aleut and Tlingit alongside English. The mission also became the root of Orthodoxy in North America as a whole. The diocese Veniaminov founded moved its seat to San Francisco and then to New York, and is the ancestor of today's Orthodox Church in America. Herman's grave on Spruce Island is still a place of pilgrimage.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Holy Ascension, Unalaska, Alaska — the parish Veniaminov served, and a National Historic Landmark
Spruce Island, Alaska — Saint Herman's hermitage and grave, a pilgrimage site for Orthodox Christians

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Latin American Catholicism
movements.informalName: The Church of the New Republics
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: patronato dossiers, records from the Reforma era, the acts of the 1899 Plenary Council, and documents from Brazil's religious question.
movements.relationsSummary: Independence brought the patronato fights and Rome's slow recognition of the new governments. Liberal and clerical factions clashed, most sharply in Mexico's Reforma. Rome pursued the Romanization of the continent's church, culminating in the 1899 Latin American Plenary Council. Brazil's imperial church faced its own conflicts with the state.
movements.why: When Spanish America's new republics claimed the same right to appoint bishops the Spanish crown once held, Rome took a generation to recognize either the governments or their nominees, leaving dioceses vacant and seminaries shut. Mexico's Reform laws stripped the church of its property in the 1850s and Brazil imprisoned two of its own bishops in the 1870s, while ordinary Catholics kept their confraternities, patronal feasts and household saints going with far fewer priests than Europe had.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (window; the independence century); end 1906 era cap; NO continuesAs from VII.17 (the E8 prose-continuity ruling’s own logic — edge/prose, not identity) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Spanish crown had run the church in its American empire under a papal grant, appointing the bishops and collecting the tithes. When the colonies won independence the new republics claimed exactly the same right, and Rome — which had backed the crown — took decades to recognize either the governments or their nominees, leaving dioceses vacant and seminaries shut for a generation. What followed was a long fight between liberals and clericals over land, schools, cemeteries and marriage. Sharpest in Mexico, where the Reform laws of the 1850s stripped the church of its property and drove it out of public life, and loudest in Brazil, where two bishops were tried and imprisoned in the 1870s. Rome answered by tightening its grip, importing European clergy and religious orders, rebuilding seminaries on Roman lines, and in 1899 summoning the bishops of the whole continent to Rome for a first Latin American Plenary Council. Underneath all of it the devotional life of ordinary Catholics — confraternities, patronal feasts, pilgrimage shrines, household saints — carried on much as before, often with very few priests.
movements.teaser: Spanish America and Brazil, 1815 to 1906 — a church that lost its king, waited a generation for Rome to recognize its bishops, and was fought over by every new republic.
voices: Benito Juarez — the Mexican president whose Reform laws separated church and state and confiscated the church's property
Gabriel Garcia Moreno — the president of Ecuador who consecrated his republic to the Sacred Heart and governed it as a Catholic state
Vital Maria Goncalves de Oliveira and Antonio de Macedo Costa — the Brazilian bishops tried and imprisoned in the religious question of the 1870s
Leo XIII — who convened the first Latin American Plenary Council at Rome in 1899
movements.legacy: This is the century that made Latin America's church what it is: a Roman-aligned hierarchy laid over a much older popular Catholicism, with far fewer priests per head than Europe had, and a long habit of arguing with the state. The 1899 council was the first time the continent's bishops met as a single body, and the continental conferences that followed — Rio in 1955, Medellin in 1968 — grew from that precedent. Latin America is still home to the largest share of the world's Catholics.

movements.name: Ethiopian Christianity — Tewodros to Menelik
movements.informalName: The Church of the Re-founded Empire
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: royal chronicles, records of the Boru Meda settlement of 1878, and mission-era accounts written by outsiders.
movements.relationsSummary: Tewodros II ruled from 1855 to 1868. Yohannes IV settled the Tewahedo doctrinal question at the Council of Boru Meda in 1878. Menelik II won the decisive victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896.
movements.why: Tewodros II seized church lands and tried to bring the clergy under his own control, a quarrel that ended with a British army at Magdala and his suicide in 1868. A decade later Yohannes IV settled a two-century theological argument over how Christ's divinity and humanity are united at the Council of Boru Meda, even as the church that ruling bound together still had to receive its own head, the abun, from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1855 (Tewodros II [S]); end 1900 seamless to IX.20; NO continuesAs back to VI.25 (205-year gap — disclosure bridges); forward continuesAs to IX.20 written at this Freeze (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: After a century in which Ethiopia's emperors were figureheads and the regional lords ruled, a provincial soldier crowned himself Tewodros II in 1855 and set out to remake the empire. And its church, whose lands he seized and whose clergy he tried to bring under his hand, until his quarrel with Britain ended with a redcoat army at Magdala and his suicide in 1868. His successor Yohannes IV settled a doctrinal argument that had divided Ethiopian theologians for two centuries: at the Council of Boru Meda in 1878 he ruled for the Tewahedo position on how Christ's divinity and humanity are united, and enforced it as the empire's single teaching. Menelik II then did what no other African ruler managed in that century — at Adwa in 1896 he destroyed an invading Italian army and kept his country independent. And Ethiopia entered the twentieth century as an ancient Christian state that had never been colonized, its church still receiving its head, the abun, from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt.
movements.teaser: Ethiopia, 1855 to 1900 — an emperor who fought his own church, a council that settled a two-century argument about Christ, and the only African army to defeat a European one and keep its country.
voices: Tewodros II — the emperor who re-founded the empire and broke with the church over its lands and privileges
Abuna Salama III — the Egyptian-appointed metropolitan who clashed with Tewodros and pressed for a single doctrinal settlement
Yohannes IV — who convened the Council of Boru Meda in 1878 and made the Tewahedo formula the empire's one teaching
Menelik II — victor at Adwa in 1896, who kept Ethiopia independent and expanded it far to the south
Empress Taytu Betul — Menelik's consort, a force in the Adwa campaign and in the church's affairs alike
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the largest of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches, and both things this century settled are still in place: the Tewahedo doctrine ruled at Boru Meda, and the independence Adwa secured. The one arrangement that did change came later — the church received its first Ethiopian bishops in 1929 and its own patriarch in 1959, ending sixteen centuries of taking its head from Alexandria. Adwa itself became a byword far beyond Ethiopia, a rallying point for Pan-Africanism and, in the Caribbean and the Americas, for movements that looked to Ethiopia as the image of an Africa that had never been conquered.

movements.name: Dutch Neo-Calvinism & the Secession Churches
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: the Afscheiding's own acts from 1834, Kuyper's writings, the Christian Reformed Church's records from 1857, and the 1892 union documents.
movements.relationsSummary: The Afscheiding secession of 1834 led American emigrants to found the Christian Reformed Church in North America in 1857. Abraham Kuyper led a second secession, the Doleantie, in 1886, founded the Free University in 1880, and brought the two streams together in the 1892 union that formed the Gereformeerde Kerken in Nederland.
movements.why: When Hendrik de Cock's congregation walked out of the Dutch national church in 1834, the state fined them and billeted soldiers on them for holding illegal services. Fifty years later Abraham Kuyper led a second, larger secession on a bigger idea, that Christ's claim covers every sphere of life, each with its own proper authority, and built a university, a newspaper and a political party to carry it out rather than withdraw from society or dissolve into it.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1834 (the Afscheiding [S]); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: In 1834 a village pastor in Groningen, Hendrik de Cock, was suspended for preaching the old Reformed doctrines against what he took to be the liberalism of the national church, and his congregation walked out with him. The Afscheiding that followed was a secession of mostly poor and rural people, who were fined and had soldiers billeted on them for holding illegal services. Many emigrated, and in 1857 their American cousins founded what became the Christian Reformed Church in North America. Fifty years after de Cock, Abraham Kuyper — journalist, politician, theologian — led a second and larger secession, the Doleantie of 1886, and in 1892 brought most of the two streams together. Kuyper's idea was always bigger than a church. That Christ's claim covers every sphere of life, each with its own proper authority, so believers should build their own schools, university, newspaper and political party rather than either withdraw from society or dissolve into it. He founded the Free University in Amsterdam in 1880 and served as prime minister of the Netherlands from 1901 to 1905.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands and the American Midwest, 1834 to 1906 — Calvinists who walked out of the national church twice, and then built a university, a newspaper and a governing party.
voices: Hendrik de Cock — the Groningen pastor whose 1834 suspension began the Afscheiding
Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer — the historian and politician whose anti-revolutionary politics prepared the ground Kuyper built on
Abraham Kuyper — theologian, newspaper editor, founder of the Free University, and prime minister of the Netherlands from 1901 to 1905
Herman Bavinck — the movement's systematic theologian, whose Reformed Dogmatics is still in use
Albertus Van Raalte — who led a colony of Seceders to Michigan in 1847
movements.legacy: The churches are still here: the Dutch Reformed families at home, most of them since 2004 inside the Protestant Church in the Netherlands, and in North America the Christian Reformed Church with its schools and colleges. Kuyper's larger idea travelled furthest. Sphere sovereignty and a Christian worldview applied to scholarship, politics and the arts became a standing tradition in Reformed thought and shaped a great deal of evangelical higher education in North America. It also travelled in a direction Kuyper's heirs still argue about, supplying vocabulary that South African theologians later adapted in defence of apartheid.

movements.name: Russian Evangelicals — Stundists to the Baptist Union
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the movement's own hymnody and congregational records, plus documentation of its persecution under Konstantin Pobedonostsev.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew from the Stundist Bible-study movement among Ukrainian peasants in the 1860s and the Pashkovite circle in St Petersburg from 1874, joining as the Russian Baptist Union in 1884. Persecuted under the ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev, and in tension with the Russian Orthodox Church of the same era. These congregations are the direct ancestors of the Soviet-era Initsiativniki Baptist movement that followed.
movements.why: Ukrainian peasants working alongside German colonists in the 1860s began holding Bible study meetings their neighbors called Stunden, hours, and read Russia's own new translation of Scripture for themselves. A decade later, a guards colonel named Vasily Pashkov opened his St Petersburg house to preaching that servants and nobles attended side by side, a movement the state answered with exile, broken-up meetings and children taken from their parents, since leaving the Orthodox Church was a crime as well as a sin.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1860 (the Stundist movement, 1860s [S]); end 1906 era cap; the direct ancestors of IX.12’s Initsiativniki (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: In the 1860s Ukrainian peasants working alongside German colonists in the southern provinces began meeting for the Bible studies their neighbours called Stunden, hours — reading the Scriptures for themselves in the Russian translation then appearing. Reading became conversion, and conversion became congregations. The movement then met a second one coming from the opposite end of society. From 1874 in St Petersburg, aristocrats converted under the preaching of the English evangelist Lord Radstock gathered around Colonel Vasily Pashkov, who opened his house for meetings that servants and nobles attended together. The strands joined in a Russian Baptist Union in 1884, and the state answered with everything it had — Pashkov exiled, meetings broken up, children removed from Stundist parents, families deported. Since leaving the Orthodox Church was a crime as well as a sin. The toleration decree of 1905 gave them their first legal breathing space in forty years.
movements.teaser: Ukraine and Russia, 1860 to 1906 — peasants who read the Bible in their own language and aristocrats who read it in a palace, and both of them breaking the law.
voices: Nikita Voronin — baptized in the river at Tiflis in 1867, conventionally counted the first Russian Baptist
Ivan Ryaboshapka and Mikhail Ratushny — among the earliest Ukrainian Stundist leaders
Lord Radstock — the English evangelist whose 1874 mission converted a circle of the Russian aristocracy
Vasily Pashkov — the guards colonel who opened his St Petersburg house to preaching and was exiled for it in 1884
Konstantin Pobedonostsev — the Holy Synod's chief lay officer, who directed the state's campaign against them
movements.legacy: These congregations are the ancestors of Russian and Ukrainian evangelical Protestantism as it now exists. The Baptist and Evangelical Christian unions descended from them survived the Soviet century, went through their own painful split in the 1960s between those who registered with the state and those who refused, and are today, with the Pentecostals, the largest Protestant presence across the former Soviet Union. Emigrants carried the tradition abroad as well, into Slavic Baptist communities in North and South America and Germany that are still identifiably from this root.

movements.name: Azusa Street & Early Pentecostalism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a self-documenting record — the mission's own paper The Apostolic Faith, Seymour's 1915 Doctrines and Discipline, and participants' memoirs read beside the hostile press file. Its 1920s end was classified at the Freeze as an episode-end of a still-living tradition: the mission's decline after 1909 and Seymour's death in 1922 close the episode, not the movement, and the copy already names the continuation. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: RICH and self-documenting (The Apostolic Faith paper; participants' memoirs)
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Holiness + Black Church worship; parent of most of this era's family
movements.why: The revival that broke out on Azusa Street in Los Angeles in April 1906 grew from two streams already flowing together, Holiness worship and Black church worship, and it spread not by hierarchy but by print: the mission's own newspaper, The Apostolic Faith, went out free and started meetings in places its founders never visited. Local papers mocked it as a "Weird Babel of Tongues," but William Seymour kept leading the mission until his death in 1922, and almost every Pentecostal church that exists today traces back to what happened on that street.
movements.dateRationale: End 1920s KEPT and classified (b) — episode-end of a still-living tradition: the mission's decline after 1909 and Seymour's death in 1922 [S] close the episode, not the movement; the copy already names the continuation (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The Apostolic Faith (Los Angeles, 1906-1908, 13 issues)
sources.note: The mission's own newspaper.

sources.work: Frank Bartleman, Azusa Street (orig. How Pentecost Came to Los Angeles, 1925); participant recollections (Valdez, Catley)
sources.note: Participant memoirs written years after the events, shaped by each author's own perspective.

sources.work: William J. Seymour, The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission (1915)
sources.note: The Black founder's own church order, including revisions made after 1913 - a document often overlooked in popular accounts of the revival.

sources.work: Los Angeles Times, 'Weird Babel of Tongues' (18 Apr 1906) and the hostile press file; early periodical web (Confidence 1908-, Bridegroom's Messenger)
sources.note: Hostile press coverage - contemptuous and racially charged - but still valuable evidence for dating events and identifying who took part.

sources.work: Cecil M. Robeck Jr., The Azusa Street Mission and Revival (2006); Espinosa, William J. Seymour (Duke, 2014); Wacker, Heaven Below (Harvard, 2001)
Allan Anderson, An Introduction to Pentecostalism (CUP, 2004; 2nd ed. 2013/14); CHC vol. 9 (McLeod, 2006)

movements.longDescription: The revival on Azusa Street in Los Angeles began in April 1906, and it came out of two streams already running — the Holiness movement, and Black church worship. What made it travel was that the mission printed its own newspaper. The Apostolic Faith ran to thirteen issues between 1906 and 1908, went out free from Los Angeles, and was read by people who then started meetings of their own on the strength of it. William J. Seymour led the mission and set down how it was to be ordered in The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission in 1915. The city's press mocked it from the first weeks — the Los Angeles Times ran 'Weird Babel of Tongues' on 18 April 1906 — and participants answered with accounts of their own, Frank Bartleman's among the best known. The mission itself declined after 1909, and Seymour died in 1922. By then what began there was long past its own address.
movements.teaser: Los Angeles, 1906 to the 1920s — a revival born out of Holiness and Black church worship that became the parent of nearly every movement in this era's family, documented as it happened in its own newspaper, The Apostolic Faith.
voices: William J. Seymour — led the Azusa Street mission and published its Doctrines and Discipline in 1915
The Apostolic Faith — the mission's own paper, thirteen issues between 1906 and 1908, which carried the revival to readers who never set foot in Los Angeles
Frank Bartleman — participant whose account of the revival, published in 1925, is one of the fullest written from inside it
The remembering participants — Valdez, Catley and others, whose later recollections are much of what is known about who was actually in the room
movements.legacy: The revival's own episode closed in the 1920s; the tradition it started did not. Almost every movement in this era's Pentecostal family runs back through here, from the Global South churches of the later century to Africa's independent churches. The denominations formed fast: the Church of God in Christ turned Pentecostal in 1907 and the Assemblies of God organized in 1914, and the argument over the doctrine of God that produced Oneness Pentecostalism broke out inside the same young movement in 1913. What travelled furthest was not a doctrine but a way of meeting — testimony, song, and the expectation that anyone present might speak.

movements.name: The 1904-07 Revival Family (Wales; Mukti India; Pyongyang Korea)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on journalists' and missionaries' near-verbatim records of three revivals that broke out independently. Its 1910 end was classified at the Freeze as an episode-end — the wave subsided; the churches did not — and the Korean origin lines banked at the Era 9 gate were landed on this row at the same time. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich (verbatim revival journalism; mission records; Korea's own church histories)
movements.relationsSummary: These revivals arose independently of the Azusa Street revival happening around the same time, rather than descending from it — revival broke out in more than one place at once. Korea's revival grew out of earlier missionary and indigenous groundwork: Horace Allen's arrival in 1884, Underwood and Appenzeller in 1885, the Nevius method adopted in 1890, and Sŏ Sang-yun's earlier work distributing scripture.
movements.why: Revival broke out almost at once in three unconnected places -- Wales in 1904, the Mukti mission in India in 1905, and a Bible conference in Pyongyang in 1907 -- and none of the three descended from the others or from Azusa Street. Journalists and missionaries recorded each one nearly as it happened, from the Western Mail's daily reports on Wales to Minnie Abrams's account of Mukti, leaving three separate beginnings rather than one single source.
movements.dateRationale: End 1910 KEPT and classified (b) — episode-end: the 1904–07 wave subsided c. 1910 [S] while the churches it left continue; start 1904 is the era's one legal single crossing of the 1906 boundary, banked at the Era 9 gate (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: Wales: Western Mail revival supplements ('Awstin', 1904-05); W. T. Stead, The Revival in the West (1905); Evan Roberts via journalism and War on the Saints (1913, with Penn-Lewis)
sources.note: First-hand journalism from the time, plus later material written after Roberts' own breakdown - each carries its own advocacy angle.

sources.work: Mukti: Pandita Ramabai's own mission press (Mukti Prayer-Bell); Minnie Abrams, The Baptism of the Holy Ghost & Fire (1906)
sources.note: The founder's own mission press record, and the revival's theology set out by a woman co-worker - influence that reached as far as Chile by 1909.

sources.work: Pyongyang: Korean church histories' own accounts (Kil Son-ju); William N. Blair's eyewitness account (with Bruce Hunt as The Korean Pentecost and the Sufferings Which Followed, Banner of Truth, 1977)
sources.note: Korea's own church histories, alongside a missionary's eyewitness account compiled and published years later.

sources.work: R. Tudur Jones, Faith and the Crisis of a Nation: Wales 1890-1914 (ET 2004); Sung-Deuk Oak, The Making of Korean Christianity (Baylor, 2013)
CHC vol. 9 (McLeod, 2006)

movements.longDescription: Three revivals broke out within a few years of each other in three parts of the world, and none of them descended from the others or from Azusa Street. In Wales the revival ran through 1904 and 1905 and was reported almost daily in the Western Mail by a correspondent writing as 'Awstin', with Evan Roberts as its public face; W. T. Stead published The Revival in the West in 1905. At Pandita Ramabai's Mukti mission in India it came in 1905, and Minnie Abrams, who worked there, described what happened in The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire the following year. In Korea it began in January 1907, at a Bible conference at the Presbyterian seminary in Pyongyang, on ground that Korean colporteurs and foreign missionaries had been working since the 1880s. Three separate beginnings, recorded almost verbatim as they happened, which is why this map keeps them together rather than tracing them to a single source.
movements.teaser: Wales, Mukti in India, and Pyongyang in Korea, 1904 to 1910 — three revivals that broke out independently of each other and of Azusa Street, recorded almost verbatim by the journalists and missionaries who were there.
voices: Evan Roberts — the public face of the Welsh revival of 1904–05
'Awstin' — the Western Mail correspondent whose near-daily reports are the fullest running record of the Welsh revival
Pandita Ramabai — founder of the Mukti mission, whose own press published the Mukti Prayer-Bell
Minnie Abrams — worker at Mukti, whose The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire (1906) described the revival from inside it
Kil Sŏn-ju — among the Korean church's own leading figures in the Pyongyang revival, recorded in Korean church histories
Sŏ Sang-yun — the Korean colporteur whose congregation at Sorae stood before the missionaries reached it
movements.legacy: The wave subsided around 1910; the churches did not. Korea's church in particular grew out of this decade and the decades just before it — Horace Allen's arrival in 1884, Underwood and Appenzeller in 1885, the Nevius method adopted in 1890 — and it went on growing long after the revival wave had passed. The three revivals together are the standing argument that revival is polygenetic: it broke out in unconnected places at nearly the same time, which is a harder and more honest fact than any single point of origin. The journalism, the mission presses and the Korean church's own histories they generated are still the record.

movements.name: The East African Revival (Balokole)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its soft decade-end was the one case in the era's sweep where a documented event could replace it: the end moved to 1977, the martyrdom of Archbishop Janani Luwum, with the fellowships' persistence inside East African Anglicanism named as the living continuation. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; testimony culture generated records; oral-history projects still gathering
movements.relationsSummary: African-led within (and often against) mission Anglicanism; martyrs include Janani Luwum
movements.why: The revival began around 1930 at the mission station at Gahini in Rwanda, when African and missionary Christians started confessing sin to each other out loud, in public. Those who joined were called balokole, "the saved ones," and they carried the movement through Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania on testimony, shared meetings, and a hymn, "Tukutendereza Yesu," still sung today. Archbishop Janani Luwum, killed in 1977, remains its best-known martyr.
movements.dateRationale: End 1970 → 1977 on a documented event: the martyrdom of Archbishop Janani Luwum, 16/17 Feb 1977 [S] — the ONE case in this era's sweep where a documented event replaces a soft decade-end, and the "1930s-1970s" string already contains it. Class (b): the fellowships persist inside East African Anglicanism [S], named as the living continuation (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: Balokole testimony culture: convention records (Kabale 1935-), fellowship records, 'Tukutendereza Yesu'; Nagenda's addresses; Kivengere, I Love Idi Amin (1977)
sources.note: The movement's own testimony genre, and published African voices from within it.

sources.work: Joe Church, Quest for the Highest (1981)
sources.note: A missionary's documentary memoir from Gahini - written from outside the African leadership of a movement that arose within, and often against, mission Anglicanism.

sources.work: The Janani Luwum martyrdom record (1977; Westminster Abbey martyrs 1998)
Derek R. Peterson, Ethnic Patriotism and the East African Revival (CUP, 2012); Kevin Ward & Emma Wild-Wood (eds.), The East African Revival: History and Legacies (Ashgate, 2012)
sources.note: The current standard scholarly works; the Ward/Wild-Wood volume includes oral-history material.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9; Sanneh/Walls world-Christianity frames

movements.longDescription: The East African Revival began around 1930 at the mission station at Gahini in Rwanda, where African and missionary Christians started confessing sin to one another out loud and in public. Those who joined were called balokole, the saved ones. It spread through fellowship meetings and through conventions, at Kabale from 1935 and then elsewhere, with testimony given openly and the hymn 'Tukutendereza Yesu' sung wherever they gathered. It ran through Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania as well as Rwanda, and it was led by Africans inside the mission Anglicanism that had planted the church — often against it, since a movement that asked bishops and catechists alike to confess in public was not always welcome. Its record is unusually communal: the testimony culture generated its own written material, and oral-history projects are still gathering the rest from people who remember it.
movements.teaser: Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, 1930s to 1970s — a revival led by Africans inside, and often against, the mission Anglicanism that had planted the church, whose martyrs include Janani Luwum.
voices: William Nagenda — one of the revival's best-known African leaders, whose addresses are part of its written record
Festo Kivengere — Ugandan bishop and evangelist, author of I Love Idi Amin (1977)
Joe Church — participant whose Quest for the Highest (1981) is an account of the beginnings from inside them
Janani Luwum — Archbishop of Uganda, killed in February 1977; the revival's best-known martyr
The convention record — the fellowship and convention papers from Kabale onward, in which ordinary balokole speak for themselves
movements.legacy: The revival ran as a wave into the 1970s and the wave subsided; the fellowships did not, and they persist inside East African Anglicanism to this day, with their meetings, their confession practice and their hymn intact. It gave the East African churches a generation of African leadership formed outside missionary control, and it left a large body of testimony that historians have only recently begun to work through. Janani Luwum is commemorated among the twentieth-century martyrs on the west front of Westminster Abbey, unveiled in 1998.

movements.name: African-Initiated Churches (Harrist; Aladura; Zionist/ZCC; Kimbanguist)
movements.statusWord: Researched — strong candidate (Era 10 Step 0; c2 run per body — Harrist/Aladura cleared on the community limb, Kimbanguist and ZCC open)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), and treated per body throughout as a family row must be. Its start was deepened to the 1880s on the family's own historiography, and the Kimbanguist church's dated documentary arc — 2005 doctrine, the 2008 Nkamba reversal, the 2021 ecumenical exclusion — was recorded as a disclosed divergence rather than harmonized. The criterion's tenth live application ran here: cleared on the community limb for the Harrist and Aladura mainstreams, open for the Kimbanguist question, and open with its sourcing constraint named for the ZCC, which publishes little by its own choice. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich and improving (own archives, liturgies, oral histories; colonial-record gravity severe)
movements.floorNote: Honest per-branch notes, each on a dated published text. The Harrist and Aladura mainstreams are creedally conventional by their own constitutions [S]. The Kimbanguist church's documentary arc is carried dated and disclosed rather than harmonized: a moderate official doctrine dated 2005, revoked at the July 2008 Nkamba assembly in favour of the popular teaching (Kimbangu as the Holy Spirit incarnate, the three sons as the Trinity's incarnations), with exclusion from the organized ecumenical fellowship following in 2021 — the church having been the first African-initiated church admitted to the World Council of Churches, in 1969 (verified). The ZCC question is recorded as an OPEN question with its sourcing constraint named: the church publishes little by its own choice and no published confession exists to cite, so the person-defined question stays open rather than answered — a question only the body itself could settle is recorded, not asked. A living body can change its confession; every clause here describes a dated text, never the faith of a member.
movements.relationsSummary: Children of mission churches + Pentecostal currents + African initiative irreducible to either
movements.why: William Wadé Harris walked through the Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast between 1913 and 1915, preaching and baptizing, and the churches that trace to him still bear his name. Others rose on their own ground: Simon Kimbangu's ministry in Congo began in March 1921 and ended within months in a colonial court, while Engenas Lekganyane founded the Zion Christian Church in South Africa in 1924. Each carries its founder's legacy forward differently, from Nigeria's Aladura congregations to the ZCC's annual pilgrimage at Moria.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1900 → the 1880s on the family's own historiography: Nehemiah Tile (1880s, verified) and Mangena Mokone's Ethiopian Church (Nov 1892, verified); string "1900s-present" → "1880s-present". This row crosses the 1906 boundary on EITHER branch of the fork — the branch changes the crossing's depth, not its existence — and the crossing is disclosed and single (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: Harrist: Harris's teaching via hearers' records (1926 Benoit interview notes); the Harrist churches' later catechisms and liturgies
sources.note: Harris himself left almost no writing of his own, so this rests on others' records of what he taught. The prophet's own era and the later church's own records are kept as distinct layers.

sources.work: Aladura: Cherubim & Seraphim founding records (Orimolade & Abiodun, 1925); CAC records around Babalola's 1930 revival; Church of the Lord (Aladura) constitutions, Ositelu's writings
sources.note: The churches' own liturgies and constitutions. A woman co-founder was present at the origin of the movement; her later marginalization is part of the record.

sources.work: Kimbanguist: the 1921 colonial military-court trial record; the EJCSK's own catechetical/doctrinal publications; the 1969 WCC admission and later trinitarian-controversy record
sources.note: The trial record comes from a hostile colonial court, so it should be read with that bias in mind.

sources.work: Zionist/ZCC: Engenas Lekganyane founding (1924/25); the ZCC's practice-borne record (Moria pilgrimage, badges, oral tradition); early Zionist links to Zion City/Dowie via outside pens
sources.note: The church publishes little by its own choice; its record lives mainly in practice - pilgrimage, badges, and oral tradition - rather than in print.

sources.work: Bengt Sundkler, Bantu Prophets in South Africa (1948; 2nd ed. 1961); J. D. Y. Peel, Aladura (OUP/IAI, 1968); Marie-Louise Martin, Kimbangu (Blackwell, 1975); Anderson, African Reformation (2001)
AIC adherence numbers: World Christian Encyclopedia, 3rd ed. (2019), compared with the churches' own self-reported figures
sources.note: The World Christian Encyclopedia discloses when its figures rely on self-reported input. The ZCC and Kimbanguist numbers here are the churches' own figures; no independent count exists for either.

movements.longDescription: From the 1880s onward Africans began founding churches of their own rather than staying inside the missions. Nehemiah Tile left the Methodists to form the Thembu National Church in the 1880s, and in November 1892 Mangena Mokone founded the Ethiopian Church in South Africa. Later waves went further. William Wadé Harris walked through the Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast between 1913 and 1915 preaching and baptizing, and the churches that followed him bear his name. In Nigeria the Aladura churches grew from the 1920s and 1930s — the Cherubim and Seraphim, founded in 1925 by Moses Orimolade and Christianah Abiodun; the Christ Apostolic Church around Joseph Babalola's revival of 1930; the Celestial Church of Christ from 1947. In the Congo, Simon Kimbangu's ministry began on 18 March 1921 and ended within months before a colonial military court. In South Africa, Engenas Lekganyane founded the Zion Christian Church in 1924. Each of these carries its founder's legacy forward differently, which is why this map takes them one at a time.
movements.teaser: West and southern Africa and Congo, 1900s to today — churches planted by missions and then remade on African terms, from the Harrist and Aladura movements to the Kimbanguist church and the ZCC, each carrying its own founder's legacy forward differently.
voices: Nehemiah Tile — founder of the Thembu National Church in the 1880s, among the first to leave a mission church to start his own
Mangena Mokone — founded the Ethiopian Church in November 1892
William Wadé Harris — whose 1913–15 trek through the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast is known largely through the notes of people who heard him
Moses Orimolade and Christianah Abiodun — founders of the Cherubim and Seraphim in 1925
Joseph Babalola — whose revival of 1930 gathered the Christ Apostolic Church around it
Simon Kimbangu — whose ministry began on 18 March 1921 and whose trial before a colonial military court that same year is one of the movement's founding documents
Engenas Lekganyane — founder of the Zion Christian Church in 1924, whose successors have led it since
movements.legacy: These are living churches, several of them very large. The Zion Christian Church's pilgrimage to Moria is central to its life, and the Kimbanguist church was the first African-initiated church admitted to the World Council of Churches, in 1969. Their congregations travelled with African migration and are now planted across Europe, which is a later chapter on this map. They also changed the scholarship: Bengt Sundkler's Bantu Prophets in South Africa (1948) and J. D. Y. Peel's Aladura (1968) made these churches a standard subject rather than a footnote to mission history, and the churches' own archives, liturgies and oral traditions are steadily being gathered.

movements.name: The Chinese Church - Indigenous & Suffering
movements.statusWord: Researched — strong candidate (Era 10 Step 0; c2 run per body, genuinely open under the safety clause)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), with safety binding every line of it. The criterion's eleventh live application ran here on published texts only and stays genuinely open, with the 2009 Christian Research Institute reassessment carried as its dated counter-note; the November 1998 house-church Confession of Faith was named as the row's dated own-voice anchor. No non-public person or community is identified, and where honest assessment would need unsafe specificity the finding is recorded open with the constraint named. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Uneven by circumstance: rich founder corpora and testimony literature; thin-and-unsafe exactly where growth was greatest
movements.floorNote: Founder-defined branches — especially the Little Flock's line from Watchman Nee to Witness Lee — are best judged on their own published texts: Nee's own writings, and Lee's Recovery Version and local-churches teaching. The Christian Research Institute reversed its own earlier classification of this tradition in a 2009 reassessment, worth naming honestly, and how each of these bodies stands doctrinally remains a genuinely open, body-by-body question. The clearest trinitarian, creed-close voice in this family is the house-church movement's own Confession of Faith from November 1998. Throughout, no living person or specific community is named, in keeping with the real safety concerns this tradition still faces today.
movements.relationsSummary: The clearest living echo of the house churches of Christianity's first two centuries, when congregations met quietly under pressure with no institutional standing.
movements.why: Chinese Christians who owed nothing to foreign missions began founding their own churches in the 1920s: Wei Enbo's True Jesus Church in 1917, Watchman Nee's Little Flock in 1922, and the Jesus Family in 1927. Their leaders wrote prolifically and paid for it -- Nee was imprisoned from 1952 to 1972, and Wang Mingdao from 1955 to 1980 -- and much of the church has gone on meeting in homes ever since, led by people with no institutional standing. That pattern, congregations meeting quietly under pressure, echoes the house churches of Christianity's first two centuries.

sources.work: Watchman Nee, The Spiritual Man (1928) and Little Flock literature, including the Nee-to-Lee succession corpus published through Living Stream Ministry; Wang Mingdao, Wushi nian lai (1950; ET A Stone Made Smooth, 1981) and 'We, Because of Faith' (1955); John Sung's diaries, posthumously compiled by his family
True Jesus Church records (1917-present); Jesus Family records (1920s-40s)
sources.note: The True Jesus Church holds a Oneness-family confession of faith, distinct from mainstream trinitarian doctrine.

sources.work: The state-church contest: the Christian Manifesto (1950) and TSPM records; denunciation-campaign records; imprisonment records (Nee 1952-72; Wang 1955-80)
sources.note: These records include both official, state-aligned documents and material produced under coercion, offering a fuller picture from both sides.

sources.work: Note on sourcing: current house-church directories, network data, and information that could identify living, non-public believers are deliberately not used here
sources.note: Real people could be put at risk by identifying them, so anything about the church's present-day state here rests only on published, publicly available figures and standard scholarship — never on unpublished or identifying material.

sources.work: Lian Xi, Redeemed by Fire: The Rise of Popular Christianity in Modern China (Yale, 2010); Daniel Bays, A New History of Christianity in China (Wiley-Blackwell, 2012)
Chinese Christian numbers: Pew 2011 (approximately 67 million) versus TSPM/CCC official figures versus movement claims
sources.note: Pew's figure is independently cross-checked; the official (TSPM/CCC) and movement figures are self-reported. The real spread between these different counts is the honest picture, not collapsed into a single number.

movements.longDescription: In the 1920s Chinese Christians began founding churches that owed nothing to the foreign missions. Wei Enbo founded the True Jesus Church in Beijing in 1917; Watchman Nee's Little Flock assemblies date from 1922; the Jesus Family from 1927. Their leaders wrote copiously — Nee's The Spiritual Man appeared in 1928, and Wang Mingdao published his own account of fifty years in 1950 — and the itinerant preacher John Sung kept diaries his family later compiled. After 1950 the Christian Manifesto and the Three-Self Patriotic Movement reorganized Protestant church life under the state; Wang Mingdao published 'We, Because of Faith' in 1955 and was imprisoned from 1955 until 1980, and Watchman Nee was imprisoned from 1952 until 1972. Much church life has gone on since outside registered structures, and in November 1998 house-church leaders published a joint Confession of Faith. No living person and no present-day community is named here: what is known is thinnest and least safe to make public exactly where the growth has been greatest, and that is a fact about the church itself, not only about the available sources.
movements.teaser: China, 1920s to today — house churches carrying forward the pattern of the earliest Chinese Christianity, from the Little Flock's Nee-then-Lee line onward, its record thinnest and most unsafe to document exactly where its growth has been greatest.
voices: Wei Enbo — founder of the True Jesus Church in Beijing in 1917
Watchman Nee — whose The Spiritual Man (1928) and Little Flock literature are the largest founder corpus here; imprisoned from 1952 to 1972
Wang Mingdao — author of a fifty-year account published in 1950 and of 'We, Because of Faith' (1955); imprisoned from 1955 to 1980
John Sung — itinerant preacher whose diaries survive in compilations edited by his family
The signatories of the house-church Confession of Faith of November 1998 — published together, and for safety left unnamed here
movements.legacy: It is a living church and, by any count, a very large one — though how large is genuinely contested. A Pew study in 2011 put the number of Christians in China at around 67 million, while official Three-Self figures and the movements' own claims fall elsewhere, and the spread between them is itself worth knowing. The founder corpora are read far outside China. The longest inheritance may be the shape rather than the size: congregations meeting in homes, led by people with no institutional standing, carrying on through decades in which the alternative was prison. That pattern is the map's strongest living echo of the house-churches of the first two centuries.

movements.name: The Confessing Church
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its tradition is genuinely closed, so it was assessed under the standing method unchanged rather than under the living-era protocol — the one era-10 row the addendum does not claim. Barmen's drafting is cross-referenced to the mainline century entry added at this Freeze rather than carried twice.
movements.sourcing: RICH: Barmen, circular letters, Finkenwalde's records, prison letters - and a record that refuses hagiography (it names its own silences)
movements.relationsSummary: Lutheran/Reformed lines under catastrophe
movements.why: When the Nazi state moved to take over the German Protestant churches in 1933, pastors organized in resistance, and a synod at Barmen in May 1934 declared that the church has one Word to obey, Jesus Christ, and no other. Dietrich Bonhoeffer ran an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde until it was shut down in 1937, writing Discipleship and Life Together out of that community before his own imprisonment. The movement's own historians are honest that its fight was mostly about the church's own freedom, and that its near-silence about what was happening to Jews is part of that story too.

sources.work: The Barmen Theological Declaration (May 1934); the Bethel Confession draft (1933); the Dahlem resolutions (Oct 1934)
