sources.note: The movement's confessional core in its own words.

sources.work: Bonhoeffer: Discipleship (1937), Life Together (1939), Letters and Papers from Prison (1951, ed. Bethge; critical DBW editions)
sources.note: Bethge's own editorial hand shaped the earlier published text; the critical edition resolves that.

sources.work: The working record: circular letters (Rundbriefe), Finkenwalde records (1935-37), Pfarrernotbund records, Niemoller's Dahlem sermons
The Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt (Oct 1945); the 1936 memorandum to Hitler; the record of the movement's own limits and silences
Gestapo and church-ministry files; Deutsche Christen publications
sources.note: These are the state's own hostile files, alongside the church's records — each clearly a different kind of source, from opposite sides of the conflict.

sources.work: Victoria Barnett, For the Soul of the People (OUP, 1992); Scholder, The Churches and the Third Reich (ET 2 vols, 1987-88); Bethge, Dietrich Bonhoeffer (ET rev. 2000); CHC vol. 9
sources.note: Standard secondary histories of the Confessing Church and Bonhoeffer's life.

movements.longDescription: When the Nazi state and the pro-Nazi 'German Christians' moved to reorganize the German Protestant churches in 1933, a minority refused. Pastors organized an emergency league; a synod at Barmen in May 1934 adopted a declaration, drafted by Karl Barth, that the church has one Word to hear and obey, Jesus Christ, and no other; and the Dahlem synod that October declared itself the lawful church. Dietrich Bonhoeffer ran an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde from 1935 until it was shut down in 1937, and wrote Discipleship and Life Together out of that community. In 1936 the movement sent a memorandum to Hitler. Its own record refuses to flatter it: the church struggle was largely about the church's own freedom, and the near-silence about what was being done to Jews is named by the movement's own historians as part of the story. In October 1945 the survivors issued the Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt.
movements.teaser: Germany, 1933 to 1945 — Lutheran and Reformed Christians who signed the Barmen Declaration against the catastrophe overtaking their church, leaving behind Finkenwalde's records and prison letters, and a record honest enough to name its own silences.
voices: Karl Barth — drafted the Barmen Theological Declaration of May 1934
Martin Niemöller — organizer of the pastors' emergency league, whose Dahlem sermons survive
Dietrich Bonhoeffer — directed the Finkenwalde seminary from 1935 to 1937 and wrote Discipleship (1937) and Life Together (1939); his prison letters were published in 1951
Eberhard Bethge — Bonhoeffer's friend, correspondent and first editor, without whom the prison letters would not exist
The circular letters — the Rundbriefe by which the movement's scattered pastors kept in contact under surveillance
movements.legacy: The Confessing Church ended with the war, and this map treats it as a closed story rather than a living one. What it left is out of all proportion to its twelve years. The Barmen Declaration is a confessional text in Reformed and Lutheran churches worldwide, cited well beyond Germany whenever a church has had to say what it will not concede to a state. Bonhoeffer's Letters and Papers from Prison, edited by Bethge and published in 1951, is read far outside the church struggle it came from. And the Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt set a pattern — a church saying plainly what it had failed to do — that other churches have used since.

movements.name: Catholic Lay Renewal Traditions (Catholic Worker; Focolare; Charismatic Renewal; L'Arche)
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (Era 10 Step 0; c2 likely-cleared per body on the community limb)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), assessed as four distinct movements rather than one tradition. The criterion's twelfth live application ran per body and likely-cleared on the community limb — all four institutionalized beyond their founders in documented form — and the L'Arche founder-abuse record was given its dates: the movement's own commissioned inquiry of 2020 and the independent Study Commission report of 2023. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich per movement
movements.floorNote: Person-defined checks apply to several founder-charism movements - run movement by movement, and likely-cleared on the community limb at the Era 10 Freeze: all four institutionalized beyond their founders in documented form [S]. L'Arche's founder-abuse record is part of any honest telling and carries its dates — the movement's own commissioned inquiry of 2020 and the independent Study Commission report of 2023 [both S], its own published reckoning. The clear concerns the transferability of authority, not the founder's conduct; the two are not blurred.
movements.relationsSummary: Children of the long Catholic renewal line
movements.why: Four movements, each begun by lay Catholics and still running today: Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin's Catholic Worker in 1933, with its newspaper and houses of hospitality; Chiara Lubich's Focolare in 1943; the Charismatic Renewal that began on a retreat weekend at Duquesne University in 1967; and Jean Vanier's L'Arche in 1964, where people with and without intellectual disabilities share a household. L'Arche's own telling includes the abuse committed by Vanier himself, documented in inquiries the movement commissioned and published in 2020 and 2023.

sources.work: Catholic Worker: Dorothy Day, The Long Loneliness (1952), Loaves and Fishes (1963); The Catholic Worker paper (1933-); Maurin's Easy Essays
sources.note: The movement's own voice, in its founders' and its own newspaper's words.

sources.work: Focolare: Chiara Lubich's writings; the movement's General Statutes (church-approved, dated revisions)
Catholic Charismatic Renewal: Duquesne weekend testimonies (Feb 1967); Ranaghan & Ranaghan, Catholic Pentecostals (1969); the Malines Documents (1974-, Suenens)
sources.note: The movement's first book, and its own effort at theological self-regulation in the Malines Documents.

sources.work: L'Arche: Jean Vanier, Community and Growth (1979), founding record (1964); AND L'Arche International's 2020 inquiry findings + the 2023 independent Study Commission report on Vanier's abuse
sources.note: The movement's own published inquiry documents into Vanier's abuse - one of the clearest examples of an institution publicly reckoning with its founder's wrongdoing.

sources.work: Mel Piehl, Breaking Bread (1982); scholarly literature on each movement (thinner for Focolare and the Charismatic Renewal, and partly written by insiders)
sources.note: The 2023 L'Arche commission report is itself scholarly-grade work.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9 (Part I movements coverage)

movements.longDescription: Four Catholic movements, all begun by lay people, all still running. Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin founded the Catholic Worker in 1933: a newspaper, houses of hospitality, and a refusal of war that cost them readers. Chiara Lubich began Focolare in 1943. The Catholic Charismatic Renewal began on a retreat weekend at Duquesne University in February 1967 and reached parishes across the world within a decade; Cardinal Suenens's Malines Documents, from 1974, worked out how it and the wider church would live together. Jean Vanier founded L'Arche in 1964, communities in which people with and without intellectual disabilities share a household. The map treats these as four distinct movements rather than one tradition, because that is what they are — and it does not tell L'Arche's story without the abuse committed by its founder, documented in the inquiry L'Arche International commissioned and published in 2020 and in the independent study commission's report of 2023.
movements.teaser: Global, 1930s to today — the Catholic Worker, Focolare, Charismatic Renewal and L'Arche, four distinct lay movements assessed on their own terms, L'Arche's telling honestly including its founder's own record of abuse.
voices: Dorothy Day — co-founder of the Catholic Worker, author of The Long Loneliness (1952) and Loaves and Fishes (1963)
Peter Maurin — the other co-founder, whose Easy Essays set out the movement's programme in verse
Chiara Lubich — founder of Focolare in 1943; the movement's General Statutes carry her rule in church-approved form
Kevin and Dorothy Ranaghan — participants in the Catholic charismatic beginnings, whose Catholic Pentecostals (1969) is its first widely read account
Léon-Joseph Suenens — the cardinal whose Malines Documents, from 1974, gave the renewal its working relationship with the wider church
The L'Arche communities — whose members have carried the movement on, and whose organization commissioned and published the 2020 inquiry and the 2023 study commission report into its founder
movements.legacy: All four are still going. Catholic Worker houses of hospitality still operate and the paper still appears. Focolare is an international movement with statutes approved by Rome. The Charismatic Renewal reshaped ordinary parish life across the Catholic world within a generation. L'Arche continues, and its handling of its own founder's record — commissioning an inquiry, publishing what it found, then commissioning a second and independent study — has become a reference point for how a movement can tell the truth about the person who started it.

movements.name: Latin American Base Communities
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its 1990s end was classified at the Freeze as an episode-end of a still-living tradition — the base-community contraction after the 1990s — and its copy gained the living-continuation clause it was the one such row to lack. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich - participatory documents by nature (Solentiname's peasant commentaries are a published inside voice); martyr records
movements.relationsSummary: Pentecostal churches grew fast among the same poor communities in Latin America at the same time as the base communities, a pairing worth noting side by side. The base communities themselves contracted after the 1990s, but the pastoral practice they pioneered, and the communities' own heirs, continue inside Latin American church life today.
movements.why: From the 1960s, poor Catholics across Latin America began meeting in small groups to read the Bible against their own week, a practice the bishops backed at Medellín in 1968. At Solentiname in Nicaragua, Ernesto Cardenal published four volumes of what his peasant neighbors actually said about the Sunday gospel, one of the few places anywhere poor people's theology survives in their own words. Many of these communities' people were killed for it, among them Archbishop Óscar Romero, shot at the altar in March 1980.
movements.dateRationale: End 1990s KEPT and classified (b) — episode-end: the base communities' contraction after the 1990s [S]; the living continuation clause added to this row's copy at the same Freeze (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: CELAM II Medellin conclusions (Aug-Sept 1968): La Iglesia en la actual transformacion de America Latina a la luz del Concilio; Puebla (1979)
Ernesto Cardenal, El Evangelio en Solentiname (4 vols, from 1975; Orbis ET); CEB intereclesial assembly records (Brazil, 1975-)
sources.note: Published inside voice - verbatim commentary from the peasant participants themselves.

sources.work: Martyr records: Romero's homilies and diary (d. 1980, canonized 2018); the four US churchwomen (1980); the UCA Jesuits (1989); Rutilio Grande (1977)
sources.note: The truth-commission records come from an adversarial legal process and should be read with that in mind.

sources.work: Gustavo Gutierrez, Teologia de la liberacion (CEP Lima, 1971; Orbis ET A Theology of Liberation, 1973); Boff, Ecclesiogenesis (1977; ET 1986); the 1984/1986 CDF instructions
sources.note: The CDF instructions are included as the record of institutional tension over liberation theology, representing both sides.

sources.work: John Burdick, Looking for God in Brazil (California, 1993); Penny Lernoux, Cry of the People (1980)
sources.note: Lernoux's book is advocacy journalism rather than a neutral academic study.

sources.work: David Martin, Tongues of Fire (Blackwell, 1990), with Pew's 2006 survey data as a comparison; CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: From the 1960s, in Brazil and then across Latin America, small groups of poor Catholics began meeting to read the Bible together, often led by a lay coordinator or a catechist, and usually reading the gospel against their own week. At Medellín in 1968 the Latin American bishops met and gave the practice their backing. Ernesto Cardenal published four volumes of the conversations his peasant neighbours at Solentiname had about the Sunday gospel, beginning in 1975 — one of the few places anywhere you can read poor people doing theology in their own words, printed as they said them. Gustavo Gutiérrez had named the theology in 1971. Many of these communities' people were killed: Rutilio Grande in 1977, Óscar Romero at the altar in March 1980, four American churchwomen later that year, six Jesuits of the UCA in 1989. Rome's doctrinal office issued two instructions on liberation theology, in 1984 and 1986.
movements.teaser: Brazil and Central America, 1960s to 1990s — small communities of the poor who read and discussed scripture together and published their own commentary, as at Solentiname, growing up alongside the Pentecostal revival reaching the same poor.
voices: Óscar Romero — archbishop of San Salvador, whose homilies and diary survive; assassinated in March 1980 and canonized in 2018
Ernesto Cardenal — who transcribed and published the Solentiname community's own commentary on the gospels from 1975
The peasants of Solentiname — whose recorded conversations are the movement's published inside voice
Gustavo Gutiérrez — whose Teología de la liberación (1971) gave the movement's theology its name
Leonardo Boff — whose Ecclesiogenesis (1977) argued that the base communities were the church being born again from below
Rutilio Grande — the Salvadoran priest killed in 1977, three years before Romero
movements.legacy: The base communities contracted after the 1990s, and the movement is no longer what it was — but the tradition lives on: the pastoral practice, the small reading groups and the communities' own heirs continue inside Latin American church life. Romero was canonized in 2018. The Solentiname volumes remain in print in several languages. Pentecostal churches grew fast among exactly the same poor at exactly the same time, and any account of one that leaves out the other is not describing what happened.

movements.name: Emigre Orthodoxy & the Paris School
movements.informalName: Émigré Orthodoxy and the Paris School
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its 1970 end was classified as an episode-end and given the anchor the record already held: the OCA's autocephaly of 1970, the Paris generation's institutional handoff, received at this same Freeze by the American Orthodoxy entry added here. A genealogy nuance was recorded alongside — the Bulgakov/Berdyaev renaissance stands beside the Optina thread rather than simply continuing it. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: RICH (Schmemann's Journals; Mother Maria Skobtsova's life and martyrdom; institute records)
movements.relationsSummary: The Russian Revolution scattered a generation of Orthodox monks, thinkers and parishioners across Europe, many settling in Paris. Its roots run through more than one strand of Russian religious life — the Optina monastic tradition and the religious-philosophical renaissance associated with Sergei Bulgakov and Nikolai Berdyaev both feed into it. Much of English-speaking Orthodoxy today descends from this Paris generation.
movements.why: The Russian revolution scattered a generation of Orthodox monks, thinkers and parishioners across Europe, and many landed in Paris, where the St Sergius Institute opened in 1925. Mother Maria Skobtsova ran a hostel there, sheltered Jews under the German occupation, and died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945. Vladimir Lossky's Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church, written in French and published in 1944, put Orthodox theology in front of Western readers for the first time.
movements.dateRationale: End 1970 KEPT and classified (b) — episode-end with the anchor the record already held: the OCA's autocephaly of 1970 [S], the Paris generation's institutional handoff, received at this Freeze by IX.48 (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: Alexander Schmemann, The Journals of Father Alexander Schmemann 1973-1983 (SVS, 2000); For the Life of the World (1963)
Mother Maria Skobtsova: essays (Essential Writings, Orbis 2003); Ravensbruck death (31 Mar 1945); canonization (2004)
sources.note: A woman's leadership and martyrdom at the center of this movement's story.

sources.work: St Sergius Institute records (1925-); Bulgakov's corpus WITH the 1935-37 Sophia controversy file (both sides); Florovsky, Ways of Russian Theology (1937); Lossky, Mystical Theology (1944); YMCA Press
sources.note: Institute records, with the Sophia controversy documented from both sides. This movement's roots run through more than the Optina monastic tradition - equally through the religious-philosophical renaissance associated with Bulgakov and Berdyaev.

sources.work: Antoine Arjakovsky, The Way: Religious Thinkers of the Russian Emigration in Paris and Their Journal (ET Notre Dame, 2013); Michael Plekon, Living Icons (2002)
CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: The Russian revolution scattered a whole church's worth of thinkers, monks and parishioners across Europe, and a remarkable number of them landed in Paris. The St Sergius Institute was founded there in 1925 and became the centre of it. Sergei Bulgakov's theology drew a controversy of its own between 1935 and 1937, argued in print on both sides; Georges Florovsky's Ways of Russian Theology (1937) called the emigration back to the Greek fathers; Vladimir Lossky's Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church, written in French and published in 1944, put Orthodox theology in front of Western readers who had never had it. YMCA Press printed what they wrote. Mother Maria Skobtsova ran a hostel in Paris, sheltered Jews under the occupation, and died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945. The next generation — Alexander Schmemann, John Meyendorff — carried the work to America, and Schmemann's journals from 1973 to 1983 record what that cost and what it was for.
movements.teaser: Paris and then the world, 1920s to 1970s — the Optina monastic tradition scattered by revolution and rebuilt in exile, its record kept in Alexander Schmemann's journals and in Mother Maria Skobtsova's life and martyrdom.
voices: Sergei Bulgakov — St Sergius's leading theologian, whose work drew the controversy of 1935–37, argued on both sides in print
Georges Florovsky — whose Ways of Russian Theology (1937) called the emigration back to the Greek fathers
Vladimir Lossky — whose Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church (1944) introduced Orthodox theology to a Western readership
Mother Maria Skobtsova — poet and nun who ran a Paris hostel, sheltered Jews under the occupation, died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945, and was canonized in 2004
Alexander Schmemann — whose For the Life of the World (1963) and journals from 1973 to 1983 are read far outside Orthodoxy
John Meyendorff — historian and theologian of the same generation, who carried the school's work into American academic life
movements.legacy: The Paris generation's own episode closed around 1970, with the handoff its institutions had been building toward: the Orthodox Church in America received autocephaly in 1970, and St Vladimir's Seminary in New York became the school this tradition had built in a second country. Much of English-speaking Orthodoxy is descended from here. Skobtsova was canonized in 2004. Schmemann's For the Life of the World is still put into students' hands in every tradition, and Lossky is still the book people are given when they ask what Orthodox theology actually says.

movements.name: The Coptic Monastic & Sunday-School Revival
movements.informalName: The Coptic Monastic and Sunday-School Revival
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its 1940s start was kept rather than deepened, with the Habib Girgis material disclosed instead of absorbed: his teaching from the 1890s and the 1918 General Sunday School Committee sit before this window, and the two research runs diverge on whether the 1918 year is verified — so no date string rests on it. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich (both renewal streams wrote copiously; living memory; new martyrs in the present century)
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of the map's longest unbroken lane - back to the Desert itself
movements.why: Habib Girgis built a church-wide Sunday-school movement from the 1890s that trained generations of teachers and, later, bishops, while from mid-century the Egyptian desert monasteries, long emptying, filled again under Patriarch Kyrillos VI. The church has kept adding to its list of martyrs in the present century: the twenty-one Coptic laborers killed in Libya on 15 February 2015 were entered into the church's own calendar of saints and given an icon that same year. This is a church that names its dead rather than remembering them only in the abstract.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1940s KEPT over the 1918 branch, with the Habib Girgis material DISCLOSED rather than absorbed: his teaching runs from the 1890s and the General Sunday School Committee dates to 1918, both before this window — and the two research runs diverge on that year (the survey verified it; the independent sources run could not page-verify it and holds it [S]), so no date string rests on it. The ratified VIII.13→IX.10 chain already discloses the 34-year gap (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: Habib Girgis (1876-1951): catechetical writings, curricula, the Sunday-School movement's organization (c. 1918) and magazine; canonized 2013
sources.note: Girgis's own Arabic-language corpus; the Suriel study is the fullest English-language treatment of it.

sources.work: Matta El-Meskeen (Matthew the Poor): Orthodox Prayer Life (ET SVS 2003) and the St Macarius corpus; Kyrillos VI papers (1959-71); Shenouda III's books (1971-2012)
sources.note: The monastic stream's own voice - the Wadi Natrun repopulation's theological record.

sources.work: The new martyrs: the 21 Libya martyrs (15 Feb 2015) - the church's own synaxarium addition and icon (2015); Mosebach, The 21 (ET 2019)
sources.note: Mosebach's own account is literary journalism rather than academic history, worth reading as such.

sources.work: Bishop Suriel, Habib Girgis: Coptic Orthodox Educator and a Light in the Darkness (SVS Press, Coptic Studies 2, 2017); S. S. Hasan, Christians versus Muslims in Modern Egypt (OUP, 2003)
CHC vol. 5, ch. 21 'Coptic Christianity in modern Egypt' (O'Mahony); CHC vol. 9
sources.note: Standard reference works on modern Coptic Christianity.

movements.longDescription: Two renewals ran together in the Coptic Orthodox Church and remade it. The first was catechetical. Habib Girgis, born in 1876, taught and wrote from the 1890s and built a church-wide Sunday-school movement, organized around 1918, that trained a generation of lay teachers and then of bishops. The second was monastic: from the middle of the century the desert monasteries, which had been emptying, were repopulated, and the movement gathered pace under Kyrillos VI, patriarch from 1959 to 1971. Matthew the Poor, of the monastery of St Macarius, wrote a body of spiritual work that is read well outside Egypt. Shenouda III, who came out of the Sunday-school generation, was patriarch from 1971 until 2012 and published steadily throughout. And the church has gone on adding to its martyrology in the present century: the twenty-one Copts killed in Libya on 15 February 2015 were entered in the synaxarium and given an icon in the same year.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 1940s to today — a monastic and Sunday-school revival continuing the map's longest unbroken lane back to the Desert itself, with new martyrs added to its record in this century.
voices: Habib Girgis (1876–1951) — the catechist and writer who built the Coptic Sunday-school movement; canonized in 2013
Kyrillos VI — patriarch from 1959 to 1971, under whom the monastic repopulation gathered pace
Matthew the Poor — of the monastery of St Macarius, whose Orthodox Prayer Life and wider corpus are read outside Egypt
Shenouda III — formed in the Sunday schools, patriarch from 1971 to 2012, and a prolific writer throughout
The twenty-one — the Coptic labourers killed in Libya on 15 February 2015, added to the church's own synaxarium and given an icon the same year
movements.legacy: It is a living church whose lane on this map runs back, unbroken, to the desert fathers themselves. The Sunday schools are still the church's teaching system and still the route by which much of its clergy is formed. The monasteries are full again. Girgis was canonized in 2013, and Matthew the Poor's books have found readers in traditions with no connection to Egypt at all. The 2015 martyrs are commemorated liturgically, which is what this church has always done with its dead: not remembered in the abstract, but named.

movements.name: Global South Pentecostal Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1). It was the known first hit of the era's prose sweep, and the sweep's words were applied here: the prosperity-gospel line, previously a present-tense characterization of a living family, now stands on dated texts and on the row's own bounded-window rule. Scale claims about this family are carried on the contemporary register — an independent counter named, or the figure marked as self-report. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich but unevenly mediated; only per-community windows (one body, one country, one generation) are honest build shapes
movements.floorNote: The prosperity-gospel current is named on dated texts, not characterized in the present tense: the Lausanne Movement's own published critique documents [S] and named churches' own statements are where the argument is on record, and the row's own bounded-window rule governs any assessment — which community, which decades. Scale claims about this family ride the contemporary register: the 600-million-class totals are self-report or definitional aggregate until an independent counter is named, and the definitional spread is itself the real datum.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Azusa + AIC lines; the map's present edge
movements.why: By the second half of the century, the weight of Pentecostal Christianity had shifted south, carried by churches founded in the Global South by people from it: the Redeemed Christian Church of God in Nigeria in 1952, Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul in 1958, the Igreja Universal in Brazil in 1977. These churches argue fiercely among themselves over prosperity teaching, and that argument is on the public record in their own sermons and in the published critiques of the Lausanne movement and African evangelical theologians who reject it.

sources.work: RCCG records (1952–, Holy Ghost Congress); Yoido Full Gospel Church (1958–, Cho, The Fourth Dimension, 1979); Assembleias de Deus (1911–); Igreja Universal (1977–, Macedo); El Shaddai (1984, Velarde)

The prosperity-gospel tension in these churches' own voices: prosperity teaching in their own published sermons, and the published critiques from within the same Pentecostal family (Lausanne evaluations; African evangelical theologians' rebukes)
sources.note: The prosperity-gospel debate as this family of churches argues it out itself, with both sides represented from the inside.

sources.note: The survey standard, majority-world-centered.

Pew's Spirit and Power (2006) and Global Christianity (2011); World Christian Encyclopedia, 3rd ed. (2019); and denominations' own self-reported counts

Denominations' own self-reported numbers are less independently verifiable, and the widely repeated figure of 600 million should always be read with that complication in mind.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9 (Part I Pentecostalism coverage)

movements.longDescription: By the second half of the century the weight of Pentecostal Christianity had moved south, and the churches carrying it were mostly founded in the Global South by people from it. The Assembleias de Deus in Brazil date from 1911; the Redeemed Christian Church of God was founded in Nigeria in 1952; Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul from 1958; the Igreja Universal in Brazil from 1977; El Shaddai in the Philippines from 1984. They are not one tradition and this map does not pretend otherwise — only a bounded window — one body, one country, one generation — describes anything real here. The family's sharpest internal argument, over prosperity teaching, is on the record in the family's own published words: in the sermons that teach it, and in the critiques published by the Lausanne movement and by African evangelical theologians who reject it.
movements.teaser: Brazil, Nigeria, Ghana, Korea and the Philippines, 1950s to today — Pentecostalism's present edge, descended from Azusa Street and Africa's independent churches alike, its argument over the prosperity gospel carried on the record in the movement's own published critiques rather than described from outside.
voices: David Yonggi Cho — founder of Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul in 1958, whose The Fourth Dimension (1979) circulated worldwide
The Redeemed Christian Church of God — founded in Nigeria in 1952; its Holy Ghost Congress records are its own account of its scale
Edir Macedo — founder of the Igreja Universal do Reino de Deus in Brazil in 1977
Mike Velarde — founder of El Shaddai in the Philippines in 1984
The family's own critics — the Lausanne movement's published evaluations and African evangelical theologians' published rebukes of prosperity teaching, argued inside the family rather than about it
movements.legacy: This is the map's present edge rather than a finished story. Numbers here need care: the figures in the hundreds of millions that circulate come partly from denominational self-counts and partly from surveys using different definitions of who is being counted, and the spread between them tells you as much as the totals do. What is not in doubt is the direction of travel. Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity is now largely a Global South matter, and this map carries a separate entry for the congregations these churches have planted back in Europe. The scholarship has followed: Anderson, Martin, Kalu and others have made this the central subject of world Christianity rather than its margin.

movements.name: Persecuted-Church Traditions of the Communist Era (Initsiativniki Baptists; Romania's Lord's Army)
movements.informalName: The Persecuted Church of the Communist Era
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its 1991 end was classified as a documented institutional terminus — the dissolution of the USSR ended the persecution regime that defines the row — with its member movements' continuing life said plainly in its copy. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich via samizdat and post-1991 archives (the Council of Prisoners' Relatives' bulletins are first-rank ordinary persecution literature)
movements.relationsSummary: Kin of the Chinese suffering church
movements.why: In the Soviet Union, a group of Baptist ministers broke in 1961 with the state-registered union and ran their own underground press; their Council of Prisoners' Relatives began issuing bulletins in 1964 that listed arrests and confiscations by name, week by week. In Romania, the Lord's Army, founded by the priest Iosif Trifa in 1923, continued under Communist rule, and its hymn-writer Traian Dorz left prison memoirs behind. When the Soviet archives opened after 1991, the persecutors' own files could finally be read alongside the persecuted's.
movements.dateRationale: End 1991 KEPT and classified (a) — documented institutional terminus: the dissolution of the USSR ended the persecution regime that DEFINES this row [S]; the member movements live on, and the copy says so (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.note: First-rank grassroots persecution literature - documentation led largely by prisoners' wives and mothers.

sources.note: The movement's theology expressed in song, written under persecution.

sources.note: These records come from the persecuting state's own files and archives.

sources.note: Outside observers writing with an advocacy position; Sawatsky is the standard scholarly account.

sources.work: Owen Chadwick, The Christian Church in the Cold War (Penguin, 1992); CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: Under Communist rule, believers who would not accept the terms the state offered went underground, and left an extraordinary paper trail doing it. In the Soviet Union a group of Baptist ministers broke in 1961 with the registered union over state control of church life; they were called the Initsiativniki, after their initiative group, and they ran their own press, Khristianin. Their Council of Prisoners' Relatives — the relatives of imprisoned believers — began issuing bulletins in 1964 listing arrests, sentences, searches and confiscations, name by name. Georgi Vins's Testament from Prison reached the West in translation in 1975. In Romania the Lord's Army, founded in 1923 by the priest Iosif Trifa around his weekly paper, went on under Communist rule; Traian Dorz wrote hymns and prison memoirs. When the archives opened after 1991, the persecutors' own files could be read alongside the persecuted's.
movements.teaser: The USSR and Romania, 1945 to 1991 — Initsiativniki Baptists and Romania's Lord's Army, kin to the Chinese suffering church, documented in samizdat and in the Council of Prisoners' Relatives' bulletins from inside the underground.
voices: Georgi Vins — Initsiativniki leader whose Testament from Prison was published in English in 1975
The Council of Prisoners' Relatives — who compiled and circulated the bulletins from 1964, first-rank documentation of ordinary persecution
Iosif Trifa — the Romanian priest who founded the Lord's Army in 1923 and edited its weekly paper
Traian Dorz — the Lord's Army's hymn-writer, whose prison memoirs survive
Michael Bourdeaux — who gathered this material in the West from the 1960s; the Keston archive is largely his doing
movements.legacy: The Communist-era persecution these movements faced ended with the fall of Communism across the Eastern bloc, including the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991; the movements themselves live on. The samizdat these communities produced is now recognized as among the best documentation anywhere of what religious persecution actually looks like from underneath — not martyrologies written afterwards but bulletins written that week, listing who had been taken and from where. The Keston archive preserves much of it. The pattern of unregistered congregations refusing the state's terms is kin to what happened in China over the same decades, a real historical relation rather than a coincidence.

movements.name: Messianic Judaism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), with its double-direction sensitivity carried. Its floorNote's confessional statement was given its dates at this Freeze, and the boundary with the largely gentile Torah-observance current was drawn rather than blurred: that current is the separate entry added at this same gate, and the two worlds' own publications draw the line. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate (recent, self-documenting, contested from multiple sides)
movements.floorNote: Mainstream confessions are trinitarian — no plain A1 question for those bodies; assessed per specific body as always, and now with dates: the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations (founded 1979) states it in "Defining Messianic Judaism" (2005) [S], and the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America in its own statement of faith [S]. A living body can change its confession; these are dated readings of published statements.
movements.relationsSummary: Messianic Judaism raises again a question as old as the church itself: whether a person can be fully Jewish and a follower of Jesus. That question was the first argument the early church ever had, among the first Jewish believers in Jesus, and this movement brings it back in living form.
movements.why: From the 1960s and 1970s, Jewish believers in Jesus began forming congregations that kept Sabbath, festivals and Hebrew liturgy rather than joining gentile churches. The Hebrew Christian Alliance of America, founded in 1915, renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance in 1975, a change of name that was also a change of self-understanding. David Stern's Complete Jewish Bible, published in 1998, and the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations' 2005 statement "Defining Messianic Judaism" are among the clearest attempts to say what the movement actually is.

sources.work: The movement's own institutional statements: the Hebrew Christian Alliance of America's 1915 statement of faith, renamed the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America's in 1975; the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations' 1979 doctrinal basis and later statements; and Jews for Jesus's publications from 1973 (Rosen)
David Stern, Messianic Jewish Manifesto (1988), Complete Jewish Bible (1998); Mark Kinzer, Postmissionary Messianic Judaism (Brazos, 2005)
sources.note: The movement's own theological range in print, from Stern to Kinzer.

sources.work: Jewish communal responses to the movement (counter-missionary literature; denominational positions) and Christian responses from the supersessionism debate
sources.note: This material is genuinely contested from multiple directions, and both sides are represented on their own terms.

sources.work: Carol Harris-Shapiro, Messianic Judaism (Beacon, 1999); Dan Cohn-Sherbok, Messianic Judaism (2000); Yaakov Ariel, Evangelizing the Chosen People (UNC, 2000)
sources.note: Three outside scholarly accounts, each written from a different position toward the movement.

sources.work: David Rudolph & Joel Willitts (eds.), Introduction to Messianic Judaism (Zondervan, 2013)
sources.note: Messianic Judaism's own scholarly base, distinct from the separate Hebrew Roots movement.

sources.work: Congregation and adherent counts: the MJAA/UMJC's own self-reports vs. scholarly estimates and the Pew 2013 US Jewish survey
sources.note: The self-reported figures should be read as self-reports; the survey and scholarly estimates are more independently grounded, though who counts as Messianic Jewish is itself contested from both directions.

movements.longDescription: Jewish believers in Jesus are as old as the church, but the modern congregational movement is recent. From the 1960s and 1970s, Jewish believers began forming congregations that kept Jewish practice — Sabbath, festivals, Hebrew liturgy — rather than joining gentile churches. The Hebrew Christian Alliance of America, founded in 1915, renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America in 1975, and the change of name was also a change of self-description. The Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations followed in 1979 and set out its position in a document called 'Defining Messianic Judaism' in 2005. Jews for Jesus, founded in 1973, took a more evangelistic shape. The movement's own writers have argued about what it is: David Stern's Messianic Jewish Manifesto appeared in 1988 and his Complete Jewish Bible in 1998, and Mark Kinzer's Postmissionary Messianic Judaism in 2005. It is argued about from outside in two directions at once, by Jewish communal bodies and in Christian debates over supersessionism.
movements.teaser: Israel and North America, 1960s to today — a living return of Christianity's oldest contested question, deliberately echoing the map's own first-century Nazoraean entry, and requiring double care because its sensitivities run in both Jewish and Christian directions at once.
voices: Moishe Rosen — founder of Jews for Jesus in 1973
David Stern — author of the Messianic Jewish Manifesto (1988) and translator of the Complete Jewish Bible (1998)
Mark Kinzer — whose Postmissionary Messianic Judaism (2005) argued the movement's case in its most demanding form
The Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations — founded in 1979; its 'Defining Messianic Judaism' (2005) is the movement's most-cited own statement
The Messianic Jewish Alliance of America — the Hebrew Christian Alliance of 1915 under the name it took in 1975
movements.legacy: It is a living movement, with congregations in Israel and North America and a body of published self-definition unusually dense for its size. Its Bible translation and its congregational liturgies have circulated well beyond it. Its lasting significance on this map is the question it keeps open rather than the institutions it has built: whether a person can be fully Jewish and a follower of Jesus was the first thing the church ever argued about, and this movement puts it back in living form. Counting it is hard — the congregations' own figures and outside estimates differ, and nothing independent settles it.

movements.name: Ecumenical Community Traditions - Taize & Iona
movements.informalName: The Communities of Taizé and Iona
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (Era 10 Step 0; c2 CLEARED on the documented founder-to-successor transition)

Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.

Iona's own institutional continuation carries the same limb.
movements.relationsSummary: Deliberate heirs of monastic lines - Iona literally on Columba's island
movements.why: George MacLeod founded the Iona Community in 1938 and set it to rebuilding the abbey on Columba's own island, a project that took until 1965. Roger Schutz began the community at Taizé in France two years earlier, in 1940, and from the 1970s young people started arriving by the thousands, for meetings held every year since 1978. When Brother Roger was murdered in 2005, the community simply continued, first under Brother Alois and then, from 2023, Brother Matthew.

sources.note: Two founder-to-successor transitions, documented in the community's own dated announcements.

sources.note: The community's own rule, publications, and sung theology.

sources.note: Documented in the communities' own institutional records.

sources.note: Spink's biography was written with the community's authorized access - worth keeping in mind as a positioning factor.

movements.longDescription: Two communities, founded two years apart, that set out to be modern heirs of the old monastic ones. George MacLeod founded the Iona Community in 1938 and set it to rebuilding the abbey on Columba's own island — a work that took until 1965 — on the conviction that worship and labour and politics belong together. Roger Schutz began the community at Taizé in France in 1940; its Rule was written in 1954, and from the 1970s young people began arriving in large numbers, with a Council of Youth in 1974 and European meetings held annually from 1978. Both are ecumenical by design, with members from many churches and none of the usual boundaries between them. Brother Roger was murdered on 16 August 2005, and the community continued under Brother Alois and then, from 2023, Brother Matthew.
movements.teaser: France and Scotland, 1938/1940 to today — Taizé and Iona, ecumenical communities built as deliberate heirs of older monastic lines, Iona's community set literally on Columba's own island.
voices: George MacLeod — founder of the Iona Community in 1938, author of Only One Way Left (1956)
Roger Schutz — founder of Taizé in 1940 and author of its Rule (1954); murdered on 16 August 2005
Brother Alois — Roger's successor, under whom the community continued, handing on in turn to Brother Matthew in 2023
John Bell — of the Iona Community's Wild Goose worship group, whose songs and liturgies are sung far outside Scotland
The Letters from Taizé — the community's own running correspondence with the young people who come to it
movements.legacy: Both communities are still going and both still take visitors. Taizé's European meetings have been held every year since 1978, and Iona's Wild Goose material, much of it by John Bell, is in hymnals across the English-speaking world. Their passage through the death of a founder is itself part of what they leave: Taizé's continuation under Alois and then Matthew is one of the clearest documented cases anywhere on this map of a community outliving the person who began it.

movements.name: Oneness Pentecostalism
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — Jesus'-name modalism at own-confession strength where a dated text is staged, and recorded OPEN where it is not (the record-mandated Era 10 disposition); register retained
movements.statusDescription: The register's record-mandated disposition for this era — assigned to this run by the row's own record — formally RECORDED at the Era 10 Freeze, staged per body. Its 1993 end was found to rest on no event in either research run and was corrected to the present. The person-defined criterion's fourteenth live application also ran here and found the criterion inapplicable: there is no single founder to test, so the disposition runs on floor grounds alone. Register retained. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich own record
movements.floorNote: Formally disposed at the Era 10 Freeze, per body and on dated texts, as this row's own record assigned. The formation record is verified: the April 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting and McAlister's baptismal sermon, the 1914 rebaptisms [S], and the Assemblies of God's 1916 Statement of Fundamental Truths (verified) — the documented rupture text, own-voice on BOTH sides. UPCI: its Articles of Faith stand in the annually republished Manual, and any assessment cites them BY MANUAL YEAR — the citation is staged, though the current text's own wording remains [S] this session. PAW: no current statement is named anywhere in this era's research — only an undated "Minute Book / statement of faith" [S] — so the per-body sub-finding is recorded OPEN with the gap named rather than filled; the body is the oldest of these and was historically interracial while the white bodies separated, and its own telling carries that. ALJC (1952 merger [S]): no current statement is staged in any input; recorded OPEN with the gap named. Two packing seams are disclosed on purpose: the True Jesus Church (1917 Beijing, verified) sits between this row and IX.5, and La Luz del Mundo (packed in IX.16) descends from the same 1914 [S] Mexican Apostolic milieu. c2 is null deliberately and argued: no single founder — McAlister, Ewart, Cook and Haywood, multiple bodies from the start, all outgrown — so there is no person-ground to test and the disposition runs on floor grounds alone. A living body can change its confession; every clause here describes a dated text, never the faith of any member.
movements.relationsSummary: Oneness Pentecostalism grew directly out of the wider Pentecostal movement that followed the Azusa Street revival. Two other traditions trace back to the same roots: the True Jesus Church, founded in Beijing in 1917, and La Luz del Mundo in Mexico, which descends from the same 1914 Mexican Apostolic revival.
movements.why: In April 1913, at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting, R. E. McAlister preached that the baptisms recorded in Acts were performed in the name of Jesus alone, and the following year Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook baptized each other on that basis. When the Assemblies of God adopted an explicitly trinitarian statement of faith in 1916, the ministers who could not sign it left and formed their own bodies, among them the interracial Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, long led by G. T. Haywood. Baptism in the name of Jesus alone is still what a visitor to these churches notices first.
movements.dateRationale: End 1993 → PRESENT: class (c) unsupported artifact — no 1993 event exists in any indexed history in either research run, and the UPCI's own annual record runs unbroken past it; the living-era protocol's known first case, confirmed. String "1913 onward" → "1913-present"; start 1913 stands (the April 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting) (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.note: The UPCI's own confession, reissued annually — its own dated, own-voice statement of faith. The record runs unbroken well past any particular closing date sometimes given for this movement.

sources.note: The 1913-16 split is documented in confessional terms on both sides. Ewart's own account is a retrospective, insider one.

sources.work: The Black Oneness lineage: G. T. Haywood's writings and hymns; PAW records (sustained interracialism; the 1924 separations; the 1945 UPCI merger's racial dimension)
sources.note: Part of the movement's own record, in the voices of Black Oneness leaders and congregations themselves.

sources.work: David A. Reed, 'In Jesus' Name': The History and Beliefs of Oneness Pentecostals (Deo, 2008); Talmadge French, Our God Is One (1999); Daniel Ramirez, Migrating Faith (UNC, 2015)
sources.note: Reed writes as an insider scholar; Ramirez covers the Apostolic borderlands wing specifically.

sources.work: Oneness constituency figures
sources.note: The UPCI's and other bodies' self-reports should be read as self-reports; the World Christian Encyclopedia's 2019 figure is a more independently cross-checked aggregate, distinct from those self-reported numbers.

movements.longDescription: In April 1913, at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting, R. E. McAlister preached on baptism and observed that the baptisms recorded in Acts are performed in the name of Jesus. The following year Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook baptized one another on that basis, and the question tore through the young Pentecostal movement. In October 1916 the Assemblies of God adopted its Statement of Fundamental Truths, an explicitly trinitarian confession, and the ministers who could not sign it left — so the rupture stands documented in each side's own words. Several bodies followed. The Pentecostal Assemblies of the World is the oldest, Oneness from 1916, and was interracial through decades in which other Pentecostal bodies separated by race; the separations of 1924, and the racial dimension of the 1945 merger, are part of its own telling, and G. T. Haywood was among its leaders. The United Pentecostal Church International was formed by a merger vote on 25 September 1945 and publishes its Articles of Faith in a Manual reissued each year.
movements.teaser: North America and then worldwide, from 1913 — a Pentecostal current inseparable from Azusa Street's own aftermath, distinguished by the Jesus'-name baptismal practice and modalist confession its own named bodies state in their own published statements of faith.
voices: R. E. McAlister — whose April 1913 baptismal sermon at Arroyo Seco opened the question
Frank Ewart — rebaptized in 1914, and later author of The Phenomenon of Pentecost (1947), the movement's own history of its beginnings
Glenn Cook — the other party to the 1914 rebaptisms
G. T. Haywood — leader in the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, whose writings and hymns are part of the movement's own record
The Assemblies of God's Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916) — the trinitarian confession whose adoption occasioned the departure, and the other half of the documented rupture
movements.legacy: These are living churches with congregations worldwide, and their distinguishing practice — baptism in the name of Jesus — is what a visitor notices first. Their scale is hard to fix: the figures in circulation are the bodies' own, without an independent count to check them against. Two seams run outward from this story. The True Jesus Church, founded in Beijing in 1917, shares the same Pentecostal roots; and La Luz del Mundo in Mexico descends from the same Mexican Apostolic revival of 1914.

movements.informalName: Iglesia ni Cristo, The Way, the Unification Church, and La Luz del Mundo

Iglesia ni Cristo: registered 27 Jul 1914 (verified); the Manalo messenger (Sugo) claim per the church's own history pages (own-voice, verified); doctrine per its own published teaching in Pasugo, from Feb 1939 (verified) — its website's belief pages are undated, so citations use dated Pasugo articles [S]; two generations of succession survived (1963, 2009 [S]). La Luz del Mundo's Oneness descent is the disclosed seam with IX.15; Iglesia ni Cristo is the Philippine lane's largest missing body, and the row-split question that follows from it stays open.
movements.why: Four separately founded movements: Iglesia ni Cristo, registered in the Philippines in 1914, whose magazine Pasugo has carried its teaching since 1939; The Way International, which grew out of Victor Paul Wierwille's radio ministry in the 1940s; the Unification Church, founded in Seoul in 1954 by Sun Myung Moon; and La Luz del Mundo, founded in Guadalajara in 1926 and still led by an apostle in succession from its founder. Each has its own scripture, founder claim and history, told here on its own terms rather than as one shared story.

movements.longDescription: Four separately founded bodies are carried together here for the map's economy, not because they share a confession — they do not, and each is described from its own published texts. Iglesia ni Cristo was registered in the Philippines on 27 July 1914; its own history presents Felix Manalo as God's messenger for the last days, and its magazine Pasugo has published its teaching since February 1939. The Way International began as Victor Paul Wierwille's Vesper Chimes radio ministry in 1942 and took its later name in 1955; his Power for Abundant Living appeared in 1971 and Jesus Christ Is Not God in 1975, a title that states its own position. The Unification Church, now the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, was founded in Seoul on 1 May 1954 by Sun Myung Moon, whose Divine Principle appeared in Korean in 1966. La Luz del Mundo was founded in Guadalajara on 6 April 1926 by Eusebio Joaquín González, and is led by an apostle in succession from him.
movements.teaser: The Philippines, North America, Korea and Mexico, from 1914 — Iglesia ni Cristo, The Way International, the Unification Church and La Luz del Mundo, four separately-founded bodies packed on one register row for roster economy rather than for any shared confession, each assessed on its own published texts.
