Sun Myung Moon — founder of the Unification Church on 1 May 1954; the Divine Principle (1966) is its foundational text
Eusebio Joaquín González — founder of La Luz del Mundo in Guadalajara on 6 April 1926, first in its line of apostles
movements.legacy: All four continue, and all four have passed through at least one succession — Iglesia ni Cristo twice, in 1963 and 2009; The Way through two changes of leadership; the Unification Church into a contested succession after Sun Myung Moon's death in 2012; La Luz del Mundo in 1964 and again in 2014. Iglesia ni Cristo's own counts run to millions and it is the largest church founded in the Philippines; no independent count is cited here. Court records are part of these bodies' public record too: The Way's leadership changes ran alongside litigation, and La Luz del Mundo's current leader was convicted in California in 2022 following a guilty plea. Those are matters of public record and part of any honest telling.

movements.name: Branch Davidians & Apocalyptic Splinters
movements.informalName: The Branch Davidians and the Apocalyptic Splinters
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — person-defined ground in extreme form, on the movement's own texts (Era 10 Step 0); a closed movement, its dates made honest; register retained
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and kept for the map's own honesty at this family's edge, with its dates made honest: the window-fill band was replaced with the real 1929–1993, whereupon its end becomes a documented terminus and its not-living flag coheres instead of contradicting a present-day fill. Remnant existence is disclosed only in those terms — no present community and no non-public person is identified. Register retained.
movements.floorNote: Three generations of leadership each left their own writings: the founder, his successors, and an unfinished theological work from the group's final leader. In each case, authority rested on a named individual's own revelation or interpretation — an especially pronounced example of a movement built on one person's claim to reveal truth, rather than on a shared community confession.
movements.relationsSummary: Victor Houteff broke from Adventism in 1929, and his followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco in 1935. Leadership passed to the Branch group under Ben and Lois Roden in 1955, then to David Koresh in the 1980s. A federal siege from 28 February to 19 April 1993 ended in a fire that killed seventy-six people. Much of what is known about how the siege ended comes from the government side — congressional hearings and the Danforth Report — since the community itself did not survive to tell its own account.
movements.why: Victor Houteff broke from Adventism in 1929 and published his reform message as The Shepherd's Rod, and his followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco in 1935. Leadership passed to Ben and Lois Roden's Branch group in 1955 and then to David Koresh in the 1980s. On 28 February 1993 a federal raid began a siege that ended on 19 April in a fire that killed seventy-six people, leaving Koresh's own exposition of the seven seals unfinished.
movements.dateRationale: "20th c." / 1906–2026 → 1929–1993: class (c) window-fill artifact fixed at BOTH ends — Houteff's Shepherd's Rod, 1929, and the fire of 19 Apr 1993 (both verified). The end thereby becomes a class (a) documented terminus and living:false coheres with it instead of contradicting a present-day fill (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The movement's own texts: Houteff, The Shepherd's Rod (vol. 1 1930, vol. 2 1932); Ben and Lois Roden's Branch publications; Koresh's unfinished Seven Seals manuscript (1993, via Tabor & Gallagher)
sources.note: An offshoot of Seventh-day Adventism.

sources.work: The 1993 Waco siege record: congressional hearings; the Danforth Report (2000)
sources.note: The community's end is documented mostly by the state that besieged it, a one-sided record worth reading critically.

sources.work: Tabor & Gallagher, Why Waco? (California, 1995); Kenneth Newport, The Branch Davidians of Waco (OUP, 2006)
sources.note: The two standard scholarly works; Newport traces the full lineage from Houteff to Koresh.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: In 1929 Victor Houteff began circulating a reform message inside Adventism that his church rejected, and published it as The Shepherd's Rod in 1930 and 1932; his followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco, Texas, in 1935. A Branch group formed under Ben Roden in 1955 and was later led by his wife Lois. David Koresh took leadership in the 1980s. On 28 February 1993 a federal raid began a siege that ended on 19 April in a fire that killed seventy-six people, and Koresh's exposition of the seven seals was left unfinished. What was already an extreme case of authority resting on one person is now known to most people through the fire — and the surviving record of the ending is largely the state's: congressional hearings, and the Danforth Report of 2000.
movements.teaser: North America, 1929 to 1993 — named here only for the map's own honesty at this family's edge: an extreme case of authority claimed by a single founder, from Houteff's break with Adventism to the fire that ended it.
voices: Victor Houteff — began the Shepherd's Rod movement in 1929 and published its founding volumes in 1930 and 1932
Ben and Lois Roden — under whom the Branch group formed in 1955 and continued
David Koresh — leader from the 1980s, whose unfinished exposition of the seven seals, written in 1993, survives
The state's record — the congressional hearings and the Danforth Report of 2000, which are most of what exists about the ending, and were written by one of the parties to it
movements.legacy: The community at Mount Carmel was destroyed in 1993, and the movement ended there. Small remnant groups exist, but no present-day member is named or described. What survives publicly is the scholarship the siege provoked — Tabor and Gallagher's Why Waco? (1995) and Kenneth Newport's study of 2006 — which asked what the group actually believed, a question the congressional hearings had largely not asked, and which changed how researchers and law-enforcement agencies approach religious groups under siege.

movements.name: Progressive Christianity (a broad label, not one movement)
movements.statusWord: A label, not one movement — no entry-level finding, ever (Era 10 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Held to its own law at the Era 10 Step 0 run: no entry-level finding was made on the label, and none ever will be. What the run did instead was date the illustrations, recast the why-clause on published statements rather than on communities in the aggregate, and give the label the history it lacked — the mainline century entry added at this same Freeze is its missing parent, named in both directions. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Varies entirely by community - the label names many very different bodies
movements.floorNote: Progressive Christianity is not one doctrinal position — the label covers very different congregations and networks, so any assessment of specific claims applies only to a particular body's own dated confession, never to the whole label. As one example: ProgressiveChristianity.org, founded in 1994, has published its "8 Points" in several revisions over the years, each its own dated statement — illustrative of one organization, not a confession for the whole movement, and any citation needs to specify which year's version is meant.
movements.relationsSummary: Progressive Christianity covers mainline progressive congregations, post-evangelical networks, and much in between, with the emerging church of the 1990s and 2000s as its most documented expression. It descends from the mainline century of liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy, which hands off to it around 1990.
movements.why: Progressive Christianity is a label, not one movement: it covers old mainline parishes with a century of history behind them, congregations founded within the last decade, and simply readers of particular books, with no single founder or confession linking them all. The Center for Progressive Christianity, founded in 1994, has published and revised its own set of guiding points more than once, each version its own dated statement.

sources.work: The Center for Progressive Christianity's '8 Points' (organization founded 1994, with successive dated revisions - each revision its own dated statement)
Gary Dorrien, The Making of American Liberal Theology (WJK, 3 vols: 2001, 2003, 2006)
sources.note: Traces the intellectual genealogy of American liberal theology.

sources.work: David Hollinger, After Cloven Tongues of Fire (Princeton, 2013); Diana Butler Bass, Christianity for the Rest of Us (2006)
sources.note: Hollinger is the standard account of the mainline trajectory; Bass writes as a participant-adjacent journalist, useful for describing the movement's present state.

sources.work: Claims that this is a 'fast-growing current'
sources.note: Claims of fast growth currently rest on journalism and self-description. Survey data from Pew and PRRI don't measure 'progressive Christianity' as a defined category, so these growth claims can't be checked against independent data.

movements.longDescription: This is a label rather than a movement, and the map treats it as one. 'Progressive Christianity' is used by mainline congregations, by post-evangelical networks, by individual writers and by organizations with no relation to one another, and the communities it covers differ from each other as much as they differ from anyone else. Some of them are old mainline parishes with a century of denominational history behind them; some are congregations founded in the last decade; some are simply readers of particular books. There are organizations that give the label a content: the Center for Progressive Christianity, founded in 1994, publishes a set of points that it has revised more than once, and each revision is its own dated document. But no confession, no founder and no membership covers the label as a whole — which is exactly why this map never judges it as a category, and asks about a specific community's own published statement instead.
movements.teaser: Global, contemporary — a label spanning mainline progressive congregations, post-evangelical networks and everything between, deliberately never judged as one category since the same label falls on both sides of the map's own floor.
voices: The Center for Progressive Christianity — the organization founded in 1994 whose successive dated revisions of its '8 Points' are the label's most-cited own text
Gary Dorrien — whose three volumes on the making of American liberal theology (2001, 2003, 2006) trace the lineage the label sits in
David Hollinger — historian of what became of mainline Protestantism after its institutional peak
Diana Butler Bass — whose Christianity for the Rest of Us (2006) described mainline congregations that had found a second life
The congregations themselves — each of which, on this map, speaks only for itself
movements.legacy: It is a current still in motion, and a fast-growing one by most accounts, so what it leaves behind is not yet a settled matter. Two things can be said now. It has a history that reaches further back than the word does: the mainline century of liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy is its parent, and hands off to it around 1990. And it has a documented movement expression in the emerging church of the 1990s and 2000s, which is where most of the writing and conference records actually are. The label itself is doing something a movement cannot: giving very different congregations a word they can find each other by.

movements.name: The Sayfo & the Syriac Diaspora
movements.informalName: The Sayfo and the Syriac Diaspora
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), and confirmed at the Freeze as the Syriac lane's resumption exactly as the Era 9 record ruled. A scope note was added naming the Assyrian wing's own arc, which would otherwise vanish inside a Syriac-Orthodox-shaped row. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: survivor testimony, diaspora church archives, living memory - trauma-informed care required
movements.relationsSummary: This is the modern continuation of the ancient Syriac Christian tradition, whose recorded history had gone quiet after about 1300 — a silence living Syriac communities experience as erasure, named honestly here rather than smoothed over. It covers the Assyrian, Church of the East wing as well as the Syriac Orthodox wing, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975, a split within the Church of the East in 1968, and the 1994 Common Christological Declaration with Rome.
movements.why: In 1915, Syriac Christians across eastern Anatolia were massacred and driven from their homes in what survivors called the Sayfo, the sword; Joseph Naayem, a survivor and priest, published his account, Shall This Nation Die?, within six years. What followed was a century of relocation: the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate moved to Homs in 1933 and then Damascus in 1959, while exiled communities of the Church of the East regathered as far away as Chicago. The Assyrian wing of this history kept writing its own hard chapters, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975 and a Common Christological Declaration with Rome in 1994.

sources.work: Survivor testimony and contemporary documentation: oral histories (incl. Gaunt's appendices); Joseph Naayem, Shall This Nation Die? (1921); the Assyro-Chaldean delegation documents (Paris 1919); missionary/consular eyewitness records
sources.note: Some of this material was recorded by missionaries and consular officials rather than survivors themselves.

sources.work: Diaspora church archives: Syriac Orthodox patriarchal records through displacement (Homs 1933, Damascus 1959); Church of the East exile records (Chicago); Tur Abdin records; European diaspora parish registers
sources.note: The communities' own institutional records, tracing their continuation through displacement.

sources.work: David Gaunt, Massacres, Resistance, Protectors: Muslim-Christian Relations in Eastern Anatolia During World War I (2006)
sources.note: The seminal study, drawing on Russian, Ottoman and Western archives together with oral histories.

sources.work: Gaunt, Atto & Barthoma (eds.), Let Them Not Return: Sayfo (Berghahn, War and Genocide 26, 2017)
sources.note: The first scholarly edited collection on the Sayfo, marking the topic's arrival in mainstream academic scholarship.

sources.work: Naures Atto, Hostages in the Homeland, Orphans in the Diaspora (2011); Brock et al., The Hidden Pearl (2001); 2015 centenary commemoration records; CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: In 1915 the Syriac Christians of eastern Anatolia and the surrounding regions were massacred and driven out — the Sayfo, the sword. Tur Abdin, the Syriac Orthodox heartland, and Urmia, where the Church of the East had its own communities, were emptied by killing and flight. Survivors testified almost at once: Joseph Naayem published Shall This Nation Die? in 1921, and an Assyro-Chaldean delegation put its case at the Paris peace conference in 1919. What followed was a century of relocation. The Syriac Orthodox patriarchate moved to Homs in 1933 and to Damascus in 1959; Church of the East exile communities gathered in Chicago and elsewhere; European diaspora parish registers now record families whose villages no longer have them. The Assyrian side of the story has its own twentieth century, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975, a split in 1968, and a Common Christological Declaration with Rome in 1994.
movements.teaser: Tur Abdin and Urmia, then the worldwide diaspora, 1915 to today — the Syriac church's longest lane on the map, carried forward after a silence since around 1300 that its living communities read as erasure.
voices: Joseph Naayem — survivor and priest whose Shall This Nation Die? (1921) is among the earliest published testimony
The Assyro-Chaldean delegation at Paris, 1919 — which put the communities' own case to the peace conference
The survivor oral histories — gathered from the 1980s onward and published in collections and in David Gaunt's appendices
The diaspora parishes — whose registers across Europe and North America are the community's continuing record of itself
Naures Atto — whose Hostages in the Homeland, Orphans in the Diaspora (2011) is a Syriac scholar's account of what the dispersal did
movements.legacy: The lane is alive and the communities are still here, mostly somewhere other than where they started. Their scholarship has become substantial in a single generation — Gaunt's 2006 study, the collection Let Them Not Return (2017), and the centenary commemorations of 2015 that put the Sayfo into public view in Europe. On this map the entry does one more thing: it carries the oldest lane on the whole atlas honestly into the present, after a silence from around 1300 that living Syriac Christians read, understandably, as erasure. The silence is named rather than smoothed over, and this is where the lane resumes.

movements.name: Modern Ethiopian & Eritrean Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its 1900 start stands as the seamless receiver of the Ethiopian re-foundation century written at the Era 9 gate. One correction to this row's own relations line is drafted and BANKED rather than written at this Freeze, to be applied whenever the row is next opened. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: living memory, church archives, persecution-era records
movements.relationsSummary: Tawahedo under empire, occupation and the Derg's persecution; the P'ent'ay evangelical movement; continuation of a lane that previously ended at 1500
movements.why: Italian occupying forces massacred the monks of Debre Libanos in 1937, and decades later Ethiopia's Communist Derg deposed the country's patriarch, Tewophilos, in 1976 and killed him in 1979 -- a history the Tawahedo church now keeps as part of its own liturgical memory. Alongside it, a Protestant evangelical movement called the P'ent'ay grew fastest precisely while it was forced underground under the Derg. Eritrea's church, autocephalous since 1993, has faced its own severe pressure: Patriarch Antonios was deposed and held under house arrest from 2006 until his death in 2022.

sources.work: Tawahedo institutional record: 1959 autocephaly (Abune Basilios); Italian occupation records (1936-41, Debre Libanos massacre 1937); Derg era - Tewophilos deposed 1976, killed 1979; the church's own Derg-era martyrology; post-1991 patriarchal disputes and 2018 reconciliation
sources.note: Some of these records come from a hostile occupying power and from the state that later persecuted the church.

sources.work: P'ent'ay movement's own record: Kale Heywet and Mekane Yesus (EECMY) records, incl. the EECMY's 1972 letter on holistic ministry; underground growth under the Derg
sources.note: A significant own-voice document from 1972, along with records from the persecution era.

sources.work: Eritrea: 1993 autocephaly; Patriarch Antonios deposed/house arrest 2006 (d. 2022); post-2002 evangelical persecution records
sources.note: These records come through church factions and human-rights monitors, both of which bring their own advocacy angle.

sources.work: John Binns, The Orthodox Church of Ethiopia: A History (I.B. Tauris, 2017); Tibebe Eshete, The Evangelical Movement in Ethiopia (Baylor, 2009)
sources.note: The current standard works on each of the two main strands.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: The Ethiopian Tawahedo church entered the twentieth century as an ancient national church under a Coptic hierarchy, and spent the century becoming self-governing under a series of shocks. The first Ethiopian bishops were consecrated in 1929; Italy occupied the country from 1936 to 1941, and massacred the monks of Debre Libanos in 1937; the church received its own patriarch in 1959. The Derg's revolution deposed Patriarch Tewophilos in 1976 and killed him in 1979, and the church's own martyrology from those years is its record of what followed. Alongside all this a Protestant evangelical movement, the P'ent'ay, grew fast — the Kale Heywet and Mekane Yesus churches among them, the latter publishing a much-quoted letter on holistic ministry in 1972 — and grew fastest underground under the Derg. Eritrea's church became autocephalous in 1993; its Patriarch Antonios was deposed and held under house arrest from 2006 until his death in 2022.
movements.teaser: Ethiopia and Eritrea, 1900 to today — the Tawahedo church carried through empire, occupation and the Derg's persecution, alongside the P'ent'ay evangelical movement, continuing a lane the map had previously left off at 1500.
voices: Abune Basilios — the first Ethiopian patriarch, from 1959
The monks of Debre Libanos — massacred by the occupying Italian forces in 1937
Patriarch Tewophilos — deposed by the Derg in 1976 and killed in 1979
The Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus — whose 1972 letter on holistic ministry is among the best-known documents of African Protestant self-definition
Patriarch Antonios of Eritrea — deposed and held under house arrest from 2006 until his death in 2022
movements.legacy: Both churches are living, and the Tawahedo is one of the largest ancient churches anywhere, with its own canon, calendar, liturgical language and fasting discipline intact after a century that took the state away twice. The evangelical movement that grew beside it is now a large minority in its own right, and the two have an unresolved relationship that any honest account has to name. The Derg-era martyrology is part of the church's own liturgical memory. Ethiopia's patriarchal disputes ran on after 1991 and were reconciled in 2018; Eritrea's church remains under severe pressure.

movements.name: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Underground
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its 1989 end was classified as a documented institutional terminus — the church's legalization, and the model case the living-era protocol names for this class. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: post-1991 archives (including the persecutors' own), survivor testimony, samizdat
movements.relationsSummary: The world's largest banned church - clandestine ordinations, bishops in the Gulag, emergence intact in 1989; continuation of VI.20
movements.why: In March 1946, a synod at Lviv dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church -- with every one of its own bishops already under arrest and none present to agree to it. For the next forty-three years priests were ordained in secret and liturgies held in apartments and forests, while Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj spent from 1945 to 1963 in the camps. When the church was finally legalized in 1989, it came back with its hierarchy, parishes and people still intact.
movements.dateRationale: End 1989 KEPT and classified (a) — documented institutional terminus: the church's legalization, the living-era protocol's own model case for this class (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The liquidation record: the 1946 Lviv 'Sobor' records (staged synod, all bishops already arrested); NKVD/KGB files opened post-1991
sources.note: These records come from the persecuting state's own archives.

sources.work: The confessors' own record: Sheptytsky's pastoral letters (incl. 'Thou Shalt Not Kill', 1942); Slipyj's Gulag letters and memoirs (1945-63); clandestine ordination and underground-liturgy records via survivor testimony
Samizdat: the Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Ukraine (1984-, Terelya's initiative group)
sources.note: The underground church's own self-documentation from the late Soviet period.

sources.work: Bohdan R. Bociurkiw, The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church and the Soviet State (1939-1950) (CIUS, 1996); Keston archive Ukraine files
sources.note: Bociurkiw is the standard scholarly work; the Keston archive is advocacy-positioned.

sources.work: The 1989 legalization and the records of the church's emergence intact in 1989-91; CHC vol. 9; Chadwick
sources.note: Marks the end of the underground period; the church itself continued afterward.

movements.longDescription: In March 1946 a synod was convened at Lviv that dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church. Every one of the church's bishops had already been arrested, and none took part. What followed was forty-three years as the largest banned church in the world: priests ordained in secret, liturgies in apartments and forests, bishops in the Gulag. Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky's pastoral letters — among them one from 1942 headed 'Thou Shalt Not Kill' — went on being read through the underground years, and his successor Josyf Slipyj spent from 1945 to 1963 in the camps before his release. From 1984 an initiative group circulated a Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Ukraine in samizdat. In 1989 the church was legalized, and it came out with its hierarchy, its parishes and its people intact — which is not what the state had been counting on.
movements.teaser: Ukraine, 1946 to 1989 — the world's largest banned church, consecrating clergy in secret and enduring bishops sent to the Gulag until it emerged still intact in 1989.
voices: Andrey Sheptytsky — the metropolitan whose pastoral letters, among them 'Thou Shalt Not Kill' (1942), were read throughout the underground years
Josyf Slipyj — his successor, in the camps from 1945 until his release in 1963, whose letters and memoirs survive
The clandestine clergy — ordained in secret and serving in apartments and forests, documented mainly through survivor testimony
Yosyp Terelya — whose initiative group began circulating the Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Ukraine in samizdat in 1984
The persecutors' own files — the NKVD and KGB records opened after 1991, which document the church from the other side
movements.legacy: Legalization in 1989 ended the underground, and the church that emerged is now the largest of the Eastern Catholic churches. Its survival is the standing counter-example to the assumption that a church without buildings, seminaries, publishing or legal existence will simply fade — it did none of those things for four decades and came back whole. The record it left is unusual in having both halves: the confessors' own letters and testimony, and the archives of the agencies that hunted them, which can now be read side by side.

movements.name: The Russian New Martyrs & the Catacomb Church
movements.informalName: The Russian New Martyrs and the Catacomb Church
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its 1991 end was classified as a documented institutional terminus, and the continuesAs write from the Optina elders found in the file but unlisted in the Era 9 record was RATIFIED here: the field tracks the institution's chronological identity-chain inside Russia, which does not displace the separate emigre relation the Paris School entry also carries. The lane's next story — the post-Soviet revival — is a named gap, not a silence. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich post-1991: state archives, martyrologies, oral-history projects
movements.relationsSummary: The century's largest persecution of Christians - Solovki, Butovo, the catacomb communities, thousands of canonized new martyrs; the Optina tradition carried through catastrophe
movements.why: Thousands of clergy, monastics and laypeople were shot at the Butovo firing range outside Moscow in 1937 and 1938 alone, while the ancient Solovki monastery became a prison camp. When Metropolitan Sergius declared loyalty to the Soviet state in 1927, the church split, and those who refused to commemorate him in the liturgy followed bishops like Joseph of Petrograd into hidden catacomb communities instead. In August 2000, the Moscow patriarchate canonized these new martyrs and confessors by the thousands.
movements.dateRationale: End 1991 KEPT and classified (a) — documented institutional terminus: the dissolution of the USSR; the lane's next story (the post-Soviet revival) is a NAMED GAP, not a silence (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: State archives post-1991: Butovo execution lists (1937-38), Solovki records, clergy/laity case files
sources.note: These are the persecutor's own records — some of the era's most extensive documentation, but produced by the state carrying out the persecution, not by its victims.

sources.work: The church's own documents, both sides: Tikhon's 1918 anathema; Sergius's 1927 Declaration AND the catacomb/True-Orthodox rejections (Joseph of Petrograd; the non-commemorators)
sources.note: The catacomb church's founding documents are this exchange itself, presented from both sides.

sources.work: Martyrologies and canonizations: the ROC Jubilee Council canonization (Aug 2000); ROCOR's 1981 parallel act; the PSTGU new-martyrs database; oral-history projects
Father Arseny (Russian, 1990s; English translation from SVS Press) - historicity debated; Solzhenitsyn's Gulag as literary-documentary context
sources.note: This is openly a composite, hagiographic account, not a straightforward historical record.

sources.work: William C. Fletcher, The Russian Orthodox Church Underground, 1917-1970 (OUP, 1971); Nathaniel Davis, A Long Walk to Church (Westview, 1995); Chadwick; CHC vol. 9
sources.note: Fletcher wrote before the Soviet archives opened, so his methodology is now dated. Davis wrote in the archival era, after they opened.

movements.longDescription: The Russian Orthodox Church went into 1917 as an established state church and came out of the Soviet century as the object of the largest persecution of Christians in history. Patriarch Tikhon issued an anathema in 1918. Clergy, monastics and laypeople were shot or sent to the camps in numbers still being counted: the Butovo firing range outside Moscow accounted for thousands in 1937 and 1938 alone, and the Solovki monastery became a prison camp. In 1927 Metropolitan Sergius issued a Declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state, and the church divided over it — those who refused went into the catacomb communities, following bishops like Joseph of Petrograd and refusing to commemorate Sergius in the liturgy. The archives opened after 1991, and with them the case files: names, charges, dates, sentences. In August 2000 the Moscow patriarchate canonized the new martyrs and confessors in their thousands.
movements.teaser: The USSR, 1917 to 1991 — the century's largest persecution of Christians, from Solovki and Butovo to underground catacomb communities and thousands of new martyrs later canonized.
voices: Patriarch Tikhon — who issued the anathema of 1918 and led the church into the persecution
Metropolitan Sergius — whose Declaration of 1927 divided the church and is preserved with its rejections alongside it
Joseph of Petrograd — among the bishops who refused the Declaration; the non-commemorators followed him into the catacomb communities
The Butovo lists — the execution records of 1937–38, now published name by name
The new martyrs — canonized in their thousands by the Jubilee Council of August 2000, after the Russian Church Abroad's parallel act of 1981
movements.legacy: The persecution ended with the Soviet Union in 1991, and the church that survived it is very much alive; what happened to it after 1991 is a further story this map names as a gap rather than pretending to cover. What this century left is a martyrology of a scale the church has had to build new instruments to hold — the new-martyrs database built after the archives opened, the Butovo lists, oral-history projects still running. It also left an unresolved argument the church continues to have with itself, about the 1927 Declaration and what compliance cost, which the surviving documents from both sides keep open.

movements.name: The Post-Vatican-II Parish Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the easiest carrier case on the roster, since the council's own texts are the dated carriers. The prose sweep's words were applied: the traditionalist tension is now anchored to its dated documents rather than described as a present state of feeling. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich: council documents plus parish-level studies, oral histories, living memory
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Second Vatican Council as it was lived in parishes: Mass in the vernacular, lay ministries, and in 1972 the restoration of the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, reviving a catechumenate pattern from Christianity's first centuries. The council's own documents — Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), Lumen Gentium (1964), and Gaudium et Spes (1965) — carry these changes. The tension with traditionalists who preferred the older Latin rite is documented in the church's own successive rulings: Ecclesia Dei (1988), Summorum Pontificum (2007), and Traditionis Custodes (2021).
movements.why: The Second Vatican Council's liturgy constitution, promulgated on 4 December 1963, changed what most Catholics actually experienced on a Sunday: Mass in their own language, readers and ministers drawn from the pews, parish councils. In 1972 the church restored the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, bringing back a first-century pattern of preparing converts that had lain dormant for fifteen centuries. The disagreement over the older Latin rite has never fully settled, and the church has kept restating its own position in dated documents: Ecclesia Dei in 1988, Summorum Pontificum in 2007, Traditionis Custodes in 2021.

sources.work: The council's own documents: Sacrosanctum Concilium (4 Dec 1963), Lumen Gentium (21 Nov 1964), Dei Verbum and Gaudium et Spes (1965); the Missal of Paul VI (1969/70); the RCIA (1972)
sources.note: These are the council's own official texts, published by the Vatican. The RCIA restored the ancient catechumenate pattern for preparing converts.

sources.work: The lived-parish record: parish-level oral histories, congregational studies, vernacular-liturgy adoption records, lay-ministry and parish-council records
sources.note: This shows the council as it was lived in ordinary parish paperwork. The published sociological studies are the accessible record of it.

sources.work: The traditionalist-grief record: Lefebvre's 1974 Declaration; SSPX (1970; 1988 consecrations, excommunications lifted 2009); Summorum Pontificum (2007); Traditionis Custodes (2021)
sources.note: This traces both the traditionalist grief and the church's shifting official response, in the church's own dated documents, presented evenhandedly.

sources.work: John W. O'Malley, What Happened at Vatican II (Harvard, 2008); Alberigo & Komonchak (eds.), History of Vatican II (5 vols, 1995-2006); Mark Massa, The American Catholic Revolution (OUP, 2010)
CHC vol. 9 (the papacy chapter in Part I)

movements.longDescription: The Second Vatican Council opened in 1962, and what it changed most was the ordinary Sunday. Sacrosanctum Concilium, the constitution on the liturgy, was promulgated on 4 December 1963; Lumen Gentium on the church followed on 21 November 1964; Dei Verbum and Gaudium et Spes came in 1965; the revised Missal of Paul VI appeared in 1969 and 1970. In parishes this meant Mass in the language people spoke, readers and ministers of communion drawn from the pews, and parish councils. In 1972 the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults restored the ancient catechumenate — a first-century pattern coming back after fifteen centuries. Not everyone welcomed it: Archbishop Lefebvre published a declaration in 1974, and the argument over the older rite is documented in the church's own successive rulings, Ecclesia Dei in 1988, Summorum Pontificum in 2007 and Traditionis Custodes in 2021.
movements.teaser: Global, 1962 to today — the Second Vatican Council as lived event: vernacular liturgy, lay ministries, and the RCIA restoring the ancient catechumenate, with the tension over the older rite carried on its own dated documents from 1988 to 2021.
voices: The council's own documents — Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), Lumen Gentium (1964), Dei Verbum and Gaudium et Spes (1965), the documents this tradition actually runs on, each with its date on it
Paul VI — under whom the revised Missal was promulgated in 1969–70 and the adult catechumenate restored in 1972
The parishes — whose oral histories, council minutes and lay-ministry records are where the council can be seen actually landing
Marcel Lefebvre — whose declaration of 1974 and the Society of St Pius X mark the resistance, argued through the documents of 1988, 2007 and 2021
John W. O'Malley — whose What Happened at Vatican II (2008) is the standard account of how the council actually proceeded
movements.legacy: This is how most of the world's Catholics have worshipped for two generations, which makes it one of the largest continuous formation traditions on the map. The restored catechumenate has become the ordinary route by which adults enter the Catholic Church. The vernacular liturgy and lay ministries have been so thoroughly absorbed that they now read as normal rather than as a change. The argument over the older rite is unresolved and is carried, on this map, on its own dated documents rather than described as a mood.

movements.name: Lausanne-Era Global Evangelicalism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), and it carries the era's best-documented self-description ladder — a three-dated confession series from Lausanne 1974 through Manila 1989 to Cape Town 2010. Its region coding was corrected at the Freeze to match its own record, which has been global in prose since it was written, and the counter-pole relation to the conciliar ecumenical movement was written here for the first time, in both directions. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally; as a TRADITION it is diffuse - the bounded-window rule applies doubly
movements.relationsSummary: At the 1974 Congress, Global South voices — chiefly the Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar — argued for holding evangelism and social responsibility together, bending the whole movement toward what became known as integral mission. It works as a network rather than a denomination, restating itself through a series of dated documents: the Lausanne Covenant (1974), the Manila Manifesto (1989) and the Cape Town Commitment (2010). It stands as a counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement centered on Geneva — two different twentieth-century answers to how separated churches should act together.
movements.why: At the Lausanne Congress in July 1974, the Latin American theologians René Padilla and Samuel Escobar argued that evangelism and social responsibility could not be separated, and they won enough of the room to bend the whole movement in that direction -- which is why "integral mission" is now a Lausanne word. What came out of the congress was not a denomination but a network built around a document, the Lausanne Covenant, and the movement has restated itself twice more since, in the Manila Manifesto of 1989 and the Cape Town Commitment of 2010.
movements.dateRationale: No date change (the 1974 Congress is the row's principled start). Recorded at the Freeze: the regions[] array read ["North America","North Europe"] while this row's own region field, teaser and relations line have said Global since they were written — the sources run's coding mismatch, corrected here to carry the Global South (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The Lausanne Covenant (1974; drafting committee chaired by John Stott; adopted at Lausanne, 16-25 July 1974); Manila Manifesto (1989); Cape Town Commitment (2010); Seoul Statement (2024)
sources.note: John Stott and Samuel Escobar served on the drafting committee.

sources.work: Let the Earth Hear His Voice (ed. J. D. Douglas, 1975) - the congress's own record, incl. Rene Padilla's and Samuel Escobar's addresses
sources.note: This is the congress's own record of the Global South delegates' argument for integral mission, in their own words.

sources.work: The network's institutional record: Lausanne consultations and occasional papers; WEA and national fellowship records
sources.note: These records document the movement as a network rather than a formal denomination.

sources.work: Brian Stanley, The Global Diffusion of Evangelicalism: The Age of Billy Graham and John Stott (IVP, 2013); Bebbington/Noll evangelicalism-history series
sources.note: Stanley's book is considered the standard history of this network.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9; Noll, The New Shape of World Christianity

movements.longDescription: Evangelicals from around the world met at Lausanne from 16 to 25 July 1974, and what came out of it was not a denomination but a network with a document. The Lausanne Covenant was drafted by a committee chaired by John Stott and adopted at the congress, and the congress's own record, Let the Earth Hear His Voice, was published the following year with the addresses in it — including those of the Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar, who argued that evangelism and social responsibility could not be separated. That argument won enough of the room to change the movement's direction, which is why 'integral mission' is a Lausanne word. The movement has restated itself twice more since, in the Manila Manifesto of 1989 and the Cape Town Commitment of 2010, and again at Seoul in 2024 — a chain of dated statements of what it takes itself to be, unusual in its consistency.
movements.teaser: Global, 1974 to today — the movement launched at the Lausanne Congress, where Global South voices bent world evangelicalism toward integral mission, organized ever since as a network rather than a denomination.
voices: John Stott — chaired the drafting committee of the Lausanne Covenant in 1974
René Padilla — whose Lausanne address pressed the case for integral mission and is printed in the congress's own record
Samuel Escobar — the other leading Latin American voice at the congress, arguing the same case
The congress record — Let the Earth Hear His Voice (1975), which prints what was actually said rather than what was later remembered
The three statements — the Lausanne Covenant (1974), the Manila Manifesto (1989) and the Cape Town Commitment (2010), the movement's own account of itself at three dates
movements.legacy: It is a living network rather than a church, and that is the point: it convenes, publishes and connects, and the churches doing the work belong to other bodies entirely. Its covenant is still the most widely subscribed evangelical statement of the last fifty years, and 'integral mission' — evangelism and social action held together — has become mainstream evangelical language largely because of what the Global South delegates said in 1974. It stands as the counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement centred on Geneva: two different answers, from the same century, to the question of how separated churches should act together.

movements.name: African Diaspora & Reverse-Mission Churches in Europe
movements.informalName: The African Diaspora Churches in Europe
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). Named carrier bodies were proposed for its assessment rather than a finding made on the current as such, and where the record declines to pick one the no-single-confession shape is recorded rather than papered over. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate and growing: church archives, sociological studies, living voices
movements.relationsSummary: Within a single lifetime, the direction of Christian mission has reversed: churches once planted in Africa by European missionaries are now planting congregations back among Europeans. It continues a pattern as old as Christianity itself — faith travelling with people who have been scattered from their homes.
movements.why: Within a single lifetime the mission map turned over: churches that European missionaries once planted in Africa are now planting congregations back among Europeans. The Redeemed Christian Church of God, founded in Nigeria in 1952, opened Jesus House in London in 1994, the same year Sunday Adelaja founded the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv. Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations had already been meeting in European cities since the 1960s, the earliest layer of what people now call reverse mission.

sources.work: The churches' own records: KICC (London, 1992, Ashimolowo); RCCG European parish-planting records; Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations (Kyiv, 1994, Adelaja); Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations in Europe from the 1960s
sources.note: This includes the Ukraine church founded by Sunday Adelaja. The 1960s start date is anchored by the earliest Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations in Europe, each with its own documented record.

sources.work: Afe Adogame, The African Christian Diaspora (Bloomsbury, 2013); Gerrie ter Haar, Halfway to Paradise: African Christians in Europe (1998)
sources.note: These are the field's standard works; ter Haar's is the pioneering study.

sources.work: Claims that a particular church is the 'largest congregation in Europe/UK'
sources.note: These claims come from the churches' own self-reports and from journalism, not independent verification. Sociological studies such as the London Church Census are the nearest independent counts available.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9
sources.note: The scholarly literature on this movement is still young, so the source base here is kept deliberately compact rather than padded out.

movements.longDescription: Within a single lifetime the mission map turned over. Churches that European missionaries had planted in Africa began planting congregations in Europe, first among migrant communities and then well beyond them. Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations were meeting in European cities from the 1960s. The Redeemed Christian Church of God, founded in Nigeria in 1952, opened British parishes from the 1980s and Jesus House in London in 1994. Matthew Ashimolowo founded Kingsway International Christian Centre in London in 1992. Sunday Adelaja founded the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv in 1994. The phrase that has attached to them, reverse mission, describes a real inversion: churches once planted by European missionaries now planting congregations back among Europeans.
movements.teaser: The UK, Germany, the Netherlands and Ukraine, 1960s to today — the mission map inverted within a single lifetime, as churches once planted by Europeans now plant their own congregations back among them.
voices: Matthew Ashimolowo — founder of Kingsway International Christian Centre in London in 1992
Sunday Adelaja — founder of the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv in 1994
The Redeemed Christian Church of God — Nigerian-founded in 1952, planting British parishes from the 1980s and opening Jesus House in London in 1994
The Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations — meeting in European cities from the 1960s, the earliest layer of this story
Afe Adogame — whose The African Christian Diaspora (2013) is the standard scholarly account
movements.legacy: This is a current still in progress rather than a finished chapter, and it is not one confession: the churches involved come from several different African traditions and answer to their own bodies. Claims that one or another is the largest congregation in Britain or in Europe circulate widely and rest mostly on the churches' own counts. What is clear is that the direction of Christian mission has reversed within living memory, and that European Christianity's growing edge is often African. It is also the map's newest instance of its oldest pattern: the faith travelling with people who have been scattered.

movements.name: Ratana Church & Pacific Adjustment Movements
movements.informalName: The Rātana Church and the Pacific Movements
movements.statusWord: Floor question carried, question-framed — the office-defined c2 run recorded (Era 10 Step 0); the mangai question stays genuinely open
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run with its question-framing retained. The criterion's sixteenth live application ran here — the first reuse of the office-defined law made at the Era 9 gate — and the question stays genuinely open: the office persists by succession, which cuts toward the community limb. Its composite tail was named minimally rather than left unnamed, since per-body assessment is impossible until the packed bodies have names. Register retained. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: movement's own records, political covenant documents, scholarship
movements.floorNote: Genuine per-body questions, held as questions. The dated locus is the movement's own published hymns and prayers — the Rātana creed's faithful angels and the mangai [S] — rather than any claim about what living adherents think: the mangai's mediating role in the church's own prayer is what raises the floor and interpretive-fidelity questions, and the question is put to those texts. The person-defined criterion ran here as the first reuse of the office-defined law made at the Era 9 gate: person-ground extends to an OFFICE only where the office is a single irreplaceable locus, and here the office persists by succession (Rātana died in 1939 [S]; the church continued under the tumuaki line [S]), which cuts toward the community limb. The question stays open, per body, on the church's own liturgical texts.
movements.relationsSummary: These movements grew out of Pacific mission Christianity combined with indigenous initiative and leadership. Te Haahi Rātana was established in 1925, following Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana's vision of 8 November 1918. A similar pattern appears elsewhere in the Pacific, most notably in Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church, founded in the Solomon Islands in 1960.
movements.why: After a vision in 1918, Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana founded Te Haahi Rātana in 1925 in Aotearoa New Zealand; the church calls him the mangai, the mouthpiece, a title woven into its own creed and hymns. The movement became a political force as well as a religious one, taking a Treaty of Waitangi petition to London in 1924 and holding all four Māori parliamentary seats by 1943. Similar movements arose elsewhere in the Pacific, among them Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands, founded in 1960.

sources.work: The movement's own records: T. W. Ratana's recorded utterances; the church's creed, prayers, and service book (the mangai's place in the church's own liturgical texts); Ratana Pa records; Te Whetu Marama
sources.note: The church was formally registered in 1925; the founding vision came earlier, on 8 November 1918. Some of these texts are in Māori.

sources.work: Political covenant documents: the 1936 Ratana-Savage meeting and alliance record; the four Maori seats by 1943; the 1924 Treaty petition delegation to London
sources.note: This archive holds both the movement's faith and its political alliances together.

sources.work: J. M. Henderson, Ratana: The Man, the Church, the Political Movement (Reed, 1972); Keith Newman, Ratana Revisited: An Unfinished Legacy (Reed, 2006)
sources.note: Te Ara serves as the more accessible reference source here.

sources.work: The Pacific adjustment family: the movements' own records where published; the adjustment-movement scholarship on Pacific prophet-led churches
sources.note: Each movement in this family is treated on its own terms rather than generalized as a whole. This is the thinnest part of the source base here, and that is acknowledged openly.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9
sources.note: Its coverage of the Pacific is limited to chapter level.

movements.longDescription: In November 1918 Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana had a vision in Aotearoa New Zealand, and a healing ministry began around him from that year. In 1925 the movement was established as an independent church, Te Haahi Rātana, and Rātana himself was known as the mangai, the mouthpiece — a role that appears in the church's own creed, prayers and hymns alongside the faithful angels. The movement was political as well as religious from early on: a delegation took a Treaty of Waitangi petition to London in 1924, an alliance with the Labour Party was formed after a meeting with Michael Joseph Savage in 1936, and by 1943 the movement held all four Māori parliamentary seats. Rātana died in 1939 and the church has continued under the tumuaki who followed him. Other Pacific movements of a similar shape belong beside it, among them Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands, from 1960.
movements.teaser: Aotearoa New Zealand and the Pacific, 1925 to today — churches born of Pacific mission Christianity and indigenous initiative together, among them Te Haahi Ratana and Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church, with the mangai's mediating role in the movement's own published prayer carried as a question rather than a verdict.
voices: Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana — whose vision of 8 November 1918 began the movement; the church calls him the mangai and he died in 1939
Te Whetu Marama — the movement's own paper, part of the record it keeps of itself
The church's creed, prayers and hymns — where the mangai's place is actually set down, and therefore where any question about it has to be put
Michael Joseph Savage — the Labour leader whose 1936 meeting with the church sealed a political alliance still remembered annually
Silas Eto — founder of the Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands in 1960, the named example of the Pacific movements carried alongside
movements.legacy: Te Haahi Rātana is a living church and a continuing force in New Zealand public life; the annual gathering at Rātana Pā is a fixture of the political calendar, and the alliance made in 1936 is still referred to by both sides. The movement gave Māori Christianity an institutional form that was not a mission's, at a time when almost nothing else was on offer. The questions this map records about it — what the mangai's mediating role means, put to the church's own prayers rather than to its members — are held here as questions, in the terms the church's own texts set.

movements.name: The Armenian Church after the Genocide (Medz Yeghern)
movements.informalName: The Armenian Church after the Genocide
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), with the Etchmiadzin/Cilicia tension carried inside it rather than given a row. The seam behind it was corrected against the census at the Freeze: the Zartonk century ends at 1906, not 1915, so the join to this row is a disclosed nine-year gap, not the seamless one an earlier reading claimed. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: survivor testimony, diaspora archives, post-1991 records, living memory - trauma-informed care as with the Sayfo
movements.relationsSummary: This is the modern continuation of one of Christianity's oldest churches, tracing back to antiquity in the Caucasus, and it shares a history of suffering under Soviet rule with other churches from the region. The 2015 centenary canonization of roughly one and a half million genocide victims is, by most accounts, the largest canonization in Christian history.
movements.why: In 1915 the Armenian genocide left the church's homeland base destroyed, its clergy killed and its dioceses emptied, and what survived did so by moving — the Holy See of Cilicia relocated to Antelias, Lebanon, in 1930, while Etchmiadzin endured under Soviet rule. On 23 April 2015, at Etchmiadzin, the church canonized roughly one and a half million genocide victims, by most accounts the largest canonization in Christian history. It is now home to a worldwide diaspora that outnumbers the church in Armenia itself.

sources.work: Survivor testimony: Grigoris Balakian, Armenian Golgotha (1922; ET 2009); Zoryan Institute and USC Shoah Foundation Armenian oral-history collections; diaspora parish survivor records
sources.note: These survivor testimonies are treated with the same trauma-informed care given to accounts of the Sayfo.

sources.work: The church's institutional record through catastrophe: Holy See of Cilicia to Antelias (1930); Etchmiadzin under Soviet rule (Khoren I killed 1938); the Cold-War diaspora split between the sees (both sides' records); post-1991 re-establishment
sources.note: Records from both sides of the diaspora split are included here.

sources.work: The 2015 canonization of the genocide's victims (23 Apr 2015, Etchmiadzin) - the church's own canonization rite and documents
Raymond Kevorkian, The Armenian Genocide: A Complete History (I.B. Tauris, 2011); Ronald Grigor Suny, 'They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else' (Princeton, 2015)
sources.note: These are the two standard scholarly works on the genocide.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9; Hratch Tchilingirian's church-and-diaspora sociology

movements.longDescription: In 1915 the Armenian population of Anatolia was destroyed, and the church went with the people — clergy killed, dioceses emptied, whole regions left without a parish. What survived did so by moving. Grigoris Balakian, a priest who lived through it, wrote his account in 1922. The Holy See of Cilicia relocated to Antelias in Lebanon in 1930. Etchmiadzin, the mother see, continued inside the Soviet Union under severe constraint; Catholicos Khoren I was killed in 1938. In the Cold War the two sees divided along the politics of the diaspora, a division dated to 1956 whose records both sides kept. After 1991 the church in Armenia was re-established in a country of its own again. On 23 April 2015, at Etchmiadzin, the church canonized the victims of the genocide — roughly one and a half million people, in what is by most accounts the largest canonization in Christian history.
movements.teaser: Anatolia to Armenia and the worldwide diaspora, 1915 to today — a church carrying the Medz Yeghern forward, whose 2015 centenary canonization of roughly 1.5 million victims stands, by most accounts, as the largest in Christian history.
voices: Grigoris Balakian — priest and survivor whose Armenian Golgotha (1922) is among the fullest first-hand accounts
Catholicos Khoren I — killed in 1938 under Soviet rule
The survivor oral histories — gathered by the Zoryan Institute and the USC Shoah Foundation, and in diaspora parish records
The diaspora parishes — from Beirut to Los Angeles, which carried the church's institutional life when its homeland could not
The canonization of 23 April 2015 — the church's own liturgical act for roughly 1.5 million victims
movements.legacy: The church is alive in Armenia and in a diaspora that now outnumbers it, and it is one of the oldest continuously existing churches anywhere — the Caucasus lane on this map runs from the fourth century straight through to it. The 2015 canonization gave the genocide a liturgical place rather than only a historical one. The Cold War split between Etchmiadzin and Antelias has eased but shaped generations of diaspora life. And the whole record of this century has to be handled the way its own communities handle it: as living memory, not distant history.

movements.name: The Emerging Church & Post-Evangelical Movement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). Its 2015 end was kept and its rationale written to say plainly what it is: a judgment, not a documented terminus — no institutional end exists to point to — which is exactly the distinction the living-era protocol requires be made explicitly. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich and digitally self-documenting (books, blogs, conference records) - though platform decay makes the archive fragile, an honest preservation note
movements.floorNote: A3 per-body: the movement deliberately held confessional questions open - some bodies affirm the creedal content plainly, others reinterpret it; assessed per community, never by label
movements.relationsSummary: Child of late evangelicalism meeting the postmodern turn; overlaps new-monastic communities; parent-influence on IX.31; the most documented movement expression of the broader progressive current (IX.18)
movements.why: Beginning in the late 1990s, younger evangelical leaders in North America, Britain and Australia used books, blogs and loose networks like Emergent Village to question a church they felt was answering questions nobody was asking. The conversation deliberately left confessional questions open rather than settling them, and Rob Bell's 2011 book Love Wins split it wide open over what happens after death. Its record survives mostly on blogs that have since largely link-rotted.
movements.dateRationale: Window c. 1990–2015 KEPT, and the rationale WRITTEN to say plainly what the end is: a JUDGMENT, not a documented terminus — no institutional end exists (platform decay; network dissolution c. 2013 [S]) — per the living-era rule that the two be distinguished explicitly; living:true stands, the continuations already named (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The movement's own books: McLaren, A New Kind of Christian (2001), A Generous Orthodoxy (2004); Bell, Velvet Elvis (2005), Love Wins (2011, with the split it provoked); Tomlinson, The Post-Evangelical (1995); Tickle, The Great Emergence (2008)
sources.note: These are the movement's own foundational, dated texts, theorizing itself as it went.

sources.work: The network/conference/blog layer: Young Leaders Network/Terra Nova to Emergent Village (c. 1997-2001); conference records; the blogosphere (2002-2012, link-rotted; Internet Archive captures as de-facto archive); Greenbelt (UK)
sources.note: This material has decayed as the platforms hosting it have gone offline; the Internet Archive is what preserves it now.

sources.work: D. A. Carson, Becoming Conversant with the Emerging Church (2005)
sources.note: This is written from outside the movement, by one of its sharpest evangelical critics, which makes it valuable for dating where the movement's boundaries were contested.

sources.work: Gerardo Marti & Gladys Ganiel, The Deconstructed Church: Understanding Emerging Christianity (OUP, 2014); Tony Jones's insider accounts
sources.note: Marti and Ganiel's book is the standard sociological study; Jones writes as a movement insider.

sources.work: The wind-down of Emergent Village and the movement's dispersal, described in its own late self-assessments

movements.longDescription: In the late 1990s a set of conversations began among younger evangelical leaders in North America, Britain and Australia who thought the church they had been formed in was answering questions nobody was asking. It ran through networks rather than institutions — the Young Leaders Network, then Terra Nova, then Emergent Village from around 2001 — and through books and an enormous volume of blogging. Dave Tomlinson's The Post-Evangelical came out in Britain in 1995; Brian McLaren's A New Kind of Christian in 2001 and A Generous Orthodoxy in 2004; Rob Bell's Velvet Elvis in 2005 and Love Wins in 2011, the second of which split the conversation open. Phyllis Tickle's The Great Emergence (2008) tried to say what was happening while it was still happening. The movement deliberately held confessional questions open rather than settling them, which is why this map assesses its communities one at a time.
movements.teaser: North America, the UK and Australia, c. 1990 to 2015 — late evangelicalism meeting the postmodern turn, self-documented in books, blogs and conference records now fragile with the platforms that carried them.
voices: Brian McLaren — whose A New Kind of Christian (2001) and A Generous Orthodoxy (2004) were the conversation's most-read books
Dave Tomlinson — whose The Post-Evangelical (1995) named the British side of it first
Rob Bell — whose Velvet Elvis (2005) and Love Wins (2011) reached furthest and cost most
Phyllis Tickle — whose The Great Emergence (2008) attempted the movement's own historical self-account
The blogs — the movement's real archive between 2002 and 2012, now largely link-rotted and surviving through the Internet Archive
movements.legacy: The conversation dissipated: Emergent Village wound down around 2013, and this map's 2015 close is a judgment about a movement running out rather than a record of any institutional end — nothing closed, and the map says so plainly. Its people are still here, and its questions went on into the deconstruction communities of the following decade and into the broader progressive current. It also leaves a preservation problem worth naming: a movement that documented itself almost entirely on platforms is one whose archive decays with them, and the Internet Archive is doing more to preserve it than any library.

movements.name: Dispensational Prophecy Culture
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), assessed through its dated mass-texts as a culture row must be. Its 31-year overlap with the Brethren entry was disposed of by acknowledgment rather than re-dating — the honest shape of a culture outliving its formation body — and the teaser's present-tense claim about millions of living readers was re-anchored to those dated texts. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich: conference records (Niagara onward), the Scofield Bible's notes as mass formation text, prophecy charts, bestsellers from Late Great Planet Earth to Left Behind
movements.relationsSummary: This popular culture grew out of Plymouth Brethren teaching, carried forward through the Bible-institute tradition. It reached a mass audience mainly through print: the Scofield Reference Bible (1909, revised 1917), Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), and the sixteen Left Behind novels (1995–2007). Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement is its clearest institutional anchor.
movements.why: Beginning with the Niagara Bible Conference's prophecy teaching in the 1870s, this way of reading scripture in distinct dispensations leading to a rapture spread less through preaching than through print: the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909 put the scheme in footnotes that readers met every time they opened the text. Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth in 1970 and the sixteen Left Behind novels published between 1995 and 2007 carried it to a mass audience far larger than any single denomination.
movements.dateRationale: NO re-date: the 31-year overlap with Frozen VIII.23 (1827–1906) is acknowledged and kept — the honest shape of a culture outliving its formation body, on the Kollyvades precedent. VIII.23 carries the formation, this row the culture; a 1906 start would orphan the Niagara and prophecy-conference decades that VIII.23's record does not carry. Start c. 1875 is a disclosed single crossing (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

movements.longDescription: This is not a doctrine so much as a way of reading, and it reached more people than most denominations do. Its formation is older than the era: the Niagara Bible Conference met annually from the 1870s to 1897 and adopted a fourteen-point creed in 1878, and prophecy conferences from 1878 onward taught a reading of scripture divided into dispensations with a rapture ahead. What carried it to the millions was print. The Scofield Reference Bible of 1909, revised in 1917, put the scheme in the notes at the foot of the page, so that a reader met it every time they opened the text. Clarence Larkin's Dispensational Truth (1918) put it on charts. Then came the bestsellers: Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth in 1970 and the sixteen Left Behind novels between 1995 and 2007, whose sales figures are the measure of how far this way of reading actually travelled.
movements.teaser: North America and then worldwide, c. 1875 to today — Plymouth Brethren teaching turned into popular culture through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909/1917), prophecy charts and bestsellers from Late Great Planet Earth (1970) to the Left Behind series (1995–2007), whose sales records are the measure of how widely the rapture became a way of reading.
voices: The Niagara Bible Conference — meeting annually to 1897, whose fourteen-point creed of 1878 is the culture's earliest formal statement
C. I. Scofield — whose Reference Bible (1909, revised 1917) taught the scheme in footnotes to readers who never attended a conference
Clarence Larkin — whose Dispensational Truth (1918) turned it into charts that hung in classrooms for decades
Hal Lindsey — whose The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), written with Carlson, took it onto the mass market
Tim LaHaye and Jerry B. Jenkins — whose Left Behind novels (1995–2007) made it a sixteen-volume work of popular fiction
movements.legacy: The culture is alive and its texts stay in print. It gave a large part of English-speaking Protestantism a default way of reading the Bible and a default expectation about how history ends, carried more by study notes, charts and novels than by any pulpit. It has institutional anchors — Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement among them — but it never needed a denomination. It also produced its own opposition: the reading of the Bible as one story fulfilled in Jesus, carried elsewhere on this map, is in large part a reaction against the chart. The scholarship on it is now substantial, from Sandeen and Weber to Boyer's When Time Shall Be No More (1992) and Hummel's study of 2023.

movements.relationsSummary: Child of evangelical pragmatism; small-group systems as formation technology; the worship-music culture (Hillsong and kin) as its global carrier; tension-sibling of IX.31, which often narrates leaving it
movements.why: From 1975, when Willow Creek Community Church designed its Sunday service for people who don't go to church, a model built on small groups and contemporary worship spread from American suburbs worldwide, carried in part by songs written by Hillsong, founded in Australia in 1983, and now sung far beyond anyone's knowledge of where they came from. In 2007 Willow Creek's own REVEAL study turned that same rigor on itself, asking whether its programs were forming anyone spiritually at all.

movements.longDescription: From the mid-1970s a particular way of building a church spread out of American suburbs and then around the world. Willow Creek Community Church was founded in 1975 on the premise that the Sunday service should be designed for the person who does not go to church, with the actual formation happening in small groups during the week. Saddleback followed in 1980, and Rick Warren's The Purpose Driven Church (1995) put the method into a book other pastors could work from. Behind both lay the church-growth school, and Donald McGavran's Understanding Church Growth (1970). The Willow Creek Association, from 1992, exported the model by conference and manual. The other great carrier was music: Hillsong, founded in Australia in 1983, became a global publisher of congregational songs, and licensing data shows how widely they were sung. The movement studies itself unusually hard — Willow Creek's own REVEAL research from 2007 questioned whether its programmes were forming anyone.
movements.teaser: North America and then worldwide, c. 1975 to today — evangelical pragmatism built into small-group systems and a worship-music culture, Hillsong among them, that carried the megachurch model around the globe.
voices: Bill Hybels — founder of Willow Creek in 1975; the Willow Creek Association from 1992 carried the model worldwide
Rick Warren — founder of Saddleback in 1980 and author of The Purpose Driven Church (1995)
Donald McGavran — whose Understanding Church Growth (1970) supplied the movement's underlying theory
Hillsong — founded in Australia in 1983, whose catalogue from the early 1990s onward, 'Shout to the Lord' among it, is what most congregations actually encountered
The REVEAL study — Willow Creek's own published research from 2007, in which the movement audited its own formation claims
movements.legacy: The model is everywhere and is now simply what many people picture when they picture a church: a stage, a band, a sermon in plain speech, and a small-group system underneath. Its worship music is sung in congregations that have no idea where it came from. The past decade has also put a series of collapses on the public record — the dissolution of Mars Hill in 2014, the investigation into Ravi Zacharias published in 2021, and Hillsong's governance crises of 2021 and 2022 — and those documents are now part of the movement's own record too. So is the scholarship: the Hartford Institute's research and Kate Bowler's Blessed (2013) study it as a serious subject rather than a curiosity.

movements.name: Deconstruction & Ex-vangelical Communities
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 10 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — and it is the recency floor's first live case. It fails the marker's time prong: its namable anchors run from 2016. It is RETAINED at this Freeze by Mark's hand-selection with that recency named on the record, on the strength of institutionalization legible across independent sources, a survived founder-adjacent transition, and this row's unique stake — the map here maps its own visitors. The reconstruction half of the story lands inside this row and its relations rather than as a row of its own. Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Abundant but platform-fragile (podcasts, online communities, memoirs); living people at every point - consent and safety care alongside sourcing
movements.floorNote: A3 per-body by the nature of the thing: its published memoirs, podcasts and community writing record journeys landing everywhere from leaving faith entirely to rebuilding within it — the spectrum IS the community's defining feature, and it is read off that published layer rather than asserted about people.
movements.relationsSummary: This movement grew out of crises within evangelicalism, echoing questions earlier generations of Christians have also asked about their own churches. Published accounts show no single destination: some people leave the faith altogether, while others move toward Orthodoxy, Catholicism — many through the Coming Home Network, founded in 1993 — or Anglicanism, a path traced back to Robert Webber's work in the 1980s and the founding of the Anglican Church in North America in 2009. Its earliest datable landmarks go back to 2016, making it one of the youngest currents on record.
movements.why: Since the 2010s, people formed in evangelical churches have worked out what they still believe in public — in podcasts, online communities and memoirs rather than in congregations, a current Blake Chastain named 'exvangelical' in 2016. Rachel Held Evans's books and the Evolving Faith conference she co-founded with Sarah Bessey in 2018 gave it a gathering place that continued after her death in 2019. The published record shows no single destination: some leave the faith altogether, while others land in Orthodoxy, Catholicism, Anglicanism or progressive congregations.
movements.dateRationale: No date change. Recorded instead under the recency floor: this row's namable anchors run from 2016 ("exvangelical" coined July 2016, verified) — under the twenty-year marker on time — and it is RETAINED by Mark's hand-selection with that recency named and logged, on institutionalization legible across independent sources (Evolving Faith founded 2018, verified), a survived founder-adjacent transition (the conference continued after Held Evans's death, 4 May 2019, verified), and this row's unique stake (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)
