movements.longDescription: Since the 2010s a large number of people formed in evangelical churches have been publicly working out what they still believe, and doing it in podcasts, online communities and memoirs rather than in congregations. Blake Chastain coined 'exvangelical' as a hashtag in 2016 and it named something already happening. Rachel Held Evans published Searching for Sunday in 2015 and Inspired in 2018 and, with Sarah Bessey, founded the Evolving Faith conference in 2018; when Evans died in May 2019 the conference continued. Joshua Harris made public statements in 2019 about leaving the faith. Christianity Today's podcast The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill, released across 2021, gave the whole current a shared reference point. What the published record shows is not one destination but many: some people leave faith altogether, some rebuild it somewhere else, and the spread is the defining feature rather than an untidiness in the data.
movements.teaser: Digital-native, North America and beyond, c. 2010s to today — documented in podcasts, online communities and memoirs whose published record shows journeys landing everywhere from rebuilding faith to leaving it, and counting, by the project's own account, among this map's own visitors.
voices: Rachel Held Evans — author of Searching for Sunday (2015) and Inspired (2018), co-founder of Evolving Faith in 2018; died in May 2019
Sarah Bessey — Evolving Faith's other co-founder, under whom the conference continued
Blake Chastain — who coined 'exvangelical' in 2016, giving the current a name it did not have
Joshua Harris — whose public statements in 2019 about leaving the faith are among the most widely discussed of these journeys
The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill — Christianity Today's 2021 podcast, the current's most widely shared published document
The memoir shelf — the published accounts by named public authors, whose personal stories fill out the wider picture
movements.legacy: This is a current still forming: its earliest datable landmarks go back only to 2016, making it one of the youngest movements described here. So far it has produced a publishing category, a conference, a subject of study within the sociology of religion, and a large number of people who describe their own journeys in public. The destinations that recur in these published accounts include Orthodoxy, Catholicism, Anglicanism and progressive congregations — a real range, not a single ending point. Its archive is fragile, because the platforms that hold it are.

T. Wright's writing to BibleProject, co-founded in 2014, whose videos and podcast now reach tens of millions. It stands as a direct alternative to reading the Bible as a chart of the future, and it has become a common place for people leaving evangelical churches to re-root their faith.

movements.longDescription: A way of reading the Bible as a single story, running from creation to Jesus and outward from him, has spread across evangelical and mainline churches since about 1990 without ever becoming an organization. Lesslie Newbigin's The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989) set the terms by asking what the church is for in a culture that has heard the story and moved on. Dallas Willard's The Divine Conspiracy (1998) put the kingdom back at the centre of discipleship. N. T. Wright's academic volumes — The New Testament and the People of God (1992), Jesus and the Victory of God (1996) — and his popular ones, Simply Christian (2006) and Surprised by Hope (2008), carried it to a general readership. Scot McKnight's The King Jesus Gospel (2011) argued the point about the gospel itself. And BibleProject, co-founded in 2014 by Tim Mackie and Jon Collins, animated it: short videos, a podcast and a free classroom, reaching an audience that runs into the tens of millions.
movements.teaser: North America and the UK, then the world by digital platform, c. 1990 to today — a reading of the Bible as one story fulfilled in Jesus, carried from Newbigin through Willard and Wright to BibleProject's video and classroom ecosystem, reaching tens of millions.
voices: Lesslie Newbigin — whose The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989) stands at the head of this lineage
Dallas Willard — whose The Divine Conspiracy (1998) made the kingdom the centre of ordinary discipleship
N. T. Wright — whose academic and popular books from 1992 onward carried the reading furthest
Scot McKnight — whose The King Jesus Gospel (2011) pressed the argument about what the gospel actually is
Tim Mackie and Jon Collins — co-founders of BibleProject in 2014, whose videos and classroom are where most people meet this reading now
movements.legacy: It is a teaching current with real formation texture — reading plans, classroom cohorts, church curricula — rather than a body with members, and this map takes that at face value. What it has done is give a generation an alternative to reading the Bible as a chart of the future: story rather than scheme, which puts it in direct rivalry with the dispensational reading culture carried elsewhere here. It has also become a common re-rooting place for people who left evangelical churches and wanted somewhere to stand. No standard scholarly account of it yet exists, which is itself worth saying: it is being described here earlier than the literature has caught up.

movements.name: Fundamentalism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14). Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich and largely self-published: The Fundamentals (12 volumes, 1910–1915, about three million copies distributed), the Niagara Creed (1878), A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield's 'Inspiration' (Presbyterian Review, April 1881), denominational controversy records, and the movement's own periodicals.
movements.floorNote: No question — the movement's stated cause was the historic doctrinal content itself
movements.relationsSummary: Fundamentalism grew out of the Niagara Bible Conference of the 1870s and the Princeton doctrine of biblical inerrancy set out in 1881, decades before it took its name in 1920. It defended traditional Christian doctrine against theological liberalism, as in J. Gresham Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923), and suffered public defeats at the Scopes trial in 1925 and in Princeton Seminary's reorganization in 1929. Much of its constituency later moved into the neo-evangelical movement through the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942, Fuller Seminary in 1947, and Billy Graham's break with separatism in 1957, while its independent Baptist and separatist churches continued on their own. The political mobilization that began with the Moral Majority in 1979 also traces back to this movement, one step beyond its own historical window.
movements.why: The name arrived in 1920, when Curtis Lee Laws called for 'battle royal for the Fundamentals' in the Watchman-Examiner, but the movement was older: twelve volumes called The Fundamentals, financed by Lyman Stewart and given away in some three million copies between 1910 and 1915, defended the doctrine of scripture A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield had set out in 1881. Public defeats followed — the Scopes trial in 1925, Princeton Seminary's reorganization in 1929 — before much of its constituency moved into the neo-evangelical world through the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942 and Billy Graham's 1957 break with separatism, while its independent Baptist and separatist churches carried on.
movements.dateRationale: Episode window c. 1910–1970s as drafted: start at The Fundamentals (12 vols., 1910–1915, verified); end at the documented neo-evangelical handoff (NAE 1942, Fuller 1947, the 1957 Graham break [all S]). The pre-1906 Niagara/Princeton decades ride as a disclosed reach-back on the IX.29 shape. Living:true — an episode end, not an obituary; the separatist continuation is named in copy (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

movements.longDescription: The word arrived in 1920: Curtis Lee Laws, writing in the Watchman-Examiner, proposed calling those willing to do 'battle royal for the Fundamentals' fundamentalists, and the name stuck. The movement was older than the word. The Niagara Bible Conference had met annually from the 1870s until 1897 and adopted a fourteen-point creed in 1878; A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield published 'Inspiration' in the Presbyterian Review in April 1881, giving the doctrine of scripture its most exacting American statement. Between 1910 and 1915 twelve volumes called The Fundamentals were published, financed by Lyman Stewart and given away — around three million copies. The Presbyterian General Assembly adopted a five-point doctrinal deliverance in 1910. Then came the public defeats and the separations: the Scopes trial in July 1925, Princeton Seminary reorganized in 1929 with Westminster founded in answer, and new denominations of their own from the 1930s.
movements.teaser: North America and then beyond, c. 1910 to the 1970s — the institutional-conservative side of the fundamentalist–modernist rupture, from the Niagara Creed and Princeton's doctrine of inspiration to the twelve volumes of The Fundamentals and the name coined in 1920, ending at the neo-evangelical handoff while the separatist world it formed lives on.

A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield — whose 'Inspiration' (Presbyterian Review, April 1881) is the movement's foundational statement about scripture
The Fundamentals — twelve volumes published between 1910 and 1915, financed by Lyman Stewart and distributed free in around three million copies
J. Gresham Machen — whose Christianity and Liberalism (1923) argued the case at its most rigorous
W. B. Riley — organizer of the World's Christian Fundamentals Association in 1919, the movement's first attempt at an institution
movements.legacy: The movement is alive; this window is not its whole life. It closes at a documented handoff rather than a death — the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942, Fuller Seminary in 1947, and Billy Graham's break with separatist fundamentalism in 1957 carried much of its constituency into the neo-evangelical world that this map picks up again at Lausanne. What stayed behind kept going: the independent Baptist and separatist congregations and their institutions are still here. The political mobilization that began with the Moral Majority in 1979 sits one step past this window, and this map notes that connection here rather than giving it a world of its own. George Marsden's Fundamentalism and American Culture (1980) remains the standard account.

movements.name: The Social Gospel
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14).
movements.sourcing: Rich own corpus: Washington Gladden's Applied Christianity (1886), Walter Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907, which went through thirteen printings in five years) and A Theology for the Social Gospel (1917), Charles Sheldon's In His Steps (1896), and the Social Creed of the Churches (1908).
movements.floorNote: The Social Gospel's defining claim was about the Kingdom's social scope — how far Christian faith obligates believers toward social reform — not a dispute over the doctrine of God. 'What would Jesus do?' is treated here as a devotional reading practice within the movement, not as a separate movement of its own.
movements.relationsSummary: This was the social-reform wing of the same era, beginning with Washington Gladden in 1886, Rauschenbusch's pastorate in Hell's Kitchen from that same year, and Charles Sheldon's novel in 1896. Its core period ran from 1907, when Christianity and the Social Crisis appeared, to Rauschenbusch's death in 1918. The Federal Council of Churches' 1908 Social Creed anchors it to the mainline Protestant tradition that later absorbed its stream into its own social agencies. Reinhold Niebuhr's 1932 critique challenged the movement's optimism from within that same broader current.
movements.why: In 1886 Washington Gladden published Applied Christianity the same year Walter Rauschenbusch took a pastorate on the edge of New York's Hell's Kitchen, an experience that turned his theology toward social reform; his Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) went through thirteen printings in five years. Charles Sheldon's 1896 novel In His Steps put the same impulse into a question anyone could ask before acting — what would Jesus do — while the Federal Council of Churches adopted the movement's own Social Creed in 1908. Rauschenbusch's death in 1918 and the war's blow to reform-minded optimism effectively ended the movement, though its stream flowed on into the mainline denominations' own social agencies.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1886–1918 as drafted: start 1886 (Gladden's Applied Christianity [S]; Rauschenbusch's Hell's Kitchen years from 1886 [S]) — a disclosed pre-1906 reach-back, one of the run's two candidate-side straddles; end 1918, story-own (Rauschenbusch's death, verified, plus the war's blow to the movement's optimism [S]). The 1907–1918 gravity window rests on two verified anchors and is therefore R6-legal (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

movements.longDescription: In 1886 Washington Gladden published Applied Christianity, and in the same year Walter Rauschenbusch took a pastorate on the edge of Hell's Kitchen in New York, where what he saw of tenement life reorganized his theology. He and others formed the Brotherhood of the Kingdom in 1892. His Christianity and the Social Crisis appeared in 1907 and went through thirteen printings in five years, and A Theology for the Social Gospel followed in 1917. Charles Sheldon's novel In His Steps (1896) put the same instinct into a form anyone could use: asking, before each decision, what Jesus would do. In 1908 the newly formed Federal Council of Churches adopted the Social Creed of the Churches — the movement's clearest institutional mark, and the ancestor of the denominational social statements that came after it.
movements.teaser: Urban, industrial North America, c. 1886 to 1918 — the rupture's social-reform side, from Gladden's Applied Christianity and Rauschenbusch's Hell's Kitchen years to the Social Creed of 1908, ending with Rauschenbusch's death and the war's blow to the movement's optimism, its stream absorbed into the mainline's own agencies.
voices: Walter Rauschenbusch — pastor from 1886 on the edge of Hell's Kitchen, author of Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) and A Theology for the Social Gospel (1917)
Washington Gladden — whose Applied Christianity (1886) opened the movement's published record
Charles Sheldon — whose novel In His Steps (1896) turned the movement's question into a practice ordinary readers could take up
The Brotherhood of the Kingdom — the working fellowship Rauschenbusch and his friends formed in 1892
The Social Creed of the Churches (1908) — the Federal Council of Churches' own statement, and the movement's clearest institutional mark
movements.legacy: The movement itself ended. Rauschenbusch died in 1918, and the war took the confidence out of a theology built on the expectation that the kingdom was arriving through reform; Reinhold Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) later made the criticism stick. But the stream did not stop — it was absorbed into the mainline denominations' own social agencies, and the mainline century that follows on this map is its named heir. The Social Creed of 1908 stands behind the denominational social statements that followed it. And In His Steps left something odder and more durable: the question 'what would Jesus do' is still in circulation, a century after the novel that put it there.

movements.name: The Mainline Century — Liberal Protestantism & Neo-Orthodoxy
movements.informalName: The Protestant Mainline and Its Theologies
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14). Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich academic and institutional record: Fosdick's sermon of 21 May 1922, Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923), the Auburn Affirmation of January 1924, Barth's Römerbrief (1919/1922), Bultmann's 'New Testament and Mythology' (1941), Tillich's Systematic Theology (1951–63), Federal and National Council of Churches records, and denominational archives.
movements.floorNote: Where this tradition reaches into the present, it's best judged body by body, not as one label — the same approach used for Progressive Christianity, which this current hands off to around 1990. The record spans confessional reaffirmation, like the Barmen Declaration of 1934, and non-realist reinterpretation, and each body and text needs its own accounting rather than one judgment covering the whole current.
movements.relationsSummary: This tradition reaches back to Schleiermacher and the historical-critical scholarship of the nineteenth century, including the Briggs heresy trial of 1891–93 and Harnack's work around 1900, and took institutional shape with the Federal Council of Churches in 1908. The fundamentalist-modernist controversy — Fosdick's sermon in 1922, Machen's reply in 1923, and the Auburn Affirmation in 1924 — stands in tension with fundamentalism as its opposite pole. From within liberal theology, Barth's turn to neo-orthodoxy (1919/1922) was carried further by Niebuhr, Bultmann, and Tillich; Barth's line also runs into the Confessing Church and the Barmen Declaration. The National Council of Churches, formed in 1950, and the World Council of Churches are this tradition's institutional and conciliar homes. Membership peaked in the mid-1960s and then declined, and this current hands off around 1990 to what is now called progressive Christianity.
movements.why: Harry Emerson Fosdick's 1922 sermon 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' and J. Gresham Machen's reply the following year opened a rupture that the Auburn Affirmation, eventually signed by some 1,300 mainline clergy, answered from the liberal side. From inside that same world, Karl Barth's Romans commentary opened a neo-orthodox turn that Reinhold Niebuhr, Rudolf Bultmann and Paul Tillich each carried further, while the seminaries that trained the denominations' clergy watched membership peak in the mid-1960s before its long decline began.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1900–1990 as drafted: start 1900 with the reach-back to Schleiermacher and the historical-critical century disclosed [S] — the run's second candidate-side straddle; end fork resolved at c. 1990 over the 1974 branch, meeting IX.18's start seamlessly (the 1974 branch would have left 1974–1990 silent). Episode end, living:true, continuation named (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

movements.longDescription: This is the world the mainline Protestant seminaries built and the mainline denominations taught. Its reach-back runs to Schleiermacher and to the historical-critical century — the Briggs heresy trial of 1891 to 1893 in America, Harnack's What Is Christianity? in 1900 — and its institutional face arrived with the Federal Council of Churches in 1908. The public rupture came in the 1920s: Harry Emerson Fosdick preached 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' on 21 May 1922; J. Gresham Machen answered with Christianity and Liberalism in 1923; and the Auburn Affirmation, released on 9 January 1924 with about 150 signatures and eventually some 1,300, answered from the other side. Then the ground moved again from inside: Karl Barth's Romans commentary of 1919, rewritten in 1922, opened the neo-orthodox turn against the liberal theology that had formed the field, and Reinhold Niebuhr, Rudolf Bultmann and Paul Tillich each reshaped the field in turn.
movements.teaser: North America, Germany and Britain, c. 1900 to 1990 — the academic and institutional side of the same rupture, from Fosdick's 1922 sermon and Machen's reply through Barth, Bultmann and Tillich, the seminaries serving as the denominations' teaching offices until the lane hands off to the contemporary progressive label.
voices: Harry Emerson Fosdick — whose sermon of 21 May 1922 gave the controversy its most quoted title
The signers of the Auburn Affirmation — about 150 at its release on 9 January 1924, some 1,300 in the end
Karl Barth — whose Romans commentary (1919, rewritten 1922) opened the neo-orthodox turn, and who later drafted Barmen
Reinhold Niebuhr — whose Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) turned the same criticism on social optimism
Rudolf Bultmann — whose 'New Testament and Mythology' (1941) set the terms of a generation's argument about how the New Testament is read
Paul Tillich — whose Systematic Theology, published between 1951 and 1963, was the era's most ambitious attempt at a whole account
movements.legacy: The mainline denominations are alive; what closed around 1990 is this particular century of theirs. Their membership peaked in the mid-1960s and turned down after that, and the current that carries their questions now goes under the contemporary progressive label, which this map treats as their continuation. Their institutional legacy is large: the National Council of Churches from 1950, the World Council of Churches in Geneva, and a network of seminaries that trained the denominations' clergy and produced much of the century's biblical and theological scholarship. Barth's line ran into the Confessing Church, whose Barmen Declaration he drafted. And the argument with fundamentalism, fought out in dated documents on both sides, is the one this map draws as a standing tension rather than a settled question.

movements.name: New Calvinism (Young, Restless, Reformed)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14). Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich and well-documented: Collin Hansen's naming article (Christianity Today, September 2006) and book (2008); the networks' own founding records (The Gospel Coalition from 2005, Together for the Gospel from 2006, Acts 29 from 1998); John Piper's Desiring God (1986); conference and publishing archives; and the Mars Hill record, including its 2014 dissolution announcement and Christianity Today's podcast The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill (2021).
movements.floorNote: No plain-reading question — confessionally Reformed-evangelical by its institutions' own dated statements (TGC founding documents 2005 [S])
movements.relationsSummary: This is the 2000s conservative Reformed resurgence built around John Piper, church-planting and publishing networks such as The Gospel Coalition (2005–07) and Together for the Gospel (2006–2022), and Acts 29, founded in 1998. It grew out of the wider evangelical world, and one of its early leaders, Mark Driscoll, had first been part of the emerging church movement before his Reformed turn. Acts 29 continued after removing Driscoll and Mars Hill Church in 2014. The Mars Hill collapse that followed also became a landmark story within the deconstruction and ex-vangelical movement's own accounts of leaving evangelical churches.
movements.why: Collin Hansen named the current 'Young, Restless, Reformed' in a 2006 Christianity Today article, but its roots ran through John Piper's Desiring God (1986) and church-planting networks like Acts 29, founded in 1998, and institutions like The Gospel Coalition, launched with its Confessional Statement in 2007. Its record includes its crises as plainly as its growth: Acts 29 removed Mark Driscoll and Mars Hill from the network in August 2014, and Mars Hill announced its own dissolution that October.
movements.dateRationale: Start fork resolved at c. 1998 as drafted (Acts 29 founded 1998, verified), over the 1986 Piper and 2005–07 institutional-wave branches; end present (living). R7 recency stated rather than hidden: the institutional wave sits at the twenty-year line and passes on the succession and institutionalization prongs (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

movements.longDescription: In September 2006 Christianity Today ran a piece by Collin Hansen called 'Young, Restless, Reformed', and it gave a name to something already under way: a wave of younger American evangelicals adopting Reformed theology, organized through networks rather than through denominations. Its most-cited earlier text was John Piper's Desiring God (1986). Its church-planting turn came earlier than its name — Mars Hill in Seattle in 1996, and the Acts 29 network founded in 1998 by David Nicholas with Mark Driscoll — and its institutional wave came after: The Gospel Coalition, initiated by D. A. Carson and Tim Keller in 2004, first meeting in 2005, launched with its Confessional Statement in 2007; Together for the Gospel, whose first conference was in 2006. It ran on conferences, seminaries and publishing rather than on denominations, and it crossed a great many of them. Hansen's book followed in 2008.
movements.teaser: North America and then the digital world, c. 1998 to today — the 2000s conservative Reformed resurgence named in Christianity Today in 2006, built on Acts 29, The Gospel Coalition and Together for the Gospel, and marked as much by its founder crises as by its growth.
voices: Collin Hansen — whose Christianity Today article of September 2006 and book of 2008 named the movement
John Piper — whose Desiring God (1986) is the current's most-cited earlier text
D. A. Carson and Tim Keller — who initiated The Gospel Coalition in 2004; its Confessional Statement was adopted at the 2007 launch
Acts 29 — founded in 1998 by David Nicholas with Mark Driscoll, and the movement's church-planting arm
The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill — Christianity Today's twelve-part podcast by Mike Cosper (2021), the fullest published account of the movement's best-known collapse
movements.legacy: It is a living current, and a young one — its institutional wave only crosses twenty years now, which this map states rather than hides. Its record includes its crises, all of them on the public record and all dated: Mark Driscoll handed the Acts 29 presidency to Matt Chandler in March 2012; in August 2014 Acts 29 removed Driscoll and Mars Hill from the network by its own published statement; Mars Hill's dissolution was announced on 31 October 2014. Acts 29 continued, and The Gospel Coalition continues; Together for the Gospel held its last conference in 2022. The Mars Hill collapse is also a landmark in someone else's story — it recurs constantly in the deconstruction communities' own published accounts, and this map wires that seam in both directions.

movements.name: Indonesian Christianity — the Independent Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14). Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: the HKBP's own records of its 1930 independence as the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies, Indonesian church histories such as Aritonang and Steenbrink's, and testimonies from the 1965–71 Timor revival.
movements.relationsSummary: The HKBP, the Batak church, became fully independent in 1930 and is now among the largest Lutheran bodies in the world. Between 1965 and 1966, in the wake of mass political violence and a new state requirement that every citizen declare a religion, church membership grew rapidly across the archipelago. A revival swept through Timor from 1965 to 1971 in the same period. Indonesian church life since has continued under the state ideology of Pancasila, with periodic episodes of persecution.
movements.why: The Batak church, the HKBP, became the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies in 1930 and is now among the largest Lutheran bodies anywhere. Between 1965 and 1971 a revival swept through Timor — recounted in Mel Tari's widely read but disputed Like a Mighty Wind (1971) and evaluated more carefully on the ground by George Peters in 1973 — in the same years that a state requirement to declare a religion, following the violence of 1965-66, drove rapid church growth across the archipelago.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1906 — the era-boundary start of the era-10 segment the Frozen E9 Q3 fork left for this gate to create; first in-window anchor the HKBP's independence, 1930 (verified); end present (living) (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The HKBP's own records: the church's independence in 1930 as the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies
sources.note: The HKBP's own institutional record of its 1930 independence.

sources.work: Mel Tari, Like a Mighty Wind (1971), with the GMIT revival-team records
sources.note: The Timor revival's own participant account, though scholars have contested how much it may be embellished.

sources.note: The on-site critical evaluation, written specifically as a corrective to Tari's account, weighing the political context that shaped the conversions.

sources.work: Jan Aritonang and Karel Steenbrink (eds.), A History of Christianity in Indonesia (Brill, 2008)
sources.note: The standard survey, covering this period.

movements.longDescription: Indonesia holds one of the largest Christian populations in the Muslim-majority world, and its churches have been running themselves for most of a century. The Batak church, the HKBP, became independent in 1930 — the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies — and is among the largest Lutheran bodies anywhere. The archipelago's Christianity is regional rather than national: Sumatra, Java, Timor and the eastern islands each have their own story. Two of the century's turning points fall close together. Between 1965 and 1971 a revival ran through Timor, whose best-known account, Mel Tari's Like a Mighty Wind (1971), is disputed for embellishment, and whose most careful evaluation, George W. Peters's Indonesia Revival: Focus on Timor (1973), was written on the ground. And after the violence of 1965 and 1966, in a state that required every citizen to declare a religion, church membership grew very fast — a growth that cannot honestly be told apart from its context.
movements.teaser: Sumatra, Java, Timor and the wider archipelago, 1906 to today — the HKBP self-governing from 1930, the crisis growth of the mid-1960s and the Timor revival, one of the largest Christian communities in the Muslim-majority world carried past 1906 at last.
voices: The HKBP — the Batak church, self-governing since 1930 and among the largest Lutheran bodies in the world
Mel Tari — whose Like a Mighty Wind (1971) carried the Timor revival to a global readership, and whose account is contested
George W. Peters — whose Indonesia Revival: Focus on Timor (1973) is the on-site critical evaluation, and whose corrective relation to Tari is part of the record
The GMIT revival teams — the Timorese church's own teams, whose records document the revival from inside it
The archipelago's congregations — whose life under Pancasila, and through the periodic episodes of persecution, is the century's ordinary story here
movements.legacy: These are living churches, and large ones, in a country where Christians are a minority and their position is periodically contested. The HKBP's independence in 1930 stands as an early institutional marker of the whole twentieth-century shift from mission to self-governing church. The Timor revival gave world Pentecostalism one of its most circulated stories and, in Tari and Peters together, an unusually clear case of a movement's account and its critical evaluation surviving side by side.

movements.name: Northeast India & the Mar Thoma Church — the 20th Century
movements.informalName: The Hill Churches and Mar Thoma after 1906
movements.region: Kerala; Mizo, Khasi & Naga hills; diaspora
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14). Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: church records, revival hymnody in local languages such as lengkhawm zai, Mar Thoma synod records, and the continuing record of the Maramon Convention.
movements.relationsSummary: The Mizo revivals that began in 1906 transformed the northeastern hills, helping make Mizoram and Nagaland among the most Christian regions on earth. In Kerala, the Mar Thoma Church — which separated as a reform wing from the wider Malankara St Thomas Christian community in 1889 — grew through the same century and spread with the Malayali diaspora.
movements.why: Revival waves that ran through the Mizo hills from 1906 onward produced lengkhawm zai, hymns composed in the local language and manner of singing that are now the churches' ordinary worship, and helped make Mizoram and Nagaland among the most heavily Christian regions on earth. In Kerala, the Mar Thoma Church, the reform wing of the ancient St Thomas Christians, grew under its own indigenous leadership through the same century, gathering each year at the Maramon Convention and following its people into a worldwide diaspora.

sources.work: The hills' churches' own twentieth-century record: Mizo revival waves (1906, 1913, 1919, the 1930s); synod records under indigenous leadership; the continuing composition of lengkhawm zai
sources.note: The revival hymnody described earlier is now this church's own mainstream practice. Records are largely in local languages, which limits outside access.

sources.note: The standard reference for both wings' continuations.

sources.note: The standard account for the northeast hills.

movements.longDescription: Two very different Indian Christian worlds are carried together here, both of them twentieth-century continuations of older stories. In the northeast hills, revival waves ran through the Mizo country from 1906 and again in 1913, in 1919 and through the 1930s, and out of them came lengkhawm zai — hymns composed in the local language for the local way of singing, which is now the churches' ordinary practice rather than a curiosity. Within a few generations Mizoram and Nagaland became, on the usual counts, among the most heavily Christian regions on earth. In Kerala, the Mar Thoma Church — the reform wing of the ancient St Thomas Christians — went through its own century under indigenous leadership, with the annual Maramon Convention as its great gathering, and sent congregations out with the diaspora.
movements.teaser: Kerala, the Mizo, Khasi and Naga hills and the diaspora, 1906 to today — revival waves from 1906 that made Mizoram and Nagaland among the most Christian regions on earth, alongside the Mar Thoma Church's own century and its scattering abroad.
voices: The Mizo revival waves — from 1906 and recurring through the 1930s, remembered in the churches' own synod records
Lengkhawm zai — the indigenous hymnody composed out of the revivals, and the hills' churches' continuing mainstream practice
Abraham Mar Thoma and his successors — under whom the Mar Thoma Church passed through its twentieth century
The Maramon Convention — the Mar Thoma Church's annual gathering and one of its longest continuous records of itself
The diaspora parishes — Mar Thoma congregations planted wherever Malayali families settled
movements.legacy: Both are living churches. Their hymnody is one of the clearest cases anywhere of a Christian tradition composing in its own musical language rather than translating someone else's. The Mar Thoma Church is a worldwide body with parishes on several continents and a continuing place in Indian ecumenical life. On this map they complete a chain: the nineteenth-century entries for both regions stopped at 1906 with nothing to hand on to, and this is where they continue.

movements.name: The Malankara Churches — Orthodox & Jacobite
movements.informalName: The Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14). Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: synod and Catholicate records, the 1934 constitution, the litigation record including the 1958 and 2017 Supreme Court rulings, and diaspora parish records.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1912, Patriarch Abdul Masih II's consecration of a Catholicos split the community into an autocephalous wing, the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church, and a patriarchal wing, the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church loyal to the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch. A constitution followed in 1934. A mid-century reunion broke down in 1975 when the patriarch deposed the Catholicos, and the dispute has continued in India's courts, most recently in a 2017 Supreme Court ruling. Both wings belong to the same account here, since the division itself is the story. Together they carry forward the ancient St Thomas Christian tradition, alongside the Mar Thoma Church, the reform wing that separated earlier, in 1889.
movements.why: In 1912 Patriarch Abdul Masih II consecrated a Catholicos for Malankara, splitting Kerala's ancient St Thomas Christian community into an autocephalous Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and a patriarchal Jacobite Syrian Christian Church loyal to the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch. A reunion in 1958 held for a generation until the patriarch deposed the Catholicos in 1975, reopening a division fought out ever since in India's civil courts, most recently in a Supreme Court ruling of 2017, over parishes, properties and endowments.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1912 (the Catholicate consecration under Patriarch Abdul Masih II, verified); end present (living) (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The dated sequence of events: the 1912 consecration of Baselios Paulose I as Catholicos of the East by Patriarch Abdul Masih II; the 1958 Supreme Court ruling and reconciliation; the 1975 re-split; the Supreme Court rulings of 1995 and 2017
sources.note: The dated backbone of this history.

sources.work: The two churches' own records: Malankara Orthodox synodal records and the Catholicate centenary literature (2012); Jacobite Syrian Christian Church and patriarchate counter-documentation
sources.note: Both churches' own institutional voices are represented here, side by side.

sources.work: The Indian court record from 1913 to the present, including the Vattipanam suit and the 2017 Supreme Court ruling
sources.note: A century of church doctrine argued out before civil courts. Both parties to the dispute authored this record in roughly equal measure, so neither side's account should be read as neutral.

sources.work: Robert Eric Frykenberg, Christianity in India: From Beginnings to the Present (Oxford, 2008)
sources.note: Covers the split; dedicated English-language monographs on this twentieth-century schism remain thin.

movements.longDescription: In 1912 Patriarch Abdul Masih II consecrated a Catholicos of the East for Malankara, and the ancient St Thomas community in Kerala divided into two: an autocephalous party, the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church, and a patriarchal party, the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church, which holds to the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch. A constitution followed in 1934. A Supreme Court ruling in 1958 brought a reunion that held for a generation; in 1975 the patriarch deposed the Catholicos and the split reopened. Further Supreme Court rulings came in 1995 and in 2017. This is a century of ecclesiology argued in civil courts — over parishes, properties and endowments as much as over jurisdiction — and both parties have written the record, since both have been litigants throughout.
movements.teaser: Kerala and the worldwide diaspora, 1912 to today — the ancient St Thomas majority carried at last: the 1912 Catholicate, a constitution in 1934, mid-century reunion and the renewed split of 1975, and a century of ecclesiology argued before India's civil courts.
voices: Patriarch Abdul Masih II — whose consecration of a Catholicos for Malankara in 1912 begins the division
The Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church — the autocephalous wing, with its Catholicate and its centenary literature of 2012
The Jacobite Syrian Christian Church — the patriarchal wing, whose counter-documentation is the other half of the record
The 1934 constitution — the document both wings have argued about ever since
The court record — from the Vattipanam suit onward to the Supreme Court rulings of 1958, 1995 and 2017, written by both parties at once
movements.legacy: Both churches are alive, both are substantial, and both have gone worldwide with the Kerala diaspora, with parishes across many countries. They carry the St Thomas tradition's liturgical life forward, and their continued existence is why that tradition is not only a matter of the distant past. The court record runs as recently as the Supreme Court ruling of 2017.

movements.name: The Georgian Orthodox Church Restored
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 10 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 10 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-14). Under the Living-Era Protocol Addendum V1.0 — ratified at this Freeze — this status is a dated reading of a living tradition, not a permanent verdict.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the 1917 restoration acts, Soviet-era persecution records, the 1943 Moscow recognition and 1990 Constantinople tomos, and patriarchate records, including those from Ilia II's patriarchate since 1977.
movements.relationsSummary: Alongside the Armenian church, this is one of the Caucasus region's modern anchors. Georgia's bishops unilaterally restored the church's autocephaly on 25 March 1917, reversing Russia's 1811 abolition of it. Ambrosi's 1922 protest memorandum and trial, and the Soviet decades that followed, tested the restored church before Moscow recognized it in 1943 and Constantinople in 1990. Since the Soviet Union's end, the church has held a strong role in Georgia's national life.
movements.why: Georgia's church had been autocephalous since antiquity until Russia abolished that status in 1811; in March 1917, without waiting for anyone's permission, an assembly of Georgian bishops, clergy and laypeople declared it restored, and a council that September elected Kyrion II as Catholicos-Patriarch, who was dead within a year under circumstances still unresolved. Recognition came slowly from two directions — Moscow acknowledged the restoration in 1943, Constantinople only in 1990 — after decades of Soviet rule that also saw Ambrosi tried in 1922 for a protest memorandum.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1917 (autocephaly restored by Georgia's bishops, 25 Mar 1917, verified — against the 1811 abolition the Frozen E9 gap ruling disclosed); end present (living) (Era 10 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-14)

sources.work: The dated sequence of events: autocephaly restoration declared 12 (25) March 1917 by an assembly of bishops, clergy and laity; the September 1917 council electing Catholicos-Patriarch Kyrion II; Russian recognition in 1943; Constantinople's tomos in 1990
sources.note: The 1917 and 1943 dates are well documented (National Archives of Georgia; Orthodox History); the exact status of the 1990 tomos is less certain, though the event itself is agreed.

sources.work: The church's own restoration documents: the March 1917 declaration and council acts; Kyrion II's correspondence with Moscow; the record of the Soviet persecution that followed

movements.longDescription: Georgia's church had been autocephalous since antiquity until that status was abolished in 1811 and the church absorbed into the Russian one. On 12 March 1917 by the old calendar — 25 March by the new — an assembly of Georgian bishops, clergy and laypeople declared the autocephaly restored, without waiting for anyone's permission; a council that September elected Kyrion II as Catholicos-Patriarch. Kyrion was dead by 1918 in circumstances the record itself leaves unresolved. Ambrosi submitted a protest memorandum in 1922 and was put on trial for it. Then came the Soviet decades, which fell on this church as heavily as on any. Recognition came slowly and from two directions: Moscow acknowledged the restored autocephaly on 31 October 1943, and Constantinople issued its tomos on 4 March 1990. Ilia II has been Catholicos-Patriarch since 1977.
movements.teaser: Georgia in the Caucasus, 1917 to today — autocephaly restored by the country's own bishops in March 1917 against the abolition of 1811, carried through the Soviet decades to recognition by Moscow in 1943 and by Constantinople in 1990.
voices: The assembly of March 1917 — bishops, clergy and laypeople together, who declared the autocephaly restored rather than requesting it
Kyrion II — elected Catholicos-Patriarch at the council of September 1917 and dead by 1918, in circumstances the record leaves open
Ambrosi — whose protest memorandum of 1922 was answered with a trial
The restoration documents — the March 1917 declaration, the council acts, and the correspondence with Moscow that followed
Ilia II — Catholicos-Patriarch since 1977, through the Soviet decades and after
movements.legacy: It is a living national church, and one with an unusually strong place in its country's public life. Its restored autocephaly, declared unilaterally in 1917 and recognized in 1943 and 1990, is now uncontested. On this map the entry answers a question left open at the previous era's close: whether the Caucasus lane resumes at all after 1811. It does, here. The English-language scholarship on the modern Georgian church remains thin, and that thinness is named rather than papered over.

movements.longDescription: In 1906 the United States religious census listed the Churches of Christ separately from the Disciples of Christ for the first time — a bureaucratic act that recorded a division which had been widening for a generation. David Lipscomb's own correspondence with the Census Bureau is part of how that listing came about. What was listed was the a cappella wing: congregations that sing without instruments and recognize no authority above the local congregation. Their journals did the work an office would have done elsewhere — the Gospel Advocate, the Firm Foundation and others carried the arguments, the news and the appeals for money. They founded colleges, sent missionaries widely, and divided again in the middle of the century over whether congregations could support institutions in common. They confess the content of the historic creeds while refusing to make subscription to any creed a test, and they say so plainly.
movements.teaser: North America's upper South and then the world, 1906 to today — the a cappella wing of the Stone-Campbell movement from the federal census listing that recorded the division, keeping the parent's refusal of creed-subscription while teaching the creeds' own content.
voices: David Lipscomb — whose correspondence with the Census Bureau is part of the record of the 1906 listing, and whose Gospel Advocate shaped the wing
The journals — the Gospel Advocate, the Firm Foundation and their rivals, which functioned as the movement's nervous system in place of a headquarters
The colleges — founded and funded congregationally, and the movement's principal formation institutions
The congregations — which, on this movement's own understanding, are the whole visible church and answer to no one above themselves
movements.legacy: It is a living body, in North America and well beyond it through a century of mission work. Its a cappella singing is the thing a visitor notices first, and it is still the practice. Its refusal of denominational machinery has held remarkably well — there is still no headquarters to write to — and its mid-century division over institutional cooperation produced a continuing non-institutional stream inside it.

movements.relationsSummary: This is the Disciples of Christ wing that emerged from the 1906 division, later reorganizing itself into a denomination through the 1968 Restructure known as 'The Design.' It was a founding member of the ecumenical movement, joining the Federal Council of Churches in 1908 and the World Council of Churches in 1948. It also underwent a second division: congregations that became the independent Christian Churches had been meeting apart since 1927 at the North American Christian Convention and were listed separately in denominational yearbooks by 1971.
movements.why: After the 1906 division, the Disciples of Christ kept their instruments and their national organization, becoming founding members of the Federal Council of Churches in 1908 and the World Council of Churches in 1948 before adopting a 1968 plan called 'The Design' that turned a movement of congregations into a denomination. That step came after decades of quiet separation: congregations that became the independent Christian Churches had been meeting apart at the North American Christian Convention since 1927 and were listed separately in the yearbooks by 1971 — one plea for Christian unity having produced three distinct streams.

movements.longDescription: The other side of the 1906 division took the opposite road. The Disciples of Christ kept their instruments and their national organizations, joined the Federal Council of Churches at its founding in 1908 and the World Council of Churches at its founding in 1948, and in 1968 adopted a plan called the Restructure — 'The Design' — that turned a movement of congregations into a denomination. But that step cost them a second division, which had been forming for decades: the independent Christian Churches had been meeting separately at the North American Christian Convention since 1927, and by 1971 they were listed separately in the yearbooks. So one nineteenth-century plea for Christian unity ended up producing three distinct streams.
movements.teaser: North America and then the world, 1906 to today — the Disciples wing after the 1906 division, with a second division disclosed inside it as the independent Christian Churches went their own way, and a denomination formed by the Restructure of 1968.
voices: The Restructure of 1968 — 'The Design', the Disciples' own constitutional self-description
The North American Christian Convention — meeting from 1927, the independent Christian Churches' gathering and the mark of the second division
The Disciples' ecumenical record — founding membership of the Federal Council of Churches in 1908 and of the World Council of Churches in 1948
The congregations of both streams — which went on cooperating locally in many places long after the yearbooks separated them
movements.legacy: Both streams are alive. The Disciples' ecumenical commitment is institutional — they were founding members of both the Federal Council in 1908 and the World Council in 1948 — which is what their founding plea for unity became; the independent Christian Churches remain a large, congregationally governed stream. The irony is not lost on either of them: a movement founded to end division has divided twice.

movements.relationsSummary: This is the twentieth-century continuation of the Black church tradition. The Great Migration remade it as an urban, northern institution; the Church of God in Christ rose from 1907; the National Baptist Convention split in 1915; the civil rights movement grew out of these congregations, with Martin Luther King Jr and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957; and James Cone's writings opened the field of Black theology. Its worship traditions also share roots with the Pentecostal movement that grew out of the Azusa Street revival.
movements.why: The Great Migration carried Black congregations out of the rural South and into northern cities, remaking a whole religious culture within a generation; the Church of God in Christ took its Pentecostal turn out of Memphis in 1907 and grew into one of the century's major denominations, while the National Baptist Convention split in 1915. From the 1950s these congregations were the civil rights movement's infrastructure — Martin Luther King Jr. worked out of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957 — and at the end of the 1960s James Cone's books opened Black theology as a field of its own.

movements.longDescription: The Great Migration moved Black Americans out of the rural South in enormous numbers, and the church moved with them: congregations founded in the North and in the cities, and a whole religious culture remade in a generation. The Church of God in Christ, which took its Pentecostal turn in 1907 out of Memphis, rose fast and became one of the century's major bodies. The National Baptist Convention split in 1915. From the 1950s the congregations were the civil-rights movement's infrastructure: Martin Luther King Jr and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957, worked out of them, and much of what survives of that movement's own voice is sermons. At the end of the 1960s James Cone published the founding works of Black theology, in 1969 and 1970, and opened a field in the seminaries that had not existed before them.
movements.teaser: The United States, 1906 to today — the Great Migration remaking the Black church urban and northern, COGIC's rise from 1907, the National Baptist split of 1915, the civil-rights church and Black theology: the future the map's nineteenth-century entry named and no row had carried.

The National Baptist bodies — whose 1915 division is one of the century's defining institutional events in Black church life

The preachers of the movement — whose sermons are the largest surviving body of its own voice
James Cone — whose founding works of Black theology, published in 1969 and 1970, opened an academic field that did not exist before them
movements.legacy: It is a living tradition and, by any reckoning, one of the first-order Christian stories of the twentieth century. It supplied the civil-rights movement with its buildings, its money, its networks and much of its language, and the sermon remains the form in which a great deal of American public moral argument still gets made. Black theology became a field with its own literature and its own critics. And on this map the entry answers a debt: the nineteenth-century Black church entry ends in 1906 pointing forward to 'the civil-rights church' as its own future, and until now nothing carried it.

movements.longDescription: Ellen White died on 16 July 1915, and the movement she had helped found carried on without the person whose writings had shaped it — which is itself one of the plainest facts about it. Its confession settled in public over the following decades. In 1931 the church's yearbook carried a statement of twenty-two beliefs, explicitly trinitarian; in 1980 the General Conference session at Dallas adopted the Fundamental Beliefs, twenty-seven of them, restating the same. Between those two documents the church became a genuinely global body, and it kept documenting itself with the thoroughness it has had since the beginning: General Conference minutes, yearbooks, statistical reports, periodicals. Its own internal arguments, including the long controversy that followed the book Questions on Doctrine, are on that same public record rather than hidden in it.
movements.teaser: North America and then the world, 1906 to today — the Adventist church after Ellen White's death in 1915, its confession explicitly trinitarian in the 1931 yearbook statement and again in the Fundamental Beliefs of 1980, its self-documentation as compulsive as ever.

The General Conference record — minutes, yearbooks and statistics, kept with unusual thoroughness and publicly available
The church's own internal debates — carried in its own periodicals rather than settled quietly
movements.legacy: It is a living worldwide church. Its own count runs to some twenty-two million members; no independent counter is named here, and the figure should be read as the church's own. Its self-documentation is unusually thorough, which makes it one of the better-documented denominations of its size. On this map it does one specific job: the nineteenth-century Adventist entry left a question about this church's confession open by name, to be settled when the twentieth century could be looked at, and the 1931 and 1980 documents are where the church itself settles it, in its own words and on the record.

movements.longDescription: On 3 April 1960 Dennis Bennett told his congregation in Van Nuys, California, that he had spoken in tongues. The announcement is conventionally taken as the start of the charismatic movement inside the historic Protestant churches, and it went where the earlier Pentecostal revival had not: into mainline Protestant parishes, whose members mostly stayed where they were. Bennett published his own account, Nine O'Clock in the Morning, in 1970. Alongside it and overlapping it came the Jesus movement, roughly 1967 to 1972, which reached young people outside the churches altogether and brought a great many of them in — Calvary Chapel, begun in 1965, became its best-known institutional home, and the music that came out of it changed what congregational worship sounds like. The Vineyard association formed in 1982, at the edge of this window, as the wave handed on to what came next.
movements.teaser: North America, the UK and then the world, 1960 to the 1980s — Dennis Bennett's Van Nuys announcement, the mainline charismatic wave, Calvary Chapel and the Jesus movement, closing at the Vineyard's founding as the wave subsided and the churches it left carried on.
voices: Dennis Bennett — whose announcement of 3 April 1960 is the movement's conventional starting point, and whose Nine O'Clock in the Morning (1970) is his own account of it
Calvary Chapel — begun in 1965 and the Jesus movement's best-known institutional home
The Jesus movement — roughly 1967 to 1972, documented as much in journalism and memoir as in church records
The Vineyard association — formed in 1982, at the window's edge, and the handoff to the next wave
The movement's periodicals — the newsletters and magazines through which mainline charismatics found each other before anyone had organized them
movements.legacy: The wave subsided; the bodies it created did not, and Calvary Chapel and the Vineyard are ongoing associations with churches worldwide. Its longest effect is probably musical: the worship style that came out of the Jesus movement is now the default in a very large part of English-speaking Protestantism, whether or not the congregations singing it know where it came from. It also seeded what followed — the megachurch and seeker movement and, later, the church-planting networks of the 2000s both grew in ground this renewal had turned over. The Catholic side of the same renewal is carried elsewhere on this map, alongside the other Catholic lay movements.

movements.relationsSummary: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 set three streams running: the International Missionary Council, founded in 1921; Life and Work, from 1925; and Faith and Order, from 1927. These converged into the World Council of Churches, constituted at Amsterdam in 1948, with the missionary council merging in at New Delhi in 1961. Orthodox churches are members, while the Roman Catholic Church works alongside it without joining. It stands as a counterpart to the Lausanne movement of 1974, the evangelical alternative answer to the same question of how divided churches should work together, and it grew out of the institutional world built by mainline liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy.
movements.why: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 left three currents running — the International Missionary Council, founded in 1921, and the Life and Work and Faith and Order movements of the 1920s — and they converged in the World Council of Churches, constituted at Amsterdam in 1948 with 147 member churches, with the missionary council joining at New Delhi in 1961. It is a council of churches rather than a church itself, with no authority over its members and no confession of its own; Orthodox churches belong to it, while the Roman Catholic Church works alongside it without joining.

movements.longDescription: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 left three currents running, which came together over the following decades. The International Missionary Council was founded in October 1921; Life and Work, concerned with the churches' common action in society, took shape in 1925; Faith and Order, concerned with the doctrinal questions that divided them, in 1927. The last two merged into the World Council of Churches, constituted at Amsterdam on 22 August 1948 with 147 member churches, and the International Missionary Council joined them at New Delhi in 1961. It is a council of churches, not a church: it has no authority over its members and no confession of its own, and each member body keeps its own. Orthodox churches are members. The Roman Catholic Church is not, and works with it in other ways.
movements.teaser: Geneva and the world, 1921 to today — Edinburgh 1910's three streams converging in the World Council of Churches: the International Missionary Council in 1921, Amsterdam's 147 churches in 1948, and the merger at New Delhi in 1961.
voices: The Edinburgh generation — whose 1910 conference set three currents running and whose watchword generation built what followed
The International Missionary Council — founded in October 1921, and merged into the World Council at New Delhi in 1961
The Amsterdam assembly of 22 August 1948 — 147 churches constituting the World Council, whose acts are the institution's founding record
Faith and Order and Life and Work — the two movements, from 1927 and 1925, whose merger the council actually was
The member churches — each of which speaks for itself, since the council speaks for none of them
movements.legacy: It is a living institution and the century's principal experiment in getting separated churches to act and argue together in one room. Its assemblies and its Faith and Order work have produced a large body of shared statements on questions that had divided churches for centuries, and its member churches have used them. This map draws it as the counter-pole to the Lausanne movement of 1974 — two different answers, from the same century, to the question of how churches that disagree should work together — and as the institutional home of the mainline century that built it.

movements.longDescription: In 1907 Rome moved against what it called modernism: the decree Lamentabili and the encyclical Pascendi condemned it, and in 1910 an anti-modernist oath was required of clergy and teachers. Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell were at the centre of it. The argument was the same one about history, scripture and doctrine that would break American Protestantism apart in the 1920s, running inside Catholicism a generation earlier. Then it turned. Divino Afflante Spiritu, in 1943, reopened the biblical scholarship Pascendi had closed. The worker-priest experiment sent clergy into ordinary workplaces. The nouvelle théologie went back behind the manuals to the fathers and to the liturgy. All of that, contested at the time, became the seedbed of the council. And there were the wars, including the record of Pius XII, which has a historiography of its own and is still argued about.
movements.teaser: Rome and the Catholic world, 1906 to 1962 — the modernist crisis and the anti-modernist oath, then Divino Afflante Spiritu reopening what Pascendi had closed, the worker-priests and the nouvelle théologie forming the council's seedbed on the eve of its opening.
voices: Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell — the scholars at the centre of the modernist crisis, whose published work drew the condemnations of 1907

Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943) — the encyclical that reopened Catholic biblical scholarship
The nouvelle théologie — the theologians who went back to the fathers and the liturgy, and whose work the council would draw on
The worker-priests — clergy who took industrial jobs, and one of the period's most argued-over experiments
movements.legacy: The church is the same church, and this half-century is a chapter in its life rather than a movement that ended: it runs to the eve of the council in 1962 and hands straight on. What this period left behind is the council itself. Almost everything the Second Vatican Council did had been prepared in these decades — the biblical scholarship released in 1943, the liturgical movement, the return to the church fathers, and the questions the worker-priests raised about where the church actually is.

movements.longDescription: Orthodoxy came to North America with immigrants and stayed, for most of a century, an affair of ethnic parishes, each answering to a church somewhere else. In 1970 the Orthodox Church in America received autocephaly, and an immigrant church became, at least in part, an American one. Then something less expected: in 1987 the Evangelical Orthodox Church — seventeen parishes and around two thousand people, formed by former evangelical leaders — was received into the Antiochian Archdiocese. Peter Gillquist told that story in Becoming Orthodox in 1989. A convert literature grew with it, and Ancient Faith Radio began broadcasting in 2004. Hank Hanegraaff, a public figure in American evangelicalism, was chrismated on Palm Sunday, 9 April 2017. A newer wave of converts has arrived through the deconstruction era's own channels; how large it is rests on parish reports and journalism, since no independent national count exists.
movements.teaser: North America, 1970 to today — the ethnic-parish century maturing into an American church with the OCA's autocephaly, the Evangelical Orthodox Church received into the Antiochian Archdiocese in 1987, and a convert wave now running through the deconstruction era's own channels.
voices: Peter Gillquist — who led the Evangelical Orthodox Church into the Antiochian Archdiocese in 1987 and wrote Becoming Orthodox (1989)
The seventeen parishes received in 1987 — around two thousand people, and the pathway's founding generation
Frederica Mathewes-Green — whose Facing East is among the convert literature's best-known books
Ancient Faith Radio — broadcasting since 2004, and the media layer through which much of the newer wave first encounters Orthodoxy
Hank Hanegraaff — the public figure chrismated on Palm Sunday, 9 April 2017, a public act by a public figure
movements.legacy: This is a living and currently growing edge of a very old church. It is jurisdictionally plural — several overlapping jurisdictions on the same soil, which is an anomaly by Orthodoxy's own canons and a fact of North American life. It receives the Paris school's handoff: the autocephaly of 1970 is the institutional close of the émigré generation's story and the opening of this one, and St Vladimir's Seminary sits at the join. It is also one of the destinations that recur in the published accounts of people leaving evangelical churches, and this map wires that relation on those published accounts rather than on any guess about motives. Amy Slagle's fieldwork of 2011 remains the one dedicated scholarly study.

movements.relationsSummary: This is a largely gentile Torah-observance movement, distinct from Messianic Judaism, a movement of Jewish believers — the two traditions' own publications draw that distinction themselves. It takes shape through Torah study groups, Sabbath- and feast-keeping congregations, and digital teaching ministries. It has two historical roots: the Sacred Name movement of the 1930s, and a newer wave connected to First Fruits of Zion, founded in 1992.
movements.why: Since the 1990s a largely gentile current of Christians has taken up Torah observance — keeping the Sabbath and biblical feasts — through congregations and, increasingly, online teaching ministries; its own publications are careful to distinguish it from Messianic Judaism, a movement of Jewish believers. Its best-documented institution, First Fruits of Zion, founded in 1992, published a public shift in 2009 away from teaching 'One Law' toward what it called Divine Invitation, a change the movement's One-Law side answered in print. It has an older root too, in the Sacred Name movement of the 1930s, whose periodical The Faith dates from 1937.

movements.longDescription: Since the 1990s a largely gentile current of Christians has taken up Torah observance — keeping the Sabbath and the biblical feasts — in congregations, Torah study groups and, above all, online. It is not Messianic Judaism, which is a movement of Jewish believers, and the two worlds' own publications draw that line themselves. Its best-documented institution is First Fruits of Zion, founded in 1992, whose own teaching changed in public: in 2009 Boaz Michael and D. Thomas Lancaster set out in Messiah Journal a shift away from 'One Law' toward what they called Divine Invitation, and the One-Law side answered in print — the clearest dated record of the argument running inside this current. Digital ministries followed, 119 Ministries among them from around 2010, though founding dates for many of them simply cannot be established. There is an older root as well: the Sacred Name movement of the 1930s, out of Adventist and Church of God (Seventh Day) circles, whose periodical The Faith dates from 1937.
movements.teaser: North America and digital-native, c. 1990s to today — a largely gentile Torah-observant current of Sabbath- and feast-keeping congregations and digital teaching ministries, deliberately distinct from Messianic Judaism, whose own publications draw the line.
voices: First Fruits of Zion — founded in 1992, and the current's most institutionally legible body
Boaz Michael and D. Thomas Lancaster — whose 2009 Messiah Journal piece set out the shift from 'One Law' to Divine Invitation
The One-Law side — whose published rebuttals of 2009 are the other half of the movement's one well-documented argument
The digital teaching ministries — 119 Ministries and its kind, from around 2010, whose material is abundant and whose institutional records are thin
The Sacred Name layer — the 1930s movement out of Adventist and Church of God (Seventh Day) circles, whose periodical The Faith dates from 1937
movements.legacy: This is a current in progress rather than a settled tradition, and this map says so. Institutionally it is thin — a handful of publishers and congregational networks, and a great deal of video — which makes it genuinely hard to describe: no central body, no shared confession, and no independent count of any kind, so every figure in circulation comes from self-report or journalism. What it has done is put a question back into ordinary Christian conversation that most churches had long considered settled: what, if anything, the Torah asks of gentile believers. Its individual bodies differ widely from one another, and the map assesses them one at a time.
